ORDINANCE: #ZA2026-11-02 (B) AGENDA SECTION: Consent ISSUE: Final reading of an ordinance to annex approximately 0.74+/- acres of property located at 1187 Hwy 501 Business. APPLICANT(S): The Earthworks Group (agent) PIN(s): 367-12-04-0002 CURRENT ZONING: Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) PROPOSED ZONING (upon annexation): City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) BACKGROUND: The applicant is requesting annexation of the subject property in connection with proposed commercial development requiring connection to City utility services. The property is currently vacant. Development plans for the property were initially submitted to Horry County for review. Because the proposed development requires City utility service, annexation into the City is required before the property may connect to those services. Following annexation, the proposed development will be subject to the City’s applicable development review and permitting requirements. The property is located along Hwy 501 Business within the Red Hill community. This portion of the corridor contains a mixture of commercial and industrial development and has previously been identified by City Council as an area of interest for future annexation. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: Most adjacent properties remain within Horry County’s jurisdiction and are zoned Highway Commercial (HC). One parcel located directly behind the subject property is zoned Horry County Heavy Industrial (HI). Properties within the City limits adjacent to or near the property are zoned Forest Agriculture (FA) and Highway Commercial (HC). The surrounding development pattern is predominantly commercial and industrial. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s future land use map designates the subject property as Highway Commercial (HC). Pursuant to Section 3.2.10 of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), the HC district is intended to provide suitable locations for automobile-oriented commercial activities associated with major highway corridors, while reducing traffic congestions and enhancing the aesthetic character of the City. 3 -- 3 of 106 -- STAFF REPORT Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-11-02 (B) The requested HC zoning classification is consistent with the Future Land Use Map designation, the property’s current Horry County zoning, and the established development pattern along this portion of Hwy 501 business. PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION (and public hearing): Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the requested zoning upon annexation at their October 8, 2026 meeting and recommended approval. CITY COUNCIL: City Council approved first reading of the ordinance annexing the subject property at its September 8 meeting. City Council approved first reading of the ordinance assigning the HC zoning district to the subject property at its October 19 meeting. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Approve Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-11-02 (B) to annex the subject property. ATTACHMENTS: GIS Maps; Annexation petition 4 -- 4 of 106 -- ORDINANCE #ZA2026-11-02 (B) AN ORDINANCE TO ANNEX INTO THE CITY LIMITS OF CONWAY, APPROXIMATELY 0.74 +/- ACRES OF PROPERTY, IDENTIFIED BY PIN: 36712040002 AND LOCATED AT 1187 HWY 501 BUSINESS, TO INCLUDE ALL WATERWAYS, ROADS, AND RIGHTS-OF- WAY ADJACENT TO THE PROPERTY. SECTION 1. FINDINGS OF FACTS: WHEREAS, Section § 5-3-150, Code of Laws of South Carolina (1976) as amended, provides a method of annexing property into a city or town by a petition signed by all persons owning real estate in the area requesting annexation; and WHEREAS, A proper petition has been filed with the City of Conway by one hundred percent (100%) of the freeholders owning one hundred percent (100%) of the assessed value of the contiguous property herein described, petitioning for annexation of the property to the City of Conway under the provisions of SC Code of Laws, Sec. § 5-3-150(3); and WHEREAS, The area comprising said property is contiguous to the City of Conway and meets all statutory requirements for annexation; and WHEREAS, It appears to City Council that annexation would be in the best interest of property owners and the City. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED by the Mayor and Council of the City of Conway, South Carolina, duly assembled and with authority of same, pursuant to Sec. § 5-3-150, Code of Laws of South Carolina (1976), as amended, the following described property is hereby annexed to and made part of the City of Conway, to wit: Approximately 0.74+/- acres of property identified by PIN: 367-12-04-0002 and located at 1187 Hwy 501 Business. Upon annexation, the property shall become subject to the City’s jurisdiction for the rendition of all applicable municipal services. This annexation includes all waterways, roads, and rights-of-way adjacent to the property. For a more specific description of said property, see attached map(s). SECTION 2. APPLICATION OF ZONING: The official zoning map of the City of Conway shall be amended by separate ordinance following Planning Commission review and recommendation in accordance with S.C. Code § 6-29-760. SECTION 3. EFFECTIVE DATE: The annexation is effective as of the date of the final reading of this Ordinance. 5 -- 5 of 106 -- RATIFIED BY CITY COUNCIL, duly assembled, this 2 day of November , 2026. APPLICANT(S): The Earthworks Group (agent) PIN(s): 367-12-04-0002 CURRENT ZONING: Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) PROPOSED ZONING (upon annexation): City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) BACKGROUND: The applicant has petitioned to annex approximately 0.74 +/- acres located at 1187 Hwy 501 Business in connection with a proposed commercial development requiring connection to City utility services. The property is currently vacant. Development plans were initially submitted to Horry County for review. Because the proposed development requires City utility service, annexation into the City is required before the property may connect to those services. The prior submission to Horry County does not constitute approval by the City. Following annexation, the development plans must be submitted to the City and reviewed for compliance with the Unified Development Ordinance and all applicable City development, utility, building, and permitting requirements. The property is located along Hwy 501 Business within the Red Hill community. This portion of the corridor contains a mixture of commercial and industrial development. Council approved first reading of the ordinance annexing the subject property at its September 8 meeting. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: Most adjacent properties remain within Horry County’s jurisdiction and are zoned Highway Commercial (HC). One parcel located directly behind the subject property is zoned Horry County Heavy Industrial (HI). Adjacent and nearby properties within the City limits are zoned Highway Commercial (HC) and Forest Agriculture (FA). The surrounding development pattern is predominantly commercial and industrial, with additional undeveloped land in the area. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s Future Land Use Map designates the subject property as Highway Commercial (HC). 18 -- 18 of 106 -- STAFF REPORT Final Reading of Ordinance # ZA2026-11-02 (I) Pursuant to Section 3.2.10 of the Unified Development Ordinance, the Highway Commercial district is intended to provide suitable locations for automobile-oriented commercial activities associated with major highway corridors while reducing traffic congestion and enhancing the aesthetic character of the City. The requested City HC zoning classification is consistent with the Future Land Use Map, maintains a zoning classification comparable to the property’s existing Horry County zoning, and is compatible with the established commercial and industrial development pattern along this portion of Hwy 501 Business. The requested Highway Commercial (HC) zoning classification is not directly consistent with the Industrial future land-use designation. However, the property is already developed with an established commercial use and is currently zoning Highway Commercial by Horry County. The requested HC zoning would maintain a comparable zoning classification upon annexation and would not represent an expansion of industrial development into the Hwy 501 corridor. The HC district is intended to accommodate commercial uses serving the traveling public and the broader community, particularly along major transportation corridors. APPLICANT(S): DCD Investments LLC PIN(s): 369-12-03-0002 CURRENT ZONING: Horry County Single Family Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF-20) PROPOSED ZONING (upon annexation): Light Industrial (LI) BACKGROUND: The applicant has petitioned to annex approx. 5.79± acres located along Liz Lane and at the end of Webb Lane. The annexation request was submitted in connection with the proposed development of the property and the anticipated need to connect to City utility services. The property is currently vacant. The applicant has indicated an intention to develop the property as an outdoor storage facility limited to storage of recreational vehicles. A substantial portion of the property is encumbered by a power transmission easement. A Santee Cooper electrical substation is located across Liz Lane from the subject property. The transmission easement may provide some physical separation between portions of the proposed development area and the adjoining residential neighborhood. City Council approved first reading of the annexation ordinance at its September 8, 2026 meeting. Following first reading, Planning Commission held the required public hearing and considered the applicant’s requested Light Industrial zoning classification upon annexation. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: Most adjacent/nearby properties remain within Horry County’s jurisdiction and are zoned Single Family Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF20) and Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) districts. Adjacent and nearby properties within the City limits are zoned Residential (R), Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1), and Highway Commercial (HC). The surrounding area includes established residential properties, undeveloped land, the power transmission corridor, and the Santee Cooper electrical substation located across Liz Ln. The surrounding development pattern is predominantly residential or undeveloped rather than industrial. 13 -- 13 of 408 -- STAFF REPORT Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-11-02 (A) COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s future land use map designates the subject property as Low-Medium Density Residential (R-1). This designation generally supports detached single-family residential development and other uses compatible with low- to medium-density residential development. Per Section 3.2.3 of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), the R-1 district is to provide for the preservation and expansion of areas for low to medium density, detached single-family residential development in the City of Conway. The district shall present a relatively spacious character, promote quiet, livable neighborhoods, and prohibit uses that are incompatible with the residential character of the surrounding areas. The requested Light Industrial (LI) zoning classification is not consistent with the Future Land Use Map designation or the predominantly residential development pattern surrounding the property. Although the applicant’s intended recreational vehicle storage use may generate less traffic, noise, and operational activity than many other uses permitted within the LI district, zoning applies to the property rather than to a particular owner or development proposal. Approval of LI zoning would allow any use permitted within the district, subject to the applicable requirements of the UDO, and could not be limited exclusively to recreational vehicle storage. PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION (and public hearing): Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the requested zoning upon annexation at its October 8, 2026 meeting. Adjacent property owners spoke in opposition and expressed concerns regarding the compatibility of Light Industrial zoning with the established residential properties in the surrounding area. Following the public hearing and consideration of the requested zoning, its inconsistency with the Future Land Use Map, the surrounding residential development pattern, and the comments received from adjacent property owners, Planning Commission recommended disapproval of the proposed Light Industrial zoning classification upon annexation. STAFF ANALYSIS: At First Reading, staff supported allowing the annexation and zoning review process to proceed based, in part, on the applicant’s stated intention to use the property for relatively low-intensity recreational vehicle storage and the physical characteristics created by the power transmission easement and nearby electrical substation. Following the Planning Commission public hearing and further review of the requested zoning, staff finds that those circumstances do not overcome the broader land-use concerns associated with the request. 14 -- 14 of 408 -- STAFF REPORT Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-11-02 (A) The transmission infrastructure does not establish an industrial development pattern, and the easement does not separate the entire property from nearby residential uses. More importantly, the requested LI zoning could not be conditioned or limited to recreational vehicle storage and would authorize the full range of uses permitted within the LI district. Because Planning Commission recommended disapproval of the requested zoning, staff does not recommend completing the annexation with the proposed LI classification. No alternative City zoning classification has been requested, reviewed through the required public-hearing process, or recommended for the property. Approval of annexation under these circumstances would leave the City without an acceptable zoning classification ready to accompany the property upon annexation. Staff therefore recommends that the annexation not proceed to final approval. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Staff recommends disapproval of Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-11-02 (A), annexing the subject property, based on the following: • The requested LI zoning is inconsistent with the Future Land Use Map; • The surrounding zoning and development pattern is predominantly residential; • LI zoning could not be restricted to the applicant’s proposed recreational vehicle storage use; • Adjacent property owners spoke in opposition and raised concerns regarding compatibility with the surrounding residential area; • Planning Commission recommended disapproval of the proposed LI zoning upon annexation; and • No alternative City zoning classification has completed the required review process to accompany the annexation. PURPOSE AND INTENT PURPOSE. The primary purpose of this PD is to establish a unified development framework for the coordinated development of commercial, multifamily residential, open space, and supporting infrastructure uses within the Property. The PD is intended to ensure that the individual development areas function as components of an integrated development rather than as separate, unrelated projects. The PD establishes the permitted uses, maximum development intensity, development standards, access and circulation framework, open space commitments, environmental protections, and design requirements applicable to the Property. Development shall be designed to provide appropriate transitions between commercial and residential uses, protect surrounding properties from incompatible impacts, and promote safe and efficient circulation within and surrounding the project. Development shall occur in substantial conformity with the approved Master Plan and the specific standards contained in this PD. Impacts to wetlands and other environmentally sensitive areas shall be avoided or minimized. Wetlands designated for preservation on the approved Master Plan shall remain undisturbed except for impacts specifically identified in this PD and authorized by the applicable local, state, and federal agencies. INTENT. This PD is established to: 1. Encourage innovative site design that cannot be achieved through strict application of conventional zoning districts; 2. Promote the integrated and orderly development of the Property under a unified development concept; 3. Establish definite permitted uses, maximum development intensities, development standards, and open space commitments; 4. Establish compatible relationships and appropriate transitions among uses within the PD and between the Project and surrounding properties; 5. Coordinate the construction and timing of transportation, utility, stormwater, and other infrastructure necessary to serve the project; 6. As identified for preservation on the approved Master Plan, protect wetlands, drainage features, open space, and other environmentally sensitive areas identified for preservation on the approved Master Plan; 115 -- 115 of 408 -- 5 207285624.v3 7. Provide an integrated vehicular and pedestrian circulation system that connects the commercial, residential, open space, and outlot areas while minimizing unnecessary access points; 8. Allow only those site-specific modifications to the UDO that are expressly identified and approved as part of this PD and that provide an equal or better planning and design outcomes; and 9. Ensure that development is consistent with the Comprehensive Plan and applicable land development regulations. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY A traffic impact study was conducted for the proposed Mill Pond Road Commercial development in accordance with SCDOT guidelines. The proposed development is located on the north side of US 501, west of Mill Pond Road in Conway, South Carolina. The development is expected to consist of 236 multi-family housing units, 270,310 square feet of retail, 13,780 square-feet of high turnover sit-down restaurant, 13,000 square feet of fast-food restaurant, a 3,500 square-foot coffee shop and a 4,800 square foot gas station/convenience store. The development is anticipated to be constructed by the end of 2029. Direct access to the site is expected to be provided through full movement driveways to Camelot Street, full movement driveways to Lochwood Lane and full movement access to Richardson Street. A turn lane analysis was conducted at the site accesses utilizing the Build (2029) volumes. Based on the build out volumes, there are no turn lanes recommended at the site accesses. The capacity analysis indicates that the intersection of US 501 and Richardson Street is expected to see higher side street delays in both the no-build and build conditions. The intersections of US 501 and Camelot Street as well as Mill Pond Road and Camelot Street are expected to see high side street delays with the addition of the proposed development trips. As stated previously, a traffic signal is warranted at both intersections. The build improved scenario shows the intersection of US 501 and Camelot Street operating at LOS C or better and the intersection of Mill Pond Road and Camelot Street operating at LOS B or better with the addition of the traffic signals. The intersection of US 501 and Mill Pond Road is expected to see a drop in LOS from the no-build to build scenarios. It is recommended to construct a westbound right turn lane on US 501 at Mill Pond Road with an overlap in addition to a second southbound left turn lane on Mill Pond Road at US 501 to increase the capacity of the intersection. The build improved scenario demonstrates the improved delays. The intersection of Mill Pond Road and Lochwood Lane is expected to see a significant increase in delays from the no-build to build scenario. Therefore, it is recommended to construct a second egress lane on Lochwood Lane. The build improved scenario shows the decreased delays with the additional egress lane. The site access capacity analysis indicates that all approaches of the site accesses are expected to operate at LOS B or better in all scenarios. Therefore, there are no recommendations at the site accesses based on the capacity analysis. 158 -- 158 of 408 -- Mill Pond Road Commercial | v Recommendations: US 501 and Camelot Street: • Install a traffic signal at the intersection of US 501 and Camelot Street. • Re-stripe the TWLTL on US 501 to consist of a westbound left turn lane on US 501 at Horry Avenue with 150 feet of storage. • Construct a second egress lane on the southbound approach of Camelot Street at US 501: a left- through lane and a 100-foot right turn lane. TRAFFIC IMPACT ANALYSIS 3.1. Turn Lane Analysis A turn lane analysis was conducted at the site accesses utilizing the Build (2029) volumes. Based on the build out volumes, there are no turn lanes recommended at the site accesses. Refer to Appendix B for the turn lane warrants with volumes graphed. 3.2. Signal Warrant Analysis A signal warrant analysis was performed for the intersection of US 501 and Camelot Street as well as Mill Pond Road and Camelot Street utilizing the Build (2029) volumes. The signal warrant utilizes the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) criteria. Thirteen-hour counts were collected for both intersections. Estimated trips from the proposed development were added to the estimated no-build volumes for the 13 hours analyzed to determine the Build scenario volumes. Hourly trip generation was generated based on hourly vehicle distributions from the 12th Edition of the ITE Trip Generation Manual. The Build (2029) volumes from the peak hour capacity analysis were used for the 7-8 AM and 5-6 PM hours, as the methodology for estimating those trips was assumed to be more precise. The intersection of US 501 and Camelot Street was analyzed under existing conditions. The intersection meets the thresholds for all three of the required warrants. Therefore, it is recommended to install a traffic signal at the intersection of US 501 and Camelot Street. The intersection of Mill Pond Road and Camelot Street was analyzed under existing conditions. The intersection meets the thresholds for all three of the required warrants. Therefore, it is recommended to install a traffic signal at the intersection of Mill Pond Road and Camelot Street. Refer to Appendix F for the MUTCD Signal Warrants, 13-hour volumes and trip generation. 3.3. Intersection LOS Analysis Using the existing, no-build, and build traffic volumes, intersection analyses were conducted for the study intersections under Existing (2026) conditions, No-Build (2029) conditions, and Build (2029) conditions. This analysis was conducted using the Transportation Research Board’s Highway Capacity Manual (HCM 6 th Edition) methodologies of the Synchro, Version 12 software. Intersection level of service (LOS) grades range from LOS A to LOS F, which are directly related to the level of control delay at the intersection and characterize the operational conditions of the intersection traffic flow. I ask you to deny a plan that would make filling wetlands a condition of building a shopping center. I have advised the South Carolina Office of Resilience (SCOR), served on WaterSC, and serve on the leadership committee of the South Atlantic Salt Marsh Initiative (SASMI). Due to my experience in and coastal environmental knowledge gained through this work, my position is that wetlands should not be filled for any project. They hold and filter water, support wildlife, and give floodwaters room to spread before they reach homes, roads, and schools. Our wetlands are vital natural resources to the Gullah/Geechee Nation. According to the South Carolina Environmental Law Project’s account of the applications, this development would fill nearly five acres of wetlands connected to Crabtree Swamp and Crabtree Canal. The submitted plan also places a gas station and underground fuel tanks in a wetland. The Gullah/Geechee Sea Island Coalition has been working with the US Environmental Protection Agency and our state to remove underground storage tanks in order to protect our environmental and human health. Therefore, we wouldn’t support a project that is placing more of these in these critical areas that are impacted by sea level rise and storms. The proposed pavement and rooftops would add runoff near neighborhoods, roads, and Conway High School. These wetlands drain through the Crabtree system toward the Waccamaw River. Before voting, you should require a public accounting of the full wetland footprint, drainage changes, flood risk, and potential effects of a fuel release during a storm. 233 -- 233 of 408 -- After Crabtree Swamp was channelized after a devastating flood in the 1960s, public agencies invested in addressing erosion and flooding. This proposal would put those investments in jeopardy. In Chapter 7 of the 2025 SC Water Plan, WaterSC calls on decision-makers to recognize the connection between water quality and water quantity and to maintain the health of state waters. Filling wetlands would remove natural flood storage while increasing the burden on constructed stormwater controls to protect downstream water quality. The Strategic Statewide Resilience and Risk Reduction Plan, Executive Summary, which was written by the South Carolina Office of Resilience, recommends that municipalities use the best available data to restrict new development in flood-prone areas, even where FEMA maps do not designate a special flood hazard area. It calls for resilience to shape zoning and land-use decisions. It also identifies wetlands as places that absorb excess water and recommends conserving natural flood protection. Conway has an opportunity to put those recommendations into practice before the land is changed. The South Atlantic Salt Marsh Initiative Plan seeks to protect and restore the functions of existing salt marshes. It calls for reducing harm from adjacent development, protecting water quality through natural buffers and setbacks, controlling erosion and polluted runoff, and giving planning agencies feedback when a proposed project could damage wetlands. Its aim is to retain the benefits that functioning marshes provide to people and wildlife. SASMI addresses tidal marshes; I cite it here for a sound planning principle that also applies to Crabtree’s wetlands: keep functioning wetlands in place and address the effects of development these wetlands. A stormwater pond should not be presumed to replace the full protection of wetlands that have been filled. The WaterSC, SCOR, and SASMI plans are guidance that your city should use as you review this and other such applications. Together, they give Conway strong reason to protect this watershed. The City of Conway should not approve a development layout that depends on filling wetlands while the Department of Environmental Services and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers still have questions about the proposed impacts. We support the Planning Commission recommending denial, and City Council denying the rezoning. Before any further vote, please make the wetland delineation, flood and drainage analysis, alternatives, and agency responses available to the public. The Proposed Project Will Degrade Water Quality in Crabtree Swamp and the Waccamaw River. South Carolina has long recognized that wetlands “are valuable habitat for wildlife and plant species and serve as hydrologic buffers, providing for absorption of storm water runoff and aquifer recharge, [therefore] commercial development is discouraged in these areas.” CMP at p. III-40. As recognized in the South Carolina Coastal Management Program Document, wetlands are valuable habitat that should not be filled indiscriminately. CZMP-62 § IX(B). The Clean Water Act contains similar language. 40 C.F.R. 230.41(b) (wetland fill may reduce “the system’s productivity” and “can degrade water quality by obstructing circulation patterns that flush large expanses of wetland systems” and may “change the wetland habitat for fish and wildlife”). Among the factors DES must both consider and address in reaching a determination about water quality impacts of this project are “(a) whether the activity is water dependent and the intended purpose of the activity; (b) whether there are feasible alternatives to the activity; (c) all potential water quality impacts of the project, both direct and indirect, over the life of the project including: (1) impact on existing and classified water uses; (2) physical, chemical, and biological impacts, including cumulative impacts; (3) the effect on circulation patterns and water movement; (4) the cumulative impacts of the proposed activity and reasonably foreseeable similar activities of the applicant and others.” S.C. Code Ann. Regs. § 61-101 F. 3. (a)-(c). DES “shall condition the certification upon compliance with all measures necessary to minimize adverse effects, including stormwater management.” S.C. Code Ann. Regs. § 61-101 F. 4. This project is not water dependent, there are likely feasible alternatives, and there will be direct and indirect water quality impacts. The construction process and presence of impervious surfaces would generate significant stormwater runoff, which will introduce pollutants and litter into nearby waterways. Studies show that impervious surfaces significantly increase stormwater runoff compared to natural areas. On average, only 15% of rainfall on pervious surfaces becomes runoff, whereas 90% of rainfall on impervious surfaces becomes runoff, carrying pollutants with it.2 The project area is located in wetlands associated with Crabtree Swamp and Crabtree Canal, which discharge into the Waccamaw River.3 Polluted runoff is a major threat to water quality for the swamp and the river, 2 See https://cms7files1.revize.com/birmingham/Document_Center/Department/Treasurers%20Office/Property%20Tax% 20Information/A1_Runoff%20Potential.pdf. 3 Attachment A, Corps Restoration Project, p. 1; Attachment B, Crabtree Plant Survival. 242 -- 242 of 408 -- 3 contributing to declines in plant and animal diversity in affected waterbodies.4 The proposed project includes retail shops, a grocery store, restaurants, a coffee shop, a fuel station, and extensive associated parking lots. Buffers carry out the important functions of preventing erosion, reducing pollution, and protecting wildlife.5 Of particular concern is the fuel station, which is currently proposed to be located in a wetland. The fuel station will likely require underground storage tanks. The Applicant Failed to Provide Adequate Information on the Project Purpose and Alternatives. South Carolina law requires a presentation of alternatives when making decisions about activities with water quality impacts. The state’s regulations implementing the Clean Water Act also emphasize the importance of considering alternate plans: “In assessing the water quality impacts of the project, the Department will address and consider the following factors… whether there are feasible alternatives to the activity.” S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 61-101(F)(3). “Certification will be denied if… there is a feasible alternative to the activity, which reduces adverse consequences on water quality and classified uses.” S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 61-101(F)(5) (emphasis added). The Clean Water Act itself requires a search for alternatives: “Except as provided under section 404(b)(2), no discharge of dredged or fill material shall be permitted if there is a practicable alternative to the proposed discharge which would have less adverse impact on the aquatic ecosystem.” 40 C.F.R. § 230.10(a). An alternative is considered practicable if it is “available and capable of being done after taking into consideration cost, existing technology, and logistics in light of overall project purposes.” 40 C.F.R. § 230.10(a)(2). For projects that are not water-dependent, such as this one, the CWA regulations create a presumption that practicable alternatives exist that do not involve impacts to special aquatic sites like wetlands. 40 C.F.R. § 230.10(a)(3). The Applicant has the burden of demonstrating that practicable alternatives do not exist. Despite these clear regulatory mandates, the Applicant has not provided a description of the project purpose nor satisfied its burden of clearly demonstrating that no practicable alternative exists. The public notice does not clearly articulate the project purpose, but instead, merely states that, “[t]he project purpose requires contiguous developable area and road frontage limiting the practicability of complete avoidance of all wetlands.” Without further explanation, the asserted needs for a “contiguous developable area” and “road frontage” appear to reflect the Applicant’s preferred layout rather than an actual necessity. Courts have recognized that while the Corps must consider the applicant’s project objectives, it cannot allow overly narrow purpose definitions that artificially constrain the alternatives analysis. See Sylvester v. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, 882 F.2d 407, 409 (9th Cir. 1989) (“[A]n applicant cannot define a project in order to preclude the existence of any alternative sites and thus make what is practicable appear impracticable.”). 17 See EPA https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2015-09/documents/bbfs3cost.pdf; https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2017-10/documents/lid_fs10_rainfall_epa_508.pdf; https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2018-08/documents/bbfs11space508.pdf; https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2015-09/documents/bbfs4aesthetics.pdf. 18 http://www.scseagrant.org/pdf_files/Stormwater_Assessment_Report_WEB.pdf. 245 -- 245 of 408 -- 6 The public notice lacks an alternatives analysis, particularly regarding an evaluation of offsite alternatives and onsite configurations that would further minimize or avoid wetland impacts. The public notice does not identify whether alternative project locations were considered or whether different designs within the proposed site were explored to achieve the project purpose with fewer wetland impacts. For a non-water-dependent project, the failure to adequately consider or document these alternatives raises serious concerns about compliance with the Clean Water Act guidelines. The deficiencies in the public notice, including the lack of a description of the project purpose and a clear demonstration that practicable alternatives are unavailable, prevent the public from meaningfully evaluating the project’s compliance with regulatory standards. The Applicant has failed to justify the proposed impacts. Therefore, the Corps must either deny the permit application or require the applicant to submit a revised public notice with sufficient information, followed by an extension of the public comment period. IV. Conclusion For the reasons set forth above, we ask that the application be denied. Authority and Purpose. Section 206 of the Water Resources Development Act of 1996 provides authority for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) to carry out aquatic ecosystem restoration and protection projects if the Secretary of the Army determines that the project will improve the quality of the environment and is in the public interest while being cost-effective. This study was initiated following receipt of a December 3, 2014 letter request from Horry County seeking assistance from the USACE to develop ecological restoration along one or more waterbodies located in Horry County, South Carolina. Prior to channelization to support development, Crabtree Swamp was a bottomland hardwood wetland ecosystem. Historic channel modifications resulted in dredge material placement on the streambanks, disconnecting the floodplains and adjacent wetlands from the channel. As more intense urban land uses replaced agricultural uses, with subsequent increased stormwater runoff, reaches of Crabtree Swamp started to exhibit associated stressors such as bank failure, erosive channel velocities, incising and scouring, loss of aquatic life habitat, episodic flooding, invasive vegetation, and blockages that prevented aquatic life passage. Crabtree Swamp is now an incised, trapezoidal channel with little remaining structural diversity, and prone to bank failures. The lack of aquatic habitat and physical barriers are inhibiting aquatic life passage. The purpose of this project is to restore aquatic habitat and improve stream functions by restoring floodplain connectivity and improving bedform diversity. This will provide flood storage capacity and, when combined with the removal of invasive species and re-planting of the riparian zone with native woody tree and shrub species, will allow for a more natural riverine ecosystem. c. Crabtree swamp is located in the Kingston Lake Watershed (HUC 03040206-08-03) in northeastern SC. The swamp flows around the City of Conway and discharges into the Waccamaw River. Since the 1960's, the US Army Corps of Engineers have dredged an eight-mile canal through the swamp to prevent and control flooding. The dredge materials were piled onto the adjacent banks, creating a very steep, unstable levee system that isolated the remaining floodplain, increased water velocities, and eliminated habitat and fish spawning grounds. Horry County and the City of Conway, with assistance from federal agencies and two universities, are restoring the natural floodplain to stabilize the canal and improve water quality. In April 2009, a half-mile stretch along one streambank was restored by removing dredge materials, regrading the bank slopes and revegetating with native trees, shrubs and wetland plants. Their health status has been assessed periodically and data archived in GIS datalayers. By restoring the natural floodplain, the energy of the floodwater is dissipated, permitting deposition of sediment and improved water quality. Partners learned important lessons such as the need for 1) strong partner commitment; 2) overall coordination; 3) maintenance guidelines; 4) project assessment and sharing results; and 5) enabling natural processes. Future restoration work is needed to address continuing erosion and water quality problems in unrestored stream reaches. A second segment of the canal is being restored in 2012. INTRODUCTION The Waccamaw River is a blackwater river that flows from Lake Waccamaw, NC, and winds through Conway on its way to the mouth of Winyah Bay in Georgetown, SC. Crabtree canal, a channelized tributary, and the adjacent swamp are part of the Kingston Lake watershed that is approximately 20 sq. mi. in area and represents a major conduit for water through Conway before discharging into the Waccamaw. The canal runs approximately eight miles through Conway, in northeastern Horry County, SC (see Figure 1.) Crabtree Canal, as it is now known, was the solution to major flooding in Conway after a storm event that dropped 10.38 inches of rain in a 14 hour period on June 6th, 1964. The rising water caused major transportation corridors in Conway (U.S. highways 701, 501, and 378) to be closed or impassable. Approximately $4,000,000 in tobacco crops were destroyed by flooding, as well as small businesses and homes suffering severe damage. Farmers and residents declared Crabtree swamp was harmful to their livelihood. Farmers and land owners petitioned the state to establish the Crabtree Watershed Conservation District for the purposes of funding. Mayor Huckabee, George Jenkins Sr. and Col. S. Y. Coker of the US Army Corps of Engineers (USACOE) spearheaded the flood control project. Through this effort, the swamp was dredged and channelized, in an effort to prevent future flooding from destroying residential, commercial, and agricultural areas. In 1965-66, the USACOE excavated a 6.5-mile canal through Crabtree Swamp to improve drainage, piling the dredged materials along the bank, effectively cutting off the floodplain. Another 1.5 miles was channelized in the 1980’s. Over time, the canal banks have steepened due to the increased water flow through the canal (Figure 2a), causing bank instability and increased erosion rates. Channelization of the formerly winding swamp has significantly impacted the hydrology of the ecosystem, affecting the frequency, degree and duration of flooding. Water quality has also declined. 262 -- 262 of 408 -- The area around Conway has experienced a change in land use over the past 50 years, shifting from an agricultural to an urban landscape. The increase in the impervious surfaces within the watershed causes the water flow in Crabtree Canal to be flashy during rain events. Currently, Crabtree Canal is listed on South Carolina’s 303(d) list of impaired waters for dissolved oxygen and fecal coliforms. The waters also experience high suspended sediment concentration after rain events. The net effect of these impairments has been to diminish the quality of aquatic habitat in the Crabtree Canal. OBJECTIVES A watershed management plan was developed for the Kingston Lake Watershed in 2010 (Libes and Fuss 2010). The restoration of Crabtree Canal was included as an action item. To implement this component of the watershed management plan, Horry County, the City of Conway, and Coastal Carolina University devised a restoration plan to improve conditions in Crabtree Canal that was based on findings from a hydrological and pollution source tracking study completed in 2008 and a floral survey of adjacent swamps performed in 2009. In May 2009, construction began at the chosen demonstration site to reconnect the floodplain along a ½- mile segment of one bank of Crabtree Canal (Figures 1 and 2b). A second ½-mile segment is undergoing restoration, 0.3 miles upstream of the first site on the opposite bank. The three main objectives of the floodplain restoration are to: 1) slow the flow of water; 2) increase water storage; and 3) reduce erosion (Fuss et al. 2010.) The restoration was designed by Coastal Carolina and Clemson Universities, in collaboration with the City of Conway and Horry County. Expert advice in selection of suitable indigenous plants was provided by Dr. Will Conner (Professor of Forestry and Natural Resources, Clemson University). Species were selected to encompass a broad range of plants indigenous to southeastern bottomland hardwood swamps. Permission to engage in this work was obtained from the property owners in the Crabtree Watershed Conservation District who signed a Memorandum of Understanding in 2008 with Horry County and the City of Conway to partner on restoration efforts (Fuss et al. 2010). The main objective was to restore a more natural bank slope and revegetate the project site with indigenous trees and shrubs. Restoring a site’s hydrology is the most important factor to consider in a bottomland hardwood restoration (Allen et al 2001; Clewell and Lee 1990). An additional objective of the project was to provide accessible recreation for the community, to help them reconnect with this important resource. METHODS The first phase of the restoration began in 2009, when ½-mi along one streambank was restored by removing the original dredge materials and re-grading the bank slopes. The restored floodplain was re-vegetated with indigenous trees, shrubs and wetland plants. In May 2009, 251 trees (11 species) and 297 shrubs (7 species) were planted across an 18’-wide aquatic zone and a 42’-wide upland zone. Species indigenous to local hardwood floodplain swamps were obtained from local nurseries in sizes ranging from 3 to 50 gallons. Several 100-ft long segments of pre-planted wetland carpets, with about 12 species of native emergent vegetation were installed at elevations above, at, and below the mean water line. These carpets were constructed using 5 foot wide coir mats and were made by Charleston Aquatics, Inc. The plantings had been grown out to a height of about 1 foot prior to planting. The planting plan was designed to test which species were best suited to the aquatic and upland zones. To track survival rates, the plants were tagged with a unique identification number and locations recorded with a Real Time Kinematic (RTK) GPS. Their health status has been assessed periodically and data archived in GIS datalayers. The trees have been retagged over the years as Table 1. Tree and shrub conditions were classified as either: 1) Green; 2) Mixed (brown and green); 3) Brown; 4) Dead; and 5) Mixed with New Growth. “Green” surviving trees were regarded as 100% green, whereas “Dead” trees were considered 0% green. For a tree to be considered “Mixed”, at least 50% of the tree had to be brown and to be considered “Brown”, less than 20% of the tree would be green. “Mixed/ new growth” meant that there was evidence of new growth. RESULTS Since the planting of 548 trees and shrubs in May 2009, tree status has been assessed at least once a year. The results are presented in Table 1. In July 2012, the overall survival rate was found to be 66% with 361 of the planted flora being observed as either “green”, “mixed” or “mixed with new growth”. High mortality rates (<50% survival) were exhibited by seven species: Atlantic white cedar, beauty berry, black gum, swamp ti ti , eastern red cedar, southern red oak, and sugarberry. Note that three of these species had low planting numbers (Atlantic white cedar, sugarberry, and southern red oak). Six species had very high survival rates (≥75%), i.e., button bush, bald cypress, dahoon holly, river birch, persimmon and green ash. Note that the tree counts performed in May and October 2010 were likely incomplete as more of the trees tagged in 2009 were counted in May 2011. The total trees counted over time should decline as dead trees fall to the ground and are potentially washed downstream. DISCUSSION As shown in Figure 3, plant mortality was highest in areas subject to high-energy floodwater regimes, i.e. the aquatic zone. This area also had a higher percentage of plants categorized as mixed, a sign of stress. Data are available to infer flood inundation frequencies and hence how species survival relates to floodplain function. Since species were deliberately planted to test tolerance to challenging environmental conditions, individual species survival rates reflect effects of less than optimal plantings. Native plants that have volunteered at the restoration site include blue vervain (Verbena hastate) and groundsel bush (Baccharis halimifolia), both of which have colonized the section closest to the channel. Along the upper border, long leaf pine (Pinus palustris) and sweet gum (Liquidambar styraciflua) have re-populated open spaces. The original stand of persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) has multiplied, leading to a survival rate >100% as some recruits were tagged during the 2011 monitoring effort. A site maintenance plan has been implemented to manage invasive species and to guide brush trimming. Invasive species include Johnsongrass (Sorghum halepense) in the aquatic zone and Alligator weed (Alternanthera philoxeroides) in the channel. Chinese tallow (Triadica spp.), rattlebox (Crotalaria spp), and Chinese/Japanese privet (Ligustrum spp) are found in the in the upland border. A second segment of floodplain is being restored with planting scheduled for winter 2012. This site is located 0.3-mile upstream of the first segment on the opposite streambank. Based on the survival results from the first restoration, which was designed as a pilot to guide future efforts, this second segment will be planted with a lower density of trees and shrubs. A test plot will also be seeded with native grasses. It will be important to continue to monitor plant status at the site, not only to watch for early detection of invasive or nuisance species, but to monitor natural revegetation to be sure that desired species are colonizing the site. Some plant species may have limited dispersion mechanisms that won’t be mimicked in the newly restored site. Due to extensive development and channelizing of the former swamp upstream of the project site, there may Figure 3. GIS datalayer showing status of planted trees following a survey conducted in July 2012. 265 -- 265 of 408 -- be limited opportunity for some species to recolonize the site. Natural regeneration has been found to be effective when the desired bottomland hardwood ecosystem is found in close proximity to the restoration site (Allen et al. 2001). Efforts to restore hydrologic conditions at a site in the Savannah River watershed have resulted in colonization of plants that in the future will provide a similar canopy to pre-disturbance conditions, likely due to the project site being directly adjacent to the targeted ecosystem (Nelson et al. 2000). One lesson learned is the importance of establishing a written maintenance plan that all stakeholders have agreed to. In 2009, herbicide spraying in a utility right of way killed several hundred willows that are not included in Table 1. In 2010, mowing led to the death of several trees. As a result, a maintenance plan was formulated and adopted by all the project partners. Nevertheless, in the 2012 survey, tree damage was observed that could be tied to a recent over application of herbicide intended to control invasive species in a utility right of way. Some of these services, or functions, include protecting and improving water quality, providing fish and wildlife habitats, storing floodwaters, and maintaining surface water flow during dry periods. These beneficial services, considered valuable to societies worldwide, are the result of the inherent and unique natural characteristics of wetlands. Functions Versus Values Wetland functions include water quality improvement, floodwater storage, fish and wildlife habitat, aesthetics, and biological productivity. The value of a wetland is an estimate of the importance or worth of one or more of its functions to society. For example, a value can be determined by the revenue generated from the sale of fish that depend on the wetland, by the tourist dollars associated with the wetland, or by public support for protecting fish and wildlife. Although large-scale benefits of functions can be valued, determining the value of individual wetlands is difficult because they differ widely and do not all perform the same functions or perform functions equally well. Decision- makers must understand that impacts on wetland functions can eliminate or diminish the values of wetlands. Water storage. Wetlands function like natural tubs or sponges, storing water and slowly releasing it. This process slows the water’s momentum and erosive potential, reduces flood heights, and allows for ground water recharge, which contributes to base flow to surface water systems during dry periods. Although a small wetland might not store much water, a network of many small wetlands can store an enormous amount of water. The ability of wetlands to store floodwaters reduces the risk of costly property damage and loss of life—benefits that have economic value to us. For example, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers found that protecting wetlands along the Charles River in Boston, Massachusetts, saved $17 million in potential flood damage. Water filtration. After being slowed by a wetland, water moves around plants, allowing the suspended sediment to drop out and settle to the wetland floor. Nutrients from fertilizer application, manure, leaking septic tanks, and municipal sewage that are dissolved in the water are often absorbed by plant roots and microorganisms in the soil. Other pollutants stick to soil particles. In many cases, this filtration process removes much of the water’s nutrient and pollutant load by the time it leaves a wetland. Some types of wetlands are so good at this filtration function that environmental managers construct similar artificial wetlands to treat storm water and wastewater. Wetlands are considered valuable because they clean the water, recharge water supplies, reduce flood risks, and provide fish and wildlife habitat. In addition, wetlands provide recreational opportunities, aesthetic benefits, sites for research and education, and commercial fishery benefits. Leaking Underground Storage Tanks (USTs): One of the most significant sources of contamination at gasoline stations is leaking USTs. Over time, corrosion, structural failures, or improper installation or maintenance can cause USTs to leak petroleum products, resulting in soil and groundwater contamination. 2. Spills and Overfills: Spills and overfills during fuel delivery, tank filling, or vehicle refueling can result in immediate contamination of soil and potential migration of contaminants into groundwater. 3. Surface Water Contamination: Runoff from gasoline station facilities, including parking lots, fueling areas, and service bays, can carry contaminants such as petroleum hydrocarbons, heavy metals, and other pollutants into nearby surface water bodies, potentially causing water quality issues. 4. Vapor Intrusion: Vapors from gasoline and other petroleum products stored in underground tanks can migrate through the soil and enter buildings, posing health risks to occupants through inhalation exposure. 5. Soil Contamination: Soil surrounding gasoline station facilities can become contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbons and other hazardous substances due to leaks, spills, and other activities. Contaminated soil may require remediation to prevent further migration of contaminants and protect human health and the environment. 6. Groundwater Contamination: Leakage from USTs and spills can result in the contamination of groundwater with petroleum hydrocarbons and other chemicals. Contaminated groundwater can migrate off-site, posing risks to drinking water supplies and ecological receptors. 7. Secondary Contamination: Gasoline station facilities may also contain other sources of contamination, such as underground hydraulic lifts, solvents used in vehicle maintenance, and chemicals stored for cleaning or maintenance purposes. Approval of LI zoning would not restrict the property exclusively to recreational vehicle storage. It would allow the property to be used for any use permitted within the LI district, subject to the applicable requirements of the UDO. The conventional LI district does not provide a mechanism for staff or City Council to condition the zoning approval on the applicant’s stated intention to limit the property exclusively to recreational vehicle storage. Although the transmission easement may provide separation from portions of the adjoining neighborhood, it does not separate the entire property from nearby residential areas. ISSUE: Consideration of the Transfer of Camelot Street and Depot Road from SCDOT into the City Street Network BACKGROUND: The City is considering accepting two roads currently maintained by the South Carolina Department of Transportation (SCDOT) into the City Street Network. Each proposed transfer is associated with a project that would benefit from local coordination and management of the adjoining roadway. As part of the Mill Pond Road Commercial Development, the City is considering accepting Camelot Street from SCDOT. Incorporating the street into the City Street Network would allow the City to more directly coordinate roadway improvements and maintenance with the development and the surrounding street network. As part of the Kingston Ferry project, the City is also considering accepting Depot Road from SCDOT. This transfer would occur after SCDOT completes its road project. Bringing Depot Road into the City Street Network would allow the City to coordinate the roadway with access and operations associated with Kingston Ferry. Accepting these roads would also mean accepting ongoing maintenance responsibilities and future costs. Before either transfer is finalized, staff should confirm the limits of the roadway and right of way to be transferred, inspect the pavement and drainage facilities, identify any needed repairs, and establish the maintenance responsibilities and estimated costs to the City. For Camelot Street, this review should also identify any roadway improvements associated with the commercial development and who will be responsible for completing them. For Depot Road, acceptance should be contingent upon completion of the SCDOT project and verification that the completed work is in satisfactory condition. The resolution anticipates completion of the improvements within five years and a maximum term of thirty years for related debt obligations. It schedules a public hearing for November 16, 2026, at 4:00 p.m. in City Hall Council Chambers. The City Clerk would publish the resolution once a week for two successive weeks, with the final publication at least ten days before the hearing. Adoption of this resolution is a preliminary step. Establishment of the district would require a subsequent ordinance. At the developer’s request, that ordinance would not become effective until the developer has acquired all property within the district and provided written notice to the City. RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends approval of the resolution to move forward with consideration of the Mill Pond Improvement District and hold the public hearing on November 16, 2026. The completed Improvement Plan should be attached before adoption and publication of the resolution. 389 -- 389 of 408 -- RESOLUTION NO. 2026 - ___ A RESOLUTION DESCRIBING THE MILL POND IMPROVEMENT DISTRICT AND IMPROVEMENT PLAN TO BE EFFECTED PURSUANT TO TITLE 5, CHAPTER 37 OF THE CODE OF LAWS OF SOUTH CAROLINA 1976, AS AMENDED, INCLUDING PROPERTY WITHIN THE IMPROVEMENT DISTRICT TO BE IMPROVED, THE PROJECTED TIME SCHEDULE FOR THE ACCOMPLISHMENT OF THE IMPROVEMENT PLAN, THE ESTIMATED COST AND THE AMOUNT OF THE COST TO BE DERIVED FROM ASSESSMENTS, BONDS, OR OTHER GENERAL FUNDS, TOGETHER WITH THE PROPOSED BASIS AND RATES OF ASSESSMENTS TO BE IMPOSED WITHIN THE IMPROVEMENT DISTRICT; CALLING AND PROVIDING NOTICE FOR A PUBLIC HEARING; AND OTHER MATTERS RELATING THERETO 390 -- 390 of 408 -- BE IT RESOLVED BY THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF CONWAY, SOUTH CAROLINA, AS FOLLOWS: Section 1 Findings. The City Council of the City of Conway (the (“City Council”) the governing body of the City of Conway, South Carolina (the “City”), hereby makes the following findings of fact in connection with the adoption of this resolution (this “Resolution”): (a) The City is an incorporated municipality located in Horry County, South Carolina, which possesses all powers granted to municipalities by the Constitution and general laws of the State of South Carolina (the “State”). (b) Pursuant to Title 5, Chapter 37, Code of Laws of South Carolina 1976, as amended (the “Act”), governing bodies of the municipalities of the State are authorized to acquire, own, construct, establish, install, enlarge, improve, expand, operate, maintain and repair, and sell, lease, and otherwise dispose of any improvement and to finance such acquisition, construction, establishment, installation, enlargement, improvement, expansion, operation, maintenance, and repair, in whole or in part, by the imposition of assessments in accordance with the Act, by special district bonds, by general obligation bonds of the municipality, by revenue bonds of the municipality, or from general revenues from any source not restricted from such use by law, or by any combination of such funding sources. The City Council constitutes a “governing body” (within the meaning of Section 5-37-20(5) of the Act). (c) At the request of RP Conway Mill Pond, LLC (the “Developer”), the City Council is considering the creation of an “improvement district” (within the meaning of Section 5-37-20(3) of the Act) pursuant to the provisions of the Act, to be referred to as the Mill Pond Improvement District (the “Improvement District”). At the request of the Developer, the ordinance establishing the Improvement District shall not be effective until such time as the Developer has acquired all real property within the Improvement District and has provided the City with written notice of such acquisition, at which time the Developer will be the “owner” (within the meaning of Section 5-37-20(6) of the Act) of the real property included within the Improvement District. (d) Pursuant to the Act, the Developer has requested that the City establish the Improvement District in accordance with an “improvement plan” (within the meaning of Section 5-37-20(4) of the Act) entitled “Improvement Plan for the Mill Pond Improvement District,” which is attached to this Resolution at Exhibit A (the “Improvement Plan”). The Improvement Plan contemplates the creation of the Improvement District and the provision of certain public infrastructure and improvements for the benefit of the real property within the Improvement District (collectively, the “Improvements”), which constitute “improvements” within the meaning of Section 5-37-20(2) of the Act. (e) The Improvements contemplated under the Improvement Plan are expected to largely be located within the boundaries of the Improvement District, except for those Improvements specifically discussed in the Improvement Plan that may be located outside of the boundaries thereof, which the City Council specifically finds and determines are necessary to make Improvements within the Improvement District effective for the benefit of the real property inside the Improvement District; however, to the extent that certain Improvements may ultimately be located or relocated in public rights of way adjacent to or in the immediate vicinity of the 391 -- 391 of 408 -- 3 Improvement District, the City Council hereby finds and determines that such Improvements confer a benefit upon the real property within the Improvement District or are necessary to make Improvements within the Improvement District effective for the benefit of the real property inside the Improvement District. (f) Pursuant to the Act, the cost of the Improvements may be paid by the imposition of an “assessment” (within the meaning of Section 5-37-20(1) of the Act) upon the real property in the Improvement District (“Assessments”) or by obligations of the City secured by the Assessments. (g) The City desires to establish the Improvement District pursuant to the Act in order to provide moneys through Assessments to fund the cost of the Improvements set forth in the Improvement Plan. Section 2 Improvement Plan. The Improvement Plan, which is attached at Exhibit A to this Resolution and incorporated herein by this reference, describes or sets forth the Improvement District, the Improvements and the estimated cost of the Improvements, the projected time schedule for the accomplishment of the Improvement Plan, the estimated source of funds to defray the cost of the Improvements, the method of repayment of the borrowings expected to defray the cost of the Improvements, and the proposed basis and rates of Assessments to be imposed within the Improvement District. Section 3 Improvement District. The Improvement District shall consist of approximately 51.12 acres of real property and public rights of way, or portions thereof, more particularly described in Exhibits A1 and A2 to the Improvement Plan on which development is expected and certain existing public rights of way adjacent to such real property. Section 4 Description of Improvements. Subject to the terms set forth in the Improvement Plan, the City Council finds that the future development within the Improvement District requires the acquisition and construction of the Improvements, as described and more particularly identified in the Improvement Plan. Section 5 Projected Time Schedule. Based upon information provided by the Developer, the City estimates that the construction of the Improvements will be completed within five years. The City expects that Improvement Plan will be accomplished upon the final debt service payment for the debt obligations that may be issued by the City in connection with the financing of the Improvements, which are expected to have a maximum term of thirty years. Section 6 Estimated Cost of Improvements; Amount to be Derived from Assessments. The total estimated, uninflated cost of all potential Improvements is approximately $6,797,524. The estimated amount of the total cost of the Improvements to be derived from the Assessments or bonds secured by Assessments is $3,000,000. The actual costs of the Improvements and the amounts thereof to be derived from Assessments are likely to vary from these estimates. Section 7 Proposed Basis and Rates of Assessments. Assessments shall be imposed upon the real property in the Improvement District based upon such real property’s expected development classification and each such development classification’s pro-rate share of 392 -- 392 of 408 -- 4 Assessments, according to the procedures set forth in an assessment roll, which shall include an assessment methodology, and an accompanying report on the basis of the Assessments, which shall establish an assessment allocation methodology which fairly reflects the benefits derived from the Improvements. The methodology and procedure for allocating the Assessments will provide that as real property within the District is subdivided, the development classifications for the resulting subdivided real property parcels, reflecting the expected development use(s) of each resulting parcel, as well as the quantity of the expected development use, will be utilized to allocate the Assessments to the subdivided real property parcels. In each case, the sum of the Assessments on all parcels resulting from a subdivision must equal the total Assessments on the single parcel in question prior to the subdivision. Assessments may not be imposed upon (i) any real property located outside of the Improvement District; (ii) any real property located within the Improvement District that does not receive a special benefit from the Improvements; or (iii) the Improvements. In addition, Assessments may not be imposed on any real property that is owned by the City or any other a public entity, expressly reserved for use by the City or any other public entity, or irrevocably offered to the City or any other public entity. Section 8 Public Hearing. Pursuant to Section 5-37-50 of the Act, the City Council hereby orders a public hearing on the question of the establishment of the Improvement District, to be held on Monday, November 16, 2026, at 4:00 p.m. in the City Hall Council Chambers at 229 Main Street, Conway, South Carolina 29526. Section 9 Publication of Resolution and Notice of Public Hearing. Pursuant to Section 5-37-60 of the Act, the City Clerk shall cause this Resolution to be published once a week for two successive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation within the City and the final publication shall be at least ten days prior to the date of the scheduled public hearing. Section 10 Severability. The provisions of this Resolution are hereby declared to be separable and if any section, phrase or provision shall for any reason be declared by a court of competent jurisdiction to be invalid or unenforceable, such declaration shall not affect the validity of the remainder of the sections, phrases and provisions hereunder. Section 11 Effective Date. This Resolution shall be effective upon its adoption. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-10-05 (D), to amend Article 8 – Off-Street Parking & Loading, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding driveway throat length as well as parking requirements for Shopping Centers v. Strip Commercial. Hucks stated that this proposed amendment to Article 8 addresses 2 separate site design issues: parking requirements for strip commercial developments and minimum driveway throat lengths. The first change concerns parking. Earlier this year, Council adopted amendments to the Unified Development Ordinance that included separate definitions for ‘shopping center’ and ‘strip commercial’, recognizing that they are different development types. However, the parking table within Article 8 of the UDO still combines both uses under one standard requiring a minimum of one parking space per 275 sq. ft. of gross floor area. The shared standard has not always worked well in practice. A large shopping center typically has substantial common parking areas shared among numerous tenants. Strip commercial centers are generally smaller, have fewer total parking spaces, and are often constructed before the final tenant mix is known. Often, the shell of the building is all that’s built, while each individual tenant is responsible for an upfit for their individual unit. As a result, a strip commercial building may meet the parking requirement when constructed but have too few spaces to accommodate high-turnover uses, such as a restaurant, or other tenants that propose high turnover uses. The proposed amendment would leave the shopping center standard unchanged but establish a separate parking range for strip commercial development. Strip commercial buildings would be required to provide at least one space per 150 sq. ft. of gross floor area and a maximum of one space per 100 sq. ft. For example, a 7,500 sq. ft. strip commercial building currently requires only 27 parking spaces. Under the proposed standard, it would require a minimum of 50 spaces and a maximum of 75. The maximum number is not required; it simply allows additional parking where the anticipated tenant mix warrants it. In short, the amendment establishes a more realistic minimum while allowing sufficient parking capacity to accommodate a broader range of tenants over the life of the development. Hucks stated that the second part of the amendment establishes driveway throat length standards. Driveway throat length is the unobstructed distance between the public street and the first internal location where a vehicle can turn, park, enter a drive aisle, or encounter another conflicting traffic movement. The UDO does not currently establish a minimum throat length standard. Without adequate space, vehicles entering a development may have to stop almost immediately because of internal parking or traffic movements. That can cause following vehicles to slow or stop within the public roadway. This is an issue that has already been seen at some of the fast-food establishments along Church Street at certain 28 -- 28 of 48 -- September 21, 2026 6 times of the day. The proposed minimums are: 20 feet for residential development entrances; 30-50 feet for small commercial and strip commercial developments; and 200- 250 feet for shopping centers and big box retail establishments. Where a range is provided, the Technical Review Committee would determine the required distance during site plan review based on the size and intensity of development, anticipated traffic volume, roadway classification, driveway location, internal circulation, and any applicable traffic impact analysis. Hucks said that Planning Commission held a public hearing on the proposed amendments at its September 3 meeting, and recommended approval, including the language establishing criteria for the varying lengths. Staff recommended approval of first reading of the proposed amendments. There was some discussion regarding possibly increasing the parking space size in a future amendment. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Goldfinch to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-10-05 (D), amending Article 8 of the UDO as presented. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. BACKGROUND: The proposed amendment addresses two separate but related site-design matters: 1. Differentiating the parking requirements for strip commercial developments and shopping centers; and 2. Establishing minimum driveway throat-length requirements. Parking Requirements: On May 4, 2026, the City Council adopted Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04(O), which added separate definitions for “Shopping Center” and “Strip Commercial.” The definitions recognize that these are different forms of commercial development. However, Table 8.3 (Parking Requirements) currently combines both uses under the category “Commercial Strip Center / Shopping Center” and applies the same minimum parking requirement of one space per 275 square feet of gross floor area. The shared parking ratio can produce substantially different results for the two development types. A large shopping center typically provides a substantial common parking area shared among numerous tenants. Strip commercial developments are generally smaller, provide fewer total parking spaces, and may divide those spaces among several tenant locations. Strip commercial buildings are also frequently constructed before the final tenant mix is known. Although development may satisfy the minimum parking requirement when initially constructed, the number of spaces provided may later be insufficient to accommodate a restaurant or another higher-turnover use. Parking for a strip commercial development is calculated based on the building’s total gross floor area, not the number of individual tenant spaces. However, when a building is divided among multiple tenants, all customer and employee parking must be accommodated within the total number of spaces provided for the development. The proposed amendment would separate “Shopping Center” and “Strip Commercial” within Table 8.3 – Parking Requirements. Shopping centers would remain subject to the existing minimum requirement of one space per 275 square feet. Strip commercial developments would be subject to the following parking range: • Minimum: One space per 150 sq. ft. of gross floor area; and • Maximum: One space per 100 sq. ft. of gross floor area. 37 -- 37 of 48 -- STAFF REPORT Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-10-05 (D) For example, a 7,500 sq. ft. strip commercial building currently requires a minimum of 27 parking spaces. Under the proposed amendment, the same building would require a minimum of 50 spaces. The maximum permitted parking would increase from 44 to 75 spaces. The amendment would not require every strip commercial development to provide the maximum number of permitted spaces. It would establish a more realistic minimum while allowing sufficient capacity to accommodate a broader range of tenants over the life of the development. Driveway Throat Length Article 8 does not currently establish minimum driveway throat-length requirements. Driveway throat length is the unobstructed distance between the intersecting public street and the first internal location where a vehicle can turn, park, enter a drive aisle, or encounter another conflicting traffic movement. When sufficient throat length is not provided, vehicles entering a development may be required to slow or stop immediately after leaving the public street due to parking movements, internal intersections, drive aisles, or vehicle queues. This can cause following vehicles to slow or stop within the public roadway, increasing the potential for traffic conflicts and abrupt braking. The proposed amendment would establish the following driveway throat-length standards: Development Standards: Proposed required throat length: Residential development – subdivision entrances 20-feet Small commercial sites and strip commercial developments 30-50 feet Shopping centers and big box retail establishments 200-250 feet Larger and more heavily traveled developments require greater throat lengths to accommodate entering vehicles and potential queues. The proposed standards are intended to improve internal circulation, reduce conflicts near site entrances, and prevent vehicle queues from extending into public streets. Because the proposed standards include ranges for certain commercial developments, additional criteria are necessary to determine the applicable throat length within each range. Staff proposed language authorizing TRC to make that determination based on site-specific conditions. PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing and recommended approval of the proposed amendments at their September 3, 2026 meeting. Planning Commission also recommended including the following language, or similar language, to govern the administration of the proposed throat-length ranges: “Where a range is provided, the required driveway throat length shall be determined by Technical Review Committee (TRC) based on the size and intensity of 38 -- 38 of 48 -- STAFF REPORT Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-10-05 (D) the development, anticipated traffic volume, roadway classification, driveway location, internal circulation, and recommendations of an approved traffic impact analysis, where applicable.” STAFF ANALYSIS: Separating the parking requirements for shopping centers and strip commercial developments will align Table 8.3 with the definitions adopted by City Council in May 2026. The revised strip commercial parking standard will also provide greater flexibility for changes in tenant occupancy while reducing the potential for parking shortages and spillover parking. Establishing minimum driveway throat lengths will address a site-access standard currently absent from the UDO. Adequate throat length will improve internal circulation and reduce the potential for vehicles entering a development to queue or stop within the adjoining public roadway. The additional language recommended by Planning Commission will allow the applicable throat length within each range to be determined based on the scale, intensity, traffic characteristics, and design of the proposed development. CITY COUNCIL: City Council approved first reading of the ordinance at its September 21 meeting. STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends approval of Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-10-05 (D).
