title: CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES 10.5.26
text: October 5, 2026 1 CITY OF CONWAY CITY COUNCIL MEETING CONWAY CITY HALL 229 MAIN STREET, CONWAY MONDAY, OCTOBER 5, 2026 PRESENT: Mayor Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor Pro Tem Beth Helms, Amanda Butler, William Goldfinch, Julie Hardwick, Justin Jordan, Larry White. STAFF: Adam Emrick, City Administrator; Mary Catherine Hyman, Deputy City Administrator; John Rogers, Deputy City Administrator; Jeff Leveille, Technology Services Director; Jason Perzan, Fire Chief; Reggie Jenerette, Solid Waste Director; Jessica Hucks, Planning and Development Director; Dale Long, Police Chief; Timmy Williams, Hospitality and Beautification Director; Ashley Smith, Parks and Recreation Director; Kelli Thomas, Deputy PIO; Bobby Wallace, Fleet Maintenance Director; Brandon Harrelson, Public Works Director; Ted Dudley, Public Utilities Director; Kym Wilkerson, Planning and Development Deputy Director; and Alicia Shelley, City Clerk. OTHERS: There were approximately 20 others in attendance. CALL TO ORDER: Mayor Blain called the meeting to order. INVOCATION/PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE: Jordan gave the invocation and led the Pledge of Allegiance. The requirements for posting notice of this meeting under South Carolina’s Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) were met. CONSENT AGENDA: A. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-10-05 (A), to annex approximately 26.98 +/- acres of property located at 585 & 605 Century Circle (PIN 383-00-00-0344). B. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-10-05 (C), to rezone approximately 26.98+/- acres of property located at 585 & 605 Century Circle from Horry County Planned Unit Development (PUD) district to the City of Conway Institutional (IN) district (PIN 383-00-00-0344). C. Approval of September 21, 2026 City Council Meeting Minutes APPROVAL OF CONSENT AGENDA: Motion: Butler made a motion, seconded by Hardwick to approve the October 5, 2026 consent agenda. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. SPECIAL PRESENTATION: A. Presentation of Longevity Awards – September 2026 – 5 Years: China Boggs, Police; 5 Years: Traci Salley, Court; 5 Years: Carson Keeling Jr, Public Works; 5 Years: -- 1 of 6 -- October 5, 2026 2 Robert Maclin, Public Works; 5 Years: Gregory Holt, Public Works; and 10 Years: Eddie Busby, Hospitality & Beautification – Emrick and Hardwick presented the longevity awards to those in attendance. Keeling and Holt were absent. B. Presentation of a Proclamation recognizing October as Breast Cancer Awareness Month – Blain presented the Breast Cancer Awareness Proclamation to Suncera Johnson. SECOND/FINAL READING Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-10-05 (D), to amend Article 8 – Off-Street Parking & Loading, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding driveway throat length as well as parking requirements for Shopping Centers v. Strip Commercial. Hucks stated that this item is up for second reading as an amendment to Article 8 regarding parking requirements and driveway throat lengths. Staff provided an overview of the proposed amendments at the September 21 meeting and first reading was approved. Hucks said that staff understands that since first reading occurred there have been some concerns expressed about the proposed amendment, specifically the amendment to the parking requirement for commercial strip centers. Hucks then showed some examples in a presentation. Goldfinch thanked staff for all the work and said that he had come to learn a lot more about this amendment. Goldfinch said that some of the challenges that were not heard last time need to be presented and recommended that this be sent back to Planning Commission. Goldfinch said that he was contacted by people that have never reached out to him since his service on council and he thinks there are some legitimate concerns that need to be aired. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Jordan to send this amendment back to Planning Commission for further review and allow for public hearing. Hardwick asked for examples of specific concerns. Goldfinch said there were lots, and it is not unusual to see businesses with drive through lines out into the highway. Goldfinch said there are lots of retail, professional and commercial uses that don’t have that pattern at certain times of the day. Goldfinch said that a few years back council moved public hearings to Planning Commission but said that if it is challenging in the future, he did not mind listening to the public hearings since council ultimately makes the decisions. Hardwick said that she listened to that Planning Commission meeting and that the commission seemed to be thorough in their questioning. Goldfinch said he was told that some felt they heard the prosecution but not the defense. Some don’t know about it until it hits the newspaper. Goldfinch said that he is asking to hit the pause button so that everyone can understand it. Hardwick said that her concern is that staff recommended it and it has been through the appropriate process. -- 2 of 6 -- October 5, 2026 3 Hucks said that nothing is waiting for this amendment to be passed and that sending it back to Planning Commission won’t delay anything. Hucks said that although staff did adhere to state law, the city does not have a mechanism to contact all that could be affected by proposed text amendments. Emrick said that having a more sound review from Planning Commission does not hurt anything and is what he would recommend. Hucks said this amendment would go back to Planning Commission on November 5. Vote: Blain, Goldfinch, Jordan, Butler, Helms voted yes. White, Hardwick voted no. Motion carried with a 5-2 vote. CONSIDERATION: Consideration of upgrading Intersection Project at Janette Street and 701 S to include mast arms – Emrick stated that the city has been waiting on this project for many years and it is finally coming to fruition. Emrick said that the intersection of Janette Street and 701 is one of the most dangerous intersections in the city and SCDOT is finally reengineering and redoing the intersection. There will be a signal at the intersection, and the question for council is whether that signal is upgraded to a mast arms signal or the traditional cabling across the street. Emrick said that the additional cost for the mast arms is $350,000 and staff does not believe it is worth $350,000 to upgrade to mast arms in that location but wanted council to consider it. Goldfinch asked if there was an opportunity for a grant. Emrick said no, that this was an aesthetic upgrade. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Helms, to disapprove the mast arms upgrade. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. PUBLIC INPUT: None Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Goldfinch to close public input. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. CITY ADMINISTRATOR’S REPORT: Emrick informed Council of the following: • WWII Memorial at Collins Park ribbon cutting - Monday November 9 at 11 a.m. • Cypress Basin has won another statewide award. This time from the SC Chapter of the American Planning Association. The Cypress Basin Project was selected for Outstanding Planning Project, and the award will be presented at the SCAPA Fall Conference in Columbia later this week. -- 3 of 6 -- October 5, 2026 4 • Depot Road is under construction. SCDOT is doing a full depth reclamation project on Depot Road, basically removing all road materials and reworking them to improve the base layers before applying asphalt. They hope to finish by November. • Depot Road construction aligns well with the beginning of construction for the Kingston Ferry. Contractors will begin clearing the path for this project through the swamp to tie into the other side of the river from the Riverwalk. Staff walked the pathway last week, looking for pathways that would preserve the most trees and offer the best views of this pristine ecological system. • The weather did not fully cooperate this weekend for the first official weekend of Halloween, but the Big Booginning was a hit. Data shows about a 36% increase this year for the kickoff event over last year. • A couple of Halloween related items, this week: Tuesday - Cobweb Candy Day, Tunes from the Tombs, the weekly coaches’ show from Chantis; Thursday - Witches, Wizards & Wine; Friday - Casper at the Terrace; Saturday - Chicora Car Club Car Show; and next week is Nightmare on Elm Street on the 13th , the Ghost Walk, Hotel Transylvania and the Coffin Races. • Emrick said that he mentioned the Great Pumpkin Oak at the last meeting and again stated that if you haven’t seen it, it is quite a sight, and it is completely full of pumpkins, all from the Community. • The Citizens Academy started last week and will continue through mid-November. Emrick thanked the folks that have signed up and are learning more about how the city works, from an inside perspective. • MASC is in town with their Regional Advocacy Meeting at 5th & Main tomorrow at 11 a.m. • There is no Workshop tonight, but two Executive Session items on the agenda. Goldfinch said that he talked to Meteorologist Jamie Arnold at the Halloween kickoff and Arnold told him not to worry about the drought, that in February the Waccamaw River will spill over due to the strong El Nino winter. Helms asked Emrick to explain what is going on with Christmas lights. Emrick said that there is a misconception in the community that the city is not doing Christmas at all, and that is not the case. The drive through light show would discontinue in its current location but the lights will be moved to other areas of the city – parks, Cypress Basin, all around the city. Emrick said that the city is not getting rid of Christmas - Christmas will be bigger but in a different way. Hardwick clarified that Under the Lights 5K was cancelled but there are still others such as the Reindeer Run. COUNCIL INPUT: Hardwick − Thanked staff for the great surprise of the Halloween decorations in council chambers and said that the City of Halloween has been fantastic so far. − Wished the Mayor a Happy Birthday and all sang. -- 4 of 6 -- October 5, 2026 5 Jordan − Thanked Helms and Emrick for addressing the Celebration of Lights and said that unlike the poorly written article, Conway is not cancelling Christmas. Goldfinch − Wished the Mayor a Happy Belated Birthday. − Spoke of how much chaos for everyone that the Christmas article on social media created. White − Spoke of the sidewalks on 378 that was considered at the last meeting and said that the next day there was an article about the lack of sidewalks at Conway High School when kids are crossing Highway 501. White said if we build it, they will come – recommends installing sidewalks now instead of allowing the fee in lieu. − White said that he met a family on the opening night of Halloween who had recognized him at a city council meeting. White warned all to be careful what you are doing when not at the meeting because people are watching. − Showed a video of the Community Garden - thanked and recognized the volunteers in attendance. White later said that the garden has donated crops to CAP, the Shepherds Table and individuals that have stopped on their own. Butler − Said that Thursday’s Booginning was great but asked to keep in mind for moving forward of the accessibility in the area for those with disabilities being able to see the stage. Helms − Thanked the volunteers – those that helped with the decorations and those that helped with the community garden for making Conway a better place to work, live and have fun. Blain - Ditto to all that had been expressed. EXECUTIVE SESSION: Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Helms to enter into Executive Session for the following: (A) Discussion of contractual agreement regarding a third-party lease downtown [pursuant to SC Code §30-4-70 (A) (2)]; and (B) Consideration of appointments to boards, commissions and committees [pursuant to SC Code §30-4-70(A) (1)]. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. RECONVENE FROM EXECUTIVE SESSION: Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Helms to leave Executive Session. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. POSSIBLE ACTION ON MATTERS DISCUSSED IN EXECUTIVE SESSION: Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Jordan to reappoint Donna Baxley to the Board of Zoning Appeals. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. -- 5 of 6 -- -- 6 of 6 --

ISSUE: Approval of applying for entitlement grant funding from the FY2026 Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant (JAG) Program BACKGROUND: The City of Conway is eligible to apply for $11,528 in entitlement funding through the FY2026 Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant (JAG) Program, administered by the U.S. Department of Justice. City staff propose upgrading the City’s firewall with intrusion prevention, network segmentation, and real‑time threat monitoring to safeguard police and city IT systems from cyberattacks and keep public safety services online. This purchase falls under JAG’s eligible category for planning, evaluation, and technology improvement. The grant requires no local match, but the City must expend at least the full grant amount. Any project costs exceeding the $11,528 award will be paid from the existing Technology Services Technology Budget. The total estimated project cost is $13,813. Per JAG guidelines, the grant application must be available for public review by the applicant’s governing body for a minimum of 30 days. A public notice was posted on the City website on September 8, with public comments accepted through October 9. The completed grant application is due October 16, 2026. If "Yes", provide explanation and attach PREVIEW Date: Sep 08, 2026 Workspace ID: WS01755039 Funding Opportunity Number: O-BJA-2026-172705 6 -- 6 of 249 -- 1 BJA FY26 Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant (JAG) Program – Local Formula Applicant: City of Conway, SC Project Title: Conway Police & Citywide Cybersecurity Firewall Enhancement Proposal Narrative 1) Description of the Need The City of Conway faces escalating cyber threats that jeopardize police and citywide criminal-justice information systems (records management, CAD, evidence handling). Existing firewall infrastructure is outdated and lacks modern prevention, segmentation, and monitoring, creating risks of service outages, sensitive data compromise, and evidentiary integrity loss. JAG funding will close this gap through an allowable technology improvement that strengthens information systems for criminal justice, both of which are explicitly supported uses under the program. 2) Project Design & Implementation Activities. Procure and deploy next-generation firewall hardware/software; configure security policies and network segmentation; integrate centralized logging/monitoring; and provide operations/incident-response training. Coordination. JAG funds will be coordinated with any applicable federal guidance to ensure efficient use and compliance with program requirements. No subawards will be made under this project. 7 -- 7 of 249 -- 2 3) Capabilities & Competencies Administrative capacity: The City’s Grants Office will manage the award in JustGrants and comply with JAG reporting (PMT quarterly data; performance and financial reports). Technical capacity: The City’s IT Department will implement and maintain the firewall, including configuration, monitoring, and incident tracking. Performance measurement: The City will track and report: • Number of critical criminal justice systems protected by the upgraded firewall; • Number of significant security incidents detected/blocked (quarterly). These measures align with JAG performance reporting requirements. Project Evaluations: The City does not propose a formal evaluation; it will monitor implementation and outcomes using required JAG performance reporting. 8 -- 8 of 249 -- September 8, 2026 1 CITY OF CONWAY CITY COUNCIL MEETING CONWAY CITY HALL 229 MAIN STREET, CONWAY TUESDAY, SEPTEMBER 8, 2026 PRESENT: Mayor Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor Pro Tem Beth Helms, Amanda Butler, William Goldfinch, Julie Hardwick, Justin Jordan, Larry White. Public Hearing and First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-09-21 (A), granting a non- exclusive Franchise Agreement for Mister Softee Mobile Food Truck to operate at property located along Peanut Road (PIN 367-01-04-0036). Dennis stated that the applicant is requesting approval for a new Franchise Agreement for Mister Softee. The applicant currently has an active Franchise Agreement which includes Collins Park and the Riverfront Park with the operation times being sunup to sundown 7 days a week. The applicant also agreed to cease operations on days of city approved festivals or special events without prior written permission from the event organizer. For this application the applicant has requested to set up on the vacant lot off Peanut Road near the water tower and operate from sunup to sundown 7 days a week at this location as well. Although staff is not opposed to this request staff does have some concerns. These concerns include the proximity to a heavily traveled vehicular right of way on a daily basis as well as an active pedestrian right of way during holiday festivities and other events, the proximity to an event venue that is most commonly used for weddings and the possibility of conflicting noise from the applicant’s vehicle, as well as the queuing area for the consumers as they wait to order. The applicant did fulfill the requirements of mandatory public notice across three consecutive issues of a local newspaper and the requirements for a public hearing have also been met. There was some discussion as council had concerns with operating during events such as the Farmers Market, location on parcel, 4’ queuing area, number of locations for a food truck to operate, and the distance between food trucks. There was no public input. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Goldfinch to close the public hearing. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. Motion: Butler made a motion, seconded by Blain to defer first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-09-21 (A) until more information is obtained from the applicant. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. FIRST READING: A. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-11-02 (A), to annex approximately 5.79+/- acres of property located on Liz Lane and Webb Street (PIN 369-12-03-0002). Hucks said that this item is for first reading of the ordinance to annex the subject property on Liz Lane currently zoned Horry County SF20. The annexation is being requested at this time in connection with the proposed development of the property that will require connection to city utilities. The applicant is proposing to develop an outdoor storage facility on the property that will be limited mostly to recreational vehicle storage. This property does have some unusual site characteristics. A substantial portion of the property is encumbered by a power transmission easement, and a Santee Cooper electrical substation is located directly across from this property on Liz Lane. The easement and existing 11 -- 11 of 249 -- September 8, 2026 4 utility infrastructure would provide some separation between the developable area and the adjacent residential neighborhood. Hucks said that tonight’s action is limited to first reading of the annexation ordinance. However, while the requested zoning of Light Industrial is not consistent with the city’s future land use map, which designated the property as Low/Medium Density Residential (R-1), the physical constraints of the property, its relationship to the existing electrical substation, and the low intensity nature of the proposed use may provide some support for considering a nonresidential zoning classification at this location. Hucks said that it is important to note that the zoning would apply to the property – not just to the proposed use, so any use in the Light Industrial district would be applicable to the property, subject to the standards of the UDO and not restricted exclusively to the proposed use of recreational vehicle storage. However, any development of the property will have to comply with the city’s requirements for access, buffering, screening, landscaping, lighting, stormwater, and fire access. Any improvements within the transmission easement would also require approval from Santee Cooper. Hucks stated that if first reading of the ordinance to annex is approved, Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on the request and make a recommendation regarding the proposed zoning of Light Industrial at ats October 8 meeting. The request would then be returned to council for further consideration. Hucks said that staff recommended approval of first reading of the ordinance annexing the subject property. There was some discussion regarding the easement issue. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by White to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-11-02 (A) annexing property located on Liz Lane and Webb Street. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-11-02 (B), to annex approximately 0.82+/- acres of property located at 1187 Hwy 501 Business (PIN 367-12-04-0002). Hucks stated that the property is currently vacant and zoned Horry County Highway Commercial. The applicant is requesting the city’s highway commercial zoning upon annexation. The annexation is being requested in connection to proposed commercial development that will require a connection to city utilities. Plans for the project were initially submitted to Horry County for review; however, because the development will require city services, and the adjacent property was recently annexed making this property also contiguous, the applicant must request annexation before a connection to city utilities can be provided. If successfully annexed, the property will be subject to the city’s applicable site plan review and permitting requirements. The property is within the Red Hill community, along a predominantly commercial and industrial portion of the Highway 501 business corridor. Most adjacent properties are zoned Horry County Highway Commercial, with a Heavy Industrial property located directly behind the site. Nearby properties within the city limits are zoned Highway Commercial, Forest Agriculture, and Light Industrial. The requested zoning of Highway Commercial upon annexation is consistent with the city’s future land use map, the property’s current county zoning, and the established development pattern along this portion of the Highway 501 Business corridor. Hucks said that if first reading of the ordinance annexing the subject property is approved, Planning Commission will hold a public hearing and make a 12 -- 12 of 249 -- September 8, 2026 5 recommendation of the proposed zoning at its October 8 meeting. Hucks said that staff recommended approval. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Blain to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-11-02 (B) annexing property located at 1187 Highway 501 Business. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. C. Hucks stated that this request for annexation is for property located at the intersection of Highway 501 and Gardner Lacy Road, which contains an existing Domino’s Pizza restaurant. The property is currently zoned Horry County Highway Commercial, and the requested zoning upon annexation is City Highway Commercial, so the existing use would maintain a comparable zoning classification once annexation is complete. The surrounding portion of Highway 501 is primarily commercial and light industrial in nature. Adjacent properties in the county’s jurisdiction are zoned Highway Commercial and Light Industrial. While the city’s future land use map classifies the property as industrial, similar recent annexations in connection with the same future development of the immediate area have been zoned Highway Commercial upon annexation. The subject property contains approx. 120.64+/- acres and is located along Hwy 378, and is currently within Horry County’s jurisdiction, where it is zoned Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA). The property is located within the City’s utility service area, and future development of the property will require connection to City water and sewer services. The applicant proposes to develop the property primarily for single-family residential purposes and is requesting Medium-Density Residential (R-2) zoning for the developable portions of the property. Conservation Preservation (CP) zoning is proposed for flood-prone and environmentally sensitive portions of the property, including the approximately 21-acre tract proposed to be conveyed to the City for public park and greenway purposes. A Development Agreement has been submitted in conjunction with the annexation and zoning request and is being considered separately by City Council. The Development Agreement establishes a framework for future development of the property and addresses infrastructure responsibilities, environmental protections, transportation and connectivity improvements, tree preservation and mitigation, and negotiated public benefits. Among the proposed public benefits are conveyance of approximately 21 acres to the City for public park and greenway purposes and Developer construction of approximately 2,600 linear feet of an eight-foot-wide paved walking/multi-use trail generally extending along Altman Branch from Hwy 378 to the southern side of Crabtree Canal. The Agreement requires construction of the trail and conveyance of the Park Property prior to final plat approval for the first phase of development. Portions of the property contain mapped flood hazard areas, wetlands, and other environmentally sensitive features. The proposed CP zoning is intended to provide long-term protection of areas that may be unsuitable for residential development and to establish a conservation zoning designation for the property proposed for 35 -- 35 of 249 -- STAFF REPORT Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-09-08 (J) conveyance to the City. The City's adopted Pathways and Trails Plan also identifies a future greenway/trail connection through this general area. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s future land use map designates the majority of the property as Medium-Density Residential, with a portion of the Highway 378 frontage identified as Highway Commercial (HC). The proposed R-2 zoning is generally consistent with the Future Land Use Map designation for the majority of the property and supports the proposed residential development pattern. The proposed CP zoning also supports the City's policies related to preservation of flood-prone and environmentally sensitive lands. A portion of the Hwy 378 frontage is designated Highway Commercial on the Future Land Use Map; therefore, the proposed zoning does not fully correspond with the Future Land Use Map along this portion of the frontage. Staff finds that the overall R-2 and CP zoning framework is appropriate based upon the proposed residential development pattern, environmental characteristics of the property, surrounding land uses, and the development framework established in conjunction with the proposed Development Agreement. The Developer shall complete construction of the Walking Trail and convey the Park Property to the City prior to receipt of final plat approval for the first phase of Development of the Project. (B) Adjacent Parcel Access and Reserve Roads. As a public benefit, Developer shall provide reasonable access points or curb cuts and utility stub outs to provide road and utility access to adjacent parcels, as shown on the Master Plan. The City and Developer shall mutually agree on the final location of such access roads and utility stub outs, which shall be subject to review and approval of the preliminary plat by the City as part of the subdivision plating process. All such access roads and utility stub outs shall be incorporated into the infrastructure and improvements to be constructed in connection with the phase of development of the Project for which any roads or utility infrastructure to which such access roads and utility stub outs will connect and shall be constructed along with such roads and infrastructure prior to applicable final plat approval. (C) Tree Preservation. Developer shall adhere to the City’s Tree Preservation Ordinance, as existing on the Effective Date of this Agreement and continuing throughout the Term of this Agreement; provided, however, the Parties acknowledge and agree that Tree Mitigation Plan attached hereto as Exhibit “H” (the “Tree Mitigation Plan”), along with the combined public benefits to be provided by the Developer through the conveyance of the Park Property, the construction of the Walking Trail, the provision of internal access within the Project, and the mitigation of trees shown in the Tree Mitigation Plan (collectively, the “Mitigation Obligations”) satisfy the tree mitigation requirements of the City’s Tree Preservation Ordinance and that the Tree Mitigation Plan constitutes the “tree protection plan” for the Project pursuant to Section 9.8.12 of the 55 -- 55 of 249 -- 9 UDO. The Developer shall provide written notice to any agent or contractor of the Developer performing work on the Property, any homebuilder operating within the Project, any other land developer responsible for the development of any portion of the Project (regardless of whether such other developer has been assigned Development Rights and Obligations), or other subsequent owner of the Property, or any portion thereof, of the Tree Mitigation Plan and the tree mitigation requirements of the UDO. The Developer acknowledges that the enforcement provisions of Section 9.8.15 of the UDO apply to any violations of the UDO with respect to the Tree Mitigation Plan. In the event that the Developer fails to provide the Mitigation Obligations, all provisions of the UDO with respect to tree preservation shall apply to the Project prospectively and, to the extent that the Developer has removed trees that would otherwise have been protected under the UDO, the enforcement provisions of Section 9.8.15 of the UDO shall apply with respect to the removed trees. (D) Jurisdictional and Non-Jurisdictional Waters. Jurisdictional and Non- Jurisdictional Waters of the State of South Carolina and the United States within the Project which are not mitigated, filled or otherwise modified, shall be surrounded by an undisturbed water quality buffer of not less than Thirty (30) feet in width. Developer shall not incorporate wetlands into individual lots, but shall remain within buffers, open space, and/or CP zoned property. Developer will convey all Jurisdictional and Non-Jurisdictional Waters of the State of South Carolina and the United States located within the Project to the Owner’s Association for maintenance and operation not later than the date on which the Project is complete. (E) Recording. Pursuant to Title 6, Chapter 31, Section 120 of the Code of Laws for the State of South Carolina, this Agreement shall be recorded in the public records of Horry County, South Carolina, on or before the date which is Fourteen (14) days following the date on which the City enters into this Agreement. 14. PURPOSE AND PUBLIC BENEFITS. The City finds that the development permitted or proposed herein is consistent with the City’s comprehensive plan and land development regulations and provides those public benefits described in Section 13 hereof. The purpose of this Agreement is to (i) provide a mechanism whereby the development of the Property can offset the cost of increased demand on the City caused by the development of the Property, and (ii) agree on certain public benefits, as described in Section 13 hereof. The Developer acknowledges that the provision of the public benefits described in Section 13 hereof constitutes a material portion of the City’s consideration for entering into this Agreement. 15. PROTECTION OF ENVIRONMENT AND QUALITY OF LIFE. The City and Developer recognize that development can have negative as well as positive impacts. Specifically, the City considers the protection of the natural environment and nearby waters, and the preservation of the character and unique identity of the City to be important goals. Developer shares this commitment and therefore agrees to abide by all provisions of federal, state and local laws and regulations for the handling of storm water. 16. COMPLIANCE REVIEWS. Developer, or its assigns, shall meet with the City, or its designee, at least once per year during the Term to review development completed in the prior year and the development anticipated to be commenced or completed in the ensuing year as compared to the Development Schedule. The City shall provide written notice to the Developer of the date for such compliance review not less than Five (5) business days in advance, provided such notice shall not be applicable to standard reviews and inspections otherwise performed by the City as to the improvement of the Property. The Developer must demonstrate good faith compliance with the terms 56 -- 56 of 249 -- 10 of this Agreement. The Developer, or its designee, shall be required to provide such information as may reasonably be requested by the City. The Development Schedule attached to this Agreement is only a projection, and Developer’s obligation at each respective Compliance Review shall be to reconcile the projected Development Schedule attached to this Agreement with the actual schedule of development for the Project at each respective Compliance Review. Failure to meet the Development Schedule attached to this Agreement shall not constitute a default hereunder. 17. EVENTS OF DEFAULTS; REMEDIES. (A) Notwithstanding the provisions of Section 5 above, Developer shall continuously and diligently proceed with Development Work on the Property. Developer’s failure to proceed with Development Work on the Property for a period of more than Six (6) months, other than as a result of Force Majeure, as defined below, shall constitute a Developer Default hereunder. In the event of such a Developer Default, the City shall provide written notice thereof to Developer, and Developer shall have a period of Thirty (30) days in which to cure a default by commencement of Development Work with regards to the next portion of the Property to be developed in accordance with phasing plan of the Project. (B) The failure of the Developer to comply with the terms of this Agreement and to cure such breach within thirty (30) days of the date of written notice provide by the City shall be considered a Developer Default ; provided, however, that if such breach cannot reasonably be cured within such thirty (30) day period, Developer shall not be deemed in Developer Default so long as Developer commences a cure within such period and thereafter diligently pursues such cure to completion. (C) In the event of a Developer Default, the City shall be entitled to pursue any remedy available at law or in equity, including, without limitation, withholding the issuance of building permits in accordance with the provisions of this Agreement, specific performance and the termination or modification of this Agreement in accordance with the Act; provided however no termination of this Agreement may be declared by the City absent its affording the Developer the notice and opportunity to cure in accordance with the Act. (D) “Force Majeure” for the purposes of this Agreement, means, but only to the extent that the event delays or prevents performance, any of the following: acts of God; all labor disputes; governmental or judicial regulations, legislation, or controls; inability to obtain any necessary permits, approvals, materials or services; fire, hurricane, snowstorm, unusually heavy rain, or other weather calamity or other weather-related casualty; casualty events affecting the Project or construction thereof; failure by an independent contractor to perform in accordance with its design or construction contract; and any other cause beyond the reasonable control of the Party claiming such cause of Force Majeure. 18. The proposed Harrison Tract development (which is anticipated to be constructed by 2029) is located along US 378 and will consist of 267 single-family homes. Access to the development is proposed to be provided via two (2) full access driveway(s) along US 378, all of which meet the SCDOT spacing requirements:  Project Driveway #1 is proposed to be aligned with Westbridge Boulevard along US 378; and  Project Driveway #2 is proposed to be located along US 378, approximately 800 feet west of the intersection of US 378 & Westridge Boulevard. The extent of the roadway network analyzed consisted of the eight (8) intersections of: 1. Westridge Boulevard/Project Driveway #1 & US 378; 2. S-165/El Bethel Road & US 378; 3. Mill Pond Road/Grainger Road & US 378; 4. US 501 & US 378; 5. Palmetto Street & US 701; 6. S-165/El Bethel Road/Cultra Road & US 501; 7. Mill Pond Road & US 501; and 8. Project Driveway #2 & US 378. The operation of each of these intersections (in terms of average vehicular delay and level of service) was analyzed with and without the project traffic anticipated to be generated by the Harrison Tract development. The results of the analysis indicate that the study intersections currently operate and are expected to continue to operate at an acceptable level of service with the proposed Harrison Tract development, with three (3) exception(s): The signalized intersection of US 501 & US 378 is projected to experience undesirable delay in the AM peak hour of the 2029 No Build Conditions and both peak hours of the 2029 Build Conditions. No improvements to mitigate this delay are recommended. The intersection of Palmetto Street & US 701 is projected to experience undesirable delay in the PM peak hour of the 2029 Build Conditions. However, this projected delay is likely due to the conservative nature of the HCM 7 th Edition unsignalized methodology and is not an uncommon condition for two-way stop control during the peak hours of the day. Therefore, no improvements are recommended. The signalized intersection of Mill Pond Road & US 501 is projected to experience undesirable delay in the PM peak hour of the 2029 No Build and 2029 Build Conditions. No improvements to mitigate this delay are recommended. Based on SCDOT’s Roadway Design Manual considerations, an exclusive eastbound left-turn lane along US 378 is recommended at Project Driveway #1 and Project Driveway #2. However, a two-way left-turn lane (TWLTL) currently exists along US 378 and will serve the left-turning traffic from US 378 into the Harrison Tract driveways. If the TWLTL are to be restriped per the criteria documented in Section 5D-4 of SCDOT’s Access and Roadside Management Standards (ARMS, 2008), it is recommended that the exclusive left-turn lanes each consist of a total of 330 feet, with 150 feet of storage and a 180-foot taper. 83 -- 83 of 249 -- HARRISON TRACT TIA August 2026 KINGSTON ENGINEERING COMPANY 1.1 1.0 INTRODUCTION 1.1 PROJECT BACKGROUND The purpose of this report is to document the procedures and findings of a traffic impact analysis for the proposed Harrison Tract development in accordance with SCDOT and Horry County guidelines. At a free-flowing leg of any unsignalized intersection on a two-lane urban or rural highway which satisfies the criteria in Figure 9.5-A; 2. at a free-flowing leg of any unsignalized intersection on a high-speed (50 mph or greater), four-lane urban or rural highway which satisfies the criteria in Figure 9.5-B; 3. at the free-flowing leg of any unsignalized intersection on a six-lane urban or rural highway; 4. at any intersection where a capacity analysis determines a right-turn lane is necessary to meet the overall level-of- service criteria; 5. as a general rule, at any signalized intersection where the projected right-turning volume is greater than 300 vehicles per hour and where there are greater than 300 vehicles per hour per lane on the mainline (A traffic analysis will be required if the turning volumes are greater than 300 vehicles per hour); 6. for uniformity of intersection design along the highway if other intersections have right-turn lanes; 7. at any intersection where the mainline is curved to the left and where the mainline curve requires superelevation; 8. at railroad crossings where the railroad is paralleled to the facility and is located close to the intersection and where a right-turn lane would be desirable to store queued vehicles avoiding interference with the movement of through traffic; or 9. at any intersection where the crash experience, existing traffic operations, sight distance restrictions (e.g., intersection beyond a crest vertical curve), or engineering judgement indicates a significant conflict related to right-turning vehicles; Table 5.1 below details whether the previously mentioned criteria for exclusive right-turn lanes are satisfied for each driveway. The analysis was conducted using the Transportation Research Board’s Highway Capacity Manual (HCM) 7 th Edition methodologies of the Synchro, Version 12 software for stop-controlled and signalized intersection analysis. Intersection level of service (LOS) grades range from LOS A to LOS F, which are directly related to the level of control delay at the intersection and characterize the operational conditions of the intersection traffic flow. LOS A operations typically represent ideal, free-flow conditions where vehicles experience little to no delays, and LOS F operations typically represent poor, forced-flow (bumper-to-bumper) conditions with high vehicular delays, and are generally considered undesirable. Table 5.3 summarizes the HCM 7th Edition control delay thresholds associated with each LOS grade for unsignalized and signalized intersections. Level of service A through D is considered to be acceptable LOS, while LOS E and F is considered to be undesirable. APPLICANT(S): SIS Angel LLC PIN(s): 382-04-02-0014 & 383-01-01-0006 CURRENT ZONING: Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) PROPOSED ZONING (upon annexation): City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) BACKGROUND: The applicant has submitted a petition requesting annexation of approximately 1.64+/- acres located at 1500 E. Hwy 501. The subject property consists of two parcels that are contiguous with the existing City limits. Annexation is being requested in anticipation of connecting the properties to City services. One parcel is currently vacant. The other contains an existing building and fenced storage area previously occupied by ASG, a telecommunications company. The properties were recently acquired from the applicant. No development plans or information regarding the intended future use of the properties have been provided to staff at this time. Both parcels are located within the geographic boundaries of the City’s Gateway Corridor Overlay (GCO) district. Upon annexation, future development or redevelopment of the properties will be subject to the applicant standards of the GCO. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: The surrounding properties are located within both the City and County jurisdictions. Nearby properties within the City are zoned Highway Commercial (HC). Surrounding properties within the County are zoned Highway Commercial (HC) and Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF-10) districts. Nearby uses include the Beverly Homes office, a storage facility, River of Life Church of God, and other commercial and residential uses. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s Future Land Use Map designates the property as Highway Commercial. Per Section 3.2.10 of the UDO, the Highway Commercial district is intended to provide suitable locations for automobile oriented commercial activities associated with major highway corridors, while reducing traffic congestion and enhancing the aesthetic character of the city. 185 -- 185 of 249 -- STAFF REPORT First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-11-02 (D) The requested HC zoning classification is consistent with the Future Land Use Map designation, maintains a zoning classification comparable to the properties’ existing County zoning, and is compatible with the established commercial development pattern along this portion of Hwy 501. PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION (and public hearing): If Council approves first reading of the annexation ordinance, Planning Commission will hold a public hearing and consider a recommendation on the proposed zoning at their November 5, 2026 meeting. TRC RECOMMENDATION / COMMENTS: None at this time. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Approve First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-11-02 (D) annexing the subject property. ORDINANCE: #ZA2026-10-05 (D) AGENDA SECTION: First Reading ISSUE: First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-10-05 (D) to amend Article 8 – Off-Street Parking & Loading, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding parking requirements for strip commercial developments and minimum driveway throat lengths. BACKGROUND: The proposed amendment addresses two separate but related site-design matters: 1. Differentiating the parking requirements for strip commercial developments and shopping centers; and 2. Establishing minimum driveway throat-length requirements. Parking Requirements: On May 4, 2026, the City Council adopted Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04(O), which added separate definitions for “Shopping Center” and “Strip Commercial.” The definitions recognize that these are different forms of commercial development. However, Table 8.3 (Parking Requirements) currently combines both uses under the category “Commercial Strip Center / Shopping Center” and applies the same minimum parking requirement of one space per 275 square feet of gross floor area. The shared parking ratio can produce substantially different results for the two development types. A large shopping center typically provides a substantial common parking area shared among numerous tenants. Strip commercial developments are generally smaller, provide fewer total parking spaces, and may divide those spaces among several tenant locations. Strip commercial buildings are also frequently constructed before the final tenant mix is known. Although development may satisfy the minimum parking requirement when initially constructed, the number of spaces provided may later be insufficient to accommodate a restaurant or another higher-turnover use. Parking for a strip commercial development is calculated based on the building’s total gross floor area, not the number of individual tenant spaces. However, when a building is divided among multiple tenants, all customer and employee parking must be accommodated within the total number of spaces provided for the development. The proposed amendment would separate “Shopping Center” and “Strip Commercial” within Table 8.3 – Parking Requirements. Shopping centers would remain subject to the existing minimum requirement of one space per 275 square feet. Strip commercial developments would be subject to the following parking range: • Minimum: One space per 150 sq. ft. of gross floor area; and • Maximum: One space per 100 sq. ft. of gross floor area. 230 -- 230 of 249 -- STAFF REPORT First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-10-05 (D) For example, a 7,500 sq. ft. strip commercial building currently requires a minimum of 27 parking spaces. Under the proposed amendment, the same building would require a minimum of 50 spaces. The maximum permitted parking would increase from 44 to 75 spaces. The amendment would not require every strip commercial development to provide the maximum number of permitted spaces. It would establish a more realistic minimum while allowing sufficient capacity to accommodate a broader range of tenants over the life of the development. Driveway Throat Length Article 8 does not currently establish minimum driveway throat-length requirements. Driveway throat length is the unobstructed distance between the intersecting public street and the first internal location where a vehicle can turn, park, enter a drive aisle, or encounter another conflicting traffic movement. When sufficient throat length is not provided, vehicles entering a development may be required to slow or stop immediately after leaving the public street due to parking movements, internal intersections, drive aisles, or vehicle queues. This can cause following vehicles to slow or stop within the public roadway, increasing the potential for traffic conflicts and abrupt braking. The proposed amendment would establish the following driveway throat-length standards: Development Standards: Proposed required throat length: Residential development – subdivision entrances 20-feet Small commercial sites and strip commercial developments 30-50 feet Shopping centers and big box retail establishments 200-250 feet Larger and more heavily traveled developments require greater throat lengths to accommodate entering vehicles and potential queues. The proposed standards are intended to improve internal circulation, reduce conflicts near site entrances, and prevent vehicle queues from extending into public streets. Because the proposed standards include ranges for certain commercial developments, additional criteria are necessary to determine the applicable throat length within each range. Staff proposed language authorizing TRC to make that determination based on site-specific conditions. PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing and recommended approval of the proposed amendments at their September 3, 2026 meeting. Planning Commission also recommended including the following language, or similar language, to govern the administration of the proposed throat-length ranges: “Where a range is provided, the required driveway throat length shall be determined by Technical Review Committee (TRC) based on the size and intensity of 231 -- 231 of 249 -- STAFF REPORT First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-10-05 (D) the development, anticipated traffic volume, roadway classification, driveway location, internal circulation, and recommendations of an approved traffic impact analysis, where applicable.” STAFF ANALYSIS: Separating the parking requirements for shopping centers and strip commercial developments will align Table 8.3 with the definitions adopted by City Council in May 2026. The revised strip commercial parking standard will also provide greater flexibility for changes in tenant occupancy while reducing the potential for parking shortages and spillover parking. Establishing minimum driveway throat lengths will address a site-access standard currently absent from the UDO. Adequate throat length will improve internal circulation and reduce the potential for vehicles entering a development to queue or stop within the adjoining public roadway. The additional language recommended by Planning Commission will allow the applicable throat length within each range to be determined based on the scale, intensity, traffic characteristics, and design of the proposed development. STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends approval of First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-10-05 (D), amending Art. 8 of the UDO, including the additional language recommended by Planning Commission concerning the administration of driveway throat-length ranges. PIN(s): 337-15-01-0003 CURRENT ZONING: Highway Commercial (HC) BACKGROUND: Sec. 7.1.2, Complete Streets, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) requires sidewalks to be constructed along the frontage of all properties abutting arterial and local nonresidential streets. Required sidewalks must be a minimum of five feet (5’) in width and four inches (4”) in thickness. Based on these requirements, the proposed development would ordinarily be required to construct approximately: • 275 linear feet of sidewalk along Hwy 378; and • 185 linear feet of sidewalk along Green Pond Circle. The applicant is requesting a waiver only for the approximately 275 linear feet of sidewalk required along the Hwy 378 frontage within the SCDOT right-of-way. The sidewalk required along Green Pond Circle is not included in the waiver request and will remain subject to the applicable UDO requirements. The required drainage improvements and associated fill is necessary to raise the grade sufficiently only to accommodate the sidewalk. Based on field verification and coordination conducted by the applicant, the proposed storm drainage alignment would be located directly above an existing Dominion Energy gas line. The proposed improvements would also affect the existing gas meter and could limit Dominion Energy’s ability to access and maintain its facilities. The applicant has indicated that Dominion Energy may require relocation of the transmission gas line before the proposed drainage improvements can be constructed. The anticipated relocation could take several months and cost more than $50,000. These costs would be the responsibility of the developer or contractor and not the City. The applicant further states that the enclosed drainage improvements are necessary solely to accommodate the sidewalk. The existing open ditch currently provides adequate drainage and would remain in place if the waiver if the sidewalk waiver is approved. 241 -- 241 of 249 -- STAFF REPORT Sidewalk Waiver Request – 2673 Hwy 378 Approval of the waiver therefore avoids the utility conflict, possible interruption of the utility service, project delays, and the additional cost associated with relocation of the gas line. PEDESTRIAN CONNECTIVITY: The immediate area currently lacks a continuous or interconnected pedestrian network along Hwy 378. Nearby properties, including the church located across Green Pond Circle, do not provide a continuous sidewalk connection to the subject property along Hwy 378. An existing sidewalk is located along Green Pond Circle within the City’s right-of-way. The applicant’s waiver request does not include the sidewalk required along the development’s Green Pond Circle frontage. PAYMENT IN LIEU Section 7.1.2 of the UDO authorizes City Council to approve requests to waive sidewalk installation requirements. When a waiver is approved, the UDO requires a payment in lieu of sidewalk construction unless the property qualifies for the ordinance’s limited exception for certain nonconforming properties. The subject property is not considered nonconforming, as the site is currently being developed. Therefore, approval of the waiver would require the applicant to provide the applicable payment in lieu. Based on the City’s current estimated cost of $33 per linear foot, the required payment would be: 275 linear feet x $33 per linear foot: $9,075 STAFF ANALYSIS: Staff finds that requiring sidewalk construction along the Hwy 378 frontage would create an unusual and substantial utility conflict. Constructing the sidewalk would require enclosing an otherwise functional roadside drainage ditch and may require relocation of an existing six-inch (6”) gas line. Staff also recognizes that there is currently no continuous pedestrian network along this portion of Hwy 378 to which the proposed sidewalk would connect. Considering the utility conflict, potential project delays, significant relocation costs, and limited immediate pedestrian connectivity, staff finds the requested waiver appropriate. The required payment in lieu will preserve the City’s ability to use those funds for future pedestrian improvements in a location where a more complete and functional connection can be achieved. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Approve the request to waive the installation of approx. 275 linear feet of sidewalk along the Hwy 378 frontage of the Macala Acres Commercial development, subject to payment of the required $9,075 fee in lieu of sidewalk installation. Approval of this request shall not waive the sidewalk requirement along the property’s Green Pond Circle frontage. ISSUE: Consideration of an amendment to the Wild Wing Pre Annexation Agreement that would satisfy the City's remaining reimbursement obligation through a discounted lump sum payment of $1,475,000. BACKGROUND: Several decades ago, the City entered into a pre-annexation agreement with Wild Wing Plantation that provided for reimbursement of certain approved public infrastructure costs from property taxes generated by the Wild Wing property. The reimbursement was limited to a portion of the property taxes paid to the City and continued over time until the approved obligation was satisfied. The agreement was amended on May 8, 2006, to cap the potential reimbursement associated with the applicable development areas at $5,000,000. Founders Wild Wing, LLC later became the successor to Wild Wing Company, LLC through an assignment dated April 13, 2015. The remaining reimbursement obligation is approximately $1.8 million. The reimbursement paid during the most recent year was approximately $585,000. Founders Wild Wing, LLC has agreed to accept $1,475,000 as a final payment if the amount is paid within 15 days after the amendment is executed. The proposed payment represents a reduction of at least $325,000, or roughly 18 percent, from the remaining obligation. Upon payment, the City's reimbursement obligation under this agreement would be complete. No additional annual reimbursements would be due to Founders Wild Wing, LLC. The principal benefit is certainty. The City can close a long-standing obligation at a meaningful discount and remove a recurring claim against future property tax revenue. The settlement also simplifies future budgeting and eliminates the administrative work required to calculate and process annual reimbursements. The principal cost is the immediate use of $1,475,000 in available funds. Those funds would no longer earn interest or remain available for another purpose. At a 4 percent annual return, the foregone interest would be approximately $59,000 in the first year. That cost is substantially less than the proposed reduction in the reimbursement obligation, particularly 246 -- 246 of 249 -- because recent reimbursement levels indicate that the remaining balance would otherwise be paid over a relatively short period. The amendment should be treated as a negotiated resolution of this specific agreement. It does not establish a general policy requiring the City to prepay or settle other reimbursement obligations. The City can eliminate an obligation of approximately $1.8 million for $1,475,000, save at least $325,000, and regain the full benefit of the affected property tax revenue going forward. RECOMMENDATION Approval of the Agreement as attached and authorize the City Administrator to immediately remit the sum of $1,475,000 as final settlement of this pre-annexation agreement. 247 -- 247 of 249 -- STATE OF SOUTH CAROLINA ) ) AMENDMENT TO WILD WING ) PREANNEXATION AGREEMENT COUNTY OF HORRY ) WHEREAS, the City of Conway and Wild Wing Plantation entered a pre-annexation agreement that provided for reimbursement over a period of time of certain approved infrastructure costs from property taxes paid to the City by Wild Wing Plantation on property known as Wild Wing; WHEREAS, Wild Wing Plantation has sold a portion of that property to Wild Wing Company, LLC; WHEREAS, the property conveyed to Wild Wing Company, LLC, was designated as areas D1, F, G, H and L of a development plan that was originally submitted by Wild Wingo Plantation to the City in 1999; and WHEREAS, the City and Wild Wing Company, LLC, amended the pre-annexation agreement on May 8, 2006, which amendment placed a cap of Five Million and No/100 ($5,000,000.00) Dollars on the amount of Wild Wing Company, LLC’s potential reimbursement under the pre-annexation; WHEREAS, Founders Wild Wing, LLC, a South Carolina limited liability company is the successor by assignment to Wild Wing Company, LLC by Assignment and Assumption of Pre- Annexation Agreement dated April 13, 2015, recorded April 14, 2015 in Deed Book 3812 at Page 3046, in the Office of the Register of Deeds for Horry County, South Carolina; WHEREAS, the City and Founders Wild Wing, LLC desire to further amend the pre- annexation agreement to modify the payment schedule and place on the total remaining balance to be paid to Founders Wild Wing, LLC as a reimbursement under the pre-annexation agreement. text: September 21, 2026 1 CITY OF CONWAY CITY COUNCIL MEETING CONWAY CITY HALL 229 MAIN STREET, CONWAY MONDAY, SEPTEMBER 21, 2026 PRESENT: Mayor Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor Pro Tem Beth Helms, Amanda Butler, William Goldfinch, Julie Hardwick, Justin Jordan, Larry White. SECOND/FINAL READING A. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (C), to annex approximately 120.7+/- acres of property located on Hwy 378 (PIN 337-00-00-0023). Hucks informed Council that the next 3 items all relate to the same 120.64 acres of property along Highway 378, between Mill Pond Road and Radio Lane. The items are final reading of the annexation, zoning upon annexation, and the associated Development Agreement regarding the subject property. Hucks said that the first item is the annexation that is within the city’s utility service area, and any future development of the property will require water and sewer connection. Council approved first reading of the annexation ordinance in May. Hucks said that the second item is the ordinance for the zoning upon annexation. The property is zoned Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture, and the proposed zoning is approximately 88.62 acres to the R-2 district and approximately 32.02 acres to the CP district. The R-2 portion is intended for the residential development, while the portion proposed to be zoned CP encompasses the flood zones that exist on the property, which includes the 21-acre tract that is proposed to be conveyed to the city for park and greenway purposes. Most of the property is designated R-2 on the city’s future land use map and a portion along the Highway 378 frontage is designated HC. As previously discussed, the proposed zoning does not correspond exactly with the future land use map along that portion of frontage. Staff nevertheless finds the overall R-2 and CP zoning framework appropriate given the residential development pattern, environmental characteristics of the property, surrounding land uses, and the associated Development Agreement. Hucks said that the last item is final reading of the Development Agreement. Since first reading, the developer and the city’s legal counsel have continued to work through the agreement, and the revised version resolves or substantially addresses the matters that were previously identified. The agreement established the framework for development of the property and provides for the developer’s infrastructure responsibilities, transportation improvements required through the Traffic Impact Analysis and by the city or SCDOT, public streets, and roadway connectivity to adjoining properties. It also includes several environmental and public benefit provisions. Approximately 21 acres will be conveyed to the city for park and greenway purposes, and the developer will construct approximately 2,600 linear feet of an 8-ft wide paved multi-use trail generally extending along Altman Branch from Highway 378 to the southern side of Crabtree Canal. The trail is required to be constructed and the park property conveyed prior to final plat approval for the first phase of development. The agreement also provides for a 30-ft undisturbed water quality buffer for remaining wetlands, Conservation Preservation zoning of the existing floodplain and the 21-acres to be conveyed to the city and negotiated tree-preservation and mitigation -- 2 of 11 -- September 21, 2026 3 requirements based upon the tree mitigation plan and the public benefits being provided through the proposed agreement. The agreement has an initial agreement subject to extension as provided in the agreement and includes a provision for annual compliance review as well as provisions addressing default and enforcement. There are still a few minor legal, drafting, administrative, and exhibit revisions to be completed before the agreement can be executed and recorded. Those revisions will not change the substantive terms or public benefits being considered for final reading and will not constitute a material modification of the agreement. Hucks said that Planning Commission held its public hearing on the proposed zoning upon annexation and the development agreement at its August 6 meeting and recommended approval. Council held a second public hearing on the Development Agreement and approved first reading of both the proposed zoning of the property and the associated Development Agreement on August 17. Hucks stated that staff recommended approval of final reading of all 3 ordinances for the subject property. Hucks stated that this request includes 2 parcels on Highway 378 and is being submitted in connection with a request to connect to city utilities. One parcel is wooded and undeveloped, while the other contains an existing structure that has not been in use for some time. Both parcels are currently zoned Horry County Highway Commercial and the proposed zoning upon annexation is also Highway Commercial. This portion of Highway 378 contains a mixture of uses, including commercial, industrial, and residential development, and undeveloped property. The adjoining property on one side is zoned Low/Medium Density Residential (R-1) and is part of the approved Kingston Preserve Conservation Subdivision development. This property is also near the City’s Public Works Complex. The city’s future land use map designates the parcel with frontage on Highway 378 as Highway Commercial and the rear parcel as Industrial. While the requested zoning upon annexation is not directly consistent with the future land use designation of the rear parcel, applying Highway Commercial zoning to both parcels would maintain a classification comparable to their existing county zoning, provide consistent zoning across the overall property, and remain compatible with the development pattern along Highway 378. Given the lapse in time there has been since the property has been in use, any future use would be subject to requirements for buffering, screening, lighting, access, parking, and other measures that are intended to minimize impacts on adjacent residential properties as well as requirements of the Gateway Corridor Overlay. If first reading of the ordinance to annex is approved, Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on the proposed zoning at its November 5 meeting. Hucks stated that the applicant is requesting the Institutional zoning upon annexation to facilitate development in conjunction with Coastal Carolina University Athletics, including a proposed track and field complex. The city’s future land use map designates the property as Institutional, therefore the requested zoning is -- 4 of 11 -- September 21, 2026 5 consistent with the future land use map, the proposed development, and the surrounding development pattern, which already includes university athletic facilities, commercial uses, and undeveloped property. Hucks said that Planning Commission held the required public hearing at its September 3 meeting, and recommended approval. Staff recommended approval. Motion: Helms made a motion, seconded by Jordan to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-10-05 (C) rezoning property located at 585 & 605 Century Circle. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. D. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-10-05 (D), to amend Article 8 – Off-Street Parking & Loading, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding driveway throat length as well as parking requirements for Shopping Centers v. Strip Commercial. Hucks stated that this proposed amendment to Article 8 addresses 2 separate site design issues: parking requirements for strip commercial developments and minimum driveway throat lengths. The first change concerns parking. Earlier this year, Council adopted amendments to the Unified Development Ordinance that included separate definitions for ‘shopping center’ and ‘strip commercial’, recognizing that they are different development types. However, the parking table within Article 8 of the UDO still combines both uses under one standard requiring a minimum of one parking space per 275 sq. ft. of gross floor area. The shared standard has not always worked well in practice. A large shopping center typically has substantial common parking areas shared among numerous tenants. Strip commercial centers are generally smaller, have fewer total parking spaces, and are often constructed before the final tenant mix is known. Often, the shell of the building is all that’s built, while each individual tenant is responsible for an upfit for their individual unit. As a result, a strip commercial building may meet the parking requirement when constructed but have too few spaces to accommodate high-turnover uses, such as a restaurant, or other tenants that propose high turnover uses. The proposed amendment would leave the shopping center standard unchanged but establish a separate parking range for strip commercial development. Strip commercial buildings would be required to provide at least one space per 150 sq. ft. of gross floor area and a maximum of one space per 100 sq. ft. For example, a 7,500 sq. ft. strip commercial building currently requires only 27 parking spaces. Under the proposed standard, it would require a minimum of 50 spaces and a maximum of 75. The maximum number is not required; it simply allows additional parking where the anticipated tenant mix warrants it. In short, the amendment establishes a more realistic minimum while allowing sufficient parking capacity to accommodate a broader range of tenants over the life of the development. Hucks stated that the second part of the amendment establishes driveway throat length standards. Driveway throat length is the unobstructed distance between the public street and the first internal location where a vehicle can turn, park, enter a drive aisle, or encounter another conflicting traffic movement. The UDO does not currently establish a minimum throat length standard. Without adequate space, vehicles entering a development may have to stop almost immediately because of internal parking or traffic movements. That can cause following vehicles to slow or stop within the public roadway. This is an issue that has already been seen at some of the fast-food establishments along Church Street at certain -- 5 of 11 -- September 21, 2026 6 times of the day. The proposed minimums are: 20 feet for residential development entrances; 30-50 feet for small commercial and strip commercial developments; and 200- 250 feet for shopping centers and big box retail establishments. Where a range is provided, the Technical Review Committee would determine the required distance during site plan review based on the size and intensity of development, anticipated traffic volume, roadway classification, driveway location, internal circulation, and any applicable traffic impact analysis. Hucks said that Planning Commission held a public hearing on the proposed amendments at its September 3 meeting, and recommended approval, including the language establishing criteria for the varying lengths. Staff recommended approval of first reading of the proposed amendments. There was some discussion regarding possibly increasing the parking space size in a future amendment. Hucks said that this is a request to approve “Village at Crabtree” as the name of a proposed 118-unit multifamily residential development located along El Bethel Road. The property is zoned High Density Residential (R-3), and the plans associated with the development are currently undergoing the Technical Review process. Section 10.3.8 of the UDO requires subdivision names to be approved by City Council before the plans proceed to Planning Commission for review and consideration of approval. Staff have not identified an existing subdivision or development that would create duplication. Hucks said that staff recommended approval of “Village at Crabtree” as the name of the proposed development. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Butler approving the name of the subdivision as “Village at Crabtree.” Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. Consideration of a request for a waiver of sidewalk requirements for Macala Acres Commercial Building, located at 2673 Hwy 378 (PIN 337-15-01-0003). Hucks stated that under Section 7.1.2 of the UDO, which contains the City’s complete street requirements, this commercial development, currently under construction, is required to construct approximately 275 linear feet of sidewalk along Hwy 378 and 185 feet along Green Pond Circle. The waiver request being considered is applicable to the Highway 378 frontage only. The reason the applicant is seeking a waiver is due to a significant utility conflict. According to the applicant, constructing the sidewalk on the Highway 378 side would require the existing roadside ditch to be replaced with approximately 275 feet of 24- -- 6 of 11 -- September 21, 2026 7 inch drainage pipe and additional fill to raise the grade. The proposed drainage pipe would be located directly above an existing 6-inch Dominion Energy gas line. It could also affect the existing gas meter and Dominion’s ability to access and maintain its facilities. Dominion may therefore require the gas line to be relocated before the drainage improvements can be installed. The applicant estimates that relocation could take several months and cost more than $50,000. The applicant has also indicated that the enclosed drainage improvements are needed only to accommodate the sidewalk – the existing open ditch otherwise provides adequate drainage for the site. Staff considered pedestrian connectivity in the surrounding area. There is currently no continuous sidewalk network along this portion of Hwy 378 to which the proposed sidewalk would connect. There is an existing sidewalk along Green Pond Circle in the Macal Acres subdivision, and the development will still be required to provide the sidewalk along that frontage. Hucks said that under the sidewalk waiver requirements of the UDO, approval of the waiver requires a payment in lieu of sidewalk construction. Based on 275 linear feet at the City’s current estimated cost of $33 per foot, the required payment fee in lieu amount would be $9,075. Staff recommended approval of the waiver for the Highway 378 frontage, subject to payment of the $9,075 fee in lieu. The sidewalk requirement along Green Pond Circle would remain in effect. There was discussion regarding the utility lines having to be relocated, building of sidewalks on other sections of the property, pedestrian connectivity in this area, putting sidewalks in as you go due to the growth of the city, putting sidewalks in other parts of the city that is much needed, and SCDOT right of way requirements. White, Hardwick, Helms voted no. Motion to approve carried with a 4-3 vote. C. Consideration of an amendment to the Wild Wing Pre Annexation Agreement. Emrick said that in early 2000, the city annexed several properties across the river, including Wild Wing which started in the county and was approved in the county. The city annexed it in as it was beginning to develop into a subdivision. At the time the city incentivized their annexation, and the incentive was to reimburse the developer 50% of the city’s tax collections from Wild Wing until they were reimbursed from their upfront cost of the development. In 2026, the agreement was amended to cap what that reimbursement would be and the cap was $5,000,000. The city was later approached by the developer for a reduction in the total amount owed in exchange for the city paying it upfront. Emrick said that the city currently owes $1.8 Million and has negotiated it down to $1,475,000, which is a reduction of $325,000, or roughly 18%. Goldfinch discussed the need for impact fees saying that state law handcuffs the city’s ability to utilize that impact fee and thinks the city should take this need to the statehouse and ask for help. Goldfinch said that smart development is to let the people that are moving here and have never contributed to this environment share in that funding. Emrick said that in the Country Club case the impact fee is the wrong tool because you have a developer that took something in good condition and ruined it. The developer is obligated to fix it, and the problem is what they have ruined is not on the city’s property or in the right of way. There is a financial guarantee that they will fix it, but SCDOT has not required them to do so, or they have taken that money and said they were going to fix it. Emrick said that is an issue and then said impact fees would be to make improvements because of the development not to fix things that have been broken. We do agree on the impact fee needs and that if that subdivision adds 200 homes, 400 cars, and then there is a sudden traffic problem at the intersection of Country Club and Long 107 -- 107 of 174 -- August 17, 2026 9 Avenue and a traffic light needs to go up or a roundabout, the city has no funding to do that either. Emrick said that an impact fee could fund that need. Goldfinch said that a lot of the issue is whether it is the city’s or not. This is a state road, but it is still the City of Conway. Emrick said you have identified the problem is that the city’s hands are so tied on what we can use impact money for right now that we can’t use impact money for, so we do need legislative change.
