Emrick recognized the group present who represented Conway in Denver at the National Civic League's All-America City Awards. -- 10 of 14 -- July 20, 2026 11 - Emrick shared a short video that WMBF produced about the city, setting up the presentation that was made before the panel of judges. WMBF did an outstanding job capturing not just who we are, but why who we are matters. Emrick again thanked WMBF for their support and for helping showcase our community throughout this entire process. - Emrick then had the Denver group stand and stated that for months, these individuals gave up evenings, weekends, and time with their families. They practiced over and over. They rewrote presentations, answered difficult questions, and prepared themselves to represent not just this organization, but this entire community on a national stage. - Emrick said that what impressed him the most wasn't the presentation itself, it was watching this group become a team. We had elected officials, staff members, students, volunteers, and community partners all working toward one goal. Nobody cared whose idea got used. Nobody cared who got the credit. They simply wanted Conway to be represented in the best possible way. When we stood on that stage, we told Conway's story with honesty, pride, and professionalism. Every person in this delegation represented this city with class and Emrick said he couldn't have been prouder to stand beside them. Awards come and go. What lasts is the culture we're building here. A culture where people willingly step up, work hard, and believe in something bigger than themselves. Emrick said he wanted to say thank you. Thank you for your time. Thank you for your commitment. Thank you for believing in Conway enough to invest so much of yourselves in telling its story. - Emrick showed a video that was created by Freda Funnye Johnson, one of our teammates and thanked Freda. 2. Emrick announced that in the coming weeks, city staff will be asking the people of Conway to help the city pursue Hallmark's Christmas Cities recognition. This time, it won't be our voices telling Conway's story - it will be yours. Emrick said staff will be asking residents to share the traditions, memories, and moments that make Christmas in Conway so special. If this experience in Denver taught us anything, it's that our greatest strength has never been a presentation or an application. It's the people who love this city and are willing to tell its story. I hope our community will rally behind this effort just as enthusiastically, because no one can explain the magic of Christmas in Conway better than the people who live it. 3. Emrick said that before we moved on from the All-America Cities, he wanted to point out that we did win one of only two individual city awards, the Social Media Award. This award recognized our city, and specifically our two-person Public Information Office team, for their outstanding online resident engagement, digital storytelling, and creative use of platforms like Facebook and Instagram to promote civic health. From the outset, we had a huge jump on our competitors. The introduction by the National Civic League of each City was an early tell. There were 20 cities, all individually introduced, besides Conway, the most reactions any City got on Facebook was 41. Conway had 1,200. The live stream of each City had an individual post with links to the stream and public comments. The most any City had besides Conway was 87, Conway had 230. And the tell here was that nearly across the board, the comments for Conway were positive, supportive, and expressed how much our residents love our city. There was little doubt that we deserved this award. Congratulations to June Wood, who is not here tonight, and -- 11 of 14 -- July 20, 2026 12 to Kelli Thomas, for not only the social media stuff, but for working tirelessly behind the scenes to help get us ready for Denver. 4. Police Captain Darren Alston will be retiring. Darren has served the city for over 25 years. Have no fear, though. It is his intention to come back in time for the fall and become an SRO for the City, working in the schools. 5. The Sports and Fitness Center has some fun programming coming up: a. On August 22nd , they are hosting Karaoke Night, register in advance starting this Friday b. Cooking Classes for people with different abilities is this Wednesday at 5 pm and August 12 at 5 pm. c. Art in the Park is August 8 from 5 pm to 7 pm d. Conway Superstar will be back this year on September 26, and Emrick said he has been informed that this year things will be changing just a bit to include a variety of talents 6. National Night Out and the Camp Blue graduation will be held together again this year on August 4th from 6 pm to 8 pm. 7. Emrick said that our area is in the middle of extreme drought conditions. We are between 10 and 12 inches behind normal rainfall, making this this dryest year to date in 132 years. We’ve all seen photographs of area rivers shallow enough to walk across. Early in the spring, we took some precautions in response, including turning off the splash pad. Conditions have not improved as the summer has progressed. Even the afternoon thunderstorms that are typical of summer here have not produced the rainfall that typical, or that we need. Over the last couple of weeks, we have had several internal meetings to discuss ways to further conserve our water, both as a city and as residents. While we are hopeful that the rain that is predicted for every afternoon this week produces some rainfall, we are also looking at what the next steps will have to be if we do not see considerable rainfall soon. 8. There is an Executive Session, but no Workshop. Helms asked staff to look into what can be done legally on Country Club. Goldfinch, with Blain agreeing, said that public input was the best in a while with the possibility of solutions to the problems that were spoken of regarding parking and Country Club. Jordan - Thanked the Denver crew and said that they all poured their heart and soul into the All- America City Awards Goldfinch - Congratulated the Denver team for a job well done at the All-America City Awards - Asked HR to find out how many full time/part time staff that have children under the age of 18 – said that all of those need to go get a Trump account – it is free money for those born between 2025 and 2028 and if outside that range they are still eligible for the $250 investment account - as financial opportunities like this can propel a kid that might not otherwise have an opportunity to be somewhere and can truly make a difference in a child’s life. White - Ditto to all that has been said. - Talked about the Greenville Ambassadors that were at the MASC Annual Meeting – said that they were on every corner with same-colored shirts. White asked that the city look into having volunteers with the designated shirts at special events. Butler - Said that she agreed with everything that had already been said. - Encouraged the residents to take advantage of the opportunities from the organizations that will be giving away books and supplies - said that there is an event on August 8 at Smith Jones Park. ISSUE: Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-15 (A) to amend Article 5 – Supplemental and Accessory Uses, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding requirements for mobile vending; specifically, to remove the cap on mobile vending permits and establishing revised administrative provisions. BACKGROUND: On July 21, 2025, the City Council adopted Ordinance #ZA2025-07-21(E), establishing a maximum of twenty (20) mobile vending permits for the 2026-27 fiscal year, with certain exemptions. On April 23, 2026, the annual cap was reached, effectively limiting the issuance of additional permits for the remainder of the current licensing cycle, which doesn’t start until May 1st . Since adoption, several challenges associated with the fixed cap have become evident: • Market Limitations: Once the cap is reached, otherwise qualified vendors are unable to operate within the City, limiting opportunities for small businesses and entrepreneurs. • Administrative Constraints: Modifying the number of permits currently requires a formal UDO amendment, which involves a multi-step legislative process and limits the City’s ability to respond to changing conditions in a timely manner. • Operational Flexibility: A fixed cap does not account for variations in staffing capacity, enforcement demands, or the availability of suitable vending locations throughout the year. The proposed amendment would remove the specific numerical cap from the UDO and instead establish a framework that allows the City to manage the number of permits administratively, based on defined operational and public safety considerations. PLANNING COMMISSION AND CITY COUNCIL: Planning Commission held a public hearing regarding this amendment on June 4, 2026 and recommended approval. City Council approved first reading on May 4, 2026. STAFF RECOMMENDATION: The amendment is intended to provide greater flexibility in managing mobile vending activity while maintaining appropriate oversight to ensure compatibility with surrounding uses, public safety, and available resources. Under this approach, the annual number of permits would be determined administratively by the Planning Director, in coordination with the Zoning Administrator, and Fire Marshal, based on objective factors such as enforcement capacity, site availability, and operational impacts without requiring frequent legislative updates. The established permit availability would be published annually to ensure transparency and 4 -- 4 of 233 -- consistency with application. The framework allows the City to remain responsive to changing conditions while maintaining a structured and predictable process for applicants. Staff recommends approval of the proposed amendment to Article 5 of the UDO. The basis for the appeal must be included in the request for an appeal. 11 -- 11 of 233 -- City of Conway Administrative Policy: Mobile Vending Permit Management PURPOSE The purpose of this policy is to establish a clear and consistent framework for the issuance and management of mobile vending permits within the City of Conway. The policy is intended to implement the requirements of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) by providing procedures for determining permit availability, processing applications, and managing permit allocation. By administering permit volumes through this policy, the City seeks to remain responsive to operational capacity, public safety considerations, and market conditions, while maintaining a fair, transparent, and predictable process for applicants. This policy does not create a right to a permit and shall not be interpreted as guaranteeing issuance to any applicant. ANNUAL PERMIT DETERMINATION 1. Capacity Review Prior to April 30 of each year, the Planning Director, in coordination with the Zoning Administrator and Fire Marshal, shall determine the number of mobile vending permits to be issued for the upcoming licensing cycle. 2. Evaluation Criteria This annual permit availability shall be based on the following factors: a. Availability of suitable vending locations on public and private property b. Administrative capacity for application review, inspections and enforcement c. Public health and safety considerations d. Feedback from the local business community, including organizations such as Conway Downtown Alive. 3. Public Notice The total number of permits available for the licensing cycle shall be published on the City of Conway Business License webpage prior to the opening of the application period. APPLICATION & ISSUANCE PROCEDURES 1. Submission Window Applications for permit renewals and new permits shall open 30 days prior to the expiration of the current licensing cycle. 12 -- 12 of 233 -- 2. Prioritization Process a. Renewals Existing permit holders in good standing, with no unresolved code violations, shall be provided a defined priority period to submit renewal applications. b. New Applicants Following the renewal period, any remaining permits shall be issued to new applicants on a first- come, first-served basis, based on complete application submittals. 3. Waitlist Management If the number of complete applications exceeds the number of permits available, the City shall maintain an official waitlist. Applicants will be placed on the waitlist in the order in which complete applications are received. Permits that become available due to non-renewal, revocation, or withdrawal shall be offered to waitlisted applicants in order of placement. OPERATIONAL COMPLIANCE All mobile vending permit holders shall comply with applicable provisions of the Unified Development Ordinance and all other applicable local, state, and federal regulations, including but not limited to: 1. Maintaining a current food safety inspection report from the South Carolina Department of Agriculture (SCDA), as applicable. 2. Maintaining general liability insurance in accordance with the South Carolina Business License requirements (see SC Business License Handbook) and as specified in the UDO. 3. Proper waste management, including the removal of all trash and debris generated within a 25-foot radius of the vending unit. MID-CYCLE ADJUSTMENTS The number of permits established for a licensing cycle may be adjusted during that cycle only in response to documented: 1. Public safety concerns 2. Infrastructure or site capacity limitations 3. Significant changes in administrative or enforcement capacity. Any such adjustment(s) shall be documented in writing and made publicly available through the City’s website or other official means. POLICY ADMINISTRATION This policy shall be administered by the Planning Director or designee and shall be applied in a consistent and non-discriminatory manner. Administrative procedures established under this policy shall remain consistent with the requirements of the Unified Development Ordinance. 13 -- 13 of 233 -- DATE: JUNE 15, 2026 ITEM: III.B. SECOND/FINAL READING Final reading of Ordinance # ZA2026-06-01 (T), to amend Article 10 – Subdivision and land development of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to the Park and Open Space Dedication. The proposed amendment would establish new standards to calculate the fee-in-lieu of open space mitigation in the City of Conway. Hucks stated that this proposed amendment received first reading at the May 18 Council meeting. Staff wanted to provide additional clarification regarding what this amendment changes and what remains unchanged. The requirements for open space are not changing. The amount of open space 23 -- 23 of 233 -- June 1, 2026 5 required by the ordinance remains the same, the circumstances under which the fee-in-lieu may be used remains the same, and City Council retains authority to review alternatives to providing open space, including reduced fee-in-lieu amounts. What the amendment changes is the method used to calculate the fee in lieu when the fee in lieu is either required by the ordinance or requested by a developer in lieu of providing all or a portion of the required open space. Currently, the fee-in-lieu amount is based on an appraisal of the property as if the development were already completed. Because that methodology relies on a hypothetical future condition, the resulting fee can vary significantly from project to project and often cannot be determined early in the development review process. Staff have also found that these appraisals can introduce a level of subjectivity and inconsistency into what is intended to be a standardized requirement. Hucks then showed a slide giving an example of the calculations under the current ordinance versus under the proposed ordinance. Hucks said that an important point to note is that this amendment is not necessarily reducing fee- in-lieu amounts. In many cases, particularly for larger developments, the proposed fee structure could actually result in a higher fee than what may have been calculated under the current method. As a result, the amendment may encourage more onsite open space construction because developers may determine that provided the required amenities is more practical or cost-effective than paying the fee in lieu. The amendment does modify the review process. Currently, fee-in-lieu requests require review by the TRC, Planning Commission and City Council. Under the proposed amendment, if the applicant utilizes the standard fee structure that is proposed, Planning Commission may approve the request to pay the fee in lieu as part of the development review process. However, if the applicant proposes a reduced fee, land donation, offsite improvement, or other alternative compliance method, Planning Commission would review and provide a recommendation, and City Council would retain final decision-making authority. Hucks stated that staff continues to recommend approval. There was some discussion regarding requirements for active and passive open space. APPLICANT(S): Christy Douglas, David Douglas, Johnny Skipper (MBNC LLC etal) PIN(s): 399-01-02-0001 & 399-00-00-0001 CURRENT ZONING: Horry County Office/Professional/Institutional (OPI) PROPOSED ZONING: City of Conway Low-Density Residential (R) BACKGROUND: The subject properties, located on Gardner Lacy Road, are currently vacant; however, there is a powerline easement one of the properties. The applicants are requesting to annex the subject properties located on Gardner Lacy Rd, and rezone the properties to the Low-Density Residential (R) district. The properties are currently vacant. Per Section 3.2.17 of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), the intent of the R District is to provide for the preservation and expansion of areas for low density, detached single-family residential development in the City of Conway. The district shall present a relatively spacious character, promote quiet, livable neighborhoods, and prohibit uses that are incompatible with the residential nature of the surrounding area. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: One of the properties abuts a Santee Cooper distribution facility. Both properties are adjacent to the railroad right-of-way. The other side is property owned by Myrtle Beach National Property Owner’s Association (POA), as well as the Southcreek development. Southcreek, in Horry County’s jurisdiction, is zoned SF10, which is single-family residential, no mobile homes allowed, with minimum lot sizes of 10,000 sq. ft. The proposed zoning upon annexation is the city’s default zoning of R, which also requires a minimum lot size of 10,000 sq. ft. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The Future Land Use Map of the Comprehensive Plan identifies the property as Professional (P). Per Section 3.2.7 of the UDO, the intent of the P district is to accommodate office, institutional, and residential uses in areas whose character is neither exclusively business nor residential in nature. This district is intended to establish areas that provide professional services to the public, which do not materially detract from nearby 31 -- 31 of 233 -- STAFF REPORT Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-07-21 (H) residential areas. More specifically, the P district serves as a transitional zone between more intensive commercial uses and residential areas. The P district is not intended for businesses that engage in retail sales. PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION: Planning Commission held the required Public Hearing at their July 10, 2025 meeting and recommended zoning the properties Professional (P) upon annexation. STAFF ANALYSIS: Although the Future Land Use Map identifies the property as Professional (P), staff finds that the proposed Low-Density Residential (R) zoning is appropriate given the property’s location, surrounding development pattern, and physical characteristics. The subject property is adjacent to established residential development, including the Southcreek subdivision, and is separated from more intensive commercial areas by the railroad corridor and utility infrastructure. In addition, one of the parcels is encumbered by a powerline easement, which may limit future development opportunities. The proposed Low-Density Residential (R) district requires a minimum lot size of 10,000 sq. ft., which is comparable to the adjacent Southcreek subdivision and consistent with the existing residential character of the area. Staff believes the proposed zoning provides a logical transition between surrounding residential uses and adjacent infrastructure corridors. While the request is not fully consistent with the Future Land Use Map designation of Professional (P), staff finds that the proposed zoning better reflects the existing development pattern. ORDINANCE: #ZA2026-07-20 (P) AGENDA SECTION: First Reading(s) ISSUE: First reading of an ordinance to rezone approximate 10 +/- acre portion of 110 +/- acres of property located on Cultra Road and Oak Street, and adjacent to Conway Christian School. APPLICANT(S): Burroughs & Chapin Company, Inc. (Blake Arp) PIN(s): 325-00-00-0011 CURRENT ZONING: Medium-Density Residential (R-2) PROPOSED ZONING: Low/Medium Density Residential (R-1) BACKGROUND: The applicant is requesting to rezone approximately 10+/- acres in connection with a proposed subdivision and combination plat. If approved, the 10+/- acre portion would be conveyed to Conway Christian School and combined with the school’s existing campus property located adjacent to the subject property. The subject property is currently part of a larger tract containing split zoning of Conservation Preservation (CP) and Medium-Density Residential (R-2). The split zoning was originally established due to the presence of environmentally-sensitive areas and flood-prone land associated with portions of the tract. Under the City’s Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), split zoning of parcels is generally prohibited except in circumstances involving environmentally sensitive lands, where Conservation Preservation (CP) zoning is utilized to protect those areas. The proposed 10-acre subdivision area appears to be located outside of the environmentally sensitive portions of the parent tract and is intended to be combined with the adjacent Conway Christian School property, which is currently zoned Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). Rezoning the proposed subdivision area to R-1 would prevent the creation of a split-zoning condition on the newly combined parcel and maintain consistency with the zoning of the adjoining school campus. A large portion of the remaining tract will continue to contain flood-prone and environmentally sensitive areas currently zoned Conservation Preservation (CP). SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: The subject property is located adjacent to existing Conway Christian School campus and is surrounded by a mix of residential development, school/institutional uses, and undeveloped land. Surrounding zoning classifications include: • Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) • Medium-Density Residential (R-2) 143 -- 143 of 233 -- STAFF REPORT First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (P) • High-Density Residential (R-3) (Midtown Village subdivision), and • Residential districts within Horry County’s jurisdiction. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The Future Land Use Map identifies the property primarily as Medium-Density Residential (R-2), with environmentally sensitive portions of the larger tract identified for Conservation Preservation (CP), and a portion along the Cultra Rd boundary identified as Neighborhood Commercial (NC). While the proposed R-1 zoning is not identical to the Medium-Density Residential designation shown on the Future Land Use Map, it represents a less intensive residential classification than currently contemplated for the property. The requested zoning would reduce, rather than increase, the development intensity of the approximately 10-acre tract. The proposed zoning is intended to facilitate the combination of the property with the adjacent Conway Christian School campus, which is currently zoned Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). As such, the request promotes zoning consistency across the combined parcel and does not create a more intensive development pattern than currently anticipated by the Comprehensive Plan. PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION: Planning Commission held the required Public Hearing at their June 4, 2026 meeting and recommended approval to rezone the 10-acre portion of the subject property to R-1. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Staff recommends approval of First Reading to rezone the property to R-1. APPLICANT(S): Denise S Holt PIN(s): 337-08-02-0021 CURRENT ZONING: Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) PROPOSED ZONING: City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) BACKGROUND: The annexation application was submitted by the property owner as a requirement associated with a name change to the existing City utility services account. The name change is solely due to the owner’s spouse passing away. The property contains a single-family residence and restrictive covenants associated with the property has been on file since September of 1987. Council approved first reading of an ordinance annexing the subject property at their May 18, 2026 meeting. The property owner has expressed their desire not to be annexed into the City. They have lived in the home with their spouse for decades and the only reason annexation is being required is due to the name change on the City utilities account. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: The subject property is adjacent on two sides to the Woodcreek subdivision, which is located within the City limits and zoned Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). The remaining adjacent property lies within Horry County’s jurisdiction, zoned Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA), and fronts along Dunn Shortcut Road. Within this portion of Dunn Shortcut Road adjacent to the Woodcreek subdivision, only five properties – including the subject parcel – remain outside the City limits. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s Future Land Use Map also identifies the property as Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). The intent of the R-1 district is to preserve and expand areas for low- to medium-density detached single- family residential development within the City of Conway. The district is intended to maintain a relatively spacious residential character, promote quiet and livable neighborhoods, and prohibit uses incompatible with the surrounding residential environment. 155 -- 155 of 233 -- STAFF REPORT First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (Q) The proposed zoning of R-1 is consistent with the Future Land Use Map, the existing residential use of the property, and the zoning pattern of adjacent properties within the City limits. PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION: Planning Commission held the required Public Hearing at their June 4, 2026 meeting and recommended approval of the proposed zoning upon annexation. However, the board also requested that City Council give thorough consideration to the property owner's concerns during their review of the annexation request, including consideration of denial of the annexation. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Staff recommends approval of First Reading to rezone the property to R-1 upon annexation. APPLICANT(S): City of Conway PIN(s): 368-00-00-0019 CURRENT ZONING: Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) PROPOSED ZONING: Conservation Preservation (CP) BACKGROUND: The subject property, located behind Lake Busbee and adjacent to New Road, was acquired by the City in 2025 as part of the same acquisition involving the property commonly known as Lake Busbee and the former Grainger Steam Plant site. During subsequent platting activity in 2025, this portion of the overall tract was separated from the parent parcel. As a result, the property was not included in the zoning actions approved for the surrounding Lake Busbee properties and does not currently display a county or city zoning designation on GIS mapping. A significant portion of the property contains a Santee Cooper transmission line easement, while the remainder of the tract is heavily wooded and encumbered by mapped flood hazard areas and environmentally sensitive features. The surrounding Lake Busbee properties and adjacent City-owned parcels were annexed and/or rezoned in 2025 to either the Conservation Preservation (CP) district or the Waccamaw Riverfront District (WRD). The purpose of these actions was to preserve environmentally sensitive land and protect flood-prone areas. The City is seeking to annex and zone the property to Conservation Preservation (CP) in order to maintain consistency with surrounding City-owned properties and to preserve flood-prone and environmentally sensitive land. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: Surrounding properties are similar in nature and include: • common area associated with the Pecan Grove subdivision (zoned R-1) • Lake Busbee (zoned CP) • the City’s Oxidation Pond (zoned R-1) COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s future land use map also identifies the property as Conservation Preservation (CP). The intent of the CP 169 -- 169 of 233 -- STAFF REPORT First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (R) District is to provide open space for recreational uses and to protect environmentally sensitive areas and flood prone areas from residential, commercial, industrial, or other development that could adversely affect the relatively undeveloped character of the district. The proposed zoning upon annexation is consistent with the City’s Future Land Use Map, the physical characteristics of the property, and the zoning of surrounding City-owned properties. PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION: Planning Commission held the required Public Hearing on June 4, 2026 and recommended approval of the proposed zoning upon annexation. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Staff recommends approval of First Reading to rezone the property to CP upon annexation. BACKGROUND: Sec. 5.2.5 of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) currently permits the non-commercial keeping of livestock or fowl as an accessory use within the Rural Residential (RR), Rural Agriculture (RA), and Forest Agriculture (FA) zoning districts, subject to specific acreage, containment, and operational standards. The ordinance also contains limited exceptions for certain properties zoned FA and educational facilities located within the Institutional (IN) zoning district. As the City continues to grow through annexation and development, portions of the City now include or may include in the future, large residential properties exceeding twenty (20) acres in size. While these properties may be located within zoning districts that permit single-family detached dwellings, the current ordinance does not provide a mechanism for property owners to keep livestock or fowl for personal enjoyment, sustenance, passive agriculture activities, or similar non-commercial purposes unless the property is located within the RR, RA, or FA zoning districts. The proposed amendment would establish an additional allowance for properties containing twenty (20) acres or more and a single-family detached dwelling as the principal use. Such properties would be eligible to keep livestock or fowl regardless of the underlying zoning district, provided the district permits single- family detached dwellings and the property contains a single-family detached dwelling as the principal use. Livestock and fowl permitted under this provision would remain subject to all applicable requirements of Sec. 5.2.5, including standards related to acreage, animal type, containment, setbacks, nuisance prevention, and prohibitions on commercial operations. In addition to the substantive amendment, the proposed ordinance reorganizes Sec. 5.2.5 to improve readability, administration, and ease of interpretation. The current ordinance is organized primarily by animal type, which can make it difficult for property owners and staff to determine where certain permissions, restrictions, and exceptions apply. The proposed amendment restructures the section by zoning district and applicability, incorporates definitions for key terms, consolidates related standards, and clearly identifies exceptions and special circumstances. These changes are intended to make the ordinance more user-friendly while preserving the City’s existing regulations regarding nuisance prevention, animal containment, setbacks, and non-commercial use limitations. 181 -- 181 of 233 -- Staff finds that the proposed amendment provides reasonable accommodation for large residential properties while maintaining the City’s existing standards intended to protect neighboring properties from potential nuisances and adverse impacts. The proposed twenty (20) acre minimum ensures that the allowance is limited to properties of sufficient size to support the keeping of livestock or fowl in a manner that remains compatible with surrounding development patterns. PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing and recommended approval of the proposed amendments at their June 4, 2026 meeting. STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends approval of First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (S), amending Sec. 5.2.5 of the UDO as proposed. 182 -- 182 of 233 -- ORDINANCE #ZA2026-07-20 (S) AN ORDINANCE TO AMEND ARTICLE 5 – SUPPLEMENTAL AND ACCESSORY USES, OF THE CITY OF CONWAY UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE (UDO), REGARDING REVISIONS TO THE REQUIREMENTS FOR NONCOMMERCIAL KEEPING OF LIVESTOCK OR FOWL, INCLUDING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF AN ALLOWANCE FOR CERTAIN RESIDENTIAL PROPERTIES TWENTY (20) ACRES OR GREATER IN SIZE. ISSUE: Approval to purchase materials and construct a water main loop connecting Willard Road and Alford Road. BACKGROUND: The City's hydraulic system analysis, completed by AECOM Engineering, identified a water main loop between Willard Road and Alford Road as one of the most beneficial improvements that can be made to the water distribution system. The project will improve system pressure, reliability, fire protection, redundancy, and overall operational efficiency. The project will require approximately 6,000 feet of water main. While staff had hoped future development would extend this line, no development is currently anticipated in the area that would provide this improvement. The estimated material cost is approximately $300,000 and will be funded through the Water Line Upgrades Account. Utilities Department staff proposes to install the line using in-house personnel rather than a contractor. Staff estimates the project would cost more than $750,000 if constructed by contract, resulting in an estimated savings of over $450,000 through the use of City forces. In addition to improving service to existing customers, the project will create opportunities for future service connections and support continued growth in the area. FISCAL IMPACT: • Estimated Material Cost: $300,000 • Funding Source: Water Line Upgrades Account • Estimated Savings Using City Forces: $450,000 + RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends approval to purchase the necessary materials and proceed with construction of the Willard Road – Alford Road Water Main Loop Project. This project was identified through the City's hydraulic model as a priority improvement and will enhance system reliability, efficiency, fire protection, and future growth opportunities while providing substantial cost savings through the use of in-house personnel. 232 -- 232 of 233 -- 233 -- 233 of 233 --

title: CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES 6.15.26
text: June 15, 2026 1 CITY OF CONWAY CITY COUNCIL MEETING CONWAY CITY HALL 229 MAIN STREET, CONWAY MONDAY, JUNE 15, 2026 PRESENT: Mayor Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor Pro Tem Beth Helms, Amanda Butler, William Goldfinch, Julie Hardwick, Justin Jordan, Larry White. STAFF: Adam Emrick, City Administrator; Mary Catherine Hyman, Deputy City Administrator; John Rogers, Deputy City Administrator; June Wood, Public Information Officer; Jeff Leveille, Technology Services Director; Jason Perzan, Fire Chief; Reggie Jenerette, Solid Waste Director; Robert Cooper, Construction Services Director; Jessica Hucks, Planning and Development Director; Dale Long, Police Chief; Timmy Williams, Hospitality and Beautification Director; Ashley Smith, Parks and Recreation Director; Kelli Thomas, Deputy PIO; Bobby Wallace, Fleet Maintenance Director; Charlotte Peterson, Assistant Planner; Nancy Alvarez, Assistant Planner; Braxton Fleming, Deputy Public Works Director; Lynn Smith, HR Director; Ted Dudley, Public Utilities Director; Kayla Fleming, Municipal Judge; Drew Sorbello, Administration Intern; and Alicia Shelley, City Clerk. OTHERS: There were approximately 20 others in attendance. CALL TO ORDER: Mayor Blain called the meeting to order. INVOCATION/PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE: Hardwick gave the invocation and led the Pledge of Allegiance. The requirements for posting notice of this meeting under South Carolina’s Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) were met. CONSENT AGENDA: A. Final reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-15 (A) to amend Article 5 – Supplemental and Accessory Uses, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance, regarding revisions to the requirements for mobile vending; specifically, to remove the cap on mobile vending permits and establish administrative provisions. B. Approval of Mutual Aid and Law Enforcement Support Agreement between the City of Conway and the City of North Myrtle Beach Police Departments C. Approval of June 1, 2026 City Council Meeting Minutes APPROVAL OF CONSENT AGENDA: Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Butler to approve the June 15, 2026 consent agenda. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. SPECIAL PRESENTATION: -- 1 of 12 -- June 15, 2026 2 A. Employee of the Month for June 2026 – Public Safety – Perzan presented Captain Jeromy Herndon, Firefighter Dallas Watts and Firefighter Stephen Gleason with the Employee of the Month award for June 2026. B. Presentation of a Proclamation recognizing Amateur Radio Club – Blain presented Todd Rush with the Amateur Radio Club Proclamation. FINAL READING A. Final reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-07-21 (H), to annex approximately 22.88 acres of property located on Gardner Lacy Rd (PIN’s 399-01-02-0001 and 399-00-00- 0001), and request to rezone from the Horry County Office/ Professional/Institutional (OPI) district to the City of Conway Low-Density Residential (R) district. Hucks stated that this request goes back to June of last year, when the applicant was seeking to annex into the City limits ahead of any intent to develop the property. The property is currently zoned Office, Professional, Institutional (OPI) in the County’s jurisdiction and the City’s current future land use map identifies the subject property as Professional, likely a very similar district to the current county zoning. Other properties in the vicinity are zoned Industrial, Commercial Forest Agriculture, Highway Commercial and Planned Unit Development. The applicant is seeking to annex the parcels as Low-Density Residential, or the R district, which is similar to the zoning of the adjacent Southcreek subdivision, which is zoned Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed, (SF10) district, requiring a minimum lot size of 10,000 sq. ft. The R district also requires a minimum lot size of 10,000 sq. ft. While there is no immediate development plans associated with the property, the applicant has expressed an interest in completing the annexation of the property to ensure that it is within the City’s jurisdiction prior to future development or utility needs. Should the applicant choose to develop the property in a manner that is not consistent with the Low-Density Residential district, they will be required to pursue a zoning map amendment to a district that would permit the proposed use at that time. Hucks said that Planning Commission held a public hearing on the requested zoning upon annexation at their July 10, 2025 meeting and recommended that the property be zoned Professional (P) upon annexation, which they thought was more in line with the current county zoning and some of the nearby uses. Staff recommended deferral. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Blain to combine this Ordinance #ZA2025-07-21 (H) and the next Ordinance #ZA2024-09-16 (C), and defer these requests until a later date. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. Final reading of Ordinance #ZA2024-09-16 (C) to annex approximately 1.43 acres of property located at 104 Gardner Lacy Rd (PIN 399-01-04-0006), and rezone from the Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) district to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district. See previous motion. -- 2 of 12 -- June 15, 2026 3 FIRST READING: A. First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (J) to amend the Future Land Use Map of the City of Conway Comprehensive Plan for approximately 1.07+/- acres of property located on Sycamore Street from Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) to Medium-Density Residential (R-2). Hucks stated that this request is the first of two companion items involving approximately 1.07 acres of property on Sycamore Street. The applicant is requesting to amend the future land use map for the subject property, currently designated R1 to R2. The purpose of both requests is to allow for the development of townhomes on the property. The property is currently vacant and surrounded by properties zoned R1, developed primarily with detached single-family homes. While there are some properties zoned R2 in the immediate vicinity, none are contiguous to the subject property. Because townhomes require a minimum zoning classification of R2, the applicant must first obtain an amendment to the future land use map before a rezoning request can be considered. The primary question for council is whether R2 is an appropriate future land use designation for this property given its size, location, and the surrounding pattern of single-family residential development. Hucks said that Planning Commission held the required public hearing at its June 4 meeting and recommended disapproval of the future land use map amendment. Staff also recommended disapproval. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by White to disapprove first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (J) amending the future land use map for the property located on Sycamore Street (PIN 368-01-03-0072). Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (K) to rezone approximately 1.07+/- acres of property located on Sycamore Street from the Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district to the Medium-Density Residential (R-2) district. Hucks said that this is the companion item to the same 1.07-acre property on Sycamore Street and the request is to rezone the property from R1 to R2 to allow for the development of townhomes. Planning Commission held the public hearing and recommended disapproval. Staff also recommended disapproval. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Hardwick to disapprove first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (K) rezoning this property. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. C. First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (L) to rezone approximately 1.93+/- acres of property located at 235 Singleton Ridge Rd (PIN 383-10-03-0025) from the Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) district to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district upon annexation. Hucks stated that this request is for zoning upon annexation of approximately 1.93 acres located at 235 Singleton Ridge Road. The property contains an existing urgent care and medical office facility and is currently zoned Horry County Highway Commercial. Properties on both sides are in the city limits already, also zoned HC. Council approved first reading of an ordinance to annex this -- 3 of 12 -- June 15, 2026 4 property at its May 4 meeting. First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (S) to amend Article 5 – Supplemental and Accessory Uses, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to the requirements for Noncommercial Keeping of Livestock or Fowl, establishing an exception for parcels twenty (20) acres or greater in size and containing a single-family dwelling. Hucks stated that currently livestock and fowl are generally permitted only within the Rural Residential (RR), Rural Agriculture (RA) and Forest Agriculture (FA) zoning districts, subject to various standards and limitations. In the FA district, the ordinance has an exception carved out that allows noncommercial keeping of livestock or fowl on property 5 or more acres, without a principal structure, for property owners who wish to build accessory structures on the property for the keeping of these animals. As the city continues to annex larger tracts of land, staff has encountered situations where properties containing several acres of land and containing a single-family residence are located in zoning districts that do not currently allow livestock or fowl for personal, non-commercial purposes. The proposed amendment would create a limited exception for properties that: contain at least 20 acres; contain a single-family detached dwelling as the principal use; and are located within a zoning -- 7 of 12 -- June 15, 2026 8 district that permits single-family detached dwellings. Under the proposed amendment, those property owners would be allowed to keep livestock or fowl for personal, non- commercial purposes, regardless of the underlying zoning district so long as the zoning district permits single-family detached dwellings and contains a single-family detached dwelling. Importantly, all existing requirements would remain in place, including standards related to acreage, setbacks, containment, nuisance prevention, animal type, and the prohibition of commercial agriculture operations. The amendment also reorganizes the ordinance for clarity by grouping requirements based on zoning district and applicability, making the section easier for both property owners and staff to interpret and administer. Hucks said that Planning Commission held the required public hearing on June 4 and recommended approval of the amendment. PUBLIC INPUT: None CITY ADMINISTRATOR’S REPORT: Emrick informed Council of the following : • Introduced Drew Sorbello, Administration Intern. • June 23, 2026 - Ribbon cutting for Cypress Basin located at 1604 Sherwood Drive. • The new playground in the Jamestown Community is nearly completed and hope to open it in the next couple of weeks. Staff will get public messaging out on this new park, and work on signage and future improvement planning. • The Dog Park project is coming along very nicely. The new brick entrance and archway are nearly complete. • At the last Council meeting there was a concern raised about removing geese in Riverfront Park and other public spaces downtown. Federal permits are required to remove geese without running afoul of the Federal Migratory Bird Treaty Act. The City of Conway is a Bird Sanctuary by ordinance and within the Bird Sanctuary ordinance there is a provision that if the birds congregate in such numbers that they constitute a menace or nuisance there are ways to abate the nuisance. Relocation is also not considered a particularly effective long-term solution, as geese often return to their original habitat or are replaced by other geese attracted to the same environmental conditions. As a result, wildlife professionals generally recommend habitat modification, public education, and population management techniques over relocation. The most suitable solution is to plant more landscaping materials along the seawall in the open grass area of Riverfront Park. The geese are drawn to open field with an unobstructed view of the water. So, obstructing the view may deter them from habituating in Riverfront Park. That is staff’s recommendation currently. However, this will change the appearance of Riverfront Park from across the marina, so Emrick said that he wanted to make sure that this approach was okay with Council prior to implementation. There was some discussion amongst Council and directed staff to keep an eye out. • The owners of 216 Elm Street are installing a new HVAC unit and will be blocking off a parking space or two in front of their location for this on Thursday. Emrick said that if there are any issues with this to let him know. • The Parks and Recreation Department successfully launched its Rec on the Go Mobile Recreation Unit program this month. The first two stops included Collins Park and Oasis Park (Smith Jones), where staff provided games, activities, and recreation opportunities directly within neighborhoods. Additional visits are scheduled throughout the summer, including Cypress Basin and Huckabee Heights, as staff continues to expand access to recreational programming across the city. • The city’s 10-week Summer Camp Program began this month with 100 campers enrolled, reflecting strong community participation. Campers are engaged in a variety of activities, -- 10 of 12 -- June 15, 2026 11 including sports, swimming, arts and crafts, educational programming, games, and special events. The program provides a safe, structured, and enjoyable summer experience for Conway youth. • The city will be represented at the South Carolina Recreation and Parks Association State Tournament by our 10U Girls Softball Team, which will compete in North Augusta beginning Friday. The department provides participating state tournament teams with financial assistance for travel and meal expenses to support their participation and represent the City of Conway at the state level. • Volunteers are being sought for the State Special Olympics in October. For now, interested individuals can contact Ashley Smith at asmith@conwaysc.gov. • Bids are due back next week for the Kingston Ferry Project and hope to have it completed by this time next year. • Camp Blue started this week with 70 campers this year working with our Police Department. • Applications for the Mayor’s Youth Council, that will begin again in the fall, reached record numbers this year as the city received 30 applications for only 5 spots. • The Laurel Street Stormwater Project will begin in the next couple of weeks, and it must be completed by September, ahead of the October rush. Work on this project will be done at night to lessen the impact on the businesses. • Last week the city acquired rights to show games from the World Cup on the big screen at the Terrace. There is a schedule on Facebook of the games that we will be showing. The attendance for the US/Paraguay game on Friday night was strong. There was some lightening damage from the storm on Saturday night, so hopefully this will not disrupt any of the planned viewings. • The 1st Comprehensive Plan Steering Committee meeting is planned for September. Charlotte and Nancy have been hard at work on the Comp Plan and to prepare for that first meeting, they have launched a community input survey. It will be open for input until mid- September and is accessible via QR Code in many locations, including social media, flyers posted around town, the Sports and Fitness Center, Library Museum and other locations. The link will also be on the kiosks throughout downtown and the big screen at the Terrace. • Finally, we are nearing the end of our All-America Cities preparation. Next week, a contingent will fly to Denver to make our case that we deserve to be selected as one of the ten All American Cities. • Emrick said there are no Executive Sessions and no Workshops. ISSUE: Final reading of Ordinance #2026-06-01 (D) to repeal and replace Purchasing Rules and Regulations BACKGROUND: The current purchasing rules have been amended multiple times over the years, resulting in a framework that is increasingly complex and difficult to navigate. The proposed update replaces the current, complex purchasing rules with a clearer and more consistent set of guidelines. In addition, purchasing thresholds are being increased, allowing staff to avoid unnecessary quotes for lower-value purchases and focus time and resources on higher-priority procurements, while maintaining appropriate oversight and accountability. In addition, staff is currently implementing procurement software to modernize the purchasing process by improving efficiency, transparency, and consistency across all departments. The online solicitation tool will expand the vendor audience, increasing competition and helping ensure the municipality receives the best value. City Council approved first reading on May 18, 2026. RECOMMENDATION: Approve final reading as presented. 16 -- 16 of 215 -- ORDINANCE #2026-06-01 (D) AN ORDINANCE REPEALING ORDINANCE NO. 2022-06-20(H) AND ADOPTING REVISED PURCHASING RULES AND REGULATIONS WHEREAS, on June 20, 2022, Conway City Council adopted Purchasing Ordinance #2022- 06-20 (H); and WHEREAS, City Council desires to modernize the procurement process, increase efficiency, and maintain full compliance with the laws of the State of South Carolina governing political subdivisions; and WHEREAS, the adoption of updated procedures will promote open competition, transparency, and the best value in the expenditure of public funds; Therefore, be it ORDAINED, that all prior purchasing ordinances are repealed and the following Purchasing Rules and Regulations are adopted; and be it further ORDAINED, that, all ordinances or parts of ordinances in conflict herewith are, to the extent of the conflict, hereby repealed. White, Council Member ATTEST: Alicia Shelley, City Clerk First Reading: May 18, 2026 Final Reading: June 1, 2026 17 -- 17 of 215 -- CITY OF CONWAY PURCHASING RULES AND REGULATIONS SECTION 1. PURPOSE The purpose of this regulation is to: • Provide a fair and equitable procurement system • Ensure the prudent expenditure of public funds • Obtain best value for the City • Provide full and open competition • Comply with the laws of the State of South Carolina SECTION 2. DEFINITIONS The terms “supplies”, “services”, “information technology”, and “construction” shall have their commonly accepted procurement meanings. SECTION 3. PURCHASING AUTHORITY The City Administrator shall serve as the Chief Procurement Officer and may delegate authority to a Procurement Director/Purchasing Agent. The Purchasing Agent shall: • Procure all goods and services • Maintain vendor lists • Establish specifications • Ensure competition • Monitor compliance • Maintain procurement records SECTION 4. ETHICS AND LEGAL COMPLIANCE All procurement activities shall comply with: • The South Carolina Ethics Act • The SC Consolidated Procurement Code principles for political subdivisions • Anti-discrimination and anti-boycott contract requirements . 18 -- 18 of 215 -- SECTION 5. PROCUREMENT METHODS AND THRESHOLDS (A) Micro Purchases – $10,000 and below May be made without competitive quotations if the price is determined fair and reasonable. (B) Small Purchases – $10,001 to $50,000 Require a minimum of two documented quotations where practicable. Award shall be made on a best value basis. (C) Intermediate Purchases – $50,001 to $100,000 Require written quotations or informal solicitation. Public notice is not required. (D) Formal Procurements – Over $100,000 Require one of the following: • Invitation for Bids (IFB) • Request for Proposals (RFP) • Request for Qualifications (RFQ) Public notice shall be given. SECTION 6. CITY COUNCIL APPROVAL City Council approval is required for: • All contracts and purchases exceeding $100,000 The City Administrator may approve contracts at or below this amount. SECTION 7. BASIS OF AWARD Awards shall be made to the responsive and responsible offeror whose proposal is most advantageous to the City, considering: • Price • Quality • Experience • Past performance • Delivery • Life-cycle costs • Other relevant factors Award is not required to be made to the lowest price. 19 -- 19 of 215 -- SECTION 8. NEGOTIATION Negotiations are permitted: • After competitive sealed bidding when in the City’s best interest • With highest-ranked RFP firms • For sole source procurements • For emergency procurements SECTION 9. SOLE SOURCE PROCUREMENT A contract may be awarded without competition when there is only one practicably available source. A written determination is required. SECTION 10. EMERGENCY PROCUREMENTS Emergency procurements may be made when there is an immediate threat to: • Public health • Public safety • Essential services Competition shall be obtained as practicable. A written determination shall be submitted to the City Administrator. SECTION 11. EXEMPTIONS FROM COMPETITIVE PROCUREMENT The following are exempt: • Advertising and public notices • Ammunition • Casual field labor • Cooperative purchasing agreements • Elections, court costs, and settlements • Emergency debris removal • Existing bid or contract for like supplies, services, or construction • Grant-required vendor selections • Holiday Decorations • Insurance • Information technology systems and equipment • Intergovernmental agreements • Landscaping and landscaping materials • Legal, audit, and financial advisory services 20 -- 20 of 215 -- • OEM parts, vehicle parts, and warranty work • Professional services • Public art • Real property transactions • Rental of land, building, and equipment • Repair, maintenance, remodeling, renovation, construction or demolition of a single project not involving an increase in size and type of existing facility • Safety shoes and other personal protective equipment • State/Federal surplus or auction • Software, software licenses and subscriptions • Training, travel, conferences, and memberships • Used vehicles, equipment and surplus property • Utilities and regulated services SECTION 12. COOPERATIVE PURCHASING The City may purchase from: • State contracts • Other governmental contracts • National cooperative purchasing programs Without further competition. SECTION 13. PREQUALIFICATION The City may prequalify vendors for particular types of work. SECTION 14. BONDS FOR CONSTRUCTION Bid, performance, and payment bonds shall be required as determined necessary and in accordance with South Carolina law. SECTION 15. LOCAL VENDOR PREFERENCE The City of Conway shall give qualified local vendors (those with a physical business location in the city for at least twelve months and a valid city business license) a five percent bid evaluation preference on contracts of $10,000 or more, with the option to match the lowest bid when applicable, except where prohibited by funding requirements, cooperative agreements, bond restrictions, emergencies, or other city-approved waivers. SECTION 16. PROTEST PROCEDURE Any actual or prospective bidder may protest a solicitation or award by submitting a written protest within fourteen (14) days. 21 -- 21 of 215 -- SECTION 17. SURPLUS PROPERTY The Purchasing Agent may transfer, trade, or sell surplus property. All proceeds shall be deposited in the appropriate City fund. SECTION 18. FEDERAL AND STATE FUNDING When procurement involves federal or state funds, the applicable funding requirements shall control. SECTION 19. JOINT PROJECTS The City may participate in joint procurement and construction projects with other public entities when determined to be in the City’s best interest. SECTION 20. SEVERABILITY If any part of this ordinance is held invalid, the remainder shall remain in effect. SECTION 21. The applicant applied for a business license to sell and display heavy equipment. At the time of application, the UDO did not specifically define or list “heavy equipment sales and service” as a use. As such, the request was evaluated based on similar uses, including storage/shed sales and manufactured home sales, which are permitted only in the Light and Heavy Industrial zoning districts. Based on this comparison, the business license was only partially approved for sales of accessories / parts, with the condition that full heavy equipment sales, service, and repair operations would not occur on this site. Subsequently, the UDO was amended to define “heavy equipment” and establish “heavy equipment sales and service” as a specific use. That use is now permitted within industrial districts, providing clear policy direction regarding its appropriate location. Heavy equipment sales operations typically involve: • Large machinery (earth moving equipment) stored outdoors • Equipment loading and unloading / staging • Truck Traffic and deliveries • Repair and servicing activities These characteristics align more closely with industrial uses than with the Highway Commercial (HC) district. The HC district is intended to support: • Customer-oriented businesses • Clean, visible commercial activity • A consistent and attractive corridor environment The Highway Commercial (HC) district is not intended to accommodate outdoor industrial storage, heavy equipment display, or repair operations involving large machinery. 24 -- 24 of 215 -- STAFF REPORT Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-01 (E) Section 3.2.14 of the UDO establishes the Heavy Industrial (HI) district as the City’s most intensive industrial zoning classification, intended to accommodate uses such as: • Large-scale manufacturing • Processing operations • Heavy equipment storage and distribution • Uses with significant noise, traffic, or visual impacts SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: Adjacent properties are zoning Highway Commercial (HC), including: • Waste Management (sanitation service company) • Property owned by the applicant While zoned HC, some nearby uses exhibit operational characteristics more consistent with industrial activity. Additionally, properties across Hwy 378 include industrial zoning and properties within Horry County’s jurisdiction zoned, zoned Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA). COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The Future Land Use Map identifies the property as Highway Commercial. Per Section 3.2.10 of the UDO, HC district is intended to: • Serve automobile-oriented commercial activities • Provide corridor compatibility • Reduce traffic congestion • Enhance the aesthetic atmosphere of the City STAFF ANALYSIS: The City’s UDO is permissive in nature, meaning uses are allowed only where they are expressly listed. When a use is not specifically listed, it must be evaluated based on similarity to established use categories. Based on its operational characteristics, heavy equipment sales are most consistent with industrial uses, which are permitted only within industrial zoning districts. Therefore, this use is not appropriate withing the HC district. The requested rezoning to Heavy Industrial (HI) presents a broader policy consideration for Planning Commission and City Council, specifically: • Whether the corridor segment is transitioning toward industrial character; or • Whether maintaining Highway Commercial zoning along Hwy 378 remains the City’s long-term policy objective for this corridor. Additionally, the subject property is located within a major corridor subject to the Gateway Corridor Overlay, 25 -- 25 of 215 -- STAFF REPORT Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-01 (E) which is intended to promote coordinated development patterns and maintain the visual quality of entryways into the City. Approval of Heavy Industrial zoning may introduce a level of intensity that is inconsistent with these objectives and could establish precedent for similar rezonings along the corridor. Suitability of Light Industrial (LI): While the subject property is currently zoned Highway Commercial, the surrounding area includes a mix of uses that exhibit industrial characteristics, including equipment storage, contractor-type operations, and service-related activities. In addition, the subject property has historically functioned in a manner more consistent with industrial-type uses than with traditional corridor-oriented commercial development. The Light Industrial (LI) district is intended to accommodate industrial uses that are lower in intensity and more controlled in nature than those permitted in the Heavy Industrial district. LI zoning allows for: • Production, storage, and distribution activities • Industrial uses with limited impacts • Compatibility with transitional and mixed-use areas The operational characteristics of the proposed use – including outdoor equipment storage, limited customer activity, and associated vehicle traffic- are more consistent with industrial land uses and align more closely with the intent of the LI district. Rezoning to LI would: • allow the proposed use • reflect the existing development pattern in the immediate area • maintain a lower intensity than Heavy Industrial, and • provide a more compatible transition between industrial-type uses and the broader corridor. Based on the surrounding development pattern, the industrial characteristics of nearby uses, and the functional history of the subject property, the Light Industrial (LI) district may be a more appropriate zoning classification in lieu of Heavy Industrial (HI). The LI district would allow the proposed use while maintaining a lower intensity and reducing potential impacts to the Hwy 378 corridor. ISSUE: Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-01 (S) to Amend Article 5 – Supplemental and Accessory Uses, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding targeted grazing. BACKGROUND: Following multiple flood events, the City acquired numerous properties through the FEMA buyout program. These parcels, along with other vacant or difficult to maintain City-owned properties, require ongoing vegetation management to prevent overgrowth, improve neighborhood appearance, and reduce maintenance costs. Traditional mowing and clearing methods can be costly, labor intensive, and in some locations, impractical due to terrain or limited site access. An alternative approach used successfully in other communities is targeted grazing, where utilizes livestock - typically goats – to naturally manage vegetation, including brush, invasive species, and dense overgrowth. This method is environmentally friendly, reduces reliance on fuel-powered equipment and chemical herbicides, and allows for maintenance of areas that are otherwise difficult to access with conventional machinery. Targeted grazing has also demonstrated effectiveness in controlling invasive plant species and promoting long-term land health. Locally, residents may recall that Santee Cooper previously utilized goats for vegetation management along Hwy 501 in front of the Grainger plant. That effort demonstrated that managed grazing can be both practical and well received within the community. Similar programs have been implemented nationwide as a cost- effective and sustainable land management strategy. In addition to operational benefits, targeted grazing can serve as a visible example of the City’s commitment to sustainable and innovative practices. These programs often generate positive community engagement and provide educational opportunities related to environmental stewardship. From an operational standpoint, the City would lease qualifying parcels to a professional grazing service provider. The provider would be responsible for animal care, temporary fencing, transportation, and onsite supervision, while the City benefits from reduced maintenance costs and improved property conditions. The proposed amendment introduces a provision to Sec. 5.2.5 – Non-commercial Keeping of Livestock or Fowl, to allow and regulate targeted grazing strictly as a vegetation management tool on city-owned or city- controlled properties. A definition of targeted grazing was incorporated into Article 2 – Definitions in a previous text amendment. 107 -- 107 of 215 -- PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing and recommended approval of the proposed amendments at their May 7, 2026 meeting. First reading of Ordinance # ZA2026-06-01 (E), to rezone approximately 5.28+/- acres of property located at 2578 HWY 378 from the Highway Commercial (HC) district to the Heavy Industrial (HI) district (PIN 337-10-03-0010). Hucks stated that the applicant is requesting to rezone the property in order to conduct heavy equipment sales and service operations on the site. The property has been zoned Highway Commercial since annexation into the City in 2001. The request originated after the applicant applied for a business license associated with heavy equipment sales and display. At the time, the UDO did not 119 -- 119 of 215 -- May 18, 2026 5 specifically define or list ‘heavy equipment sales and service’ as a use category. Because the UDO is permissive in nature, staff had to evaluate the request based on the most similar existing use classifications within the ordinance. Hucks said that permissive in nature means that uses are only allowed where they are specifically listed within the ordinance. If a use is not listed, staff cannot simply assume it’s allowed. Instead, staff have evaluated it based on similar uses and the intent of the zoning district. In this case, staff determined that the operational characteristics of the heavy equipment sales, including outdoor equipment storage and display, loading and unloading activities, truck traffic, and repair or servicing functions, are more consistent with industrial uses than with traditional highway commercial uses. The Highway Commercial district is intended to support customer- oriented businesses, visible commercial activity, and an attractive corridor environment. It is not intended to accommodate outdoor industrial storage, heavy equipment display, or repair operations involving large machinery. As part of a recent, broader amendment to the UDO, heavy equipment sales and service were specifically defined and identified in the Use Table section of the UDO, which establishes where the use is permitted. Hucks said that under the current ordinance, the use is now permitted within the Light Industrial and Heavy Industrial zoning districts as a supplemental use. The broader policy question is whether this corridor segment should transition toward a heavier industrial character through HI zoning, or whether a lower-intensity industrial classification would be more appropriate given the surrounding context and long-term corridor objectives. Staff’s concern with the HI district along Hwy 378 is this corridor, as with the other major corridors throughout the city, are within the Gateway Corridor Overlay. This overlay is intended to maintain the visual quality and coordinated development pattern of major entryways into the city. Hucks said that the Heavy Industrial zoning is the city’s most intrusive industrial district and permits a much broader range of industrial activities than is currently being proposed. While the proposed heavy equipment sales use may be appropriate within the Light or Heavy Industrial district, staff’s primary concern is not the business itself, but rather the Heavy Industrial zoning classification and the full range of uses that could occur on the property in the future. Hucks stated that zoning runs with the land, not with the property owner. The Light Industrial district is intended for lower-intensity industrial and service- related activities, including contractor operations, warehousing, equipment-related uses, and limited outdoor storage, while Heavy Industrial is intended for larger-scale manufacturing, processing, heavy distributions, and more intensive industrial activity. Hucks said that staff also recognized that the immediate area contains several uses that exhibit industrial-type characteristics, including contractor type operations, equipment storage, sanitation related services, and properties across Hwy 378 within the County contain similar heavy equipment sales operations. For that reason, staff concluded that the Light Industrial district represents a more balanced approach. It would allow the proposed use while maintaining a lower-intensity classification along the corridor. Additionally, as part of the Comprehensive Plan update, staff intend to further evaluate and identify appropriate industrial nodes or activity areas throughout the city based on existing development patterns and long-term land use compatibility. Staff believes that this area 120 -- 120 of 215 -- May 18, 2026 6 exhibits characteristics supportive of lower-intensity industrial zoning, but not necessarily the broader range of uses that would be permitted in Heavy Industrial. Hucks said that Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the proposed zoning and recommended approval of the Light Industrial district as well at their May 7 meeting. Based on the surrounding development pattern and the operational characteristics of the proposed use, staff also recommended approval of the rezoning to Light Industrial. The proposed ordinance does NOT establish a residential or agricultural livestock use, nor does it change existing residential regulations on private noncommercial keeping of livestock or fowl in residential zoning districts. It authorizes a limited municipal maintenance activity on City-owned or City-controlled property for vegetation management purposes only. The livestock are temporary, professionally managed, and accessory to a governmental maintenance function, similar to how the city may use specialized equipment or contractors for drainage maintenance, stormwater management, or sidewalk improvements. The use of targeted grazing provides the City with an additional tool to manage difficult properties in a more environmentally sustainable and potentially more cost-effective manner while also supporting vegetation control in areas where conventional maintenance methods may not be practical. First reading of Ordinance # ZA2026-06-01 (T), to amend Article 10 – Subdivision and land development of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to the Park and Open Space Dedication. The proposed amendment would establish new standards to calculate the fee-in-lieu of open space mitigation in the City of Conway. Hucks stated that this amendment to the UDO is regarding fee-in-lieu process for required park and open space dedication associated with major residential developments. Currently, when a development does not provide all or a portion of the required open space onsite, the ordinance allows the developer to request to pay a fee-in-lieu of providing that open space. Under the existing ordinance, which has been in effect since the original adoption of the UDO in 2011, the fee is calculated using an appraisal of the property as if the development were already completed according to the submitted plans. This appraisal-based method has created several recurring issues for staff, applicants, and Planning Commission. First, because the calculation relies on hypothetical post-development appraisals, there can be significant variability in how the fee is determined from project to project. Staff have also encountered situations where appraisers themselves expressed concern or confusion with providing valuations based on future developed conditions that do not yet exist. Second, the current process requires multiple levels of review, including the Technical Review Committee, Planning Commission, and City Council approval, which increases review time and creates uncertainty for applicants regarding overall costs early in the process. Finally, the existing methodology can disproportionately impact certain types of projects, particularly infill or smaller-scale developments, where higher land values can produce substantially higher fee-in-lieu amounts that may not necessarily correlate with the actual cost of providing open space improvements. One example of this is the University Suites expansion located on Technology Blvd, in which the applicant requested to pay a fee in lieu of providing open space, but also a reduction in the amount, requiring a recommendation by Planning Commission and final approval from Council. Before Planning Commission could even consider the reduced fee in lieu amount, they first had to consider a design modification in which the applicant requested a modification from the way in which the fee in lieu was determined. Hucks said that in response to these concerns, staff evaluated 3 different alternatives which were presented to Planning Commission. PC ultimately recommended approval of what is identified as Option 1. Under option 1, the appraisal-based calculation would be replaced with a standardized flat fee structure based on deficiencies in required active and passive open space. The Unified Development Ordinance currently requires that 25% of required open space amount be active open space – such as playgrounds, amenity areas, pools or athletic courts – with the remainder allowed as passive open space. Because active open space generally involves substantially higher construction and maintenance costs than passive open space, the proposed amendment establishes 2 different flat fee amounts: (1) $12 per sq. ft. for deficiencies in active open space; and (2) $8 per sq. ft. for deficiencies 124 -- 124 of 215 -- May 18, 2026 10 in passive open space. The amounts were determined based on review of estimated development costs associated with active and passive open space improvements. Hucks said that another important component of the amendment is the review process. Under the proposed structure, if an applicant utilizes the standard fee-in-lieu structure established in the ordinance, Planning Commission may approve the fee in lieu administratively as part of the development review process. However, if the applicant proposes an alternative method, such as a reduces fee, land donation, conservation easement, or offsite improvement, that request would still require a recommendation from Planning Commission and final approval from City Council. Staff evaluated other alternatives, ranging from a fully discretionary Council review process to a single flat fee structure. Planning Commission recommended Option 1 because it represents the best balance between predictability, administrative efficiency, and retaining council oversight where flexibility or deviations are requested. Hucks emphasized that this amendment is not intended to reduce or waive the City’s open space requirements – in fact, it likely increases the fee in lieu amounts in most situations. The purpose of the amendment is to standardize the calculation methodology and create greater predictability early in the development review process. The ordinance still allows alternative compliance proposals or modified fee requests, but those situations would continue to require final approval from City Council. In short, the requirements for open space are not changing...what is changing is the method by which the fee in lieu is calculated and administered. Hucks said that staff also recommended approval of Option 1, as recommended by Planning Commission. White asked what the purpose of open space was. Hucks explained. Goldfinch asked if council would have flexibility. Hucks said yes, any deviations would come to council for approval.
