ISSUE: Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-01 (T) to amend Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to the Park and Open Space dedication requirements. The proposed amendment would establish new standards to calculate the fee in lieu of open space mitigation in the City of Conway. BACKGROUND: This text amendment was initiated in response to repeated design modification requests for major residential developments related with the fee-in-lieu of required open space dedication. Through this process, staff identified a need to standardize the method for calculating the fee in lieu in order to improve consistency, predictability, and administrative efficiency. Alternative approaches to amending Article 10, Sec. 10.3.9 have been provided in the packet. Staff recommends Option 1, as described herein. Currently, the fee-in-lieu amount is calculated based on an applicant-provided appraisal of the subject property. The applicant is required to submit a written appraisal estimating the market value of the land as if the proposed development were completed in accordance with the submitted plans. This value is then divided by the total square footage of the site to determine a per-square-foot value, which is multiplied by the amount of required open space not being provided. An additional 25% is applied to the resulting figure to establish the final fee amount. Following this calculation, the proposed fee must be presented to the Planning Commission for recommendation and subsequently approved by City Council prior to preliminary plan approval. ANALYSIS: This current fee-in-lieu process presents several challenges. First, because the calculation relies on an applicant-provided appraisal based on a hypothetical post- development condition, there is inherent variability in how market value is determined. This can result in inconsistent fee calculations across similar projects and introduce a level of subjectivity into what is intended to be a standardized requirement. Second, the current process requires multiple levels of review, including Technical Review Committee (TRC), Planning Commission, and City Council approval, prior to preliminary plan approval. This multi- step process increases review time and creates uncertainty for applicants, particularly in the early stages of development when project feasibility is being evaluated. 154 -- 154 of 215 -- Finally, the existing method can disproportionately impact certain types of development, including infill or smaller-scale projects, where higher appraised land values may result in significantly higher fee-in-lieu amounts relative to project scale. PROPOSED AMENDMENT: The proposed amendment replaces the existing appraisal-based methodology with a standardized, flat fee per square foot for deficiencies in required open space. Under the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), a minimum of 25% of required open space must be provided as active open space, with the remaining portion as passive open space. Active open space, such as amenity centers, pools, playgrounds, and athletic courts, typically involves significantly higher development and construction costs than passive open space areas. As such, the proposed amendment establishes a differentiated fee structure. Based on research of estimated costs associated with the development of both active and passive open space amenities (see supporting materials in the packet), staff recommends the following rates: • Active Open Space: $12.00 per square foot for any deficiency in required active open space • Passive Open Space: $8.00 per square foot for any deficiency in required passive open space In addition to revising the fee calculation methodology, the amendment modifies the review process for fee- in-lieu requests. Under the proposed structure: • The Planning Commission may approve fee-in-lieu requests administratively when the applicant utilizes the prescribed fee structure established in the Ordinance; and • If the applicant proposes an alternative compliance method – such as a modified fee amount, conservation easement, land donation, or offsite improvement, PC shall forward a recommendation to City Council, which will retain final decision-making authority. This approach streamlines the review process for standard applications while preserving City Council oversight for requests involving discretion or deviation from the established procedures. SUMMARY: The proposed amendment to Sec. 10.3.9(D) is intended to: • Establish a consistent and predictable fee calculation method • Reduce subjectivity associated with appraisal-based valuations • Improve administrative efficiency by streamlining the review process • Provide greater cost certainty for applicants early on in the development process • Maintain flexibility for alternative compliance methods through City Council review 155 -- 155 of 215 -- ADDED LANGUAGE (5/22/2026): The proposed changes to the open space ordinance are not intended to make it easier to avoid providing open space, and in many cases – particularly for larger developments – the proposed flat fee structure could actually result in a higher fee-in-lieu amount than what may have been calculated under the previous appraisal-based methodology. As a result, the amendment may actually encourage more onsite open space construction rather than less because developers may determine that providing the required open amenities onsite is more practical or cost effective than paying the fee in lieu. So this amendment is not reducing the City’s open space standards. In many cases, it may strengthen the incentive to actually construct open space improvements within the development itself. The amendment primarily changes the predictability and consistency of the calculation method, not the requirement for open space itself. ORDINANCE: N/A AGENDA SECTION: Consideration ISSUE: Consideration of a request for a waiver of sidewalk requirements for the Village at Crabtree, a proposed multi-family development containing 3 buildings with 117 units, located on El Bethel Road & Campton Loop. APPLICANT(S): Alex Frazier, TWG Development & Venture Engineering PIN(s): 337-06-04-0002 CURRENT ZONING: High Density Residential (R-3) BACKGROUND: Sec. 7.1.2, Complete Streets, of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) requires sidewalks to be constructed along the frontage of all properties abutting arterial or local non-residential streets. These sidewalks are required to be a minimum of five (5) feet in width, and a minimum of four (4) inches in thickness. Based on these requirements, approximately 566 linear feet (LF) of sidewalk would be required along the frontage of this proposed development on El Bethel Road and a portion of Campton Loop. The applicant has requested a waiver of the sidewalk installation requirement, pursuant to Sec. 7.1.2 of the UDO, sidewalk waivers may only be granted by City Council when there is no foreseeable pedestrian connectivity or public benefit associated with the installation of the sidewalk. Should Council approve the waiver request, the applicant would still be required to provide a payment in lieu of sidewalk construction equal to the estimated cost of installation, including associated infrastructure improvements. The payment would be utilized by the City toward future pedestrian, bikeway, and pathway improvements. Using the City’s current estimated construction cost of $33.00 per linear foot for labor, construction, grading, and clearing, the estimated payment-in-lieu of construction for the required sidewalk improvements would be $18,678.00. Staff notes that City Council has previously denied similar sidewalk waiver requests in this immediate area, including: • the adjacent Spring Oaks subdivision in 2021; and • Whittemore Park Middle School in 2022. In addition, sidewalks already exists along portions of nearby developments, including the Crabtree Commons multifamily development located on El Bethel Rd. 189 -- 189 of 215 -- STAFF REPORT Sidewalk Waiver Request – Village at Crabtree MF Although portions of the surrounding corridor remain undeveloped and do not yet contain sidewalks, staff believes the area demonstrates clear foreseeable pedestrian connectivity due to: • the presence of existing residential subdivisions; • nearby multifamily residential developments; • the proximity of Whittemore Park Middle School; • nearby commercial destinations, including Walmart and associated retail uses; and • the continued urbanization and residential growth occurring along the El Bethel Road corridor. Staff further notes that multifamily residential developments, often generate higher levels of pedestrian activity and reliance on walking connectivity to nearby schools, services, retail areas, and transit opportunities. As such, the installation of sidewalks along this corridor is consistent with the intent of the City’s Complete Streets requirements and the long-term development of a connected pedestrian network. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Staff continues to support the installation of sidewalks where required by the City’s Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) and recommends denial of the requested sidewalk waiver. The proposed development is located within an area where pedestrian activity currently exists and is continued to develop. Requiring sidewalk installation would be consistent with prior Council actions involving nearby developments and would further the City’s Complete Streets objectives by helping eliminate gaps in the pedestrian network along El Bethel Rd. Should Council determine that a waiver is appropriate, staff recommends that the applicant be required to provide the payment in lieu amount of $18,678.00 in accordance with Sec. 7.1.2 of the UDO. 190 -- 190 of 215 -- Village at Crabtree Sidewalk Waiver (red lines indicate where a sidewalk currently exist) Whittemore Park Middle School Crabtree Commons Apt.’s Spring Oaks Subdivision Oakbrook 191 -- 191 of 215 -- Parcel 2 n/f SCDOT C/O Maintenance Office Pin # 337-06-04-0001 Deed Book 3621, Page 852. Discussion of an amendment to the City of Conway Comprehensive Plan 2035, to amend the Future Land Use Map, for property located on Sycamore Street (PIN 368- 01-03-0072). Hucks stated that the applicant is seeking this amendment in conjunction with a rezoning request that would allow for development of townhomes on the property. Under -- 3 of 9 -- June 1, 2026 4 the City’s unified development ordinance, townhomes require a minimum zoning designation of medium-density residential, or R-2, and because the property is currently designated and zoned R-1, Low/Medium-Density Residential, both a future land use map amendment to the City’s Comprehensive Plan and a rezoning is necessary. The property is currently vacant and surrounded by properties zoned R-1 and developed primarily with detached single-family homes. While there are some R-2 zoned properties in the general area, there are none directly adjacent to this site. The primary question before Planning Commission and City Council is whether Medium-Density Residential is an appropriate future land use designation for this property, given its size and the surrounding pattern of single-family detached residential development, or whether the request would represent an isolated change that is inconsistent with the surrounding area. Hucks said that Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on this request as well as the request to rezone the property at their June 4 meeting, and their recommendation will be forwarded to City Council for consideration. E. Discussion of a request to rezone an approximate 10 +/- acre portion of 110 +/- acres of property located on Cultra Rd and Oak Street and adjacent to Conway Christian School (PIN: 325-00-00-0011), from the City of Conway Medium-Density Residential (R-2) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district. Hucks stated that the applicant proposes to subdivide a 10-acre portion from a larger tract located along Cultra Road and Oak Street and convey that property to Conway Christian School. The 10-acre portion is currently zoned Medium-Density Residential (R-2), while the adjacent Conway Christian School property is zoned R-1, Low/Medium-Density Residential. In order to combine the properties into a single parcel, the applicant proposes to rezone this 10-acre portion to R-1 so that the combined property has a consistent zoning classification, as split-zoning of parcels is generally prohibited. You may recall this property being annexed and rezoned within the last year, and it contains a split-zoning of R-2 and Conservation Preservation due to the environmentally sensitive and flood-prone areas. The area zoned Conservation Preservation will remain unchanged. The rezoning would apply only to the 10-acre area that is proposed to be conveyed to the school. The request is primarily administrative in nature. It does not increase density, expand development rights, or introduce a new land use, but rather reduces the intensity of the designation from R-2 to R-1 and creates consistency with the zoning of the existing school campus. Hucks said that Planning Commission will hold the public hearing on this request at their June 4 meeting and their recommendation will be forwarded to Council for consideration. SECOND/FINAL READING Final reading of Ordinance # ZA2026-06-01 (T), to amend Article 10 – Subdivision and land development of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to the Park and Open Space Dedication. The proposed amendment would establish new standards to calculate the fee-in-lieu of open space mitigation in the City of Conway. Hucks stated that this proposed amendment received first reading at the May 18 Council meeting. Staff wanted to provide additional clarification regarding what this amendment changes and what remains unchanged. The requirements for open space are not changing. The amount of open space -- 4 of 9 -- June 1, 2026 5 required by the ordinance remains the same, the circumstances under which the fee-in-lieu may be used remains the same, and City Council retains authority to review alternatives to providing open space, including reduced fee-in-lieu amounts. What the amendment changes is the method used to calculate the fee in lieu when the fee in lieu is either required by the ordinance or requested by a developer in lieu of providing all or a portion of the required open space. Currently, the fee-in-lieu amount is based on an appraisal of the property as if the development were already completed. Because that methodology relies on a hypothetical future condition, the resulting fee can vary significantly from project to project and often cannot be determined early in the development review process. Staff have also found that these appraisals can introduce a level of subjectivity and inconsistency into what is intended to be a standardized requirement. Hucks then showed a slide giving an example of the calculations under the current ordinance versus under the proposed ordinance. Hucks said that an important point to note is that this amendment is not necessarily reducing fee- in-lieu amounts. In many cases, particularly for larger developments, the proposed fee structure could actually result in a higher fee than what may have been calculated under the current method. As a result, the amendment may encourage more onsite open space construction because developers may determine that provided the required amenities is more practical or cost-effective than paying the fee in lieu. The amendment does modify the review process. Currently, fee-in-lieu requests require review by the TRC, Planning Commission and City Council. Under the proposed amendment, if the applicant utilizes the standard fee structure that is proposed, Planning Commission may approve the request to pay the fee in lieu as part of the development review process. However, if the applicant proposes a reduced fee, land donation, offsite improvement, or other alternative compliance method, Planning Commission would review and provide a recommendation, and City Council would retain final decision-making authority. Hucks stated that staff continues to recommend approval. There was some discussion regarding requirements for active and passive open space. Motion: Hardwick made a motion, seconded by Blain to approve final reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-01 (T) amending Article 10 of the UDO regarding revisions to the Park and Open Space Dedication. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. FIRST READING: A. First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-08-03 (A), to annex approximately 0.58+/- acres of property located at 921 Buccaneers Cove (PIN 382-13-01-0007). Hucks stated that this property contains an existing single-family residence within the Buccaneer’s Cove subdivision. Annexation is being requested to facilitate a name change on the City’s utility service account. Restrictive Covenants were recorded on May 1 of this year. Properties located adjacent to and behind the subject property are within the City limits, making this property contiguous. The requesting zoning of R-1 or Low/Medium-Density Residential is consistent with the City’s future land use map as well as the other properties in the Buccaneer’s Cove subdivision that have been annexed. -- 5 of 9 -- June 1, 2026 6 If annexation is approved, Planning Commission will hold the public hearing on the proposed zoning upon annexation at their July 9 meeting. Hucks said that staff recommends approval of first reading. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Butler to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-08-03 (A) annexing 921 Buccaneers Cove. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (I), to annex approximately 71.82+/- acres of property located behind property commonly referred to as “Lake Busbee” and adjacent to New Road (PIN 368-00-00-0019). (Hucks) Hucks stated that this property was acquired by the City in 2025 as part of the Lake Busbee and former Grainger steam plant acquisition. During subsequent platting activity, this portion of the tract appears to have been subdivided from the parent parcel, resulting in the property not appearing within the City or County’s zoning jurisdiction on GIS mapping. The property appears to be heavily wooded, containing a Santee-Cooper transmission line easement, and is substantially encumbered by flood-prone and environmentally sensitive areas. The surrounding Lake Busbee and adjacent City-owned parcels were annexed and/or rezoned in 2025 to either Conservation Preservation or the Waccamaw Riverfront District. This request would annex the property and assign the Conservation Preservation zoning, consistent with the Future Land Use Map and the City’s previous actions for the surrounding area. Hucks said that if first reading is approved, Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on the proposed zoning at their June 4 meeting. Staff recommends approval of first reading. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Helms to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (I) annexing the property located behind Lake Busbee and adjacent to New Road. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. CONSIDERATION: A. Consideration of a request for a waiver of sidewalk requirements for the Village at Crabtree, a proposed multi-family development containing 3 buildings with 117 units, located on El Bethel Rd & Campton Loop (PIN 337-06-04-0002). Hucks stated that this request is for a fee-in-lieu of the installation of sidewalks associated with the proposed Village at Crabtree development located on El Bethel Rd. Under the City’s Complete Streets Ordinance, approximately 566 linear feet of sidewalk would be required to be installed along the project’s frontage. The applicant has requested a waiver of this requirement. Under the Unified Development Ordinance, City Council may grant a sidewalk waiver when there is no foreseeable pedestrian connectivity or public benefit associated with the installation of sidewalks. If granted, the applicant is required to pay the fee in lieu of installation of sidewalks, which is equal to the cost of installing the sidewalk. Hucks said that staff does not believe the standard for a fee-in-lieu of the installation of sidewalk has been met in this case. The proposed development is located within an area that contains existing residential subdivisions, nearby multifamily developments, and -- 6 of 9 -- June 1, 2026 7 Whittemore Park Middle School; all of which were required to install sidewalks in conjunction with development of those properties. In fact, sidewalk waivers were denied for the Spring Oaks subdivision in 2021 and Whittemore Park Middle School in 2022. Because there is a foreseeable pedestrian connectivity and a clear public benefit associated with completing the sidewalk network along El Bethel Rd, staff recommends disapproval of the request and supports installation of the required sidewalks. Hucks said that should Council determine a waiver is appropriate, the applicant would be required to provide a payment in lieu of construction in the amount of $18,678, consistent with the requirements of the UDO. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Hardwick to deny the request for a waiver of sidewalk requirements for the Village at Crabtree. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. Consideration of a request for a waiver of sidewalk requirements for Long HVAC, located at 3191 Hwy 378 (PIN 370-04-01-0002). Hucks stated that this request is for property on Hwy 378, Long’s HVAC. Under the UDO, approximately 265 linear feet of sidewalk would be required along the property’s frontage. The applicant has requested a waiver of installation based on 2 primary factors: (1) Future roadway widening improvements associated with the Brookhaven Planned Development would impact any sidewalks installed today and would require reconstruction as part of those improvements; (2) Staff does not believe there is foreseeable pedestrian activity in the immediate area. The surrounding properties, including the Brookhaven Planned Development, airport frontage areas, and properties across Hwy 378, do not contain sidewalks or an interconnected pedestrian network. As a result, the proposed sidewalk would function as an isolated segment with no meaningful connections at either end. Hucks said that because the ordinance allows waivers when there is no foreseeable pedestrian connectivity or public benefit, staff supports the requested waiver and recommends approval of the fee-in-lieu of sidewalk installation in the amount of $8,745. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Helms to approve the request for a waiver of sidewalk requirements for 3191 Highway 378. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. C. Deferred - Consideration of approval of a special event – The Gathering on the Green Sunday Fundays on various Sundays from May – September, 2026. Rogers said that this request came before council at last meeting and the applicant is requesting to hold a special event on Sundays from June through September. Rogers stated that the questions that came from council last time were the time frame from 12-8 p.m. during the summer months, how buskers would work, the name of the event, and the competition of other businesses in the area. Thomas Festa, applicant was present to address concerns. Festa introduced Chris Lawson, Lemons and Dough food truck and said that Lawson is helping him organize the event. Fester stated that the event name would just be called Sunday Funday and the event time would be changed and held from 3-8 p.m. Festa said that he had been in contact with other businesses to see if they would want to be open for this event and he then talked about his -- 7 of 9 -- June 1, 2026 8 business. Festa said that they choose to have buskers due to vendors not having to pay for the musicians. There was more discussion regarding buskers, the type of event, heat safety, and police attendance. Helms asked if the September event could be cancelled since it is so close to the Halloween events in October. Festa said they would strike the September event. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Blain to approve the special event permit as presented. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. PUBLIC INPUT: − Judy Gerrald spoke requesting the removal of Canadian geese in the Downtown area. CITY ADMINISTRATOR’S REPORT: Emrick informed Council of the following : • The Planning Department is working on the city’s Comprehensive Plan rewrite. As part of that, the Planning Commission creates a Steering Committee to help guide the process. If any of council have specific recommendations to sit on the Steering Committee to send to the Planning Commission, please let Emrick know by the end of the week. • Mark June 23rd on your calendar for the ribbon cutting for Cypress Basin, located at 1604 Sherwood Drive. • A couple of playground updates. Work has begun building the new playground at Jamestown across from the old Jamestown Baptist Church. This is a new park location in an area that the city has been looking to add a facility for a long time. The fencing around the donated playground at the Sports and Fitness Center next to Lady Bug Park is complete. • The Dog Park has been closed for a few days so the new archway entrance can be installed and several shade trees can be planted. These projects are funded by a generous bequest from Dave and Caroly Hoyt, residents of Conway who both passed away several years ago but wanted to leave a legacy for the City. • Today, the city accepted the final delivery of two new fire engines. These trucks were originally ordered nearly three years ago and were custom fitted to the city’s needs. There is still some equipment that needs to be installed to put them into action but expect to see them on the road soon. • The Downtown Get Down Line Dancing will start on the Town Green this Friday and continue throughout the summer. • Coastal’s baseball season ended abruptly over the weekend in Tallahassee. We are spoiled by the success that we have enjoyed for the last several years, but the accomplishments of this team, making the NCAA tournament year after year is a major feat, one that Clemson and USC are both envious of. So, congratulations to Coastal Carolina University Baseball for another fantastic season. • There are two Executive Session items as outlined on the agenda, but no workshop tonight. -- 8 of 9 -- -- 9 of 9 --

ISSUE: Final Reading of Ordinance #2026-05-18 (A) to amend Article I – Redevelopment Enhancement Incentive Program, of the City of Conway Municipal Code, which provides economic incentives to develop or expand commercial businesses in the City of Conway, to expand the geographic applicability of the incentive to commercially zoned properties fronting Mill Pond Road and Sixteenth Ave. BACKGROUND: City Council previously adopted the Redevelopment Enhancement Incentive program to encourage reinvestment and economic activity along key commercial corridors within the City. The incentive currently provides for reimbursement of 100 percent of capital recovery fees for qualifying new or expanding businesses located on designated corridors. The existing ordinance applies to commercially zoned properties fronting Hwy 378 (Wright Blvd) and Hwy 701 (Main St./Fourth Ave). The proposed amendment expands eligibility to include additional corridors – specifically Mill Pond Rd and Sixteenth (16th ) Ave. This amendment is being considered in response to anticipated and ongoing commercial development activity along these corridors, which are emerging as important areas for growth and redevelopment within the City. ANALYSIS: The proposed amendment is limited in scope and does not alter the structure, eligibility requirements, or administration of the incentive program. Instead, it expands the geographic boundary in which the incentive may be applied. Mill Pond Rd and Sixteenth Ave are both strategically located corridors that provide connectivity to established commercial areas and are experiencing increased development interest. Extending the incentive to these areas is intended to: • Promote continued economic investment and redevelopment in emerging commercial corridors; • Encourage new business establishment and expansion in areas where infrastructure and accessibility support growth; • Maintain consistency in how the City incentivizes development across similarly situated commercial corridors; and • Support broader economic development goals by leveraging private investment. 5 -- 5 of 220 -- All other provisions of the ordinance remains unchanged, including: • Requirement for City Council approval of eligibility; • Execution of a formal agreement prior to issuance of a Certificate of Occupancy; • Reimbursement procedures and timelines; and • The three-year expiration period unless renewed by Council. STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends approval of final reading of the ordinance amending Article I of the City’s Municipal Code, as presented. The proposed expansion aligns with the City’s ongoing efforts to support targeted economic development and encourages reinvestment along key commercial corridors experiencing growth. ATTACHMENTS: Ordinance #2025-05-18 (A) (as proposed to be amended) 6 -- 6 of 220 -- ORDINANCE #2026-05-18 (A) AMENDING TITLE 1, CHAPTER 5, ARTICLE I – REDEVELOPMENT ENHANCEMENT INCENTIVE, OF THE CITY OF CONWAY MUNICIPAL CODE OF ORDINANCES, TO EXPAND THE APPLICABILITY OF THE INCENTIVE PROGRAM WHEREAS, the City of Conway has adopted a Redevelopment Enhancement Incentive program to encourage economic investment, redevelopment, and business growth along key commercial corridors within the City; and WHEREAS, the program provides for the reimbursement of capital recovery fees for qualifying new or expanding businesses located on designated commercially zoned properties; and WHEREAS, City Council has identified additional commercial corridors, including Mill Pond Rd and Sixteenth (16th ) Ave, as areas experiencing increased development activity and having the potential for continued economic growth; and WHEREAS, expanding the applicability of the Redevelopment Enhancement Incentive program to include these corridors will promote consistent economic development policies and encourage reinvestment in strategically important areas of the City; and WHEREAS, pursuant to applicable law and City procedures, City Council held a duly advertised public hearing on the ordinance amendment and provided an opportunity for public comment prior to taking action; and WHEREAS, City Council finds that the proposed amendment is in the best interest of the public health, safety, and welfare of the citizens of Conway by supporting economic development and enhancing commercial opportunities within the City. Now, therefore be it ORDAINED, by the City Council of the City of Conway, South Carolina, in meeting duly assembled, that Title 1, Chapter 5, Article I – Redevelopment Enhancement Incentive, of the City of Conway Municipal Code of Ordinances, shall be amended as attached hereto; and be it further ORDAINED, that all ordinances or parts of ordinances inconsistent with this Ordinance are hereby repealed to the extent of such inconsistency. EFFECTIVE DATE: This ordinance shall become effective upon adoption by City Council. 7 -- 7 of 220 -- RATIFIED BY CITY COUNCIL, duly assembled, this 18 day of May 2026. This incentive applies to any person, firm, or corporation establishing a new business or expanding an existing business in a commercial property fronting Highway 378 (Wright Boulevard), or Highway 701 (Main Street/4th Avenue), Sixteenth Avenue (16th Avenue) or Mill Pond Road. These locations shall be defined as any property with a commercial zoning designation with frontage on Highway 378 (Wright Blvd), or Highway 701 (Main Street/4th Avenue), Sixteenth Avenue (16th Avenue) or Mill Pond Road as shown on the city's official zoning map. It is the responsibility of the person, firm or corporation applying for the incentive to demonstrate that they are a new or expanding business to be eligible. All eligibility is subject to review and approval by city council. Incentives: The city administrator, on behalf of the City of Conway, may reimburse any person, firm, or corporation 100 percent of capital recovery fees. Sec. 1-5-116 Reimbursement. Reimbursement shall be made within 60 days of receiving a reimbursement request form. Reimbursements shall be made only to the person, firm, or corporation who is the agreement holder. No partial reimbursements will be made. The applicant or business must be actively operating in the qualifying commercially zoned property fronting Highway 378 (Wright Boulevard), or Highway 701 (Main Street/4th Avenue), Sixteenth Avenue (16th Avenue) or Mill Pond Road to receive reimbursement under this article. Sec. 1-5-117 Expiration. The incentive offering shall expire on the third anniversary of the passing of final reading of this article unless renewed or otherwise amended by city council prior to expiration. Sec. 1-5-118 Agreement required. No reimbursement shall be made without an agreement signed by the interested person, firm or corporation and the City of Conway prepared in accordance with the terms outlined in this article. A signed agreement must be in place prior to the issuance of a certificate of occupancy (CO). No agreements may be applied retroactively. Sec. 1-5-119 Transferability. BACKGROUND: The parcel that contains the building that last housed G&H Cabinets has recently changed ownership and has the opportunity to have new life breathed into it. The new owners are applying for certification under the South Carolina Abandoned Buildings Revitalization Act and as such need a resolution of support from the City to confirm that certain buildings within the plaza have been unoccupied for a qualifying period of time. The attached Resolution will assist the new owners in the funding of the redevelopment of the site, with the hopes that high quality national retailers will be recruited to the plaza and fill a much- needed gap in the retail availability of goods for Conway residents. RECOMMENDATION Approval of the Resolution as attached. 11 -- 11 of 220 -- STATE OF SOUTH CAROLINA ) COUNTY OF HORRY ) R E S O L U T I O N CITY OF CONWAY ) A RESOLUTION CERTIFYING THE PROPERTY IDENTIFIED AS HORRY COUNTY PIN 338-00-00-0037, AS AN ABANDONED BUILDING SITE PURSUANT TO THE SOUTH CAROLINA ABANDONED BUILDINGS REVITALIZATION ACT, CODIFIED AT TITLE 12, CHAPTER 67 OF THE CODE OF LAWS OF SOUTH CAROLINA 1976, AS AMENDED; AND OTHER MATTERS RELATED THERETO. WHEREAS, the South Carolina Abandoned Buildings Revitalization Act (the “Act”), as codified at Title 12, Chapter 67 of the Code of Laws of South Carolina 1976, as amended, was enacted to create an incentive for the rehabilitation, renovation, and redevelopment of abandoned buildings located in South Carolina; and WHEREAS, the Act provides that restoration of abandoned buildings into productive assets for the communities in which they are located serves a public and corporate purpose and results in job opportunities; and WHEREAS, Section 12-67-140 of the Act provides that a taxpayer who rehabilitates an abandoned building is eligible either for a credit against certain income taxes, license fees, or premium taxes, or a credit against local real property taxes; and WHEREAS, RP Conway Mill Pond, LLC or an affiliate, successor, or assign thereof (the “Taxpayer”) intends to rehabilitate certain real property identified as Horry County Tax Map PIN 33800000037 and more fully described on Exhibit A attached hereto and made part hereof (individually, “Parcel”); and WHEREAS, the Parcel is located entirely within the City of Conway, South Carolina (the “City”); and WHEREAS, the Taxpayer has expressed a desire to claim South Carolina state income tax credits under the Act, which shall have no negative fiscal impact on the City; and WHEREAS, Section 12-67-160(A) of the Act provides that a taxpayer may apply to the City in which an abandoned building is located for a certification of the abandoned building site, and the taxpayer may conclusively rely upon that certification in determining the credits allowed; and WHEREAS, the City and the Taxpayer, after performing their diligence activities for each Parcel, have determined that each Parcel contains at least one “abandoned building” or portion of an “abandoned building” as defined in Section 12-67- 120(1) of the Act, and the geographic area of each Parcel is consistent with the term “building site” as defined in Section 12-67-120(2) of the Act; and 12 -- 12 of 220 -- WHEREAS, the Taxpayer has requested that the City certify each Parcel as an abandoned building site under Section 12-67-160(1) of the Act in order to facilitate Taxpayer’s claim for income tax credits; and WHEREAS, given that the claim for income tax credits will have no negative fiscal impact on the City and that certification would enhance the likelihood of restoring non- productive property in the City to productive use, it appears that each Parcel meets the requirements of the Act for certification. NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the City Council of the City of Conway in meeting duly assembled, as follows: Section 1. Each Parcel satisfies the criteria for an “abandoned building” as described by Section 12-67-120(1) of the Act, namely that it has been closed continuously to business or otherwise nonoperational for income producing purposes for more than five years, and the geographic area of the “building site” on each Parcel is consistent with Section 12-67-120(2) of the Act, namely that it consists of the abandoned building itself together with the parcel of land upon which it is located and other improvements located on the parcel, provided that the area of the building site is limited to the land upon which the abandoned building is located and the land immediately surrounding such building used for parking and other similar purposes directly related to the building's income producing use. Future re-platting or re-drawing of parcel lines referenced in this Resolution shall not affect the City’s findings contained herein. Section 2. The City hereby certifies that (i) the abandoned building site is an abandoned building as defined in Section 12-67-120(1) of the Act, and (ii) the geographic area of the abandoned building site is consistent with Section 12-67-120(2) of the Act. First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-15 (A) to amend Article 5 – Supplemental and Accessory Uses, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding requirements for mobile vending permits; specifically, to remove the cap on mobile vending permits and establishing revised administrative provisions. Hucks stated that last year Council adopted a cap of 20 mobile vending permits per year, which excluded those which had a franchise agreement with the City, those that were approved as part of a special event permit, and those that were also properly licensed dining establishments in the city limits. The original cap proposed by staff was 40, but Planning Commission recommended reducing the cap to 20; in which staff recommended approval of to Council, with the caveat that those exceptions just mentioned be carved out in the ordinance. Hucks said that Horry County has a limit of 50 mobile food vending permits annually (per Art. 9 – conditional uses, Sec. 913, B.3.f.), and Myrtle Beach limits theirs to 20 annually, so when Conway set the cap at 20, it was in line with what other jurisdictions were doing, but also based on our staffing capacity at the time. The City’s cap of 20 permits was established with consideration of the regional benchmarks, as well as local staffing capacity and operational constraints. The initial cap was driven by staff capacity and overall market balance. Staff has since learned that while those concerns are still valid – having a fixed number may not be the most effective way to address them, as it is a little too rigid. This amendment addresses those concerns, but instead of a fixed cap, the number of mobile vending permits to be issued annually will be determined administratively, based on the City’s capacity to effectively manage, inspect and enforce mobile vending operations, as well as the availability of suitable locations and considerations of public health, safety and welfare. Administrative procedures will be provided in the application packet for a mobile vending permit, and applicants will be required to acknowledge them as part of the process. 23 -- 23 of 220 -- May 4, 2026 9 That way the process is transparent and consistently applied. These procedures will also be available on the City’s website. Hucks stated that Planning Commission will still have to hold a public hearing on the amendment, which is set for their June meeting, but staff does recommend approval of the amendments to the mobile vending ordinance. If council approves first reading of the amendment, State law requires that zoning regulations be applied as adopted until formally amended; however, council could direct staff to process applications that have been received that are currently waitlisted in the interim. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by White to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-15 (A) removing the cap on mobile vending permits and establishing revised administrative provisions. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. ISSUE: First reading of Ordinance #2026-06-01 (D) to repeal and replace Purchasing Rules and Regulations BACKGROUND: The current purchasing rules have been amended multiple times over the years, resulting in a framework that is increasingly complex and difficult to navigate. The proposed update replaces the current, complex purchasing rules with a clearer and more consistent set of guidelines. In addition, purchasing thresholds are being increased, allowing staff to avoid unnecessary quotes for lower-value purchases and focus time and resources on higher-priority procurements, while maintaining appropriate oversight and accountability. In addition, staff is currently implementing procurement software to modernize the purchasing process by improving efficiency, transparency, and consistency across all departments. The online solicitation tool will expand the vendor audience, increasing competition and helping ensure the municipality receives the best value. RECOMMENDATION: Approve first reading as presented. 42 -- 42 of 220 -- ORDINANCE #2026-06-01 (D) AN ORDINANCE REPEALING ORDINANCE NO. 2022-06-20(H) AND ADOPTING REVISED PURCHASING RULES AND REGULATIONS WHEREAS, on June 20, 2022, Conway City Council adopted Purchasing Ordinance #2022- 06-20 (H); and WHEREAS, City Council desires to modernize the procurement process, increase efficiency, and maintain full compliance with the laws of the State of South Carolina governing political subdivisions; and WHEREAS, the adoption of updated procedures will promote open competition, transparency, and the best value in the expenditure of public funds; Therefore, be it ORDAINED, that all prior purchasing ordinances are repealed and the following Purchasing Rules and Regulations are adopted; and be it further ORDAINED, that, all ordinances or parts of ordinances in conflict herewith are, to the extent of the conflict, hereby repealed. White, Council Member ATTEST: Alicia Shelley, City Clerk First Reading: _______________ Final Reading: _______________ 43 -- 43 of 220 -- CITY OF CONWAY PURCHASING RULES AND REGULATIONS SECTION 1. PURPOSE The purpose of this regulation is to: • Provide a fair and equitable procurement system • Ensure the prudent expenditure of public funds • Obtain best value for the City • Provide full and open competition • Comply with the laws of the State of South Carolina SECTION 2. DEFINITIONS The terms “supplies”, “services”, “information technology”, and “construction” shall have their commonly accepted procurement meanings. SECTION 3. PURCHASING AUTHORITY The City Administrator shall serve as the Chief Procurement Officer and may delegate authority to a Procurement Director/Purchasing Agent. The Purchasing Agent shall: • Procure all goods and services • Maintain vendor lists • Establish specifications • Ensure competition • Monitor compliance • Maintain procurement records SECTION 4. ETHICS AND LEGAL COMPLIANCE All procurement activities shall comply with: • The South Carolina Ethics Act • The SC Consolidated Procurement Code principles for political subdivisions • Anti-discrimination and anti-boycott contract requirements . 44 -- 44 of 220 -- SECTION 5. PROCUREMENT METHODS AND THRESHOLDS (A) Micro Purchases – $10,000 and below May be made without competitive quotations if the price is determined fair and reasonable. (B) Small Purchases – $10,001 to $50,000 Require a minimum of two documented quotations where practicable. Award shall be made on a best value basis. (C) Intermediate Purchases – $50,001 to $100,000 Require written quotations or informal solicitation. Public notice is not required. (D) Formal Procurements – Over $100,000 Require one of the following: • Invitation for Bids (IFB) • Request for Proposals (RFP) • Request for Qualifications (RFQ) Public notice shall be given. SECTION 6. CITY COUNCIL APPROVAL City Council approval is required for: • All contracts and purchases exceeding $100,000 The City Administrator may approve contracts at or below this amount. SECTION 7. BASIS OF AWARD Awards shall be made to the responsive and responsible offeror whose proposal is most advantageous to the City, considering: • Price • Quality • Experience • Past performance • Delivery • Life-cycle costs • Other relevant factors Award is not required to be made to the lowest price. 45 -- 45 of 220 -- SECTION 8. NEGOTIATION Negotiations are permitted: • After competitive sealed bidding when in the City’s best interest • With highest-ranked RFP firms • For sole source procurements • For emergency procurements SECTION 9. SOLE SOURCE PROCUREMENT A contract may be awarded without competition when there is only one practicably available source. A written determination is required. SECTION 10. EMERGENCY PROCUREMENTS Emergency procurements may be made when there is an immediate threat to: • Public health • Public safety • Essential services Competition shall be obtained as practicable. A written determination shall be submitted to the City Administrator. SECTION 11. EXEMPTIONS FROM COMPETITIVE PROCUREMENT The following are exempt: • Advertising and public notices • Ammunition • Casual field labor • Cooperative purchasing agreements • Elections, court costs, and settlements • Emergency debris removal • Existing bid or contract for like supplies, services, or construction • Grant-required vendor selections • Holiday Decorations • Insurance • Information technology systems and equipment • Intergovernmental agreements • Landscaping and landscaping materials • Legal, audit, and financial advisory services 46 -- 46 of 220 -- • OEM parts, vehicle parts, and warranty work • Professional services • Public art • Real property transactions • Rental of land, building, and equipment • Repair, maintenance, remodeling, renovation, construction or demolition of a single project not involving an increase in size and type of existing facility • Safety shoes and other personal protective equipment • State/Federal surplus or auction • Software, software licenses and subscriptions • Training, travel, conferences, and memberships • Used vehicles, equipment and surplus property • Utilities and regulated services SECTION 12. COOPERATIVE PURCHASING The City may purchase from: • State contracts • Other governmental contracts • National cooperative purchasing programs Without further competition. SECTION 13. PREQUALIFICATION The City may prequalify vendors for particular types of work. SECTION 14. BONDS FOR CONSTRUCTION Bid, performance, and payment bonds shall be required as determined necessary and in accordance with South Carolina law. SECTION 15. LOCAL VENDOR PREFERENCE The City of Conway shall give qualified local vendors (those with a physical business location in the city for at least twelve months and a valid city business license) a five percent bid evaluation preference on contracts of $10,000 or more, with the option to match the lowest bid when applicable, except where prohibited by funding requirements, cooperative agreements, bond restrictions, emergencies, or other city-approved waivers. SECTION 16. PROTEST PROCEDURE Any actual or prospective bidder may protest a solicitation or award by submitting a written protest within fourteen (14) days. 47 -- 47 of 220 -- SECTION 17. SURPLUS PROPERTY The Purchasing Agent may transfer, trade, or sell surplus property. All proceeds shall be deposited in the appropriate City fund. SECTION 18. FEDERAL AND STATE FUNDING When procurement involves federal or state funds, the applicable funding requirements shall control. SECTION 19. JOINT PROJECTS The City may participate in joint procurement and construction projects with other public entities when determined to be in the City’s best interest. SECTION 20. SEVERABILITY If any part of this ordinance is held invalid, the remainder shall remain in effect. SECTION 21. EFFECTIVE DATE This ordinance shall become effective upon final reading and adoption. 48 -- 48 of 220 -- STAFF REPORT First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (F) COUNCIL MTG DATE: May 18, 2026 AGENDA ITEM: VI.B ORDINANCE: #ZA2026-07-20 (F) AGENDA SECTION: First Reading(s) ISSUE: Petition to annex approximately 1.78+/- acres of property located at 321 Rainwood Road. APPLICANT(S): Brad Richardson, Richardson Family Holdings, LLC PIN(s): 337-10-03-0010 CURRENT ZONING: Highway Commercial (HC) PROPOSED ZONING: Heavy Industrial (HI) Light Industrial (LI) BACKGROUND: The subject property was annexed into the City in 2001 [#ZA2001-06-11(C)] and has been zoned Highway Commercial (HC) since annexation. The applicant applied for a business license to sell and display heavy equipment. At the time of application, the UDO did not specifically define or list “heavy equipment sales and service” as a use. As such, the request was evaluated based on similar uses, including storage/shed sales and manufactured home sales, which are permitted only in the Light and Heavy Industrial zoning districts. Based on this comparison, the business license was only partially approved for sales of accessories / parts, with the condition that full heavy equipment sales, service, and repair operations would not occur on this site. Subsequently, the UDO was amended to define “heavy equipment” and establish “heavy equipment sales and service” as a specific use. That use is now permitted within industrial districts, providing clear policy direction regarding its appropriate location. Heavy equipment sales operations typically involve: • Large machinery (earth moving equipment) stored outdoors • Equipment loading and unloading / staging • Truck Traffic and deliveries • Repair and servicing activities These characteristics align more closely with industrial uses than with the Highway Commercial (HC) district. The HC district is intended to support: • Customer-oriented businesses • Clean, visible commercial activity • A consistent and attractive corridor environment The Highway Commercial (HC) district is not intended to accommodate outdoor industrial storage, heavy equipment display, or repair operations involving large machinery. Section 3.2.14 of the UDO establishes the Heavy Industrial (HI) district as the City’s most intensive industrial zoning classification, intended to accommodate uses such as: 90 -- 90 of 220 -- STAFF REPORT First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-01 (E) • Large-scale manufacturing • Processing operations • Heavy equipment storage and distribution • Uses with significant noise, traffic, or visual impacts SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: Adjacent properties are zoning Highway Commercial (HC), including: • Waste Management (sanitation service company) • Property owned by the applicant While zoned HC, some nearby uses exhibit operational characteristics more consistent with industrial activity. Additionally, properties across Hwy 378 include industrial zoning and properties within Horry County’s jurisdiction zoned, zoned Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA). COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The Future Land Use Map identifies the property as Highway Commercial. Per Section 3.2.10 of the UDO, HC district is intended to: • Serve automobile-oriented commercial activities • Provide corridor compatibility • Reduce traffic congestion • Enhance the aesthetic atmosphere of the City STAFF ANALYSIS: The City’s UDO is permissive in nature, meaning uses are allowed only where they are expressly listed. When a use is not specifically listed, it must be evaluated based on similarity to established use categories. Based on its operational characteristics, heavy equipment sales are most consistent with industrial uses, which are permitted only within industrial zoning districts. Therefore, this use is not appropriate withing the HC district. The requested rezoning to Heavy Industrial (HI) presents a broader policy consideration for Planning Commission and City Council, specifically: • Whether the corridor segment is transitioning toward industrial character; or • Whether maintaining Highway Commercial zoning along Hwy 378 remains the City’s long-term policy objective for this corridor. Additionally, the subject property is located within a major corridor subject to the Gateway Corridor Overlay, which is intended to promote coordinated development patterns and maintain the visual quality of entryways into the City. Approval of Heavy Industrial zoning may introduce a level of intensity that is inconsistent with these objectives and could establish precedent for similar rezonings along the corridor. 91 -- 91 of 220 -- STAFF REPORT First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-01 (E) Suitability of Light Industrial (LI): While the subject property is currently zoned Highway Commercial, the surrounding area includes a mix of uses that exhibit industrial characteristics, including equipment storage, contractor-type operations, and service-related activities. In addition, the subject property has historically functioned in a manner more consistent with industrial-type uses than with traditional corridor-oriented commercial development. The Light Industrial (LI) district is intended to accommodate industrial uses that are lower in intensity and more controlled in nature than those permitted in the Heavy Industrial district. LI zoning allows for: • Production, storage, and distribution activities • Industrial uses with limited impacts • Compatibility with transitional and mixed-use areas The operational characteristics of the proposed use – including outdoor equipment storage, limited customer activity, and associated vehicle traffic- are more consistent with industrial land uses and align more closely with the intent of the LI district. Rezoning to LI would: • allow the proposed use • reflect the existing development pattern in the immediate area • maintain a lower intensity than Heavy Industrial, and • provide a more compatible transition between industrial-type uses and the broader corridor. PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION: Planning Commission held the required Public Hearing at their May 7, 2026 meeting and recommended approval of the Light Industrial (LI) zoning in lieu of Heavy Industrial (HI) for the property. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Based on the surrounding development pattern, the industrial characteristics of nearby uses, and the functional history of the subject property, the Light Industrial (LI) district may be a more appropriate zoning classification in lieu of Heavy Industrial (HI). The LI district would allow the proposed use while maintaining a lower intensity and reducing potential impacts to the Hwy 378 corridor. Staff recommends approval of First Reading of Ord. #ZA2026-06-01 (E), to rezone the property to Light Industrial (LI). ISSUE: First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-01 (S) to Amend Article 5 – Supplemental and Accessory Uses, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding targeted grazing. BACKGROUND: Following multiple flood events, the City acquired numerous properties through the FEMA buyout program. These parcels, along with other vacant or difficult to maintain City-owned properties, require ongoing vegetation management to prevent overgrowth, improve neighborhood appearance, and reduce maintenance costs. Traditional mowing and clearing methods can be costly, labor intensive, and in some locations, impractical due to terrain or limited site access. An alternative approach used successfully in other communities is targeted grazing, where utilizes livestock - typically goats – to naturally manage vegetation, including brush, invasive species, and dense overgrowth. This method is environmentally friendly, reduces reliance on fuel-powered equipment and chemical herbicides, and allows for maintenance of areas that are otherwise difficult to access with conventional machinery. Targeted grazing has also demonstrated effectiveness in controlling invasive plant species and promoting long-term land health. Locally, residents may recall that Santee Cooper previously utilized goats for vegetation management along Hwy 501 in front of the Grainger plant. That effort demonstrated that managed grazing can be both practical and well received within the community. Similar programs have been implemented nationwide as a cost- effective and sustainable land management strategy. In addition to operational benefits, targeted grazing can serve as a visible example of the City’s commitment to sustainable and innovative practices. These programs often generate positive community engagement and provide educational opportunities related to environmental stewardship. From an operational standpoint, the City would lease qualifying parcels to a professional grazing service provider. The provider would be responsible for animal care, temporary fencing, transportation, and onsite supervision, while the City benefits from reduced maintenance costs and improved property conditions. The proposed amendment introduces a provision to Sec. 5.2.5 – Non-commercial Keeping of Livestock or Fowl, to allow and regulate targeted grazing strictly as a vegetation management tool on city-owned or city- controlled properties. A definition of targeted grazing was incorporated into Article 2 – Definitions in a previous text amendment. 164 -- 164 of 220 -- PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing and recommended approval of the proposed amendments at their May 7, 2026 meeting. ISSUE: First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-01 (T) to amend Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to the Park and Open Space dedication requirements. The proposed amendment would establish new standards to calculate the fee in lieu of open space mitigation in the City of Conway. BACKGROUND: This text amendment was initiated in response to repeated design modification requests for major residential developments related with the fee-in-lieu of required open space dedication. Through this process, staff identified a need to standardize the method for calculating the fee in lieu in order to improve consistency, predictability, and administrative efficiency. Alternative approaches to amending Article 10, Sec. 10.3.9 have been provided in the packet. Staff recommends Option 1, as described herein. Currently, the fee-in-lieu amount is calculated based on an applicant-provided appraisal of the subject property. The applicant is required to submit a written appraisal estimating the market value of the land as if the proposed development were completed in accordance with the submitted plans. This value is then divided by the total square footage of the site to determine a per-square-foot value, which is multiplied by the amount of required open space not being provided. An additional 25% is applied to the resulting figure to establish the final fee amount. Following this calculation, the proposed fee must be presented to the Planning Commission for recommendation and subsequently approved by City Council prior to preliminary plan approval. ANALYSIS: This current fee-in-lieu process presents several challenges. First, because the calculation relies on an applicant-provided appraisal based on a hypothetical post- development condition, there is inherent variability in how market value is determined. This can result in inconsistent fee calculations across similar projects and introduce a level of subjectivity into what is intended to be a standardized requirement. Second, the current process requires multiple levels of review, including Technical Review Committee (TRC), Planning Commission, and City Council approval, prior to preliminary plan approval. This multi- step process increases review time and creates uncertainty for applicants, particularly in the early stages of development when project feasibility is being evaluated. Finally, the existing method can disproportionately impact certain types of development, including infill or 171 -- 171 of 220 -- smaller-scale projects, where higher appraised land values may result in significantly higher fee-in-lieu amounts relative to project scale. PROPOSED AMENDMENT: The proposed amendment replaces the existing appraisal-based methodology with a standardized, flat fee per square foot for deficiencies in required open space. Under the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), a minimum of 25% of required open space must be provided as active open space, with the remaining portion as passive open space. Active open space, such as amenity centers, pools, playgrounds, and athletic courts, typically involves significantly higher development and construction costs than passive open space areas. As such, the proposed amendment establishes a differentiated fee structure. Based on research of estimated costs associated with the development of both active and passive open space amenities (see supporting materials in the packet), staff recommends the following rates: • Active Open Space: $12.00 per square foot for any deficiency in required active open space • Passive Open Space: $8.00 per square foot for any deficiency in required passive open space In addition to revising the fee calculation methodology, the amendment modifies the review process for fee- in-lieu requests. Under the proposed structure: • The Planning Commission may approve fee-in-lieu requests administratively when the applicant utilizes the prescribed fee structure established in the Ordinance; and • If the applicant proposes an alternative compliance method – such as a modified fee amount, conservation easement, land donation, or offsite improvement, PC shall forward a recommendation to City Council, which will retain final decision-making authority. This approach streamlines the review process for standard applications while preserving City Council oversight for requests involving discretion or deviation from the established procedures. SUMMARY: The proposed amendment to Sec. 10.3.9(D) is intended to: • Establish a consistent and predictable fee calculation method • Reduce subjectivity associated with appraisal-based valuations • Improve administrative efficiency by streamlining the review process • Provide greater cost certainty for applicants early on in the development process • Maintain flexibility for alternative compliance methods through City Council review PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing on May 7, 2026, and recommended approval of staff’s recommendation for Option 1 of the proposed amendment. 172 -- 172 of 220 -- STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends approval of First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-01 (T), to amend the UDO as proposed and as attached hereto. 173 -- 173 of 220 -- ORDINANCE #ZA2026-06-01 (T) AN ORDINANCE TO AMEND ARTICLE 10 – SUBDIVISION AND LAND DEVELOPMENT, OF THE CITY OF CONWAY UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE (UDO), REGARDING REVISIONS TO THE REQUIREMENTS FOR PARKS AND OPEN SPACE DEDICATION, ESTABLISHING NEW STANDARDS FOR CALCULATING THE FEE-IN-LIEU OF OPEN SPACE MITIGATION. These devices allow fire trucks, when responding to emergencies, to interrupt the normal pattern of traffic lights as they approach, turning them green to clear traffic ahead of the emergency vehicles. text: May 18, 2026 1 CITY OF CONWAY CITY COUNCIL MEETING CONWAY CITY HALL 229 MAIN STREET, CONWAY MONDAY, MAY 18, 2026 PRESENT: Mayor Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor Pro Tem Beth Helms, Amanda Butler, William Goldfinch, Julie Hardwick, Justin Jordan, Larry White. PUBLIC HEARING/FIRST READING Public hearing and first reading on the Fiscal Year 2026-27 Budget - Ordinance #2026-06- 01 (C) An Ordinance to levy taxes and establish a Municipal Budget for the City of Conway, South Carolina. Willams stated that the FY 26-27 comprehensive budget totals $111,029,313, which is a 0.11% decrease over the current year’s budget. Included in that total is a cost-of-living increase of 3.3% for qualifying employees and 30 new full-time positions. Williams said that the property tax millage will increase by the cost-of-living rate of 3.3% from 98.1 mills to 101.3 mills. The Solid Waste collection fees will increase from $32 to $33. Water and sewer rates were initially projected to increase by only 3.3%; however, due to a significantly larger rate increase from Grand Strand Water and Sewer (GSWSA), the city must adjust rates accordingly to keep pace with the rising service costs, therefore water will increase by 10% and sewer will increase by 3.3%. Public Utilities and Construction Services will update fees to ensure development is paying for itself. Helms asked if there is any way to increase the capital recovery fees to pass along to the developers. Williams said that their water and sewer capital recovery fees are being increased as well. Emrick said that capital recovery fees go into a restricted fund for future capital needs and the actual operation, 10% increase won’t be the actual water service that we pay for water. Its 2 separate things, as GSWSA is also going up on their capital recovery fees tremendously as well. Emrick said that if the city does not go up on both at the same time we will be behind what we are paying for water now. Helms asked about a fee survey with tiered fees. Emrick said that a study is in the budget for next year. Williams gave an example of the rate increase for city residents and out of city resident rates. Helms said that she wanted the public to hear that the city was only going up the cost of living at 3.3% but that this 10% rate increase was pushed on the city by GSWSA. Willaims said yes, that is correct. Goldfinch stated that there has been no tax increase on city property taxes since he has been on council, increasing it to only mirror inflation. Goldfinch then stated that if the penny tax had of moved forward with Horry County, the City of Conway would have been the biggest beneficiary receiving approximately 40 mills. Hardwick asked if there were any other options other than GSWSA. Emrick said no. There was no public input. -- 2 of 14 -- May 18, 2026 3 Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Goldfinch to close the public hearing. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Blain to approve first reading of Ordinance #2026-06-01 (C) Fiscal Year 2026-27 Budget as presented. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. FIRST READING: A. First Reading of Ordinance #2026-06-01 (D) to repeal and replace Purchasing Rules and Regulations for the City of Conway, South Carolina. Kempski stated that this ordinance is to repeal and replace the purchasing rules and regulations as the current purchasing rules have been amended many times over the years, resulting in a framework that is increasingly complex and difficult to navigate. The proposed update replaces the current, complex purchasing rules with a clearer and more consistent set of guidelines. In addition, purchasing thresholds are being increased, allowing staff to avoid unnecessary quotes for lower-value purchases and focus time and resources on higher-priority procurements, while maintaining appropriate oversight and accountability. City Council approval for all contracts and purchases will increase from $25,000 to $100,000. Kempski said that staff recommended approval of first reading as presented. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Jordan to approve first reading of Ordinance #2026-06-01 (D) repealing and replacing the purchasing rules and regulations. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (F), to annex approximately 1.78+/- acres of property located at 321 Rainwood Road (PIN 324-07-03-0006). Hucks stated that this property contains an existing single-family residence, and the annexation request was submitted in accordance with city requirements for connection to city utilities. The property has been under current ownership since 1991; however, restrictive covenants were recorded on May 4, 2026. The property is essentially surrounded by similar residential zoning patterns. Properties across Rainwood Road as well as a large tract of over 200 acres are currently zoned Low/Medium Density Residential (R-1). This property and the abutting property is under the county’s jurisdiction, zoned SF40, which is a residential district that prohibits manufactured homes and requires a minimum lot size of 40,000 square feet. If first reading of the annexation is approved, Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on the proposed zoning upon annexation at their June 4 meeting. Hucks said that staff recommended approval of first reading. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Hardwick to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (F) annexing the property located at 321 Rainwood Road. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. C. Hucks stated that this annexation request was submitted as a requirement for connection to City utility services after it was determined that the existing well system would not adequately serve the property. The site contains an existing commercial building that has historically been -- 3 of 14 -- May 18, 2026 4 occupied by a few commercial uses over the years. Most recently, there have been inquiries and permit applications submitted through Horry County associated with the potential reuse of the building, including a bakery use and a pizza restaurant; however, staff notes that no final approvals or inspections have been completed through the County at this time. The property is adjacent to residentially zoned property within the City limits, so any future redevelopment or site improvements would still be subject to applicable city development standards if annexed, including access, signage, buffering and permitting requirements. From a land use perspective, the Highway Commercial zoning is consistent with the City’s future land use map designation for this portion of the Hwy. 501 corridor and is compatible with the existing commercial character of the property and surrounding highway-oriented development pattern. Hucks said that staff notes, however, that the applicant is not seeking annexation. Annexation is driven solely by the requirement to obtain a connection to city utilities rather than part of a broader redevelopment or expansion of the site. If first reading to annex the subject property is approved, the proposed zoning of the property upon annexation will be considered at the June 4 Planning Commission meeting. Hucks stated that t his property contains a single-family dwelling, and the annexation request was submitted in connection with a name change associated with the existing city utility account. The property has been under the current ownership since 2009, and restrictive covenants have been on file since 1987. If annexed, the proposed zoning upon annexation is low/medium-density residential (R-1), which is consistent with the surrounding development pattern and the City’s future land use map. The property is adjacent to the Woodcreek subdivision, which is within the City limits, zoned R-1. Properties like this one are often referred to being a donut hole, where properties are surrounded or nearly surrounded by existing city boundaries. If first reading to annex the property is approved, Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on the proposed zoning upon annexation at their June 4 meeting. Hucks said that staff recommended approval of first reading to annex the property. First reading of Ordinance # ZA2026-06-01 (E), to rezone approximately 5.28+/- acres of property located at 2578 HWY 378 from the Highway Commercial (HC) district to the Heavy Industrial (HI) district (PIN 337-10-03-0010). Hucks stated that the applicant is requesting to rezone the property in order to conduct heavy equipment sales and service operations on the site. The property has been zoned Highway Commercial since annexation into the City in 2001. The request originated after the applicant applied for a business license associated with heavy equipment sales and display. At the time, the UDO did not -- 4 of 14 -- May 18, 2026 5 specifically define or list ‘heavy equipment sales and service’ as a use category. Because the UDO is permissive in nature, staff had to evaluate the request based on the most similar existing use classifications within the ordinance. Hucks said that permissive in nature means that uses are only allowed where they are specifically listed within the ordinance. If a use is not listed, staff cannot simply assume it’s allowed. Instead, staff have evaluated it based on similar uses and the intent of the zoning district. In this case, staff determined that the operational characteristics of the heavy equipment sales, including outdoor equipment storage and display, loading and unloading activities, truck traffic, and repair or servicing functions, are more consistent with industrial uses than with traditional highway commercial uses. The Highway Commercial district is intended to support customer- oriented businesses, visible commercial activity, and an attractive corridor environment. It is not intended to accommodate outdoor industrial storage, heavy equipment display, or repair operations involving large machinery. As part of a recent, broader amendment to the UDO, heavy equipment sales and service were specifically defined and identified in the Use Table section of the UDO, which establishes where the use is permitted. Hucks said that under the current ordinance, the use is now permitted within the Light Industrial and Heavy Industrial zoning districts as a supplemental use. The broader policy question is whether this corridor segment should transition toward a heavier industrial character through HI zoning, or whether a lower-intensity industrial classification would be more appropriate given the surrounding context and long-term corridor objectives. Staff’s concern with the HI district along Hwy 378 is this corridor, as with the other major corridors throughout the city, are within the Gateway Corridor Overlay. This overlay is intended to maintain the visual quality and coordinated development pattern of major entryways into the city. Hucks said that the Heavy Industrial zoning is the city’s most intrusive industrial district and permits a much broader range of industrial activities than is currently being proposed. While the proposed heavy equipment sales use may be appropriate within the Light or Heavy Industrial district, staff’s primary concern is not the business itself, but rather the Heavy Industrial zoning classification and the full range of uses that could occur on the property in the future. Hucks stated that zoning runs with the land, not with the property owner. The Light Industrial district is intended for lower-intensity industrial and service- related activities, including contractor operations, warehousing, equipment-related uses, and limited outdoor storage, while Heavy Industrial is intended for larger-scale manufacturing, processing, heavy distributions, and more intensive industrial activity. Hucks said that staff also recognized that the immediate area contains several uses that exhibit industrial-type characteristics, including contractor type operations, equipment storage, sanitation related services, and properties across Hwy 378 within the County contain similar heavy equipment sales operations. For that reason, staff concluded that the Light Industrial district represents a more balanced approach. It would allow the proposed use while maintaining a lower-intensity classification along the corridor. Additionally, as part of the Comprehensive Plan update, staff intend to further evaluate and identify appropriate industrial nodes or activity areas throughout the city based on existing development patterns and long-term land use compatibility. Staff believes that this area -- 5 of 14 -- May 18, 2026 6 exhibits characteristics supportive of lower-intensity industrial zoning, but not necessarily the broader range of uses that would be permitted in Heavy Industrial. Hucks said that Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the proposed zoning and recommended approval of the Light Industrial district as well at their May 7 meeting. Based on the surrounding development pattern and the operational characteristics of the proposed use, staff also recommended approval of the rezoning to Light Industrial. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by White to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-01 (E) rezoning 2578 Highway 378 to Light Industrial (LI). Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. F.
