First reading of Ordinance # ZA2026-06-01 (S), to amend Article 5 – Specific Use Regulations of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to the Non-commercial Keeping of Livestock or Fowl. The proposed amendment would establish new standards and restrictions to regulate the use of targeted grazing on city owned property in the City of Conway. Hucks stated that the City owns several vacant or difficult to maintain properties throughout the City. Many city- owned parcels require ongoing vegetation management to prevent overgrowth, improve appearance, and reduce long-term maintenance costs. In some cases, traditional mowing equipment is difficult or inefficient due to terrain, drainage conditions, or limited access. This amendment would allow the City to utilize targeted grazing, typically with goats, as a controlled vegetation management tool on City-owned or City-controlled property. A grazing service provider would be responsible for fencing, transportation, supervision, and animal care, while the city benefits from a more sustainable and cost-effective maintenance method. This approach has been used successfully in other communities, including locally, where in the past, goats were used along Hwy 501 near the former Santee Cooper Grainger Steam plant for vegetation control purposes. The proposed ordinance does NOT establish a residential or agricultural livestock use, nor does it change existing residential regulations on private noncommercial keeping of livestock or fowl in residential zoning districts. It authorizes a limited municipal maintenance activity on City-owned or City-controlled property for vegetation management purposes only. The livestock are temporary, professionally managed, and accessory to a governmental maintenance function, similar to how the city may use specialized equipment or contractors for drainage maintenance, stormwater management, or sidewalk improvements. The use of targeted grazing provides the City with an additional tool to manage difficult properties in a more environmentally sustainable and potentially more cost-effective manner while also supporting vegetation control in areas where conventional maintenance methods may not be practical. Hucks said that Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the amendment at their May 7 meeting and recommended approval. Staff also recommended approval. Helms asked if the fencing would be temporary. Hucks said yes, and that the provider would install and maintain the fencing during the grazing period. Blain asked how long the goats would be on the property. Hucks said that would depend on the acreage and the number of goats. -- 8 of 14 -- May 18, 2026 9 Motion: Helms made a motion, seconded by Blain to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-01 (S) regarding non-commercial keeping of livestock or fowl on city owned property. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. I. First reading of Ordinance # ZA2026-06-01 (T), to amend Article 10 – Subdivision and land development of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to the Park and Open Space Dedication. The proposed amendment would establish new standards to calculate the fee-in-lieu of open space mitigation in the City of Conway. Hucks stated that this amendment to the UDO is regarding fee-in-lieu process for required park and open space dedication associated with major residential developments. Currently, when a development does not provide all or a portion of the required open space onsite, the ordinance allows the developer to request to pay a fee-in-lieu of providing that open space. Under the existing ordinance, which has been in effect since the original adoption of the UDO in 2011, the fee is calculated using an appraisal of the property as if the development were already completed according to the submitted plans. This appraisal-based method has created several recurring issues for staff, applicants, and Planning Commission. First, because the calculation relies on hypothetical post-development appraisals, there can be significant variability in how the fee is determined from project to project. Staff have also encountered situations where appraisers themselves expressed concern or confusion with providing valuations based on future developed conditions that do not yet exist. Second, the current process requires multiple levels of review, including the Technical Review Committee, Planning Commission, and City Council approval, which increases review time and creates uncertainty for applicants regarding overall costs early in the process. Finally, the existing methodology can disproportionately impact certain types of projects, particularly infill or smaller-scale developments, where higher land values can produce substantially higher fee-in-lieu amounts that may not necessarily correlate with the actual cost of providing open space improvements. One example of this is the University Suites expansion located on Technology Blvd, in which the applicant requested to pay a fee in lieu of providing open space, but also a reduction in the amount, requiring a recommendation by Planning Commission and final approval from Council. Before Planning Commission could even consider the reduced fee in lieu amount, they first had to consider a design modification in which the applicant requested a modification from the way in which the fee in lieu was determined. Hucks said that in response to these concerns, staff evaluated 3 different alternatives which were presented to Planning Commission. PC ultimately recommended approval of what is identified as Option 1. Under option 1, the appraisal-based calculation would be replaced with a standardized flat fee structure based on deficiencies in required active and passive open space. The Unified Development Ordinance currently requires that 25% of required open space amount be active open space – such as playgrounds, amenity areas, pools or athletic courts – with the remainder allowed as passive open space. Because active open space generally involves substantially higher construction and maintenance costs than passive open space, the proposed amendment establishes 2 different flat fee amounts: (1) $12 per sq. ft. for deficiencies in active open space; and (2) $8 per sq. ft. for deficiencies -- 9 of 14 -- May 18, 2026 10 in passive open space. The amounts were determined based on review of estimated development costs associated with active and passive open space improvements. Hucks said that another important component of the amendment is the review process. Under the proposed structure, if an applicant utilizes the standard fee-in-lieu structure established in the ordinance, Planning Commission may approve the fee in lieu administratively as part of the development review process. However, if the applicant proposes an alternative method, such as a reduces fee, land donation, conservation easement, or offsite improvement, that request would still require a recommendation from Planning Commission and final approval from City Council. Staff evaluated other alternatives, ranging from a fully discretionary Council review process to a single flat fee structure. Planning Commission recommended Option 1 because it represents the best balance between predictability, administrative efficiency, and retaining council oversight where flexibility or deviations are requested. Hucks emphasized that this amendment is not intended to reduce or waive the City’s open space requirements – in fact, it likely increases the fee in lieu amounts in most situations. The purpose of the amendment is to standardize the calculation methodology and create greater predictability early in the development review process. The ordinance still allows alternative compliance proposals or modified fee requests, but those situations would continue to require final approval from City Council. In short, the requirements for open space are not changing...what is changing is the method by which the fee in lieu is calculated and administered. Hucks said that staff also recommended approval of Option 1, as recommended by Planning Commission. White asked what the purpose of open space was. Hucks explained. Goldfinch asked if council would have flexibility. Hucks said yes, any deviations would come to council for approval. Vote: Blain, Helms, Butler, Goldfinch, Jordan, Hardwick voted yes. White voted no. Motion to approve carried with a 6-1 vote. CONSIDERATION: A. Consideration of an application for approval of Article K - Industrial Incentive for ASL Properties LLC, located at 3191 Hwy 378 (PIN 370-04-01-0002). Dennis stated that Long’s Heating & Air Conditioning is under construction of a new building for their business and the property is eligible for the Industrial Incentive. This incentive would provide the applicant with reimbursement of building permit fees, business license fees for 2 years, expedited review period of 15 days, and a reduction in the required landscaping by one letter unless abutting residential zoning districts. The applicant is also -- 10 of 14 -- May 18, 2026 11 eligible for Redevelopment Enhancement with this one and will receive reimbursements on any capital recovery fees as well. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Helms to approve the application for the Industrial Incentive. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. Consideration of approval of a bid for water line replacement project on Edgewood Circle – Dudley stated that staff is requesting approval to award the contract for the Edgewood Circle water line replacement project. This project will replace the existing 1.5- inch galvanized water line, which has required frequent repairs, and will improve fire protection within this area. On April 23, the city received 3 bids for the project and after review by staff and AECOM, Land & Development Services was determined to be the best qualified and most responsive bidder. Dudley said that funding for this project will come from the waterline upgrades account, and staff requested council’s approval to award the contract. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Goldfinch to award the contract to Land & Development Services, LLC. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. C. Consideration of approval of a local match for GSATS Emergency Vehicle Signal Preemption System Grant – Perzan stated that the Grand Strand Area Transportation Study is planning to implement the initial phases of an Emergency Vehicle Signal Preemption System in Horry County. The City of Conway has the opportunity to join the program along with Horry County and the City of North Myrtle Beach. These devices allow fire trucks, when responding to emergencies, to interrupt the normal pattern of traffic lights as they approach, turning them green to clear traffic ahead of the emergency vehicles. This grant funding will be used to launch a pilot program that will include busy intersections in the city, with transponders in nine City of Conway fire vehicles. If the pilot program proves efficacy as expected, the program may be rolled out on a wider scale in the future. It is estimated that such a system will reduce response times for the Conway Fire Department by as much as 25%. The preliminary report provided as part of the City’s Public Safety Strategic Plan established lower response times as one of the primary goals for the Fire Department over the next few years. Perzan said that the city has been asked to provide a match of $40,800 now and there is funding in the current budget that can be used for this purpose. There will be an additional match of $127,548 in a future fiscal year. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Blain to approve the local match for GSATS Emergency Vehicle Signal Preemption System grant. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. D. The proposed amendments revise the classification and regulation of certain commercial uses across multiple zoning districts. The amendments establish updated and new definitions, clarify use classifications, and implement additional use-specific standards and location-based restrictions for certain higher-impact uses, including, but not limited to: tobacco/vape/smoke shop establishments, alternative financial services (e.g., payday loan/title loan/cash advance/check-cashing services), gas/service stations (with or without convenience stores), outdoor event facilities/spaces, and similar uses. BACKGROUND: Over the past several months, staff has evaluated how certain commercial uses are regulated, particularly within the Highway Commercial (HC) zoning district and along key commercial corridors. The effort was initiated following a rezoning request involving property zoned HC and located adjacent to an established single-family residential neighborhood. While the request was ultimately denied, it highlighted broader concerns that some zoning districts currently allow higher-intensity commercial uses without sufficient standards when located near residential areas. In response, staff reviewed the Use Tables in Article 4 of the UDO and standards for certain uses in Article 5 to identify uses that: • Are permitted by right without additional standards; and • May create impacts such as traffic, noise, lighting, and extended hours of operation that are not always compatible with nearby residential uses. Staff also reviewed regulatory approaches used by comparable municipalities to identify appropriate tools for Conway. ANALYSIS: The proposed amendments establish a more consistent and targeted framework for regulating certain commercial uses. Major changes include: Article 2 – Definitions: • Updates and adds definitions to reflect current business operations; • Clarifies distinctions between similar or overlapping uses (e.g., gas stations vs. convenience stores) 90 -- 90 of 390 -- • Ensures uses are classified based on primary business activity, not business name or signage Article 4 – Use Tables: • Clarifies that only uses specifically listed are permitted • Establishes a consistent process for classifying similar or unlisted uses • Reclassifies certain uses to ensure appropriate oversight (e.g., permitted to supplemental or accessory) • Improves alignment between use classifications and applicable standards Article 5 – Supplemental and Accessory Uses (formerly “Specific Use Regulations”) • Renames and restructures the Article to focus on objective, use-specific standards • Implements location-based criteria, including separation requirements and proximity to residential areas • Adds standards addressing operational and site impacts (e.g., traffic, lighting, hours of operation) • Applies Special Exception review in limited circumstances where site-specific conditions warrant additional evaluation Nonconformities • Existing lawful uses may continue as legal nonconforming uses • Re-establishment of certain uses muse comply with current standards, including separation and location requirements. Housekeeping amendments: • Improves clarity, consistency, and internal alignment across multiple sections of the UDO. REGULATORY APPROACH The proposed amendments take a targeted approach to regulation. Rather than prohibiting uses, the amendments: • Establish objective standards to address potential impacts; • Apply separation requirements where appropriate to prevent overconcentration; • Introduce location-based criteria, particularly near residential areas; and • Use Special Exception review selectively to address site-specific conditions. CONSISTENCY WITH COMPREHENSIVE PLAN The proposed amendments are consistent with the goals of the City’s Comprehensive Plan, including: • Protection of established residential neighborhoods; • Promotion of compatible land use patterns; 91 -- 91 of 390 -- • Improved development and redevelopment of commercial corridors; and • Support for balanced and sustainable growth. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION These amendments provide clearer standards and improved tools to address location-specific impacts, rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach to all properties. The proposed amendments revise how certain commercial uses are defined, classified, and regulated across multiple zoning districts. The amendments focus on uses that may have greater potential for land use impacts. The amendments are intended to address compatibility concerns without eliminating uses that are otherwise appropriate in commercial zoning districts. The complete text of the proposed amendments are included for your review. Religious meetings / revivals in a tent or other temporary structure located in any district for a period not to exceed seven (7) days, including setup and takedown. C. Open lot sale of Christmas trees in any commercial district for a period not to exceed forty-five (45) days. Sales are limited to Christmas trees and associated holiday fare. D. Real estate sales offices associated with new developments or subdivisions, in any district, for a period not to exceed one (1) year, provided no cooking or sleeping accommodations are maintained in the structure. E. Contractor’s office and equipment shed, in any district, for a period not to exceed one (1) year, provided such office or shed is located on the property to which such office or shed is appurtenant. F. Public Educational and Public Higher Education Facilities may utilize portable classrooms and offices in any district for a period not to exceed five (5) years. Up to ten (10) structures are permitted as accessory structures to a permanent education facility. G. Accessory Residential Uses. Residential uses accessory to any of the above permitted temporary uses are prohibited, unless expressly permitted by the Zoning Administrator at the time of issuing the Temporary Certificate of Zoning Compliance. 5.3.2 Temporary Uses During a Declared Emergency A. Temporary Public Safety Uses during a Natural Disaster or Emergency. In the case of a natural disaster or other citywide emergency event, all public safety and/or public health land uses of a temporary nature that the city deems as necessary to serve the city during a time of need, as declared by the Mayor or City Council, shall be exempt from requiring a Temporary Certificate. This includes, but is not limited to: 1. Temporary emergency tents or shelters; 2. Triage care centers; 3. Mobile communications units or similar staging and care equipment; 4. Temporary structures needed to house displaced city departments and/or services. B. Private Temporary Uses during a Natural Disaster or Emergency. Private temporary uses in the case of a citywide declared emergency shall require Temporary Certificate of Zoning Compliance allowing the temporary use for a period of ninety (90) days. The Zoning Administrator may issue an extension of up to sixty (60) days if deemed necessary. The following are private temporary uses that will be considered for a temporary Certificate: 1. Mobile homes or on-site RVs and campers for displaced residents; 2. Portable storage units; 3. Dumpsters; 4. Portable toilets; 5. Other uses related to home repair or residential displacement related to said emergency. 179 -- 179 of 390 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 5 –Specific Supplemental and Accessory Uses Regulations 5-55 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended XX C. BACKGROUND (updated): This amendment is a companion to a related set of amendments addressing use classifications and supplemental standards within Articles 2, 4 and 5 of the UDO. As part of that broader effort, staff evaluated the need for a formal Special Exception process to address certain uses that, while appropriate within a zoning district, may have the potential to create site-specific impacts depending on location and operational characteristics. A Special Exception is a permitted use within a zoning district that requires case-by-case review to evaluate potential impacts, such as traffic generation, operational intensity, noise, lighting, and compatibility with surrounding properties. The purpose of the special exception process is to provide a structured and consistent mechanism for evaluating these impacts in accordance with established ordinance criteria. A special exception: • Is a permitted use within an applicable zoning district; • Is not a variance from dimensional or development standards; • Does not authorize a use that is otherwise prohibited; • Requires a finding that the proposed use complies with applicable ordinance standards and will not result in demonstrable adverse impacts; and • May be approved with reasonable conditions directly related to identified impacts and necessary to ensure compliance with the UDO. If adopted, the special exception process would require an applicant, where specified in the Use Table or in Article 5, to obtain approval from the Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA) following a duly noticed public hearing conducted in accordance with Article 14. Evaluation of Uses: As part of this process, staff evaluated a range of uses to determine whether Special Exception review was appropriate, including bed and breakfast establishments, outpatient treatment facilities, alternative financial services, adult entertainment establishments, body piercing and tattoo establishments, tobacco/vape/smoke shops, taverns/bars/nightclubs, and gas/service stations. The evaluation focused on whether existing ordinance standards – such as separation requirements, 193 -- 193 of 390 -- STAFF REPORT Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (P) operational limitations, and location-based criteria – were sufficient to address potential impacts, or whether additional discretionary review would provide a meaningful benefit. Based on this analysis, staff determined that certain uses are already adequately regulated through objective standards and do not warrant additional special exception review. These include adult entertainment establishments, taverns/bars/nightclubs, tattoo and body piercing establishments, bed and breakfast establishments, and outpatient treatment facilities, all of which are subject to existing locational, operational, and/or separation requirements within the UDO. Conversely, for selected uses, the special exception process provides an additional layer of review to address site-specific conditions that cannot be fully anticipated through objective standards alone. Proposed amendments: The proposed amendments to Articles 2, 4 and 14: • Establish a formal Special Exception process within the UDO; • Define the scope and criteria for Special Exception review; • Identify specific uses and circumstances under which special exception approval is required; and • Clarify the role of the Board of Zoning Appeals in evaluating such requests based on established criteria. These amendments are intended to work in coordination with the updated Use Table (Art. 4) and Supplemental and Accessory Use standards (Art. 5), creating a consistent framework in which: • Uses are clearly classified; • Objective standards are applied where appropriate; and • Discretionary review is used selectively to address site-specific impacts. Consistency with the Comprehensive Plan: The proposed amendments are consistent with the goals and policies of the City’s Comprehensive Plan, including: • Protection of established residential neighborhoods; • Promotion of compatible land use patterns; and • Implementation of regulatory tools that support balanced and context-sensitive development. Additional Information: The complete text of the proposed amendments are included in your packet for review. BACKGROUND: Article 12 of the UDO establishes regulations for nonconforming uses, lots, and structures. Nonconformities occur when a property or use was lawfully established but no longer complies with the current zoning regulations. As part of the City’s broader effort to modernize and clarify the UDO, staff conducted a comprehensive review of Art. 12 to address inconsistencies, improve clarity, and ensure alignment with recently proposed amendments – particularly those related to supplemental use standards in Art. 5 and the establishment of a formal Special Exception process (Art.14). These amendments are intended to create a more consistent, enforceable, and predictable framework for the treatment of nonconforming uses while reinforcing the City’s broader zoning policies. Summary of Proposed Amendments: 1. Discontinuance and Re-establishment of Nonconforming Uses • Retains the 180-day discontinuance standard for nonconforming uses. • Clarifies that inactivity – rather than the maintenance of a business license alone -determines whether a use has been discontinued. • Establishes a narrowly defined process for re-establishment through Special Exception approval by the Board of Zoning Appeals. • Requires all of the following: o Lawful prior establishment of the use o Demonstration of hardship beyond the property owner’s control o No increase in intensity, density, or impacts • Limits any re-established use 206 -- 206 of 390 -- STAFF REPORT Final reading Of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (Q) 2. Separation-Based and Location-Restricted Uses • Confirms that uses rendered nonconforming due to separation requirements, location restrictions, or special exception standards may continue as legal nonconforming uses. • Establishes that once such uses are discontinued, they may not be re-established unless they comply with current ordinance requirements. • Ensures consistency with recently proposed standards for higher-impact uses. 3. Change in Ownership • Clarifies that a legal nonconforming use may continue despite a change in ownership, tenancy, or business name, provided the use has not been discontinued. 4. Nonconforming Lots of Record • Confirms that lawfully created lots that do not meet current dimensional standards may still be used. • Requires the combination of commonly owned adjacent lots where necessary to meet minimum standards. 5. Nonconforming Structures and Sites • Clarifies provisions for expansion, reconstruction, and modification of nonconforming structures. • Ensures that improvements do not increase the degree of nonconformity. • Establishes consistent expectations for site elements such as access, parking, landscaping, and buffering. 6. Damage and Reconstruction Standards • Establishes a consistent reconstruction threshold: o Structures damaged 50% or less may be rebuilt to prior nonconforming conditions. o Structures damaged greater than 50% must be brought into full compliance. 7. Nonconforming Signs • Updates and modernizes sign provisions. • Removes outdated material-specific standards. • Clarifies allowances for maintenance, repair, and replacement. 8. General Clarifications and Housekeeping • Improves organization, terminology, and internal consistency. • Aligns Art. 12 with Art. 5 and Art. 14. • Eliminates redundant or conflicting language. 207 -- 207 of 390 -- STAFF REPORT Final reading Of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (Q) ANALYSIS The proposed amendments strengthen Art. 12 by establishing a clear and consistent framework for determining when nonconforming uses may continue, be discontinued, or be re-established. These amendments: • Clarify the circumstances under which nonconforming uses may be re-established and limit that process to narrowly defined hardship situations; • Ensure that uses subject to separation requirements or location restrictions cannot be re-established once discontinued; • Eliminating ambiguity regarding the role of the Board of Zoning Appeals and reinforce its quasi- judicial function; • Prevent the expansion or intensification of nonconforming uses over time while allowing reasonable relief in limited cases. Overall, these updates improve clarity, consistency, and enforceability, while supporting the City’s ability to manage uses with greater potential impacts. [ZA2012-09-04 (A)] 222 -- 222 of 390 -- STAFF REPORT Final reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (R) COUNCIL MTG DATE: May 4, 2026 AGENDA ITEM: III.I ISSUE: Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (R), to amend Article 2 – Definitions, Article 6 – Design Standards, Article 7 – Street Design and Circulation, Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development, and Article 12 – Nonconformities, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), establishing standards for private streets and access to substandard roads in the City of Conway. This amendment in intended to address existing lots of record that lack adequate frontage on a public street accepted for maintenance by the City, County, or State, and to establish regulations for development proposed on roads not constructed to City standards. BACKGROUND: The City’s current UDO requires all lots to front on a public street constructed to City standards and accepted for public maintenance. While this requirement is appropriate for new subdivisions, it has created challenges in situations involving: • Lots of record created prior to adoption of the UDO; • Properties annexed into the City that are served by private or substandard roads; • Existing roads that were assumed to be public but were never formally dedicated; • Roads under the jurisdiction of other entities that do not meet City standards; and • Parcels lacking adequate frontage due to historic platting patterns. Under the current ordinance, these properties may be unable to obtain building permits or certificates of occupancy unless a public street is constructed to full City standards. In many cases, this requirement is impractical due to cost, ownership constraints, or existing development patterns. These situations are becoming more frequent as the City continues to annex property and encounter legacy development patterns that were established prior to current regulations. ANALYSIS (this section updated since 1st reading) The proposed amendment establishes a coordinated framework across multiple sections of the UDO to address these conditions while maintaining the City’s standards for new development. This amendment maintains public streets as the required standard for new and major subdivisions and provides a limited, controlled framework for addressing existing conditions. Key Components of the Amendment 1. Definition of Private Road (Article 2) Adds a definition clarifying that private roads are not publicly maintained and are not part of the City street system unless constructed to City standards and formally accepted. 223 -- 223 of 390 -- STAFF REPORT Final reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (R) 2. Frontage Requirement Modification (Article 6) Revises the requirement that all lots must front on a public street to allow access via private roads or access easements in limited circumstances, as governed by Article 10. 3. Street Design Consistency (Article 7) Updates existing provisions to remove the blanket prohibition on private roads and instead allow them only where specifically permitted by Article 10. Private roads remain prohibited for major subdivisions. 4. Subdivision Regulations (Article 10) Creates a new Sec. 10.10 – Private Streets and Access to Substandard Roads, which: • Allows private roads only in limited circumstances, such as lots of record and annexed properties; • Establishes minimum design and safety standards, including fire access requirements; • Requires recorded maintenance agreements and clarifies that the City has no maintenance responsibility; • Prohibits the use of private roads for major subdivisions; • Provides administrative approval authority for individual lots of record; and • Establishes standards for development accessing substandard roads, including the ability to require improvements or deny development where adequate access cannot be provided. • Requires improvements to substandard roads or allows denial of development where adequate access cannot be achieved, including for roads maintained by other jurisdictions. 5. Nonconforming Lots (Article 12) Clarifies that legally created nonconforming lots of record may be developed, including those lacking frontage, provided access is established in accordance with Sec. 10.10. UPDATES from 1st reading: The updated ordinance establishes maintenance requirements for private roads and for substandard roads that may be improved to provide access. In these cases, property owners will be required to enter into a recorded maintenance agreement ensuring that the road is maintained by the owner(s) or a responsible entity. The ordinance further clarifies that the City will not be responsible for maintenance, repair, or reconstruction of such roads unless and until they are constructed to full City standards and formally accepted. This reflect a deferred acceptance approach, allowing access to be established while protecting the City from premature or unintended maintenance obligations. PURPOSE AND INTENT The proposed amendment is intended to: • Address longstanding issues related to access for legally created lots of record; 224 -- 224 of 390 -- STAFF REPORT Final reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (R) • Provide a clear and consistent framework for evaluating development on private or substandard roads; • Maintain public safety through minimum access and fire standards; • Protect the City from long-term maintenance obligations associated with private roads; and • Preserve existing requirements for public streets in new and major subdivisions. This amendment does not reduce development standards for new subdivisions and does not permit private roads as an alternative to required public infrastructure for new or major development. IMPACTS Positive Impacts • Provides a practical solution for development of existing lots lacking public frontage; • Reduces the need for case-by-case exceptions or informal interpretations; • Improves clarity and consistency in the UDO; • Enhances public safety by establishing minimum access standards; • Protects the City from assuming maintenance of substandard or private roads. • Reduces potential long-term financial exposure associated with premature acceptance or maintenance of substandard infrastructure. • Establishes clear maintenance responsibility for private and substandard roads, ensuring that the City does not assume long-term maintenance unless roads are constructed to full City standards and formally accepted. Potential Concerns • Perception that private roads are being broadly permitted (mitigated by limitations within the ordinance); • Requires careful administrative review to ensure compliance with access and safety standards. The 2 amendments are related and work together to update how certain commercial uses are defined, regulated and reviewed within the UDO. They are the result of a broader effort by staff over the past year. The process was initiated following a rezoning request for property zoned Highway Commercial, located adjacent to an established single-family neighborhood. While that request was ultimately denied, it highlighted broader concerns with how certain higher impact commercial uses are currently regulated – particularly when located near residential areas. In response, staff conducted a comprehensive review of the UDO to determine whether additional tools were needed to better address compatibility moving forward. Hucks said that the first amendment focuses on how uses are defined, classified and regulated and it will do the following: (1) Update definitions to reflect modern business operations; (2) Clarifies the use table so that only listed uses are permitted; (3) Applies supplemental standards rather than conditional designations for high impact uses and additional restrictions for other higher impact uses such as vape/smoke/tobacco shops, alternative financial services such as payday loans, check cashing, title loans, gas/service stations, and a new use category – outdoor event facilities or spaces. Outdoor event facilities will include standards for event size, event frequency, noise, and location, along with a requirement for special exception review to ensure compatibility with surrounding properties. Hucks said that the second amendment established the special exception review process through the Board of Zoning Appeals. This applies in limited situations where a use may be appropriate within a zoning district, but its location or surrounding context warrants additional review. This is not a variance, and it is not a rezoning. The use remains permitted, but the Board of Zoning Appeals evaluates site-specific impacts and apply reasonable conditions when necessary to ensure compatibility. Hucks said that the third amendment addresses how these regulations apply to existing uses. Existing, lawful uses can continue, however if discontinued uses that are subject to separation requirements or special exception requirements must comply with current standards of the UDO before the use can be re-established. This ensures that nonconforming situations are reduced over time. Hucks stated that the amendments also include housekeeping provisions and the addition of uses not previously defined or listed in the Use Table. These updates improve clarity, consistency, and alignment across the UD). These amendments do not prohibit uses, they clarify how uses are classified, apply targeted standards based on impacts, introduce limited additional reviews where appropriate, and provide a long-term framework for compatibility. The goal is to be a more predictable and balanced system that supports development while protecting established neighborhoods. First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (R), to amend Article 2 – Definitions, Article 6 – Design Standards, Article 7 – Street Design & Circulation, Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development, and Article 12 – Nonconformities, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance, to establish standards for private roadway in the City limits. The amendments proposed are intended to address existing lots of record that lack adequate frontage on a public street accepted for maintenance by the City, County, or State, and to establish regulations for development proposed on roads not constructed to City standards. Hucks stated that this amendment addresses a growing issue that the city is seeing with properties that were legally created or annexed into the City but do not have the required frontage on a public street constructed to City standards. Under the current ordinance, every lot must front a public street accepted for public maintenance – whether that is the county, state or city. This requirement works well for new subdivisions, but for older lots or annexed properties, it creates a situation where – even if a road exists – the property cannot be built on unless that street is constructed to full city standards. In many cases, that’s simply not practical due to cost, ownership, or existing conditions. Hucks showed a couple of slides of typical road profiles and existing streets and explained what they look like today and would look like being built to city standards. Hucks said that Council has discussed these situations several times over the last year or so. This amendment creates a limited and controlled framework to address these situations. It allows access through private roads and substandard roads, but only when: (1) Access is safe and adequate; (2) Fire requirements are met; and (3) the City can require improvements or deny development if needed. The amendment does not change standards for new development - private roads are not allowed for major subdivisions, public streets are still the standard, and the city will not maintain private roads. Hucks showed a real-world case and said that in this case, the road exists but it is not paved and is not a public road. Because ownership of the road is unclear, it can never be accepted by the City – regardless of any improvements made, and under the current ordinance, certificates of occupancy cannot be issues for any homes being built or that will be built in the future. With the proposed amendment, and with the required improvements to meet private road standards, these properties would have a path forward. This is an example of a platted street that was never constructed. Even one lot being developed would require the road to be constructed to City standards. In many of these areas – often involving inherited property – development is unlikely to occur under the current requirements. 266 -- 266 of 390 -- April 20, 2026 10 Hucks said that these examples are not isolated. As the City continues to annex property, particularly in rural areas, staff is seeing more of these situations. Even where design modifications could be granted, it doesn’t resolve the issue if the road is not public or cannot be dedicated. This amendment provides a path forward where today, there isn’t one. It allows reasonable use of property, maintains public safety, protects the city from long- term maintenance obligations – without changing requirements for major subdivisions. Hucks stated that Planning Commission held the public hearing on this amendment at their April 2 meeting and recommended approval and that staff also recommended approval. ATTACHMENT A Summary of CCU Housing (PDD) ORDINANCE # The CCU Housing PDD is located in Horry County, on South Carolina Highway 544. The project is approximately 6.81 acres and identified as PIN 382-12-04-0006 and 382-12-04-0005. The Planned Development envisions a student house community of multifamily housing and a variety of commercial uses to meet the needs of the existing and future residents of the City of Conway. The development will be accessed from Buccaneers Cove. Open space is varied and provided throughout the development in the form of passive and active features. Spatial and landscape buffer treatments around the perimeter and environmentally sensitive areas enhance and protect existing land uses, residents and the public. GENERAL PROVISIONS 1. Minimum Development Standards A. The proposed PD described herein contains 6.81 acres of land. Proposed improvements include a Mixed-Use Apartment building containing 199 residential units, clubhouse/amenity areas, and commercial space, as well as exterior recreational spaces. These improvements shall be constructed in a single phase. B. Development Standards i. Parking Requirements Paved parking spaces will be provided at a rate of 1.75 spaces per unit. A maximum of fifteen (15) consecutive parking spaces in a row shall be permitted without a landscape island or peninsula. Twenty-five percent (25%) of the required parking spaces may be compact spaces. No more than fifteen (15) compact car parking stalls shall be placed side by side or thirty (30) head-to-head. A maximum of 25% or the required parking may be located off-site. Additional parking for uses contained within the primary residential structure shall not be required. In the event uses are permitted independently and not within the primary Multifamily structure, parking requirements shall be consistent with that of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance. vi. Common Open Space Requirements A minimum of twenty-five percent (25%) of the buildable area of this PD shall be dedicated to active and passive open space. No more than 25% of pond surface area (if provided) may account for required open space. Clubhouses, courtyards, dog parks, pools, paseos, and roof-top amenities areas shall count toward Active Open Space Requirements in addition to those listed under Article 10 of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance. 288 -- 288 of 390 -- CCU Housing Planned Development District – PIN 382-12-04-0006 and 382-12-04-0005. 4. Support features may also include centralized mail delivery kiosks and recycling centers. During development various areas of the community will be targeted for sales with sales centers. These features and their associated parking areas shall not be subject to the landscaping and buffer requirements of Article V if located internal to the PD. 5. Access and Circulation Access to within the development will be via entry / exit off of Buccaneers Cove. Proposed vehicular use area is designed so that there are no cul-de-sacs or one-way traffic patterns. A sidewalk around the building and “paseo’s” at the building’s lower level will encourage walkability and pedestrian activity through and around the building. 6. ISSUE: First Reading and Public Hearing of Ordinance #2026-05-18 (A) to amend Article I – Redevelopment Enhancement Incentive Program, of the City of Conway Municipal Code, which provides economic incentives to develop or expand commercial businesses in the City of Conway, to expand the geographic applicability of the incentive to commercially zoned properties fronting Mill Pond Road and Sixteenth Ave. BACKGROUND: City Council previously adopted the Redevelopment Enhancement Incentive program to encourage reinvestment and economic activity along key commercial corridors within the City. The incentive currently provides for reimbursement of 100 percent of capital recovery fees for qualifying new or expanding businesses located on designated corridors. The existing ordinance applies to commercially zoned properties fronting Hwy 378 (Wright Blvd) and Hwy 701 (Main St./Fourth Ave). The proposed amendment expands eligibility to include additional corridors – specifically Mill Pond Rd and Sixteenth (16th ) Ave. This amendment is being considered in response to anticipated and ongoing commercial development activity along these corridors, which are emerging as important areas for growth and redevelopment within the City. ANALYSIS: The proposed amendment is limited in scope and does not alter the structure, eligibility requirements, or administration of the incentive program. Instead, it expands the geographic boundary in which the incentive may be applied. Mill Pond Rd and Sixteenth Ave are both strategically located corridors that provide connectivity to established commercial areas and are experiencing increased development interest. Extending the incentive to these areas is intended to: • Promote continued economic investment and redevelopment in emerging commercial corridors; • Encourage new business establishment and expansion in areas where infrastructure and accessibility support growth; • Maintain consistency in how the City incentivizes development across similarly situated commercial corridors; and • Support broader economic development goals by leveraging private investment. 303 -- 303 of 390 -- All other provisions of the ordinance remains unchanged, including: • Requirement for City Council approval of eligibility; • Execution of a formal agreement prior to issuance of a Certificate of Occupancy; • Reimbursement procedures and timelines; and • The three-year expiration period unless renewed by Council. STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends approval of first reading of the ordinance amending Article I of the City’s Municipal Code, as presented. The proposed expansion aligns with the City’s ongoing efforts to support targeted economic development and encourages reinvestment along key commercial corridors experiencing growth. ATTACHMENTS: Ordinance #2025-05-18 (A) (as proposed to be amended) 304 -- 304 of 390 -- ORDINANCE #2026-05-18 (A) AMENDING TITLE 1, CHAPTER 5, ARTICLE I – REDEVELOPMENT ENHANCEMENT INCENTIVE, OF THE CITY OF CONWAY MUNICIPAL CODE OF ORDINANCES, TO EXPAND THE APPLICABILITY OF THE INCENTIVE PROGRAM WHEREAS, the City of Conway has adopted a Redevelopment Enhancement Incentive program to encourage economic investment, redevelopment, and business growth along key commercial corridors within the City; and WHEREAS, the program provides for the reimbursement of capital recovery fees for qualifying new or expanding businesses located on designated commercially zoned properties; and WHEREAS, City Council has identified additional commercial corridors, including Mill Pond Rd and Sixteenth (16th ) Ave, as areas experiencing increased development activity and having the potential for continued economic growth; and WHEREAS, expanding the applicability of the Redevelopment Enhancement Incentive program to include these corridors will promote consistent economic development policies and encourage reinvestment in strategically important areas of the City; and WHEREAS, pursuant to applicable law and City procedures, City Council held a duly advertised public hearing on the ordinance amendment and provided an opportunity for public comment prior to taking action; and WHEREAS, City Council finds that the proposed amendment is in the best interest of the public health, safety, and welfare of the citizens of Conway by supporting economic development and enhancing commercial opportunities within the City. Now, therefore be it ORDAINED, by the City Council of the City of Conway, South Carolina, in meeting duly assembled, that Title 1, Chapter 5, Article I – Redevelopment Enhancement Incentive, of the City of Conway Municipal Code of Ordinances, shall be amended as attached hereto; and be it further ORDAINED, that all ordinances or parts of ordinances inconsistent with this Ordinance are hereby repealed to the extent of such inconsistency. EFFECTIVE DATE: This ordinance shall become effective upon adoption by City Council. 305 -- 305 of 390 -- RATIFIED BY CITY COUNCIL, duly assembled, this day of 2026. The property is located within the City’s utility service area, and development of the site will require connection to City water and sewer. The applicant has indicated an intent to develop the property for residential purposes consistent with the Medium-Density Residential (R-2) district, which permits a mix of residential dwelling types, including single-family detached, single-family attached, and multifamily housing. A portion of the property is located within a mapped flood hazard area, primarily along one side of the site, and extending across a small portion of the rear property line. At this time, no detailed site plan has been submitted. Given the presence of flood-prone areas, staff notes that this may present an opportunity to consider zoning these environmentally-sensitive portions of the property as Conservation Preservation (CP). This approach would be consistent with the City’s policy of protecting floodplain areas and could help avoid future development constraints or conflicts. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: The subject property is adjacent to a mix of institutional, residential, commercial, and undeveloped land: • To the rear: Conway High School (Institutional – IN) and two vacant parcels zoned Conservation Preservation (CP) • Along Radio Lane: properties zoned Highway Commercial (HC) and Low/Medium-Density (R-1) • All other adjacent properties are located in the County’s jurisdiction and zoned Highway Commercial (HC) and Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA). ORDINANCE: #ZA2026-07-20 (D) AGENDA SECTION: First Reading(s) ISSUE: Petition to annex approximately 17.87+/- acres of property located at 4183 Patterson Drive. APPLICANT(S): Joann Patterson Anderson, Agent PIN(s): 294-00-00-0024 CURRENT ZONING: Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) PROPOSED ZONING (upon annexation): Rural Residential (RR) BACKGROUND: The applicant is requesting annexation of the property in order to update the name associated with the City utility service account following the death of the property owner of record, Vetas Gowans. Documentation has been provided identifying the applicant as an heir to the property. Restrictive Covenants were recorded on April 16, 2026. The property contains an existing manufactured home and is located near Long Avenue Extension, just beyond Highway 813. Access to the property is provided via Patterson Drive, a county-owned roadway that appears to be unpaved and may not be constructed to public standards or accepted for maintenance. Patterson Drive connects to Derrick Lane, another unimproved county Rd. Under the City’s UDO, development of property requires frontage on a public street constructed to applicable standards and connected to a public street system. While the property already contains a residential dwelling, annexation into the City would subject the property to City development standards. Any future subdivision or additional development of the parent parcel would require that access be improved to meet those standards. Additionally, properties along Patterson Drive that may seek annexation in the future would be subject to the same requirements, should subdivision occur. As a result, annexation of the property at this time could create challenges related to roadway access, infrastructure improvements, and the consistent application of City standards, and may impose significant financial burdens on individual property owners seeking to develop similar properties. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: • The subject property is contiguous to an approximately 177.15+/- acre parcel annexed into the City in 2003 and zoned Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). 352 -- 352 of 390 -- STAFF REPORT First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-07-20 (D) • All other surrounding properties remain within Horry County and are zoned Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA). COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The future land use map designates the property as Rural Residential (RR). • RR District (Rural Residential) (Sec. 3.2.2): intended to preserve and expand areas for low-density single-family residential development, maintain a character, and ensure compatibility with surrounding uses. While the proposed zoning is consistent with the future land use map, the property’s access conditions present limitations relative to City development standards. PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION (and public hearing): If First Reading of the Ordinance to annex the property is approved, Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on the requested zoning upon annexation at their June 4, 2026 meeting. TRC RECOMMENDATION / COMMENTS: None at this time. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Staff recommends denial of the annexation request due to concerns regarding inadequate roadway access and the inability to meet City street standards. ISSUE: First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-15 (A) to amend Article 5 – Supplemental and Accessory Uses, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding requirements for mobile vending; specifically, to remove the cap on mobile vending permits and establishing revised administrative provisions. BACKGROUND: On July 21, 2025, the City Council adopted Ordinance #ZA2025-07-21(E), establishing a maximum of twenty (20) mobile vending permits for the 2026-27 fiscal year, with certain exemptions. On April 23, 2026, the annual cap was reached, effectively limiting the issuance of additional permits for the remainder of the current licensing cycle, which doesn’t start until May 1st . Since adoption, several challenges associated with the fixed cap have become evident: • Market Limitations: Once the cap is reached, otherwise qualified vendors are unable to operate within the City, limiting opportunities for small businesses and entrepreneurs. • Administrative Constraints: Modifying the number of permits currently requires a formal UDO amendment, which involves a multi-step legislative process and limits the City’s ability to respond to changing conditions in a timely manner. • Operational Flexibility: A fixed cap does not account for variations in staffing capacity, enforcement demands, or the availability of suitable vending locations throughout the year. The proposed amendment would remove the specific numerical cap from the UDO and instead establish a framework that allows the City to manage the number of permits administratively, based on defined operational and public safety considerations. PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission is scheduled to hold a public hearing regarding this amendment on June 4, 2026. STAFF RECOMMENDATION: The amendment is intended to provide greater flexibility in managing mobile vending activity while maintaining appropriate oversight to ensure compatibility with surrounding uses, public safety, and available resources. Under this approach, the annual number of permits would be determined administratively by the Planning Director, in coordination with the Zoning Administrator, and Fire Marshal, based on objective factors such as enforcement capacity, site availability, and operational impacts without requiring frequent legislative updates. The established permit availability would be published annually to ensure transparency and consistency with application. 380 -- 380 of 390 -- The framework allows the City to remain responsive to changing conditions while maintaining a structured and predictable process for applicants. Staff recommends approval of the proposed amendment to Article 5 of the UDO. ATTACHMENTS: Ordinance #ZA2025-07-21(E) Proposed administrative policy Proposed amendments to Sec. 5.1.16 of the UDO 381 -- 381 of 390 -- ORDINANCE #ZA2026-06-15 (A) AMENDING ARTICLE 5 – SUPPLEMENTAL AND ACCESSORY USES, OF THE CITY OF CONWAY UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE (UDO) REGARDING REQUIREMENTS FOR MOBILE VENDING PERMITS WHEREAS, Title 6, Chapter 29, of the Code of Laws of South Carolina 1976, as Amended known as the “South Carolina Local Government Comprehensive Planning Enabling Act of 1994,” enabled the City of Conway to adopt the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) of the City of Conway, South Carolina; and WHEREAS, Article 13, Sec. 13.1.7 of the UDO provides that the regulations, restrictions, and boundaries set forth in said Ordinance may from time be amended, supplemented, changed, or repealed in accordance with S.C. State Code 6-29-760; and WHEREAS, City of Conway adopted standards for mobile food vending in 2018 in response to the increasing popularity of mobile food vending; and WHEREAS, the City has experienced continued growth in mobile food vending applications in recent years; and WHEREAS, City Council desires to continue allowing mobile food vending while ensuring that such activity is conducted in a manner that protects public health, safety, and the general welfare of the community; and, WHEREAS, the existing numerical cap on mobile food vending permits has limited the City’s ability to respond to changing operational conditions, including staffing capacity, enforcement demands, and the availability of appropriate vending locations; and WHEREAS, City Council finds that establishing a flexible, criteria-based framework for determining permit availability will allow the City to more effectively manage mobile vending operations while maintaining appropriate oversight and consistency; and WHEREAS, following review and the required public hearing held by Planning Commission, it has been determined that Article 5 of the UDO should be amended to revise the requirements for mobile food vending. Now, therefore, be it ORDAINED, that the City Council of the City of Conway has determined that Article 5 – Supplemental and Accessory Uses of the Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) shall be amended as attached hereto; and be it further ORDAINED, that all ordinances or parts of ordinances inconsistent with this Ordinance are hereby repealed to the extent of such inconsistency. White, Council Member ATTEST: Alicia Shelley, City Clerk First Reading: 5/4/2026 Planning Commission Recommendation: Final Reading: 383 -- 383 of 390 -- 5.1.16 Mobile Vending The intent of this ordinance is to regulate how mobile food and beverage vendors sell food and / or non- alcoholic beverages to the public. A. Mobile vending shall be permitted with the following conditions. 1. The vendor shall obtain and carry at all times any SCDHEC (South Carolina Department of Health and Environmental Control) food handler and / or other applicable health safety licenses. 2. If the vendor wants to operate on public property or on private property under a special event permit, he or she shall obtain notarized written permission from the owner to conduct business. 3. The vendor shall obtain and carry at all times a valid City of Conway Business License. Vendors must obtain an annual zoning compliance. Food truck permits issued under this ordinance will be valid beginning on date of this Ordinance’s enactment until June 30 of the ensuing year. In the following year, a permit shall be from May 1 until April 30 of the ensuing year. [Amended 4-16-18 ZA# 2018-04-16 (B)] 4. The vendor can operate through an approved City of Conway Special Event Permit. Mobile vendors shall not be permitted to operate in the location of Special Event activities without the permission of the Special Event permit holder. 5. The vendor is subject to a background check by the Conway Police Department prior to issuance of a zoning permit. 6. The vendor shall provide a list of the items to be sold and shall be limited to selling food and non- alcoholic beverages. 7. All sales shall be made to pedestrians and bikers only. Vendors may not solicit or conduct business with persons in motor vehicles. 8. The vendor may use only music or bells to attract attention but shall not violate the noise ordinance regulations (City of Conway Code of Ordinances Sec. 9-1-21). 9. The vendor shall not operate in any manner that blocks, obstructs or restricts the free passage of vehicles or pedestrians in the lawful use of the sidewalks or highways or ingress or egress to the abutting property. The vendor shall maintain, at a minimum, four feet of passage for pedestrians and shall follow ADA (Americans with Disabilities Act) and ANSI (American National Standards Institute) Regulations. 10. Vending units shall be in compliance with all ANSI (American National Standards Institute) regulations. 11. The vendor shall be actively engaged in vending operations at all times while occupying any property. 12. The vendor shall pick up all refuse generated by his or her operation before the vending unit is moved. 13. All vending units must be self-contained with a waste receptacle. 14. The vendor shall not discharge items from any vending unit onto the sidewalk, gutter, storm inlets, streets, or planters. 15. The vendor shall keep the area surrounding their vending unit maintained in a safe, clean, orderly, and sanitary condition at all times. Mats shall be used in the food preparation area to keep the area clean. 16. No tables, chairs, fences, shade structures, or other site furniture shall be permitted. 17. Exterior storage or display of surplus refuse, equipment, materials, goods, wares, or merchandise associated with the vending unit shall be prohibited. 18. The vendor shall display, in plain view and at all times, current permits and licenses in or on their vending unit. 19. Any damage to landscape or vegetation caused by the mobile vending operation shall be immediately compensated by the vendor upon request of the City. 20. The vendor shall provide the location of an appropriate storage facility where the vending unit is when not in operation. 384 -- 384 of 390 -- 21. Excluding properly licensed dining establishments located within the City limits of Conway, as well as mobile food vending units operating in conjunction with a special event permit, The number of mobile food vending permits issued annually shall be limited to a maximum of twenty (20) each year, from May 1 st – April 30 th , and shall be done on a first-come, first-serve basis determined administratively based on the City’s capacity to effectively manage, inspect, and enforce mobile vending operations, as well as the availability of suitable locations and considerations of public health, safety, and welfare. The Planning Director, in coordination with the Zoning Administrator and Fire Marshal, shall establish the number of permits to be issued for each licensing cycle. The total number of permits available shall be published to ensure transparency and consistency. The procedures for application submission, prioritization, and waitlist management shall be established through administrative policy consistent with this Section. a. Application Completeness Applications for a mobile food vending permit shall be complete at the time of submittal. Partial or Incomplete applications will not be accepted or processed. b. Renewal Applications for Renewal of a previously issued permit does shall not guarantee that such permit will be approved or reserved approval or reservation of a permit for any subsequent licensing cycle. c. Exemptions The administrative determination of permit availability shall not apply to: i. Properly licensed dining establishments located within the City limits of Conway; ii. Mobile vending units operating in conjunction with an approved Special Event permit; or iii. Mobile vending units operating under an approved franchise agreement with the City. B. Transient Mobile Vending. In addition to the requirements in Sec. 5.1.16 A, transient mobile vending shall be permitted in the R, RA, RR, R-1, R-2, R-3, R-4, IN, HI, and LI Zoning Districts and legitimate construction sites only with the following conditions: 1. The vending unit shall not stop within 300 feet of any school, religious institution, or cemetery. 2. The vending unit shall only be stationary for a maximum of 30 minutes per stop and move at least one block before making another stop. 3. The hours of operation shall be anytime between sunrise and sunset. 4. The vehicle shall park legally. 5. The vending unit shall not stop in congested areas where it may impede or inconvenience the public or create a traffic hazard. 6. No door-to-door solicitation shall occur. 7. The vending unit shall incorporate flashing lights or signage indicating frequent stops of the vehicle. 8. Transient mobile vending may be permitted on City Property in the zones referenced in this section with the written approval of City Council. [ZA2018-12-17(A)] C. Franchise Mobile Vending. In addition to the requirements stated in Sec. 5.1.16, A, franchise mobile vending shall be permitted on Public Property in the CBD, CC, WRD, and City Parks with the following conditions: 1. Shall be granted through a franchise agreement approved by Conway City Council. 2. City Council shall determine the hours of operations. 3. City Council shall determine the approved location(s) of the vending unit. 385 -- 385 of 390 -- 4. Vendors shall not store, park, or leave any vending unit overnight on any public property. 5. The vendor shall complete a release and indemnification agreement, which will hold the City of Conway harmless for any loss, liability or damage, including expenses and costs, for bodily or personal injury, and for property damage sustained by a person as a result of the negligent installation, use, or maintenance of a permitted public space within the City of Conway. 6. The vendor shall submit a Certificate of Insurance verifying the following minimum coverage and specifically identifying the City of Conway as an additional insured. The mobile vendor will not be permitted to operate without a Certificate of Insurance. The City of Conway must be listed as the “Certificate Holder” on the Certificate of Insurance. Minimal acceptable coverage: a. Each Occurrence: $1,000,000 b. Personal Injury: $1,000,000 c. General Aggregate: $2,000,000 D. Vending on Private Property. In addition to the requirements stated in Sec. 5.1.16, A, mobile vending shall be permitted on private property in the CBD, CC, WRD, P, IN, NC, HC, LI, HI, and commercial areas of PD with the following conditions: 1. A letter and/or copy of an official lease agreement from the property owner to vend on the subject parcel must be obtained. 2. No vendor shall operate within 150 feet from the principal public entrance to any food service business, unless the adjacent food service business owner provides a notarized letter agreeing to the lesser distance. If a food services business opens within the zone after the vending unit has continuously operated the business in the location for at least 6 months, the vending unit may remain in that location. 3. The vending unit shall meet a 15’ front setback from the property line, a 10’ clearance between units, 10’ from any fire hydrant, and a 10’ emergency access setback between the unit and any buildings. If adjacent to a residential area, then the vending unit must meet the side and rear property setback requirements of its underlying zoning district. 4. A list of all requested vending sites, including property owners and physical addresses, must be provided to the City. The applicant must submit a site plan, to scale, for all proposed locations of the vending operation(s) for Commercial Plan Review by the Technical Review Committee (TRC). 5. A minimum of two (2) parking spaces must be provided per vending unit and maintained in addition to the minimum parking required for the principal business (except in the CBD, CC, and WRD Zoning Districts). 6. The vending units are to be located only on parcels with no less than a paved 30 feet driveway (except in the CBD, CC, and WRD Districts). 7. The maximum number of vending units per parcel: a. For parcels up to 10,000 sq. ft., up to two vending units may be permitted at a time; b. For parcels more than 10,000 sq. ft. and less than 20,000 sq. ft., up to three vending units may be permitted at a time; c. For parcels greater than 20,000 sq. ft. in size, a maximum of 4 vending units is permitted at the same time (with the exception of city-sponsored or special events). 8. Each vending unit may submit multiple location sites, subject to staff approval. Commercial plan review fees will apply to each location. [ZA#2018-04-16 (B); ZA2019-03-18(B)] E. Appearance. The appearance of vending units shall be approved by the Planning Department with the following conditions: 1. The vendor shall be responsible to ensure that the vending unit is in good condition, free from evidence 386 -- 386 of 390 -- of deterioration, weathering, discoloration, and rust. 2. Advertising consisting of the name and logo, and a listing of items available for sale may be displayed on the vending unit. No other form of advertising or signs shall be allowed. Additionally, the vendor shall follow the requirements in Sec. 11.2.2, Prohibited Signs, of the UDO. 3. If already constructed, the vendor shall submit three photographs and the dimensions of the vending unit. If not constructed, the vendor shall submit a copy of the plans and color renderings of the vending unit. 4. A vendor shall be entitled to appeal the decision of the Planning Department to revoke or deny a permit based on the appearance of the vending unit by submitting a Conway CAB (Community Appearance Board) Application. Appeals must be filed within thirty (30) days from the date the notice of revocation or denial is issued. The basis for the appeal must be included in the request for an appeal. 387 -- 387 of 390 -- City of Conway Administrative Policy: Mobile Vending Permit Management PURPOSE The purpose of this policy is to establish a clear and consistent framework for the issuance and management of mobile vending permits within the City of Conway. The policy is intended to implement the requirements of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) by providing procedures for determining permit availability, processing applications, and managing permit allocation. By administering permit volumes through this policy, the City seeks to remain responsive to operational capacity, public safety considerations, and market conditions, while maintaining a fair, transparent, and predictable process for applicants. This policy does not create a right to a permit and shall not be interpreted as guaranteeing issuance to any applicant. ANNUAL PERMIT DETERMINATION 1. Capacity Review Prior to April 30 of each year, the Planning Director, in coordination with the Zoning Administrator and Fire Marshal, shall determine the number of mobile vending permits to be issued for the upcoming licensing cycle. 2. Evaluation Criteria This annual permit availability shall be based on the following factors: a. Availability of suitable vending locations on public and private property b. Administrative capacity for application review, inspections and enforcement c. Public health and safety considerations d. Feedback from the local business community, including organizations such as Conway Downtown Alive. 3. Public Notice The total number of permits available for the licensing cycle shall be published on the City of Conway Business License webpage prior to the opening of the application period. APPLICATION & ISSUANCE PROCEDURES 1. Submission Window Applications for permit renewals and new permits shall open 30 days prior to the expiration of the current licensing cycle. 2. Prioritization Process a. Renewals 388 -- 388 of 390 -- Existing permit holders in good standing, with no unresolved code violations, shall be provided a defined priority period to submit renewal applications. b. New Applicants Following the renewal period, any remaining permits shall be issued to new applicants on a first-come, first-served basis, based on complete application submittals. 3. Waitlist Management If the number of complete applications exceeds the number of permits available, the City shall maintain an official waitlist. Applicants will be placed on the waitlist in the order in which complete applications are received. Permits that become available due to non-renewal, revocation, or withdrawal shall be offered to waitlisted applicants in order of placement. OPERATIONAL COMPLIANCE All mobile vending permit holders shall comply with applicable provisions of the Unified Development Ordinance and all other applicable local, state, and federal regulations, including but not limited to: 1. Maintaining a current food safety inspection report from the South Carolina Department of Agriculture (SCDA), as applicable. 2. Maintaining general liability insurance in accordance with the South Carolina Business License requirements (see SC Business License Handbook) and as specified in the UDO. 3. Proper waste management, including the removal of all trash and debris generated within a 25- foot radius of the vending unit. MID-CYCLE ADJUSTMENTS The number of permits established for a licensing cycle may be adjusted during that cycle only in response to documented: 1. Public safety concerns 2. Infrastructure or site capacity limitations 3. Significant changes in administrative or enforcement capacity. Any such adjustment(s) shall be documented in writing and made publicly available through the City’s website or other official means. POLICY ADMINISTRATION This policy shall be administered by the Planning Director or designee and shall be applied in a consistent and non-discriminatory manner. Administrative procedures established under this policy shall remain consistent with the requirements of the Unified Development Ordinance. 389 -- 389 of 390 -- DATE: MAY 4, 2026 ITEM: VII. ISSUE: Request by Impact Church to use a City-owned building leased to A Father’s Place BACKGROUND: A Father’s Place currently leases a city-owned building at 1800 Racepath Avenue. Pending approval from their board, Impact Church, which was previously housed inside the former Jamestown Baptist Church is requesting to enter into a revocable facility use agreement with A Father’s Place. City staff do not have the authority, per the lease, to authorize the agreement as such approval would need to come from council. Impact Church is proposing the following: • A Father’s Place would retain full control and oversight of the facility at all times • The use would be non-exclusive and limited to specific days/times • There would be no transfer of possession or lease rights • The arrangement would be structured as a revocable facility use agreement, not a sublease RECOMMENDATION: Approve A Father’s Place to enter into a revocable facility use agreement with Impact Church 390 -- 390 of 390 --

PUBLIC HEARING/FIRST READING Public Hearing and first reading of Ordinance #2026-05-18 (A) amending the City of Conway Municipal Code to update Article I the Redevelopment Enhancement Incentive Program, which provides economic incentives to develop or expand commercial businesses in the City of Conway. Dennis stated that City Council previously adopted the Redevelopment Enhancement Incentive program to encourage reinvestment and economic activity along key commercial corridors within the city. The incentive currently provides for reimbursement of 100 percent of capital recovery fees for qualifying new or expanding businesses located on designated corridors. The existing ordinance applies to commercially zoned properties fronting Highway 378 and Highway 701. The proposed amendment expands eligibility to include additional corridors – specifically Mill Pond Road and Sixteenth Avenue. This amendment is being considered in response to anticipated and ongoing commercial development activity along these corridors, which are emerging as important areas for growth and redevelopment within the city. There was some discussion about whether it would be beneficial to add more areas to the program at this time. Goldfinch suggested incentivizing commercial uses in residential areas. Emrick said that this could be addressed in the future land use re-write which is close to being looked at. White asked which areas of Sixteenth Avenue. Dennis explained those with commercial zoning. White asked if the residents would be notified. Dennis said yes, those within 200 ft. There was no public input. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Blain to close the public hearing. Vote: Unanimous.
