First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-15 (A) to amend Article 5 – Supplemental and Accessory Uses, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding requirements for mobile vending permits; specifically, to remove the cap on mobile vending permits and establishing revised administrative provisions. Hucks stated that last year Council adopted a cap of 20 mobile vending permits per year, which excluded those which had a franchise agreement with the City, those that were approved as part of a special event permit, and those that were also properly licensed dining establishments in the city limits. The original cap proposed by staff was 40, but Planning Commission recommended reducing the cap to 20; in which staff recommended approval of to Council, with the caveat that those exceptions just mentioned be carved out in the ordinance. Hucks said that Horry County has a limit of 50 mobile food vending permits annually (per Art. 9 – conditional uses, Sec. 913, B.3.f.), and Myrtle Beach limits theirs to 20 annually, so when Conway set the cap at 20, it was in line with what other jurisdictions were doing, but also based on our staffing capacity at the time. The City’s cap of 20 permits was established with consideration of the regional benchmarks, as well as local staffing capacity and operational constraints. The initial cap was driven by staff capacity and overall market balance. Staff has since learned that while those concerns are still valid – having a fixed number may not be the most effective way to address them, as it is a little too rigid. This amendment addresses those concerns, but instead of a fixed cap, the number of mobile vending permits to be issued annually will be determined administratively, based on the City’s capacity to effectively manage, inspect and enforce mobile vending operations, as well as the availability of suitable locations and considerations of public health, safety and welfare. Administrative procedures will be provided in the application packet for a mobile vending permit, and applicants will be required to acknowledge them as part of the process. -- 8 of 13 -- May 4, 2026 9 That way the process is transparent and consistently applied. These procedures will also be available on the City’s website. Hucks stated that Planning Commission will still have to hold a public hearing on the amendment, which is set for their June meeting, but staff does recommend approval of the amendments to the mobile vending ordinance. If council approves first reading of the amendment, State law requires that zoning regulations be applied as adopted until formally amended; however, council could direct staff to process applications that have been received that are currently waitlisted in the interim. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by White to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-06-15 (A) removing the cap on mobile vending permits and establishing revised administrative provisions. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. CONSIDERATION: Consideration of approval of a request by A Father’s Place to enter into a revocable facility use agreement with Impact Church – Rogers stated that A Father’s Place currently leases a city- owned building at 1800 Racepath Avenue. Pending approval from their board, Impact Church, which was previously housed inside the former Jamestown Baptist Church, is requesting to enter into a revocable facility use agreement with A Father’s Place. City staff does not have the authority, per the lease, to authorize the agreement as such approval would need to come from council. Impact Church is proposing the following: (1) A Father’s Place would retain full control and oversight of the facility at all times; (2) The use would be non-exclusive and limited to specific says/times; (3) There would be no transfer of possession or lease rights; and (4) The arrangement would be structured as a revocable facility use agreement, not a sublease. Blain had concerns especially with the city being short on space. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Hardwick to deny the request for A Fathers Place to enter into a revocable facility use agreement with Impact Church. The proposed amendments would establish new or additional standards and restrictions for new and/or existing regulated commercial uses, including, but not limited to, vape/smoke/tobacco shops, alternative financial services (i.e. payday loan/title loan/cash advance services), gas/service stations -- 9 of 13 -- May 4, 2026 10 (with or without convenience store), outdoor event facilities/spaces, and other high impact uses in the City of Conway. Final reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (P), to amend Article 2 – Definitions, Article 4 – Use Tables, and Article 14 – Boards and Procedures, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding the adoption of a Special Exception process and uses in which a special exception will be required. Final reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (Q), to amend Article 12 – Nonconformities, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding the re-establishment of certain uses that require Special Exception approval. Hucks said that this item was requested to be moved from consent to briefly explain a minor revision to the nonconformities section, specifically related to nonconforming advertising signs. The original amendments were intended to clarify how damage to a nonconforming sign is evaluated, but after further discussions with legal counsel it was determined that it was still possible that the language could be interpreted in different ways. Hucks said that the revised language does not change the policy or intent of the ordinance, it only provides clearer more objective standards for determining when these types of nonconforming signs can no longer be rebuilt and must comply with current sign regulations. The revisions also reduce ambiguity, limit discretionary interpretation, and ensure that the ordinance is aligned with state law. Huck said that in short, the clarifications make the ordinance more defensible and easier to administer. The overall amendments to Article 12 remain unchanged, and Planning Commission’s recommendation as well as staff’s recommendation of approval still stands. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Hardwick to approve final reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (Q) as revised. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. ISSUE: Final reading of Ordinance #2026-04-20 (C), an ordinance granting a distribution right-of-way easement to the South Carolina Public Service Authority (Santee Cooper) across property of the City of Conway adjacent to Sherwood Road (PIN 338-00-00-0024). BACKGROUND: The McKeithan Watershed Project, funded by the South Carolina Office of Resiliency (SCOR) in 2025, is approaching its final stages. As construction nears completion, planning is underway for landscaping, recreational features, and site lighting. Public Works staff have recommended the installation of Santee Cooper streetlights along the walkways, as well as electrical connections to support seasonal and holiday decorations. The proposed fixtures would match the lighting currently used in nearby developments and throughout the downtown area, ensuring visual consistency and enhancing public safety. To proceed with this work, the City must grant Santee Cooper a distribution right-of-way. The required easement would extend the full length of the distribution lines and measure 20 feet in width—10 feet on each side of the cable centerline. Establishing this easement provides the necessary clearance for energized lines, ensures access for maintenance vehicles, and protects utility infrastructure. The easement would be perpetual and would authorize Santee Cooper to enter the property as needed to operate, maintain, and service its equipment. Easements are required of property owners within the subject work area, which includes the City of Conway for the property adjacent to Sherwood Road (PIN 338-00-00-0024). City Council approved first reading of Ordinance #2026-04-20 (C) at their March 16, 2026 meeting. Technology Upgrades 1. Description of the Issue The City of Conway Police Department proposes to address a critical technology and operational gap within the Detective Division by replacing end-of-life desktop computers and obsolete field tablets with five rugged tablet computers and docking stations. Detectives currently rely on a mix of stationary desktops and older tablets that are past their useful life, frequently fail, and cannot reliably support modern, data-intensive investigative applications. This forces detectives to shuttle between the office and the field to access records and complete reports, increases administrative backlog, and reduces the timeliness and completeness of digital evidence capture. These limitations also constrain real-time information sharing with partner agencies and reduce situational awareness during field operations, which can adversely affect officer and community safety. This request aligns with the FY25 JAG NOFO’s allowable uses for equipment and technology improvement programs and the program goal to “improve the administration of the criminal justice system.” Funding the proposed equipment directly supports law enforcement program needs and will enable the department to modernize investigative workflows while complying with JAG statutory and administrative requirements. 15 -- 15 of 421 -- 2 Identified gaps and impacts • Mobility gap: Office desktops provide full functionality but no mobility; current tablets lack processing power, secure management, and reliable connectivity. • Operational delays: Investigative report turnaround and evidence documentation are delayed by device failures and the need to return to the office. • Security and compliance risk: Older devices lack modern endpoint protections and centralized device management, increasing risk to sensitive investigative data. • Cost inefficiency: Maintaining two aging device classes (desktops + tablets) increases IT support, maintenance, and replacement costs. Addressing these gaps will reduce administrative burden, improve case processing times, and strengthen officer safety and investigative outcomes. 2. Project Design and Implementation Requested items and total cost: Five (5) rugged tablet computers with docking stations and required accessories; device configuration and deployment services. Project purpose: Replace end-of-life desktops and obsolete field tablets with a single, secure, mobile platform that supports both office and field investigative workflows. Activities and timeline (Months measured from award start) 1. Procurement (Month 0–1) o Conduct competitive procurement per City and Federal purchasing rules. 16 -- 16 of 421 -- 3 o Purchase five rugged tablets, five docking stations, and required accessories and licenses. 2. Configuration and Integration (Month 1–2) o City Technology Services and vendor image devices; install RMS/CAD client, NCIC access tools, mobile reporting software, MDM agent, and endpoint protection. o Configure VPN, encryption, and role-based access controls. o Test integration with Records Management System and CAD. 3. Training and Policy Update (Month 2) o Deliver a training session for detectives and supervisors covering device operation, evidence capture best practices, secure data handling, and mobile reporting. o Update department policies for device use, chain-of-custody for digital evidence, and acceptable use. 4. Deployment (Month 2–3) o Assign devices to five detectives; install vehicle/desk docks where applicable; begin routine field use for crime-scene documentation, on-scene report writing, and real-time database queries. 5. Restrictive Covenants for the subdivision were recorded on May 6, 1988. The property currently contains a single-family dwelling and a detached garage. Properties located to the side and rear of the parcel are already within the City limits. Rezoning is being requested as a requirement of an annexation request in order to obtain a new connection to City utilities. In addition to the property receiving municipal utility services, annexation of the property brings the parcel into the City’s planning and zoning jurisdiction, consistent with surrounding properties. The requested zoning upon annexation is Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1), which is consistent with the City’s future land use map. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: Two (2) adjacent parcels fronting Maplewood Circle were annexed into the city in 2020 and 2024 and are also zoned R-1. The parcel located directly behind the subject property is owned by the City of Conway and located within the city limits. Two (2) properties directly across Maplewood Circle remain in Horry County’s jurisdiction. The surrounding area is primarily developed with single-family residential uses. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s future land use map identifies the property as Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). Per Section 3.2.3 of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), the intent of the R-1 district is to preserve and expand areas for low- to medium-density detached single-family residential development within the City of Conway. The district is intended to maintain a relatively spacious 140 -- 140 of 421 -- STAFF REPORT First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (E) residential character, promote quiet and livable neighborhoods, and prohibit uses incompatible with the surrounding residential environment. PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION: Planning Commission held the required Public Hearing and voted to recommend approval of the proposed zoning at their April 2nd meeting. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Approve First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (E) to rezone the subject property to R-1. The applications in this instance appear to be signed by the person listed as the designated agent according to the Secretary of State (Business Filings) website. A copy of the business filing with the registered agent is included in this packet. Staff has no way to dispute otherwise. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: Properties along this portion of E. Hwy 501 and is currently within Horry County’s jurisdiction. This parcel contains an existing commercial business (Skyline Signs) as well as a manufactured home located on the same property. Available records indicate the manufactured home has been present on the site since approximately 2006. Staff has not yet been able to confirm whether the manufactured home was originally permitted as a residential use under County regulations. In 2022, Horry County approved a plat combining two of the parcels associated with the property, resulting in the commercial business and the manufactured home being on the same parcel. The manufactured home is currently vacant. According to the applicant, annexation is being required in order to obtain municipal utility services, which the owner has indicated would allow the existing manufactured home to be used as a legal residence. City records indicate that water was last turned on the structure in September 2025 but was disconnected due to nonpayment. Under Horry County’s Highway Commercial zoning district, single-family (site built) residential uses are permitted; however, manufactured homes are not. Under the City’s Unified Development Ordinance, the Highway Commercial district does not permit residential uses at all, and manufactured homes are not permitted uses in the City under any zoning district. The proposed zoning upon annexation is the Highway Commercial (HC) district. However, since applying for annexation, the applicant has contended the application, stating that he does not wish to be annexed, and that his assistant signed the application, unaware of what was being signed or the purpose. When applicants are sent to the Planning & Development Department (P&D Dept.) in order to apply for annexation as a requirement of the City Utility Dept., they are provided thorough information as to why the annexation is being required, what the P&D Dept.’s role is in the annexation, and many times, applicants must leave and come back at a later time with the appropriate paperwork and/or 167 -- 167 of 421 -- STAFF REPORT First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (G) signatures, which may also include a Designation of Agent (DOA) form; however, a DOA is only required when the property owner(s) is not the person(s) signing the application The applications in this instance appear to be signed by the person listed as the designated agent according to the Secretary of State (Business Filings) website. A copy of the business filing with the registered agent is included in this packet. Staff has no way to dispute otherwise. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: Properties along this portion of E. Hwy 501 are developed with highway-oriented commercial as well as industrial uses, including retail, automotive services, manufactured home sales, a sign company, and other commercial businesses. Adjacent City zoning is Highway Commercial. The neighboring properties were annexed in 2025 as Highway Commercial (HC) and one fronting Amber Lane as Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). Adjacent County zoning includes Highway Commercial (HC), Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA), and a mix of residential zoning types. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s Future Land Use Map designates the property as Highway Commercial (HC). Per Section 3.2.10 of the UDO, the intent of the HC district is to provide compatible locations to serve the automobile oriented commercial activities in harmony with major highway developments, reduce traffic congestions and to enhance the aesthetic environment of the City. Assigning HC zoning upon annexation is consistent with both the Future Land Use Map and the existing development pattern along Highway 501. PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION: Planning Commission held the required Public Hearing and voted to recommend approval of the HC district upon annexation at their April 2, 2026 meeting. STAFF ANALYSIS: Annexation decisions are based on logical municipal growth, service provision, and consistency with the Comprehensive Plan. The zoning district applied upon annexation must follow the Future Land Use Map, which designates the properties along this corridor as Highway Commercial (HC). Staff supports annexation of the property as it would extend the City’s municipal boundaries in a logical manner. However, it is important to note that under the City of Conway UDO, the HC district does not permit residential uses, including manufactured homes. If annexed and assigned HC zoning, the manufactured home currently located on the property would be considered nonconforming to the City’s zoning regulations. As such, the structure could remain on the property as a nonconforming structure, but its use would be subject to the City’s regulations 168 -- 168 of 421 -- STAFF REPORT First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (G) governing nonconforming uses and structures. Whether the manufactured home can used for residential purposes is dependent on how the UDO would treat this nonconforming use. If the structure was “lawfully” established, meaning the structure was legally permitted by the County, then the residential use could continue as a “legal” nonconforming use. If the structure was never legally permitted, it is considered illegal, not nonconforming and illegal uses cannot be continued. Rezoning the property to a residential use would not be consistent with the City’s Future Land Use Map or the established Highway Commercial development pattern along the Highway 501 corridor. Annexation of the property does NOT constitute approval of any specific use of the property. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Approve First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (G) to rezone the subject property to HC upon annexation. ISSUE: First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (O) to amend Article 2 – Definitions, Article 4 – Use Tables, and Article 5 – Specific Use Regulations (proposed to be renamed “Supplemental and Accessory Uses), of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding revisions to permitted and conditional uses in various zoning districts. The proposed amendments revise the classification and regulation of certain commercial uses across multiple zoning districts. The amendments establish updated and new definitions, clarify use classifications, and implement additional use-specific standards and location-based restrictions for certain higher-impact uses, including, but not limited to: tobacco/vape/smoke shop establishments, alternative financial services (e.g., payday loan/title loan/cash advance/check-cashing services), gas/service stations (with or without convenience stores), outdoor event facilities/spaces, and similar uses. BACKGROUND: Over the past several months, staff has evaluated how certain commercial uses are regulated, particularly within the Highway Commercial (HC) zoning district and along key commercial corridors. The effort was initiated following a rezoning request involving property zoned HC and located adjacent to an established single-family residential neighborhood. While the request was ultimately denied, it highlighted broader concerns that some zoning districts currently allow higher-intensity commercial uses without sufficient standards when located near residential areas. In response, staff reviewed the Use Tables in Article 4 of the UDO and standards for certain uses in Article 5 to identify uses that: • Are permitted by right without additional standards; and • May create impacts such as traffic, noise, lighting, and extended hours of operation that are not always compatible with nearby residential uses. Staff also reviewed regulatory approaches used by comparable municipalities to identify appropriate tools for Conway. ANALYSIS: The proposed amendments establish a more consistent and targeted framework for regulating certain commercial uses. Major changes include: Article 2 – Definitions: • Updates and adds definitions to reflect current business operations; • Clarifies distinctions between similar or overlapping uses (e.g., gas stations vs. convenience stores) 235 -- 235 of 421 -- • Ensures uses are classified based on primary business activity, not business name or signage Article 4 – Use Tables: • Clarifies that only uses specifically listed are permitted • Establishes a consistent process for classifying similar or unlisted uses • Reclassifies certain uses to ensure appropriate oversight (e.g., permitted to supplemental or accessory) • Improves alignment between use classifications and applicable standards Article 5 – Supplemental and Accessory Uses (formerly “Specific Use Regulations”) • Renames and restructures the Article to focus on objective, use-specific standards • Implements location-based criteria, including separation requirements and proximity to residential areas • Adds standards addressing operational and site impacts (e.g., traffic, lighting, hours of operation) • Applies Special Exception review in limited circumstances where site-specific conditions warrant additional evaluation Nonconformities • Existing lawful uses may continue as legal nonconforming uses • Re-establishment of certain uses muse comply with current standards, including separation and location requirements. Housekeeping amendments: • Improves clarity, consistency, and internal alignment across multiple sections of the UDO. REGULATORY APPROACH The proposed amendments take a targeted approach to regulation. Rather than prohibiting uses, the amendments: • Establish objective standards to address potential impacts; • Apply separation requirements where appropriate to prevent overconcentration; • Introduce location-based criteria, particularly near residential areas; and • Use Special Exception review selectively to address site-specific conditions. CONSISTENCY WITH COMPREHENSIVE PLAN The proposed amendments are consistent with the goals of the City’s Comprehensive Plan, including: • Protection of established residential neighborhoods; • Promotion of compatible land use patterns; 236 -- 236 of 421 -- • Improved development and redevelopment of commercial corridors; and • Support for balanced and sustainable growth. ADDITIONAL INFORMATION These amendments provide clearer standards and improved tools to address location-specific impacts, rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach to all properties. The proposed amendments revise how certain commercial uses are defined, classified, and regulated across multiple zoning districts. The amendments focus on uses that may have greater potential for land use impacts. The amendments are intended to address compatibility concerns without eliminating uses that are otherwise appropriate in commercial zoning districts. The complete text of the proposed amendments are included for your review. PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing and voted to recommend approval of the proposed amendments at their April 2, 2026 meeting. Such determinations may be relied upon in the interpretation and administration of this Ordinance. Applicability Conditional The provisions of this Article establish supplemental Uses use and development standards applicable to certain uses shall be permitted within the zoning districts of the City. These standards address subject use-specific characteristics and a determination by the Planning Director that such use(s) conform(s) to all potential site impacts that are not fully addressed by base district regulations. Uses subject to Supplemental Use Standards, as identified in Article 4 – Use Tables, shall comply with the applicable regulations provisions set forth herein of this Article in addition to all other applicable requirements for that specific use and of the zoning district in which such the use is proposed to be located. Applications to construct or alter conditional uses shall be processed in accordance with the standards set forth herein for permitted uses. Applicable conditional uses shall be shown in Article 4, Use Tables. Uses lawfully established prior to the adoption of these standards that do not conform to the requirements of this Article shall be considered legal nonconforming and shall be subject to the provisions of Article 12 – Nonconformities, including the limitations on re-establishment of discontinued or nonconforming uses. Where this Article references zoning districts by name or by use category (e.g., residential zoning districts), such references shall be interpreted in accordance with Article 4 – Use Tables. Uses described as permitted in districts where a principal residential use is allowed shall include all zoning districts in which such residential use is permitted. Nothing in this Article shall be construed to authorize the re-establishment of a use that has lost its legal nonconforming status, except in accordance with Article 12. B. Relationship to Zoning District Regulations. The supplemental use standards in this Article apply in addition to the regulations of the district in which the use is located. Compliance with these standards shall not exempt a use from meeting all other applicable requirements of this Ordinance. C. Administrative Review and Special Exception Approval. Where expressly provided in this Article or identified in Article 4 – Use Tables, certain uses or site In addition to the conditions may require administrative review or special exception approval by the Board of Zoning Appeals in order to evaluate and mitigate site-specific impacts. set forth in this Article, the Planning Director and/or the Technical Review Committee (TRC) may require additional provisions reasonable as deemed necessary to protect the health, safety, and welfare of the general public. Such review shall be conducted in accordance with the applicable provisions of Article 14 – Board and Procedures. Special exception approval shall be based on the applicable criteria set forth in Article 14, in addition to any applicable use-specific standards identified in this Article. 5.1.1 Adult Entertainment Establishments Adult entertainment establishments include, but are not limited to: cabarets, bookstores, drive-in theaters, theaters, peep shows, adult model studios, sexual encounter centers, escort services and motels, as defined herein, and any other establishment which contains activities characterized by the performance, depiction or description of “specified sexual activities”, or “specified anatomical areas”. Adult entertainment establishments shall be permitted as conditional uses in the Light Industrial (LI) and Heavy Industrial (HI) districts provided the following requirements standards are met: A. Number. No more than one (1) adult use as classified above shall be located on any lot. B. Location. Adult entertainment establishments shall not be located closer than: 1. 1,000 feet from residential zoning districts or residential use in the City of Conway (R, RA, RR, R-1, R-2, R- 3, R-4, or residential within a MU or PD Zoning District) or equivalent residential zoning districts or use in 307 -- 307 of 421 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 5 –Specific Supplemental and Accessory Uses Regulations 5-4 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended XX Horry County. [ZA2018-12-17(A)] 2. 1,000 feet from any religious institution, day care facilities, public or private education facility, Community Support Services / Facility, Outpatient Treatment Facility, public park, public library, cemetery, or any motion picture establishment which shows G or PG rated movies to the general public on a regular basis. [ZA2019-04-01(D)] 3. 2,000 feet from any other adult use, provided that this shall not apply to any establishment or cabaret that does not provide adult entertainment more than twelve (12 times per calendar year). 4. Basis of Measurement. Distances shall be measured in a straight line from the closest property line of the parcel in which the proposed use is located to the closest property line of the parcel containing the protected use or zoning district, without regard to intervening structures, rights-of-way, or property ownership. C. Ownership Disclosure. If a person who applies to operate an adult entertainment business is an individual, he must sign the application for a permit as applicant. If a person who applies to operate an adult entertainment business is other than an individual, each individual who has a ten (10%) percent or greater interest in the business must sign the application for a permit and/or license as applicant. If a corporation is listed as owner of an adult business, or as entity which wishes to operate such business, each individual having a ten (10%) percent or greater interest in the corporation must sign the application for a permit and/or license as applicant. All corporate officers shall also sign the application. The fact that a person possesses other types of state or county permits and/or licenses does not exempt him from the requirements of obtaining a sexually oriented business permit and/or license. D. Sale and/or Consumption of Alcohol Prohibited. The sale and/or consumption of alcoholic beverages in conjunction with any adult entertainment establishment shall be prohibited. E. An adult entertainment establishment shall neither employ nor permit the admittance / patronage of any person who is under 18 years of age. F. Inspections. The management of any adult entertainment establishment shall permit representatives of the Police, Fire, Construction Services, Planning/Development Department or other City or State Agencies to inspect the premises at any time it is open for business. G. Revocation of Zoning Compliance. The Planning Director shall revoke a Certificate of Zoning Compliance, thereby suspending the operation of any adult entertainment establishment, for any of the following: 1. The giving of false or misleading information by the applicant at any time in the application process; 2. For the illegal sale of any controlled substance on the premises; 3. For the arrest and conviction of any owner or employee (unless said employee is discharged immediately) for any violation of Title 44 of the Code of Laws of South Carolina, 1976 as amended, relating to controlled substances; and/or violation of any State or Federal crime involving moral turpitude and/or violation of Title XVI, Chapters 3, 15, 23, and 25 of the Code of Laws of South Carolina, 1976, as amended; and/or for the arrest and conviction of any owner or employee for any violation of Title 16 of the Code of Laws of South Carolina, 1976, as amended; 4. Failure to permit inspections by authorized City and State agencies or personnel; 5. Violation of the age restrictions as set forth herein. H. Exterior Portions of Regulated Establishments. 1. It shall be unlawful for an owner or operator of a regulated establishment to allow the merchandise or activities of the regulated establishment to be visible from any point outside such regulated establishment. 2. It shall be unlawful for the owner or operator of a regulated establishment to allow the exterior portions of the regulated establishment to have flashing lights, or any words, lettering, photographs, silhouettes, drawings, or pictorial representations of any manner except to the extent permitted by the signage 308 -- 308 of 421 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 5 –Specific Supplemental and Accessory Uses Regulations 5-5 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended XX provisions of this section and Article 11. 3. It shall be unlawful for the owner or operator of a regulated establishment to allow exterior portions of the regulated establishment to be painted any color other than a single achromatic color. This provision shall not apply to any regulated establishment if the following conditions are met: a. The regulated establishment is a part of a commercial multi-unit center; b. The exterior portions of each individual unit in the commercial multi-unit center, including the exterior portions of the regulated establishment are painted the same color as one another or are painted in such a way so as to be a component of the overall architectural style or pattern of the commercial multi-unit center. 4. Nothing set forth herein shall be construed to require the painting of an otherwise unpainted exterior portion of a regulated establishment. I. Signage. 1. It shall be unlawful for the owner or operator or any regulated establishment or any other person to erect, construct, or maintain any sign for the regulated establishment other than one sign as provided herein. 2. Signs shall have no more than two (2) display surfaces. Each such display surface shall : a. Not contain any flashing lights; b. Be a flat plane, rectangular in shape; c. Not exceed twenty-five (25) square feet in area or greater than 5% of the façade wall; and d. Not exceed eight (8) feet in height. 3. ISSUE: First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (P) to amend Article 2 – Definitions, Article 4 – Use Tables, and Article 14 – Boards & Procedures, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding the adoption of a special exception process and uses in which a special exception will be required. BACKGROUND (updated): This amendment is a companion to a related set of amendments addressing use classifications and supplemental standards within Articles 2, 4 and 5 of the UDO. As part of that broader effort, staff evaluated the need for a formal Special Exception process to address certain uses that, while appropriate within a zoning district, may have the potential to create site-specific impacts depending on location and operational characteristics. A Special Exception is a permitted use within a zoning district that requires case-by-case review to evaluate potential impacts, such as traffic generation, operational intensity, noise, lighting, and compatibility with surrounding properties. The purpose of the special exception process is to provide a structured and consistent mechanism for evaluating these impacts in accordance with established ordinance criteria. A special exception: • Is a permitted use within an applicable zoning district; • Is not a variance from dimensional or development standards; • Does not authorize a use that is otherwise prohibited; • Requires a finding that the proposed use complies with applicable ordinance standards and will not result in demonstrable adverse impacts; and • May be approved with reasonable conditions directly related to identified impacts and necessary to ensure compliance with the UDO. If adopted, the special exception process would require an applicant, where specified in the Use Table or in Article 5, to obtain approval from the Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA) following a duly noticed public hearing conducted in accordance with Article 14. Evaluation of Uses: As part of this process, staff evaluated a range of uses to determine whether Special Exception review was appropriate, including bed and breakfast establishments, outpatient treatment facilities, alternative financial services, adult entertainment establishments, body piercing and tattoo establishments, tobacco/vape/smoke shops, taverns/bars/nightclubs, and gas/service stations. 360 -- 360 of 421 -- STAFF REPORT Amendment(s) to Articles 2 – Definitions, 4 – Use Tables, & 14 – Boards & Procedures The evaluation focused on whether existing ordinance standards – such as separation requirements, operational limitations, and location-based criteria – were sufficient to address potential impacts, or whether additional discretionary review would provide a meaningful benefit. Based on this analysis, staff determined that certain uses are already adequately regulated through objective standards and do not warrant additional special exception review. These include adult entertainment establishments, taverns/bars/nightclubs, tattoo and body piercing establishments, bed and breakfast establishments, and outpatient treatment facilities, all of which are subject to existing locational, operational, and/or separation requirements within the UDO. Conversely, for selected uses, the special exception process provides an additional layer of review to address site-specific conditions that cannot be fully anticipated through objective standards alone. Proposed amendments: The proposed amendments to Articles 2, 4 and 14: • Establish a formal Special Exception process within the UDO; • Define the scope and criteria for Special Exception review; • Identify specific uses and circumstances under which special exception approval is required; and • Clarify the role of the Board of Zoning Appeals in evaluating such requests based on established criteria. These amendments are intended to work in coordination with the updated Use Table (Art. 4) and Supplemental and Accessory Use standards (Art. 5), creating a consistent framework in which: • Uses are clearly classified; • Objective standards are applied where appropriate; and • Discretionary review is used selectively to address site-specific impacts. Consistency with the Comprehensive Plan: The proposed amendments are consistent with the goals and policies of the City’s Comprehensive Plan, including: • Protection of established residential neighborhoods; • Promotion of compatible land use patterns; and • Implementation of regulatory tools that support balanced and context-sensitive development. ISSUE: First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (Q) to amend Article 12 – Nonconformities, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding the re-established of certain uses that require special exception approval under the UDO. This amendment clarifies how nonconforming uses are discontinued, establishes a narrowly defined process for -establishment in limited circumstances, and ensures consistency with related amendments to Articles 2, 5, 6, 10 and 14 of the UDO. BACKGROUND: Article 12 of the UDO establishes regulations for nonconforming uses, lots, and structures. Nonconformities occur when a property or use was lawfully established but no longer complies with the current zoning regulations. As part of the City’s broader effort to modernize and clarify the UDO, staff conducted a comprehensive review of Art. 12 to address inconsistencies, improve clarity, and ensure alignment with recently proposed amendments – particularly those related to supplemental use standards in Art. 5 and the establishment of a formal Special Exception process (Art.14). These amendments are intended to create a more consistent, enforceable, and predictable framework for the treatment of nonconforming uses while reinforcing the City’s broader zoning policies. Summary of Proposed Amendments: 1. Discontinuance and Re-establishment of Nonconforming Uses • Retains the 180-day discontinuance standard for nonconforming uses. • Clarifies that inactivity – rather than the maintenance of a business license alone -determines whether a use has been discontinued. • Establishes a narrowly defined process for re-establishment through Special Exception approval by the Board of Zoning Appeals. • Requires all of the following: o Lawful prior establishment of the use o Demonstration of hardship beyond the property owner’s control o No increase in intensity, density, or impacts • Limits any re-established use 373 -- 373 of 421 -- STAFF REPORT Amendments to Article 12 - Nonconformities 2. Separation-Based and Location-Restricted Uses • Confirms that uses rendered nonconforming due to separation requirements, location restrictions, or special exception standards may continue as legal nonconforming uses. • Establishes that once such uses are discontinued, they may not be re-established unless they comply with current ordinance requirements. • Ensures consistency with recently proposed standards for higher-impact uses. 3. Change in Ownership • Clarifies that a legal nonconforming use may continue despite a change in ownership, tenancy, or business name, provided the use has not been discontinued. 4. Nonconforming Lots of Record • Confirms that lawfully created lots that do not meet current dimensional standards may still be used. • Requires the combination of commonly owned adjacent lots where necessary to meet minimum standards. 5. Nonconforming Structures and Sites • Clarifies provisions for expansion, reconstruction, and modification of nonconforming structures. • Ensures that improvements do not increase the degree of nonconformity. • Establishes consistent expectations for site elements such as access, parking, landscaping, and buffering. 6. Damage and Reconstruction Standards • Establishes a consistent reconstruction threshold: o Structures damaged 50% or less may be rebuilt to prior nonconforming conditions. o Structures damaged greater than 50% must be brought into full compliance. 7. Nonconforming Signs • Updates and modernizes sign provisions. • Removes outdated material-specific standards. • Clarifies allowances for maintenance, repair, and replacement. 8. General Clarifications and Housekeeping • Improves organization, terminology, and internal consistency. • Aligns Art. 12 with Art. 5 and Art. 14. 374 -- 374 of 421 -- STAFF REPORT Amendments to Article 12 - Nonconformities • Eliminates redundant or conflicting language. ANALYSIS The proposed amendments strengthen Art. 12 by establishing a clear and consistent framework for determining when nonconforming uses may continue, be discontinued, or be re-established. These amendments: • Clarify the circumstances under which nonconforming uses may be re-established and limit that process to narrowly defined hardship situations; • Ensure that uses subject to separation requirements or location restrictions cannot be re- established once discontinued; • Eliminating ambiguity regarding the role of the Board of Zoning Appeals and reinforce its quasi- judicial function; • Prevent the expansion or intensification of nonconforming uses over time while allowing reasonable relief in limited cases. Overall, these updates improve clarity, consistency, and enforceability, while supporting the City’s ability to manage uses with greater potential impacts. [ZA2012-09-04 (A)] 390 -- 390 of 421 -- STAFF REPORT Amendments to UDO (ART.’s 2, 6, 7, 10, and 12) regarding private streets and access to substandard roads COUNCIL MTG DATE: April 20, 2026 AGENDA ITEM: VI.H. ISSUE: First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (R), to amend Article 2 – Definitions, Article 6 – Design Standards, Article 7 – Street Design and Circulation, Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development, and Article 12 – Nonconformities, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), establishing standards for private streets and access to substandard roads in the City of Conway. This amendment in intended to address existing lots of record that lack adequate frontage on a public street accepted for maintenance by the City, County, or State, and to establish regulations for development proposed on roads not constructed to City standards. BACKGROUND: The City’s current UDO requires all lots to front on a public street constructed to City standards and accepted for public maintenance. While this requirement is appropriate for new subdivisions, it has created challenges in situations involving: • Lots of record created prior to adoption of the UDO; • Properties annexed into the City that are served by private or substandard roads; • Existing roads that were assumed to be public but were never formally dedicated; • Roads under the jurisdiction of other entities that do not meet City standards; and • Parcels lacking adequate frontage due to historic platting patterns. Under the current ordinance, these properties may be unable to obtain building permits or certificates of occupancy unless a public street is constructed to full City standards. In many cases, this requirement is impractical due to cost, ownership constraints, or existing development patterns. These situations are becoming more frequent as the City continues to annex property and encounter legacy development patterns that were established prior to current regulations. ANALYSIS The proposed amendment establishes a coordinated framework across multiple sections of the UDO to address these conditions while maintaining the City’s standards for new development. This amendment maintains public streets as the required standard for new and major subdivisions and provides a limited, controlled framework for addressing existing conditions. 391 -- 391 of 421 -- STAFF REPORT Amendments to UDO (ART.’s 2, 6, 7, 10, and 12) regarding private streets and access to substandard roads Key Components of the Amendment 1. Definition of Private Road (Article 2) Adds a definition clarifying that private roads are not publicly maintained and are not part of the City street system unless constructed to City standards and formally accepted. 2. Frontage Requirement Modification (Article 6) Revises the requirement that all lots must front on a public street to allow access via private roads or access easements in limited circumstances, as governed by Article 10. 3. Street Design Consistency (Article 7) Updates existing provisions to remove the blanket prohibition on private roads and instead allow them only where specifically permitted by Article 10. Private roads remain prohibited for major subdivisions. 4. Subdivision Regulations (Article 10) Creates a new Section 10.10 – Private Streets and Access to Substandard Roads, which: • Allows private roads only in limited circumstances, such as lots of record and annexed properties; • Establishes minimum design and safety standards, including fire access requirements; • Requires recorded maintenance agreements and clarifies that the City has no maintenance responsibility; • Prohibits the use of private roads for major subdivisions; • Provides administrative approval authority for individual lots of record; and • Establishes standards for development accessing substandard roads, including the ability to require improvements or deny development where adequate access cannot be provided. • Requires improvements to substandard roads or allows denial of development where adequate access cannot be achieved, including for roads maintained by other jurisdictions. 5. Nonconforming Lots (Article 12) Clarifies that legally created nonconforming lots of record may be developed, including those lacking frontage, provided access is established in accordance with Sec. 10.10. PURPOSE AND INTENT The proposed amendment is intended to: • Address longstanding issues related to access for legally created lots of record; 392 -- 392 of 421 -- STAFF REPORT Amendments to UDO (ART.’s 2, 6, 7, 10, and 12) regarding private streets and access to substandard roads • Provide a clear and consistent framework for evaluating development on private or substandard roads; • Maintain public safety through minimum access and fire standards; • Protect the City from long-term maintenance obligations associated with private roads; and • Preserve existing requirements for public streets in new and major subdivisions. This amendment does not reduce development standards for new subdivisions and does not permit private roads as an alternative to required public infrastructure for new or major development. IMPACTS Positive Impacts • Provides a practical solution for development of existing lots lacking public frontage; • Reduces the need for case-by-case exceptions or informal interpretations; • Improves clarity and consistency in the UDO; • Enhances public safety by establishing minimum access standards; • Protects the City from assuming maintenance of substandard or private roads. • Reduces potential long-term financial exposure associated with premature acceptance or maintenance of substandard infrastructure. Potential Concerns • Perception that private roads are being broadly permitted (mitigated by limitations within the ordinance); • Requires careful administrative review to ensure compliance with access and safety standards. PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing and voted to recommend approval of the proposed amendments at their April 2, 2026 meeting. Private streets shall not be approved where extension of a public street is reasonably feasible. 3. No further subdivision of lots served by a private streets shall be permitted unless such street is upgraded to City standards. 4. Private streets shall not be used to avoid the construction of public streets where such streets are otherwise required. E. Minimum Standards Private streets shall meet the following minimum requirements, unless otherwise approved by the City: 1. Minimum travel surface width: Twenty (20) feet. 2. All-weather driving surface capable of supporting emergency apparatus vehicles. 3. Adequate drainage shall be provided. 4. Turnaround facilities where required. 5. Compliance with applicable fire access requirements. 398 -- 398 of 421 -- Amendments to Articles 2, 6, 7, 10 and 12 regarding standards for private roadways F. Maintenance 1. Private streets shall be maintained by the property owner(s), homeowners’ association, or other responsible entity. 2. A recorded maintenance agreement shall be required prior to final plat approval or issuance of building permits, as applicable. 3. The City shall have no responsibility for maintenance, repair, or reconstruction of private streets and roads. 4. Public and/or non-exclusive utility easements may be required separate from or atop the roadway/access easement area, as needed. G. Plat Requirements 1. All private streets shall be clearly identified on plats with the following note: “Private street/road– not maintained by the City of Conway.” 2. Language will be required to express; the scope of use, the permanent nature of the easement, the applicable parties responsible for maintenance and cite the tenants (lots/parcels) to whom the easement is being assigned. 3. Easements for access shall meet applicable setbacks from any structures (existing or future) and shall be located in an area where travel-lanes, shoulders and drainage facilities are not obstructed. H. Administrative Approval The Planning & Development Director, or their designee, may approve private street access for individual lots of record or minor subdivisions where compliance with public street requirements would create an undue hardship due to existing conditions. Certificate of Occupancies (CO’s) for new residents will not be issued until required improvements are inspected and approved. I. Acceptance as Public Streets Private streets shall not be accepted into the City street system unless constructed or improved to meet all applicable City standards in effect at the time of dedication. 10.10.2 Access to Substandard Roads A. Applicability This section shall apply to development proposed to be accessed by a street that: 1. Is not constructed to City standards; 2. Is not publicly maintained; 3. Has unknown or unclear ownership, but clear tenant rights have been established; or 4. Is otherwise determined by the City to be substandard. B. General Requirement 1. Development shall not be approved unless safe and adequate access is provided. Access via a substandard road may be permitted only when the City determines that such access is sufficient to serve the proposed development or can be improved to meet minimum standards acceptable by the City. 2. Approval of access to a substandard road shall not be construed as acceptance of such road for public maintenance. C. Required Improvements The City may require improvements to a substandard road as a condition of development approval, including but not limited to: 1. Widening of the travel surface; 399 -- 399 of 421 -- Amendments to Articles 2, 6, 7, 10 and 12 regarding standards for private roadways 2. Construction of Auxiliary Turn Lanes, 3. Installation of an all-weather surface; 4. Drainage improvements; 5. Turnaround facilities; 6. Intersection improvements; 7. Additional access points where necessary for public safety. D. Fire Access All development served by a substandard road shall comply with applicable fire access requirements. Approval from the Fire Department may be required prior to issuance of permits. E. Limitations 1. The City may limit the number of lots or intensity of development served by a substandard road. 2. The City may deny development where adequate access cannot be provided. 3. Major Subdivisions and Substandard Roads a. Major developments shall not be approved where primary access is proposed via a substandard road, including roads maintained by another governmental entity, unless such road is improved to meet minimum standards (as determined by the Technical Review Committee) for access and public safety prior to or concurrent with development. b. Where such access is proposed, the applicant shall be responsible for securing all necessary approvals from the applicable jurisdictions and completing required improvements as a condition of development approval. F. Coordination with Other Jurisdictions Where access is provided via a road under the jurisdiction of another governmental entity, the applicant may be required to obtain approval from that entity for any necessary improvements. ISSUE: Consideration of Acceptance of a Bid for the Laurel Street Stormwater Upgrades Construction Contract BACKGROUND: The City received grant funding to improve the stormwater and water line infrastructure on Laurel St. between 3rd Avenue and 4 th Avenue through the South Carolina Rural Infrastructure Authority (SCRIA). This project includes: • Installing proposed stormwater, water, and wastewater infrastructure on Laurel St. as called out in the plans provided by AECOM. • This project consists of installing RCP ranging in sizes from 18” to 24” along with the installation concrete drainage boxes to add additional capacity and resiliency to the City’s stormwater system. The project also consists of extending a newly installed waterline and connecting in at 4th Ave. The City of Conway advertised publicly to select a firm to construct the Laurel St. Stormwater Upgrades. Proposals were required to be submitted to the city no later than March 26, 2026. Five firms submitted proposals. The bids received were: 1. Hardee Construction Services, LLC - $1,546,391 2. Green Wave Contracting, INC - $2,289,285 3. R.H. Moore Company, INC - $2,632,861 4. PSI of Conway, LLC - $2,768,608.20 5. Coastal Asphalt, LLC - $3,083,806 RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends the lowest responsible bidder, Hardee Construction Services, LLC, to construct Laurel Street Stormwater Upgrades upon RIA approval. 417 -- 417 of 421 -- DATE: APRIL 20, 2026 ITEM: VII.B. ISSUE: Purchase and install removable bollards at McCray Alley and Hiland Ave. BACKGROUND: Years ago, at the request of the Police Department, Public Works installed a large concrete barricade to prevent cut-through traffic along McCray Alley at Hiland Avenue as part of an effort to reduce crime in the area. At the time, cut-through traffic had been identified as a contributing factor to criminal activity. Since the installation of the barricade, crime in the surrounding area has decreased. However, the size and placement of the barricade have resulted in pedestrians walking around it and onto adjacent private property. Residents have expressed concerns regarding the increased and unwanted foot traffic through their yards. To address these concerns, it has been proposed that the existing barricade be removed and replaced with removable bollards. The bollards would continue to restrict vehicular access from Hiland Avenue while allowing pedestrians to pass through safely without entering private property. Installation would require five bollards across the opening at an estimated cost of approximately $6,000, including materials and labor. RECOMMENDATION: Approve the purchase and installation of removable bollards on McCray Alley at Hiland Ave. for approximately $6,000 utilizing the Council Contingency Fund. 418 -- 418 of 421 -- DATE: APRIL 20, 2026 ITEM: VII.C. ISSUE: Award of Contract - Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) System BACKGROUND: On March 3, 2026, the City received six (6) proposals for a citywide Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) system. The AMI system will modernize meter reading through real-time, two-way communication technology and will be implemented over 5–10 years. Key benefits include: • Real-time usage data for improved customer service • Faster leak detection, reducing water loss and high bills • Remote service capabilities, reducing field visits • Lower labor, fuel, and operational costs • Improved system management through better data This project represents a significant upgrade to the City’s utility system, improving efficiency, reducing long-term costs, and enhancing service to residents. Four (4) City employees evaluated and scored the proposals based on cost, system capabilities, compatibility, vendor experience, and overall value. Proposals ranged from approximately $313,000 to $5.9 million, reflecting differences in system scope, technology, and long-term capabilities. The recommended vendor was selected based on overall value and performance, not solely cost. RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends awarding the contract to Ferguson Waterworks in partnership with Sensus Meters as the most responsive and responsible proposal. 419 -- 419 of 421 -- 420 -- 420 of 421 -- DATE: APRIL 20, 2026 ITEM: VII.D. ISSUE: New LED Video Wall for the Terrace. BACKGROUND: The Terrace currently uses a projector and vinyl screen for movie nights which is outdated and difficult for citizens to see, these events have become very popular, and a new solution is recommended. This LED Video Wall will place a permanent outdoor Live display that can not only show movies in high definition but also can display various events around the City as a digital message board. Bids not including tax: − DVS: $39,235.34 14’-9”x 8’x3” 3.99P 5yr Warranty − LEDNation: $32,437.00 16’-3”x 9’x6” 2.97P 5yr Warranty − Techled: $23,989.00 15’-7”x 9’-3” 3.99P 3yr Warranty The DVS and LEDNation displays are permanently fixed walls fully serviceable from the front. The TechLed Wall is an outdoor “rental” unit. While this was a Council request for FY 26/27, there are some remaining funds in the Hospitality Fee Fund, which could be used to allow the purchase now, so the screen can be utilized this summer. RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends purchasing the LEDNation Video wall due to the size, best resolution, and 5 year warranty using Hospitality Funding. 421 -- 421 of 421 --

title: CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES 4.20.26
text: April 20, 2026 1 CITY OF CONWAY CITY COUNCIL MEETING CONWAY CITY HALL 229 MAIN STREET, CONWAY MONDAY, APRIL 20, 2026 PRESENT: Mayor Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor Pro Tem Beth Helms, Amanda Butler, William Goldfinch, Julie Hardwick, Justin Jordan, Larry White. STAFF: Adam Emrick, City Administrator; Mary Catherine Hyman, Deputy City Administrator; June Wood, Public Information Officer; Jeff Leveille, Technology Services Director; Jason Perzan, Fire Chief; Reggie Jenerette, Solid Waste Director; Robert Cooper, Construction Services Director; Ted Dudley, Public Utilities Director; Jessica Hucks, Planning and Development Director; Brandon Harrelson, Public Works Director; Dale Long, Police Chief; Timmy Williams, Hospitality and Beautification Director; Ashley Smith, Parks and Recreation Director; Kelli Thomas, Deputy PIO; Bobby Wallace, Fleet Maintenance Director; Jeff Edwards, Stormwater Manager; Charlotte Peterson, Assistant Planner; Nancy Alvarez, Assistant Planner; and Alicia Shelley, City Clerk. OTHERS: There were approximately 30 others in attendance. CALL TO ORDER: Mayor Blain called the meeting to order. INVOCATION/PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE: Blain gave the invocation and led the Pledge of Allegiance. Blain asked all in attendance to join in a moment of silence in memory of Kevin Chestnut, former Public Works Director of the City of Conway. The requirements for posting notice of this meeting under South Carolina’s Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) were met. CONSENT AGENDA: A. Final reading of Ordinance #2026-04-20 (C), an ordinance granting a distribution right-of-way easement to the South Carolina Public Service Authority (Santee Cooper) across property of the City of Conway adjacent to Sherwood Road (PIN 338-00-00-0024). B. Approval authorizing staff to apply for the FY2025 Edward Byrne Memorial Justice Assistance Grant (JAG) Program C. Approval of special event – 2026 Conway Riverfest – June 27, 2026 D. Acceptance of a bid for purchase of air compressor for the Fleet Services Department -- 1 of 15 -- April 20, 2026 2 E. Approval of a Resolution accepting dedication of roadways & drainage, and the financial guarantee for the roadway warranty for the Elmhurst Place subdivision (Rockwood Drive, Woodbrook Drive, Danby Lane, and Collinwood Drive). F. Approval of a Resolution accepting dedication of roadways & drainage, and the financial guarantee for the roadway warranty for the Hemingway Landing Phase 1A subdivision (Starlight Drive and Parkside Court). G. Approval of a Resolution accepting dedication of roadways & drainage, and the financial guarantee for the roadway warranty for the Kingston Oaks Phase 1B subdivision (King Oaks Loop, Water Oaks Way). H. Approval of special event – 4th Annual Youth Performing Arts Festival – September 26, 2026 I. Approval of a Resolution accepting dedication of roadways and drainage for the Sanctuary at Wild Wing subdivision (Sanctuary Boulevard and Willet Cove). J. Approval of March 16, 2026 City Council Meeting Minutes APPROVAL OF CONSENT AGENDA: Motion: Butler made a motion, seconded by White to approve the April 20, 2026 consent agenda. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. SPECIAL PRESENTATION: A. Employee of the month for March 2026 – Public Safety – Long presented the March 2026 Public Safety Employee of the Month award to Senior Master Police Office Jonathan Brown. B. Presentation of Longevity Awards – March 2026 – 5 Years: Evan Cullipher, Recreation; 5 Years: Zane Jones, Public Utilities; 25 Years: Amber Lewis, Police; 30 Years: Derrick Turner, Public Works; 30 Years: Reginald Hill, Police. Emrick and Butler presented the longevity awards (Cullipher, Turner and Hill were absent). C. Presentation of a Proclamation recognizing May 2026 as Lupus Awareness Month D. Presentation of a Proclamation recognizing May 2026 as ALS Awareness Month – Blain read aloud the Proclamation recognizing May 2026 as ALS Awareness Month. E. Presentation of a Proclamation recognizing Ella Sheppard as the 2026 South Carolina Girls’ Wrestling Champion (105 Pounds) – Blain presented Ella Sheppard with a proclamation as the 2026 South Carolina Girls Wrestling Champion in the 105-pound weight class. F. Presentation of a Proclamation recognizing Emma Sheppard as the 2026 South Carolina Girls’ Wrestling Champion (110 Pounds) – Blain presented Emma Sheppard with a proclamation as the 2026 South Carolina Girls Wrestling Champion in the 110- pound weight class. -- 2 of 15 -- April 20, 2026 3 G. Presentation by The Rotary Club of Conway – Steve Perry of the Conway Rotary Club presented the City Police Department with a $1,500 check to purchase equipment and thanked the city for their help with the Reindeer Run that is held by the Rotary Club every year. First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (O), to amend Article 2 – Definitions, Article 4 – Use Tables, and Article 5 – Specific Use Regulations, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding revisions to Permitted and Conditional uses in various zoning districts. The proposed amendments would establish new or additional standards and restrictions for new and/or existing regulated commercial uses, including, but not limited to, vape/smoke/tobacco shops, alternative financial services (i.e. payday loan/title loan/cash advance services), gas/service stations (with or without convenience store), outdoor event facilities/spaces, and other high impact uses in the City of Conway. First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (P), to amend Article 2 – Definitions, Article 4 – Use Tables, and Article 14 – Boards and Procedures, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding the adoption of a Special Exception process and uses in which a special exception will be required. First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (Q), to amend Article 12 – Nonconformities, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding the re-establishment of certain uses that require Special Exception approval. -- 7 of 15 -- April 20, 2026 8 Hucks stated that these amendments have been discussed with council at prior workshops as well as at budget retreat so she said she would be as brief as possible. The 2 amendments are related and work together to update how certain commercial uses are defined, regulated and reviewed within the UDO. They are the result of a broader effort by staff over the past year. The process was initiated following a rezoning request for property zoned Highway Commercial, located adjacent to an established single-family neighborhood. While that request was ultimately denied, it highlighted broader concerns with how certain higher impact commercial uses are currently regulated – particularly when located near residential areas. In response, staff conducted a comprehensive review of the UDO to determine whether additional tools were needed to better address compatibility moving forward. Hucks said that the first amendment focuses on how uses are defined, classified and regulated and it will do the following: (1) Update definitions to reflect modern business operations; (2) Clarifies the use table so that only listed uses are permitted; (3) Applies supplemental standards rather than conditional designations for high impact uses and additional restrictions for other higher impact uses such as vape/smoke/tobacco shops, alternative financial services such as payday loans, check cashing, title loans, gas/service stations, and a new use category – outdoor event facilities or spaces. Outdoor event facilities will include standards for event size, event frequency, noise, and location, along with a requirement for special exception review to ensure compatibility with surrounding properties. Hucks said that the second amendment established the special exception review process through the Board of Zoning Appeals. This applies in limited situations where a use may be appropriate within a zoning district, but its location or surrounding context warrants additional review. This is not a variance, and it is not a rezoning. The use remains permitted, but the Board of Zoning Appeals evaluates site-specific impacts and apply reasonable conditions when necessary to ensure compatibility. Hucks said that the third amendment addresses how these regulations apply to existing uses. Existing, lawful uses can continue, however if discontinued uses that are subject to separation requirements or special exception requirements must comply with current standards of the UDO before the use can be re-established. This ensures that nonconforming situations are reduced over time. Hucks stated that the amendments also include housekeeping provisions and the addition of uses not previously defined or listed in the Use Table. These updates improve clarity, consistency, and alignment across the UD). These amendments do not prohibit uses, they clarify how uses are classified, apply targeted standards based on impacts, introduce limited additional reviews where appropriate, and provide a long-term framework for compatibility. The goal is to be a more predictable and balanced system that supports development while protecting established neighborhoods. Hucks said that Planning Commission held public hearings on the proposed amendments at previous Planning Commission meetings, and recommended approval with minor -- 8 of 15 -- April 20, 2026 9 revisions and those revisions were incorporated and provided to Council. Hucks said that staff also recommended approval. Hucks further explained the use tables/charts. First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (R), to amend Article 2 – Definitions, Article 6 – Design Standards, Article 7 – Street Design & Circulation, Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development, and Article 12 – Nonconformities, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance, to establish standards for private roadway in the City limits. The amendments proposed are intended to address existing lots of record that lack adequate frontage on a public street accepted for maintenance by the City, County, or State, and to establish regulations for development proposed on roads not constructed to City standards. Hucks stated that this amendment addresses a growing issue that the city is seeing with properties that were legally created or annexed into the City but do not have the required frontage on a public street constructed to City standards. Under the current ordinance, every lot must front a public street accepted for public maintenance – whether that is the county, state or city. This requirement works well for new subdivisions, but for older lots or annexed properties, it creates a situation where – even if a road exists – the property cannot be built on unless that street is constructed to full city standards. In many cases, that’s simply not practical due to cost, ownership, or existing conditions. Hucks showed a couple of slides of typical road profiles and existing streets and explained what they look like today and would look like being built to city standards. Hucks said that Council has discussed these situations several times over the last year or so. This amendment creates a limited and controlled framework to address these situations. It allows access through private roads and substandard roads, but only when: (1) Access is safe and adequate; (2) Fire requirements are met; and (3) the City can require improvements or deny development if needed. The amendment does not change standards for new development - private roads are not allowed for major subdivisions, public streets are still the standard, and the city will not maintain private roads. Hucks showed a real-world case and said that in this case, the road exists but it is not paved and is not a public road. Because ownership of the road is unclear, it can never be accepted by the City – regardless of any improvements made, and under the current ordinance, certificates of occupancy cannot be issues for any homes being built or that will be built in the future. With the proposed amendment, and with the required improvements to meet private road standards, these properties would have a path forward. This is an example of a platted street that was never constructed. Even one lot being developed would require the road to be constructed to City standards. In many of these areas – often involving inherited property – development is unlikely to occur under the current requirements. -- 9 of 15 -- April 20, 2026 10 Hucks said that these examples are not isolated. As the City continues to annex property, particularly in rural areas, staff is seeing more of these situations. Even where design modifications could be granted, it doesn’t resolve the issue if the road is not public or cannot be dedicated. This amendment provides a path forward where today, there isn’t one. It allows reasonable use of property, maintains public safety, protects the city from long- term maintenance obligations – without changing requirements for major subdivisions. Hucks stated that Planning Commission held the public hearing on this amendment at their April 2 meeting and recommended approval and that staff also recommended approval. Goldfinch asked why the streets in the new neighborhoods can’t be private and give the city an easement. There was some discussion and Emrick said staff would research and bring back to council. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by White to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04 (R), amending the UDO to establish standards for private roadway in the City limits. Blain - Said that the Chamber Salute to Education reception was on March 18 and that Jordan’s daughter was the scholarship recipient. - Mentioned several events and commended all on jobs well done – March 20 was the Chris Ray celebration thanked Perzan and Jarrett Wallace, March 25 was the Citizens Academy, March 31 was a celebration at Conway High School for the Sheppard twins for winning the State Championships in wrestling, and April 11 was the sports jamboree at the Rec Center. - Repeated things that were said today that made a lot of sense to her: Pride in your community is infectious and local pessimists overpower nonvocal optimists. WORKSHOP: Wetland Buffer Requirements – Edwards informed Council that jurisdictional wetland buffers are still under the EPA and Army Corps of Engineers but nonjurisdictional wetland buffers are no longer protected. Edwards said that City of Conway wetland buffers are no longer protected therefore staff proposed that nonjurisdictional wetland buffers be 50 feet with the minimum of 30 feet. Edwards said that jurisdictional wetland buffers are 30 feet. -- 14 of 15 -- -- 15 of 15 --

Each parcel contains a single-family dwelling. Properties directly across Cottage Lane and to the rear of the subject parcels are already within the City limits. Annexation is being requested in order to connect to City utility services, following a name change associated with the existing City utility service account. The applicant requested that the properties be zoned Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) upon annexation. However, the City’s Future Land Use Map identifies the area as Highway Commercial (HC). Because of this designation, staff does not support assigning residential to the properties and recommends that the properties be zoned Highway Commercial (HC) upon annexation to maintain consistency with the Comprehensive Plan and the surrounding land use pattern. Although the parcels are currently developed with single-family homes, the HC zoning district would not require removal of the existing residences. The homes would be allowed to continue as legal nonconforming residential uses, but expansion of the residential use in the future would be limited, if not prohibited, under the HC district (i.e. could not expand outside of the existing building footprint). SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: The properties are bordered on two sides by parcels already located within the City limits and zoned HC. Adjacent properties immediately to the sides are vacant lots, while properties across Cottage Lane and to the rear include commercial uses such as fast-foot establishments and other highway-oriented businesses, all zoned HC within the City limits.
