Motion carried. SPECIAL PRESENTATION: A. Presentation of Employee of the Month for January 2026 – Public Service – A. Smith presented Tristan Casper with the Employee of the Month award. B. Presentation of the 2025 City of Conway Audit Report - Nathan Skipper, Smith Sapp CPAs – Nathan Skipper of Smith Sapp CPAs gave a brief overview of the independent auditor’s report regarding the City’s Annual Comprehensive Financial Report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2025. FIRST READING: A. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-02-02 (C) to rezone approximately 0.22 +/- acres of property located at 250 Chevy Chase Drive (PIN 367-13-01-0031) from the Horry County Residential, including mobile homes (MSF10) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district upon annexation. Hucks stated that first reading of the ordinance to annex this property was approved at the December 1, 2025 council meeting, which is required in accordance with city requirements for connection to utility services. The property is currently zoned Horry County MSF10, which is a residential district that includes manufactured homes on minimum lot sizes of 10,000 square feet. The requested zoning upon annexation is R-1, which is consistent with the zoning of other properties that have been annexed in recent years, as well as the city’s future land use map. Hucks said that Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the proposed zoning of the property at their January 8, 2026 meeting and recommended approval. Hucks stated that staff also recommends approval of R-1 zoning. Motion: Jordan made a motion, seconded by Butler to approve first reading of Ordinance #2026-02-02 (C) zoning the property at 250 Chevy Chase Drive to City of Conway R-1. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-02-02 (D) to rezone approximately 50.64 +/- acres of property located on E. Country Club Drive (PIN 339-00-00-0026), from the City of Conway Low/ Medium Residential (R-1) to the City of Conway Conservation Preservation (CP). Hucks stated that this item was discussed at the January 5 council meeting. The property is now owned by the city, and the city is seeking to rezone the property to CP for protection of the environmentally sensitive and flood prone areas the property contains. Planning Commission held the required public hearing at their January 8, 2026 meeting and recommended approval of the proposed zoning. Hucks said that staff also recommends approval of the CP zoning. -- 3 of 10 -- January 20, 2026 4 Motion: Helms made a motion, seconded by Goldfinch to approve first reading of Ordinance #2026-02-02 (D) rezoning the property on E. Country Club Drive to CP. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. C. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-03-16 (C) to annex approximately 0.2 +/- acres of property located at 1326 Cottage Lane (PIN 338-10-02-0007). Hucks stated that this property is located directly behind the parcel that has frontage on Church Street and Cottage Lane that was recently annexed and rezoned to Highway Commercial, in conjunction with the abutting property. The property is currently vacant, and the applicant is seeking to annex the property for future commercial development. Two other parcels on Cottage Lane on the other side of the subject property are also going through the annexation and rezoning process, so annexation of this property further closes this donut hole in the city, leaving just one property on Cottage Lane not within the city’s jurisdiction. Hucks said that Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on the proposed zoning upon annexation to Highway Commercial at their February 5 meeting, and their recommendation will be forwarded to council along with first reading of an ordinance to one the property Highway Commercial Hucks said that this ordinance is for first reading of annexation only, in which staff recommends approval. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Butler to approve first reading of Ordinance #2026-03-16 (C) annexing the property at 1326 Cottage Lane. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. CONSIDERATION: A. Consideration of the approval of changing the name for a new single-family development located on East Country Club Drive from “Rivers Edge Village” to “Homestead” (PIN 339-00-00-0025). Hucks said that this development is located on East Country Club Drive, between Highway 905 and Long Avenue Ext. Council approved the current name, Rivers Edge Village, at their May 6, 2024 meeting. The preliminary plans for this development were approved in October of last year. the applicant is seeking to rename the approved development, which is a Conservation Subdivision, to “Homestead.” Hucks said that in accordance with the UDO, council must review and approve all subdivision names. Hucks said that staff does recommend approval of the proposed name change. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Blain to approve the subdivision name change to “Homestead.” Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. Consideration of the approval of a resolution authorizing a fee in lieu of open space for the proposed expansion of University Suites, located on Technology Blvd (PIN 383-10-03-0020). Hucks stated that University Suites, located on Technology Blvd, is being expanded to include an additional 24 units on the opposite side of the street. This property was rezoned last year in conjunction with the original University Suites development to the R-3, or high-density residential district. The property is 1.75 acres in size, and there are 24 units proposed for construction. The requirements for open space -- 4 of 10 -- January 20, 2026 5 have been amended a few times over the last 10 or so years, and a 2016 amendment included a revision requiring that a fee in lieu of open space be provided when less than one acre of open space is calculated using the formula determining the amount of open space. This was because the amount of open space being required at the time for some of the developments would not have been compliant with the open space suitability standards in effect at that time. How the total amount of open space that is determined has also been amended, to a much simpler formula, which now requires that there be 1,000 sq. ft. of open space for each lot or unit in a proposed development. This means that there would need to be a minimum of 44 lots or units proposed to meet the minimum standard for providing open space onsite (43,560 sq. ft.). Hucks said that in addition to the requirement to submit a fee in lieu of providing open space when less than one acre is required, the applicant is required to submit a written appraisal of the market value of the land to be developed, as if the development has been completed; in other words, post-development value. As part of the applicant’s request for preliminary plan approval, which is considered by Planning Commission, the applicant requested a design modification from the appraisal requirements, requesting that the contracted amount for the property be accepted in determining the dollar amount for the open space fee in lieu. Planning Commission approved the design modification request, and granted preliminary plan approval, contingent upon final review and approval of the Technical Review Committee. Hucks stated that a separate request considered on the same agenda was for the same project, asking for approval of the fee in lieu amount of open space, but in a reduced amount, which is required to receive a recommendation by Planning Commission before being considered by Council, based on the following factors: (1) This is an infill development, an expansion of an existing student housing project that already contains open space amenities, including an outdoor pool, amenity center, a dog park, among other things, that will be available for use by the new residents; and (2) Although the open space areas shown to be provided on this site do not meet the minimum standards, there is some passive open space being provided, in addition to the fee in lieu. Hucks said that Planning Commission considered the second request for the reduced fee in lieu amount at their January 8, 2026 meeting. Part of the discussion included the amount of open space that was already in place for the existing University Suites, which was approved under a different regulatory framework when previously zoned as a Planned Development and the open space was calculated very differently at that time. Because the open space that does exist is considered nonconforming, it cannot be credited toward the requirement for the proposed expansion. The open space ordinance currently in effect sets a standard method for calculating the fee based on the value of the land, the size of the site, and the amount of open space that would otherwise be required, plus a 25% surcharge, which was adopted as part of the most recent amendments to the open space ordinance. Using that method, and the contracted amount that was approved by Planning Commission via a design modification, the full fee in lieu of providing open space onsite is $223,800. Planning Commission considered the applicant’s request to reduce the fee in lieu amount that is calculated, based on the value of the land via the method they approved, and did not reach consensus on the fee in lieu amount. Two motions were made; -- 5 of 10 -- January 20, 2026 6 neither received a majority. It was split 3/3 both times. As a result, the applicant’s request was denied. Hucks stated that the question is not whether open space is required but in applying the policy that is in effect, whether the proposed fee in lieu amount is sufficient for this project. Based on the number of units proposed, the ordinance calculates the amount of open space required to be 24,000 sq. ft.; a little more than half an acre. As previously stated, using the applicant’s own contracted amount, the fee in lieu amount would otherwise be $223,800, when you take into account the 25% additional fee that is required. The applicant is requesting approval of a reduced fee in lieu amount of $52,152.86, based on the reasons previously provided, and citing in their application that the project only lacks 6,991 sq. ft. of “suitable” open space if the requirement for the fee in lieu for less than one acre of open space did not exist. Hucks said that staff’s determination and recommendation is based on a few factors: − The formula for determining the fee in lieu of open space is designed to approximate the cost of acquiring and developing new open space when a project creates demand for new park land. In this case, the city would have to acquire roughly half an acre of land elsewhere. The standard calculation works best for large, standalone developments where residents will rely entirely on new or offsite public facilities, not ones that have private amenities nearby. − This project is a small, infill expansion, not a new, isolated development. Residents will have access to private amenities directly across the street, which already serves a similar population. As a result, the demand this project places on City parks and recreation facilities could be considered much less than what the formula in the ordinance assumes. The assessed fee ($223,800) reflects a hypothetical cost based solely on land value, not actual use or impact. − Applying the full fee in this case could unintentionally discourage infill development in areas the city wants it, pushing development farther out where infrastructure and services are more costly, contributing towards urban sprawl. A reduced fee supports the City’s broader goals of efficient land use, student housing near campuses, and minimizing sprawl, while still complying with the ordinance. Staff’s recommendation is to approve a reduction in the fee in lieu amount to $65,191.008, which includes an additional 25% fee on top of the applicant’s proposed fee of $52,152. This approach balances the ordinance requirements with proportionality – the fee still contributes to city open space but does not over-penalize an infill project that is already leveraging existing infrastructure. Goldfinch has concerns with the fee in lieu amount as University Suites was built in 2007 and the requirements were different then. Hucks explained that this is a new part and not part of the original development but has the same owners and is an expansion of the original directly across the street. Blain said that she agrees with Goldfinch and is willing to charge the owners with a lesser fee. -- 6 of 10 -- January 20, 2026 7 Helms also agreed with Goldfinch but had concerns about traffic in that area. Hucks said that Technology Blvd is a city road and the residents would be able to just walk across the street. Hucks added that staff is working on options for situations such as this moving forward. Emrick explained the open space fund. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Blain to approve staff’s recommendation for a reduction in the fee in lieu amount to $65,191.08. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. PUBLIC INPUT: − Lizzy Marlowe – spoke to council in opposition of the buffer ordinance from 2018. − Tonya Robinson – spoke on behalf of community members that are in opposition of a sports complex being placed on the former Whittemore Elementary site and supports a community center at this location. Asked who made the decision to make this site a sports complex. There was no further public input. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Jordan, to close public input. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. CITY ADMINISTRATOR’S REPORT: Emrick informed Council of the following: − Staff has started decorating for Valentine’s Day and hope to have everything out by February 1. Decorations will be left up until February 23 and then staff will start switching to Spring and Easter. − The wreaths on the bridge will come down tonight. − Emrick reminded council that in 6 weeks, we will be getting ready to leave for our annual Budget Retreat and if there are any specific requests from City Council for retreat consideration, please get those to him as soon as possible so that there is time to review them and prepare a presentation for consideration. − Staff was requested to do a speed survey at Laurel Street, near 5th Avenue. This study was conducted in November. The posted speed on Laurel is 25mph and the average speed was 28.87 mph. This indicates that there is not a speed issue on Laurel at this location worthy of further consideration. − As you all aware, we have a major Stormwater project happening throughout the Conwayborough and Snowhill adjacent neighborhoods. This is a grant funded, extremely tight time window, massive project that will upgrade the stormwater infrastructure from Pine Street all the way to Kingston Lake. This project both replaces aging stormwater pipes and upsizes them, making the drainage systems more effective in heavy rain events and adding lifespan to the network. Mary Catherine Hyman will now give a more detailed update on this project, where it now stands and what future impacts may result from it. -- 7 of 10 -- January 20, 2026 8 Hyman updated council on the road closures for the following stormwater improvements: • Pine Street Outfall • Beaty Street Outfall • Park View Road • Graham and Long Roads • Highway 701 and Boundary • Ackerrose Drive in Rosehaven • Ridgewood Drive • Blue Bell Lane • Moore Lane • Laurel Street Drainage • ERF at Fourth and Laurel Emrick continued by saying: − The mayor mentioned at the outset of the meeting that two of our Council Members are in Columbia today, representing the City at Hometown Legislative Action Day. This event serves as a centralized forum for local government leaders to inform themselves about legislative developments, advocate for their communities, and cultivate productive dialogue with state policymakers. − There are some large culverts under Mill Pond Road that have settled, creating two big dips in the road before reaching Church Street. Mill Pond is down to one lane in that area to fix some joints in the culverts and then King Asphalt will come through and resurface that area when the temperatures rise and get it scheduled. − The serious threat of a winter storm this weekend begins on Saturday and continues into Sunday, with sub-freezing temperatures continuing past that. The main concern is ice, especially from freezing rain. Temperatures near or below freezing could cause rain to freeze on roads, bridges, trees, and power lines. Even a small amount of ice can make travel dangerous and may lead to slick roads and possible power outages. The city has begun necessary preparations, and we are continuing to monitor forecasts closely. Emrick said he will keep Council updated as updates are received. − John Rogers has begun to work on the next Citizens Academy which will kick off in the Spring. − There are Department Head reports from Lynn Smith in HR, Chief Long in Police and Robert Cooper in Construction Services. − No workshop, but there are a couple of Executive Session items as outlined in the agenda. L. Smith, Cooper and Long all gave brief departmental reports. There was some discussion about police officer incentives for those hired that are already certified, parking citations for those in the fire zones at Food Lion, and the recently purchased Jamestown property. -- 8 of 10 -- January 20, 2026 9 COUNCIL INPUT: Helms − Thanked the Fire Department for having Santa on the firetrucks riding through the neighborhoods. − Asked for the Budget Books early − Asked about special Olympics volunteers − Hope everyone enjoyed MLK day off. Butler - Commended the Conway Horry County MLK Committee for a wonderful event honoring the life and legacy of Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. - Thanked the community members that reached out to her about the Whittemore Elementary School site. Butler went on to say that the site is historic, and the history is not being erased or replaced. Voices are being heard. Wants everyone to be more transparent and to be integral in the efforts to honor and remember that site. Butler said that she opens and welcomes any dialogue and says that she will do her part to make sure that she not only listens but also speaks on behalf of those that have come to her with their concerns. Butler stated that we are 1 Conway and are stronger together; and said there are times when we all must come together for a common cause, and she believes that this is one of the causes. The site is important and will continue to be important and it is the city’s job to remember that site. Butler pledges to make sure she communicates more effectively with the community and the remaining council members concerning that site. Goldfinch and Blain said that Butler was very well said in her remarks. EXECUTIVE SESSION: Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Jordan to enter into Executive Session for the following: (A) Consideration of appointments to boards, commissions and committees [pursuant to SC Code §30-4-70(A) (1)]; (B) Discussion regarding Potential Acquisition of Property on Sherwood [pursuant to SC Code §30-4-70 (A) (2)]; and (C) Discussion of Employment of an Employee in the Police Department [pursuant to SC Code §30-4-70 (A) (1)]. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. RECONVENE FROM EXECUTIVE SESSION: Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Helms to leave Executive Session. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. POSSIBLE ACTION ON MATTERS DISCUSSED IN EXECUTIVE SESSION: Motion: Helms made a motion, seconded by Jordan to uphold the decision of the grievance committee’s recommendation regarding an employee in the Police Department. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. ADJOURNMENT: Motion: Butler made a motion, seconded by Goldfinch, to adjourn the meeting. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. -- 9 of 10 -- -- 10 of 10 --

STATE OF SOUTH CAROLINA } COUNTY OF HORRY } R E S O L U T I O N CITY OF CONWAY } EXPRESSING GRATITUDE TO BO FLAVOR AND THE BOJANGLES FRANCHISE ON CHURCH STREET FOR THEIR INVESTMENT, HOLIDAY SPIRIT, COMMUNITY PARTNERSHIP, AND EXEMPLARY ACHIEVEMENTS WHEREAS, Bo Flavor, the local franchise owner of the Bojangles restaurant located on Church Street, has made a significant investment in the City of Conway through the construction of a new, beautifully designed store that enhances the visual character and economic vitality of the corridor; and, WHEREAS the Church Street Bojangles has been recognized across the entire Bojangles system as one of the absolute best- of-the-best restaurants in the franchise, distinguished for its quality, service, operations, and leadership; and, WHEREAS, this excellence is exemplified by Felicia Tracy, who has earned national recognition as the Best General Manager in the United States for the Bojangles franchise – a historic and remarkable achievement that brings great pride to Conway; and, WHEREAS, Bo Flavor and their team have consistently demonstrated a deep commitment to community partnership, actively participating in and elevating Conway’s unique culture and seasonal celebrations by consistently participating in the City Tree Lighting and the Sensory Tree Lighting events; and, WHEREAS, during October 2025, the Church Street Bojangles transformed into “Boojangles,” delighting residents and visitors with a fully themed, spooky, playful Halloween makeover that aligned perfectly with Conway’s identity as Halloween, South Carolina, strengthening the city’s seasonal branding and joy; and, WHEREAS, during December 2025, Bo Flavor continued this tradition of creativity and community engagement by converting the store into “Bojingles,” a festive, Christmas-themed experience decorated from top to bottom, embodying the warmth, cheer, and magic of Conway’s holiday season; and, WHEREAS, these transformations – from Boojangles to Bojingles – have become beloved local attractions, drawing families, visitors, and community members to celebrate the holidays, take photographs, and share in the spirit that Bo Flavor and the store’s leadership have helped cultivate; and, WHEREAS, the outstanding achievements of the store and its General Manager, together with its joyful holiday transformations, demonstrate exceptional corporate citizenship and showcase how local businesses can meaningfully contribute to Conway’s identity, culture, and quality of life; and, WHEREAS, the City Council wishes to express its gratitude for these contributions, recognizing that the efforts of Bo Flavor, Felicia Tracy, and the Church Street Bojangles team have strengthened community pride, enhanced Conway’s holiday programming, and enriched the experiences of residents and visitors alike. NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED by the City Council of the City of Conway that: 1) The City of Conway extends its sincere appreciation to Bo Flavor and the entire Bojangles team on Church Street for their significant investment in Conway’s business community and their outstanding contributions to Conway’s culture and holiday traditions. 2) The Council recognizes and celebrates Church Street Bojangles as one of the top-performing restaurants in the entire Bojangles franchise system, a distinction that brings honor to the City of Conway. 3) The Council commends Felicia Tracy for her extraordinary accomplishment in being named the Best General Manager in the Nation, and expresses pride in her leadership, professionalism, and dedication. 4) The Council further applauds the creativity, energy, and enthusiasm displayed in transforming the restaurant into Boojangles and Bojingles, which have become cherished elements of Conway’s community identity. 5) A copy of this Resolution shall be presented to Bo Flavor and Felicia Tracy and placed in the official records of the City of Conway as a lasting expression of appreciation and recognition. IN WITNESS WHEREOF, this Resolution is hereby adopted and made a part of the City Records this 5th day of January 2026. Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor William M. Goldfinch IV, Mayor Pro Tem Amanda Butler, Council Member Julie Ann Hardwick, Council Member Beth Helms, Council Member Justin D. Jordan, Council Member Larry A. White, Council Member ATTEST: Alicia Shelley, City Clerk 4 -- 4 of 134 -- ITEM: V.B. STATE OF SOUTH CAROLINA } COUNTY OF HORRY } R E S O L U T I O N CITY OF CONWAY } HONORING DONZELLE’S RESTAURANT WHEREAS, Since its founding in 1962 by Donzelle and Dick Dickerson, Donzelle’s Restaurant has welcomed generations of Conway residents, students, travelers, and friends to its doors - serving not only meals, but warmth, hospitality, and a sense of home; and, WHEREAS Donzelle’s earned its reputation as a cherished gathering place - a spot where life’s everyday moments and milestone celebrations unfolded over home-cooked fare, friendly conversation, and consistent kindness; many Conway families and visitors consider it a cornerstone of their memories; and, WHEREAS, Over more than sixty years, Donzelle’s has become woven into the social and cultural fabric of Conway, contributing to the city’s identity, character, and community spirit; and, WHEREAS, the long-standing success of Donzelle’s stands as a testament to the dedication of its owners and staff, who through decades of work built more than a business – they built a legacy of hospitability and belonging; and, WHEREAS, Although the restaurant closed at the end of 2025, and a beloved era will draw to an end, the impact of Donzelle’s will endure in the memories and hearts of those who passed through its doors; and, WHEREAS, the City of Conway believes it is fitting and proper to formally recognize Donzelle’s for its steadfast service, enduring contributions, and the role it played in shaping community bonds over multiple generations. NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED by the City Council of the City of Conway that: 1) The City Council expresses its deep gratitude and heartfelt appreciation to Donzelle’s Restaurant for more than six decades of service, hospitality, and community building. 2) The Council recognizes that Donzelle’s was far more than a place to eat – it was a home away from home, a gathering place for friends and families, and a link between past, present, and future generations of Conway residents. 3) The Council acknowledges the dedication, hard work, and kindness of the owners and staff, whose commitment sustained Donzelle’s through decades of change and helped define its character. 4) The Council affirms that the closing of Donzelle’s marks the end of a treasured chapter in Conway’s history – but also the preservation of its legacy through the many lives it touched, and memories made within its walls. 5) A copy of this Resolution shall be presented to the Dickerson family, and a certified copy shall be entered into the permanent records of the City of Conway, to honor and preserve its legacy for future generations. IN WITNESS WHEREOF, this Resolution is hereby adopted and made a part of the City Records this 5th day of January 2026. Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor William M. Goldfinch IV, Mayor Pro Tem Amanda Butler, Council Member Julie Ann Hardwick, Council Member Beth Helms, Council Member Justin D. Jordan, Council Member Larry A. White, Council Member ATTEST: Alicia Shelley, City Clerk 5 -- 5 of 134 -- ITEM: V.C. STATE OF SOUTH CAROLINA } COUNTY OF HORRY } R E S O L U T I O N CITY OF CONWAY } HONORING SINGLETON’S GROCERY WHEREAS, Singleton’s Grocery has served the City of Conway and its surrounding neighborhoods for generations, standing as a reliable and welcoming cornerstone of daily life for countless families; and, WHEREAS as one of Conway’s long-standing, family-run establishments, Singleton’s Grocery provided more than groceries – it offered familiarity, friendship, and a sense of belonging that only a neighborhood store can create; and, WHEREAS, Over the years, Singleton’s Grocery became a trusted gathering place where community members shared stories, checked in on one another, and experienced the warmth of local hospitality that defines Conway’s character; and, WHEREAS, the store’s longevity is a testament to the dedication of the Singleton family and all who worked alongside them, whose kindness, consistency, and customer service made the store a beloved part of the Conway community; and, WHEREAS, Singleton’s Grocery has contributed to the stability and identity of its neighborhood by providing essential goods, supporting local families, and serving as an anchor point during times of growth, challenge, and change; and, WHEREAS, with the store’s closing, the City of Conway marks the end of an era and recognizes the deep sense of nostalgia and gratitude felt by generations who relied on Singleton’s Grocery as part of their daily routine and community life; and, WHEREAS, it is fitting and proper that the City of Conway capture and preserve the significance of Singleton’s Grocery in the community’s history, honoring its service and celebrating its legacy. NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED by the City Council of the City of Conway that: 1) The City of Conway hereby extends its heartfelt appreciation to Singleton’s Grocery for its decades of loyal service, steadfast presence, and meaningful contributions to Conway’s community life. 2) The City Council recognizes that Singleton’s Grocery was more than a business – it was a neighborhood cornerstone that fostered connection, stability, and shared experience among Conway residents. 3) The Council honors the commitment and personal dedication of the owners and employees whose work built and maintained a store known for its friendliness, reliability, and service. 4) The Council acknowledges the closure of Singleton’s Grocery as a significant moment in Conway’s story and affirms that its legacy will continue in the memories of those who grew up, shopped, visited, and found community within its walls. 5) A copy of this Resolution shall be presented to the Singleton family following the closing of the store and placed in the permanent records of the City of Conway so that future generations may remember its service and contributions. IN WITNESS WHEREOF, this Resolution is hereby adopted and made a part of the City Records this 5th day of January 2026. Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor William M. White, Council Member ATTEST: Alicia Shelley, City Clerk 6 -- 6 of 134 -- December 1, 2025 1 CITY OF CONWAY CITY COUNCIL MEETING CONWAY CITY HALL 229 MAIN STREET, CONWAY MONDAY, DECEMBER 1, 2025 PRESENT: Mayor Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor Pro Tem William Goldfinch, Amanda Butler, Julie Hardwick, Beth Helms, Justin Jordan and Larry White. STAFF: Adam Emrick, City Administrator; Mary Catherine Hyman, Deputy City Administrator; John Rogers, Deputy City Administrator; June Wood, Public Information Officer; Jeff Leveille, Technology Services Director; Jason Perzan, Deputy Fire Chief; Reggie Jenerette, Solid Waste Director; Robert Cooper, Construction Services Director; Lynn Smith, Human Resource Director; Ted Dudley, Public Utilities Director; Jessica Hucks, Planning and Development Director; Brandon Harrelson, Public Works Director; Dale Long, Police Chief; Timmy Williams, Hospitality and Beautification Director; Kayla Fleming, Municipal Judge; Ashley Smith, Recreation Director; Kelly Thomas, Deputy PIO; David Crotts, Procurement and Inventory Division Chief; Katie Dennis, Planner; and Alicia Shelley, City Clerk. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. SPECIAL PRESENTATION: A. Recognition of 2025 Artist of the City of Conway Christmas Card Contest – Blain recognized Fernanda Loredo Martinez as the City of Conway Christmas card contest winner. B. Recognition of 2024 CP Quattlebaum Design Award Recipients – Blain presented the following Quattlebaum Awards: − Mercy Baptist Church – Outstanding Restoration of a Non-residential Building (absent) − 1215 Grede Court – Outstanding New Construction of a Residential Building (absent) − 1109 Whopping Crane, Phill McNelis and Julie Blais – Outstanding New Construction of a Residential Building − Palmetto Taps, Brian Von – Outstanding Signage Project − Diamond Shores LLC, Collins Walk Subdivision – Outstanding Signage Project (absent) − SOS Health Care – Outstanding contribution to quality development, restoration, landscape or design by an organization or individual C. E. Discussion of a request to rezone approximately 0.44+/- acres of property located along Hwy 701 N. / N. Main Street (PIN 325-13-01-0013), from the City of Conway 8 -- 8 of 134 -- December 1, 2025 3 Low/ Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district. Hucks stated that this property is currently zoned R-1 and the applicant is seeking to rezone the property for future potential development under the HC district. The city’s future land use map identifies the property as HC, which is a zoning intended to accommodate auto-dependent commercial development. The HC district is typically located along major arterial and highway corridors where auto-dependent development can occur, while also promoting orderly growth, coordinated access, and functional corridor aesthetics, such as those that are listed in the City’s Gateway Corridor Overlay, which this property will be subject to if developed commercially. Property on either side of this property is zoned HC. Property across from it is zoned Horry County Heavy Industrial. Property located behind the subject property is the Ivy Glen development, which is zoned R-1. Hucks said that Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on the request at their December 11 meeting and their recommendation will be forwarded with first reading of the ordinance to rezone the subject property. Hucks explained the buffer requirements in the HC district abutting the Ivy Glen development. SECOND READING: Second Reading of Ordinance #2024-11-18 providing for the establishment of the Riverfront Downtown Redevelopment Project Area, the approval of the Riverfront and Downtown Redevelopment Plan, and financing of redevelopment projects, and other matters related thereto. Rogers stated that this is second reading for the Riverfront Downtown Redevelopment Project area and introduced Attorney Gary Pope. Pope gave a brief overview on the consideration of second reading of the TIF plan stating that it encompasses 449 acres and 296 parcels of property. The boundaries of the Redevelopment Area include and encompass a significant portion of the city’s downtown commercial area and riverfront, particularly including certain area around First, Second, Third, Fourth, and Fifth Avenues between Kingston Lake and the Waccamaw River on the north and Highway 501 on the South, and also including the former Santee Cooper property between First Avenue, Highway 501, and the Waccamaw River. Pope said that the cost of the Redevelopment Project is estimated at $78,900,000. Second Reading allows the city to set the tax value as of December 31 of last year and that gives a base line of future investment to count towards the increment. The school district and Horry County have reserved their rights to participate and are currently planning to negotiate over the course of the coming months. Pope said that this sets the baseline value for the district to allow the city to move forward with the downtown redevelopment plan and also gives a basis to negotiate with the county and school district. There was some discussion regarding the notice to the property owners within the plan, and the process of adding properties to the plan. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Blain to approve second reading of Ordinance #2024-11-18 . Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. 9 -- 9 of 134 -- December 1, 2025 4 FIRST READING: A. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-02-02 (A) to annex approximately 0.22+/- acres of property located at 250 Chevy Chase Drive (PIN 367-13-01-0031). Hucks stated that this is a request to annex the subject property, which is being requested in accordance with city requirements for connection to city utilities. The property was transferred into the current owner’s name in October, and restrictive covenants were recorded on November 10. One property directly beside the parcel is already within the city limits, which was annexed in 2011 and zoned R-1. Property directly across from the parcel is also within the city limits, zoned FA although currently undeveloped. With the exception of the undeveloped parcel and the elementary school, this area is primarily residential in nature. Nearby surrounding properties, although not contiguous, were annexed in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2023, and in June of this year; all of which are zoned R-1. Hucks said that if first reading of the ordinance to annex is approved, Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on the requested zoning at their meeting in January 2026 and that staff does recommend first reading to annex the subject property. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Jordan to approve first reading of Ordinance #2026-02-02 (A) annexing the property at 250 Chevy Chase Drive. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-02-02 (B) to annex approximately 18.26+/- acres of property located at 1071 & 1059 Academy Drive (PIN 382-00-00-0009). Hucks stated that council discussed this property and the potential for annexation at a council workshop a couple of months ago, where the applicant had approved plans and permit for rectory home for St. James Catholic Church, ready for pickup at Horry County Code Enforcement. When attempting to pay their water tap fees, the applicant was informed of the requirement to request annexation. The consensus of council at the workshop was that annexation would not be appropriate at this time, due to the fact that the only property on Academy Drive that would need city services, aside from city water, would be this property. However, that application is still required to request annexation. Restrictive covenants were recorded for the property on November 20, 2025. Hucks said that staff recommended against annexation of the property at this time. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Butler to deny first reading of Ordinance #2026-02-02 (B) annexing the property at 1071 & 1059 Academy Drive. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. CONSIDERATION: Consideration of City Assistance to Blackwater Market for Restroom Cleaning and Stocking (October – December) – Emrick said that this was a request from Russell Fowler of Blackwater Market to designate its on-site restrooms as public restrooms during the peak visitation months of October through December. They have requested that the city consider assisting with daily 10 -- 10 of 134 -- December 1, 2025 5 cleaning and the stocking of restroom supplies during this period. Emrick said it would require an MOU, there are pros and cons, but it is an atypical situation. There was discussion concerning how often the city’s public restrooms are cleaned, the need to bring in porta potties, the labeling of the restrooms as public, liability concerns, overuse issues that may fall back on the city, MOU as a test run for December 2025, the city completely taking over ownership, responsibility of repairs when needed, and the cleaning schedule. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Goldfinch authorizing the administrator to enter into a 1-month MOU with the owners of the Black Water Market for help with the daily cleaning and stocking of their restroom for public use and then come back to council for further assistance. Vote: Blain, Goldfinch, Jordan, White, Butler, Helms voted yes. Hardwick voted no. Motion carried 6-1. PUBLIC INPUT: − Lizzy Marlowe – spoke to council regarding the buffer behind her home at the dentist office saying that it encroaches on her property and, she said that she was attacked by a satanic decoration while entering city hall. CITY ADMINISTRATOR’S REPORT: Emrick informed Council of the following: • The city’s Technology Services Department is testing out some new hardware for the Christmas season. They are installing a parking lot sensor at the Town Green parking to be able to monitor the amount of vehicles in and out of the parking lot and determine the available parking spaces in the lot. This can then be made available to the public via a dashboard. If it works well for Christmas, staff can add more parking lots in the future. • IT is also working at adding a real time people counter to existing infrastructure. This will allow us to know, in real time, the number of people in certain areas of the City at any given moment. We will continue to use the other service that we subscribe to for the next year, and compare the data we have from the two sources. • On Wednesday, at 1 pm, the Police Department is hosting a drop-in to celebrate the retirement of Sgt. Michelle Johnson, at the Public Safety Building. • The Christmas Tree Lighting is this Thursday at 6 pm. Make travel plans now to avoid the traffic congestion. This Friday, the Mayor’s Youth Council will lead the event, showing a double feature of the Grinch who Stole Christmas, the 2000 version, 11 -- 11 of 134 -- December 1, 2025 6 followed by the original 1968 version. They are also leading a Toys for Tots drive at the movie night, so bring a toy with you. • The Reindeer Run is this Saturday beginning at the Conway Marina. • Arbor Day celebration is this Saturday from 11am-3 pm in the Terrace. This year’s Arbor Day will be a larger event than usual as we commemorate the 40th year of Conway being a Tree City USA city. • The Holiday Market is at the Sports and Fitness Center this Saturday beginning at 9 am. • A Christmas to Remember, where our Police and Fire Department take kids who may otherwise not have a Christmas, shopping, is this Saturday at noon. This year they are meeting at the Town Green to kick off the day. • The 8th Annual Rivertown Regatta, Christmas Boat Parade is Saturday at dusk. • The Under the Lights 5k is the 10th at 6 pm beginning at the Marina. • The Sensory Friendly Christmas Tree Lighting is on the 11th at 6 pm at Riverfront Park. Make sure you are at the starting point of the parade no later than 9:45 am. • Gave a shout out to our Parks and Recreation Department. Goldfinch wants the city to be the leader and encourage local cities and counties to have requirements in place where new neighborhoods have development agreements with enhancement fees to subsidize the expense of growth. Goldfinch wants to reignite the discussion, get more aggressive and go to the state with all concerns. Emrick discussed the COLA in this area, removal of the income tax in South Carolina, growth in Horry County, traffic congestion in downtown Conway, infrastructure improvements, construction of bridges, development agreements with enhancement fees, and impact fees. White encouraged the city to communicate with the other entities. Blain said there are many opportunities to do that with the League of Cities being one. ORDINANCE: N/A AGENDA SECTION: Special Presentation ISSUE: Discussion of a request to rezone approximately 50.64 +/- total acres of property located on E. Country Club Dr., from Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district to the Conservation Preservation (CP) district. APPLICANT(S): City of Conway PIN(s): 339-00-00-0026 CURRENT ZONING: Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) PROPOSED ZONING: Conservation Preservation (CP) BACKGROUND: The subject property, E/S Country Club Dr.; Parcel B, was transferred from Snow Hill Company to the City of Conway on March 21st, 2025 with the intent to preserve the flood zones and wetlands. The property is currently zoned Low/medium Density Residential (R-1) and is vacant. Per Section 3.2.15 per the UDO, the Conservation Preservation (CP) serves to provide needed open space for general outdoor and indoor recreational uses, and to protect environmentally sensitive areas and flood prone areas from the encroachment of any residential, commercial, industrial, or other uses capable of adversely affecting the relatively undeveloped character of the district. The request is not in accordance with the Future Land Use map as it is identified as Low Density Residential; however, surrounding properties are zoned Conservation Preservation (CP). Zoning the property to Conservation Preservation (CP) is consistent with the City’s goal to protect environmentally sensitive areas containing flood zones from residential development. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: The property abuts a residential development currently under construction, zoned R-1 and is surrounded by uninhabited, wood wetlands zoned R-1 in the city limits or SF-20 if in the unincorporated area of the county. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s future land use map identifies the property as Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). Per Section 3.2.3 of the UDO, the intent of the R-1 district is to provide for the preservation and expansion of areas for low to medium density, detached single-family residential development in the City of Conway. The district shall present a relatively spacious character, promote quiet, livable neighborhoods, and prohibit uses that are incompatible with the residential nature of the surrounding area. PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION (and public hearing): Planning Commission will hold the public hearing on this request at their January 8th meeting, after which their recommendation will be forwarded to City Council. ORDINANCE: #ZA2026-03-16 (B) AGENDA SECTION: First Reading ISSUE: Petition to annex approximately 0.43+/- acres of property located at 1322 & 1324 Cottage Lane APPLICANT(S): Sara Jo Lewis PIN(s): 338-10-02-0006, & - 0005 CURRENT ZONING: Horry County Residential, mobile homes allowed (MSF10) PROPOSED ZONING (upon annexation): Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) BACKGROUND: The subject property, identified as Lot 4 1322 Cottage Lane & Lot 5 1324 Cottage Lane’s restrictive covenants were recorded on November 26, 2025. Both properties contain one single-family dwelling. Properties abutting the rear and directly across Cottage Lane from the subject parcel are already within the city limits. Annexation is being requested as a requirement to connect to city services following a name change to the city utility service account. The applicant is requesting Low/ medium Density Residential (R-1) which is not supported by the Future Land Use Map, which identifies the subject properties as being Highway Commercial (HC). The zoning district HC would not prevent the homes from being used as residencies it would simply restrict the ability to expand the use in the future, as the existing residential structures would become legal nonconforming uses under the HC district. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: The properties are surrounded on two sides by properties already in the city limits and zoned HC. The properties on either side of the parcels are vacant wooded lots with the rear abutting property being commercial uses like fast food establishments among others all zoned HC in the city limits. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s future land use map identifies the property as Highway Commercial (HC). Per Section 3.2.10 of the UDO, the intent of the HC district is to provide compatible locations to serve the automobile oriented commercial activities in harmony with major highway developments, reduce traffic congestions and to enhance the aesthetic atmosphere of the City. PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION (and public hearing): Planning Commission is scheduled to hold the public hearing and consider the proposed zoning upon annexation at their February 5th mtg. Upon annexation, the property shall become subject to the City’s jurisdiction for the rendition of all applicable municipal services. This annexation includes all waterways, roads, and rights-of-way adjacent to the property. For a more specific description of said property, see attached map(s). SECTION 2. Code § 6-29-760. SECTION 3. title: CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES 1.5.26
text: January 5, 2026 1 CITY OF CONWAY CITY COUNCIL MEETING CONWAY CITY HALL 229 MAIN STREET, CONWAY MONDAY, JANUARY 5, 2026 PRESENT: Mayor Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor Pro Tem Beth Helms, Amanda Butler, William Goldfinch, Julie Hardwick, Justin Jordan and Larry White. STAFF: Adam Emrick, City Administrator; Mary Catherine Hyman, Deputy City Administrator; John Rogers, Deputy City Administrator; June Wood, Public Information Officer; Jeff Leveille, Technology Services Director; Jason Perzan, Fire Chief; Reggie Jenerette, Solid Waste Director; Robert Cooper, Construction Services Director; Lynn Smith, Human Resource Director; Ted Dudley, Public Utilities Director; Jessica Hucks, Planning and Development Director; Brandon Harrelson, Public Works Director; Dale Long, Police Chief; Timmy Williams, Hospitality and Beautification Director; Kayla Fleming, Municipal Judge; Ashley Smith, Parks and Recreation Director; Kelli Thomas, Deputy PIO; Bobby Wallace, Fleet Maintenance Director; Allison Williams, Finance Director; David Crotts, Procurement and Inventory Division Chief; and Alicia Shelley, City Clerk. OTHERS: There were approximately 65 others in attendance. CALL TO ORDER: Mayor Blain called the meeting to order. INVOCATION/PLEDGE OF ALLEGIANCE: Jordan gave the invocation and led the Pledge of Allegiance. The requirements for posting notice of this meeting under South Carolina’s Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) were met. ADMINISTRATION OF OATHS OF OFFICE: Oaths of Office were administered during the swearing in ceremonies for the Council members that were re-elected in the November 2025 Municipal Election. Those included Council Member Amanda Butler, Council Member William Goldfinch, and Council Member Beth Helms. CONSENT AGENDA: A. Approval of a Resolution recognizing Bojangles B. Approval of a Resolution honoring Donzelle’s Restaurant C. Approval of a Resolution honoring Singleton’s Grocery D. Approval of December 1, 2025 Council Meeting Minutes -- 1 of 11 -- January 5, 2026 2 APPROVAL OF CONSENT AGENDA: Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Hardwick to approve the January 5, 2026 consent agenda. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. ELECTION OF MAYOR PRO TEM FOR 2026: Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Butler to elect Helms as Mayor Pro Tem for 2026 by acclamation. There was no objection, and the motion carried unanimously. SPECIAL PRESENTATION: A. Presentation of a Resolution recognizing Bojangles – Blain presented the Bojangles Franchise and Bo Flavor with a Resolution for their investment, holiday spirit, community partnership and exemplary achievements. B. Presentation of a Resolution honoring Donzelle’s Restaurant – Blain presented Donzelle’s Restaurant with a Resolution honoring them for their sixty plus years of business in Conway. C. Presentation of a Resolution honoring Singleton’s Grocery – Blain presented Singleton’s Grocery with a Resolution honoring them for serving the Conway area for generations. D. Presentation of Longevity Awards – December 2025 – 15 Years – Julius “Mike” Alford, II, Solid Waste – Emrick and Butler presented Mike Alford with his longevity award. E. Presentation by the Conway Rotary Club – David Welborn thanked Council and staff for allowing the Reindeer Run for 18 years. F. Discussion of a request to rezone approximately 50.64+/- acres of property located on E. Country Club Drive (PIN 339-00-00-0026), from the City of Conway Low/ Medium Residential (R-1) district to the City of Conway Conservation Preservation (CP) district. Hucks stated that this property was transferred to the city in March of 2025 with the development of the adjacent property. The current zoning is R-1, and the city is requesting to rezone the property to CP, as a significant amount of the property contains a flood zone. This item is for discussion only and Planning Commission will review the requested zoning and hold a public hearing on the proposed zoning at their January 8 meeting. At Blain’s request, Hucks briefly explained the CP district. FIRST READING: A. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-01-20 (F) to rezone approximately 0.15+/- acres of property located at 182 Quail Run (PIN 383-09-04-0040), from Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF10) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district. Hucks stated that this property is within the Quail Village development near the university. Annexation is being requested -- 2 of 11 -- January 5, 2026 3 due to the requirements to connect to city services due to a change in ownership. Restrictive Covenants have been on file since June 2010. Eight other lots within this subdivision have been annexed over the last several years, with the adjacent lot being annexed in 2023. The requested zoning upon annexation is R-1, which is consistent with the zoning of the other lots that have been annexed. Hucks said that council approved first reading of the annexation at the November 3 council meeting, and Planning Commission recommended approval of the requested zoning of R-1 upon annexation at their December 11 meeting. If first reading of the ordinance to zone the property is approved, final reading of both ordinances, to annex and to rezone the property, will be forwarded for consideration at the January 20 council meeting. Hucks said that staff recommends approval. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Butler to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-01-20 (F) rezoning the property at 182 Quail Run to City of Conway R-1. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-01-20 (G) to rezone approximately 0.37+/- acres of property located at 801 Donald Street (PIN 369-12-04-0002), from Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF10) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district. Hucks stated that this property is within the Sam Johnson subdivision near Cates Bay Highway, and this request came about due to the city requirement for annexation when a property changes ownership that will connect to city utilities or when there is a change in the name on the utility account. The restrictive covenant has been on file for this property since 1987. Eleven other properties within this subdivision have been annexed over the years and with the adjacent parcel annexed in 2023. The requested zoning upon annexation is R-1, which is consistent with the zoning of the surrounding properties as well as the city’s future land use map. Hucks said that City Council approved first reading of the ordinance to annex the subject property at their November 17 meeting, and PC recommended approval of the proposed zoning upon annexation at their December 11 meeting. If first reading of the ordinance to zone the property R-1 is approved, final reading of both ordinances will be forwarded for consideration at the January 20 council meeting. Hucks said that staff recommends approval. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Helms to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-01-20 (G) rezoning the property at 801 Donald Street to City of Conway R-1. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. C. First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-01-20 (H) to rezone approximately 0.4+/- acres of property located at 5007 Presbyterian Drive (PIN 383-08-02-0010), from Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF10) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district. Hucks stated that this property is within the College Park subdivision near Highway 501 and this request is a result of the city requirements to annex for a connection to city utilities, with restrictive covenants on file since 1998. Sixteen or so other properties have been annexed over the last several years, with the adjacent parcel annexed in 2007. The requested zoning upon annexation -- 3 of 11 -- January 5, 2026 4 is R-1, which is consistent with the other residential properties within the College Park development as well as the city’s future land use map. Hucks said that City Council approved first reading of the ordinance to annex this property at their November 17 meeting and Planning Commission recommended approval of the requested R-1 zoning at their December 11 meeting. If first reading of this ordinance is approved, final reading of both ordinances will be forwarded for consideration at the January 20 council meeting. Hucks said that staff recommends approval. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Jordan to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-01-20 (H) rezoning the property at 5007 Presbyterian Drive to City of Conway R-1. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. D. First reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-01-20 (I) to rezone approximately 0.44+/- acres of property located on Hwy 701 N / Main Street (PIN 325-13-01-0013), from City of Conway Low/Medium Density Residential (R-1) district to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district. Hucks stated that this property is currently zoned R-1 and the applicant is seeking to rezone the property to HC district, which is consistent with the zoning of other properties with frontage along Highway 701 North as well as the city’s future land use map. Hucks said that Planning Commission held the public hearing on the request and recommended approval of the requested zoning of HC at their December 11 meeting. Hucks said that staff recommends approval. Motion: Butler made a motion, seconded by Hardwick to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-01-20 (I) rezoning the property at Highway 701 N / Main Street to HC. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. White requested that staff add business names to the aerial map. E. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-03-16 (A) to annex approximately 1+/- acres of property located at 3000 Hwy 378 (PIN 337-16-04-0011). Hucks stated that this property is the location of what used to be a used car dealership. The property was transferred to the current owners in October 2025; however restrictive covenants were recorded for this property in 1991. In order to connect to city utilities, the new owners must request annexation in accordance with city requirements. The rear adjacent property as well as the property on one side is within the city limits. The city’s future land use map identifies the property as HC, and the requested zoning upon annexation, if approved, is also HC. Hucks said that Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on the requested zoning upon annexation at their February 5 meeting and following their recommendation a proposed ordinance to zone the property HC will be forwarded for consideration separately from the annexation ordinance. Hucks said that staff recommends approval of first reading of the ordinance to annex the subject property. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Helms to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-03-16 (A) annexing the property at 3000 Highway 378. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. -- 4 of 11 -- January 5, 2026 5 F. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2026-03-16 (B) to annex approximately 0.43+/- acres of property located at 1322 & 1324 Cottage Lane (PINs 338-10-02-0005 & 338- 10-02-0006). Hucks stated that both properties contain a single-family dwelling, owned by the same individual. Annexation is being requested in order to connect to city utilities in accordance with city requirements and restrictive covenants were recorded in November of 2025. More recently, the city rezoned 2 parcels at the corner of Cottage Lane and Church Street from R1 district to the Highway Commercial district, which was consistent with the city’s future land use maps and previous uses of the property. In this case, the reverse is true. Neither of these parcels are within the city, and both are currently zoned Horry County HC and contain a single-family residence, which, unless the county has amended their ordinance to exclude, single-family is permitted within their version of the HC district. The applicant is requesting to be zoned R-1 upon annexation; however, R-1 is not consistent with the city’s future land use map, no surrounding properties are zoned R-1, and the parcels do not exceed the 3-acre minimum to not be considered spot zoning. The issue of the zoning is something that Planning Commission will consider at their February 5 meeting, and it is possible that if the R-1 district is recommended a future land use map amendment will be necessary. Hucks said that what is being considered for first reading today is just the annexation portion of the request, which Hucks said staff does recommend approval. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by White to approve first reading of Ordinance #2026-03-16 (B) annexing the property at 1322 & 1324 Cottage Lane. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. CONSIDERATION: A. Consideration of the approval of a proposed name, “Elmhurst Place,” for a new subdivision located on Rockwood Drive and Medlen Parkway. (PIN 338-00-00-0032). Hucks stated that this proposed development directly abuts the Elmhurst development located on Medlen Parkway and was once a future phase or extension of that development. However, the property has changed hands, and the new developers now have plans in review for what was Phase 5 of Elmhurst, to be named, Elmhurst Place. City ordinance requires that council review and adopt all proposed subdivision names. Hucks said that staff does recommend approval of the requested name. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by White to approve the name of Elmhurst Place. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. Consideration of a Special Event – Porchfest 2026 – February 15, 2026 – Hillary Howard of Conway Downtown Alive presented a special event, Porchfest to be held on February 15, 2026 from 12 Noon to 6:00 p.m. Porchfest will be held on 22 various porches with 28 bands performing. Conway Downtown Alive is requesting road closures on Laurel Street, Seventh Avenue and Elm Street. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Hardwick to approve the special event, 2026 Porchfest, as presented. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. -- 5 of 11 -- January 5, 2026 6 C. Consideration of a request to extend the Camp Bonfire Special Event Permit – Rogers stated that the Bonfire would like to expend their special event permit that was approved for October 1, 2025 through January 1, 2026 from 11 a.m. to 9 p.m. on Wednesday through Sunday. The Bonfire has been using the vacant lot next to them to host Camp Bonfire with propane campfire pits with chairs and a temporary building to serve drinks. Rogers said that the first benchmark of the MOU agreement is September 4, 2026. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Blain to extend the special event permit to September 4, 2026. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. Hardwick asked for an estimated time for groundbreaking of a future building at this site. Rogers said that the MOU in place says that the initial phase which would include construction would be 3 years from contract, which would be September 4, 2028 D. Consideration of approval to replace a Police Department vehicle (Long) Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Goldfinch to approve the replacement vehicle for the Police Department. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. PUBLIC INPUT: − Lizzy Marlowe – spoke to council in opposition of the buffer ordinance from 2018. There was no further public input. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Goldfinch, to close public input. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. CITY ADMINISTRATOR’S REPORT: Emrick informed Council of the following: 1. Wished all a Happy New Year. 2. Emick said that despite this year’s Christmas season being a short one and having one of the few Thursday nights rained out, it was a very successful holiday season. The city welcomed 272,600 people downtown during the month of December. This is an increase of 14.2% over last year. It is the largest number of people ever to be downtown in December. Emrick said that his favorite piece of Christmas data, though, is, with the help of our fantastic volunteers, staff adopted out nearly 3,600 retired elves of the north pole. 3. Last February, Emrick gave an update on the number of visitors to our downtown. Emirck’s quote from then, “This calendar year (2025), for the first time ever, we are likely to hit 2 million visitors to our downtown.” When he said this, he said he was being optimistic, but not unrealistic. Emrick said that he is excited to report that in the calendar year 2025, Conway had 2.8 million people visit downtown. An increase of 15.7% over 2024. To put that number into perspective, Hilton Head Island welcomes 2.5 million visitors annually. -- 6 of 11 -- January 5, 2026 7 4. Emrick said that his prediction for 2026 would be very close to 3 million number this year. To achieve that, however, staff will need some help from Ed Piotrowski and Jamie Arnold. The single biggest impact on our numbers is the weather. 5. At the request of the Wild Wing neighborhood, staff conducted a Speed Study on Woodstork Drive. The posted speed limit in Wild Wing is 25 mph. The average speed in the neighborhood was 29.75 mph. This would not warrant any additional measures to limit speed. However, the posted speed limit signs are not the traditional speed limit signs, rather they are smaller and were installed by the Wild Wing HOA. There is a question about the enforceability of the speed limit in this area given their lack of uniformity with our city speed limit signs. If any action were to be taken there, the installation of appropriate speed limit signs would be that recommendation. 6. Emrick gave a brief update on some of the projects that the city completed during 2025: a. The Parks Master Plan was completed and is already being implemented. b. The Riverwalk Extension was completed and opened last February. c. The city took ownership of 825 acres from Santee Cooper, including the Steam plant site, the former ash ponds and Lake Busbee d. Town Green project was completed, including the construction and opening of the downtown Splash Pad. e. Holiday Alley was completed, making pedestrian safety and connectivity a highlight of our downtown and allowing the holiday celebrations to dictate infrastructure, while at the same time, making further connections between downtown and the riverfront. f. The restroom facilities at Riverfront Park were rebuilt, after finding former flood damage that was too great to make easy repairs, the bathrooms were upgraded to better fit the vernacular of downtown. g. With the help of the South Carolina Department of Commerce, staff completed a Strategic Plan for the City, which will help guide the city in decision making in the upcoming years. h. The city expanded the National Register of Historic Places Downtown District, adding 59 properties to the district. i. The new Crabtree Pump Station came online in 2025. This project was partially grant funded, partially funded by GSWSA and the City and will provide capacity on the city sewer lines which will allow for future growth and provide relief during flooding events that are used to overwhelm the city sewer system in this area. j. The roof on the Ken Senn building was replaced. k. An infield groomer was purchased by the Recreation Department in August and placed into service. This will dramatically improve the quality of our baseball fields. l. The parking lots at the Oasis Pool, the Dog Park and Sports complex were all paved. m. A new humidifier was installed at the indoor pool, beginning the end-of-life replacement work that is needed to maintain the center in high quality. -- 7 of 11 -- January 5, 2026 8 n. Resurfaced 7 miles of roadways, with 5 of those miles being City roads. Repaired nearly 4 miles of sidewalks. o. For the first time ever, the city Fire Department is 100% EMT certified. Despite being a new endeavor, the certification of the city’s 39 fire fighters was achieved in less than two years. A remarkable achievement that will greatly benefit our city. 7. Emrick highlighted the big projects underway for this year: a. Chestnut Bay is 100% engineered, but since the funding for this stormwater project was cancelled, staff are looking for other funding sources to build this flood relief project in the Sherwood neighborhood. b. The Kingston Ferry is nearly completed with engineering, and staff is waiting on permitting from SCDES and Army Corps. Hopefully by this time next year, the city will be almost ready for a ribbon cutting. The ferry itself will be purchased soon using grant funds. c. The McKeithen Outfall project has been cleared and excavation for the stormwater pond is underway. The project should be completed in June. d. Drainage improvements and redesign of Park View Road is underway. Improvements to the ditch at 16th Avenue will be completed by next week and the remainder of the work will begin in February. e. The Pine/Beaty/Kingston Outfall project is well underway with a completion date of June. f. The utility relocation that is required as part of the 701N widening project is still awaiting bids and staff is working with GSWSA to determine if they would like to upsize the water lines during this process. g. The new Sherwood Pump Station is nearly online, once power is installed and final inspection, it should be ready. h. City crews are also finishing up the surveying work on Medlen Parkway to rework the sewer force main. Medlen also has extensive stormwater completed recently and sidewalks are being installed where this work was done. i. Working on the survey, work for a new water line on Highway 905. j. Working with a group to install a new historic marker at Collins Park to commemorate the Norton Twins. This project will hopefully be completed this year. k. The new park for New Road has playground equipment in storage ready for installation once the space is cleared and ready to go. A survey of the property has been ordered, and this park will be phased with some happening in this fiscal year and some in the next. l. The reconstruction of the Press Box at the Sports and Fitness Center is waiting on staff to draw up plans and have structural engineering to begin. Then it can be bid out for construction. m. New pavilions for Collins Park are being fabricated and will hopefully be installed by the end of February. -- 8 of 11 -- January 5, 2026 9 n. A new community Center and Park are in the planning stages for the Whittemore Area, and new fields are coming to the former Whittemore Elementary School site. o. New gas pumps will be installed at the Marina by the end of January. p. The indoor pool at the Sports and Fitness Center is ready for repainting. Bids are due by the middle of this month and will commence shortly thereafter. q. Upgrades to the Senior Center are underway. r. Field improvements are underway at the site by the Dog Park. s. The Crabtree Greenway Extension is 90% completed with engineering and waiting for SCDOT easements to finish engineering and move on to construction. t. ERF #4, which will accommodate Stella’s, River City Café, Crooked Oak, Leone’s and more, is on schedule, with brick being installed currently and all infrastructure in place - hope for completion in late winter. u. Engineering of Phase one of the Ash ponds project is underway. Survey work is 90% completed along with a preliminary site plan. Wetland/survey work was approved in December. v. Hawthorne Park has completed engineering and awaiting SCDED Land Disturbance Permits. Construction will begin as soon as permits are in hand. w. Rosehaven Drainage improvements are expected to begin in January. Box culverts have been ordered, and the contractor is awaiting delivery. x. Laurel Street downtown has some drainage issues that we hope to be able to address. The engineering on these improvements has been completed, and we are awaiting SCDOT permits. Hope to bid it out by the end of January. y. The city has brought in a consultant to work with our Police and Fire Departments and evaluate operations to make sure we are prepared adequately for the future and make recommendations to that end. This process is underway and hope to have recommendations by late winter. z. Encouraged council to get budget items to him soon. 8. No department head reports and no workshops, but there is a lengthy Executive Session still ahead. Goldfinch gave a shoutout to the Fire Department for all having EMT certifications. Goldfinch recommended handing over the 350 acres of waterfowl habitat to Ducks Unlimited with certain provisions. Emrick said that he reached out to Ducks Unlimited but had not heard back but will keep the conversation going. Blain suggested that smaller vehicles are looked at for the fire department. Emrick said that he hopes the consultants will be able to make recommendations for those items. COUNCIL INPUT: Helms - Told everyone Happy New Year. - Said it was a humbling experience to be reelected - looking forward to a second term and being nominated as the Mayor Pro Tem. -- 9 of 11 -- January 5, 2026 10 - Appreciate staff and all their hard work with the holidays. Butler - Said that being on council has been a humbling experience, thanked all the citizens and looks forward to working with everyone for the next 4 years as the city continues to grow. White - Said that the lady at 1908 Racepath Avenue inquired about getting a street sign at the alley that goes from Racepath to Ninth Avenue and possibly getting it renamed Lawrence Alley. Emrick said that staff would look into it. - Asked about the requirements for someone wanting to produce a movie in Conway. Emrick said that the applicant may need a special event permit but can coordinate with Wood or himself. Goldfinch - Honored to be back for another 4 four years and working with everyone. - Commended Bojangles and Singletons Grocery. Jordan - Congratulated Helms, Butler and Goldfinch on their reelection. - Congratulations to all for the 2.8 million visitors. Hardwick - Congratulated the returning Council members. - Thanked staff, volunteers and all citizens for making possible the 2.8 million visitors. - Excited about Porchfest. - Said that the fireworks on New Years Eve were phenomenal and told everyone Happy New Year. Blain - Welcomed colleagues back for another term. - Proud of Conway and is glad she gets to choose Conway to be her home. - Hats off to employees and she appreciates all. WORKSHOP: None EXECUTIVE SESSION: Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Helms to enter into Executive Session for the following: (A) Consideration of appointments to boards, commissions and committees [pursuant to SC Code §30-4-70(A) (1)]; (B) Discussion of potential contractual agreement regarding City lease of property [pursuant to SC Code §30- 4-70 (A) (2)]; (C) Discussion of an Economic Development Opportunity named Project Smokestacks [pursuant to SC Code §30-4-70 (A) (5)]; and (D) Discussion of contractual matter with Horry County Community Land Trust [pursuant to SC Code §30-4-70 (A) (2)]. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. -- 10 of 11 -- -- 11 of 11 --

ORDINANCE: #ZA2025-12-01 (A) AGENDA SECTION: Consent ISSUE: Petition to annex approximately 0.39+/- acres of property located at 4 Clemson Road. APPLICANT(S): Daniel Bachand ETAL PIN(s): 383-15-02-0010 CURRENT ZONING: Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF10) – min. lot size of 10,000 sq. ft. PROPOSED ZONING (upon annexation): Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) BACKGROUND: The subject property, identified as Lot 29, Block B of the Coastal Heights Subdivision, was transferred to the current owners on September 24, 2025. Restrictive Covenants were recorded on September 23, 2025. The property contains a single-family dwelling. Properties abutting the side, rear and across the street of the subject parcel are within the city limits. Annexation is being requested as a requirement for a name change to the city utility service account. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: The property abuts a vacant lot in the city limits, zoned HC and a residential lot, zoned R-1. Across the street is Conway Medical Center, zoned IN and County, including SF10 (Residential, no mobile homes allowed, on min. lot sizes of 10,000 sq. ft.), containing residential dwellings. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s future land use map identifies the property as Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). Per Section 3.2.3 of the UDO, the intent of the R-1 district is to provide for the preservation and expansion of areas for low to medium density, detached single-family residential development in the City of Conway. The district shall present a relatively spacious character, promote quiet, livable neighborhoods, and prohibit uses that are incompatible with the residential nature of the surrounding area. PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION (and public hearing): Planning Commission held the required Public Hearing at their November 6th mtg and voted to rezone the property to R-1 upon annexation. CITY COUNCIL: City Council approved first reading of the ordinance to annex the subject property at their October 6th meeting. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Approve Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-12-01 (A) to annex the subject property. SECTION 1. FINDINGS OF FACTS: WHEREAS, Section § 5-3-150, Code of Laws of South Carolina (1976) as amended, provides a method of annexing property into a city or town by a petition signed by all persons owning real estate in the area requesting annexation; and WHEREAS, A proper petition has been filed with the City of Conway by one hundred percent (100%) of the freeholders owning one hundred percent (100%) of the assessed value of the contiguous property herein described, petitioning for annexation of the property to the City of Conway under the provisions of SC Code of Laws, Section § 5-3-150(3); and WHEREAS, The area comprising said property is contiguous to the City of Conway and meets all statutory requirements for annexation; and WHEREAS, It appears to City Council that annexation would be in the best interest of property owners and the City. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED by the Mayor and Council of the City of Conway, South Carolina, duly assembled and with authority of same, pursuant to Section § 5-3-150, Code of Laws of South Carolina (1976), as amended, the following described property is hereby annexed to and made part of the City of Conway, to wit: Approximately 0.39+/- acres of property identified by PIN: 383-15-02-0010 and located at 4 Clemson Road. Upon annexation, the property shall become subject to the City’s jurisdiction for the rendition of all applicable municipal services. This annexation includes all waterways, roads, and rights-of-way adjacent to the property. For a more specific description of said property, see attached map(s). SECTION 2. Code § 6-29-760. SECTION 3.
