title: CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES 10.20.25
text: October 20, 2025 1 CITY OF CONWAY CITY COUNCIL MEETING CONWAY CITY HALL 229 MAIN STREET, CONWAY MONDAY, OCTOBER 20, 2025 PRESENT: Mayor Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor Pro Tem William Goldfinch, Amanda Butler, Julie Hardwick, Beth Helms, Justin Jordan and Larry White. STAFF: Adam Emrick, City Administrator; Mary Catherine Hyman, Deputy City Administrator; John Rogers, Deputy City Administrator; June Wood, Public Information Officer; Jeff Leveille, Technology Services Director; Le Hendrick, Fire Chief; Reggie Jenerette, Solid Waste Director; Robert Cooper, Construction Services Director; Lynn Smith, Human Resource Director; Chris Weatherford, Public Utilities Deputy Director; Rock Rabon, Fleet Maintenance Director; Jessica Hucks, Planning and Development Director; Brandon Harrelson, Public Works Director; Dale Long, Police Chief; Allison Williams, Finance Director; Timmy Williams, Hospitality and Beautification Director; Kayla Fleming, Municipal Judge; Ashley Smith, Recreation Director; and Alicia Shelley, City Clerk. OTHERS: There were approximately 10 others in attendance. CALL TO ORDER: Mayor Blain called the meeting to order. Butler gave the invocation and led the Pledge of Allegiance. The requirements for posting notice of this meeting under South Carolina’s Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) were met. CONSENT AGENDA: A. Approval of Purchase of Construction Services Vehicle (budgeted) B. Approval of October 6, 2025 Council Meeting Minutes APPROVAL OF CONSENT AGENDA: Motion: Butler made a motion, seconded by White to approve the October 20, 2025 consent agenda. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. SPECIAL PRESENTATION: A. Presentation of Employee of the Month for October 2025 – Public Service – Hucks presented the Public Service Employee of the Month award to Bradley Todd. B. Presentation of a Proclamation Recognizing Breast Cancer Awareness – Blain presented the Breast Cancer Awareness Proclamation to those in attendance. -- 1 of 8 -- October 20, 2025 2 FIRST READING: A. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-11-03 (B) to rezone approximately 2.15+/- acres of property located at 1001 Creel Street (PIN 368-08-01-0103) from the Horry County General Residential (GR) district to the City of Conway Professional (P) district upon annexation into the City of Conway. Hucks stated that the ordinance to annex the subject property was given first reading at the September 15 Council meeting. The applicant is seeking to zone the property Professional upon annexation. It’s currently zoned General Residential under Horry County’s jurisdiction. The City’s future land use map identifies the property as low/medium-density residential (R-1); however, properties on either side of the subject property as well as property across the street are zoned Professional. Creel Street contains a mixture of uses, including residential, medical, childcare, and other office related uses. Currently, the property contains one single-family dwelling, which is a permitted use in the professional district. Staff is not aware of any plans for the use of the property if the rezoning is granted. Hucks said that Planning Commission held the public hearing on the request at their October 2 meeting and recommended approval of the Professional district upon annexation of the property. Staff also recommended approval. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Goldfinch, to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-11-03 (B) rezoning the property at 1001 Creel Street to City of Conway Professional. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-11-03 (C) to amend Article 2 – Definitions, Article 4 – Use Tables, & Article 6 – Design Standards, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding the requirements and subdistricts of the Waccamaw Riverfront District (WRD). Hucks stated that this proposed amendment is being presented for consideration to provide clarity and consistency within the Waccamaw Riverfront zoning district, and would eliminate the sub-districts of the WRD, which is currently split between WRD-1 and WRD-2. There is nothing in the Unified Development Ordinance defining the parameters of the WRD-1 vs. the WRD-2 subdistricts, and there is no definition provided distinguishing between the two subdistricts. Per the definition of the Waccamaw Riverfront District, the intent of the district is to provide for the physical, social, and economic development of the City’s riverfront area. However, several of the properties that are zoned WRD do not have direct access to the riverfront. Section 6.4.1 of Article 6 provides a requirement for the WRD-1 district that all ground level floors of any building in WRD-1 be devoted to permitted uses that are outlined in the Use Tables of Article 4, aside from residential uses; with residential uses permitted on upper floors only. Recently, the city acquired approximately 224 acres that was zoned WRD-2 upon annexation because many of the areas included in those parcels do not have direct access to the riverfront, including property across Marina Drive and the property on the other side of Highway 501 on New Road. However, with the City’s riverfront being expanded by acquiring this acreage, in keeping with the intent of the Waccamaw Riverfront District, the mixed-use component is necessary on areas with direct access to the riverwalk to maintain public access and stimulate pedestrian activity. As such, this amendment eliminates the -- 2 of 8 -- October 20, 2025 3 sub-districts and instead proposes to include a requirement that properties to be developed that adjoin the riverwalk contain a mix of uses, with ground level floors devoted to one or more of the permitted commercial uses in the district and restricting residential (multifamily style) to upper-level floors. Hucks said that the Use Tables in Article 4 have also been revised as part of this amendment to reflect this change. Additionally, there are a few housekeeping changes included as part of the amendment. Hucks stated that Planning Commission held the public hearing on the amendment at their October 2 meeting and recommended approval. Staff also recommended approval of the proposed amendments. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Butler, to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-11-03 (C) as presented. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. C. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-11-03 (D) to amend Article 2 – Definitions and Article 13 – Administrative Agencies and Functions, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), to establish provisions for requiring a Development Agreement (DA) for developments that involve a zoning map amendment and/or annexation into the City of Conway. Hucks stated that this amendment was originally discussed at this year’s budget retreat, and again at a workshop a few meetings ago. One of the issues that staff has researched over the past several months is whether the requirement for a development agreement existed in other localities and whether requiring a development agreement as a condition of annexation or rezoning was in accordance with state law. The South Carolina Local Government Development Agreement Act expressly authorizes cities and counties to enter into such agreements with property owners, but these agreements must be voluntary. However, they may accompany zoning approvals and annexations. By adopting a development agreement through the statutory and public notice process, the right to attach development agreements to an annexation and/or rezoning is considered to be legally defensible. Staff emphasizes that such agreements must be voluntary between the City and the applicant and must be adopted in accordance with state law - both parties must agree to the terms of the agreement. With the annexation of large tracts of land, such as the Warden Station PD or the Brookhaven PD, Council asked that staff prepare options for requiring development agreements for certain types of development. In accordance with state law, there are 2 threshold requirements for a DA: 1) the property must contain a minimum of 25 acres of uplands or highlands, such as acreage that is above the 100-yr flood plain, and 2) the length of the agreement varies with the size of the property. For instance, property up to 250 acres of highland is limited to an agreement term of 5 years and property with 250-1000 acres of upland is limited to 10 years. Properties with 1000-2000 acres of upland are limited to 20 years. The contents of a DA must include several items, such as the property description, owners, the duration of the agreement, permitted uses, public facilities, dedication of land for public purpose, permits needed, and a schedule for completion of the development, among other things. -- 3 of 8 -- October 20, 2025 4 There are two places in South Carolina that staff found that typically require development agreements as part of the approval of a Planned Development District, and that was Hardeeville and North Myrtle Beach. Hucks said that she had heard that NMB has started requiring them for all development, but Hucks said that had not been verified. Hucks said that at the last Council workshop this issue was discussed, one of the biggest issues discussed was the threshold for requiring an agreement. The general consensus was for any annexation and/or rezoning of property that would permit residential uses and proposed to contain 150 lots or units. Additionally, the requirement would only apply to properties seeking annexation into the city limits or property proposed to be rezoned, not property already in the city and zoned for residential development, as those properties already have by-right development. Hucks stated that Planning Commission considered the amendment at their October 2 meeting and held the public hearing. Staff presented 2 options: Option 1 - included a threshold of 150 lots/units on a minimum of 25 acres of upland or, Option 2 - leave the requirement up to Council, and instead, under the applicability section of the ordinance, state that “Council, as a condition to annexation and/or rezoning of a property, may require the property owner and/or developer to enter into a development agreement for any development whether residential or nonresidential, when it is determined that such an agreement is necessary to protect the public health, safety, and general welfare of the citizens of Conway.” Planning Commission’s preference was to lower the threshold to 50 lots or units and to remove the standard for the property to contain 25 acres or that proposed to include the minimum number of lots or units. That was a valid concern because what the city does not want is to have someone wishing to annex large tracts that is not proposing a residential development but instead intends to build a few or only one house for themselves. However, the issue with how it’s worded now is it gives those who may seek annexation or rezoning of property a way to get around the requirement for a development agreement as is illustrated here - If they have 100 acres, they could divide the property in a way that keeps the number of lots or units under the threshold of 50 or if there is a way it could be subdivided to where each tract would contain less than 25 acres of uplands, they could build a multifamily project that contains more than 50 units, regardless of the overall acreage when less than 25 acres is considered upland. In this example, the parent tract is split into 3, 33-acre tracts, and each one avoids the minimum threshold but once all 3 tracts have been developed, 247 lots or units are built. This conundrum is probably why there is nothing too specific in any ordinance across the state, except for where it’s specified that a planned development district may be accompanied by a development agreement. Hucks told Council that staff wanted to present the 2 options for consideration for first reading as well and included 2 separate ordinances: one that includes PC’s recommendation, and one that provides the more general language, which gives Council the discretion to require a development agreement for any project which meets the minimum standards for such an agreement. This amendment is not time-sensitive, so if there is a desire to defer the amendment at this time, if there is something that council -- 4 of 8 -- October 20, 2025 5 would like staff to look into further, that would not be a problem. If this is something council would like to advance to final reading, staff recommends approval of first reading of the version that gives Council the discretion to require or not require a development agreement – regardless of the number of lots or units proposed or whether its residential or commercial in nature. There was much discussion regarding parcels being subdivided to get around the 25 acres, restrictions on developers being about to subdivide, multiple uses on the parcels, future council decisions, comp plan as a tool, and protecting the citizens that are already living here. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Goldfinch, to approve staff’s recommendation of Option 2 for first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-11-03 (D). Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. PUBLIC INPUT: - Jimmy Hammond spoke to council regarding retired employees’ health insurance. CITY ADMINISTRATOR’S REPORT: Emrick informed Council of the following: • The Mayor’s Youth Council has had two meetings so far this school year. Skyler Platt was elected as the 3rd Junior Mayor. The entire Council will be attending one of our future Council meetings. • Visitor data for Halloween through Friday of last week shows 46.2% over last year, which includes the rainout Saturday and Sunday from two weekends ago. It does not include this past Saturday which saw the most people downtown in its history. Staff expects the data to show Downtown had 40,000 people or more. • Having that many people for the first time means there are some issues to work out before this upcoming weekend, and those plans are being worked on now. • There were numerous reports of restaurants running out of food, 3+ hour wait times, and people leaving Halloween hungry. Adding a few more food trucks this weekend to help address the demand. • Staff is working on Christmas planning and building and have heard from many out- of-town visitors that they are thinking about a return trip to see what’s done in December. Since the bar has been set high, the city needs to execute. • This week features Phantom of the Opera at the First United Methodist Church, the Chamber of Commerce’s Coffin Races, Scare on the Square Professional Wrestling, The UFO Festival, the Monster Mash on Millpond and a lot of Trunk or Treats and Fall Festivals. • The final Citizen’s Academy is this Wednesday, and they will learn where all the Holiday Decorations are stored. -- 5 of 8 -- October 20, 2025 6 • Reminder that the City of Halloween Game at Coastal Football is the 30th against Marshall and is expected to be a Halloween extravaganza. • On the 31st, in addition to Halloween, there is a home football game at Conway High School, which will be rebranded to Halloween High School for the game. • The Coastal Homecoming Parade is on Friday, November 7th at 4 p.m. downtown. Transportation for Council will be provided to ride in the parade. • Three items on the agenda for Executive Session, but no workshop tonight. • Department Head report from Brandon Harrleson in Public Works. There was much discussion regarding Halloween, including traffic control, control over the traffic lights, various road closures, and the possibility of putting flashing lights on top of the crosswalk stands. Harrelson gave Council a year-to-date report on the Public Works Department. COUNCIL INPUT: Helms − Rode the Pedal Pub for a birthday party and said it was fun. Helms spoke to operator of the Pedal Pub and said business had not been as good possibly due to traffic flow or not being able to have alcohol. − Said that she appreciated the visitors and while downtown Saturday she met people from all over. − Appreciates all of staffs’ hard work. − Hopes that Halloween volunteers also show up for Christmas. Butler − Said that everything Downtown looks amazing, Riverwalk is great and wants to make sure that it is accessible to all citizens, even citizens with disabilities. Butler asked the Administrator if the city was following the ADA guidelines. Emrick said yes and that those areas are being upgraded where deficiencies were found. Emrick said that last year the sidewalks on Laurel were redone as they were found to be too narrow. Holiday Alley was a mulch pathway and now pavement has been added to make it accessible. Emrick said that there is a stair walk in the middle of the Riverwalk but there was no way to get over the railroad trestle without it and it meets code because each end is accessible, but the stairs was the only way to make it connectible. Emrick said once the city owns the railroad tracks there may be a way to retro fit to make more ADA accessible. − Has concerns with Smith Jones and wondered about putting more cameras out. Emrick said that there are cameras on the city side of it that face multiple locations but putting city cameras on private property is tricky. Emrick said that staff can check on putting more out where the city owns and make sure that there is coverage around the perimeter. White − Requested to use the Pedal Pub for the Christmas Parade. -- 6 of 8 -- October 20, 2025 7 Goldfinch − Told staff to keep up the great work, and continue to push council out of their comfort zones as Goldfinch says that council is learning and growing through those successes. Goldfinch said he was reminded at the budget retreat of the challenges that the community faced in a period of time was this motivation to do something new to grow. − Encouraged all to read the book, Performative Outrage. − Thanked staff and best colleagues in the world for pushing him to go out of his comfort zone and Goldfinch feels he is a better person for doing so. Jordan − Said that Saturday downtown was insane and mind boggling to see – heard from business owners that are setting record numbers – able to generate revenue now to get them through the drier months is a great thing to see. − Thanked all. Hardwick − Thanked all staff and volunteers for their hard work with decorating Downtown - said she has sat for hours meeting, talking and watching everyone from all over the country as they are coming by with smiles on their faces. − Asked staff and council to look at congratulating Anto’s as he brought home a world title for his pizza while in Italy. Darren Smith, SC Chef Ambassador also helped Anto’s in that process. − Theatre of the Republic starts the Wizard of Oz this weekend. − The Children’s Festival was very well attended. − Read a Facebook post commending Council and then encouraged all to get out and vote early. Blain − Told all that on her visit to Salt Lake City last week she toured a tiny housing project that starts with transition sheltering with mental health services, medical services, more training on how to get a job, keep a job, managing money, and how to get started all over again. Blain wants to look beyond what happens after the shelter and spoke of what was built in this housing project that she toured. Asked staff to start planning where this could exist in the city. − Blain said that she also promoted the City of Halloween, South Carolina while in Salt Lake City. − Read 2 testimonials supporting the Halloween transition. EXECUTIVE SESSION: Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Helms, to enter into Executive Session for the following: (A) Discussion on Contractual Matters Incident to Retirees Health Insurance [pursuant to SC Code §30-4-70 (A) (2)]; (B) Discussion of an Economic Development Opportunity named Project Smokestacks [pursuant to SC Code §30-4-70 (A) (5)]; and (C) Review of Contract Terms with AT&T for Lease of Space on the Gardner Lacy Water Tower [pursuant to SC Code §30-4-70 (A) (2)]. -- 7 of 8 -- -- 8 of 8 --

ORDINANCE: #ZA2025-10-06 (C) AGENDA SECTION: Consent ISSUE: Final Reading of an ordinance to amend Articles 1 – Preamble, 3 – Zoning Districts, 6 – Design Standards, 13 – Administrative Agencies and Functions, and Article 14 – Boards and Procedures. BACKGROUND: The proposed amendments are part of a larger effort to clean up several parts of the UDO, which has been in process since early 2024. In addition to this cleanup effort, some of the proposed amendments will address recent guidance provided by the Municipal Association with respect to the process for annexation and zoning of property. Going forward, Council will consider annexation and zoning map amendments as separate ordinances. These changes are outlined in Article 13. Several of these amendments are simply relocation of the UDO from Article 6 to Article 13. Other amendments include, but are not limited to, the following: • Article 1 has been amended to include several provisions, such as an intent and purpose, applicability of the UDO, transition rules/vested rights, limitation of liability, among other legal provisions. The “preamble” of the UDO will be moved to an appendix in Article 1. • Article 3: moved the CCU Neighborhood Overlay ordinance to Article 6, to be in the overlay section of the UDO, similar to the GCO, VCO, and MSO are located. • Article 6: removed language to add to Article 13 instead. • Article 14: Minor revisions to the language regarding the BZA and TRC. These amendments are attached for your reference. PLANNING COMMISSION: In addition to holding the required public hearing, Planning Commission reviewed the proposed amendments and recommended unanimous approval of the amendments at their Sept. 4th mtg. STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Approve Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-10-06 (C). 34 -- 34 of 223 -- ORDINANCE #ZA2025-10-06 (C) AMENDING ARTICLE 1 – PREAMBLE, ARTICLE 3 – ZONING DISTRICTS, ARTICLE 6 – DESIGN STANDARDS, ARTICLE 13 – ADMINISTRATIVE AGENCIES AND FUNCTIONS, AND ARTICLE 14 – BOARDS AND PROCEDURES, OF THE CITY OF CONWAY UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE (UDO), REGARDING REQUIREMENTS ANNEXATION AND AMENDMENTS TO THE CITY’S OFFICIAL ZONING MAP, AMENDMENTS RELATED TO CITY BOARDS AND PROCEDURES, AND REVISIONS IN LANGUAGE WITHIN THESE ARTICLES OF THE UDO FOR CLARITY AND CONSISTENCY. WHEREAS, pursuant to Title 6, Chapter 29 of the Code of Laws of South Carolina 1976, as Amended known as the “South Carolina Local Government Comprehensive Planning Enabling Act of 1994” enabled the City of Conway to adopt the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) of the City of Conway, South Carolina; and WHEREAS, Article 13, Section 13.1.7 of the UDO provides that the regulations, restrictions, and boundaries set forth in said Ordinance may from time be amended, supplemented, changed, or repealed in accordance with S.C. Whenever any provision of this Ordinance refers to or cites a section of the South Carolina Code of Laws and that section is later amended, this Ordinance shall be deemed amended to refer to the amended section. 1.1.3 Jurisdiction This Ordinance shall apply to all property (land, buildings, structures, and uses) located within the corporate limits of the City of Conway, South Carolina, as permitted by law, and as may be expanded, contracted, or modified from time to time. 1.1.4 Applicability A. All development and use of land within the City of Conway shall conform to the requirements of this Ordinance. B. The provisions of this Ordinance shall apply to all zoning, land subdivision, site development, signage, landscaping, and related land use activities occurring after its effective date, unless specifically exempted. C. Applicability to Governmental Facilities. To the extent allowed by law, the provisions of this ordinance shall apply to development by the County, State, or federal government or its agencies, departments, or corporate services, or on land owned or otherwise controlled by the County, State, or federal government. 1.1.5 Relationship to Other Laws A. Where this Ordinance imposes a greater restriction than imposed by other local ordinances, regulations, private covenants, or agreements, the provisions of this Ordinance shall control. B. Compliance with this Ordinance does not relieve any person from complying with other applicable local, state or federal laws or regulations. C. Private Restrictions / Covenants 1. In accordance with SC Code of Laws § 6-29-1145, as amended, local planning agencies are required to inquire in application for a permit if the parcel of land is restricted by a recorded covenant that prohibits the proposed activity. Nothing within this Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) shall be construed to authorize the use of any land or structure in a manner that violates private deed restrictions, covenants, or other private agreements governing the use of land. The City of Conway does not enforce private deed restrictions or covenants and assumes no responsibility for interpreting or enforcing such agreements. 41 -- 41 of 223 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 1 – General Provisions 3-3 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended xx, xx xxxx 1.1.6 Severability If any section or provision of this Ordinance (UDO) is declared invalid or unconstitutional by a court of competent jurisdiction, such declaration shall not affect the validity of this Ordinance (UDO) as a whole or any part thereof which is not specifically declared to be invalid or unconstitutional and shall continue in full force and effect. 1.1.7 Effective Date This Ordinance (UDO) shall take effect and be enforced from and after the date of its adoption by the City Council for the City of Conway, and supersedes and repeals any previous zoning, subdivision, or development regulations by the City of Conway to the extent of any conflict. 1.1.8 Preamble (Informational Reference) The City’s policy goals and planning philosophy underlying this ordinance are described in the Preamble, which is the original Ordinance adopting the Unified Development Ordinance, Ordinance 2011-12-12 (A), and is attached as Appendix A – Preamble, to this Article. Section 1.2 Purpose and Intent 1.2.1 Purpose and Intent The purpose and intent of the UDO is to guide development in accordance with the City’s Comprehensive Plan and existing and future needs of the City. The UDO is enacted and designed to exercise the full range of authority available to the City in accordance with State law to: A. Provide for adequate light, air, and open space; B. Prevent the overcrowding of land; C. Avoid undue concentration of population; D. Lessen congestion in the streets; E. Facilitate the creation of a convenient, attractive and harmonious community; F. Protect and preserve scenic, historic, or ecologically sensitive areas; G. Regulate the density and distribution of populations and the uses of buildings, structures, and land; H. Facilitate the adequate provision and availability of public facilities or services; I. Secure safety from fire, flood, and other dangers; and J. Further the public welfare in any other regard specified by the City Council. 1.2.2 Conformance with the Comprehensive Plan This ordinance is intended to ensure that all development within the City’s jurisdiction is in accordance with the Comprehensive Plan and implements the planning policies adopted as part of the Comprehensive Plan in furtherance of the general health, safety, and welfare of the citizens of the City of Conway. The district shall present a rural character, promote quiet, livable neighborhoods, and prohibit uses that are incompatible with the residential nature of the surrounding area. 3.2.3 Low/Medium Density Residential (R-1) The intent of the R-1 District is to provide for the preservation and expansion of areas for low to medium density, detached single-family residential development in the City of Conway. [Amended 12/17/18 #ZA2018-12-17(A)] 3.2.4 Medium Density Residential (R-2) The intent of the R-2 District is to provide areas for medium density attached, detached, semi-attached and multi- family residential development in the City of Conway, and to prohibit uses that would substantially interfere with the development or continuation of residential structures in the District. 3.2.5 High Density Residential (R-3) The intent of the R-3 District is to provide areas for high-density attached, detached, semi-detached, and multifamily residential development in the City of Conway and to prohibit uses that would substantially interfere with the development or continuation of residential structures in the District. 3.2.6 Traditional Residential (R-4) The intent of the R-4 District is to allow undeveloped parcels of land to be subdivided and developed in a manner that utilizes traditional residential neighborhood principles that were common in the early part of the 20th Century. More specifically, the district is intended to provide for the configuration of blocks, lots, streets, open spaces, and other amenities that lend to creating a sense of community and social interaction. The characteristics of such developments generally include rectangular block configurations where streets run parallel and perpendicular to one another, intersect at or near 90-degree angles, and form blocks of similar size and shape. Centrally located open space for community recreation and leisure is required in order to compensate for the uniquely smaller lots of such developments. Service alleys providing access to the rear of lots are necessary in order to accommodate vehicular storage and public utility services. The design aspect of the individual homes is as critical to the creation of the sense of community as the design standards of the platted subdivision. Typically, homes should be built closer to streets and on raised foundations. More specifically, the intent of the PD District is to permit: A. Flexibility in design to take the greatest advantage of natural land, trees, historical and other features; B. Accumulation of large areas of usable open space for recreation, preservation of natural amenities, and provision of community facilities; C. Creation of a variety of residential and compatible neighborhood arrangements that give the home occupant greater choice in selecting types of environments and living units; D. Clustering of one residential type for better use of land and open space; E. Allowance of sufficient freedom for the developer to take a creative approach to the use of land and related physical development, as well as utilizing innovative techniques to enhance the visual character of the city; F. Efficient use of land which may result in reduction in development and maintenances cost of street and utility systems; G. Simplification of the procedure for obtaining approval of proposed developments through simultaneous review by the city of proposed land use, site consideration, lot and setback consideration, public needs and requirements, and health and safety factors. 52 -- 52 of 223 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 3 – Zoning Districts 3-7 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended July 21, 2025 3.3.3 Mixed Use Flexible Zone (MU) The intent of the Mixed-Use Flexible Zone is to encourage a mix of residential, professional and limited commercial development throughout the City of Conway that does not create excessive demands for vehicular parking. The requirements of the district are designed to promote mixed uses and provide a transition between residential and commercial properties and minimizing adverse effects to adjoining properties. The Mixed-Use District is a ‘floating zone’ which is defined as a zone that is described in the text of a zoning ordinance, but is unmapped (S.C. Code of Laws, Title 6, Chapter 29). Once a property is designated Mixed Use, it will then be mapped by amending the Official Zoning Map of the City of Conway. Intent. Residential design standards are not an attempt to stifle design but are meant to inspire good architectural design while protecting and enhancing the aesthetic and visual character of residential developments within the City of Conway. More specifically, to: 1. avoid monotony in design; 2. protect and preserve the character of residential areas within the city and permit continued development of a compatible nature on vacant properties that are or will be proposed for residential development within the city limits; 3. enhance the character and function of city streets; 4. promote original and high-quality design, and reduce tract or production-style homes; 5. maintain and enhance property values through appropriate aesthetic and functional design considerations; 6. deemphasize garages as major visual elements along local residential streets; 7. encourage design details, which add visual interest and encourage outdoor living spaces; and 8. implement the city’s goals and objectives within the city’s comprehensive plan related to providing a mix of housing types and promoting quality site development and design that enhances Conway’s sense of place within neighborhoods. A. To hear and decide appeals where it is alleged the City Planner Zoning Administrator or their designee, erred in an order, requirement, decision, or determination. To hear and decide appeals for variances in specific cases when a strict application of the zoning ordinance would cause an unnecessary hardship, and approval of such variance would not be contrary to public interest or undermine the spirit of the zoning ordinance. The fact that property may be used more profitably if a variance is granted is not grounds for a variance. The Board may attach conditions to a variance that address location, character, or other features of a proposed building, structure, or use, in order to protect the established property values in the surrounding area or to promote the public health, safety, or general welfare of the community. The Board may grant a variance for an unnecessary hardship if it makes and explains in writing all of the following findings. 1. Extraordinary conditions: There are extraordinary and exceptional conditions pertaining to the particular piece of property. 2. Other Property: The extraordinary and exceptional conditions do not generally apply to other property in the vicinity. 3. Utilization: Because of the extraordinary or exceptional conditions, the application of the ordinance to a particular piece of property would effectively prohibit or unreasonably restrict the utilization of the property. 4. Detriment: The authorization of a variance will not be of substantial detriment to adjacent property or the public good, and the character of the district will not be harmed by granting a variance. BACKGROUND: The city’s footprint is extending to more rural areas of the county, and several large tracts are shown as being Forest Agriculture (FA) on the future land use map; many of them exceeding 100 acres in size. The intent of the FA district is to establish and preserve areas for agricultural or passive recreation. Most agricultural uses require structure(s) for farming equipment or stables for animals. However, the current language of the UDO would not permit such structures without there being a principal use and structure (i.e. in conjunction with a single-family dwelling). The proposed amendment carves out an exception for the FA district only for the ability to have accessory structures relating to farming; particularly, the keeping of livestock / fowl, without the requirement to have a principal structure, but with conditions, including that it would be applicable to parcels zoned FA that are a minimum of 5 acres in size. This amendment also includes other revisions relating to the noncommercial keeping of livestock / fowl and adds the Rural Residential (RR) district as one of the districts in which the use is permitted as a conditional use. The amendments are included on the following pages. Note that the amendments are applicable to “noncommercial” activities, not commercial activities. Commercial agriculture uses in FA already require a minimum lot size of 5 acres. ISSUE: Accommodations Tax Advisory Committee Funding Recommendations BACKGROUND: The City received $192,628.80 from the State Accommodations Tax for FY 24-25. SC Code of Laws (Section 6-4-10) details how these funds are allocated: 1. The first $25,000 to the General Fund 2. The balance remaining must be allocated as follows: a. 5% of balance to General Fund b. 30% of balance to the City’s selected designated marketing organization (Conway Downtown Alive) c. 65% of balance to tourism related expenses The Accommodations Tax Advisory Committee is tasked with reviewing applications and making a recommendation on how to allocate the 65% balance of $108,958.72 plus the $7,435.25 rollover from FY 2024. title: CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES 10.6.25
text: October 6, 2025 1 CITY OF CONWAY CITY COUNCIL MEETING CONWAY CITY HALL 229 MAIN STREET, CONWAY MONDAY, OCTOBER 6, 2025 PRESENT: Mayor Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor Pro Tem William Goldfinch, Amanda Butler, Julie Hardwick, Beth Helms, Justin Jordan and Larry White. STAFF: Adam Emrick, City Administrator; Mary Catherine Hyman, Deputy City Administrator; John Rogers, Deputy City Administrator; June Wood, Public Information Officer; Jeff Leveille, Technology Services Director; Le Hendrick, Fire Chief; Reggie Jenerette, Solid Waste Director; Robert Cooper, Construction Services Director; Lynn Smith, Human Resource Director; Chris Weatherford, Public Utilities Deputy Director; Rock Rabon, Fleet Maintenance Director; Jessica Hucks, Planning and Development Director; Brandon Harrelson, Public Works Director; Dale Long, Police Chief; Allison Williams, Finance Director; Timmy Williams, Hospitality and Beautification Director; and Alicia Shelley, City Clerk. OTHERS: There were approximately 35 others in attendance. CALL TO ORDER: Mayor Blain called the meeting to order. Hardwick gave the invocation and led the Pledge of Allegiance. The requirements for posting notice of this meeting under South Carolina’s Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) were met. CONSENT AGENDA: A. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-15 (C) to annex approximately +/-0.39 acres of property located at 5206 Columbia Street (PIN 383-08-03-0002). B. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-10-06 (A) to rezone approximately 0.39+/- acres of property located at 5206 Columbia St. (PIN 338-08-03-0002) from the Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF10) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district upon annexation into the City of Conway. C. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-15 (B) to annex approximately +/-10.66 acres of property located at or near the corner of Hwy 501 and Hwy 548 (PIN’s 326- 00-00-0026 and 326-09-03-0006). D. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-10-06 (B) to rezone approximately 10.68 +/- acres of property located at the intersection of Hwy 548 & Hwy 501 (PINs 326-00-00- 0026 & 326-09-03-0006) from Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) district to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district upon annexation into the City of Conway. -- 1 of 11 -- October 6, 2025 2 E. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-10-06 (C) to amend Article 1 – Preamble, Article 3 – Zoning Districts, Article 6 – Design Standards, Article 13 – Administrative Agencies and Functions, and Article 14 – Boards and Procedures, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding requirements for annexation and amendments to the city’s official zoning map, amendments relating to City Boards and procedures, and revisions to language in these Articles of the UDO for clarity and consistency. F. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-10-06 (D) to amend Article 4 – Use Tables and Article 5 – Specific Use Regulations, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding requirements for noncommercial keeping of livestock or fowl and related accessory uses and/or structures in the Forest Agriculture (FA) zoning district. G. Final Reading of Ordinance #2025-10-06 (E) approving the execution of a quit claim deed for property in the Pecan Grove Subdivision, specifically the parcels identified as PINs 368-15-03-0033 & 368-15-03-0035. H. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-10-06 (F) to amend the City of Conway Comprehensive Plan to adopt the 2025 Conway Parks and Recreation Master Plan. I. Approval of Purchase of Public Works Vehicles (budgeted) J. Approval of a Special Event – North Conway Baptist Church Community Outreach Fall Festival – October 19, 2025 K. Approval of a Special Event – 2025 CCU Homecoming Parade – November 7, 2025 L. Approval of Purchase of Planning & Development Vehicle (budgeted) M. Approval of September 15, 2025 Council Meeting Minutes APPROVAL OF CONSENT AGENDA: Motion: Butler made a motion, seconded by Hardwick to approve the October 6, 2025 consent agenda. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. SPECIAL PRESENTATION: A. Presentation of a Proclamation honoring Annsley Vick – Blain presented Annsley Vick with a proclamation honoring her achievements. B. Presentation of a Proclamation honoring the Palmetto Literacy Council – Blain presented a proclamation honoring the efforts and successes of the Palmetto Literacy Council to Dodi Hodges, Executive Director and Tonya Robinson, Board Member. -- 2 of 11 -- October 6, 2025 3 C. Presentation by Horry County Solid Waste Authority – On behalf of the Solid Waste Authority, Esther Murphy presented the city, particularly the Solid Waste and Hospitality and Beautification Departments with a plaque for their Environmental Awareness. D. Presentation by Denley Caughman – Denley Caughman gave a presentation to council on the operations of the Kingston Joinery and invited everyone to the open house scheduled for October 18, which will spotlight the latest reproduction of “The Lincoln Chair.” FIRST READING: A. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-12-01 (A) to annex approximately 0.34 acres of property located at 4 Clemson Road (PIN 383-15-02-0010). Hucks stated that this property is within the Coastal Heights subdivision, at the corner of Singleton Ridge Road. Several lots within this subdivision have been annexed over the years as a result of the existing homes being sold and new accounts set up to receive city utility services. This particular property was sold to the current owner in September of this year, and restrictive covenants were recorded. This particular property appears to be owner-occupied. Hucks said that the city’s future land use map identifies the property as R-1 (low/medium density residential). If first reading of annexation is approved, the request to amend the zoning map for this property will be considered by Planning Commission at the November 6 meeting. Following Planning Commission’s recommendation, the ordinance for the amendment to the city’s zoning map will be considered at the next available council meeting. Hucks said that staff recommends approval of first reading to annex the subject property. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Helms, to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-12-01 (A) annexing the property at 4 Clemson Road. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-12-01 (B) to annex approximately 0.19 acres of property located at 503 University Forest Drive (PIN 383-01-02-0002). Hucks stated that this property is located in the University Forest subdivision. The request to annex was submitted by the Power of Attorney for the property owner, which is now an estate property, as the property owner has passed away. This triggered the requirement to request annexation, as the utility account was being transferred to another individual’s name. Restrictive covenants were recorded on September 23 of this year. Sanitation services are not currently provided in this subdivision, no other lots in the subdivision have been annexed to date, and each request that has been considered for annexation over the years has been denied by council. Hucks said that staff does not recommend annexation of this property. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Blain, to deny first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-12-01 (B) annexing the property at 503 University Forest Drive. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. -- 3 of 11 -- October 6, 2025 4 CONSIDERATION: A. Consideration of approval of a name for new subdivision located on Mill Pond Road and Tortoise Drive, proposed to be named “The Reserve at Millpond” (PIN 338-00- 00-0018). Hucks stated that the proposed development is currently being reviewed by the Technical Review Committee (TRC). Planning Commission approved the subdivision plan contingent on approval of TRC, along with the proposed street names at their October 2 meeting. There are 234 in common townhome units proposed for this property and the main access will be provided from existing city roads – Tortoise Drive and Turtle Creek Drive. In accordance with Section 10.3.18 of the city’s Unified Development Ordinance, all subdivision names must be reviewed and approved by city council. Hucks said that the proposed name of “The Reserve at Millpond” has been reviewed by TRC and staff recommends approval of the requested subdivision name. Motion: Butler made a motion, seconded by Jordan, to approve the subdivision name of “The Reserve at Millpond.”. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. Consideration of Accommodations Tax Advisory Committee Funding Recommendations - Mungo thanked council for allowing those to serve on the Accommodations Tax Committee (ATAX) and said he appreciated each of the committee members for taking the time out of their schedules to serve on it. Mungo acknowledged Russell Fowler, committee member that was in attendance. Mungo gave a special thanks to Allison Williams for all her help in preparing the advertisements, receiving the applications, preparing the ATAX spreadsheet and setting up the meetings. The committee reviewed each application to make sure the requests fit the tourism related expenditures that is set up in the Accommodations Tax guidelines. The funds available from the tourism related expenditures for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2025 totaled $116,393.97. The committee recommended a disbursement of $116,390.00 to four separate agencies and that would allow the committee to carry over $3.97 to year 2026. The committee’s recommendation was as follows: • Conway Chamber of Commerce - $35,000 for advertising of Riverfest and additional advertisements. • Conway Downtown Alive - $56,890 for advertising of approximately 21 major events throughout the year. • Waccamaw Market Cooperative - $6,500 for advertising for the Conway Farmers Market. • Theatre of the Republic - $18,000 for advertising for musical productions, comedies, Coastal Youth Theatre, and special programs throughout the year. Mungo said that the committee feels that these requests fall within the Accommodations tax law to promote tourism and enlarge its economic benefit through advertising, promotion and providing those facilities and services which enhance the ability of the City of Conway to attract and provide for tourists. -- 4 of 11 -- October 6, 2025 5 Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Helms, to approve the recommendation of the Accommodations Tax Committee as presented. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. C. Consideration of the Replacement of the HVAC Unit at the Public Safety Building – Rogers stated that the existing Trane HVAC unit at the Public Safety building has reached the end of its useful life and is in dire need of replacement. A new Trane unit will reduce operating costs, increase energy efficiency, and improve comfort conditions within the facility. To obtain the most competitive pricing, staff proposes utilizing the OMNIA cooperative purchasing agreement, which is an approved government contract. Rogers said that staff recommends proceeding with the purchase and installation of a new 50-ton packaged commercial rooftop Trane unit through the OMNIA cooperative agreement. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Butler, to approve staff to proceed with the purchase and installation of the new HVAC unit at the Public Safety Building as presented. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. PUBLIC INPUT: − Denise Linderson spoke to council regarding the development going in behind Midtown Village and requested that speed bumps be installed on McDougal and that the new development use the easement at Conway Christian School. − Sue Tayor spoke to council regarding the development going in behind Midtown Village and voiced traffic concerns, use of easement on Cultra, wetlands buffer and infrastructure. − Tiffany Edwards spoke to council regarding the traffic congestion on Palmetto Street on the Highway 701 S. end. − Christin Whedon-Darling spoke to council regarding the development going in behind Midtown Village and voiced concerns with traffic, wetlands, and the animals in the now wooded area. − Kennedi Poole voiced her concerns to council regarding handicap accessibility downtown, especially along the sidewalks and the riverwalk. − Tim Poole voiced concerns regarding ongoing crime problems at Crane Creek Apartments and asked council to enforce the nuisance laws. CITY ADMINISTRATOR’S REPORT: Emrick informed Council of the following: • Congratulated Conway High School on a big win over North Myrtle Beach in football last Friday night. Hoping that brought a little bit of momentum to carry -- 5 of 11 -- October 6, 2025 6 into Friday’s game vs. Myrtle Beach to bring the Victory Bell back to Conway. The win also moves the Tigers into a tie in the Beach Region for first place. • Said he would mention Halloween one time. The data for October 1st through 3rd shows that the city is up 98% in visitor traffic from last year during the same three days. Restaurants are reporting record sales. Staff is looking at some improvements for pedestrian safety before this weekend. • The Smoke on the Waccamaw BBQ Festival is this weekend, and Tru Soul is playing Friday night at the Old Tennis Center. • The Citizen’s Academy has been very successful thus fare. Great feedback from the participants. For sure, this will be a program that the city continues. • Horry County’s Charters of Freedom Dedication is scheduled for 10 a.m. at the Horry County Museum. The City of Conway is a sponsor of this project, which displays the Constitution, the Declaration of Independence, the Bill of Rights and the Civil Rights Act. • There are multiple workshop items for discussion and an Executive Session. The workshops are: o Discussion of the concept of a food truck corral o Property on Hwy 701 and Copperhead Road o The Train Depot o County acceptance of a permit for parcel requiring annexation on Academy Drive Goldfinch said that he would love to see the Citizens Academy continue. Goldfinch also recommended that we have a FAQ or Did you Know section to promote on our different outlets to educate folks on hot topics. Helms asked if people could buy Halloween t-shirts. Emrick said that the city provided employees with shirts but that others could buy at Papa’s or Conway Downtown Alive. Everyone sang Happy birthday to Smith. White asked about the safety of visitors Downtown. Emrick said that staff were looking into options and possibly closing Laurel Street between Second and Third Avenues. Butler inquired about expanding decorations to Highway 378. Emrick said that first staff try to keep them all within walking distance and the city does not own frontage on Highway 378 and does not have power at the Smith Jones property. Emrick said that the goal is to expand the footprint in the future and that staff could look into putting some pumpkins out in that area. COUNCIL INPUT: Helms − Said that she had a couple of calls about doing something at Collins Park for the tennis teams that won State Championships. − Thanked staff for all of the hard work and looks forward to continuing through Christmas. -- 6 of 11 -- October 6, 2025 7 Butler − Said that staff has done an amazing job with the decorations and thanked them as she realizes it will be busy until the end of the year. White − Said ditto to all that had been said. Goldfinch − Reminded everyone that there is the Charter of Freedom Dedication at the Museum on October 15. Jordan − Said that everyone said it well that staff has crushed it, and to keep on keeping on. Looks forward to the next few months of the good craziness – thanks to staff. Hardwick − Encouraged everyone to get Downtown and enjoy all that is happening – Hallmark Halloween. Blain − Said that when she told Emrick on Wednesday night, “Look at what you have done” – she meant it to all staff – phenomenal job. − Said that she is attending a conference with the Solicitors Office this week and people from all around the state are aware of what is going on in Conway. − Gave kudos to everyone involved, including the volunteers, in helping with making Halloween a success. − Asked staff to look into accounts that have their water bills drafted and allow those not to receive an envelope each month. WORKSHOP: Academy Drive Annexation – Hucks informed Council that this is another situation where a permit was applied for at the county, is approved and ready to be picked up, but the county cannot issue the permit until the water receipt is provided from the city. This property is contiguous, so the applicant would be required to request annexation. The issue, other than the general rule is for the property owner to request annexation, is that everything was reviewed at the county, and in order for the city to issue the permit and perform all of the necessary inspections, the applicant would need to re-apply for permitting at the city. The county could send us everything they have, but aside from the fact that there would likely be little to no refund issued since they did conduct all of the plan reviews, the applicant would have to start over at the city, and there are likely requirements the city has that the county does not. The most obvious one is probably the requirement to have sidewalks. There are none on Academy Drive, which is a county road. So, while the permit is ready for pickup, in order for the city to take over everything, it would need to be annexed first. This would also require Planning Commission review. The earliest this property -- 7 of 11 -- October 6, 2025 8 could be in the city limits would be November 17, and that is with first reading of the annexation and zoning map amendment ordinances being given ahead of Planning Commission review. Staff could review the plans in the interim, but again, it does not mean that everything would be the same, and there may be requirements that the county doesn’t have that the city does. Hucks said that another possibility is that first reading could be given but final reading held off until the county issues a Certificate of Occupancy. However, this has been an issue in the past and staff is usually left to keep in constant contact with the county to see if a CO is about to be issued because they do not inform city staff when it happens. Staff ran into that with Pinnacle Storage, and during construction, the property was sold so the process had to start all over again. Thankfully, the property owners were willing to annex but it could have become a legal issue had they not. Hucks then pointed out that there are no other properties on Academy Drive that are in the city limits. Hucks stated that staff is looking for direction on how they would like staff to proceed in this situation: Require annexation now and have everything transferred to the city, with the probability that additional requirements will be applicable to this property that are not required by the county; or hold first reading of the annexation and zoning map amendment and hold final reading off until all CO’s have been issued. Hucks said that the applicant was present and may be able to provide council with more info if needed. Applicant, Shawn Becker added that city water meters are on the property, the residential home is for the church leadership and churches do not have to pay property taxes in South Carolina. Becker said that there would be no revenue coming into the city. Becker said if annexation is applied for the city may not want the parcel in the city. Becker would like to pay the water fees and get the receipt to Horry County so that the permit could be issued. There was discussion regarding restrictive covenants and staff’s likely recommendation not to annex. Emrick said that procedurally, the applicant would need to apply for annexation, file restrictive covenants, and then the applicant can get the paid water receipt to proceed with Horry County. The only risk with that is if Council does change their mind and annex the property then the applicant would have to start over. Council showed a consensus that they do not support annexation. Food Truck Corral – Hucks informed Council that a couple of months ago, staff was approached about the possibility of using the vacant space on Laurel Street, which is privately owned, as a type of outdoor event space. What makes this different from a “special event” is that the property owner would like to construct a permanent pergola, or decorative entrance, possible have a stage for live music, and tables and chairs with 2 food trucks set up onsite. It could be that the site would be used primarily by one specific business, or it may be that the space would be available for events. The issue for this property is that it isn’t tied to a brick-and-mortar establishment, and there may be building code issues, such as the requirement for an onsite restroom for patrons, to utilize. Most cities and towns simply refer to this type of use as a special event, or in some cases, a food truck -- 8 of 11 -- October 6, 2025 9 corral or garden. The county has something called a “rural tourism permit” which is for agricultural properties that want to have event facilities, farms open to the public, and things of that nature. These types of permits are not permitted outright – they must receive what’s called a “special exception” through the County’s board of zoning appeals. A “special exception” is a use that is permitted within a zoning district but requires review and approval of the board of zoning appeals, so that it can be determined that the proposed use meets specific standards and the general intent of the district and would not be detrimental to surrounding properties. In these instances, a public hearing is required, and BZA has the ability to impose conditions on the proposed use. Other uses also require a special exception in several other municipalities in South Carolina, but the city does not currently have this type of process. Hucks said that staff is looking at writing an ordinance that would be considered by Council to adopt a special exception process for certain types of uses, and this could be one of those uses. Several names for this type of use have been considered, such as an outdoor event permit, or a local tourism permit. Hucks said that there is also a concept of the same type of use for the property beside the water tower, which is referred to as the tractor shed, to show what that could look like if the same concept was applied there. Hillary Howard of Downtown Alive added that she has talked to downtown businesses and the city is in dire need of more outdoor space to be in an organized space in the empty lots and grassy areas. Howard thinks it would be a great addition in the Central Business District. There was some discussion regarding being permanent, bathrooms, parking, type of permit, and that the property owner would be responsible. Council asked staff to proceed with an ordinance. Highway 701 S. & Copperhead Road – Hucks informed Council that staff met with a potential developer for this site a few weeks ago, who is interested in annexing the property into the city. The only contiguity they have is the Warden Station property on the other side of Highway 701 South. However, the property is outside of the city’s utility service area so annexation would never be required. Before the applicants officially submit, staff recommended that they workshop this with Council and explain why annexation of the property would be beneficial to the city and discuss what their plans include. There are 2 things that staff could be of benefit if it were to be annexed and developed in the city: 1 – staff could recommend to City Council that the portions within the flood zone come in as Conservation Preservation, ensuring that no homes were built in the flood zone, and 2 – the city’s design standards, which are stricter than the county’s, would be implemented as part of the requirements for development. Charles Suggs with G3 Engineering further explained the request saying that under the County’s regulations the entire 120 acres would be residential development with potential for encroachments into wetlands within the flood plain. Suggs said that he believes that the city offers great benefit in their ordinance in that it could not only be a great project for G3’s client but also the city residents. Suggs said that they would be looking to retain a commercial outparcel along the Highway 701 Pitch Landing corridor for Neighborhood Services to benefit the community and only be seeking to rezone the upland acreage to potentially the R-2 zoning district and restrict any development in any flood plain to remain undeveloped in perpetuity. Suggs said that this would -- 9 of 11 -- October 6, 2025 10 preserve 55 acres that would remain undeveloped, and it would be a better project under the city’s regulations. There was some discussion regarding the zoning districts and the possibility of a Development Agreement. Train Depot – Hucks gave Council the background on the train depot saying that this property has been an issue as far as whose jurisdiction it’s in for some time now. Until last week, the train depot was not located on parcel of property; it was located within the railroad ROW, so there was never a PIN attached to it, and it was shown as being fee simple ROW much like City roads are. Since the fire that occurred here, the county has reached out to the city’s GIS staff for information, as they too are actively trying to verify the jurisdiction that the property is in. According to city records, they receive in-city water rates, trash pickup and are part of the city’s police sector. However, the property has not paid city taxes since it was never an actual parcel that could be taxed. After much research, what likely occurred was that whenever the property was sold from one rail line to another, there were exceptions carved out in the actual deed like what you see here – the most recent one in 2015, that deeds the ROW but not the Conway Train Depot and provides a detailed property description including where the property boundaries for the train depot begin and end. While I am no expert on deed work, one could assume that at some point, there probably should have been a plat done that executes the deed describing this exception and showing property , and likely older deeds as well; however, even going back as far as 1921, staff was not able to find anything that did that. And now, with the likelihood that the current owners would like to pull permits to repair the train depot, or maybe for insurance purposes, the deed that was recorded in 2015 was most likely used to create the property boundaries that now exist. So, while the city does annex rights of way adjacent to properties when properties are annexed, the train depot, while it ”appeared” as ROW on both the City and County GIS layer, it was not because had a plat been executed the first time the railroad was sold that excluded the property containing the train depot, this would have been a parcel and not right of way that would have been part of the annexation of adjacent property (specifically, the Rescue Squad site that was annexed in 1999). If there was a recent plat done, staff is not aware of its existence. If the county believes that the property is in the city, they would have sent whoever was looking to have the plat reviewed by the City and that is not the case. Land records do not indicate a recent plat has been recorded either. Hucks stated that with the probability of the property being either sold or redeveloped for commercial use, staff wanted to bring this issue to Council. 1 – the property receives in-city water rates and there are no restrictive covenants. This means that the current owner would have to voluntarily annex. 2 – if and when they attempt to submit plans or permits to repair any damage to the structures, they have to apply to the county or the city. The question is, which one? Without having more information than what we have been able to find, it’s staff’s opinion that this parcel is within the county’s jurisdiction, not the City of Conway. They already have city water, so the current owners don’t have to request annexation unless the current utility service is proposed to be extended, such as building an additional structure on the site. If the property is sold, then the new owner, who will be required to obtain a new account in their name, will also be required to request annexation. When all of that occurs, council will have the opportunity to annex, but not until then. -- 10 of 11 -- -- 11 of 11 --

Consideration of Obtaining Ownership of Depot Road – Hyman said that the city has been wanting to expand the trails network of the city, with the most recent being the riverwalk expansion. The next phase will be the ferry landing that will connect the city’s existing riverwalk, a ferry across the river, and a boardwalk through the swamp that will intersect with Depot Road. Emrick had the great idea that the city take over Depot Road from SCDOT and turn it into a one-way road with a multi-purpose path with a bike lane and a pedestrian walkway within that road as part of the network. Hyman showed a map of what the city is proposing for Depot Road to create a one way coming from 501 Business to Dobros Road, then two-way to Highway 90. The hope is that this would connect to a trail system along the railroad right of way that would eventually connect to Coastal Carolina University. During this design process staff realized that it made sense for the city to take over Depot Road. Staff reached out to SCDOT and discovered that DOT has funding to reconstruct the road. After discussions with city staff and DOT staff, plans were made for DOT to move forward with reconstruction of the road and then Depot Road be given to the city. DOT will not stripe it and will leave it up to the city to stripe with the multi-purpose path. Depot Road still has to get approved by Columbia DOT, but staff recommends the city take over Depot Road once constructed to make part of the trail system for the city. Goldfinch asked that the city be flexible for whatever reason to reverse traffic if needed due to a hurricane evacuation or a wreck. 29 -- 29 of 185 -- September 2, 2025 3 Hardwick asked for the timeline. CITY ADMINISTRATOR’S REPORT: Emrick informed Council of the following: • Holiday Alley is nearing completion. The concrete is completed; the curbing is going this week. The conduit has been laid for multiple electrical connections, music and cameras where needed. Landscaping will go in next week and the skeletons will go up immediately after. Great work to all of our crews and staff who have had a hand in this project on a quick timeline. • Special thanks to CCAR, who did a wonderful job helping city staff finish up the Splash Pad and the redesigned parking lot landscaping. • The Ribbon cutting for the Splash Pad and all Town Green improvements is this Thursday at 3:30 p.m. 30 -- 30 of 185 -- September 2, 2025 4 • The river is finally falling back to normal levels which is a relief. Had Hurricane Erin come ashore while the river was in flood stage, the city would have been in some serious trouble. During the month of August Conway had 8.2 inches of rain which is well above the normal 5.3 inches for the month. Making this near the top 5-10% of the wettest Augusts in the last 50 years. Emrick said he thinks this needs to be stated, the flooding we experienced over the last few weeks, which resulted in no property damage in the City, was caused by excessive rain. It was not caused by development. The drought that the city had early in the year was caused by below normal rainfall, not by development. Ideally, the city will have a few more weeks with below normal rainfall, so the river and the basins can fully drain. This will give capacity during the heart of the remainder of the Hurricane season. • In just 29 days, Halloween begins. As such, you will all start to see the transformation starting this week. And it’s going to be amazing. Staff estimates that the city will have over 200 events during the month and staff has been fielding questions for weeks already from people who are very excited to come see the magic of Conway. • Before Halloween, though, is September 11. The city will have our annual recognition of the day during the morning hours when the towers fell on the Main Street Bridge. If you’ve not experienced it, it’s simple and impactful. • The Citizens Academy starts tomorrow afternoon and Emrick believes there are a few spaces remaining. If interested, just show up tomorrow at 2 p.m. and staff will get you an application then. 25 people have signed up at this time. • There will be a short Workshop discussing updates to Title 7 and 8 of the Municipal Code and there are also multiple Executive Sessions tonight as detailed on the agenda. Goldfinch thanked staff for pushing forward with the Citizens Academy. Goldfinch said that it took him years to listen to engineers and hydrologists to understand that responsible development does not cause flooding, and people will argue that until the end. Then asked Emrick to give his opinion on development – is it an argument to be made because you just don’t want it. Emrick said that flooding is the argument of the day against development, when it is not flooding its traffic, not traffic then its school overcrowding, if its not school overcrowding its because there is no Publix. Someday when we have a Publix, it will be because we don’t have a Kroger. City is a very desirable place to live, everyone wants to live here and when the ones that move here then they don’t want anyone else to live here. That is not uncommon for places that are growing as fast as the city is. The challenge is that if the city were to close the doors and say no one else builds –#1 it is not legal, #2 no one would be able to afford to live here. Emrick said that people are still going to move here, people will still create the demand. If the supply is cut off, then no one will be able to afford to live here because everything is supply and demand. Emrick said that there is a housing shortage national wide and the reason that the housing prices have doubled is because Conway does not have enough housing. People continuously fight about every house that is built. 31 -- 31 of 185 -- September 2, 2025 5 COUNCIL INPUT: Helms − Gave appreciation to staff especially with Emrick’s favorite time of the year and all the holidays coming up. − Mentioned hospitality tax while on the radio, saying how that money is what pays for the decorations and the more money spent downtown is more money the city has to spend on decorations. These decorations do not come from the residents’ tax base or tax bill, and Helms said it is important for the citizens to understand. − Looks forward to all the things that are coming. White − Invited the community at large to Bethel AME Church on September 6 at 3 p.m. for a viewing of “One Last Breath” about the Daniel Simmons story. Hardwick − Excited about Halloween and thinks it will be the best Conway has seen. Blain − Read a letter from Blake Hendrick praising Parks and Recreation summer counselors, Mikal Moody, Junior Hemingway and Tristan Casper. WORKSHOP: Review of Title 7 – Rogers informed Council that the city is required to update its business license ordinance every 2 years. The updates are provided by the Municipal Association. This year’s updates will be included with the updates to the code of ordinances later this year. Review of Title 8 – Rogers told Council that Title 8 covers vehicles and said the following are a few of the changes: − Sec. 8-3-2 regulates coach tours, and the Chamber of Commerce will be removed as the point of contact for coach tours. − Sec. 8-3-2 is updated to clarify language on mobile billboards to match language in recent court decisions. The ban on mobile billboards will remain. − Sec. 8-1-17 Truck Routes is confusing, and the updates focus on clarifying language. US 378 from Church Street to Main Street will be removed from the list of allowable routes, pending SCDOT approval. Trucks are allowed to access Mill Pond Road from Main Street to Wright Blvd., as well as El Bethel Road. − The other changes in Title 8 are basically scriveners’ errors. ORDINANCE: #ZA2025-10-06 (C) AGENDA SECTION: First Reading ISSUE: First Reading of an ordinance to amend Articles 1 – Preamble, 3 – Zoning Districts, 6 – Design Standards, 13 – Administrative Agencies and Functions, and Article 14 – Boards and Procedures. BACKGROUND: The proposed amendments are part of a larger effort to clean up several parts of the UDO, which has been in process since early 2024. In addition to this cleanup effort, some of the proposed amendments will address recent guidance provided by the Municipal Association with respect to the process for annexation and zoning of property. Going forward, Council will consider annexation and zoning map amendments as separate ordinances. These changes are outlined in Article 13. Several of these amendments are simply relocated from Article 6. Other amendments include, but are not limited to, the following: • Article 1 has been amended to include several provisions, such as an intent and purpose, applicability of the UDO, transition rules/vested rights, limitation of liability, among other legal provisions. The “preamble” of the UDO will be moved to an appendix in Article 1. • Article 3: moved the CCU Neighborhood Overlay ordinance to Article 6, to be in the overlay section of the UDO, similar to the GCO, VCO, and MSO are located. • Article 6: removed language to add to Article 13 instead. • Article 14: Minor revisions to the language regarding the BZA and TRC. These amendments are attached for your reference. PLANNING COMMISSION: In addition to holding the required public hearing, Planning Commission reviewed the proposed amendments and recommended unanimous approval of the amendments. STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends approval of First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-10-06 (C). 61 -- 61 of 185 -- ORDINANCE #ZA2025-10-06 (C) AMENDING ARTICLE 1 – PREAMBLE, ARTICLE 3 – ZONING DISTRICTS, ARTICLE 6 – DESIGN STANDARDS, ARTICLE 13 – ADMINISTRATIVE AGENCIES AND FUNCTIONS, AND ARTICLE 14 – BOARDS AND PROCEDURES, OF THE CITY OF CONWAY UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE (UDO), REGARDING REQUIREMENTS ANNEXATION AND AMENDMENTS TO THE CITY’S OFFICIAL ZONING MAP, AMENDMENTS RELATED TO CITY BOARDS AND PROCEDURES, AND REVISIONS IN LANGUAGE WITHIN THESE ARTICLES OF THE UDO FOR CLARITY AND CONSISTENCY. Whenever any provision of this Ordinance refers to or cites a section of the South Carolina Code of Laws and that section is later amended, this Ordinance shall be deemed amended to refer to the amended section. 1.1.3 Jurisdiction This Ordinance shall apply to all property (land, buildings, structures, and uses) located within the corporate limits of the City of Conway, South Carolina, as permitted by law, and as may be expanded, contracted, or modified from time to time. 1.1.4 Applicability A. All development and use of land within the City of Conway shall conform to the requirements of this Ordinance. B. The provisions of this Ordinance shall apply to all zoning, land subdivision, site development, signage, landscaping, and related land use activities occurring after its effective date, unless specifically exempted. C. Applicability to Governmental Facilities. To the extent allowed by law, the provisions of this ordinance shall apply to development by the County, State, or federal government or its agencies, departments, or corporate services, or on land owned or otherwise controlled by the County, State, or federal government. 1.1.5 Relationship to Other Laws A. Where this Ordinance imposes a greater restriction than imposed by other local ordinances, regulations, private covenants, or agreements, the provisions of this Ordinance shall control. B. Compliance with this Ordinance does not relieve any person from complying with other applicable local, state or federal laws or regulations. C. Private Restrictions / Covenants 1. In accordance with SC Code of Laws § 6-29-1145, as amended, local planning agencies are required to inquire in application for a permit if the parcel of land is restricted by a recorded covenant that prohibits the proposed activity. Nothing within this Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) shall be construed to authorize the use of any land or structure in a manner that violates private deed restrictions, covenants, or other private agreements governing the use of land. The City of Conway does not enforce private deed restrictions or covenants and assumes no responsibility for interpreting or enforcing such agreements. 68 -- 68 of 185 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 1 – General Provisions 3-3 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended xx, xx xxxx 1.1.6 Severability If any section or provision of this Ordinance (UDO) is declared invalid or unconstitutional by a court of competent jurisdiction, such declaration shall not affect the validity of this Ordinance (UDO) as a whole or any part thereof which is not specifically declared to be invalid or unconstitutional and shall continue in full force and effect. 1.1.7 Effective Date This Ordinance (UDO) shall take effect and be enforced from and after the date of its adoption by the City Council for the City of Conway, and supersedes and repeals any previous zoning, subdivision, or development regulations by the City of Conway to the extent of any conflict. 1.1.8 Preamble (Informational Reference) The City’s policy goals and planning philosophy underlying this ordinance are described in the Preamble, which is the original Ordinance adopting the Unified Development Ordinance, Ordinance 2011-12-12 (A), and is attached as Appendix A – Preamble, to this Article. Prevent the overcrowding of land; C. Avoid undue concentration of population; D. Lessen congestion in the streets; E. Facilitate the creation of a convenient, attractive and harmonious community; F. The characteristics of such developments generally include rectangular block configurations where streets run parallel and perpendicular to one another, intersect at or near 90-degree angles, and form blocks of similar size and shape.
