Intent. Residential design standards are not an attempt to stifle design but are meant to inspire good architectural design while protecting and enhancing the aesthetic and visual character of residential developments within the City of Conway. More specifically, to: 1. avoid monotony in design; 2. protect and preserve the character of residential areas within the city and permit continued development of a compatible nature on vacant properties that are or will be proposed for residential development within the city limits; 3. enhance the character and function of city streets; 4. promote original and high-quality design, and reduce tract or production-style homes; 5. maintain and enhance property values through appropriate aesthetic and functional design considerations; 6. deemphasize garages as major visual elements along local residential streets; 7. encourage design details, which add visual interest and encourage outdoor living spaces; and 8. implement the city’s goals and objectives within the city’s comprehensive plan related to providing a mix of housing types and promoting quality site development and design that enhances Conway’s sense of place within neighborhoods. B. Interpretation. In their interpretation and application, the provisions of this ordinance shall be held to the minimum requirements necessary to protect and promote economic growth and stability, as well as the aesthetic appeal of the City of Conway. Exceptions. Intent: Non-residential architectural design standards protect and enhance the aesthetic and visual character of various developments within the City of Conway. In particular, the purpose is to encourage and better articulate positive visual experiences throughout the City of Conway and to provide for economic growth and stability through the preservation of property values. The design review process is not intended to stifle innovative architecture but to assure respect for surrounding uses and reduce incompatible and adverse impacts on the visual experience. B. P, NC, HC, CC, CBD, GCO, and VCO: Properties that are located outside of the HDRDs shall be reviewed and approved by the Planning Department and shall meet the following architectural design standards: 1. All elevations of a structure shall be in harmony with one another in terms of scale, proportion, detail, material and color. 2. All structures within a proposed development, including gasoline station canopies, shall utilize a uniform architectural theme and shall be designed to create a harmonious whole. The district is intended to establish areas that provide professional services to the public, which do not materially detract from nearby residential areas. More specifically this district should serve as a transitional zone between more intensive commercial areas and residential areas. ISSUE: First reading of an Ordinance approving the execution of a quit claim deed for property in the Pecan Grove Subdivision, specifically the parcels identified as PIN #36815030033 & 36815030035. BACKGROUND: Phase 1 of the Pecan Grove Subdivision (in 2005) was initially developed with a portion of a street known as Pecan Way, shown as running between Lot 21 and Lot 70 (renumbered as Lot 22 on the Phase 2 plat). Pecan Way was intended to provide access to undeveloped lands of the developer. However, during the design of Phase 2, it was determined that the adjacent property could not be developed due to the run of Bear Swamp. As a result, the Phase 2 plat, as recorded, deleted Pecan Way and combined that area into Lots 21 and 22. The complication arises because, prior to recording the Phase 2 plat (in 2009), the developer had already conveyed the subdivision streets, including Pecan Way, to the City (in 2008) in accordance with the Phase 1 plat. Consequently, Lot 21 was never conveyed in accordance with the Phase 2 plat, resulting in a clouded title. Houses were constructed on both Lot 21 (PIN #36815030033) and Lot 22 (PIN #36815030035) years ago, and this title issue only came to light during a recent resale of one of the homes. A quit claim deed from the City would resolve the title issues for both parcels. RECOMMENDATON: Approve first reading of Ordinance #2025-10-06 (E). 179 -- 179 of 185 -- ORDINANCE #2025-10-06 (E) AN ORDINANCE APPROVING THE EXECUTION OF A QUIT CLAIM DEED FOR PROPERTY IN THE PECAN GROVE SUBDIVISION (PIN #36815030033 & PIN #36815030035) WHEREAS, Phase 1 of the Pecan Grove Subdivision included a roadway known as Pecan Way, shown as running between Lot 21 and Lot 70; and WHEREAS, prior to the recording of the Phase 2 plat, the developer conveyed all subdivision streets, including Pecan Way, to the City of Conway; and WHEREAS, upon approval and recording of the Phase 2 plat, Pecan Way was deleted and the area formerly designated as right-of-way was combined into Lots 21 and 22; and WHEREAS, Lot 21 (PIN #36815030033) was never conveyed as described on the Phase 2 plat, resulting in a discrepancy in legal descriptions and a cloud on title; and WHEREAS, the recorded Phase 2 plat sufficiently describes the combined parcels and only results in a minor 71-square-foot adjustment to Lot 21; and WHEREAS, Lot 22 (PIN #36815030035) has consistently used the Phase 2 plat as its legal description, and a quit claim deed from the City is necessary to resolve the title issues created by the prior conveyance of Pecan Way; WHEREAS, houses have been built on both parcels for several years, and this title issue came to light only recently during the resale of one of the homes; WHEREAS, pursuant to S.C. Code 5-7-40, a municipality may sell, alien, convey or lease property it owns by Ordinance. NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED by the Mayor and City Council of the City of Conway, South Carolina, that: The City hereby approves and authorizes the execution of a Quit Claim Deed to resolve the discrepancies related to Pecan Way as shown on the Phase 1 plat of the Pecan Grove Subdivision; said Quit Claim Deed shall convey any and all interest of the City in and to the portion of Pecan Way formerly located between Lots 21 and 22, as depicted on the Phase 2 plat of the Pecan Grove Subdivision, relating specifically to PIN #36815030033 and PIN #36815030035.; and the City Administrator is authorized to execute the Quit Claim Deed on behalf of the City, and the City Clerk is directed to attest and record the same. ISSUE: Resolution of commitment to provide a local match for a Municipal Association of South Carolina Big Idea Grant BACKGROUND: The Municipal Association of South Carolina launched the IMPACT Fund, an acronym for “Innovative Municipal Projects for Advancing Change and Transformation,” in 2025, consisting of two grants programs. The City proposes to apply for MASC’s Big Idea Grant, which is designed to fund bold, creative and forward-thinking ideas. Staff has identified a need for a splash pad to be located at Smith Jones Park. The pool renovation at Smith Jones Park utilized the City’s remaining HUD CDBG entitlement funds and initial plans for the site included a splash pad. However, the budget did not allow for the addition of a splash pad at the time of pool renovation. As part of the application, MASC requires council to pass a resolution committing to the minimum required match of $5,000. If approved, the application will be submitted by Friday, September 26, 2025. RECOMMENDATION: Adopt the proposed resolution committing the City of Conway to provide a local match for a MASC Big Idea Grant to fund a splash pad at Smith Jones Park. 182 -- 182 of 185 -- STATE OF SOUTH CAROLINA ) COUNTY OF HORRY ) RESOLUTION CITY OF CONWAY ) RESOLUTION COMMITTING THE CITY OF CONWAY TO PROVIDING A LOCAL MATCH FOR A MUNICIPAL ASSOCIATION OF SOUTH CAROLINA BIG IDEA GRANT AND FOLLOWING ITS PROCUREMENT POLICY WHEN SECURING SERVICES AND PRODUCTS WITH GRANT FUNDS BE IT RESOLVED BY THE COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF CONWAY, here assembled on this _15th day of September 2025, that the Conway City Council hereby commits to provide a local match of at least $ 5,000, which equals the minimum 5% local match required by the Municipal Association of South Carolina, to support the City’s application for a Big Idea Grant in the amount of $100,000. These grant and local matching funds will be used for a splash pad at Smith Jones Park. BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the Council will follow its procurement policy adopted in accordance with SC Code of Laws Section 11-35-50 when securing all services and products purchased with funds awarded from a Big Idea Grant. This resolution is made in regard to the submission of an application for Big Idea Grant funds to the Municipal Association of South Carolina on or before the application deadline of September 26, 2025. Motion carried. SPECIAL PRESENTATION: A. Recognition of Volunteers – Harry recognized the holiday decorating volunteers that were in attendance and thanked all 146 that have signed up to help. B. Presentation of Employee of the Month for September 2025 – Public Safety – Captain Carter presented the Employee of the Month award to Sergeant Shane Carter. C. Presentation of Hero Awards – Goldfinch presented Nikki Goldman and Nickey Richardson with Hero Awards. FIRST READING: A. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-10-06 (A) to rezone approx. 0.39+/- acres of property located at 5206 Columbia St. (PIN 338-08-03-0002) from the Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF10) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district upon annexation into the City of Conway. Hucks stated that the applicant is requesting annexation and zoning of this property due to the property being sold and the requirement of the current owners to connect to City utilities. Adjacent properties were annexed in May and August of 2024, making this property contiguous. Several other properties within the College Park subdivision have been annexed over the years. The requested zoning upon annexation is R-1. First reading of the ordinance to annex the subject property was approved at the August 18 Council meeting. If first reading of the ordinance to zone the property to the R- 1 district is approved, final reading of the ordinance to annex the subject property and the ordinance to zone the property R-1 upon annexation will be scheduled for the October 6 Council meeting. Hucks said that Planning Commission held a public hearing on the request to zone the property to R-1 upon annexation at their September 4 meeting, and recommended approval. Staff also recommends approval of the ordinance to zone this property R-1 upon annexation. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Hardwick, to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-10-06 (A) rezoning the property located at 5206 Columbia Street to R-1. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. Hucks stated that the applicants are intending to develop the property commercially, and because city utilities are going to be needed, they are required to request annexation. The city’s future land use map identifies the property as HC, and the requested zoning upon annexation is also HC. City Council gave first reading of the ordinance to annex this property at their August 18 meeting. If first reading of the ordinance to zone the property HC upon annexation is approved, final reading of both the ordinance to annex the property and to zone the property HC will be considered at the October 6 Council meeting. Hucks said that Planning Commission held a public hearing on the request at their September 4 meeting, and recommended approval of the requested zoning upon annexation. Staff also recommends approval of zoning the property Highway Commercial upon annexation. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Helms, to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-10-06 (B) rezoning the property located at the intersection of Hwy 548 and Hwy 501 to HC. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. C. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-10-06 (C) to amend Article 1 – Preamble, Article 3 – Zoning Districts, Article 6 – Design Standards, Article 13 – Administrative Agencies and Functions, and Article 14 – Boards and Procedures, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding requirements for annexation and amendments to the city’s official zoning map, amendments relating to City Boards and procedures, and revisions to language in these Articles of the UDO for clarity and consistency. Hucks stated that this amendment is part of a larger clean-up amendment that includes several articles of the UDO. There have been some changes in the process for annexations and zoning changes, in that the annexation is occurring separately from the zoning change. While annexation of property is a legislative function, amendments to the City’s official zoning map require a review and recommendation by Planning Commission prior to the annexation and requested zoning becoming final. In cases where annexation is either requested or required, Planning Commission will only consider the proposed zoning after Council has approved first reading of an ordinance to annex the property. Thereafter, once Planning Commission has held the public hearing and made a recommendation on the proposed zoning, the ordinance to rezone the property will be forwarded for first reading and subsequently, if approved, both ordinances to annex and zone the property will be forwarded for final reading on the next available council agenda. This process will be outlined in Article 13 of the UDO. These changes codify flexibility while ensuring that zoning decisions are always consistent with state requirements for Planning Commission review and public input. Hucks said that also proposed is a name change to Article 1, from Preamble to General Provisions, which include several items not currently within the UDO, that will apply to the entire UDO, such as a purpose and intent statement, applicability of the UDO, transition rules and vested rights, fees and exemptions from fees, limitation of liability – which are all common inclusions in any zoning ordinance or UDO. -- 3 of 10 -- September 15, 2025 4 Hucks said that the remaining amendments to the other articles include cleanup items that staff has been working on for several months, which has been an ongoing initiative since originally discussed with Council during the 2024 budget retreat. All of these amendments seek to clarify terms, ensure consistency across the UDO, update procedural standards, correct inconsistencies, and modernize for readability, and streamline the process for annexation and zoning map amendments. Hucks stated that Planning Commission held the public hearing on the proposed amendment at their September 4 meeting and recommended approval. Staff also recommends approval of the amendments. Motion: Butler made a motion, seconded by Helms, to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-10-06 (C) amending Articles 1, 3, 6, 13 and 14 of the UDO. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. D. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-10-06 (D) to amend Article 4 – Use Tables and Article 5 – Specific Use Regulations, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding requirements for noncommercial keeping of livestock or fowl and related accessory uses and/or structures in the Forest Agriculture (FA) zoning district. Hucks stated that as the city’s footprint starts extending to the more rural areas of the county, there are several properties where the future land use map designates these properties as FA; many of them exceedingly even 100 acres in size. Staff did a random sampling of 30 properties – from 2 acres in size to 277 acres in size, all shown as FA on the future land use map, and the average size of a single property shown as FA is 52 acres. The intent of the FA district is to establish and preserve areas for agricultural or passive recreation. Currently, the UDO allows for noncommercial keeping of livestock in the Rural Agriculture (RA) and FA districts but limits it to one such animal for every 2 acres. One of the key amendments being recommended is that accessory structures related to livestock or fowl — things like barns, chicken coops, or fencing — be permitted even when there’s not a house on the property, but only when the lot is at least 5 acres in size. Hucks said also proposed is including the Rural Residential (RR) district, which requires a minimum lot size of one acre, as one of the districts in which noncommercial keeping of livestock or fowl is permitted, subject to the same conditions. Hucks said that other changes to the ordinance include relocation of some of the provisions within the ordinance so that the requirements for the noncommercial keeping of livestock or fowl is clear and consistent throughout the ordinance. Hucks stated that Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the amendments at their September 4 meeting and recommended approval. One of the questions posed by Planning Commission was why the 5-acre minimum size was proposed. The 5-acre minimum ensures that the property has appropriate space to support animals without creating potential conflicts with adjacent properties that may be primarily residential. The 5-acre minimum also creates a clear distinction between suburban scale residential lots and parcels that are truly agricultural or rural in nature. 5 acres is large -- 4 of 10 -- September 15, 2025 5 enough to avoid conflicts, small enough to remain accessible, and consistent with regional practice. Staff also recommends approval of the amendments. White asked if someone has animals on their property but do not have 5 acres, what would they have to do with the animals. Hucks said they can still have animals but it would be as a secondary accessory use. For example, if someone had 4 acres, they could have 2 cows or 2 horses because only 1 per 2 acres are allowed. For chickens, it is only 1 per 1 acre so there would still be a limitation. In FA they would not have to have a house but a farm building on the 5 acres without a principle dwelling. Goldfinch stated that this was in response to a citizen being allowed to have horses on 5 acres or rather selling to DR Horton and having homes put on it. Goldfinch says anytime the city does something like this is a good thing and he appreciates staff for taking the initiative to work through to make the changes. Motion: Jordan made a motion, seconded by Helms, to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-10-06 (D) amending Articles 4 and 5 of the UDO. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. E. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-11-03 (A) to annex approximately 2.15+/- acres of property located at 1001 Creel Street (PIN 368-08-01-0109). Hucks said that the applicant is requesting annexation into the city, and upon annexation, the requested zoning is Professional. The property is within the city’s utility service area, so any changes to the property, such as it being sold, a change from residential to commercial, would require that annexation be requested. The property is currently zoned Horry County General Residential. The city’s future land use map identifies the property as Low-Density Residential (R-1); however, properties on either side of it and one on the opposite side of Creel Street, are zoned Professional. At this time, staff is unaware of any proposed plans for the subject property. Hucks said if first reading of the annexation is approved, Planning Commission is scheduled to hold a public hearing on the request and make a recommendation at their October 2 meeting. The property is considered a donut hole in the city limits, and therefore, staff does recommend approval of first reading of the ordinance to annex the property. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Helms, to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-11-03 (A) to annex 1001 Creel Street. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. F. First Reading of Ordinance #2025-10-06 (E) approving the execution of a quit claim deed for property in the Pecan Grove Subdivision, specifically the parcels identified as PINs 368-15-03-0033 & 368-15-03-0035. Hyman said that his issue goes back a couple of decades but was just recently brought to light with the sale of a home. The Pecan Grove Subdivision was developed in 2005 and as part of that Phase 1, a stub out was proposed as Pecan Way which was highlighted on the map shown. In 2008 when Phase 2 came about they combined the stub out and made it another lot. Hyman said the problem is that after -- 5 of 10 -- September 15, 2025 6 they created the stub out but before they changed the lots, they deeded that stub out to the city, which has created a cloud on the title. Houses were built decades ago and sold several times but with a recent title search it came to light. A quit claim deed from the city would clear that title and staff recommended approval of this ordinance for first reading. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Butler, to approve first reading of Ordinance #2025-10-06 (E). Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. CONSIDERATION: A. Consideration of a Resolution of Commitment to Provide a Local Match for a MASC Big Idea Grant – Hyman stated that that city is proposing to apply for MASC’s Big Idea Grant, which is designed to fund bold, creative and forward-thinking ideas. Staff has identified a need for a splash pad to be located at Smith Jones Park. As part of the application, MASC requires council to pass a resolution committing to the minimum required match of $5,000. If approved, the application will be submitted by the September deadline. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Jordan, to approve the Resolution committing the City of Conway to provide a local match for a MASC Big Idea Grant. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. Consideration of Bid for Public Works Annual Concrete Contract – Edwards stated that the contract for sidewalk repairs and improvements expired on September 12, 2025. The city sent out a bid request and the bid opening was August 13, 2025. Four bids were received with GeoWorks, LLC being the low bidder overall. Edwards said that staff recommends that Council approve the contract with GeoWorks for the period of September 16, 2025 to September 16, 2026 per the bid summary sheet unit prices. White asked if the city had a list of sidewalks to be repaired. Edwards said yes and staff adds to it as needed. Goldfinch asked who identifies the sidewalks. Edwards said that the city has an inspector that tries to identify before the residents. Emrick said that they are also identified at Budget Retreat. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Hardwick, to approve staff’s recommendation to award the annual contract to GeoWorks, LLC for sidewalk repairs and improvements. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. Goldfinch stated that prior to this meeting that a meeting was scheduled so that this council could learn more about what happened in 2008 as none of present council was here or staff was not in the positions that they are today. Goldfich urged the retirees to be patient as council learns what happened in 2008. CITY ADMINISTRATOR’S REPORT: Emrick informed Council of the following: • Emrick gave an update on Holiday Alley, encouraging all to walk through it when leaving tonight, asked council to thank any staff that had a hand in it. themed ribbon cutting for Holiday Alley will be scheduled shortly. • The first Mayor’s Youth Advisory meeting of the year is this Thursday with 9 new members joining the Council and 4 returning. • The Conway High School Homecoming Parade is this Friday. The parade starts promptly at 4 p.m., • The Conway Superstars competition is September 27th at 3:30 at the McCown Auditorium at the Horry County Museum on Main Street. This annual event showcases some of the best vocal talent in Conway and is completely free for the public to enjoy. • Halloween prep work is underway. The canopy lights in the trees are being replaced this week with new ones, and the pumpkins will go out next week. The rest of downtown is buzzing with items being placed and then tweaked to get them right, with two weeks left to put a bow on it. • The first big event of Halloween is the Big Boo-Ginning. This is the costumed march that begins at 4th and Kingston and ends at the Town Green with a concert. The Halloween calendar is growing daily and staff expects it to hit 300 events before October begins. • Two new partner events have been added that will run all month - Crazy Sister’s Halloween Pirate Adventure will operate pirate ship rides on the Waccamaw and Murder Beach Productions will operate a haunted house style maze at the old tennis center. Both of these events will run all month and allow the city to add new amazing events without having to staff them! • The city has also partnered with a few other groups to sponsor props or events. HGTC is sponsoring our Halloween movie series at the Terrace (the Terror). Every Friday night in October, plus two Sensory Friendly movies at the Sports and Fitness Center are sponsored by HGTC. The Barndo Co., that build barndominiums, is building a Halloween themed barndominium filled with fun on lower Laurel Street. And OrthoSC is getting in on the spirit and is building a huge spider on the Riverwalk that you can walk under. -- 7 of 10 -- September 15, 2025 8 • The Halloween Hustle, Public Safety Day, the Labor of Love Craft Fair, and the first appearance of Fuego the Marsh Tacky Horse all take place on October 4. • On the 10th and 11th, will once again be the Smoke on the Waccamaw, the BBQ cook off, Chicora Car Club is having a Car Show, Falktoberfest at Falk Chiropractic, the Fall Fest by Horry County Family Outreach is at Lady Bug Park, and the Horry County Museum is having Local Ghost Stories • The weekend of the 17th, kicks off on the 16th with s Skeleton Disco at Kingston Park, its also the Ghost Walk Week from Conway Downtown Alive, and the Theater of the Republic’s Youth Performing Arts Festival. • Emrick said he could go on, but the calendar is so full and it’s going to be a magical year for sure. • Department reports tonight are from Judge Kayla Fleming and from Jeff Leveille. Emrick shared that for the second year in a row, Conway has made the HGTV’s top 40 Most Charming Downtowns in America list. Emrick congratulated Council for this pretty awesome achievement. Helms said she was asked Friday night at Coppers why the band had to stop playing at 10 p.m. and asked if the noise ordinance could be amended. Emrick said staff would bring that back to council to discuss at a workshop. Hardwick has concerns at the brick crossing on Second Avenue at Holiday Alley with cars not stopping for people. ORDINANCE: #ZA2025-09-02 AGENDA SECTION: Consent ISSUE: Final Reading of an ordinance to annex approx. +/-0.35 acres of property located at 152 Lander Drive APPLICANT(S): Andrew & Carrie LoMonaco PIN(s): 383-15-01-0046 CURRENT ZONING: Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF10) PROPOSED ZONING (upon annexation): Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) BACKGROUND: The property was transferred to the current owners in May of 2024. It is unknown as to why annexation has not been required until now; however, in instances where property receives city utilities and is contiguous to the city limits, annexation must be requested at the time services are requested. If the property is not yet contiguous at the time in which city services are requested, a restrictive covenant is typically required to be recorded, which bounds current and future owners to annexation requirements should the property become contiguous in the future. The legal residence of the current owners is not a local address. The property is located within the Coastal Heights subdivision. The abutting property was annexed in 2018 and property directly across the road was annexed in 2013, making this property contiguous. There are 3 other lots on Lander Drive that are within the City limits and 20 other lots on Clemson Rd that have been annexed into the City, to date; all of which are within the Coastal Heights subdivision. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: The Coastal Heights subdivision is a single-family neighborhood, containing single-family detached dwellings on roughly quarter-acre parcels. The CCU Hackler Course abuts the homes within the subdivision, which is not in the city limits. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s future land use map identifies the property as Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). Per Section 3.2.3 of the UDO, the intent of the low/medium-density residential district is to provide for the preservation and expansion of areas for low to medium density, detached single-family residential development in the City of Conway. The district shall present a relatively spacious character, promote quiet, livable neighborhoods, and prohibit uses that are incompatible with the residential nature of the surrounding area. PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the request to zone the property Low/Medium Density Residential (R-1) at their August 7th mtg. and recommended approval of the R-1 zoning district upon annexation. CITY COUNCIL: City Council approved first reading of the annexation at their August 4th mtg. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Approve final reading of ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (A). ORDINANCE: #ZA2025-09-02 (E) AGENDA SECTION: Consent ISSUE: Final reading of an ordinance to amend the official zoning map of the City of Conway, to assign the Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) zoning district to a recently annexed parcel (PIN 383-15-01-0046), consisting of approx. 0.35+/- acres, located at 152 Lander Dr. APPLICANT(S): Andrew & Carrie LoMonaco PIN(s): 383-15-01-0046 CURRENT ZONING: Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF10) PROPOSED ZONING (upon annexation): Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) BACKGROUND: The property was transferred to the current owners in May of 2024. It is unknown as to why annexation has not been required until now; however, in instances where property receives city utilities and is contiguous to the city limits, annexation must be requested at the time services are requested. If the property is not yet contiguous at the time in which city services are requested, a restrictive covenant is typically required to be recorded, which bounds current and future owners to annexation requirements should the property become contiguous in the future. The legal residence of the current owners is not a local address. The property is located within the Coastal Heights subdivision. The abutting property was annexed in 2018 and property directly across the road was annexed in 2013, making this property contiguous. There are 3 other lots on Lander Drive that are within the City limits and 20 other lots on Clemson Rd that have been annexed into the City, to date; all of which are within the Coastal Heights subdivision. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: The Coastal Heights subdivision is a single-family neighborhood, containing single-family detached dwellings on roughly quarter-acre parcels. The CCU Hackler Course abuts the homes within the subdivision, which is not in the city limits. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s future land use map identifies the property as Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). Per Section 3.2.3 of the UDO, the intent of the low/medium-density residential district is to provide for the preservation and expansion of areas for low to medium density, detached single-family residential development in the City of Conway. The district shall present a relatively spacious character, promote quiet, livable neighborhoods, and prohibit uses that are incompatible with the residential nature of the surrounding area. CITY COUNCIL: Approved 1st reading to annex at their August 4th meeting (Ord. ZA2025-09-02 A). Council approved 1st reading of the ordinance to zone the property R- 1 upon annexation at their August 18th mtg. RECOMMENDED ACTION: Approve final reading of Ord. ISSUE: Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (D), granting a non-exclusive franchise agreement to Myrtle Beach Party Bike LLC d/b/a Pedal Pub Conway located at the parking lot at 7 Elm Street as well as City owned roadways. BACKGROUND: Amanda Sijbrandji, owner of Myrtle Beach Party Bike LLC is requesting a non-exclusive franchise agreement with the City of Conway to operate Pedal Pub Conway from 7 Elm Street as well as along City owned roadways. She has requested to use 7 Elm Street as the pickup and drop-off location for the Pedal Pub Tours on a Pedal Pub Bike that has a capacity of holding 16 people. The tours will travel along City owned roadways in Downtown Conway. In order to utilize public property such as streets, parking, sidewalks, and public docks for private enterprise, a vendor must enter into a Franchise Agreement with the City. A franchise is the extension of a privilege to use the streets, parking and other City-owned amenities for which the franchisee does not have a legal right to do without permission of the governing body. The franchise agreement allows the franchisee to use City property in the requested manner which exceeds or differs from the customary uses. The franchise agreement is a contract between the City and the franchisee which governs the use of the City property. A franchise agreement does not give exclusive use to the franchisee. For a Franchise Agreement to be valid, it must receive two readings of City Council as an Ordinance. Prior to the first reading, the applicant must have placed a legal line advertisement, noting the meeting, in a newspaper of general circulation, three different days, with the third ad running no later than seven calendar days before the first reading. JULY 21, 2025 CITY COUNCIL WORKSHOP: The applicant presented a Power Point presentation and gave an explanation of the requested franchise agreement as well as addressing several questions from Council. AUGUST 18, 2025 CITY COUNCIL MTG: City Council approved first reading of the ordinance for the franchise agreement at their August 18th meeting. RECOMMENDATION: Approve final reading of Ordinance ZA2025-09-02 (D). 25 -- 25 of 96 -- ORDINANCE #ZA2025-09-02 (D) AN ORDINANCE APPROVING A NON-EXCLUSIVE FRANCHISE AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE CITY OF CONWAY AND MYRTLE BEACH PARTY BIKE LLC, D.B.A. PEDAL PUB CONWAY, FOR THE OPERATION OF A PEDAL PUB PARTY BIKE FROM 7 ELM STREET THROUGHOUT DOWNTOWN CONWAY. BE IT ORDAINED BY THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF CONWAY: WHEREAS the downtown area of the City of Conway has numerous offerings including restaurants, shops and a Riverwalk as well as civic and business offices; and, WHEREAS a steel and aluminum frame party bike will be a downtown attraction; and, WHEREAS creating a vibrant downtown and encouraging public use of the many businesses is of interest to the City of Conway; and, WHEREAS the Pedal Pub offers tours throughout downtown Conway; and, WHEREAS the Pedal Pub offers Public and Private tours; and WHEREAS the Pedal Pub offers routes that are chosen to not impede traffic; and, WHEREAS the Pedal Pub is equipped with several safety features and is able to fit within a normal parking spot; and, WHEREAS the City Council sees the benefit in providing a non-exclusive Franchise Agreement to allow the Pedal Pub in the City; Therefore: BE IT ORDAINED, that the Conway City Council in council duly assembled does hereby approve the attached non-exclusive Franchise Agreement between the City of Conway and Myrtle Beach Party Bike LLC d/b/a Pedal Pub Conway, effective this 2 day of September, 2025. 26 -- 26 of 96 -- DONE AND RATIFIED BY CITY COUNCIL duly assembled this 2 day of September, 2025. ZA2025-09-02 H, amending Article 2 – Definitions, Article 4 – Use Tables, and Article 5 – Specific Use Regulations, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding requirements for Day Care Facilities. BACKGROUND: The issue of the City’s different types of child care options arose out of an inquiry from a prospective childcare provider looking to open a part-time child-care facility in a strip mall setting. Currently, the City’s ordinance does not address part-time child care, or any other type of child care which the state deems to be “legally exempt”, meaning the child care center / program is open less than four (4) hours per day, no more than two (2) days per week, and on an irregular schedule, such as on school holidays. Upon closer review, staff looked at ways to include more options for child care within the UDO, compliant with state law, without compromising the safety and security of children. There were several factors considered when drafting the proposed amendments: • According to a 2024 article from the Children’s Trust of South Carolina, one of the most significant reasons for the lack of workforce participation is the shortage of childcare. Childcare challenges center around three primary factors: access, affordability, and quality. - Access: 42% of South Carolinians live in a childcare “desert”, meaning there are 3 young children for every licensed “spot.” - Affordability: the low supply of available slots drive up costs. The average cost for center-based childcare for an infant (in 2024) is approximately $9,000 per year. - Quality: finding high-quality childcare can be a challenge due to the high (employee) turnover rates and poor employee compensation. • Disparities relating to childcare (cost; access) disproportionately affect low-income and minority families because they limit workforce participation, and exacerbate inequalities in education, health and economic opportunities. Even middle-income families struggle to afford high-quality childcare, and subsidy programs often have long waiting lists or strict eligibility requirements. • Many localities include childcare regulations in their ordinances that create a barrier to home-based providers, such as requirements for home modifications, and zoning codes – including Conway’s, have not been updated to accommodate home-based care. These requirements also disproportionately affect minority or low-income women, who are most likely to seek licensing for an in-home childcare program. - Lack of centralized coordination between the multiple agencies who provide oversight of childcare (i.e. DSS, First Steps, DHEC) contribute to the gaps in service, inefficiencies, and frustration of families and providers trying to navigate the complex systems in place. 37 -- 37 of 96 -- STAFF REPORT FINAL READING OF ORDINANCE #ZA2025-09-02 (H) What changes are advocated by the American Planning Association? • Reviewing current regulations regarding childcare facilities and amend, as needed, to remove barriers to parents entering or re-entering the workforce. • Support legislation (i.e. zoning amendments) which provide for childcare in locations convenient to neighborhoods and in public facilities such as schools, recreation centers and social service centers. Procedures should not be overly burdensome and should be related to size and land use impacts associated with the proposed facility. • Remove obstacles to group and family childcare in all zoning districts, in safe and appropriate locations for children. • Support legislation (local or state) which provides for small childcare homes as permitted land uses in all zoning districts without standard home occupation restrictions. • Support federal, state and local legislation providing for childcare needs assessments and for planning to be performed at the state and local level. Where the proposed amendments included in the proposed ordinance could make a real impact: • Permits family and group child care homes in residential areas as conditional uses, removing a major zoning barrier; • Provides economic opportunities for individuals looking to become a family or group child care home provider; • Aligns local definitions and use standards with DSS categories, helping to prevent conflicts; • Helps small providers navigate compliance without confusion; • Helps reduce regulatory burdens for home-based providers. While the proposed amendments are a first step in addressing child care disparities at a local regulatory level, there are still opportunities to strengthen equity impacts for low-income families, minority entrepreneurs, and working parents with nontraditional schedules. Cultra Road contains a mix of residential and commercial uses, with a majority of it being residential in nature. Most of the properties that have been annexed along Cultra Road are on the same side as the subject property, with the exception of the Ivy Glen subdivision, closer to Hwy 701 North and some properties closer to Hwy 501. White Oak Estates, Tiger Grand, Rivertown Row North, and the Kingston Bay subdivision, are all within the city limits and with the exception of Tiger Grand, are zoned Medium-Density Residential. Hucks said that what makes this property different from some of these surrounding developments is the amount that is within a flood zone. A large portion of the property is within the AE flood zone and a very small fraction of the parcel, on the Oak Street side, is within a floodway. In 2023, Council adopted an ordinance that permits the split zoning of properties upon annexation or rezoning when properties seeking annexation and/or rezoning were being considered that contained environmentally sensitive areas. The ordinance gives Planning Commission the ability to recommend Conservation Preservation zoning on portions of properties containing these environmentally sensitive areas, giving council the ability to zone those portions CP upon annexation. Hucks said that first reading of the ordinance to annex the subject property was approved at the August 4 council meeting. There was discussion during first reading of the ordinance to annex the property regarding the commercial zoning shown on the future land use map and whether or not that portion could be zoned commercially upon annexation, or whether a PD would be more appropriate. Although the future land use map shows that portion as being commercial; given the flood zone that goes through the center of the property, staff has concerns with commercial development being that close to a flood zone area. Commercial development is going to have more impervious surface area, so when it rains, the stormwater runoff would likely flow into the flood zone faster and in greater volume than if it were residential yards, making a greater impact to the displacement of flood waters. There is also a concern with the potential for environmental contamination from oil and other pollutants that come from certain types of commercial development, and that could create environmental hazards beyond the flood zone. Hucks stated that earlier this year, staff were approached by someone wanting to open a limited childcare facility within a commercial strip center, providing baby-sitting services for parents who need childcare services for doctors’ appointments, to run errands or go shopping, and similar needs. Planning Commission originally reviewed amendments in February, but staff recommended it be deferred so that staff could do a deeper dive into state law as well as review what other places in South Carolina have in place for childcare. Currently, the UDO does not address childcare that the state deems “legally exempt” from licensing requirements, which means the childcare facility is open for less than 4 hours per day, no more than 2 days per week, and operates on an irregular schedule, such as on school holidays. Hucks said that staff looked at various ways that includes more options for providing child care within the UDO while remaining compliant with state law and without compromising the safety and security of children, while also considering factors related to disparities in Access, Lack of Affordability, inflexible zoning, support for working families, aligning 79 -- 79 of 96 -- August 18, 2025 8 with state standards, and the quality of childcare. Some of the statistics that staff came across include: • 42% or more of South Carolinians live in a childcare desert, meaning that for every licensed spot, there are 3 children needing childcare. In Conway, for example, the average wait time for a spot for an infant is a year or longer for center-based care. • The low supply of available childcare slots drives up costs. The average cost for center- based childcare in 2024 was more than $9,000 per year. • Finding high-quality childcare is a challenge due to high employee turnover rates and poor employee compensation. • The disparities in lack of childcare options disproportionately affect low-income and minority families because they limit workforce participation and exacerbate inequalities in education, health and economic opportunities. • Many localities include childcare regulations in their ordinances that create a barrier to those seeking to offer home-based childcare as an alternative, including Conways, as these regulations have not been updated to accommodate home-based care. Hucks said that staff also reviewed the standards and policies surrounding childcare; specifically, those recommended by the American Planning Association, which include: • Reviewing and amending regulations that are barriers to parents who are entering or reentering the workforce • Support changes that will allow childcare in locations convenient to neighborhoods and in public facilities – such as schools or recreation centers, • Remove obstacles to group and family childcare in all zoning districts, and • Allow for home-based childcare in all zoning districts without standard home occupation restrictions. Hucks stated that the proposed amendments are a first step at addressing childcare disparities at the local level. They include: • Lessening restrictions for family and group home childcare by allowing family childcare homes (up to 6 children) in any residential district and group childcare (7-12 children) in the RR, RA, and the P districts as a conditional use, with requirements for residency, hours of operation, and prohibition on signage and overnight care, with the goal of helping small providers navigate compliance without confusion and to some degree, reduces regulatory burdens for home-based providers; • Separate after-school programs or similar childcare programs from residential and institutional care, with conditions on each; • Provides general standards that are applicable to all childcare types, and requires that owners or operators are responsible for compliance with all federal, state, and local laws, which would include licensing requirements; and • Aligns local definitions of the different types of daycare facilities with DSS categories which will help prevent conflicts. WORKSHOP: Hucks introduced the following possible UDO amendments: • Tinting of windows in the commercial HDRD – Hucks said that some businesses downtown are seeking to install window tint or that have installed window tint who are now having to remove it. The Community Appearance Guidelines provides appropriate and inappropriate methods when constructing or rehabilitating in one of the Historic Design Review Districts. When it comes to windows, the guidelines for the commercial historic design review district provides standards for displays and transom windows. While preservation is the ultimate goal, there are circumstances that warrant replacement. In those instances, one of the inappropriate practices includes the installation of smoked, mirrored, or tinted window glass or film because it limits valuable product display capability and reflects the street scene back to the pedestrian and has an inappropriate character for the traditional downtown environment. The guidelines suggest gaining shade through deep awnings or canopies. Hucks said that some stores downtown use other methods, which are not regulated, including curtains and blinds. Staff have had complaints from some store owners about the damage caused to their products by not being able to tint their windows or by the limitation of signage being installed on the windows. Hucks said that what is not clear in the guidelines is whether this should only apply to existing display or transom windows, or to actual buildings on the national register, or applicable to any property within a national register district, such as the downtown commercial district that was recently expanded. The Secretary of the Interior has specific guidance in the Standards for Rehabilitation regarding energy retrofits and preservation of historic character in one of their preservation briefs stating that “highly tinted or mirrored films that substantially alter the appearance of windows from the exterior are generally not appropriate for historic buildings”. Hucks gave alternative methods that could be considered, such as: • Films or coatings that are non-reflective, non-metallic and neutral (limit percentage like with car windows) • Tinting that does not alter the visual appearance of the glass • Tinting that is applied to the interior surface of the building • Options that are reversible and do not damage the glass • From NPS illustrated guidelines (2011), “applying nonreflective UV or heat- reducing film on the interior of historic windows in a manner that does not damage glass or alter character may be recommended”. 84 -- 84 of 96 -- August 18, 2025 13 Hucks said that many of the newer window options come preloaded with tint now, and unless the building itself is on the national register, where the building official is able to exempt the building from having to comply with certain building codes, high impact glass is required, and much of that includes a degree of tint manufactured into the glass. The question is for buildings with new windows, or seeking to install new windows, should the standards be applicable to the buildings on the national register, or continue to apply to all buildings within the Historic Design Review Districts, regardless of the national register status. BACKGROUND: The City of Conway owns a parcel at the intersection of Laurel Street and Fourth Avenue in the downtown district, currently used for public parking. A portion of this lot is slated to be redeveloped into the 4th Environmental Refuse Facility (ERF). The facility will include a garbage compactor and a designated grease collection area, enclosed within an attractive brick structure. This ERF will serve nearby businesses and restaurants by consolidating refuse and grease collection into a single, centralized location. The facility will eliminate the need for multiple individual containers outside establishments, improving both efficiency and aesthetics in the downtown district. Only one contractor, Hardee Construction Services LLC, submitted a proposal in the amount of $249,672.00, which exceeded the project’s budget. In accordance with the South Carolina Consolidated Procurement Code, the procurement officer is authorized to negotiate in good faith. City procurement staff engaged with the contractor to reduce costs, resulting in negotiated savings through adjustments to the project scope. Reductions were achieved by modifying the scope of asphalt pavement removal, catch basins/snouts, and drainage pipes. In addition, the City’s Public Utilities Department will perform water meter adjustments and install new water service, allowing these items to be removed from the contract. As a result, Hardee Construction Services LLC agreed to a revised proposal totaling $215,522.25. If approved by City Council, the City will enter into contract negotiations with Hardee Construction Services LLC immediately. This project will be funded through a grant from the South Carolina Department of Commerce and the City’s Hospitality account. title: CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES 9.2.25
text: September 2, 2025 1 CITY OF CONWAY CITY COUNCIL MEETING CONWAY CITY HALL 229 MAIN STREET, CONWAY TUESDAY, SEPTEMBER 2, 2025 PRESENT: Mayor Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor Pro Tem William Goldfinch, Amanda Butler, Julie Hardwick, Beth Helms, Justin Jordan and Larry White. STAFF: Adam Emrick, City Administrator; Mary Catherine Hyman, Deputy City Administrator; John Rogers, Deputy City Administrator; June Wood, Public Information Officer; Jeff Leveille, Technology Services Director; Le Hendrick, Fire Chief; Reggie Jenerette, Solid Waste Director; Robert Cooper, Construction Services Director; Lynn Smith, Human Resource Director; Ted Dudley, Public Utilities Director; Bobby Wallace, Fleet Maintenance Deputy Director; Ashley Smith, Recreation Director; Kayla Fleming, Municipal Judge; Kym Wilkerson, Planning and Development Deputy Director; Braxton Fleming, Public Works Deputy Director; Darren Alston, Police Captain; Allison Williams, Finance Director; Timmy Williams, Hospitality and Beautification Director; Katie Dennis, Planner; and Alicia Shelley, City Clerk. OTHERS: There were approximately 10 others in attendance. CALL TO ORDER: Mayor Blain called the meeting to order. Goldfinch gave the invocation and led the Pledge of Allegiance. The requirements for posting notice of this meeting under South Carolina’s Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) were met. CONSENT AGENDA: A. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (A) to annex approximately +/-0.35 acres of property located at 152 Lander Drive (PIN 383-15-01-0046). B. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (E) to rezone approximately 0.35+/- acres of property located at 152 Lander Dr. (PIN 383-15-01-0046) from the Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF10) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density residential (R-1) district upon annexation into the City of Conway C. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (D), granting a non-exclusive franchise agreement between Pedal Pub and Global Leisure Management (GLM), to provide Downtown Pedal Pub tours, no alcohol allowed, with a pickup and drop off from the property located at 7 Elm Street, owned by the City of Conway (PIN 367-08-01-0001). D. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (G) to amend Article 2 – Definitions and Article 5 – Specific Use Regulations, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding requirements for Educational Facilities. -- 1 of 6 -- September 2, 2025 2 E. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (H) to amend Article 2 – Definitions, Article 4 – Use Tables, Article 5 – Specific Use Regulations, and Article 6 – Design Standards, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding requirements for Day Care Facilities. F. Approval of the Purchase of Equipment for the Public Utilities Department (budgeted) G. Approval of Special Event – Conway High School Homecoming Parade – September 19, 2025 H. Approval of August 18, 2025 Council Meeting Minutes APPROVAL OF CONSENT AGENDA: Motion: Hardwick made a motion, seconded by White to approve the September 2, 2025 consent agenda. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. SPECIAL PRESENTATION: Presentation of August 2025 Longevity Awards – 5 Years: Sara Prince, Police; 10 Years: Allison Williams, Finance; 15 Years: Brian Cummings, Fire Emrick and Jordan presented the longevity awards. CONSIDERATION: A. Consideration of Obtaining Ownership of Depot Road – Hyman said that the city has been wanting to expand the trails network of the city, with the most recent being the riverwalk expansion. The next phase will be the ferry landing that will connect the city’s existing riverwalk, a ferry across the river, and a boardwalk through the swamp that will intersect with Depot Road. Emrick had the great idea that the city take over Depot Road from SCDOT and turn it into a one-way road with a multi-purpose path with a bike lane and a pedestrian walkway within that road as part of the network. Hyman showed a map of what the city is proposing for Depot Road to create a one way coming from 501 Business to Dobros Road, then two-way to Highway 90. The hope is that this would connect to a trail system along the railroad right of way that would eventually connect to Coastal Carolina University. During this design process staff realized that it made sense for the city to take over Depot Road. Staff reached out to SCDOT and discovered that DOT has funding to reconstruct the road. After discussions with city staff and DOT staff, plans were made for DOT to move forward with reconstruction of the road and then Depot Road be given to the city. DOT will not stripe it and will leave it up to the city to stripe with the multi-purpose path. Depot Road still has to get approved by Columbia DOT, but staff recommends the city take over Depot Road once constructed to make part of the trail system for the city. Goldfinch asked that the city be flexible for whatever reason to reverse traffic if needed due to a hurricane evacuation or a wreck. -- 2 of 6 -- September 2, 2025 3 Hardwick asked for the timeline. Hyman said DOT intends to let the project in March with the hope that construction can start a month or two after. Helms asked if it could be two ways to the Santee Cooper campground. Helms then clarified but they would still be able to come in one way and out of the other and didn’t need two-way. Hyman said yes. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by White, to approve staff to move forward with the process of obtaining Depot Road from SCDOT. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. Consideration of Selection of Contractor to build the ERF located at the city-owned Parking Lot at Laurel Street and Fourth Avenue – Hyman said that this lot is slated for ERF #4 which will consolidate refuse and grease collection for several businesses which increases the aesthetics and reduces stops for solid waste staff. The project was advertised publicly and only received one contractor proposal, which was over budget. City procurement staff worked with the contractor to reduce the contractor cost to bring it within the city’s budget by reductions which were achieved by modifying the scope. Public Utilities will do a portion of the work in house to bring within the budget. As a result, the contractor has agreed to modify the price within the budget and the city’s engineers have approved the changes as well. This project will be funded through a grant from the South Carolina Department of Commerce and the rest by the City’s Hospitality account. Hyman said that staff recommend moving forward with the contractor. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Hardwick, to approve staff’s recommendation to award the contract to Hardee Construction Services LLC for construction of the ERF to be located at the city owned parking lot at Laurel Street and Fourth Avenue. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. PUBLIC INPUT: − Jimmy Hammond presented a letter to Council to read regarding retiree insurance benefits. CITY ADMINISTRATOR’S REPORT: Emrick informed Council of the following: • Holiday Alley is nearing completion. The concrete is completed; the curbing is going this week. The conduit has been laid for multiple electrical connections, music and cameras where needed. Landscaping will go in next week and the skeletons will go up immediately after. Great work to all of our crews and staff who have had a hand in this project on a quick timeline. • Special thanks to CCAR, who did a wonderful job helping city staff finish up the Splash Pad and the redesigned parking lot landscaping. • The Ribbon cutting for the Splash Pad and all Town Green improvements is this Thursday at 3:30 p.m. -- 3 of 6 -- September 2, 2025 4 • The river is finally falling back to normal levels which is a relief. Had Hurricane Erin come ashore while the river was in flood stage, the city would have been in some serious trouble. During the month of August Conway had 8.2 inches of rain which is well above the normal 5.3 inches for the month. Making this near the top 5-10% of the wettest Augusts in the last 50 years. Emrick said he thinks this needs to be stated, the flooding we experienced over the last few weeks, which resulted in no property damage in the City, was caused by excessive rain. It was not caused by development. The drought that the city had early in the year was caused by below normal rainfall, not by development. Ideally, the city will have a few more weeks with below normal rainfall, so the river and the basins can fully drain. This will give capacity during the heart of the remainder of the Hurricane season. • In just 29 days, Halloween begins. As such, you will all start to see the transformation starting this week. And it’s going to be amazing. Staff estimates that the city will have over 200 events during the month and staff has been fielding questions for weeks already from people who are very excited to come see the magic of Conway. • Before Halloween, though, is September 11. The city will have our annual recognition of the day during the morning hours when the towers fell on the Main Street Bridge. If you’ve not experienced it, it’s simple and impactful. • The Citizens Academy starts tomorrow afternoon and Emrick believes there are a few spaces remaining. If interested, just show up tomorrow at 2 p.m. and staff will get you an application then. 25 people have signed up at this time. • There will be a short Workshop discussing updates to Title 7 and 8 of the Municipal Code and there are also multiple Executive Sessions tonight as detailed on the agenda. Goldfinch thanked staff for pushing forward with the Citizens Academy. Goldfinch said that it took him years to listen to engineers and hydrologists to understand that responsible development does not cause flooding, and people will argue that until the end. Then asked Emrick to give his opinion on development – is it an argument to be made because you just don’t want it. Emrick said that flooding is the argument of the day against development, when it is not flooding its traffic, not traffic then its school overcrowding, if its not school overcrowding its because there is no Publix. Someday when we have a Publix, it will be because we don’t have a Kroger. City is a very desirable place to live, everyone wants to live here and when the ones that move here then they don’t want anyone else to live here. That is not uncommon for places that are growing as fast as the city is. The challenge is that if the city were to close the doors and say no one else builds –#1 it is not legal, #2 no one would be able to afford to live here. Emrick said that people are still going to move here, people will still create the demand. If the supply is cut off, then no one will be able to afford to live here because everything is supply and demand. Emrick said that there is a housing shortage national wide and the reason that the housing prices have doubled is because Conway does not have enough housing. People continuously fight about every house that is built. -- 4 of 6 -- September 2, 2025 5 COUNCIL INPUT: Helms − Gave appreciation to staff especially with Emrick’s favorite time of the year and all the holidays coming up. − Mentioned hospitality tax while on the radio, saying how that money is what pays for the decorations and the more money spent downtown is more money the city has to spend on decorations. These decorations do not come from the residents’ tax base or tax bill, and Helms said it is important for the citizens to understand. − Looks forward to all the things that are coming. White − Invited the community at large to Bethel AME Church on September 6 at 3 p.m. for a viewing of “One Last Breath” about the Daniel Simmons story. Hardwick − Excited about Halloween and thinks it will be the best Conway has seen. Blain − Read a letter from Blake Hendrick praising Parks and Recreation summer counselors, Mikal Moody, Junior Hemingway and Tristan Casper. WORKSHOP: Review of Title 7 – Rogers informed Council that the city is required to update its business license ordinance every 2 years. The updates are provided by the Municipal Association. This year’s updates will be included with the updates to the code of ordinances later this year. Review of Title 8 – Rogers told Council that Title 8 covers vehicles and said the following are a few of the changes: − Sec. 8-3-2 regulates coach tours, and the Chamber of Commerce will be removed as the point of contact for coach tours. − Sec. 8-3-2 is updated to clarify language on mobile billboards to match language in recent court decisions. The ban on mobile billboards will remain. − Sec. 8-1-17 Truck Routes is confusing, and the updates focus on clarifying language. US 378 from Church Street to Main Street will be removed from the list of allowable routes, pending SCDOT approval. Trucks are allowed to access Mill Pond Road from Main Street to Wright Blvd., as well as El Bethel Road. − The other changes in Title 8 are basically scriveners’ errors. EXECUTIVE SESSION: Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Jordan, to enter into Executive Session for the following: (A) Discussion regarding Potential Acquisition of Property in the Jamestown Area [pursuant to SC Code §30-4-70 (A) (2)]; (B) Discussion regarding Potential Acquisition of Property in the Sherwood Park Area [pursuant to SC -- 5 of 6 -- -- 6 of 6 --

ISSUE: Public Hearing and First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025- 09-02 (D), granting a non-exclusive franchise agreement to Myrtle Beach Party Bike LLC d/b/a Pedal Pub Conway located at the parking lot at 7 Elm Street as well as City owned roadways. BACKGROUND: Amanda Sijbrandji, owner of Myrtle Beach Party Bike LLC is requesting a non-exclusive franchise agreement with the City of Conway to operate Pedal Pub Conway from 7 Elm Street as well as along City owned roadways. She has requested to use 7 Elm Street as the pickup and drop-off location for the Pedal Pub Tours on a Pedal Pub Bike that has a capacity of holding 16 people. The tours will travel along City owned roadways in Downtown Conway. In order to utilize public property such as streets, parking, sidewalks, and public docks for private enterprise, a vendor must enter into a Franchise Agreement with the City. A franchise is the extension of a privilege to use the streets, parking and other City-owned amenities for which the franchisee does not have a legal right to do without permission of the governing body. The franchise agreement allows the franchisee to use City property in the requested manner which exceeds or differs from the customary uses. The franchise agreement is a contract between the City and the franchisee which governs the use of the City property. A franchise agreement does not give exclusive use to the franchisee. For a Franchise Agreement to be valid, it must receive two readings of City Council as an Ordinance. Prior to the first reading, the applicant must have placed a legal line advertisement, noting the meeting, in a newspaper of general circulation, three different days, with the third ad running no later than seven calendar days before the first reading. JULY 21, 2025 CITY COUNCIL WORKSHOP: The applicant presented a Power Point presentation and gave an explanation of the requested franchise agreement as well as addressing several questions from Council. RECOMMENDATION: Staff has concerns with enforcement issues as well as “Open Containers” on State Roads (Third Avenue) and therefore recommends disapproval of this Franchise Agreement. At the very least, staff would suggest that the agreement be approved as a “pilot program” for a three (3) month period, and in three months, Council can revisit the issue and approve a more permanent agreement with Pedal Pub if it desires. 72 -- 72 of 173 -- ORDINANCE #ZA2025-09-02 (D) AN ORDINANCE APPROVING A NON-EXCLUSIVE FRANCHISE AGREEMENT BETWEEN THE CITY OF CONWAY AND MYRTLE BEACH PARTY BIKE LLC, D.B.A. PEDAL PUB CONWAY, FOR THE OPERATION OF A PEDAL PUB PARTY BIKE FROM 7 ELM STREET THROUGHOUT DOWNTOWN CONWAY. APPLICANT(S): Development Resource Group (DRG) LLC PIN(s): 325-00-00-0011 CURRENT ZONING: Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) PROPOSED ZONING (upon annexation): Medium- Density Residential (R-2) & Conservation Preservation (CP BACKGROUND: The subject property is proposed to be annexed into the City for residential development. The property is within the city’s utility service area, thus requiring annexation to be requested. Surrounding developments – Rivertown Row North, Kingston Bay and Elmhurst, are also zoned Medium-Density Residential (R-2). Midtown Village, which directly abuts this property, is zoned High-Density Residential (R-3). A large portion of the subject property is located within the AE flood zone, which runs through the middle of the parcel (see attached maps). While development is permitted within flood zones, provided the affected property meets the required elevation, staff does not support rezoning portion(s) of property within a flood zone to a district that would permit residential development. In 2023, Council adopted an ordinance that permits parcels containing environmentally sensitive areas to be split- zoned, which is otherwise prohibited, with such areas being zoned Conservation Preservation (CP) upon annexation of property or when property is proposed to be rezoned. Given that there is a small portion of the property within the floodway, in which no development can occur, and that the general area has been prone to flooding, should annexation proceed, this would be an opportunity to discuss the possibility of zoning the portions within a flood zone / floodway to CP with the applicant. In this instance, the applicant would need to submit a survey showing the areas within the flood zone / floodway so that they could be mapped accordingly should the split zoning be preferred. SURROUNDING USES / ZONING: Surrounding in-City zoning includes Neighborhood Commercial (NC), High-Density Residential (R-3), Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1), and Medium-Density Residential (R-2). The area is primarily single-family residential, with limited established commercial uses. There is a gas station/convenience store (Sun House) with a few tenant spaces containing limited commercial uses, including a dog grooming business, immediately adjacent to the subject property. 92 -- 92 of 173 -- STAFF REPORT First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (F) Surrounding County zoning includes mostly residential, including Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF20) on 20,000 sq. ft. min. lot sizes, and Residential, including mobile homes (MSF20), also on 20,000 sq. ft. min. lot sizes. Abutting property is also zoned Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA). The John T. Henry Auction location is near the subject property, which is also zoned CFA. Horry Electric is also nearby, on the opposite side of Cultra Rd, which is zoned Office/Professional/Institutional (OPI). COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s future land use map provides three (3) future land use designations for the subject property. For the portion with frontage along Cultra Rd, the future land use is shown as Neighborhood Commercial (NC). Per Section 3.2.9 of the UDO, the NC district is intended to provide small-scale retail and service uses for nearby residential areas. Dimensional requirements and design standards of the district are intended to promote compatibility to surrounding residential areas and accommodate pedestrian use and access. Strip commercial development, designed primarily to accommodate vehicular access and parking, and development that is insensitive or incompatible with the scale and character of the surrounding residential areas, is discouraged in this district. A larger portion of the property is shown as Conservation Preservation (CP) on the city’s future land use map. Per Section 3.2.15 of the UDO, the intent of the CP district is to provide needed open space for general outdoor and indoor recreational uses, and to protect environmentally sensitive areas and flood prone areas from the encroachment of any residential, commercial, industrial, or other uses capable of adversely affecting the relatively undeveloped character of the district. The portion abutting Midtown Village and Conway Christian School is shown as High-Density Residential on the future land use map. Per Section 3.2.5 of the UDO, the intent of the high-density residential district is to provide areas for high-density attached, detached, semi-attached, and multifamily residential development in the City of Conway and to prohibit uses that would substantially interfere with the development or continuation of residential structures in the district. Dear Planning Director, I am writing to formally express my objection to the proposed annexation and rezoning of approximately 107.75 acres located on Cultra Road and Oak Street from Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) to City of Conway Medium-Density Residential (R-2). My concerns are as follows: 1. Environmental Impact: The development will result in the removal of a significant number of trees, which not only affects local wildlife and natural beauty but also increases the risk of flooding. Trees play a vital role in stormwater absorption, and their removal could exacerbate flooding during hurricanes and severe storms, which are common in our area. 2. Infrastructure Limitations: Conway’s current infrastructure is not equipped to handle the additional traffic and population growth this development would bring. The city has only two, two-lane bridges for daily commuting. These bridges are in disrepair and will only cause further issues for current homeowners in Conway. 3. Traffic and Road Safety: The roads in and around Conway are already congested. Additional residential development will increase traffic volume, leading to longer commute times, higher accident risks, and more wear and tear on public roads. 4. Overdevelopment Concerns: New housing developments are already being constructed on all sides of our community. This proposal adds to the rapid expansion without adequate planning for schools, emergency services, and utilities, which will negatively affect the quality of life for current residents. I urge the Planning Commission and City Council to consider these concerns seriously and to prioritize sustainable development that aligns with the capacity of Conway’s infrastructure and environmental resilience. Thank you for your attention to this matter. In accordance with the requirements to connect to city utilities, the applicant is required to request annexation. Restrictive Covenants were recorded on July 29, 2025. This easement would not provide the access required if annexed into the city limits. The required frontage onto a public roadway, maintained by the city, county or state is not present. As such, if annexed, the property owner would not be able to obtain a permit for construction of a dwelling unless the city’s requirements for access were met. The back half of the property is located within the AE flood zone. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: The property abuts the Oakbrook development (city limits, zoned R- 2). ORDINANCE: #ZA2025-09-02 (H) AGENDA SECTION: First Reading ISSUE: Amendments to Article 2 – Definitions, Article 4 – Use Tables, and Article 5 – Specific Use Regulations, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding requirements for Day Care Facilities. BACKGROUND: The issue of the City’s different types of child care options arose out of an inquiry from a prospective childcare provider looking to open a part-time child-care facility in a strip mall setting. Currently, the City’s ordinance does not address part-time child care, or any other type of child care which the state deems to be “legally exempt”, meaning the child care center / program is open less than four (4) hours per day, no more than two (2) days per week, and on an irregular schedule, such as on school holidays. Upon closer review, staff looked at ways to include more options for child care within the UDO, compliant with state law, without compromising the safety and security of children. There were several factors considered when drafting the proposed amendments: • According to a 2024 article from the Children’s Trust of South Carolina, one of the most significant reasons for the lack of workforce participation is the shortage of childcare. Childcare challenges center around three primary factors: access, affordability, and quality. - Access: 42% of South Carolinians live in a childcare “desert”, meaning there are 3 young children for every licensed “spot.” - Affordability: the low supply of available slots drive up costs. The average cost for center-based childcare for an infant (in 2024) is approximately $9,000 per year. - Quality: finding high-quality childcare can be a challenge due to the high (employee) turnover rates and poor employee compensation. • Disparities relating to childcare (cost; access) disproportionately affect low-income and minority families because they limit workforce participation, and exacerbate inequalities in education, health and economic opportunities. Even middle-income families struggle to afford high-quality childcare, and subsidy programs often have long waiting lists or strict eligibility requirements. • Many localities include childcare regulations in their ordinances that create a barrier to home- based providers, such as requirements for home modifications, and zoning codes – including Conway’s, have not been updated to accommodate home-based care. These requirements also disproportionately affect minority or low-income women, who are most likely to seek licensing for an in-home childcare program. 151 -- 151 of 173 -- STAFF REPORT FIRST READING OF ORDINANCE #ZA2025-09-02 (H) - Lack of centralized coordination between the multiple agencies who provide oversight of childcare (i.e. DSS, First Steps, DHEC) contribute to the gaps in service, inefficiencies, and frustration of families and providers trying to navigate the complex systems in place. What changes are advocated by the American Planning Association? • Reviewing current regulations regarding childcare facilities and amend, as needed, to remove barriers to parents entering or re-entering the workforce. • Support legislation (i.e. zoning amendments) which provide for childcare in locations convenient to neighborhoods and in public facilities such as schools, recreation centers and social service centers. Procedures should not be overly burdensome and should be related to size and land use impacts associated with the proposed facility. • Remove obstacles to group and family childcare in all zoning districts, in safe and appropriate locations for children. • Support legislation (local or state) which provides for small childcare homes as permitted land uses in all zoning districts without standard home occupation restrictions. • Support federal, state and local legislation providing for childcare needs assessments and for planning to be performed at the state and local level. Where the proposed amendments included in the proposed ordinance could make a real impact: • Permits family and group child care homes in residential areas as conditional uses, removing a major zoning barrier; • Provides economic opportunities for individuals looking to become a family or group child care home provider; • Aligns local definitions and use standards with DSS categories, helping to prevent conflicts; • Helps small providers navigate compliance without confusion; • Helps reduce regulatory burdens for home-based providers. While the proposed amendments are a first step in addressing child care disparities at a local regulatory level, there are still opportunities to strengthen equity impacts for low-income families, minority entrepreneurs, and working parents with nontraditional schedules. The amendments included reflect the amendments recommended by PC.
