Providers may include public or private schools, religious institutions, licensed child care centers, community-based organizations, or private individuals. Programs operating fewer than four (4) hours per day and/or fewer than two (2) days per week may qualify as legally exempt child care operations under S.C. Code § 63-13-20, provided they meet all applicable state and local requirements. This includes irregularly scheduled programs (i.e., during school holidays), and does not include licensed child day care centers, Family Child Care Homes, or Group Child Care Homes, unless otherwise specified in Section 5.1.7 of this Ordinance. • Child Day Care Facilities: Any facility, other than a private residence, that provides care, supervision, or guidance for minor children unrelated to the owner or operator, for more than four (4) hours per day and/or more than two (2) days per week. Such facilities are required to be licensed by the South Carolina Department of Social Services (DSS) in accordance with applicable state regulations. This term includes child care centers and group programs operated for compensation, whether for profit or nonprofit, and excludes in-home child care operations such as Family Child Care Homes and Group Child Care Homes. • Family Child Care Homes: A full-time, owner-occupied private residence, in which the owner or operator resides and provides child care to no more than six (6) children at any one time, including the provider’s own children and any related children under the age of 12. Such homes must be licensed or registered with the S.C. Department of Social Services (DSS), as required by S.C. Code § 63-13-820. • Group Child Care Homes: A full-time, owner-occupied private residence, in which the owner or operator resides and provides care to seven (7) to twelve (12) children at any one time, including the provider’s own children and any related children under the age of 12. Group Child Care Homes must be licensed by the S.C. Department of Social Services (DSS) in accordance with S.C. Child care providers must be licensed or registered if they: • Operate 4 or more hours a day • Operate more than 2 days a week • Care for children in your home and you care for more than 1 family not related to you Types of Care: All South Carolina child care programs are required to be one of the following: licensed, registered, approved, or legally exempt. Requirements are determined by provider type. The state defines four types of child care: • Child Care Center—A center that is licensed for 13 or more children can be commercial, faith-based, or school-based. • Group Child Care Home—A facility within a residence occupied by the operator that cares for 7 to 12 children; The number includes those living in the residence and children who are related to the operator, must be licensed. • Family Child Care Home—A facility within a residence occupied by the operator that cares for no more than 6 children; The number includes those living in the residence and children who are related to the operator; Family Child Care Centers must be registered but may choose to be licensed. • Legally-Exempt Operations—Child care center-based programs open less than 4 hours a day and/or open on school holidays; Not allowed for Family Child Care Homes or Group Child Care Homes. NOTE: Many parents rely on family members, friends, or neighbors who provide care. These types of care are not registered or licensed but are regulated. How to Become a Licensed Child Care Provider: Step 1. Attend Orientation. Interested parties will receive an application packet prior to orientation that will have all the required forms needed to apply. In addition, they will be able to ask any questions related to the process and provide resources specific to the county/town where the facility may be located. Interested parties should review the dates and times of orientation meetings available, on our website and call the Region that will monitor their location at the telephone number assigned to their specific regional office at scchildcare.org/ providers/new-applicant-orientation/ to attend orientation. Step 2. If required, submit architectural plans to the Chief Fire Marshal at the DSS Child Care Licensing Central Office: SC Department of Social Services Child Care Licensing Attn: Chief Fire Marshal P.O. Box 1520 Columbia, SC 29202-1520 Step 3. After attending orientation and the architectural plans have been approved by the Chief Fire Marshal at Child Care Licensing, the applicant must submit the Zoning Approval letter or form, the application to apply, and the fire and health inspection request to the local Child Care Licensing Regional Office that will monitor the location of the child care facility. Step 4. Once the above items have been submitted to Child Care Licensing, they will be assigned a Licensing DSS Brochure 501 (JAN 24) 169 -- 169 of 173 -- Specialist and must complete the additional required documents located in the application packet. Those items should be completed and submitted for Child Care Licensing review. Step 5. During the review of the application, the Fire and Health Inspector and Child Care Licensing will contact them for an inspection visit. If everything meets the regulatory requirements, their application will be submitted for approval. When approved, a provisional license will be issued. Step 6. After the provisional license has been issued and the child care facility has operated with 13 or more children enrolled for at least 45 days, Child Care Licensing will re-visit to complete their full evaluation. If no deficiencies, the application will be submitted for a regular license. How SC Licensing Works: Licensing is managed by the SC Division of Early Care and Education at the SC Department of Social Services (SCDSS). Child Care Licensing regulates approximately 2,400 child care providers, through four regional offices. There are several key functions that build safe, healthy environments for children: 1. Inspections: These help to ensure that providers comply with state laws and regulations through a yearly unannounced inspection. All regulated child care providers including legally-exempt and Family, Friend and Neighbor providers will receive the required annual health and safety inspections. 2. State and Federal Comprehensive Background Checks: As required by state law, federal and state background checks must be conducted on all child care staff members who work in child care facilities. More information on background checks can be found at scchildcare.org/providers/in-state-background-check- requirements. Required background checks include: • SC Child Abuse and Neglect Central Registry & Database checks and out of state Abuse and Neglect checks if child care staff lived out of SC in the past 5 years. o For all center-based care, licensed, registered, and legally exempt o Licensed and registered home child care facilities o Family, Friend, and Neighbor checks for providers enrolled in the SC Scholarship Program • In-state and National Sex Offender Database checks for all child care facility types, including legally exempt child care facilities and Family, Friend and Neighbor providers • State and Federal fingerprinting for all child care facility types, including legally exempt child care facilities and Family, Friend and Neighbor providers The State of South Carolina uses a digital fingerprint service. Find the complete information at sc.state.identogo.com. 3. Investigations: Child Care Licensing investigates complaints against regulated facilities and reports of facilities or individuals operating without a license or registration. 4. Regulation: A state Advisory Committee is responsible for reviewing the regulations regarding their improvement. Staff to Child Ratios: The following staffing ratios apply at all times children are present on the premises at a child care center and during activities away from the center. Age Staff-to-Child Ratios Birth to one year 1:5 One to two years 1:6 Two to three years 1:8 Three to four years 1:12 Four to five years 1:17 Five to six years 1:20 Six to twelve years 1:23 DSS Brochure 501 (JAN 24) 170 -- 170 of 173 -- DATE: AUGUST 18, 2025 ITEM: VI.H. ISSUE: First reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-10-06 (A) to adopt the 2025 Conway Parks & Recreation Master Plan and incorporate it by reference in the Comprehensive Plan. BACKGROUND: In April 2024, the City of Conway advertised publicly to select a firm to provide professional design services for a City of Conway Parks Master Plan, and the team of Greenberg Farrow + Brandstetter Carroll Inc was chosen. A portion of this Master plan is funded by a grant awarded from the SC Department of Parks, Recreation & Tourism Park and Recreation Development Fund (PARD). Over the past year, City staff has been working with the design team, including: • Needs assessment and inventory of all existing facilities • Defining the mission, vision, values, goals and objectives for Parks, Recreation facilities, and their usage • Providing short, intermediate, and long-range management and development plans for recreation, park and facility planning • Establishing priorities and recommendations for existing and future park and facility development, including types of parks, size of parks, timing of development, and developer-led allocation of park lands • Developing a systematic plan that maximizes the park, recreation, and natural open space opportunities for Conway residents. • Identify appropriate staffing needs to support park maintenance operations and recreation operations • Future trends recommendations • Providing recommendations for physical improvements to existing and future recreation and park facilities to create a uniform and cohesive look and feel that is distinctly Conway, including branding and signage A public hearing will be held at Planning Commission prior to final reading. RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends approval of First Reading. 171 -- 171 of 173 -- ORDINANCE #ZA2025-10-06 (A) AMENDING THE CITY OF CONWAY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN BY ADOPTING THE 2025 CONWAY PARKS & RECREATION MASTER PLAN WHEREAS, Pursuant to Title 6, Chapter 29 of the Code of Laws of South Carolina 1976, as Amended known as the "South Carolina Local Government Comprehensive Planning Enabling Act of 1994" sets forth requirements of local governments with Zoning Ordinances; and WHEREAS, South Carolina Code §6-29-520 establishes the requirements to create, amend and recommend Comprehensive Planning elements, which requires the City of Conway Planning Commission is to review and make a recommendation to City Council; and WHEREAS, prior to adoption of component of the Comprehensive Plan, a public hearing shall be held after no less than 30 days' public notice has been placed in a newspaper of general circulation; and WHEREAS, The City of Conway Planning Commission will review the 2025 Conway Parks & Recreation Master Plan at its October 2, 2025 meeting; and WHEREAS, following the public hearing, the City Council of the City of Conway has determined the Comprehensive Plan of the City of Conway should be amended to include the 2025 Conway Parks & Recreation Master Plan: Therefore be it ORDAINED by the City Council of the City of Conway, in Council duly assembled, the Comprehensive Plan of the City of Conway be amended by adopting and including the 2025 Conway Parks & Recreation Master Plan as part of the Community Facilities element; and be it further ORDAINED that all ordinances or parts of ordinances inconsistent with this Ordinance are hereby repealed to the extent of such inconsistency EFFECTIVE DATE: This ordinance shall become effective upon final reading approval. 172 -- 172 of 173 -- DONE AND RATIFIED BY CITY COUNCIL duly assembled this day of _______________________, 2025. title: CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES 8.18.25
text: August 18, 2025 1 CITY OF CONWAY CITY COUNCIL MEETING CONWAY CITY HALL 229 MAIN STREET, CONWAY MONDAY, AUGUST 18, 2025 PRESENT: Mayor Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor Pro Tem William Goldfinch, Amanda Butler, Julie Hardwick, Beth Helms, Justin Jordan and Larry White. STAFF: Adam Emrick, City Administrator; Mary Catherine Hyman, Deputy City Administrator; John Rogers, Deputy City Administrator; June Wood, Public Information Officer; Jeff Leveille, Technology Services Director; Le Hendrick, Fire Chief; Reggie Jenerette, Solid Waste Director; Robert Cooper, Construction Services Director; Lynn Smith, Human Resource Director; Ted Dudley, Public Utilities Director; Rock Rabon, Fleet Maintenance Director; Ashley Smith, Recreation Director; Kayla Fleming, Municipal Judge; Kym Wilkerson, Planning and Development Deputy Director; Brandon Harrerlson, Public Works Director; Dale Long, Police Chief; Allison Williams, Finance Director; Timmy Williams, Hospitality and Beautification Director; and Alicia Shelley, City Clerk. OTHERS: There were approximately 15 others in attendance. CALL TO ORDER: Mayor Blain called the meeting to order. White gave the invocation and led the Pledge of Allegiance. The requirements for posting notice of this meeting under South Carolina’s Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) were met. CONSENT AGENDA: A. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-08-04 (D), to annex approximately 1.08+/- (total) acres of property located on Cypress Circle at Conway Medical Center (PIN’s 383-15-02-0024, -0025, - 0026, -0027, and -0028), and rezone from the Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) district to the City of Conway Institutional (IN) district. B. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-08-04 (E), to annex approximately 1.34+/- acres of property located off 16th Ave and Elizabeth Street, behind the Coastal Shopping Center (PIN 338-10-02-0018), and rezone from the Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) district to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district. C. Final Reading of Ordinance #2025-08-18 (A) authorizing the sale of certain real property in the City of Conway located along the Conway Riverfront. D. Approval of August 4, 2025 Council Meeting Minutes -- 1 of 16 -- August 18, 2025 2 Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Helms to remove Agenda Item III.B. from the Consent Agenda and discuss after the First Readings - Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025- 08-04 (E), to annex approximately 1.34+/- acres of property located off 16th Ave and Elizabeth Street, behind the Coastal Shopping Center (PIN 338-10-02-0018), and rezone from the Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) district to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. APPROVAL OF CONSENT AGENDA: Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Jordan to approve the August 18, 2025 consent agenda as amended. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. SPECIAL PRESENTATION: Presentation of Employee of the Month for August 2025 – Public Works – Dudley presented Zane Jones with the Employee of the Monday award. PUBLIC HEARING AND FIRST READING: Public Hearing and First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (D), granting a non- exclusive franchise agreement between Pedal Pub and Global Leisure Management (GLM), to provide Downtown Pedal Pub tours with a pickup and drop off from the property located at 7 Elm Street, owned by the City of Conway (PIN 367-08-01-0001). Wilkerson stated that the applicants are requesting a non-exclusive franchise agreement with the City of Conway to operate Pedal Pub Conway from 7 Elm Street as well as along city owned roadways. The applicants have requested to use 7 Elm Street as the pickup and drop-off location. A franchise is the extension of a privilege to use the streets, parking and other City owned amenities for which the franchise does not have a legal right to do without permission of the governing body. For a Franchise Agreement to be valid, it must receive two readings of City Council as an Ordinance. Prior to the first reading, the applicant must have placed a legal line advertisement, noting the meeting, in a newspaper of general circulation, three different days, with the third ad running no later than seven calendar days before the first reading. The applicants gave a presentation to council on July 21, 2025 explaining the requested franchise agreement as well as addressing several questions from Council. Wilkerson said that staff has concerns with enforcement issues as well as “open containers” on State Roads (Third Avenue) and therefore recommends disapproval of this Franchise Agreement. At the very least, staff suggested that the agreement be approved as a “pilot program” for a three- month period, and in three months, Council could revisit the issue and approve a more permanent agreement with Pedal Pub if it desires. There was discussion regarding a consumption zone, no alcohol allowed on bike, a pilot program and the pick-up location. There was no public input. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Butler, to close the public hearing. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. -- 2 of 16 -- August 18, 2025 3 Thomas Palmieri and Angie Goeppinger, representatives from Pedal Pub stated that they presented the request with no alcohol. There was more discussion that involved special events, the business name, and larger cities that allow participants to BYOB. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Goldfinch, to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (D) granting the franchise agreement without allowing alcohol on the Pedal Pub bike. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. FIRST READING: A. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (E) to rezone approximately 0.35+/- acres of property located at 152 Lander Dr. (PIN 383-15-01-0046) from the Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF10) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density residential (R-1) district upon annexation into the City of Conway. Hucks stated that this property is being considered for annexation as a result of the requirement to connect to city utilities. The property is currently zoned SF10 in Horry County’s jurisdiction and is within the Coastal Heights subdivision. The abutting property was annexed in 2018 and property directly across Lander Drive was annexed in 2013 There are 23 other lots in the Coastal Heights subdivision that have been annexed over the years. The requested zoning upon annexation is the R1 district, which is consistent with the zoning assigned to the other lots that have been annexed into the city within the subdivision. Hucks said that City Council approved first reading of an ordinance to annex the subject property at their August 4 meeting. Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the proposed zoning upon annexation at their August 7 meeting and recommended approval. Hucks said that staff also recommends approval of the proposed zoning of R1 upon annexation. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Butler, to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (E) zoning 152 Lander Drive to City of Conway Low/Medium-Density residential (R-1). Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (F) to rezone approximately 109.13 +/- acres of property located at or near the corner of Cultra Rd. and Oak Street (PIN 325-00-00-0011) from the Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) district to the City of Conway Medium-Density Residential (R-2) district and the Conservation Preservation (CP) district upon annexation into the City of Conway. Hucks stated that the applicant is requesting to rezone the subject property to Medium- Density Residential (R-2) and Conservation Preservation upon annexation into the City limits. The property is within the city’s utility service area, so they would be required to request annexation for connection to city utilities. The property is currently zoned Commercial Forest Agriculture in the county’s jurisdiction. The city’s future land use map has 3 different future land use designations for the subject property: Neighborhood Commercial (NC) along the frontage of Cultra Road, CP for the large portion within a flood zone, and High-density residential (equivalent to the R-3 district) on the portions abutting -- 3 of 16 -- August 18, 2025 4 the Midtown Village subdivision and the Conway Christian School. Cultra Road contains a mix of residential and commercial uses, with a majority of it being residential in nature. Most of the properties that have been annexed along Cultra Road are on the same side as the subject property, with the exception of the Ivy Glen subdivision, closer to Hwy 701 North and some properties closer to Hwy 501. White Oak Estates, Tiger Grand, Rivertown Row North, and the Kingston Bay subdivision, are all within the city limits and with the exception of Tiger Grand, are zoned Medium-Density Residential. Hucks said that what makes this property different from some of these surrounding developments is the amount that is within a flood zone. A large portion of the property is within the AE flood zone and a very small fraction of the parcel, on the Oak Street side, is within a floodway. In 2023, Council adopted an ordinance that permits the split zoning of properties upon annexation or rezoning when properties seeking annexation and/or rezoning were being considered that contained environmentally sensitive areas. The ordinance gives Planning Commission the ability to recommend Conservation Preservation zoning on portions of properties containing these environmentally sensitive areas, giving council the ability to zone those portions CP upon annexation. Hucks said that first reading of the ordinance to annex the subject property was approved at the August 4 council meeting. There was discussion during first reading of the ordinance to annex the property regarding the commercial zoning shown on the future land use map and whether or not that portion could be zoned commercially upon annexation, or whether a PD would be more appropriate. Although the future land use map shows that portion as being commercial; given the flood zone that goes through the center of the property, staff has concerns with commercial development being that close to a flood zone area. Commercial development is going to have more impervious surface area, so when it rains, the stormwater runoff would likely flow into the flood zone faster and in greater volume than if it were residential yards, making a greater impact to the displacement of flood waters. There is also a concern with the potential for environmental contamination from oil and other pollutants that come from certain types of commercial development, and that could create environmental hazards beyond the flood zone. Additionally, Council adopted strict design standards for residential development, and if zoned commercially, there is no control over what business is built there if it is permitted in that zoning district. Neighborhood commercial, as the future land use map shows, would permit small scale retail and services for nearby areas. Some of the uses could include a doctor’s office, a beauty salon, a restaurant, a fitness center or gym, a furniture show room, several types of professional services, retail establishments, for example – a Dollar General or a grocery store, a nursery / garden center, a funeral home or mortuary, a bar or tavern, and a gas station, to name a few. Limiting development to residential gives the community a better idea of what will be built there, and will likely result in less impervious surface ratios, resulting in less stormwater runoff into those environmentally sensitive areas. Hucks said that there was also discussion as to whether the development would provide affordable housing. While that is not something that the city can actually require from a developer, there are things that the city could do to promote affordable housing. This can be done through zoning and land use adjustments, such as allowing smaller lot sizes and -- 4 of 16 -- August 18, 2025 5 narrower lot widths, through inclusionary zoning (i.e. elimination of single-family only zoning), providing incentives to developers, such as density bonuses or permit fee reductions, and partnering with non-profits or housing authorities. Hucks stated that when requests to annex and rezone property, staff considers the following factors: (1) Consistence with the Comprehensive Plan; (2) Effect of the annexation and rezoning on surrounding properties; (3) Whether existing infrastructure is adequate; and (4) Environmental / Economic impacts. Hucks said that the applicant has agreed to zone the areas containing the flood zone and flood way as Conservation Preservation, which guarantees protection of those areas in perpetuity. The city has strict residential design standards, ensuring that new homes built in the development will be held to a higher standard than if developed in the county. Hucks continued to say that the current zoning of CFA in the county permits single-family dwellings, townhomes, and manufactured homes, on ½-acre lots, which could be built across the entire property, including the flood zone, and is currently a development permitted by-right under the current zoning. CFA also permits commercial development, some of which could be to the detriment of surrounding properties if developed on the property, such as: commercial animal raising facilities, livestock or agriculture auction facilities, vehicle/equipment repair services, including boat service or other repair services, a firearm training and sports facility, funeral home, crematory and mortuary, trade shops, restaurants and bars, gas stations, mini warehouses/self-storage, and campers / recreational vehicles for temporary living accommodations, to name a few. Hucks stated that similar, but larger properties to the one being considered have ultimately been annexed into the city limits for residential development. Planning Commission held a public hearing at their August 7 meeting; however, staff recommended that the item be deferred so that the request could be readvertised to correct the property PIN. Planning Commission will consider the request at their September 4 meeting, and their recommendation will be forwarded to Council with final reading of both the ordinance to annex and the ordinance to rezone the property, should first reading be approved. Hucks said that annexation of property ensures that development of the property is consistent with the City’s vision for growth and protection of environmentally sensitive areas. Therefore, staff recommends approval of first reading to zone the property Medium- Density Residential and approximately 43 acres in Conservation Preservation upon annexation. Council discussed smaller lot sizes and incentives to attract affordable housing, commercial uses inside communities, putting a road through a CP, 45% being zoned CP, open space, preventing homes in CP. Rob Wilfong further explained the request saying that the development is going to take place and whether in the city or county there are different hoops to go through. -- 5 of 16 -- August 18, 2025 6 Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Hardwick, to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (F) rezoning the property located at the corner of Cultra Road and Oak Street to R2 and CP . Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. C. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-15 (A) to annex approximately +/-1.57 acres of property located at 2373 West Road (PIN 337-11-03-0017). Hucks stated that this property is part of what was a minor subdivision split from the parent parcel in 2002, which created 3 additional parcels. It is currently vacant and is contiguous to the city by the Oakbrook subdivision. Restrictive covenants were recorded July 29 of this year, so the applicant is likely trying to obtain city utilities at this time and therefore is requesting annexation. The only access to the property is via a 50’ easement that was created when the property was subdivided, which is not a legal means of access for these lots if it were within the city limits. Some of the property is within a flood zone and the future land use map identifies the property as being Conservation Preservation. Hucks said that Planning Commission is scheduled to hold a public hearing on the request at their September 4 meeting, if first reading of the annexation is approved. Hucks stated that due to the issue with access and flooding concerns, staff recommends disapproval. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Helms, to deny first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-15 (A) annexing 2373 West Road. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. D. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-15 (B) to annex approximately +/-10.66 acres of property located at or near the corner of Hwy 501 and Hwy 548 (PIN’s 326-00-00- 0026 and 326-09-03-0006). (Hucks) Hucks stated that the applicants are intending to develop the property commercially, and because city utilities are going to be needed, they are required to request annexation. The city’s future land use map identifies the property as Highway Commercial (HC), and the requested zoning upon annexation is also HC. Planning Commission will hold a public hearing on the requested zoning at their September 4 meeting, should first reading of the annexation be approved. Hucks said that staff does recommend approval of first reading to annex the property. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Blain, to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-15 (B) annexing the property at the corner of Highway 501 and Highway 548. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. E. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-15 (C) to annex approximately +/-0.39 acres of property located at 5206 Columbia Street (PIN 383-08-03-0002). Hucks stated that this property is in the College Park subdivision and was transferred into the current owner’s name on August 4, 2025. Restrictive Covenants were recorded on August 6, 2025 and the property contains a single-family dwelling. Property abutting this parcel was annexed in May 2024 and property directly across the street was annexed in August 2024. Annexation is being requested due to the requirements for connection to city services. Hucks said that Planning Commission is scheduled to consider the proposed zoning upon annexation at their September 4 meeting and that staff recommends first reading to annex the subject property. -- 6 of 16 -- August 18, 2025 7 Motion: Butler made a motion, seconded by Blain, to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-15 (C) annexing the property at 5206 Columbia Street. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. F. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (G) to amend Article 2 – Definitions and Article 5 – Specific Use Regulations, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding requirements for Educational Facilities. Hucks stated that recently Horry County Schools sought to rezone the property where the former Whittemore Park Middle School is located to Institutional. This building will be utilized to house their Conway area adult education program, which will contain a limited childcare function, a therapeutic learning center, the districts JROTC program, administrative offices and other functions. There were concerns with rezoning the property to Institutional, even though the current future land use map shows the future land use as Institutional, due to the permitted uses in the district and if the school district ever sold the property, what it could potentially be used for, given its proximity to the neighboring residential area. The proposed amendments include a revised definition of an educational facility, as well as amendments to the conditional use standards for educational facilities. The goal of the amendments is to better define what an educational facility is and entails, and to ensure that the proposed uses of the former middle school fall within the guidelines or functions of an educational facility, including the limited childcare function. Hucks said that Planning Commission held a public hearing on the proposed amendments and recommended approval. Hucks said that staff also recommends approval. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Jordan, to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (G) regarding requirements for educational facilities. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. G. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (H) to amend Article 2 – Definitions, Article 4 – Use Tables, Article 5 – Specific Use Regulations, and Article 6 – Design Standards, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding requirements for Day Care Facilities. Hucks stated that earlier this year, staff were approached by someone wanting to open a limited childcare facility within a commercial strip center, providing baby-sitting services for parents who need childcare services for doctors’ appointments, to run errands or go shopping, and similar needs. Planning Commission originally reviewed amendments in February, but staff recommended it be deferred so that staff could do a deeper dive into state law as well as review what other places in South Carolina have in place for childcare. Currently, the UDO does not address childcare that the state deems “legally exempt” from licensing requirements, which means the childcare facility is open for less than 4 hours per day, no more than 2 days per week, and operates on an irregular schedule, such as on school holidays. Hucks said that staff looked at various ways that includes more options for providing child care within the UDO while remaining compliant with state law and without compromising the safety and security of children, while also considering factors related to disparities in Access, Lack of Affordability, inflexible zoning, support for working families, aligning -- 7 of 16 -- August 18, 2025 8 with state standards, and the quality of childcare. Some of the statistics that staff came across include: • 42% or more of South Carolinians live in a childcare desert, meaning that for every licensed spot, there are 3 children needing childcare. In Conway, for example, the average wait time for a spot for an infant is a year or longer for center-based care. • The low supply of available childcare slots drives up costs. The average cost for center- based childcare in 2024 was more than $9,000 per year. • Finding high-quality childcare is a challenge due to high employee turnover rates and poor employee compensation. • The disparities in lack of childcare options disproportionately affect low-income and minority families because they limit workforce participation and exacerbate inequalities in education, health and economic opportunities. • Many localities include childcare regulations in their ordinances that create a barrier to those seeking to offer home-based childcare as an alternative, including Conways, as these regulations have not been updated to accommodate home-based care. Hucks said that staff also reviewed the standards and policies surrounding childcare; specifically, those recommended by the American Planning Association, which include: • Reviewing and amending regulations that are barriers to parents who are entering or reentering the workforce • Support changes that will allow childcare in locations convenient to neighborhoods and in public facilities – such as schools or recreation centers, • Remove obstacles to group and family childcare in all zoning districts, and • Allow for home-based childcare in all zoning districts without standard home occupation restrictions. Hucks stated that the proposed amendments are a first step at addressing childcare disparities at the local level. They include: • Lessening restrictions for family and group home childcare by allowing family childcare homes (up to 6 children) in any residential district and group childcare (7-12 children) in the RR, RA, and the P districts as a conditional use, with requirements for residency, hours of operation, and prohibition on signage and overnight care, with the goal of helping small providers navigate compliance without confusion and to some degree, reduces regulatory burdens for home-based providers; • Separate after-school programs or similar childcare programs from residential and institutional care, with conditions on each; • Provides general standards that are applicable to all childcare types, and requires that owners or operators are responsible for compliance with all federal, state, and local laws, which would include licensing requirements; and • Aligns local definitions of the different types of daycare facilities with DSS categories which will help prevent conflicts. Hucks said that Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the amendments at the August 7 meeting, and recommended approval. Staff also recommends approval of the amendments. -- 8 of 16 -- August 18, 2025 9 There was discussion regarding federal, state and local laws, safety concerns at entrances and at strip malls, parking standards, and helping daycare operators with more options while remaining compliant with all laws and regulations. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Helms, to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-09-02 (H) regarding requirements for daycare facilities. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. Moved from Consent Agenda Item III.B. - Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-08- 04 (E), to annex approximately 1.34+/- acres of property located off 16th Ave and Elizabeth Street, behind the Coastal Shopping Center (PIN 338-10-02-0018), and rezone from the Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) district to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district. Hucks said that this is a situation where staff received plans for review and all of the parcels that they own that were going to be combined for the shopping center. Staff then realized that one of the parcels was not in the city. 1.05 of the 1.34 acres of this parcel is in the flood zone so there is an opportunity, which will have no impact on the development because it is a stormwater parcel, to take the 1.05 acres and zone it to Conservation Preservation. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Helms, to approve final reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-08-04 (E) as written except for a portion which will be contained as Conservation Preservation that represents the flood zone portion of the parcel. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. H. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-10-06 (A) to adopt the 2025 Conway Parks and Recreation Master Plan and incorporate it by reference in the Comprehensive Plan. Hyman said that last year the city advertised publicly to select a firm to provide professional services to create the Parks and Recreation Master Plan. Over the past year staff have been working with those consultants to make that plan a reality and there have been a lot of stakeholder meetings, surveys, and lots of questions and meetings to dig in and see what was needed for the City of Conway. Hyman introduced Jessica Wise, Greenberg Farrow and Keith Rodenhauser, Brandstetter Carroll who gave Council an update on the Parks and Recreation Master Plan. Wise and Rodenhauser highlighted the purpose of the plan; using the plan and what’s included; the project process – evaluate, engage, envision, plan; plan recommendations including places, programs, parks, and people; action plan; and the executive summary. Blain said that it is the Whittemore Elementary School, not Whittemore Park. White asked about the cut off for the splash pad. Emrick said that there would be a workshop held at the next meeting to discuss it. Emrick then gave Council the following 4 options (1)Technology that will allow it to turn off is $3,000 up front and then $5,000 annually; (2) Lifeguard on site that would cost $50,000 per year; (3) If storms are in the forecast, staff would have to climb into the cabinet and turn off for the day; and (4) Allow parents to govern themselves and their children. -- 10 of 16 -- August 18, 2025 11 There was discussion regarding the on and off switch and having someone on site, when someone is not available to turn off during a storm, and data with lightning strikes at a splash pad. Blain stated that the electricity should be wired outside of the cabinet so that a human can turn it off without having to climb in. Blain believes that liability is heavy, water draws lightning, people don’t take great care over their children when lightning is in eminent danger and that the city needs to be able to turn the water off. Emrick said if there is a button to push there still has to be someone to push it and the city would have to pay them. There was more discussion regarding liability. WORKSHOP: Hucks introduced the following possible UDO amendments: • Tinting of windows in the commercial HDRD – Hucks said that some businesses downtown are seeking to install window tint or that have installed window tint who are now having to remove it. The Community Appearance Guidelines provides appropriate and inappropriate methods when constructing or rehabilitating in one of the Historic Design Review Districts. When it comes to windows, the guidelines for the commercial historic design review district provides standards for displays and transom windows. While preservation is the ultimate goal, there are circumstances that warrant replacement. In those instances, one of the inappropriate practices includes the installation of smoked, mirrored, or tinted window glass or film because it limits valuable product display capability and reflects the street scene back to the pedestrian and has an inappropriate character for the traditional downtown environment. The guidelines suggest gaining shade through deep awnings or canopies. Hucks said that some stores downtown use other methods, which are not regulated, including curtains and blinds. Staff have had complaints from some store owners about the damage caused to their products by not being able to tint their windows or by the limitation of signage being installed on the windows. Hucks said that what is not clear in the guidelines is whether this should only apply to existing display or transom windows, or to actual buildings on the national register, or applicable to any property within a national register district, such as the downtown commercial district that was recently expanded. The Secretary of the Interior has specific guidance in the Standards for Rehabilitation regarding energy retrofits and preservation of historic character in one of their preservation briefs stating that “highly tinted or mirrored films that substantially alter the appearance of windows from the exterior are generally not appropriate for historic buildings”. Hucks gave alternative methods that could be considered, such as: • Films or coatings that are non-reflective, non-metallic and neutral (limit percentage like with car windows) • Tinting that does not alter the visual appearance of the glass • Tinting that is applied to the interior surface of the building • Options that are reversible and do not damage the glass • From NPS illustrated guidelines (2011), “applying nonreflective UV or heat- reducing film on the interior of historic windows in a manner that does not damage glass or alter character may be recommended”. -- 12 of 16 -- August 18, 2025 13 Hucks said that many of the newer window options come preloaded with tint now, and unless the building itself is on the national register, where the building official is able to exempt the building from having to comply with certain building codes, high impact glass is required, and much of that includes a degree of tint manufactured into the glass. The question is for buildings with new windows, or seeking to install new windows, should the standards be applicable to the buildings on the national register, or continue to apply to all buildings within the Historic Design Review Districts, regardless of the national register status. Hillary Howard with Conway Downtown Alive spoke in opposition of window tinting. Council agreed with Howard and advised staff to keep the requirements in place • Article 1 – General Provisions, Article 3 – Zoning Districts, Article 6 – Design Standards, Article 13 – Administrative Agencies, and Article 14 – Boards and Commissions (clean up and related to annexation / zoning process) – Hucks said that this amendment will be part of a larger clean-up amendment that will include Article 1, 3, 6, 13 and 14 of the UDO. Some changes that are already taking place are how annexations and zoning changes will proceed, in the annexation occurring separately from the zoning change. This change ensures compliance with the guidelines put forth by the Municipal Association. Bottom line is that while the annexation is a legislative function, completely up to City Council, the zoning to be assigned to the property upon annexation should be reviewed and recommended by Planning Commission. In order to be more efficient, staff is taking the annexation and zoning separately, and in cases where annexation is requested, Planning Commission will only consider the proposed zoning when Council has approved first reading of an ordinance to annex the property. If approved, Planning Commission’s recommendation for zoning will be sent to Council for first reading, and then both ordinances will proceed for final reading on the same agenda. Other amendments to some of the other article’s center around the zoning amendment process. Hucks said that other amendments that will be included is a name change to Article 1, from Preamble to General Provisions, which will include several items not currently within the UDO, that will apply to the entire UDO, such as a purpose and intent statement, applicability of the UDO, transition rules and vested rights, fees and exemptions from fees, limitation of liability – which are all common inclusions in a zoning ordinance or UDO. Council advised staff to proceed. Hucks said that this amendment would be at the September 15 meeting for first reading. • Accessory Uses / Structures in FA District – Hucks said that as the city’s footprint starts extending to the more rural areas of the county, there are several properties where the future land use map designates these properties as Forest Agriculture: many of them exceedingly even 100 acres in size. The intent of the FA district is to establish and preserve areas for agricultural or passive recreation. Currently, the UDO allows for noncommercial keeping of livestock in the Rural Agriculture and FA districts but limits it to one such animal for every 2 acres. Staff is considering amending the UDO to create a new conditional use in -- 13 of 16 -- August 18, 2025 14 the FA district only which would allow for parcels that are 5 acres or larger to have livestock, such as horses, cows, etc., along with related accessory buildings, for noncommercial use, and not requiring it as only being secondary to a residence. Hucks said that staff wanted to see if this was something council wanted staff to look into further. Right now, it’s only permitted as an accessory use to a residence on the same lot, and only one animal per 2 acres. There are not currently a lot of parcels in the city limits zoned FA, and certainly not many zoned the same exceeding 5 acres, but for those that meet the proposed conditions, it does provide an opportunity for allowing a use that per the definition of the district, meets the intent of the FA district. Council advised staff to look into further. • Threshold for Development Agreements (DA) – Hucks said that this was discussed at budget retreat so staff looked at options for requiring a DA, and the most important thing to note is that DA’s must be voluntary. You can adopt requirements for DAs for those seeking discretionary actions, such as a zoning change or annexation, but it’s not recommended as an outright mandate. Requiring a DA for properties seeking to rezone for residential development or annexation into the city for the same could be required to coordinate via a DA. The minimum threshold recently discussed was when the property in question is 50 acres in size or larger and/or 150+ lots or units were proposed. If council was comfortable with that number or acreage, staff would draft an ordinance to that effect, and it could be an amendment that is considered by PC as soon as September. Council advised staff to look into further. • Uses in Highway Commercial and Light Industrial – Huck said that this request came out of a recent zoning amendment that was proposed for a property on Hwy 701 North, currently zoned HC that is also adjacent to an established single-family neighborhood. There may be other uses that council will want to consider looking at as far as whether they should be permitted in the HC district, but a majority of the uses are consistent with the uses you would typically see in the HC district, which is a district that serves automobile- oriented uses. 2 uses that stuck out to staff that have been discussed previously are tobacco shops and financial institutions. Not because those 2 uses themselves are an issue, but similar uses, like a vape shop, or a payday loan service establishment. There’s been discussions about limiting vape shops, and payday loan providers, or cash advance places, are often considered predatory lenders because of their lending practices that disproportionately target vulnerable populations. i.e. exorbitant interest rates and fees, debt traps, lack of transparency, targeting vulnerable populations. These types of businesses cannot be outright banned, but where they operate can be. They can be defined separately in the UDO, the districts they operate in can be limited, and stricter zoning standards, the amount within a certain area, setback or buffers can be implemented, etc. Vape shops often over concentrate in certain corridors or areas, such as low income or minority areas, and clustering of these establishments contribute to blight, reduce diversity of services, and give a perceived degradation of the quality of the area. These too can be defined separately within the UDO, separation requirements, and other means. -- 14 of 16 -- August 18, 2025 15 Hucks said that staff has not completed a draft of an amendment but have begun doing research and asked if there are other uses Council wants staff to look at, they would be happy to do so. • Roadway Standards – Hucks said that this item was discussed at budget retreat as well, but this seems to be an issue that staff is encountering more with requests on infill development, or development of existing lots of records in the city limits. There are several examples that can be provided, with each of them having entirely different circumstances: some are not fronting a road that is owned by the city or state, some which front a city road that is not currently installed, some that an easement exists, like the property considered for annexation that has an easement created for access that is allowed in the county but not the city. In all cases, if someone applies for a permit for a residential dwelling, if legal access is not present, they have to obtain that before the permit is issued. That could be having the road installed and then dedicated to the public or even purchasing abutting property in order to combine with the subject property so that the lot has the required frontage. Bottom line is that all lots have to front a public road and cannot be an “island” not connected to the public street system. Hucks said that staff does not propose to create any exemptions or exceptions for any new lots that are created. This would be applicable only to existing lots of record that do not meet the requirement to front a public street. For those lots of record, already in the city limits, staff could create exemptions from the current requirements, with conditions, one of them being the requirement to obtain a design modification from Planning Commission. Other options could include allowing the road to be installed to meet emergency apparatus standards, which require a dust free surface, and appropriate turnaround, and then a maintenance agreement with the city being recorded. It could mean, if the road is currently “private”, to require the road to meet the minimum emergency vehicle standards and it remain private; however, this could result in issues that warranted the requirement for all roads to be public in the first place because you may get a lot of complaints about the road condition over time for lack of maintenance by the property owners who live on that particular road. Hucks said that staff wanted to see what Council was comfortable with and then proceed with drafting a text amendment for consideration, hopefully within the next couple of months. Public Works will need to review any proposed amendments to make sure there would be no issues on their end with whatever is proposed as well. It was decided that this item would come back to Council for Workshop in the future. Hwy 501, New Road, Ash Pond Road, Marina Drive, Elm Street, and Laurel Street (PIN’s 368-00-00-0008 and -0015), and upon annexation, rezone from the Horry County Heavy Industrial (HI) district, City of Conway Light Industrial (LI) district and City of Conway High-density Residential (R-3) district to the City of Conway Waccamaw Riverfront District (WRD) (1) (2). BACKGROUND: The City is seeking to annex and rezone these properties that were recently acquired to the Waccamaw Riverfront District (WRD). The WRD districts, 1 & 2, are considered a special use district; similar to that of a Planned Development (PD) district or the Mixed Use (MU) Flexible Zone district. Section 3.3.1 of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) defines the WRD as the following: The intent of the WRD District is to provide for the proper physical, social, and economic development of the City’s riverfront area in order to protect, promote and improve the public health, safety, morals, convenience, order, appearance, prosperity, and general welfare, including but not limited to: safeguarding the cultural, scenic, economic, environmental, and social heritage of the Waccamaw Riverfront on behalf of the City, Horry County and South Carolina; providing for adequate light, air, and public open space; encouraging efficient and economic practices in the process of development and redevelopment; making adequate provision for pedestrian and vehicular traffic; supporting the wise and efficient expenditures of public funds promoting safe and proper drainage; protecting lives and properties from the hazards of flooding; safeguarding water quality; promoting attractive and economically beneficial community and architectural appearance; protecting valuable wetlands trees, and other vegetation; encouraging natural and environmentally sound shoreline stabilization, promoting economic prosperity for the district and the City, and providing for adequate public access to the river and its shores. The Waccamaw Riverfront District (WRD) is broken down into two (2) sub-districts for zoning purposes: WRD-1 and WRD-2. The only difference between the two is that WRD-1 has specific requirements for certain uses in new buildings, and limitations on multifamily residential – in that it may only occupy second (upper) floors of buildings, not ground floors. Surrounding Zoning / Uses: While most of these properties are vacant, or containing ponds, there are still a couple of buildings on one of the properties, where the smoke stacks were once located, which is zoned Horry County Heavy Industrial (HI). Property across Hwy 501 on New Rd zoned Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1), Conservation Preservation (CP), Light Industrial (LI) and Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA). 4 -- 4 of 155 -- CITY OF CONWAY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN: The Future Land Use Map of the Comprehensive Plan identifies a majority of the property as Conservation Preservation (CP) and a small portion, where the smoke stacks and other structures were once located, as Light Industrial (LI). PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the request at their July 10th meeting and recommended approval of the request to annex and rezone the property to Waccamaw Riverfront District (WRD) (1) (2). CITY COUNCIL: City Council approved First Reading of the ordinance to annex the subject property, along with the proposed zoning of WRD (1) and (2) at their July 21st meeting. ISSUE: Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-08-04 (B), to rezone 533+/- acres of property (PIN 368-00-00- 0014) located on Hwy 501 E. (Church Street), known as Lake Busbee, from the Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district to the Conservation Preservation (CP) district. BACKGROUND: The City is seeking to rezone this recently acquired property, commonly known as Lake Busbee, to the Conservation Preservation (CP) district. The intent of the CP District is to provide needed open space for general outdoor and indoor recreational uses, and to protect environmentally sensitive areas and flood prone areas from the encroachment of any residential, commercial, industrial, or other uses capable of adversely affecting the relatively undeveloped character of the district. Surrounding Zoning / Uses: Most of the properties located on New Rd are zoned Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1), apart from some that are Conservation Preservation (CP), Light Industrial (LI) and Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA). Other zoning includes Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) and Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF10) districts. Surrounding uses include residential, a community dog park, a waste treatment facility, and vacant property. CITY OF CONWAY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN: The Future Land Use Map of the Comprehensive Plan also identifies the property as Conservation Preservation (CP). PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the request at their July 10th meeting and recommended approval of the request to rezone the property to Conservation Preservation (CP). CITY COUNCIL: City Council approved First Reading of the ordinance to rezone the property to CP at their July 21st meeting. BACKGROUND: The applicants submitted annexation and rezoning applications on June 6th for the subject property. The requested zoning upon annexation is the Highway Commercial (HC) district. The property is currently zoned Highway Commercial (HC) in Horry County. The intent of the HC District is to provide compatible locations to serve the automobile oriented commercial activities in harmony with major highway developments, reduce traffic congestions and to enhance the aesthetic atmosphere of the city. Surrounding Zoning / Uses: Surrounding properties are a mix of commercial, institutional and residential. Abutting property is Mixed-Use (MU) and Institutional (IN). Property across Todd Blvd is Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF6) and currently contains a single-family residence. Property located across Hwy 544 is zoned Institutional and is owned by the University. CITY OF CONWAY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN: The Future Land Use Map of the Comprehensive Plan also identifies the property as Highway Commercial (HC). PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing at their July 10th meeting and recommended approval of rezoning the property to Highway Commercial (HC) upon annexation. ISSUE: Update to Title 8-4-3, Golf Carts, of the City of Conway Code of Ordinances BACKGROUND: Earlier this year, the state legislature updated state laws regarding the use of golf carts in public areas. As part of this update, the legislature empowered municipalities to create ordinances that are more tailored to their communities. Among those changes, cities are able to allow or restrict access on certain highways within the city limits. They are also able to dictate how far golf carts may travel from their registered address and at what times they may legally travel. Council discussed various options at the June 16 meeting and made some changes at first reading on July 21, 2025. Attached is an ordinance that creates the following new rules within the city limits: - Golf carts may operate on public streets between 6:00 am and 11:00 pm. - Golf carts may operate within a four-mile radius from their registered address. - Golf carts may not operate on certain roads regardless of speed limit. These roads are Millpond, Cultra, and El Bethel. - Golf carts may operate on certain primary highways where the speed limit is 35 or lower. This includes portions of 3rd Avenue, 4th Avenue, Main Street, and 16th Avenue. RECOMMENDATION: Approve final reading of an update to Title 8-4-3 Golf Carts, of the City of Conway code of ordinances. 38 -- 38 of 155 -- ORDINANCE #2025-08-04 (G) AN ORDINANCE TO AMEND SECTION 8-4-3 OF THE CITY OF CONWAY CODE OF ORDINANCES RELATIVE TO OPERATION OF GOLF CARTS WHEREAS, Title 8, Chapter 4 of the City of Conway Code of Ordinances regulates the ownership and operation of golf carts within the municipal limits of Conway, and; WHEREAS, the South Carolina Legislature has amended state laws relative to the authority and powers of local governments to regulate golf carts within their respective jurisdictions, and; WHEREAS, Conway City Council strives to make the streets of its city safe and accessible for all visitors and citizens. NOW, THEREFORE, be it ordained, by the Mayor and the members of the City Council of the City of Conway, South Carolina, that the changes outlined below to Section 8-4-3 of the Conway Code of Ordinances are hereby adopted. Sec. 8-4-3 Operation of golf carts. (a) A permitted golf cart may be operated within 4 miles of the address on the registration or within 4 miles of a point of ingress and egress to a gated community, if the address is within a gated community. (b) Golf carts may only be operated on public streets or designated public golf cart pathways between the hours of 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM, unless excepted as part of a special event permit. (c) Unless otherwise designated in Section 8-4-3(j), golf carts may only travel along secondary highways and local streets with a posted speed limit of 35 miles per hour or less. (d) Unless otherwise designated in Section 8-4-3(k), golf carts may not operate on state primary highways. This is not meant to prohibit crossing such highway while operating in compliance with Section 8-4-3(c). (e) A person operating a golf cart must be at least 16 years of age and hold a valid driver’s license. (f) The operator of a permitted golf cart operating on a public street or pathway must have in his possession the registration certificate issued by the Department of Motor Vehicles, proof of liability insurance, and his driver’s license. (g) It shall be unlawful for an operator to carry more persons at one time than the golf cart is designed to carry. (h) Golf carts are prohibited from traveling upon city sidewalks. (i) Golf carts may operate upon designated golf cart pathways regardless of the posted speed limit of any adjacent highway. APPLICANT(S): Development Resource Group (DRG) LLC (agents) PIN(s): 325-00-00-0011 CURRENT ZONING: Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) PROPOSED ZONING (upon annexation): Medium-Density Residential (R-2) BACKGROUND: The subject property is proposed to be annexed into the City for residential development. The property is within the city’s utility service area, thus requiring annexation to be requested. Surrounding developments – Rivertown Row North, Kingston Bay and Elmhurst, are also zoned Medium-Density Residential (R-2). Midtown Village, which directly abuts this property, is zoned High-Density Residential (R-3). A large portion of the subject property is located within the AE flood zone, which runs through the middle of the parcel (see attached maps). While development is permitted within flood zones, provided the affected property meets the required elevation, staff does not support rezoning portion(s) of property within a flood zone to a district that would permit residential development. In 2023, Council adopted an ordinance that permits parcels containing environmentally sensitive areas to be split- zoned, which is otherwise prohibited, with such areas being zoned Conservation Preservation (CP) upon annexation of property or when property is proposed to be rezoned. Given that there is a small portion of the property within the floodway, in which no development can occur, and that the general area has been prone to flooding, should annexation proceed, this would be an opportunity to discuss the possibility of zoning the portions within a flood zone / floodway to CP with the applicant. In this instance, the applicant would need to submit a survey showing the areas within the flood zone / floodway so that they could be mapped accordingly should the split zoning be preferred. SURROUNDING USES / ZONING: Surrounding in-City zoning includes Neighborhood Commercial (NC), High-Density Residential (R-3), Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1), and Medium-Density Residential (R-2). The area is primarily single-family residential, with limited established commercial uses. There is a gas station/convenience store (Sun House) with a few tenant spaces containing limited commercial uses, including a dog grooming business, immediately adjacent to the subject property. Surrounding County zoning includes mostly residential, including Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF20) on 20,000 sq. ft. min. lot sizes, and Residential, including mobile homes (MSF20), also on 20,000 sq. ft. min. lot sizes. Abutting property is also zoned Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA). 111 -- 111 of 155 -- STAFF REPORT/ISSUE PAPER The John T. Henry Auction location is near the subject property, which is also zoned CFA. Horry Electric is also nearby, on the opposite side of Cultra Rd, which is zoned Office/Professional/Institutional (OPI). COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s future land use map provides three (3) future land use designations for the subject property. For the portion with frontage along Cultra Rd, the future land use is shown as Neighborhood Commercial (NC). Per Section 3.2.9 of the UDO, the NC district is intended to provide small-scale retail and service uses for nearby residential areas. Dimensional requirements and design standards of the district are intended to promote compatibility to surrounding residential areas and accommodate pedestrian use and access. Strip commercial development, designed primarily to accommodate vehicular access and parking, and development that is insensitive or incompatible with the scale and character of the surrounding residential areas, is discouraged in this district. A larger portion of the property is shown as Conservation Preservation (CP) on the city’s future land use map. Per Section 3.2.15 of the UDO, the intent of the CP district is to provide needed open space for general outdoor and indoor recreational uses, and to protect environmentally sensitive areas and flood prone areas from the encroachment of any residential, commercial, industrial, or other uses capable of adversely affecting the relatively undeveloped character of the district. The portion abutting Midtown Village and Conway Christian School is shown as High-Density Residential on the future land use map. Per Section 3.2.5 of the UDO, the intent of the high-density residential district is to provide areas for high-density attached, detached, semi-attached, and multifamily residential development in the City of Conway and to prohibit uses that would substantially interfere with the development or continuation of residential structures in the district. PLANNING COMMISSION RECOMMENDATION: PENDING Planning Commission is scheduled to consider the proposed zoning upon annexation at their August 7th mtg. DATE OF PUBLIC HEARING: Scheduled August 7, 2025 TRC RECOMMENDATION / COMMENTS (if applicable): None; however, the Police Dept. requested additional information. RECOMMENDED ACTION: The property, if developed, will receive city utility services. Staff recommends approval of first reading to annex the subject property and refer to Planning Commission for consideration of the requested zoning of R-2 as well as consideration of split zoning to zone the environmentally sensitive areas to CP upon annexation.
