Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-02-18 (C) to amend Article 9 – Landscape and Buffering, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding Landscape, Buffer, and Tree Preservation Requirements. Hucks stated that this ordinance received first reading at the February 3 Council meeting. As previously presented, the biggest amendment to the tree preservation ordinance is removing it from the general code and codifying it into the Unified Development Ordinance, since Planning & Development facilitate the Tree Board meetings and permits for tree removals are issued by the Planning Department. Hucks said that other changes include: - Appeals of the decisions of tree board would be appealable to the Board of zoning appeals rather than to City Council; - Reduction in the threshold for what is considered a landmark life oak tree from 30” DBH to 24” DBH; - Remove Crepe Myrtles and Redwood trees from the protected tree list as well as add the Tulip, Red Cedar, and Tupelo trees to the protected tree list; - Added definitions, clarified the tree mitigation process, and removed certain penalties Hucks said that following First Reading, several issues regarding maintenance responsibilities of trees in certain locations were discussed amongst staff, and whether trees in public rights of way were the responsibility of the city, individual property owners, or HOA’s, as streets within residential subdivisions are required to be public and ‘street trees’ are required to be planted in the rights of ways. Article 9 of the Unified Development Ordinance specifies that “street trees” shall be maintained by the property owner and/or the HOA in perpetuity. However, while routine maintenance of street trees may prevent them from becoming a nuisance or a hazard, there may be instances when the city’s fire or 65 -- 65 of 161 -- April 7, 2025 Page 3 of 11 sanitation trucks may have issues with tree limbs or branches in relation to these trucks when servicing the neighborhood. Additionally, the Tree Preservation Ordinance, as it’s currently written in the general code, is currently under the public works chapter of the code, and their policies and procedures for tree pruning varies from the requirements of the Unified Development Ordinance, in that there is nothing specified that separates from required street trees in newer, residential developments, or from long-established residential areas, even those not within a subdivision, with regard to maintenance of trees within rights-of-way. The general code currently states that the arborist may have hazard trees or public nuisance trees on public or private property pruned in the interest of public safety, and that a notification in the form of a door hanger will be used to alert the residents that crews will be in the area within a 3- day period and contact information will be provided on the door hanger including name and phone number for the city’s beautification department. This was specifically discussed at the recent budget retreat as well. This language has likely been in the ordinance since it was last amended in 2007 and has not been the general practice. Typically, if a tree is a hazard, in most cases, something is done as soon as possible to prevent damage to streets, vehicles, or to prevent injury to pedestrians. Also, our staff typically work closely with public works staff to let them know about any specific areas (outside of subdivisions) that need attention, regardless of whether it is city or state road. Staff also receive a lot of requests from residents for trees to either be removed or pruned that are located within the right of way in front of their home OR on their private property but with limbs extending over the right of way. If the tree is on private property and the tree is NOT a landmark live oak tree, no pruning permit is required. If the tree is a landmark live oak, they must receive a pruning permit from our department. The current amendment proposes to strike through the aforementioned language. The previous paragraph in the same section will have language added to specify that the City reserves the right to prune any tree deemed to be a hazard tree or public nuisance tree, whether on public or private property, in the interest of public safety. Additionally, another section will be added to clarify that any property that requires the installation of street trees shall be required to adhere to the requirements for street trees and the proper pruning of such trees. As with any other standard or requirement within the Unified Development Ordinance, violations of the requirements of the ordinance are subject to penalties, as provided in Article 15 of the ordinance. Since first reading staff also updated the recommended plant list in the landscaping requirement section of Article 9 to revise the mature heights and widths of certain trees and removed the invasive species list and instead specified that no invasive species that is identified in the current version of the South Carolina Invasive Species Exotic Plant list will be allowed in the City of Conway. Hucks said that staff recommended approval of final reading of the proposed amendment, with the changes included since first reading. Hucks said that the next item on the agenda is a repeal of the general code. ISSUE: Special Presentation of a request to rezone approximately 1.4+/- acres of property located at the corner of Davidson Rd and Hwy 501 (PIN’s 383-08-02-0003 & -0002) from the Professional (P) district to the Highway Commercial (HC) district. BACKGROUND: The applicant submitted a rezoning application for the subject properties on April 1, 2025. The properties are already in the city limits, zoned Professional (P). These properties are lots 1 and 2 on block 8 of the College Park subdivision (see attached plat of College Park). The lots are currently vacant; however, they are encumbered by power transmission line easements, as are several other surrounding lots, which will restrict any type of development. Lot 1 (PIN 383-08-02-0003) is approx. 0.74 acres and Lot 2 (PIN 383- 08-02-0002) is approx. 0.66 acres. The proposed use of the property is not known at this time. Proposed Zoning of Property: The applicant is seeking to rezone the properties to the Highway Commercial (HC) zoning district. Per Section 3.2.10 of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), the intent of the HC district is to provide compatible locations to serve the automobile oriented commercial activities in harmony with major highway developments, reduce traffic congestions and to enhance the aesthetic atmosphere of the City. Surrounding uses/Zoning Districts: These parcels front Hwy 501. Lot 1 is a corner lot, adjacent to Davidson Road. There is nothing on either side of these lots, and properties on either side are zoned Professional. Properties directly behind the subject property is zoned R-1; also, part of the College Park Subdivision. While developed in the county, several parcels were annexed into the city limits over the years, including the lots that front Hwy 501. University Baptist Church is located on lots 1-4 on block 9 of College Park. Declaration of Restrictive Covenants Staff was recently made aware of the existence of restrictive covenants for the College Park Subdivision, from when the development was originally created in 1967, recorded in Deed Book 371 at Page 517 (at Horry County Register of Deeds). Building regulations provided in the restrictions is limited to single- family dwellings only, not to exceed two stories in height. Uses are limited to private family residences together with appropriate and approved outbuildings. Further, the restrictions strictly prohibit commercial activity within the College Park subdivision. The restrictions described within the Declaration of Restrictive Covenants are in effect for an initial 20- year period, and then automatically extended for successive periods of 5 years each, unless an instrument signed by the then owners of a majority of lots within the subdivision has been recorded, agreeing to change in the covenants, limitations or restrictions – in whole or in part. There was such an amendment filed in 1996 for lots 1-4 of block 9 of the subdivision, which subsequently allowed a church with amenities to be constructed on said lots. However, the amendment did not include any revisions to any of the other lots within College Park. In fact, page 3 of the amendment specifically states that “except as changed, amended, 79 -- 79 of 161 -- or modified herein, the subdivision Declaration of Restrictions, and any amendment thereto, shall remain in full force, virtue and effect.” While deed restrictions / restrictive covenants are a civil matter, and it is not required by the local planning agency to determine whether such restrictions exist, once we have received notice of their existence, the local planning agency does have the ability to deny plans that would otherwise violate such restrictions. However, they are not enforced by the local planning agency. More specifically: SC Code of Laws, Section § 6-29-1145. Determining existence of restrictive covenant; effect. A. In an application for a permit, the local planning agency must inquire in the application or by written instructions to an applicant whether the tract of land or parcel of land is restricted by any recorded covenant that is contrary to, conflicts with, or prohibits the permitted activity. B. If a local planning agency has actual notice of a restrictive covenant on a tract or parcel of land that is contrary to, conflicts with, or prohibits the permitted activity: 1. In the application for the permit; 2. From materials or information submitted by the person or persons requesting the permit; or 3. From any other source including, but not limited to, other property holders, the local planning agency must not issue the permit unless the local planning agency receives confirmation from the applicant that the restrictive covenant has been released for the tract or parcel of land by action of the appropriate authority or property holders or by court order. C. As used in this section: 1. “actual notice” is not constructive notice of documents filed in local offices concerning the property and does not require the local planning agency to conduct searches in any records offices for filed restrictive covenants. CITY OF CONWAY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN: The future land use map of the Comprehensive Plan identifies the property as Highway Commercial (HC). Per Section 3.2.10 of the UDO, the intent of the HC district is to provide compatible locations to serve the automobile oriented commercial activities in harmony with major highway developments, reduce traffic congestions and to enhance the aesthetic atmosphere of the City. ISSUE: First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-05-19 (D) to rezone approximately 8.5+/- acres of property located on Technology Blvd (PIN’s 383-10-03-0020 and -0026) from the Planned Development (PD) and Highway Commercial (HC) districts to the High-Density Residential (R-3) district, and a request to rezone 0.02+/- acres of property located on Technology Blvd (PIN 383-10-03-0027) from the Planned Development (PD) district to the High-Density Residential (R-3) district. BACKGROUND: The applicant submitted a rezoning application for the subject property in March 2025. The properties are already in the city limits, zoned Planned Development (PD) district and Highway Commercial (HC). Two of the parcels include the University Suites Planned Development, with the small .02-acre parcel containing the pump station for University Suites. The other property, across Technology Blvd, is zoned Highway Commercial and is located directly behind the Food Lion shopping center. The applicant proposes to construct 24 multifamily units on the 1.75-acre parcel. Proposed Zoning of Property: The applicant is seeking to rezone the properties to High-Density Residential (R-3). Per Section 3.2.5 of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), the intent of the R-3 district is to provide areas for high-density attached, detached, semi-attached, and multifamily residential development in the City of Conway and to prohibit uses that would substantially interfere with the development or continuation of residential structures in the district. Existing surrounding uses/Zoning Districts: These parcels are located behind the Food Lion shopping center, which is zoned HC. It abuts an established single-family residential neighborhood (Coastal Heights), mostly zoned Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF10); however, several lots within this development have been annexed into the city over the last few years and are zoned Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). The subject properties also abut property zoned Institutional (IN) that is owned by Horry-Georgetown Technical College (HGTC). The properties are within walking distance to a shopping center, several food establishments, medical offices, a hospital, and both HGTC and Coastal Carolina University (CCU). There are already sidewalks along Technology Blvd, and there are several outlets for vehicular access to Hwy 501. Proposed use of property: Two of the three parcels are already developed, with no changes to those parcels currently planned. One of those developed parcels is the pump station for the University Suites development, owned by Grand Strand Water & Sewer Auth. The vacant parcel currently zoned Highway Commercial is proposed to contain 24 multifamily units. A site plan has been provided by the applicant. The request was reviewed by the City’s Technical Review Committee, and no concerns were provided by any city department regarding this request. 114 -- 114 of 161 -- CITY OF CONWAY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN: The future land use map of the Comprehensive Plan identifies the property as Highway Commercial (HC). Per Section 3.2.10 of the UDO, the intent of the HC district is to provide compatible locations to serve the automobile oriented commercial activities in harmony with major highway developments, reduce traffic congestions and to enhance the aesthetic atmosphere of the City. PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the request at their April 3rd meeting and ultimately recommended approval of the request to rezone the property to High-Density Residential (R-3). However, Planning Commission did express concerns with additional traffic on Technology Blvd; particularly at the intersection with Victory Lane and Horry-Georgetown Blvd, as this area is heavily traveled by pedestrians who visit the Abilities Beyond Barriers establishment (formerly known as Horry County Disabilities and Special Needs) and the SC Dept. of Employment and Workforce. Planning Commission discussed the need for a traffic study of Technology Blvd. Staff explained that for this type of rezoning request, a traffic study is not typically required; however, Article 7 – Streets and Circulation, of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) was amended a few years ago, as part of a broader amendment, giving the Technical Review Committee (TRC) the authority to require a traffic study of any proposed major subdivision development that it determines may have an impact on the road network or functionality, at the expense of the developer. When full civil plans are submitted for review, this will be further studied to determine if a traffic study is warranted for the additional units. ISSUE: First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-04-07 (D) to rezone approximately 7.8+/- acres of property located on (North) Main Street and Chicora Blvd (PIN 338-03-02-0006) from the Highway Commercial (HC) district to the High-Density Residential (R-3) district. BACKGROUND: The applicant submitted a rezoning application for the subject property in January 2025. The property is already in the city limits, zoned Highway Commercial (HC). The property is currently vacant. The applicant is seeking to rezone the property to High-Density Residential (R-3) in order to develop the property as multifamily; more specifically, a workforce housing community. Per Section 3.2.5 of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), the intent of the R-3 district is to provide areas for high-density attached, detached, semi-attached, and multifamily residential development in the City of Conway and to prohibit uses that would substantially interfere with the development or continuation of residential structures in the district. Gateway Corridor Overlay (GCO) District: The subject property is also within the Gateway Corridor Overlay (GCO). Per Section 3.4.2 of the UDO, the intent of the overlay district is to create a commercial corridor that is well planned and attractive through the implementation of consistent design standards. The provisions of this section will ensure that the design quality of new development in the city’s identified gateway corridors are held to high standards. This section (GCO) shall not apply to detached single-family residential dwellings being used for residential purposes. Per Section 6.5.2, A. – Purpose, of the UDO, the GCO is established to provide standards relative to accessibility, appearance, and safety in the development of commercial, industrial, multifamily residential, and office projects that utilize highway corridors are their primary means of access. Per Section 6.5.2, B. – Applicability, the GCO district shall extend 500 feet from the right-of-way line on properties along these highways (90, 378, 501, 501 Bus., 701 (South and North), and 905). Surrounding uses/Zoning Districts: The subject property abuts the Chicora development, a single-family neighborhood, zoned R-1 (low/medium-density residential). Other properties beside and across from the subject property are zoned Highway Commercial (HC). There is no other property zoned R-3 (high-density residential) in the nearby surrounding area. The property on the opposite side of Chicora Blvd (currently vacant) had previously been proposed and approved for a grocery store (KJ’s) to be developed. CITY OF CONWAY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN: The future land use map of the Comprehensive Plan identifies the property as Highway Commercial (HC). Per Section 3.2.10 of the UDO, the intent of the HC district is to provide compatible locations to serve the automobile oriented commercial activities in harmony with major highway developments, 128 -- 128 of 161 -- reduce traffic congestions and to enhance the aesthetic atmosphere of the City. PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the request at their March 6th meeting and recommended disapproval of the request to rezone the property to High-Density Residential (R-3), although it was not unanimous. Several residents of the Chicora neighborhood were present and gave public input, in opposition to the request. Their concerns included traffic along Chicora Blvd and Hwy 701, crime, stormwater drainage and flooding issues. APRIL 7, 2025 – CITY COUNCIL WORKSHOP: City Council held a workshop with the applicant at their April 7, 2025 meeting to discuss the applicants request in more detail. STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Workforce housing and affordable / attainable housing is needed in and around Conway. The costs of housing has increased significantly over the past several years; specifically post-Covid, with many people relocating to the area from other parts of the country, the shortage in housing supply, as well as inflation. Adequate housing is not always attainable for many individuals who work in and around our community, such as our teachers, nurses, police, firefighters, and others in similar professions, as these individuals make too much money to qualify for low-income housing and not enough money to purchase a home. Housing affordability a much broader issue than just the zoning of property. Lack of affordability / attainability of housing cannot be solved just by rezoning properties to districts that allow higher density. While zoning districts which would allow higher densities could add to the housing supply if properties are developed as zoning (density) allows, what staff must consider when reviewing a request to rezone property is whether the requesting zoning is appropriate for the subject property. The Comprehensive Plan must first be consulted to see if the proposed rezoning is consistent with the plan and the future land use map. Other factors that can influence recommendations and decisions regarding rezoning requests include, but are not limited to: • Current and proposed land use; • How the requesting zoning would affect nearby properties (and public opposition); • Whether existing infrastructure is adequate and if not, what infrastructure may be necessary; • Environmental impacts (wetlands, flood zones, etc.); • Economic impacts; • Past decisions for similar requests; • Recommendation of Planning Commission The property is currently zoned Highway Commercial (HC), as is all other surrounding properties fronting on either side of Hwy 701 N. (N. Main St.). The Future Land Use Map also identifies the property as HC. There is no property in the immediate area that is already zoned R-3. There is property zoned R-2 (medium-density residential) on Cultra Rd / Oak Street and Boundary Street; none of which 129 -- 129 of 161 -- front a major corridor. There are no flood zones on the subject property; however, the adjacent property is within a flood zone as well as properties across the road, and areas near this portion of Hwy 701 North have been known to flood during major rain events. However, if developed as proposed, it’s likely there would be less impervious surface area resulting from the development than if it were to be developed commercially, resulting in less stormwater runoff. There is strong opposition from the neighboring community to this request, with concerns related to traffic, crime, and flooding; as previously mentioned. Council has previously denied rezoning requests for zoning other than what the future land use map shows for properties along major corridors in the city (Hwy 501 bypass), in an effort to preserve these commercial corridors. Finally, Planning Commission recommended disapproval of the requesting zoning of R-3. Based on these factors, including the recommendation of Planning Commission, staff recommends disapproval of the request. 130 -- 130 of 161 -- ORDINANCE # ZA2025-04-07 (D) AN ORDINANCE TO REZONE APPROXIMATELY 7.8+/- ACRES OF PROPERTY LOCATED ON (NORTH) MAIN STREET AND CHICORA BLVD (PIN 338-03-02-0006) FROM THE CITY OF CONWAY HIGHWAY COMMERCIAL (HC) DISTRICT TO THE CITY OF CONWAY HIGH-DENSITY RESIDENTIAL (R-3) DISTRICT. The site will also include a covered patio area and a playground. title: CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES.5.5.25
text: CITY OF CONWAY CITY COUNCIL MEETING CONWAY CITY HALL 229 MAIN STREET, CONWAY MONDAY, MAY 5, 2025 PRESENT: Mayor Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor Pro Tem William Goldfinch, Amanda Butler, Julie Hardwick, Beth Helms, Justin Jordan and Larry White STAFF: Adam Emrick, City Administrator; Mary Catherine Hyman, Deputy City Administrator; John Rogers, Deputy City Administrator; June Wood, Public Information Officer; Jeff Leveille, Technology Services Director; Jessica Hucks, Planning and Development Director; Dale Long, Police Chief; Rock Rabon, Fleet Maintenance Director; Reggie Jenerette, Solid Waste Director; Kayla Fleming, Municipal Judge; Brandon Harrelson, Public Works Director; Ashley Smith, Parks and Recreation Director; Robert Cooper, Construction Services Director; Timmy Williams, Hospitality and Beautification Director; Allison Williams, Finance Director; Lynn Smith, Human Resource Director; Ted Dudley, Public Utilities Director; and Debbie Smith, Executive Assistant. CALL TO ORDER: Mayor Blain called the meeting to order. Brandon Wilson of Ekklesia Christian Church gave the invocation and led the Pledge of Allegiance. The requirements for posting notice of this meeting under South Carolina’s Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) were met. CONSENT AGENDA: A. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-05-05 (A), granting a non-exclusive franchise agreement to Mister Softee Mobile Food Trucks (three total) to operate within Collins Park and Riverwalk Park. B. Final reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-05-05 (B) to amend Articla 10 – Subdivision and Land Development, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding the requirements for the renaming of existing streets. C. Approval to Amend a Franchise Agreement with the SCPSA. D. Approval of the 2025 Emergency Operations Plan. E. Approval of a Purchase for a Replacement Vehicle Extrication Tool – Fire Department (budgeted). F. Approval of a memorandum of Understanding between Coastal Carolina University and the City of Conway. G. Approval of April 7, 2025, Council Meeting Minutes. -- 1 of 7 -- APPROVAL OF CONSENT AGENDA: Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Goldfinch to approve May 5, 2025 consent agenda. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. SPECIAL PRESENTATION: A. Presentation of a Proclamation recognizing May 2025 as National Tennis Month – Mayor Blain presented the proclamation to Ms. Carolyn Williams. B. Presentation of a Proclamation honoring the American Legion Post III – Mayor Blain read the proclamation, but no one was present to receive it. C. Presentation of a Proclamation recognizing Apraxia Awareness – Mayor Blain read and presented the proclamation to Ms. Beth Ann Sawicki. D. Presentation of a Proclamation recognizing Earth Day – Mayor Blain read and presented the proclamation to Mr. John Friestad. E. Discussion of a request to rezone approximately 1.4+/- total acres of property located at the corner of Davidson Road and East highway 501 (PIN’s 383-08-02-0003 & 383- 08-02-0002) from the Professional (P) district to Highway Commercial (HC) district. Hucks stated the applicant submitted a rezoning application for lots 1 and 2 on block 8 of the College Park subdivision. The properties are already in the city limits, zoned Professional (P) and are currently vacant; however, they are encumbered by power transmission line easements, as are several other surrounding lots, which will restrict any type of development. Lot 1 (PIN 383-08-02-0003) is approximately 0.74 acres and Lot 2 (PIN 383-08-02-0002) is approximately 0.66 acres. The request is to rezone the properties to the Highway Commercial (HC) zoning district. The College Park Subdivision holds restrictive covenants which date back to 1967, when the development was originally developed. Building regulations provided in the restrictions is limited to single-family dwellings only, not to exceed two stories in height. Uses are limited to private family residences together with appropriate and approved outbuildings. Further, the restrictions strictly prohibit commercial activity within the College Park subdivision. The restrictions described within the Declaration of Restrictive Covenants are in effect for an initial 20-year period, and then automatically extended for successive periods of 5 years each, unless an instrument signed by the then owners of a majority of lots within the subdivision has been recorded, agreeing to change in the covenants, limitations or restrictions – in whole or in part. Hucks said the Planning Commission considered the request at their May 1st meeting and recommended disapproval. First Reading will be on the May 19th agenda for consideration. -- 2 of 7 -- FIRST READING: A. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-05-19 (A) to annex approximately 0.41 acres located at 125 Ole Cedar Lane (PIN 339-05-04-0002), and rezone from the Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF20) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district. Dennis stated the annexation application was submitted by Charles Foster, property owner, as a requirement to connect to city utility services. The property, which contains an existing single-family home is located adjacent to the Clearbrook subdivision – recently annexed large parcel off John Doctor Road. A restrictive covenant was recorded on April 10, 2025. The Technical Review Committee (TRC) all approved the annexation except for Sanitation; the reason - having no place to turn the truck around. Staff recommended the request be disapproved. Motion: Mayor Blain made a motion, seconded by Helms, to disapprove first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-05-19 (A). Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-05-19 (C) to annex approximately 20.4+/- acres of property located on Hwy 501 (PIN’s 326-15-03-0002, 326-00-00-0042 and 337-03-01-0026) and request to rezone from the Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) and Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) zoning districts to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district. Hucks stated the applicant submitted the annexation and rezoning application for the subject property requesting to assign Highway Commercial (HC) zoning to the properties upon annexation. The properties are currently in the county’s jurisdiction, zoned Highway Commercial (HC) and Commercial Forest and Agriculture (CFA). The property is currently vacant. Mayor Blain expressed concern that residential property is directly behind the subject property. Goldfinch expressed concern that if not approved, the current zoning would create a “donut hole” and anything could be put on the property. Hucks stated the Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the proposed request at their April 3rd meeting and recommended approval of the request to annex and rezone the property to Highway Commercial (HC). Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by White, to approve first reading of Ordinance#ZA2025-05-19 (C). Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. C. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-05-19 (D) to rezone approximately 8.5 +/- acres of property located on Technology Blvd (PIN’s 383-10-03-0020 and -0026) from the Planned Development (PD) and Highway Commercial (HC) districts to the High-Density Residential (R-3) district, and a request to rezone 0.02+/- acres of property located on Technology Blvd (PIN 383-10-03-0027) from the Planned Development (PD) district to the High-Density Residential (R-3) district. Hucks -- 3 of 7 -- stated this request includes 3 parcels; 2 of which are known as the University Suites Planned Development, with one being the pump station parcel for the development. The other parcel is currently vacant and currently zoned Highway Commercial. The applicant is requesting to rezone these 3 parcels to the Highway Density Residential District (R-3) to construct 24 additional units on the vacant property zoned Highway Commercial, across from the University Suites development. These parcels are located behind Food Lion shopping center and abuts an established single-family residential neighborhood (Coastal Heights), mostly zoned Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed. Hucks stated the Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the request at their April 3rd meeting and expressed concerns with additional traffic on Technology Blvd but ultimately recommended approval of the request to rezone the property to High-Density Residential (R-3). Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Goldfinch, to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-05-19 (D). Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. D. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-04-07 (D) to rezone approximately 7.8+/- acres of property located on (North Main Street and Chicora Blvd (PIN 338-03- 02-0006) from the Highway Commercial (HC) district to the High-Density Residential (R-3) district. Hucks stated the subject property is currently in the city limits, zoned Highway Commercial (HC) and is vacant. The request is to rezone the property to High-Density Residential (R-3) to develop the property as multifamily; more specifically, a workforce housing community. The subject property is in the Gateway Corridor Overlay and abuts the Chicora development, a single-family neighborhood, zoned R-1 (low-medium-density residential). Other properties beside and across from the subject property are zoned Highway Commercial (HC). There is no other property zoned R-3 (high-density residential) in the nearby surrounding area. The property on the opposite side of Chicora Blvd (currently vacant) had previously been proposed and approved for a grocery store (KJ’s) to be developed. The future land use map of the Comprehensive Plan identifies the property as Highway Commercial (HC). White and Blain expressed concerns about comments made during the April 7, 2025, City Council Workshop. Hardwick stated that she is not against workforce housing; she would vote to deny the request regardless of the type of housing based on the city’s Comprehensive Plan and Gateway Corridor Plan that is currently in place. Goldfinch suggested a meeting for Council to discuss housing in the City of Conway. Motion: Hardwick made a motion, seconded by Jordan, to deny first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-04-07 (D). Vote: Hardwick, Jordan, Goldfinch, Blain, Butler and Helms voted yes, with White voting no. Motion carried 6-1. -- 4 of 7 -- CONSIDERATION: Consideration of changing the name of a proposed subdivision on Hemingway Chapel Road, from “Hemingway Chapel Landing” to “Hemingway Landing” (PIN 369-00-00-0021), across from the New Castle subdivision. Hucks stated that the agenda was incorrect, and the name is to be changed to Hemingway Landing. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Helms, to approve the name change from Hemingway Chapel Landing to Hemingway Landing. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. PUBLIC INPUT: - George Ulrich addressed the Council asking if the city could offer grocery stores incentives to move to the area. The incentives would help offset building costs. He also thanked Adam Emrick and the staff for keeping Conway alive and interesting. CITY ADMINISTRATOR’S REPORT: Emrick informed Council of the following: • Emrick said that a few walked the pathway of the boardwalk that will be part of Kingston Ferry, wading through the swamp from Depot Road to where the landing will be on the river across from the Riverwalk. This area will be, without any further connections, a destination worth seeing. • GSATS (Grand Strand Area Transportation Study) has identified four separate locations to improve access management and safety within the city through grant funding. Federal funding is now available to implement these projects and GSATS will apply for $6.3 million to design and construct better and safer access management on both Church Street and north Main Street. A match will be required, but only if the city gets the grant and even then, not until FY 26/27 at the earliest. • Emrick encouraged all to attend on Tuesday, May 13th at 1 p.m. as there will be a dedication of the new brick wall at Lakeside Cemetery. • Emrick also encouraged all to attend on May 16th at 11 am for the groundbreaking ceremony for Health Care Partners’ new 30,000 sq ft facility on 4th Avenue. • Emrick said that later this week, John, MC and himself would be attending the SC Community Development Association Annual Meeting. Emrick said that staff is presenting on Halloween and hopefully bringing back more good ideas for Conway. • Emrick stated that the city has an open grant for stormwater improvements to Pine Street and Beaty Street that will upgrade and improve the infrastructure in this area all the way to its outfall at Kingston Lake. Staff hopes to have bids in on all phases of this project later this month and will likely have them on a Council calendar in late -- 5 of 7 -- June or early July for approval. The city is in a bit of a time crunch on this project due to delays in permitting, but staff is confident that all deadlines for the grant will be met. Construction will begin late summer or early fall with a completion deadline of June 1, 2026. • Emrick thanked Nevada Milleur, Timmy Williams and all of those who participated in the Great American Cleanup event that took place on Saturday. o There were 67 total volunteers that picked up 880 pounds of litter, more than 60 bags full. Targeted areas were Depot Road, Boundary Street, Oak Street, Medlen Parkway, Ernest Finney Avenue, Westridge Blvd, Smith Jones Park, 9th Avenue, Hemingway Chapel Road, Lochwood Lane, and Mill Pond Road. • The city has had several requests from the public for sidewalks to be installed on Medlen Parkway. The recent development of Oak Tree Farms and a new Town Home project called Bay Village, which is next to Oak Tree Farms, both have been required to add sidewalks to the road front of Medlen. Staff is working on two large infrastructure projects on Medlen right now, a drainage project and a sewer project. After both are completed, staff can try to fill sidewalks in to make a more complete network and meet the requests of the community there. But it will take a while before that is possible and likely, this will not happen until next budget season. • First reading of the budget will be on the next agenda with final reading scheduled for the first meeting in June. • Thank you to the Mayor’s Youth Council for their work this year. And thank you to John Rogers and the other staff members who assisted him this year to make it successful. There is a nationwide shortage of people entering the workforce who want to do what we do. Hopefully, the Youth Council is introducing just enough of local government to spark an interest that may resonate with these young leaders moving forward. • On May 22nd, at 1 pm, the city will celebrate City Hall 200, the 200th birthday of this building and the oldest public building in Horry County. Please put this on your calendar as it should be a fun and informative afternoon commemorating a milestone in our city’s history. • There is no workshop tonight, but there is an Executive Session to discuss Board Appointments. COUNCIL INPUT: Hardwick said that she was so excited to see the youth council and thanked the Mayor and staff. Hardwick also said she is super excited about the trail and where it will go. Hardwick congratulated all the high school and college graduates. Goldfinch talked about the joinery that is in the old Visitors Center adjacent to Presbyterian Church and would like to invite him to a council meeting to help promote -- 6 of 7 -- -- 7 of 7 --

Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the request at their March 6 meeting. Several people spoke in opposition to the request. Their concerns included traffic on Highway 701 and Chicora Blvd, stormwater drainage and flooding, and crime. Ultimately, Planning Commission recommended disapproval of the request to rezone to R-3; however, it was not a unanimous decision. Hucks said that the applicant has stated that the intended use of the property is multifamily but would be workforce housing. Staff certainly agrees that not only workforce housing, but affordable and attainable housing is very much needed in the community, given the increased cost associated with housing; especially since the Covid pandemic. However, what staff must consider when reviewing a request to rezone property is whether the requested zoning district is appropriate for the property. Staff’s foremost responsibility is to the comprehensive plan, and whether the request is consistent with the plan. Additional factors can include how the rezoning will affect nearby properties, whether existing infrastructure is adequate and if not – what is needed, environmental and economic impacts there could be, past decisions that have been made for similar requests and the recommendation of Planning Commission. In the case of this property, which is zoned Highway Commercial, all surrounding properties with frontage on Highway 701 are also zoned HC. The future land use map of the comprehensive plan identifies these properties as HC as well. There is no other property in the vicinity that is zoned R-3. The closest to this would be properties on Boundary Street zoned R-2; however, these properties do not have frontage on Highway 701. Additionally, while there are no identified flood zones on this property, portions of the property on the other side of Chicora Blvd are within a flood zone, and Highway 701 has been prone to flooding very close to the subject property. ISSUE: Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-02-18(C), amending Article 9 – Landscaping and Buffering, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding Landscape, Buffer, and Tree Preservation requirements. BACKGROUND: Staff is proposing an amendment to Article 9 that would codify the Tree Preservation Ordinance, currently part of the city’s general code, into the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO). There are additional amendments proposed to Article 9, part of a broader cleanup initiative of the UDO, that would provide needed clarification on commonly misinterpreted aspects of Article 9 as well as to ensure consistency with other Articles of the UDO that have also been amended over the past couple of years. Amendments to the Tree Preservation Ordinance, other than codification into the UDO include, but are not limited to the following: 1. Redirect appeals of the Conway Tree Board from City Council to the Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA); 2. Removal of trees from the protected tree list (remove: Crape Myrtle and Dawn Redwood); 3. Addition of native trees to the protected tree list (add: Cottonwood; Tulip tree; Red Cedar tree; Tupelo tree; Iron Tree); 4. Reduce the size of a landmark (live oak) tree from the current 30 inches DBH to 24 inches DBH; 5. Addition of requirements for a Tree Protection Plan in conjunction with plans for clearing, grading, grubbing, and site construction; 6. Clarify requirements for tree removal permits for non-residential development and major subdivision developments; and 7. Housekeeping changes throughout the ordinance to ensure a more uniform and concise understanding of the processes and terminology used throughout the ordinance. These items include clarity of the process of tree mitigation, clarification of penalties for improper removal of protected or landmark trees, and clarification on definitions that were commonly misinterpreted. RECOMMENDATION: Since first reading of the ordinance at the February 3rd Council meeting, an issue arose regarding who is responsible for removal of trees on private properties when such trees may pose a public safety issue or hazard due to dead limbs or the health of the tree itself, which have been in effect since at least 2007. Staff has made an amendment to the ordinance that clarifies responsibilities to be consistent with the requirements of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO). Staff recommends approval of final reading of the ordinance, with the changes that have been made since First Reading of the ordinance. 46 -- 46 of 124 -- ORDINANCE #ZA2025-02-18(C) AMENDING ARTICLE 9 – LANDSCAPING AND BUFFERING, OF THE CITY OF CONWAY UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE (UDO), REGARDING LANDSCAPE, BUFFER AND TREE PRESERVATION REQUIREMENTS. Section 9.1 – Intent and Purpose 9.1.1 Intent A. The requirement and regulation of landscaping in the City of Conway is a critical public concern. Requirements and regulations for landscaping are necessary in order to preserve and enhance the aesthetic beauty of the city and promote the safety and general welfare of its residents. More specifically, the intent of the landscape ordinance is to: 1. Provide buffering between non-compatible land uses. 2. Protect, preserve, and promote aesthetic appeal and scenic beauty. 3. Reduce noise pollution and air pollution. 4. Reduce storm water run-off. 5. Filter and reduce glare from artificial light sources. 6. Purpose. Through the use of Best Management Practices (BMP’s) to protect onsite and offsite water resources, a variety of BMP’s can preserve site hydrology and maintain or reduce pre-development run-off volumes and rates. New development shall minimize off-site stormwater runoff, promote on-site filtration, and minimize the discharge of pollutants to ground and surface water. Every development over three acres shall at all times have in place a plan approved by the City of Conway that articulates sustainable stormwater management initiatives. In addition to other requirements set by the City of Conway, the Storm Water Management Plan shall include storm water management performance standards. Post development peak discharge rates should not exceed pre- development peak rates. B. Storm Water Management Performance Standards 1. Provisions for Stormwater Management. a. Rate Control. Storm water drainage systems shall manage the peak rate of discharge from the Development, incorporating the maximum permissible release rate allowed by the City of Conway. Untreated, direct stormwater discharges to wetlands or surface waters are not allowed. b. Volume Control. Storm water drainage systems shall reduce the volume of runoff from a development by one of the following measures: 1) Capture first one-half inch of runoff from all impervious surfaces in accordance with volume control BMP’s; or 2) achieve a fifteen (15) percent reduction in impervious surfaces from existing conditions. 2. Provisions for Sediment and Erosion Control. Erosion and sediment controls must be implemented to remove 80% of the average annual load of total suspended solids. C. Stormwater Management Design Techniques. Multiple Storm Water Management Techniques (Best Management Practices or BMPs) shall be applied to a development parcel in order to accomplish the above stated rate and volume controls. BMPs shall include the following methods of infiltration. 1. Bioswale. Bio-swales are open, linear channels that filter stormwater as the water flows through vegetation to the discharge point. Although their width and length vary as needed to achieve function, at a minimum they are two feet wide at the bottom and have a maximum slope of 2.5:1. Rain will not stand for more than four (4) hours in a bioswale before infiltrating. A bioswale often includes a perforated pipe for emergency overflow situations. 2. Filter Strips. A landscape strip usually underlain by open graded aggregate with no fines. 3. Permeable Pavers. A paving system that allows water to move through the driving surface into the stone base below. Permeable pavers are individual clay or concrete pavers that provide a solid ground surface and strong enough to take heavy loads, like large vehicles, while at the same time allowing water to filter through the surface and reach the underlying soils. Permeable pavers shall be utilized in commercial and residential paved areas such as parking lots, sidewalks, storage yards, building entryways, plazas and patios. Design requirements include the following: a. Use surface material that allows infiltration. b. A minimum 6-inch depth of aggregate base/storage bed shall be used below the permeable pavement surface. c. Provide positive drainage from the permeable surface (slope surface at 1% to 2%). 73 -- 73 of 124 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 9 – Landscaping, and Buffering and Tree Preservation Standards 9-26 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended xx-xx-xxxx d. Perforated overflow pipe design shall be designed and evaluated by project engineer or geotechnical engineer. 4. Vegetated Roof. A vegetated roof system designed to detain rain water on the building’s roof. In general, the vegetated roof is planted with species adaptable to drought conditions. 5. Cistern. A closed system that re-uses rain water for various landscape uses and/or internal building recycling. 6. Rain Garden. A vegetated garden space that filters rain water. Few communities can actually boast that they build streets around trees as Conway does. Few communities attach names and historical significance to particular trees as Conway does. The live oak trees, which line many streets within the city, are probably the city's most prized and most protected natural resource. Local legend has it that when the large oaks along Main Street were threatened by the construction of the railroad in 1887, Mrs. Mary Beaty, who lived near the Wade Hampton Oak, appeared with a loaded shotgun and demanded that the construction workers "touch not a single bough." The actions of Mary Beaty have inspired the citizens of Conway to actively protect the live oak trees as well as certain other native tree species. It is felt that Mrs. Beaty's actions that day were the genesis of tree protection, not only in Conway, but in the State of South Carolina. 9.8.2 Intent A. The intent of the City of Conway tree protection ordinance is to accomplish the following: 1. To provide for the protection, preservation, proper maintenance, and use of trees and woodlands; 2. To minimize disturbance and prevent damage from erosion and destruction of the natural habitat without denying the reasonable use and enjoyment of the property within the city; 3. To protect trees and woodlands (including other forms of vegetation) for their economic support of local property values and for their natural beauty, wilderness character, or geological, ecological or historical significance; 4. To address the public concern for these valued natural resources in the interest of health, safety, and general welfare of the residents of the City of Conway; 5. To encourage the beautification, air-cooling and purification, noise abatement, property value enhancement and the other attributes of trees within a city; 6. To naturally control flooding and erosion, moderate noise pollution, dust, and other airborne pollutants, moderate the city climate and shelter and feed wildlife; 7. To enable citizens to prevent and control the spread of diseases, to preserve trees in the path of development, and to avoid the unnecessary cost associated with sewer clogging, sidewalk replacement and tree-related accidents. 9.8.3 Applicability This chapter The provisions of this ordinance shall apply to all trees of any type all trees identified as being protected or landmark trees, as described herein, that are located on public or private property inside the city limits of the City of Conway, South Carolina. Please refer to Section 9.8.10, Tree permits required, for the applicability of each type of permit. 9.8.4 Jurisdiction Administration The city arborist, zoning administrator, or their designee shall be responsible for the administration of all provisions of this chapter and for public tree management, and The city arborist shall be assisted in his/her the administration of these regulations by the Conway tree board, as provided for in Section 9.8.6 established below. 75 -- 75 of 124 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 9 – Landscaping, and Buffering and Tree Preservation Standards 9-28 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended xx-xx-xxxx 9.8.5 Tree City USA A. ISSUE: Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-02-18 (D), to amend Title 3 – Public Works, Chapter 4 – Tree Preservation, and Title 5 – Planning and Development, of the City of Conway Code of Ordinances, regarding the Tree Preservation Ordinance. BACKGROUND: Currently, Title 3, Chapter 4 of the City of Conway Code of Ordinances currently assigns the responsibilities of the Tree Preservation Ordinance to the City Arborist and the Tree Board (also the Community Appearance Board) and also directs appeals of the tree board decisions to City Council. Staff has been working on amendments to the Tree Preservation Ordinance that would remove the ordinance from the general code and insert it into the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), which is already being enforced through the Planning & Development Dept. One of the biggest reasons for doing so is to move the appeals process for appeals of the Tree Board to the Board of Zoning Appeals, which is consistent with the process of other municipalities in the state. In doing so, appeals of the decisions of tree board could first be considered by the Board of Zoning Appeals rather than City Council, and before any appeal is filed in circuit court. Amendments regarding revisions to Article 9 – Landscaping and Buffer Requirements, of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), can be reviewed in Ordinance ZA2025-02-18 (C). This amendment to the general code is solely to repeal the Tree Preservation Ordinance from Title 3, Chapter 4 of the General Code and Title 5 – Planning & Development. No. ZA99-10-25(B). Sec. 3-4-1 - Introduction. The preservation of trees and natural vegetation is deeply rooted in the history of Conway and is a critical public concern. Few communities can actually boast that they build streets around trees as Conway does. Few communities attach names and historical significance to particular trees as Conway does. The live oak trees, which line many streets within the city, are probably the city's most prized and most protected natural resource. Local legend has it that when the large oaks along Main Street were threatened by the construction of the railroad in 1887, Mrs. Mary Beaty, who lived near the Wade Hampton Oak, appeared with a loaded shotgun and demanded that the construction workers "touch not a single bough." The actions of Mary Beaty have inspired the citizens of Conway to actively protect the live oak trees as well as certain other native tree species. It is felt that Mrs. Beaty's actions that day were the genesis of tree protection, not only in Conway, but in the State of South Carolina. (Ord. No. 2007-11-12(A), 11/12/07) Sec. 3-4-2 - Intent. The intent of the City of Conway tree protection ordinance is to accomplish the following: (a) To provide for the protection, preservation, proper maintenance, and use of trees and woodlands; (b) To minimize disturbance and prevent damage from erosion and destruction of the natural habitat without denying the reasonable use and enjoyment of the property within the city; (c) To protect trees and woodlands (including other forms of vegetation) for their economic support of local property values and for their natural beauty, wilderness character, or geological, ecological or historical significance; (d) To address the public concern for these valued natural resources in the interest of health, safety, and general welfare of the residents of the City of Conway; (e) To encourage the beautification, air-cooling and purification, noise abatement, property value enhancement and the other attributes of trees within a city; (f) To naturally control flooding and erosion, moderate noise pollution, dust, and other airborne pollutants, moderate the city climate and shelter and feed wildlife; (g) To enable citizens to prevent and control the spread of diseases, to preserve trees in the path of development, and to avoid the unnecessary cost associated with sewer clogging, sidewalk replacement and tree-related accidents. All words in these standards have their customary dictionary definition except as specifically defined herein. The words "shall" and "must" are mandatory, and the words "may" and "should" are permissive. Technical terms used are defined as follows: (1) Area: The area of a tree, as defined in this chapter, shall be arrived at by multiplying pi (3.14, a constant) times the square of the radius of the tree (where the radius equals one and one-half (1 ½) times the diameter breast high) or the standard area formula: A = pi X r squared. (2) ANSI (current edition): American National Standards Institute. The ANSI A300 standards represent the industry consensus on performing tree care operations. (3) Caliper: A caliper measurement shall be measured six (6) inches above the soil line, or across the stump, in the event the tree has been severed at less than 12 inches above the soil line. (4) Critical root zone: That area of tree roots under the canopy measured to be no less than one and one-half (1 ½) feet in radius for every inch of trunk diameter measured four and one-half (4 ½) feet above the ground. (5) Diameter breast height (d.b.h.): The diameter measurement of a tree is measured at four and one-half (4 ½) feet above ground level and is referred to as diameter, breast high, commonly abbreviated as d.b.h. Trees consisting of two (2) or more stems in which the fork is below d.b.h. are considered as separate trees and the diameter is measured for each stem separately. If a fork occurs exactly at d.b.h., the diameter measurement is taken immediately below the enlargement caused by the fork. Measurements shall be made by use of an arborist diameter tape or arborist tree calipers. (6) Drip line: An imaginary vertical line extending downward from the outermost tips of the tree branches to ground level. (7) Grubbing: The removal of understory vegetation which does not remove any trees with a d.b.h. of four (4) inches or greater. 91 -- 91 of 124 -- (8) Hazard tree: A tree, or tree part that may be dangerous and is likely to fail and cause damage or injury, and the likelihood of failure exceeds an acceptable level of risk. ISSUE: First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-05-05 (B) to amend Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding the requirements for the renaming of existing streets. BACKGROUND: Currently, the City has no defined process for renaming existing streets that have been dedicated to the city or naming an unnamed street, with the exception of those being created in conjunction with the development of property. However, staff has received a few requests from different residents of the city to rename a city street in which they resided; the most recent one being a resident of McCray Alley, who inquired about renaming the alley to a different name, which they claimed was for public safety reasons. There is a McCray Rd located off Hwy 701 South with a Conway address, in zip code 29527. Changing of a street name that has been dedicated to the City should be limited and rare, as doing so may have a negative impact on emergency response. However, in the very rare instances that may warrant a street name change, it would be beneficial to have a process in which such requests may be facilitated. Staff reached out to Horry County about their process of renaming county roads. Horry County requires a public hearing to be held for any proposed road name changes. In addition, the property (street/road) must be posted, written notification must be provided to affected addressees, and if approved, a plat must be submitted renaming the road and a new street sign must be installed; all of which incur costs. If approved, the fee schedule for the Planning & Development Dept. will also need to be amended to reflect a $250 fee in conjunction with such requests; however, this fee was one of the fees that was included in the proposed fee schedule that was discussed at this year’s budget retreat. The proposed amendment includes a process for the renaming of a City street, which includes a requirement for a public hearing to be held and two ordinance readings by City Council. PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing at their March 6th meeting, and recommended approval of the amendment to Article 10 to adopt a process for renaming streets within the city limits.
