Synonymous with bars and taverns are other establishments, such as pubs, saloons, barrooms, tap rooms, and watering holes – all of which shall be considered a bar or tavern for the purposes of this code of ordinances. This does not include nightclubs or adult entertainment establishments, which are elsewhere defined herein. Berm: A mound of soil, either natural or man-made, intended to buffer land uses or limit access (See Section 9.3.1). Community Support Services [ZA2019-04-01(D)] • Community Support Facilities: An agency which provides a variety of support services to adult individuals, including those with disabilities, whose primary goal is to help individuals increase or maintain their independence and quality of life through interaction and participation in the community, as well as teaching concepts such as self-determination, self-advocacy and socialization and training to enhance skills they already possess or want to learn. Conditional Use: Property uses that would otherwise be undesirable in a particular zoning district, but which may be allowed given certain requirements (conditions) listed in Article 5, and subject to additional restrictions if deemed necessary by the planning staff. Conservation Areas: A tract of land that has been awarded protected status in order to ensure that natural features, cultural heritage or biota are safeguarded. A conservation area may be a nature reserve, a park, a land reclamation project, or other area. Crematory / Crematorium: A facility containing a furnace which is designed and licensed for cremation of human or animal remains. Cropland: Shall be defined as tracts of land of five (5) acres or greater, which is used for growing cultivated plants or agricultural produce, such as grain, vegetables, or fruit. Low Impact Development (L.I.D.): A common term for nonstructural stormwater measures that can be easily incorporated into any development site design to optimize the land’s ability to locally absorb stormwater, thus capturing pollutants on-site and preventing major environmental impacts downstream. Low-Impact-Development practices, such as bioretention swales, rain gardens, constructed wetlands, porous pavers, vegetated buffers, green roofs, etc., mimic the natural hydrologic absorption functions by utilizing absorptive soils and local plant communities that enhance localized treatment and infiltration of excess precipitation. Also, L.I.D. includes various cost benefits for the developer, such as less required stormwater infrastructure, irrigation water savings, nicer aesthetics, and better climate insulation through green roofs. Heavy Industrial: Heavy industry refers to production processes, which should not be located near residential or commercial uses due to the insensitive nature of the industrial activity and/or the scale of the operation. Typical uses include equipment or vehicle manufacturing, sawmills, textile dying, leather tanning, hazardous chemical production, petroleum refining, primary metal processing and production of explosives or propellants. Wholesaling, Storage, and Distribution. Wholesaling, storage and distribution use type refers to establishments or places of business primarily engaged in wholesaling, storage and bulk sale distribution including but not limited to, air handling of material and equipment other than live animals and plants. The following are wholesaling, storage, and distribution use types: • Light: Wholesaling, storage and warehousing services within enclosed structures. Typical uses include wholesale distributors, storage warehouses, or moving and storage firms. • Heavy: Distribution and handling of materials and equipment. ISSUE: Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-01-21 (J) to amend Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to requirements for conservation subdivisions. BACKGROUND: Earlier this year, Council approved a text amendment to Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development, of the UDO to correct several issues that are inconsistent or outdated, or that were inconsistent with current policy; however, two sections within Article 10 were left out of the update – Open Space Requirements and requirements for Conservation Subdivisions, due to the comprehensive nature of these amendments. Open Space amendments were recently adopted. A conservation subdivision design is an option for flexible, cluster-style development that incentivizes eco-conscience design and preserves areas of environmental and/or historical value while maintaining the prorated density of residential units for the overall site and also minimizing the impacts of the development on surrounding communities. In addition to the environmental benefits, conservation subdivisions also have economic benefits, such as reduced maintenance costs, higher property values, and reduced stormwater management costs. The amendments proposed to the Conservation Subdivision ordinance are intended to correct several flaws and inconsistencies that staff has found over the years; particularly when the Collins Jollie Conservation Subdivision was being reviewed. The main issue is the current requirement for conservation subdivisions, even when there are multiple neighborhoods owned by separate developers, to plat all of the open space and conservation areas up front and at the same time, regardless of the status of project. For this reason alone, a development agreement was adopted that allows these areas to be platted with each project/tract within the entire conservation subdivision; however, these areas must be shown on the approved Master Plan. Other changes include a reorganization of the entire ordinance, to group like requirements together, such as open space requirements, permitted uses, general requirements, and the requirements for permanent protection of open space and conservation areas. The amendments will provide clarification and better guidance for the development community when considering options for residential development of property; particularly when a conservation subdivision design is being considered. Included is Section 10.4 of the UDO containing the requirements for Conservation Subdivisions and the proposed amendments. 114 -- 114 of 256 -- PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the proposed amendment(s) at their December 12, 2024 meeting and recommended approval. It is the purpose of this section to provide flexibility in ensuring preservation of open space within a new residential development an option for flexible, cluster style development that will incentivize eco- conscience A conservation subdivision design preserves and preserve open space areas of environmental and historical value, while maintaining the prorated density of residential units for the overall site area and minimizing the impact on surrounding communities. Natural density is achieved by allowing smaller individual owned residential lots in neighborhoods that include or are adjacent to aesthetically and ecologically important areas. The goal of the design process is to identify and set aside conservation areas prior to the delineation of transportation and residential pod layouts and to integrate the preservation of such areas with the layout of the residential pods and their associated infrastructure. Open space areas include wetlands, stream buffer zones, woodlands, farmlands, playing fields, and meadows, depending on the resources of the land. The purpose of conservation subdivisions is below. 1. Preserve significant areas of land for ecological, recreational, and agricultural purposes in perpetuity. 2. Afford greater flexibility of design and placement of buildings and structures. 3. Preserve and protect exceptional terrain, natural beauty, or sites of historic interest. 4. Preserve the Waccamaw River and its streams and tributaries as natural resources. 5. Prevent flooding, erosion, and water pollution, and protect the quality and quantity of drinking water. 6. Preserve wetlands, aquifers, topographical or soil features, marine and wildlife habitat; and other features having conservation values, including views, vistas, and indigenous vegetation. 7. Promote interconnected greenways and corridors throughout the city. 8. Promote contiguous open space with adjacent jurisdictions. B. Applicability. In order to achieve these purposes, Conservation Subdivisions are permitted by right in the R, RR, RA, R-1, and R-2 zoning districts. Applicants utilizing the Conservation Subdivision design regulations shall comply with all other provisions of the Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) and all other applicable laws, except those that are incompatible with the provisions contained herein. ISSUE: Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-01-21 (K), to amend Article 6 – Design Standards, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding the creation of an Airport Overlay (AO) District. BACKGROUND: Per the South Carolina Aeronautics Commission (SCAC), airports are impacted by three-dimensional concerns as well as airspace imaginary surface penetrations that may occur off of the airport property. Certain types of development are more compatible than others with airport operations. Development in areas that are in close proximity to an airport should be more closely scrutinized that other areas in a city or county may be. https://aeronautics.sc.gov/clue-tool-and-development-near-south-carolina-airport Since the City has received annexation applications for property on Hwy 378, Juniper Bay Rd, and Dunn Shortcut Rd, known as the Brookhaven Planned Development, staff noted that several parcels/tracts are located within many of the airport’s zones that could classify the proposed uses of the Brookhaven PD as incompatible uses and/or density due to their proximity to the Conway-Horry County airport. Additionally, SC Code of Laws, Section § 55-13-5. Public Use Airport Maps; review of plans for development, states: “Each governmental body or agency receiving these maps shall ensure notice of any planned development, plat approval, or building permit issued in an airport safety zone or airport land use zone be provided to the division for review. In the event that an activity is enjoined or a condition is abated by the division contrary to a local governmental body’s decision, the governmental body proposing the land use decision shall have the right to seek recovery cost from the party responsible for creating the condition or the enjoinment or abatement of the activity. Neither the division or a local government shall be required to post a bond or other financial security as a condition to enjoining or abatement of a condition surrounding a public use airport. Land use decisions by county and municipal governments and local agencies shall take into account the presence of airport land use zones and airport safety zones and consult with the division, when possible, prior to making land use decisions within airport land use zones and airport safety zones. If the division provides comments, within thirty days, the governmental body must respond substantively in writing to each comment, separately stated before the issuance of the permit or approval. If the division believes the proposed project may have a substantial impact on aviation safety, create an imminent or foreseeable hazard to aviation safety, or result in a nuisance or an incompatible land use, the division may seek relief, including enjoining the activity or abatement of the condition giving rise to the division’s comments. SCAC defines an Airport Overlay District (AOD) as “a district described on the zoning map within which, through superimposition of a special designation, further regulations and requirements apply in addition to those of the underlying districts to which such designation is added. The Airport Overlay District is established in recognition of airport related hazards which may endanger lives and property; obstructions which effectively reduce airspace required for aircraft takeoff, landing, and maneuvering which reduce the utility of an airport and the public investment therein.” 127 -- 127 of 256 -- SCAC requires that developers submit FAA Form 7460-1 to the Obstacle Evaluation / Airport Airspace Analysis (OE/AAA) site for review. Once the developer / applicant has received the FAA analysis, the findings should be submitted to the Local Permitting Authority Official (LPO), which would be the City’s Planning & Development Dept. and/or the Construction Services Dept., in conjunction with their plan / permit submittal. The LPO should then submit a CLUE Tool case to the South Carolina Aeronautics Commission (SCAC) staff for further evaluation. Horry County has adopted an Airport Environs Overlay Zone several years ago, as part of their zoning ordinance (Art. VIII, Sec. 823), the purpose of which is to ensure current operations and future expansions of the county’s publicly-owned and operated aviation facilities are not hindered by encroachment of structures or objects into required aircraft approach paths or airspace, to ensure safety and efficiency of air navigation, to prevent conflict with land development that may result in loss of life and property, to encourage development that is compatible with airports, and to preserve and protect the public investment in Horry County’s aviation facilities. While the county does provide restrictions on building height and use of property within their overlay, it’s important to note that there are four (4) airports within Horry County; one being an international airport. Below are airport zones identified via SCAC’s “CLUE” Tool, and a snippet of the map via SCAC: Zone A – Runway Protection Zone (RPZ) Zone B1 – Inner Approach Zone Zone B2 – Outer Approach Zone Zone C – Transitional Zone *Zone D – Horizontal Zone *Zone E – Conical Zone *Zones D and E also referred to as “Airport Vicinity Zones” by SCAC. The purpose of the overlay would not necessarily be to prevent development from occurring with the vicinity of the airport, but to assist in identifying properties within the overlay to ensure that proper notification is provided to the Dept. of Airports and the FAA of any applicable requests for annexation, rezoning, development, or permits that have been submitted to the City – in accordance with SC Code of Laws § 55-13-5. This overlay would make current and future staff aware of where the proposed development falls in relation to the airport and whether or not such notification is required. ISSUE: Reaffirmation of the City’s Risk Management Policy and update on City’s safety program. BACKGROUND: The SC Municipal Insurance Trust and the SC Municipal Insurance Risk Fund’s minimum guidelines include a requirement that members (municipalities) adopt a safety/ risk management commitment towards the prevention and control of accidental loss. This statement of commitment must be adopted annually by a resolution of the governing body of the member entity. The proposed resolution is attached. Staff continues a number of initiatives with which to improve safety among city employees. Our city-wide goal is to reduce our injury and property loss experiences. The following outlines these continuing efforts: • Each employee’s safety practices and performance are evaluated and the scoring is included on his/her job evaluation. • Previous years’ loss data on injuries and property damages are monitored and trends are identified. • Monthly progress reports toward meeting safety goals are provided to department heads and City Council. Significant, unusual or reoccurring incidents are discussed at City’s management team staff meeting. • Injury and property loss incidents are reviewed by the City’s Incident Review Committee. Reviews are used to evaluate how improvements maybe implemented and similar incidents avoided in the future. This information is sent back to the department heads and discussed in the safety committee meetings. • Appropriate city employees take advantage of training opportunities provided by the Municipal Association. City employees are registered to be able to take online training thorough the Municipal Association. All operations of city departments have been evaluated and applicable safety classes are identified and conducted on an on-going basis. RECOMMENDATION: Adopt the attached resolution. 156 -- 156 of 256 -- STATE OF SOUTH CAROLINA } COUNTY OF HORRY } R E S O L U T I O N CITY OF CONWAY } RISK MANAGEMENT WHEREAS, the Mayor and City Council recognize that the prevention of accidental losses affecting employees, property, and the public will enhance the operating efficiency of city governing; and WHEREAS, a proactive loss control posture requires that sound loss prevention measures are of primary consideration and take precedence over expediency in all operations; and WHEREAS, the City endeavors to provide a work environment free of recognized hazards through the establishment and implementation of loss control policies and procedures and their subsequent amendments and additions, designed to provide protection to city employees, public and private property, and members of the public; WHEREAS, the City of Conway supports compliance with all federal and state safety regulations, provides and requires the use of personal protective equipment by all employees, and insures that all employees are advised of and understand their loss control responsibilities in the performance of their work: Therefore be it RESOLVED, that Conway City Council, as evidence of its commitment to provide a safe workplace for city employees and its efforts to prevent and control accidental loss, does hereby reaffirm its Risk Management Policy for the City of Conway. Hucks stated that staff had been in discussions with the applicant regarding annexation of these properties since 2022. The request included 2 parcels, both of which are currently being used for one business. The applicant relocated their manufactured home sales business from another site in the county’s jurisdiction to these properties. In April 2023, staff spoke with the applicant about annexation of the larger tract fronting East Cox Ferry Road, and the applicant inquired about storage of the manufactured homes. Staff informed the applicant that it was not a permitted use, but manufactured home sales would be permitted in either the Light or Heavy Industrial zoning district, provided that the site complied with the requirements for commercial development and that a sales office would also be required on the same property where the manufactured homes were displayed. Other uses discussed with the applicant included a possible amazon fulfillment center and a mini-storage facility. Around that same time, the applicant received zoning approval to obtain a business license for the property fronting Highway 501, which is zoned Horry County Highway Commercial. The use of the zoning approval issued by the county at that time was for office use only, and the condition of approval was that no outdoor display was allowed; the smaller piece of property and not the property where the storage of the manufactured homes is occurring. Hucks said that city staff emailed the County’s Planning Director at the time to inform the county of the restrictive covenants in place for the property being rezoned to RE4 and that the applicant had been aware of the requirement to annex before any development can occur on the property. The rezoning was granted, and the property is now zoned RE4, High Bulk Retail. Sometime thereafter, a large metal building that was not properly permitted was erected on the site, which is what prompted discussions between the city and the county as to how these violations could be addressed including how to remedy the situation. The biggest issue for the applicant, in addition to the current use of the property, is that for water to be provided to the site so that they could become compliant with the county, they would need water service from the city, which triggers the requirement to annex. For the city, the issue becomes that if annexed, the city would inherit a use and structures on property that were never permitted. Hucks stated that staff began working with the applicant’s attorney on how best to rectify the issues on the property. The applicant cannot come into compliance with city requirements unless and until the property is within the city’s jurisdiction. Staff, along with the City Administrator, have agreed that should the property be annexed, that staff would delay any additional enforcement to give the applicant an opportunity to apply for any needed variances from the Board of Zoning Appeals. ISSUE: Second Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-01-21 (A), granting a non-exclusive franchise agreement to Project Smashburger Mobile Food Truck at the parking lot adjacent to Fourth Avenue and Kingston Street (near Palmetto Taps). BACKGROUND: Section 5.1.16 – Mobile Vending, of the UDO, sets forth regulations for mobile vending in Conway. This ordinance allows franchise mobile vending on public property in the CBD, CC, WRD zoning districts and City parks, but only with a franchise agreement approved through City Council. A franchise is an extension of the privilege to use the streets, parking and other City owned amenities for which the franchisee does not have a legal right without permission from the governing body. The franchise agreement allows the franchisee to use City property in the requested manner which exceeds or differs from the customary uses. The franchise agreement is a contract between the City and the franchisee which governs the use of the City property. The agreement does not give exclusive use to the franchisee. The hours of operations and approved locations are determined by City Council in the franchise agreement. A certificate of insurance, as well as a release and indemnification agreement, are also required for mobile vending on public property (which the applicant has obtained). Project Smashburger has a valid City of Conway Business License, and two approved Private Property Mobile Food Vending Permits. One for Rob’s Auto Body, located at 909 Fourth Avenue and the other is for NAPA Auto Parts, located at 901 Church Street. Project Smashburger has requested a Franchise Agreement to operate the Mobile Food Truck at the following location: • The parking lot adjacent to Fourth Avenue and Kingston Street, near Palmetto Taps (PIN# 367-01-01-0032) The requested hours of operation are 5:00pm to 9:00pm on Tuesday and Thursday and Noon to 9:00pm on Friday and Saturday. For a franchise agreement to be valid, it must receive two readings at City Council as an Ordinance. To satisfy the requirements of the City Code concerning franchise agreements, the applicant published a public notice in three (3) issues of a newspaper having general circulation in the city stating the nature of the franchise and the date on which the application is to be presented to Council. The public hearing has also been advertised as required. 180 -- 180 of 256 -- JANUARY 6, 2025 CITY COUNCIL MEETING: City Council had several concerns about parking in this area of downtown. ISSUE: Second/ Final Reading of Ordinance #2025-01-21 (D) to amend Title 1, Chapter 5, Article G, of the City of Conway Code of Ordinances, an incentive program which provides economic incentives for the redevelopment of existing vacant commercial buildings 25,000 sq. ft. or greater in the City of Conway. BACKGROUND: City staff has identified the need to expand our current ordinance to provide a larger economic incentive for large locations such as those that are described within this ordinance. This ordinance was created to provide an incentive to developers to modify, reestablish, update, or completely renovate large abandoned existing facilities rather than building a new facility. This ordinance has not been used for any property yet but with the new sale of the Gator Investments property on Church Street staff is hoping to provide a larger incentive to the potential developer to aid in the redevelopment for this location as it is and has been needed for quite some time. Staff feels that the added incentive could provide a solid plan for the location that would greatly benefit the city in its entirety. Extending the reimbursement of the property taxes collected by the City of Conway for up to 10 years would provide a greater economic impact on the project cost as well as the desire to implement the best possible development design. Staff would also like to include the option of transferability for this incentive to allow developers to provide the ground work to jump start the project and have the ability to transfer a turn key renovation to a tenant. RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends approval of the proposed changes. 191 -- 191 of 256 -- ORDINANCE #2025-01-21 (D) AMENDING ARTICLE G, CHAPTER 5 – REDEVELOPMENT OF EXISTING VACANT COMMERCIAL BUILDINGS 25,000 SQUARE FEET OR GREATER INCENTIVE OF THE CONWAY MUNICIPAL CODE IN THE CITY OF CONWAY WHEREAS, The City of Conway, South Carolina, adopted a Redevelopment of Existing Vacant Commercial Buildings 25,000 square feet or greater incentive in 2009 to lessen the burden of opening or expanding a new business endeavor to help stimulate development or redevelopment in larger vacant commercial buildings; and WHEREAS, Since the creation of the ordinance, City staff has been made aware of the continued increase in financial burden a large-scale renovation on a property can have. Staff has proposed to offset such a burden by increasing the incentive reimbursement for the property taxes collected by the City from 5 years to 10 years; and allow for transferability within the ordinance as determined by City Council. WHEREAS, City Council has determined it is in the best interest of the City and its citizens to amend the redevelopment of existing vacant commercial buildings 25,000 square feet or greater incentive program: Therefore, be it ORDAINED, by Conway City Council, in council duly assembled, that the City of Conway Municipal Code shall be amended after adoption as attached hereto. EFFECTIVE DATE: This ordinance shall become effective upon final reading approval. 192 -- 192 of 256 -- RATIFIED BY CITY COUNCIL, duly assembled, this day of _______________________, 2025. This incentive program applies to any person, firm or corporation redeveloping and fully occupying an existing vacant commercial building or storefront 25,000 square feet and greater in the city limits of Conway. A vacant building shall be defined as any building or storefront which has been vacant for a period exceeding six (6) continuous months. It is the responsibility of the person, firm or corporation applying for the incentive to show that the vacancy requirement has been met. Sec. 1-5-102 Incentives. City council, at its discretion, and on a case-by-case basis, may enter into an agreement to reimburse any person, firm, or corporation any or all or any portion of the following fees: 1. The applicable water and sewer capital recovery fees up to one-half (½) of the total required fee paid. 2. The required building permit fee paid. 3. The business license fees collected by the City of Conway for as many as five (5) years. 4. The hospitality fees collected by the City of Conway for as many as five (5) years. 5. The property taxes collected by the City of Conway for as many as five (5) years. ten 10 Years Sec. 1-5-103 Reimbursement. City council shall set a reimbursement cap for any and all reimbursements on a case-by-case basis and the reimbursement clock shall begin on the date of the issuance of a business license. Reimbursement of building permit fees and capital recovery fees may be requested separately from the other applicable incentives using the Reimbursement Request Form. All other reimbursements for any calendar year shall be applied for by submitting the Reimbursement Request Form between May 1 and May 31 of the following year. Failure to provide a Reimbursement Request Form by the May 31 deadline shall result in forfeiture of reimbursements for that year as outlined in the agreement. Requests for reimbursement must contain proof of fees and or taxes paid in the previous calendar year. The city shall pay all reimbursement requests within 60 days of receiving the Reimbursement Request Form. A signed agreement must be in place prior to the issuance of a certificate of occupancy (CO). No agreements may be applied retroactively. Sec. 1-5-105 Transferability. No reimbursement agreements entered into under this article are transferable to any other person, firm or corporation, without the expressed permission approval of Conway City Council. ISSUE: First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-02-03 (B), to annex approximately 7.62+/- total acres of property located at 1705 Hwy 501 and on E. Cox Ferry Rd (PINs 383-01-02-0030 & 383-01-03-0002), and rezone from the Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) and High Bulk Retail (RE4) districts to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) and Light Industrial (LI) districts. BACKGROUND: The applicant submitted an annexation and rezoning application for the subject properties November 2024. The property is located in the city’s water utility service area and is contiguous to property in the city limits. This annexation is part of a broader enforcement issue related to the subject property that has been ongoing for a few years now. The applicant relocated his business, H&H Builders, from another property on Hwy 501 (in county’s jurisdiction) to this location, which has been owned by the applicant for some time. Both properties are still in the county’s jurisdiction; however, there were and continue to be issues related to business licensing, unpermitted structures, and uses on the subject properties, in that the county’s zoning compliance approval for the sales office is solely for a sales office only and not for any outdoor display, and a large metal building (more than 3,000 sq. ft.) in size, was erected on one of the parcels without a building permit (aerial photograph from April 2024 included in packet). Complicating matters, the properties were one parcel before being split in 2007 (plat book 221, pg. 175). The railroad right-of-way separates the two parcels. Now that they are separated, they cannot be recombined, due to the right-of-way that exists. However, both parcels include the use of manufactured homes sales, and in order for the manufactured home sales business to be compliant, the sales office, parking, etc., must be located on the same property as the display models are located; otherwise, the use is considered outdoor storage, which is prohibited except in conjunction with a permitted use. The applicant was attempting to become compliant with Horry County’s requirements; however, in order for them to do so, they would need to provide water to the unpermitted metal building on the same parcel as the displays (manufactured home units) are located on. Being that it would be an extension of (water) service, or a new service if none currently exists, the requirement to annex becomes applicable. The issue for staff is that if the property is annexed under the current condition, then the city is inheriting a use on a property that was never legally permitted on the property as well as structures that were never issued a building permit. Yet, the only way for the property to comply would include the requirement for city water to be extended to the property, which requires the applicant to request annexation. Staff has been working with the applicant’s attorney on the issues and has agreed that if Council chose to annex the properties, that they would be given the opportunity to request variances for some of the 210 -- 210 of 256 -- outstanding issues without the threat of further enforcement, pending the outcome of the variance requests, as they cannot request any variances (from the City’s requirements) until and unless the property has been annexed. If Council chooses not to annex, the applicant would need to comply with the requirements for the county. While manufactured home sales is the current use of one of the properties, the applicant has stated that they would be phasing that use out in the near future and would pursue approval to develop mini-storage and/or other commercial / industrial uses. The requested zoning upon annexation is Highway Commercial (HC) (0.47-acre parcel with frontage on Hwy 501) and Light Industrial (LI) (7.15-acre tract with frontage on E. Cox Ferry Rd). Per Section 3.2.13 – Light Industrial (LI), the intent of the LI district is to provide areas for light industrial uses, such as manufacturing, processing, repairing of goods, wholesaling, storage, packaging, distribution and retailing while ensuring adjacent and nearby properties are not adversely impacted. Surrounding uses/Zoning Districts: Adjacent properties in the city limits are zoned Light Industrial (LI) and Heavy Industrial (HI), as these properties are located within the Commerce Plaza industrial park. Property fronting Hwy 501 in the county’s jurisdiction is zoned Highway Commercial (HC). CITY OF CONWAY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN: The future land use map of the Comprehensive Plan also identifies the larger tract fronting E. Cox Ferry Rd as being Industrial, and the smaller parcel with frontage on Hwy 501 as Highway Commercial (HC). The future land use map does not distinguish between light and heavy industrial, only “industrial”, but because Light Industrial (LI) is the requested zone for the larger parcel upon annexation, that district is defined below: Per Section 3.2.13 of the UDO, the intent of the Light Industrial (LI) district is to provide areas for light industrial uses, such as manufacturing, processing, repairing of goods, storage, packaging, distribution and retailing while ensuring adjacent and nearby properties are not adversely affected. Per Section 3.2.10 of the UDO, the intent of the HC district is to provide compatible locations to serve the automobile oriented commercial activities in harmony with major highway developments, reduce traffic congestions and to enhance the aesthetic atmosphere of the City. PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the request at their January 9th meeting and recommended approval of the request to annex and rezone the properties to Highway Commercial (HC) and Light Industrial (LI). ISSUE: First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-02-03 (C) to amend Article 11 – Signage, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding general provisions, exempt and prohibited signs, sign standards by zoning district and sign type, and applications and permits for signs. BACKGROUND: Since early 2023, city staff has been going through the UDO to identify inconsistencies, typos, and other items that may be lacking within each Article of the UDO. The sign ordinance, although amended a few times through the years, has not had a comprehensive review of all sign requirements, and as part of the city’s UDO cleanup effort, staff is seeking to amend Article 11 to address several issues that have been identified through the years and/or that have caused confusion amongst staff and the sign community, as well as different interpretations. Some of the amendments include, but are not limited to: • Revisions to requirements for signage in residential zoning districts; • Addition of murals to signage that is considered to be exempt from permitting procedures, provided that it does not contain text or images that identify the business or business product(s); • Clarification of number of wall signs permitted on corner buildings or lots; • Removal of balloons as being ‘prohibited’ signage; • Revisions to requirements for EMC/LED signs – regarding distance to residential structures or properties; • Revisions to requirements for drive-thru signs (i.e. menu panel options); and • Housekeeping revisions to sign permit requirements PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission held the required public hearing and recommended approval of the proposed amendments to Article 11 at their January 9, 2024 meeting. STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends approval of Ordinance #ZA2025-02-03 (C), amending Article 11 of the UDO. 227 -- 227 of 256 -- ORDINANCE #ZA2025-02-03 (C) AMENDING ARTICLE 11 – SIGNAGE, OF THE CITY OF CONWAY UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE (UDO), REGARDING REVISIONS TO VARIOUS ITEMS CONTAINED WITHIN THIS ARTICLE. Where there is no defined sign background, the sign area is calculated by determining the number of square feet of the smallest rectangle within with a sign face can be enclosed. (see Example 1 below) In determining the area of an individual sign that has more than one face (e.g. a monument or projecting sign), the single sign face with the greatest area shall be used. ISSUE: First Reading of Ordinance #2025-02-03 (D) to amend Title 8 Motor Vehicles and Traffic, Chapter 5 Off-Highway Vehicles, of the City of Conway Code of Ordinances. BACKGROUND: The police department received complaints of ATVs being ridden on city on property. The ATVs caused rutting, started creating a trail network, and were damaging and destroying native foliage. The city has acquired numerous unimproved properties through purchase or award. There are currently no restrictions or rules in place, and the city could have some liability for allowing it to continue. A workshop was held 12/2/24, and the Council voted to move forward developing an ordinance governing ATVs, UTVs, and other vehicles on city owned property. RECOMMENDATION Review and revise as needed the proposed ordinance to add to the City of Conway Municipal Code. 252 -- 252 of 256 -- ORDINANCE #2025-02-03 (D) AN ORDINANCE ESTABLISHING RESTRICTIONS AND PENALTIES RELATED TO OFF-ROAD VEHICLE USE ON PRIVATE & PUBLIC PROPERTY WHEREAS, The Conway City Council, as the governing body of Conway, South Carolina, finds that there has been a proliferation of the use of all off-highway vehicles within public rights-of-way, utility rights-of-way, and on private and public property without the consent of the owners of such property. WHEREAS, The Conway City Council finds that the unregulated use of all off-highway vehicles disturbs the public peace and threatens the health, safety and welfare of citizens of Conway, SC; damages the integrity of public rights-of-way, utility rights-of-way and damages private and public property; causes excessive noise, property damage, and dust; constitutes a risk to the safety of operators of all off- highway vehicles and the general public; and should be regulated in order to provide for the health, safety, and welfare of Conway, SC and its citizen NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT ORDAINED, by the Conway City Council, that the City of Conway Code of Ordinances, Title 8 Motor Vehicles and Traffic, Chapter 5 Off-Highway Vehicles is hereby added to Conway Municipal Code. RATIFIED BY CITY COUNCIL, duly assembled, this day of ____________, 2025. Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor William M. Goldfinch IV, Mayor Pro Tem Amanda Butler, Council Member Julie Ann Hardwick, Council Member Beth Helms, Council Member Justin D. Jordan, Council Member Larry A. White, Council Member ATTEST: Alicia Shelley, City Clerk First Reading: _______________ Final Reading: _______________ 253 -- 253 of 256 -- Title 8 – Motor Vehicles and Traffic Chapter 5 – Off-Highway Vehicles Sec. 8-5-1 Definitions Unless the context clearly indicates otherwise, the following terms shall have the meanings ascribed herein. (1) ALL TERRAIN VEHICLE and ATV. Any motorized off-highway vehicle 50 inches or less in width, having a dry weight of 900 pounds or less, designed to travel on three or more low-pressure tires, having a seat or seats designed to be straddled or used by the operator or the operator and an additional passenger, and having an engine displacement of less than 800 cubic centimeters. (2) OFF-HIGHWAY MOTORCYCLE. Any motorized, off-highway vehicle traveling on two wheels, having a seat or saddle designed to be straddled by the operator and having handlebars for steering control. Motorcycles may be legal for highway use and still considered to be off-highway motorcycles if used for off-highway operation on trails or natural terrain. (3) OFF-HIGHWAY VEHICLE. All-terrain vehicles, off-highway motorcycles and other vehicles as defined herein. (4) OPERATE. To ride in or on and have control of an off-highway vehicle. (5) OPERATOR. The person who operates or is in actual physical control of an off- highway vehicle. (6) OTHER VEHICLES and Utility Terrain Vehicle (UTV). Any motorized recreational vehicles capable of cross-country travel on natural terrain, such as four-wheel-drive trucks and ATVs and UTVs with seating for the operator and/or additional passengers, that have an engine displacement of more than 800 cubic centimeters or total dry weight of more than 900 pounds. Vehicles not considered OTHER VEHICLES include snowmobiles, all-terrain vehicles, and motorcycles. Watercraft or aircraft or farm, logging, military, emergency, law enforcement, utility, trail grooming and construction vehicles are not considered to be OTHER VEHICLES when used for their intended purpose. (7) OWNER. A person other than a lienholder having a property interest in or title to an off-highway vehicle who is entitled to the use and possession thereof. (8) PERSON. Any individual, partnership, corporation or anybody of persons whether incorporated or not. (9) PUBLIC RIGHTS-OF-WAY. The rights-of-way of the State of South Carolina, and the municipality of Conway, SC. Sec 8-5-2 Prohibitions 254 -- 254 of 256 -- Except as otherwise provided in this code, it is unlawful to operate an off-highway vehicle upon public rights-of-way, utility rights-of-way or easements, public highways, streets, sidewalks, trails, parks and roads or upon private or public property without the written consent of the owner thereof; provided, however, that the prohibitions contained in this section shall not apply to any agent or employee of any public authority on public property or within public rights-of-way; the agent, employee or contractor for any public or private utility on property of the public or private utility or within its rights-of-way or easements; any law enforcement agency or public safety agency or any fire department, hospital or ambulance service while providing or exercising official duties and powers; or to the operation of off-highway vehicles on private property owned by the operator or for which the operator has written permission from the owner. Sec 8-5-3 Owner’s and operator’s responsibilities It is unlawful for the owner or operator of an off-highway vehicle to permit its operation on private or public property without permission of the owner or occupant; within public rights-of-way except as provided by law; or within rights-of-way of public or private utilities without the written consent of such utilities. Sec 8-5-4 Liability insurance required No off-highway vehicle as defined in this Code will be required to be insured under a liability insurance policy unless such vehicle is required to be insured under a liability insurance policy in compliance with existing or subsequently enacted statutory insurance requirements for such vehicles under South Carolina law. All vehicles, including off- highway vehicles for which state statutes require liability insurance coverage shall be insured in accordance with liability insurance requirements for motor vehicles under South Carolina Statues and laws. Any owners and operators must also comply with South Carolina Code of Laws Title 50, Chapter 26, also known as “Chandler’s Law”. Sec 8-5-5 Enforceability The provisions of this section shall be enforced by Conway Police Department, state troopers, commissioned officers of the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources and any other duly authorized law enforcement officer. Sec 8-5-6 Penalties 255 -- 255 of 256 -- Violation of any of the terms and provisions of this article herein shall be subject to the penalties provided in section 1-3-48 of this code, and a separate offense shall be deemed committed on each day or days the violation occurs or continues to occur. 256 -- 256 of 256 --

text: January 21, 2025 Page 1 of 6 CITY OF CONWAY CITY COUNCIL MEETING CONWAY CITY HALL 229 MAIN STREET, CONWAY TUESDAY, JANUARY 21, 2025 - 4:00 P.M. PRESENT: Mayor Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor Pro Tem William Goldfinch, Amanda Butler, Julie Hardwick, Beth Helms, Justin Jordan, Larry White. STAFF: Adam Emrick, City Administrator; Mary Catherine Hyman, Deputy City Administrator; John Rogers, Deputy City Administrator; June Wood, Public Information Officer; Jeff Leveille, Technology Services Director; Jessica Hucks, Planning and Development Director; Dale Long, Police Chief; Le Hendrick, Fire Chief; and Alicia Shelley, City Clerk. OTHERS: There were approximately 7 others in attendance. CALL TO ORDER: Mayor Blain called the meeting to order. Brandon Wilson of Ekklesia Christian Church gave the invocation and led the Pledge of Allegiance. The requirements for posting notice of this meeting under South Carolina’s Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) were met. CONSENT AGENDA: A. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-01-21 (B), granting a non-exclusive franchise agreement to Randall’s Culinary Creations mobile food truck to operate at the property located at 7 Elm Street. B. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-01-21 (C), to annex approximately 0.19 acres of property located at 625 Lesia Lane (PIN 382-12-01-0002), and rezone from the Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed, (SF6) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium -Density Residential (R-1) district. C. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-01-21 (E), to annex approximately 16.19+/- acres of property located at 370 Allied Drive (PIN 383-00-00-0353), and rezone from the Horry County Planned Unit Development (PUD) district to the City of Conway Light Industrial (LI) district. D. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-01-21 (F), to annex approximately 21.55+/- acres of property located at 2951 Hwy 501 and on Gardner Lacy Rd (PINs 399-00-00- 0404, 399-01-04-0002 and 400-04-02-0003), and rezone from the Horry County Limited Industrial (LI) district to the City of Conway Light Industrial (LI) district. E. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-01-21 (G), to annex approximately 11.17+/- acres of property located on East Cox Ferry Rd, near the intersection of Bellamy Rd (PIN 383-00-00-0346), and rezone from the Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) district to the City of Conway Medium-Density Residential (R-2) district. -- 1 of 6 -- January 21, 2025 Page 2 of 6 F. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-01-21 (H), to rezone approximately 0.70+/- (total) acres of property located at 1318 and 1320 Fourth Ave (PINs 368-04-01-0021 and -0022) from the Core Commercial (CC) and Medium-Density Residential (R-2) districts to the Core Commercial (CC) district. G. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-01-21 (I), to amend Article 2 – Definitions and Article 4 – Use Tables, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance, regarding revisions to various items within these Articles. H. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-01-21 (J), to amend Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance, regarding the requirements for Conservation Subdivisions. I. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-01-21 (K), to amend Article 6 – Design Standards, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance, regarding the creation of an Airport Overlay (AO) district. J. Approval of a Special Event – Stars and Strides – November 8, 2025 K. Approval of a Resolution to set forth Rules of Conduct for Public Input at City Council Meetings L. Approval of the 2025 Risk Management Resolution M. Approval of January 6, 2025 Council Meeting Minutes APPROVAL OF CONSENT AGENDA: Motion: Butler made a motion, seconded by Helms to approve the January 21, 2025 consent agenda. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. APPROVAL OF AGENDA: Motion: Hardwick made a motion, seconded by Jordan to approve the January 21, 2025 agenda. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. PUBLIC INPUT: - Michael Flowers asked Council to change the ordinance to allow Capuchin monkeys. There was no further public input. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Helms, to close public input. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. SPECIAL PRESENTATION: A. Presentation of Employee of the Month for January 2025 – Public Service – No presentation. B. Presentation of the 2024 City of Conway Audit Report - Nathan Skipper, Smith Sapp CPAs – Moved to the February 3 meeting. -- 2 of 6 -- January 21, 2025 Page 3 of 6 C. Discussion of a request to rezone approximately 0.74+/- acres of property located on Sixteenth Avenue, between Elizabeth St and Elm St (PIN 338-11-01-0049) from the Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district to the Neighborhood Commercial (NC) district. Hucks said that this rezoning application was received in December. The current zoning of the property is Low/Medium Density Residential, R-1, as is much of the surrounding property. However, the parcel abuts property zoned Highway Commercial and R-1. The applicant has not provided the proposed use of the property, but is requesting to rezone to Neighborhood Commercial, which is different than the zoning of surrounding property. However, the city’s future land use map identifies the property as Neighborhood Commercial, along with some of the adjacent parcels. Hucks said that Planning Commission is scheduled to hold the required public hearing and consider the request at their February 6 meeting. SECOND/FINAL READING: A. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-01-21 (A), granting a non-exclusive franchise agreement to Project Smashburger mobile food truck to operate at the parking lot adjacent to Fourth Ave and Kingston Street (near Palmetto Taps). Hucks stated that this request for a franchise agreement for Project Smashburger received first reading at the January 6 meeting; however, the request was amended to approve for this location on a trial basis for a period of 6 months. The location of the mobile vending unit has also been revised, now proposed to be located within 3 parking spaces directly adjacent to Kingston Street, as shown on the site plan provided. If approved, the trial period would end July 21st of this year; at which time the applicant would be required to come back to council for consideration of the full 5-year term. Council voiced concerns with the 3 parking spaces. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion to deny second reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-01-21 (A). There was much discussion regarding other options that might be available, including another location nearby, and the possibility of using the kitchen area at Palmetto Taps. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by White to amend the motion to table the request to give the applicant time to explore other options that were discussed and bring back to Council. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. Final Reading of Ordinance #2025-01-21 (D) to amend Title 1, Chapter 5, Article G of the Code of Ordinances, an incentive program which provides economic incentives for the redevelopment of existing vacant commercial buildings 25,000 sq. ft. or greater in the City of Conway. Hucks stated that this amendment to this incentive received first reading at the January 6 meeting. Since then, an additional amendment has been included for consideration under the Transferability section of the ordinance that, with approval of City Council, would allow the benefits of the incentive to be transferable, however, if Council were to approve such, the number of years for the incentives would remain unchanged. In other words, if 3 or 4 years into one property owner receiving benefits of the incentive the property were to be sold, Council could -- 3 of 6 -- January 21, 2025 Page 4 of 6 approve the transferability, but only the remaining yeas of the incentive for the property would benefit the new owner. Hucks said that staff would recommend eliminating the word permission or approval from the sentence of: No reimbursement agreements entered into under this article are transferable to any other person, firm or corporation without the expressed permission/approval of Conway City Council. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Hardwick to approve final reading of Ordinance #2025-01-21 (D). Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. FIRST READING: A. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-02-03 (A) to annex approximately 1.06 acres of property located at 4100 Hagwood Circle (PIN 324-04-02-0006), and request to rezone from the Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). Hucks stated that this request was received as a result of the requirements to reconnect to city utilities. The property was transferred into the name of the current owner on December 17, of last year, and there is an existing restrictive covenant on file for the property that was recorded in 1995. The property is located in the Maple Hill subdivision and is the only property on Hagwood Circle that has not been annexed. There is an existing single-family home on the property. Hucks said that staff recommends approval of the request. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Hardwick to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-02-03 (A). Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. B. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-02-03 (B) to annex approximately 7.62+/- (total) acres of property located at 1705 Hwy 501 and on E. Cox Ferry Rd (PINs 383-01-02-0030 & 383-01-03-0002), and rezone from the Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) and High Bulk Retail (RE4) districts to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) and Light Industrial (LI) districts. Hucks stated that this request was discussed as a special presentation item at the January 6 council meeting. The request includes two parcels, one fronting Highway 501 and the other fronting East Cox Ferry Road. The applicant is requesting to rezone the smaller parcel fronting Highway 501 to Highway Commercial and the larger tract fronting East Cox Ferry Road to Light Industrial. The properties are within the city’s utility service area and the requested zoning districts are consistent with the city’s future land use map. The annexation and rezoning of the property is the first of many steps in the applicant coming into compliance with city requirements. Hucks said that Planning Commission held the required public hearing at the January 9 meeting, and recommended approval of the request. Hucks said that staff also recommended approval. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Blain to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-02-03 (B). Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. C. First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-02-03 (C) to amend Article 11- Signage, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding general provisions, exempt and prohibited signs, sign standards by zoning district and sign type, and applications and permits for signs. Hucks said that this amendment was -- 4 of 6 -- January 21, 2025 Page 5 of 6 originally presented to council at the October 21, 2024 meeting. The amendments within Article 11 are part of the UDO cleanup initiative that staff began in 2023. While there have been amendments to Article 11 over recent years, particularly with regard to EMC/LED signage, it had not had a comprehensive review and remains as one of the most misinterpreted articles of the entire UDO, and a lot of variance requests from the signage requirements are considered by the Board of Zoning Appeals each year. Sign standards also continue to be the most violated zoning ordinance that Planning and Development staff contend with. Hucks said that Planning Commission held the required public hearing on the proposed amendments and recommended approval of the amendments at their January 9 meeting. Hucks said that staff also recommended approval. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Butler to approve first reading of Ordinance #ZA2025-02-03 (C). Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. D. First Reading of Ordinance #2025-02-03 (D) to amend Title 8 Motor Vehicles and Traffic, Chapter 5 Off-Highway Vehicles, of the City of Conway Code of Ordinances. Long stated that the city does not have the most area for adventure sports, things like riding ATV’s, dirt bikes, and things of that nature. Long said that the city has acquired a lot of property during the FEMA buyout that has been adjusted into that type of use by people that live in that area. Long thinks that the city needs to get a handle on the properties that the city owns that are unregulated. Long said that this issue was presented at workshop and that this ordinance would govern ATV’s, UTV’s and other vehicles on city owned property. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Helms to approve first reading of Ordinance #2025-02-03 (D). Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. There will be time to brief everyone on the upcoming events at the next council meeting but encouraged all to make their date night reservations now. • Emrick said that all workshop items have been moved to the next meeting. There are two Executive Sessions that were not moved, and council should move to the conference room at the conclusion of this meeting for that portion. Discussion of proposed amendments to Article 2 – Definitions and Article 4 – Use Tables, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding various revisions within these articles of the UDO. Hucks said that this proposed amendment includes Article 2-Definitions and Article 4-Use Tables in the UDO. They are part of an overall cleanup of the UDO that has been ongoing since 2023, which was also discussed at Council’s budget retreat that same year. Regarding Article 2, staff has noted several terms that are used throughout the UDO, yet have not been defined, as well as other terms that needed to be revised to either coincide with changes made in other articles within the UDO or to meet new standard definitions. For example, the term “opaque” is used throughout the UDO with regard to screening standards, yet it is not defined. Other terms, such as “multifamily”, were amended to coincide with the residential design standards for what would be considered a multifamily dwelling rather than define it based on relationships to other persons within the same dwelling. Hucks said that with regard to Article 4, the changes were minor in nature and included the deletion of duplicate uses or uses that are considered obsolete, and combining uses, such as Beauty Salons and Barber Shops, which would be allowed within the same zoning districts even though one may provide more services than the other; they are similar enough in nature to be considered like-uses. Hucks stated that staff is currently working on finalizing the amendments to Article 2 and Article 4, which will be considered by Planning Commission at their December 12 meeting. Following a public hearing on the proposed amendments, they will be forwarded to Council for first reading along with Planning Commission’s recommendations. 53 -- 53 of 260 -- December 2, 2024 Page 3 of 13 F. Discussion of a proposed amendment to Article 6 – Design Standards, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding the creation of an Airport Overlay (AO) District. Hucks said that several properties along Highway 378 and Dunn Shortcut Road have been annexed over the past couple of years. There have been 2 annexations that are within close proximity to the Conway-Horry County Airport; one of which contains several hundred acres proposed to contain both commercial and residential development – known as the Brookhaven Planned Development. South Carolina Code of Laws requires the local governmental body or agency receiving requests for a planned development, plat approval or a building permit that is within an airport safety zone to provide the information to the division of airports for review. This was done last year regarding the Brookhaven Planned Development in accordance with South Carolina code. There were no specific comments provided back to staff with regard to the annexation request; however, the county attorney at the time recommended that the city defer to the county’s Airport Environs overlay in the county zoning ordinance and advised that a large national flight school associated with the Myrtle Beach Airport’s east coast campus has begun operations and that there would likely be an increase in operations at the Conway airport. In general, development resulting in any density of significance near the ends of runways is generally discouraged. Further, the South Carolina Aeronautics Commission (SCAC) requires that developers submit an Obstacle Evaluation / Airport Airspace Analysis Form to the FAA. Once the developer receives the results of the analysis of the FAA, the findings should be submitted to the Local Permitting Authority, in this case – the city, in conjunction with their plan or permit submittals. From there, the appropriate city department, which could include Planning as well as Construction Services, would be required to submit a case to SCAC for further evaluation. Hucks said that the goal of this overlay is to provide a layer on the city’s GIS maps for current and future staff so that when annexation requests, rezoning requests, plan submittals or permit applications are received, staff is easily made aware when properties are located within the overlay and when they would be required to provide the appropriate notification. It is not intended to provide decisions on whether specific developments or permits can be approved. Therefore, unlike the county’s airport environs overlay, no specific requirements are included, only the process for notification by developers and staff. This amendment will also define the overlay, provide a map of the overlay, outline the proper review authority and information relating to the Airport Approach Zones identified by the South Carolina Aeronautics Commission’s Compatible Land Use Evaluation Tool (CLUE) Analysis. Hucks stated that Planning Commission is scheduled to hold the public hearing on the amendment at their December 12 meeting. Their recommendation will be forwarded to Council with first reading. There was some discussion regarding conversations with Horry County, height restrictions and Hemingway Chapel Road. G. Discussion of proposed amendments to Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to the requirements for Conservation Subdivisions. Hucks said 54 -- 54 of 260 -- December 2, 2024 Page 4 of 13 that the conservation subdivision design is part of Article 10 of the UDO. This section of article 10, along with open space requirements, were pulled from an overall cleanup of Article 10 that was recently adopted by Council, due to the comprehensive nature of the amendments proposed. Open space requirements were also recently adopted. A conservation subdivision design is an option for flexible, cluster style development that incentivizes eco conscience design and preserve areas of environmental and historical value while maintaining the prorated density of residential units for the overall site and minimizing the impact of the development on surrounding communities. Houses or lots in a conservation subdivision are typically located closer together, rather than spread throughout the development acreage, resulting in higher density in one or more parts of the property but also preserving larger portions of land. Additionally, there are typically fewer environmental impacts than traditional development thru a reduction in disturbed areas, minimized stormwater runoff and less impervious surface. Conservation subdivisions also have economic benefits, including higher property values, reduced maintenance costs, and reduced stormwater management costs. Hucks said that current and former staff have promoted the use of a conservation subdivision design, and Council has previously approved amendments to the UDO regarding conservation subdivisions, including the requirement for proposed developments on land exceeding 50 acres or more in size to submit a site plan for a conservation subdivision with the preliminary plans for development so that staff can determine whether a conservation subdivision design is appropriate for the site proposed to be developed. Hucks stated that the first development that was approved as a conservation subdivision was Collins Jollie, a multi-neighborhood design containing several tracts that are being developed by different owners or builders. During the plan review process, staff discovered that although multi-neighborhood designs are allowed, the requirement for all conservation and open space areas to be platted and recorded simultaneously remained unchanged; regardless of whether all tracts were at the point where final plats to create lots could be approved or not. For Collins Jollie, the solution to this issue was a development agreement, the sole purpose of which was to allow each tract to record the open space / conservation areas separately as long as such areas coincided with wetlands that have been delineated on a recent survey and were in line with the approved master plan. This amendment seeks to remedy this issue so that the requirements may be applied regardless of whether a multi- neighborhood or single neighborhood design is proposed. Other amendments, aside from reorganization of the requirements, include detailing what areas qualify for conservation areas, how maximum density is to be calculated, what areas may not count towards the net buildable area, the requirements for a Master Plan to be submitted, clarification on perimeter buffers and screening requirements, as well as appropriate instruments for permanent protection of open space, which includes the requirement for such areas to be platted as a conservation easement either before or with the final subdivision plat. Hucks said that the city has seen an increase in the number of conservation subdivisions being proposed, with 3 different approved plans and 2 others currently being reviewed. In total, there are currently 1,766 lots or units proposed within conservation subdivisions. The proposed amendments will provide needed clarification and provide better guidance to applicants and staff when considering a conservation subdivision design. 55 -- 55 of 260 -- December 2, 2024 Page 5 of 13 Hucks stated that Planning Commission is scheduled to hold a public hearing on the amendment at their December 12 meeting. Their recommendation will be forwarded to council with first reading. H. Discussion of proposed amendments to Article 9 – Landscaping and Buffering, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding Landscape, Buffer, and Tree Preservation requirements. Child Care Facilities Licensing Requirements – Hucks informed Council that staff was recently approached by an individual who is looking to open a childcare center in a shopping center with limited hours. The individual who inquired about it has several years of experience in the childcare industry and stated that the services she intends to provide would be considered legally exempt from the state’s licensing requirements for childcare centers. Staff looked at state law regarding the requirements for childcare centers, and found the following: SC Code of Laws, Ch. 13 – Childcare Facilities, Article 1, Sec. 63-13-20, defines a childcare facility as “a facility which provides care, supervision, or guidance for a minor child who is not related by blood, marriage, or adoption to the owner or operator of the facility whether or not the facility is operated for profit and whether or not the facility makes a charge for services offered by it.” This definition includes, but is not limited to, day nurseries, nursery schools, childcare centers, group childcare homes, and family childcare homes. The term does not include: Educational facilities, whether private or public, which operates solely for educational purposes; 5-yr old kindergarten programs; Kindergartens or nursery schools or other daytime programs, with or without stated educational purposes, operating no more than 4 hours a day and receiving children younger than lawful school age; Summer camps for children; Bible schools conducted during vacation periods; Childcare centers and group childcare homes owned and operated by a local church congregation or an established religious denomination or a religious college or university which does not receive state 61 -- 61 of 260 -- December 2, 2024 Page 11 of 13 or federal assistance for childcare services; and facilities that are operated for more than 4 hours a day in connection with a shopping center or service or other similar facility, where the same children are cared for less than 4 hours a day and not on a regular basis while parents or custodians of the children are occupied on the premises or are in the immediate vicinity and immediately available. These types of facilities must meet local fire and sanitation requirements and maintain documentation on these requirements on file at the facility available for public inspection. The City’s UDO defines a child daycare center is very similar to that of the state’s definition. The UDO defines “after school programs” as “any organized program which invites youth to participate outside of the traditional school day. Some programs are run by a primary or secondary school and some by externally funded non-profit or commercial organizations. Additionally, after school programs are permitted as a conditional use in most of the residential zoning districts; subject to requirements for proof of licensing or proof of exemption, limitations on hours of operation and no more than 4 consecutive hours per day, and fencing requirements for any designated play areas. After school programs are also permitted as an accessory use to all schools or religious institutions and daycare facilities in the Institutional and Professional zoning districts. The current requirements for after school programs eliminates the ability for other types of facilities, such as a part-time child-care facility located within shopping centers, to be permitted under the city’s current ordinance, even though state law exempts such facilities from licensing requirements. It also eliminates the option as far as zoning because unless the proposed facility is in the Institutional or Professional zoning districts, is an accessory use to a church or school, or is proposed to operate from a residence, the use is not allowed. Hucks said that staff wanted to bring the issue up to Council to see if there was a desire to open up the use in commercial districts in accordance with how the state permits such facilities. Even though such a facility would be considered “legally exempt,” the owner or operator of these facilities would still be required to apply for legally exempt status, meaning it would be determined by the state whether the facility is legally exempt, and this status would be required to be provided prior to the issuance of any city business license. Balloons as Signage vs. Decoration – Hucks informed Council that the city’s sign ordinance was amended a few years ago to eliminate temporary signage from the types of signs that are regulated within the city, as a result of a 2015 Supreme Court decision (Reed v. Town of Gilbert) regarding temporary signs, citing that the temporary sign regulations of the Town of Gilbert were a violation of the first amendment and the restrictions were content-based rather than content-neutral. In summary, a church installed small temporary directional signs throughout the town to inform churchgoers of where services would be held, as this particular church did not have a permanent location; however the town’s sign code contained different regulations based on the information conveyed in the signs, and the type of sign that the church had installed did not comply with the town’s sign code for that particular type of temporary directional sign. The supreme court held that a municipality cannot restrict expression because of a signs message, ideas, subject matter or content, and in most cases, content-based restrictions are considered unconstitutional unless the municipality can prove that the restrictions are narrowly tailored to serve a compelling governmental interest, such as public safety or aesthetics. In the case of the Town of Gilbert, the 62 -- 62 of 260 -- December 2, 2024 Page 12 of 13 court found that Gilbert’s sign code was NOT narrowly tailored because it allowed an unlimited number of ideological signs but placed significant limits on directional signs. The court offered some guidance on regulations that would not be considered content-based; mainly, that the sign regulations include restrictions on time, place, and manner. This could include the size of signs, sign lighting, electronic message displays, sign placement, on-premises v. off- premises signs, number of signs, sign materials, and time restrictions. Hucks stated that the reason this was brought up to Council is because Planning has had some businesses that have displayed items that could be considered “temporary” in nature and could be considered signage. The list of prohibited signs in the city’s sign ordinance lists 21 different types of signs that would be prohibited, one of those being attention-seizing or wind activated devices, such as inflatable signs, feather flags, and balloons, among other items. The argument being made by these businesses is that there are instances where decorations have been displayed – including balloons, that were not considered “signage” and were displayed for an extended period of time. Granted, the supreme court decision dealt with non-commercial signage; however, the same content-neutral restrictions would likely still apply, and as with any regulation or law, it is always possible for such regulations to be challenged if the regulations are not narrowly tailored to achieve the city’s interest; which in the case of the list of prohibited signs, exists in the interest of public safety and aesthetics. As a sidenote, to staff’s knowledge, there are no regulations that would permit balloons or similar devices for noncommercial activities, and within the UDO, the only place where balloons or other wind-activated or attention seizing device is mentioned is under the Prohibited Signs section of the UDO. Further, the UDO defines a sign as “any device designed to attract the attention of the public for commercial or advertising purposes that is attached, painted or otherwise affixed to, or a part of a building, structure, material, surface, vehicle, or object. Signs shall include any artificial light source, time or temperature units, clocks and any device that animates or projects a visual representation that attracts the attention of the public for commercial purpose. Staff does not dispute that balloons are used to attract the public’s attention for a commercial purpose is in fact a sign, based on the city’s definition of a sign. However, staff’s concern is the issue content neutrality and whether the prohibition of balloons for commercial purposes while noncommercial balloon displays are not necessarily prohibited (although not expressly permitted) would meet the strict scrutiny test if they are prohibited for commercial purposes in order to promote the public health, safety and aesthetics of the city. Hucks again said that staff wanted to present the issue to council and see if there was any interest in allowing balloons for businesses for temporary display – which would still not be permitted by the city but may provide an avenue for businesses to have balloons for special sales, promotions or a community event.
