B. Screening 1. All perimeter buffers are to provide a continuous screening in either of the following manners: a. The retention of existing mature trees, illustrated on the Landscape Plan with a notation verifying that all such trees are a minimum 5-inches in caliper and in good health; or b. The provision of supplemental plantings, consistent with a Type C Buffer as described in Table 9.2 2. Whether obtained through existing vegetation or supplemental planting, screening material should be staggered to utilize the full buffer width. Walking paths, cycling/hiking trails, or boardwalks may be permissible within the buffers, but should meander throughout to blend into the natural habitat. 10.4.7 Open Space Requirements for Conservation Subdivisions A. Permitted uses of Open Space include the following: 1. Conservation of natural, archeological or historical resources; 2. Meadows, woodlands, wildlife corridors, game preserves, or similar conservation-oriented areas; 3. Walking or bicycle trails, provided they are constructed of permeable materials; 4. Passive recreation areas, such as open fields; 5. Landscaped stormwater management facilities, community wastewater disposal systems and individual wastewater disposal systems located on soils particularly suited to such uses. Such facilities shall be located outside of Conservation Easement. 6. Easements for drainage, access, and underground utility lines. 7. General maintenance and care of vegetation within the Perimeter Buffers, Wetlands, Wetland Buffers and Riparian Corridor Zones. 8. Other conservation-oriented uses that are compatible with the purposes of this ordinance. B. Prohibited Uses of Open Space Uses of within open space may not include the following activities or uses: 1. Roads, parking lots and impervious surfaces, except as specifically authorized in the previous sections stated herein; 2. Agricultural and forestry activities not conducted according to accepted Best Management Practices; 98 -- 98 of 110 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development 10-8 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended August 19, 2024 3. Golf Courses; 4. Other activities as determined by the Applicant and recorded on the legal instrument providing for permanent protection. C. Ownership and Management of Open Space 1. Open Space may either be owned and maintained by the Homeowners/Property-owners Association or dedicated to the City of Conway conveyed to a land trust or similar conservation-oriented non-profit organization with legal authority to administer perpetual care for the land or to the City of Conway. Management Plan. An applicant shall submit an Open Space Management Plan that includes the following: a. Allocates responsibility and guidelines for the maintenance and operation of the Open Space and any facilities located thereon, including provisions for ongoing maintenance and for long-term capital improvements; b. Estimates the costs and staffing requirements needed for maintenance and operation of, and insurance for, the Open Space and outlines the means by which such funding will be obtained or provided; 2. Open Space that is to be deeded to the HOA and/or POA: a. Shall be assigned unique legal descriptions (i.e. Open Space #1, Open Space #6, etc....), and b. Shall contain a plat notation stating that “All areas shown hereon as Open Space shall remain as such in perpetuity. Open Spaces are to be owned and maintained by the HOA/POA.” D. When a Conservation Subdivision designates Open Space that is to be deeded to the HOA and/or POA and Open Space parcels that are to be subsequently deeded to a land trust, conservation-oriented organization, or to the City of Conway: 1. The parcels will need to be delineated assigning tracts to be subsequently deeded to a land trust, conservation-oriented organization or to the City of Conway as “Open Space Conservation Parcel”; and 2. the following plat notation provided “All areas shown hereon as Open Space are to be owned and maintained by the HOA and are to remain as open space in perpetuity. Those Open Spaces also designated as Conservation Parcels are to be owned and maintained by the HOA until such time that the property is conveyed to a land trust or conservation organization for perpetual care and preservation.” E. A minimum of 30% of the net buildable area of the subject property shall be left undeveloped and shall be used for both the preservation of the natural environment and human recreation. This portion of the development must be designated for perpetual ownership and maintenance by the HOA/POA. Fragmentation of Open Space should be minimized so that resource areas are not divided into numerous small parcels located in various parts of the development. D. Above-ground utility rights-of-way and small areas of impervious surface may be included within the protected Open Space but cannot be counted towards the 30% minimum area requirement. E. Access to the Open Space shall be provided either through sufficient frontage onto internal streets/sidewalk systems within the development or walking paths, cycling/hiking trails, or boardwalks constructed to give residents within the development adequate means of ingress/egress. 10.4.8 Legal Instrument for Permanent Protection A. Conservation areas shall be platted within open space and shall be protected in perpetuity by a Conservation Easement. Such easement shall be delineated either prior to or concurrent with the final subdivision plat. 99 -- 99 of 110 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development 10-9 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended August 19, 2024 1. The open space shall be protected in perpetuity by a binding legal instrument that is recorded with the deed and submitted to Horry County. The permanent conservation easement(s) are to be: a. delineated/dedicated either on the final subdivision plat or via an easement plat, previously recorded at the Horry County Register of Deeds with such plat book & page referenced and existing easement shown on the subdivision plat/final plans. b. a binding legal instrument, such as the HOA/POA restrictive covenants or easement agreement, as well as all subsequent title deeds shall incorporate by reference, the recorded plat that dedicated the easement for proper reservation of said encumbrance; c. be expressly dedicated to the City of Conway, which requires acceptance /approval by City Council or; d. be dedicated to a land trust or similar conservation-oriented non-profit organization with legal authority to accept such easements and cite the City of Conway as a successor. The organization shall be bona fide and in perpetual existence and the conveyance instruments shall contain an appropriate provision for retransfer in the event the organization becomes unable to carry out its functions, or e. be dedicated to a governmental entity with an interest in pursuing goals compatible with the purposes of this ordinance. If the entity accepting the easement is not in the City of Conway, then a third right of enforcement favoring the City of Conway shall be included in the easement. f. An equivalent legal tool that provides permanent protection, if approved by the City of Conway. g. The instrument for permanent protection shall include clear restrictions on the use of the Open Space. These restrictions shall include all restrictions contained in this article, as well as any further restrictions the Applicant chooses to place on the use of the Open Space. h. Once a legal instrument for permanent protection has been placed upon the Open Space, the Horry County Tax Assessor’s office shall be directed to reassess the Open Space at a lower value to reflect its more limited use. If the open space is used purely for passive recreational purposes and the terms of the instrument for permanent protection effectively prohibit any type of significant economic activity, then the assessment should be at a value of zero. 100 -- 100 of 110 -- DATE: DECEMBER 2, 2024 ITEM: V.I. ISSUE: Discussion of proposed amendments to Article 9-Landscaping and Buffering, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding Landscape, Buffer, and Tree Preservation requirements. BACKGROUND: Staff is proposing an amendment to Article 9 that would allow for a more clarification on commonly misinterpreted aspects of the Tree Preservation Ordinance, penalties for violations of the ordinance, as well as a more appropriate course of action for Tree Board appeals. Staff is proposing the following. 1. Codify the Tree Preservation Ordinance into the UDO. Then the Tree Ordinance falls under the purview of the Planning & Development Dept. 2. Designate that the Community Appearance Board (CAB) will continue to act as the Tree Board; however, appeals of the decisions of the Tree Board would be directed to the Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA). 3. Amend the Tree Preservation Ordinance, including the Appeals Section (Sec. 3-4-15 – Appeals), items (b) and (c) that directs appeals of the Tree Board to Conway City Council, and amend to direct appeals of the Tree Board decision to Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA). This would ensure a proper appeal process, as the appellant would then appeal decisions of the BZA to circuit court instead of City Council. 4. Begin collecting an application fee ($250) for Tree Board Appeals. Staff proposes to begin charging $250 for Tree Appeal applications. Should applicants seek to overturn the decision of the Tree Board, and these requests go to BZA, the property will need to be posted, the appeal would need to be advertised, letters would need to be sent to adjacent property owners, and decisions from the BZA would need to be mailed certified to interested parties. 5. Upon the request of tree board, staff have made some housekeeping changes throughout the ordinance to ensure a more uniform and concise understanding of the processes and terminology used throughout the ordinance. These items include clarity of the process of tree mitigation, implementation of higher penalties for improper removal of protected or landmark trees, and clarification on definitions that were commonly misinterpreted. 6. Addition and deletion, upon the request of the tree board, of trees from the protected tree list. The tree board asked to remove non-native trees, Crepe Myrtle and Dawn Redwoods, from the protected list but to rather include native trees, such as a Tulip tree, Red Cedar, and a Tupelo tree. RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends discussion of amendments the proposed amendments to the Tree Preservation Ordinance. 101 -- 101 of 110 -- DATE: DECEMBER 2, 2024 ITEM: V.J. ISSUE: Discussion of proposed amendments to Title 3- Public Works, Chapter 4-Tree Preservation, of the City of Conway Code of Ordinances, regarding the Tree Preservation Ordinance. BACKGROUND: Chapter 4 of the City of Conway Code of Ordinances assigns the duties of the Conway Tree Board to be the responsibility of the appointed members of the Community Appearance Board (CAB). The issue that faces the current Tree Board is that there is no clear direction as to the appeals process regarding their decisions. There are 3 appeals options listed in the Tree Preservation Ordinance: (a) Denial of a protected tree removal permit from City Arborist. The applicant may appeal to the Tree Board. It must be filed within 10 working days of the denial of the permit. (b) The arborist cannot grant a permit to remove a landmark tree. If the tree is determined to be a landmark tree, the applicant must request permission to remove from the Tree Board. IF the Tree Board denies the applicant a permit to remove a landmark tree, they may appeal their decision to City Council. It must be filed within 10 working days of the denial of the permit. (c) Appeal of the penalty assessed by the Tree Board. If the applicant wishes to appeal the penalty (or mitigation amount) that was assessed by the Tree Board, they may appeal to City Council. It must be filed within 10 days of the Board’s decision (or assessment). Staff has explored a couple of different options regarding the Tree Board and the appropriate Board for protected tree removal requests to be considered. In our research, staff has concluded that because Conway is a “Tree City USA”, there must be a designated “Tree Board” OR a “Tree Department”, and even with a Tree Dept., it is the opinion of the City Arborist, as well as other Cities / Towns with certified arborists that a Tree Board would still be necessary. Additionally, staff researched several cities / towns that are also a Tree City USA, and of the ones we found – all had a Tree Protection Ordinance and either a Tree Board, or in some cases, a Tree Commission. As such, staff has reached the following conclusions and suggestions for the Tree Preservation Ordinance and the appeals authority to ensure that the City does not lose its Tree City USA status and continues to strengthen its efforts in tree preservation and protection: 1. Codify the Tree Preservation Ordinance into the UDO. Then the Tree Ordinance falls under the purview of the Planning & Development Dept. 2. Designate that the Community Appearance Board (CAB) will continue to act as the Tree Board; however, appeals of the decisions of the Tree Board would be directed to the Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA). 3. Amend the Tree Preservation Ordinance, including the Appeals Section (Sec. 3-4-15 – Appeals), items (b) and (c) that directs appeals of the Tree Board to Conway City Council, and amend to direct appeals 102 -- 102 of 110 -- of the Tree Board decision to Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA). This would ensure a proper appeal process, as the appellant would then appeal decisions of the BZA to circuit court instead of City Council. 4. Begin collecting an application fee ($250) for Tree Board Appeals. Staff proposes to begin charging $250 for Tree Appeal applications. Should applicants seek to overturn the decision of the Tree Board, and these requests go to BZA, the property will need to be posted, the appeal would need to be advertised, letters would need to be sent to adjacent property owners, and decisions from the BZA would need to be mailed certified to interested parties. RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends discussion of amendments to remove the Tree Preservation Ordinance from the general code and codify into the UDO, as well as amend the Tree Preservation Ordinance to direct appeals of the Tree Board to the authority of the BZA. 103 -- 103 of 110 -- DATE: DECEMBER 2, 2024 ITEM: IX.A. text: December 2, 2024 Page 1 of 13 CITY OF CONWAY CITY COUNCIL MEETING CONWAY CITY HALL 229 MAIN STREET, CONWAY MONDAY, DECEMBER 2, 2024 - 4:00 P.M. PRESENT: Mayor Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor Pro Tem Larry White, Amanda Butler, William Goldfinch, Julie Hardwick, Beth Helms, Justin Jordan. STAFF: Adam Emrick, City Administrator; Mary Catherine Hyman, Deputy City Administrator; John Rogers, Deputy City Administrator; June Wood, Public Information Officer; Jeff Leveille, Technology Services Director; Timmy Williams, Hospitality & Beautification Director; Jessica Hucks, Planning and Development Director; Rock Rabon, Fleet Maintenance Director; Allison Williams, Finance Director; Reggie Jenerette, Solid Waste Director; Ashley Smith, Parks and Recreation Director; Brandon Harrelson, Public Works Director; Dale Long, Police Chief; Kayla Fleming, Municipal Judge; Lynn Smith, Human Resources Director; Le Hendrick, Fire Chief; Katie Dennis, Planner; David Crotts, Procurement and Inventory Division Chief; Rosanne Dates, Grants and Special Projects Division Chief; Ted Dudley, Public Utilities Director; and Alicia Shelley, City Clerk. OTHERS: There were approximately 15 others in attendance. CALL TO ORDER: Mayor Blain called the meeting to order. Blain gave the invocation and led the Pledge of Allegiance. The requirements for posting notice of this meeting under South Carolina’s Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) were met. CONSENT AGENDA: A. Final Reading of Ordinance #ZA2024-12-02 (B), to annex approximately 0.80+/- total acres of property located at 2689, 2691, 2693, 2695, 2697 and 2699 Oak Street (PIN 325-15-01-0010), and rezone from the Horry County Neighborhood Commercial (NC) district to the City of Conway Neighborhood Commercial (NC) district. C. Approval of a Special Event - Jingle Jam by First Baptist Church – December 15, 2024 D. Approval of November 18, 2024 Council Meeting Minutes APPROVAL OF CONSENT AGENDA: Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Butler to approve the December 2, 2024 consent agenda. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. PUBLIC INPUT: -- 1 of 13 -- December 2, 2024 Page 2 of 13 There was no public input. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Hardwick, to close public input. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. SPECIAL PRESENTATION: A. Recognition of 2024 Artist of the City of Conway Christmas Card Contest – Blain recognized Samantha Whyland as the 2024 Artist of the City of Conway Christmas Card Contest winner. B. Presentation of Employee of the Month for December 2024 – Public Safety – Hendrick presented David Parker as the Public Safety Employee of the Month for December 2024 C. Presentation of Longevity Awards – November 2024 – 5 Years: Rosanne Dates, Administration; 5 Years: Kym Wilkerson, Planning and Development; 5 Years: Chelci Morris, Police; 5 Years: Jeff Edwards, Public Works; 5 Years: Travis Paul, Hospitality and Beautification; 10 Years: Dan Reardon, Public Utilities – Emrick and White presented the longevity awards. D. Presentation by Taylor Garretson and Elissa Plocinik of Coastal Sea Turtle Center – Elissa Plocinik and Taylor Garretson, college graduates from CCU with a bachelor’s in marine science, presented to Council their dream of opening a sea turtle care center in Conway. They asked Council for their support and use of available space in Conway. E. Discussion of proposed amendments to Article 2 – Definitions and Article 4 – Use Tables, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding various revisions within these articles of the UDO. Hucks said that this proposed amendment includes Article 2-Definitions and Article 4-Use Tables in the UDO. They are part of an overall cleanup of the UDO that has been ongoing since 2023, which was also discussed at Council’s budget retreat that same year. Regarding Article 2, staff has noted several terms that are used throughout the UDO, yet have not been defined, as well as other terms that needed to be revised to either coincide with changes made in other articles within the UDO or to meet new standard definitions. For example, the term “opaque” is used throughout the UDO with regard to screening standards, yet it is not defined. Other terms, such as “multifamily”, were amended to coincide with the residential design standards for what would be considered a multifamily dwelling rather than define it based on relationships to other persons within the same dwelling. Hucks said that with regard to Article 4, the changes were minor in nature and included the deletion of duplicate uses or uses that are considered obsolete, and combining uses, such as Beauty Salons and Barber Shops, which would be allowed within the same zoning districts even though one may provide more services than the other; they are similar enough in nature to be considered like-uses. Following a public hearing on the proposed amendments, they will be forwarded to Council for first reading along with Planning Commission’s recommendations. -- 2 of 13 -- December 2, 2024 Page 3 of 13 F. Discussion of a proposed amendment to Article 6 – Design Standards, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding the creation of an Airport Overlay (AO) District. Hucks said that several properties along Highway 378 and Dunn Shortcut Road have been annexed over the past couple of years. There have been 2 annexations that are within close proximity to the Conway-Horry County Airport; one of which contains several hundred acres proposed to contain both commercial and residential development – known as the Brookhaven Planned Development. South Carolina Code of Laws requires the local governmental body or agency receiving requests for a planned development, plat approval or a building permit that is within an airport safety zone to provide the information to the division of airports for review. This was done last year regarding the Brookhaven Planned Development in accordance with South Carolina code. There were no specific comments provided back to staff with regard to the annexation request; however, the county attorney at the time recommended that the city defer to the county’s Airport Environs overlay in the county zoning ordinance and advised that a large national flight school associated with the Myrtle Beach Airport’s east coast campus has begun operations and that there would likely be an increase in operations at the Conway airport. In general, development resulting in any density of significance near the ends of runways is generally discouraged. Further, the South Carolina Aeronautics Commission (SCAC) requires that developers submit an Obstacle Evaluation / Airport Airspace Analysis Form to the FAA. Once the developer receives the results of the analysis of the FAA, the findings should be submitted to the Local Permitting Authority, in this case – the city, in conjunction with their plan or permit submittals. From there, the appropriate city department, which could include Planning as well as Construction Services, would be required to submit a case to SCAC for further evaluation. Hucks said that the goal of this overlay is to provide a layer on the city’s GIS maps for current and future staff so that when annexation requests, rezoning requests, plan submittals or permit applications are received, staff is easily made aware when properties are located within the overlay and when they would be required to provide the appropriate notification. It is not intended to provide decisions on whether specific developments or permits can be approved. Therefore, unlike the county’s airport environs overlay, no specific requirements are included, only the process for notification by developers and staff. This amendment will also define the overlay, provide a map of the overlay, outline the proper review authority and information relating to the Airport Approach Zones identified by the South Carolina Aeronautics Commission’s Compatible Land Use Evaluation Tool (CLUE) Analysis. Hucks stated that Planning Commission is scheduled to hold the public hearing on the amendment at their December 12 meeting. Their recommendation will be forwarded to Council with first reading. Discussion of proposed amendments to Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to the requirements for Conservation Subdivisions. Hucks said -- 3 of 13 -- December 2, 2024 Page 4 of 13 that the conservation subdivision design is part of Article 10 of the UDO. This section of article 10, along with open space requirements, were pulled from an overall cleanup of Article 10 that was recently adopted by Council, due to the comprehensive nature of the amendments proposed. Open space requirements were also recently adopted. A conservation subdivision design is an option for flexible, cluster style development that incentivizes eco conscience design and preserve areas of environmental and historical value while maintaining the prorated density of residential units for the overall site and minimizing the impact of the development on surrounding communities. Houses or lots in a conservation subdivision are typically located closer together, rather than spread throughout the development acreage, resulting in higher density in one or more parts of the property but also preserving larger portions of land. Additionally, there are typically fewer environmental impacts than traditional development thru a reduction in disturbed areas, minimized stormwater runoff and less impervious surface. Conservation subdivisions also have economic benefits, including higher property values, reduced maintenance costs, and reduced stormwater management costs. Hucks said that current and former staff have promoted the use of a conservation subdivision design, and Council has previously approved amendments to the UDO regarding conservation subdivisions, including the requirement for proposed developments on land exceeding 50 acres or more in size to submit a site plan for a conservation subdivision with the preliminary plans for development so that staff can determine whether a conservation subdivision design is appropriate for the site proposed to be developed. Hucks stated that the first development that was approved as a conservation subdivision was Collins Jollie, a multi-neighborhood design containing several tracts that are being developed by different owners or builders. During the plan review process, staff discovered that although multi-neighborhood designs are allowed, the requirement for all conservation and open space areas to be platted and recorded simultaneously remained unchanged; regardless of whether all tracts were at the point where final plats to create lots could be approved or not. For Collins Jollie, the solution to this issue was a development agreement, the sole purpose of which was to allow each tract to record the open space / conservation areas separately as long as such areas coincided with wetlands that have been delineated on a recent survey and were in line with the approved master plan. This amendment seeks to remedy this issue so that the requirements may be applied regardless of whether a multi- neighborhood or single neighborhood design is proposed. Other amendments, aside from reorganization of the requirements, include detailing what areas qualify for conservation areas, how maximum density is to be calculated, what areas may not count towards the net buildable area, the requirements for a Master Plan to be submitted, clarification on perimeter buffers and screening requirements, as well as appropriate instruments for permanent protection of open space, which includes the requirement for such areas to be platted as a conservation easement either before or with the final subdivision plat. Hucks said that the city has seen an increase in the number of conservation subdivisions being proposed, with 3 different approved plans and 2 others currently being reviewed. In total, there are currently 1,766 lots or units proposed within conservation subdivisions. The proposed amendments will provide needed clarification and provide better guidance to applicants and staff when considering a conservation subdivision design. -- 4 of 13 -- December 2, 2024 Page 5 of 13 Hucks stated that Planning Commission is scheduled to hold a public hearing on the amendment at their December 12 meeting. Their recommendation will be forwarded to council with first reading. H. Discussion of proposed amendments to Article 9 – Landscaping and Buffering, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding Landscape, Buffer, and Tree Preservation requirements. Hucks informed Council that the next item on the agenda, Title 3 – Public Works, Chapter 4 – Tree Preservation, of the City of Conway Code of Ordinances, regarding the Tree Preservation Ordinance, is included with this discussion. The ordinance is still being finalized but some of the amendments being proposed include the following: (1) Repeal the Tree Preservation ordinance from the general code and codify in Article 9 of the UDO; (2) Direct appeals of the Tree Board to be considered by the Board of Zoning Appeals prior to the option of appealing to circuit court; (3) Amend the fee schedule for the Planning Department regarding tree violation penalties and mitigation requirements; (4) Reduce the size of a live oak tree to be considered a landmark tree from 30” to 24” DBH; (5) Remove certain trees from the protected tree list and add trees to the protected tree list; and (6) Several other housekeeping changes. Hucks said provided that the 2025 Planning Commission schedule is approved at their December 12 meeting, the amendments proposed to Tree Preservation will be considered at the January 2 Planning Commission meeting. WORKSHOP: Use of Off-Road Vehicles on Allen Drive – Long said that it has been brought to the Police Departments’ attention of someone that uses the Crabtree Greenway Trail that ATV’s are utilizing this area. Long showed maps of the area explaining where Chestnut Bay fits into the area as well. Long asked Council for direction, should the ATVs be prohibited from this area, how does the police stop them from riding them in this area or should the city do anything at all. Child Care Facilities Licensing Requirements – Hucks informed Council that staff was recently approached by an individual who is looking to open a childcare center in a shopping center with limited hours. The individual who inquired about it has several years of experience in the childcare industry and stated that the services she intends to provide would be considered legally exempt from the state’s licensing requirements for childcare centers. Staff looked at state law regarding the requirements for childcare centers, and found the following: SC Code of Laws, Ch. 13 – Childcare Facilities, Article 1, Sec. 63-13-20, defines a childcare facility as “a facility which provides care, supervision, or guidance for a minor child who is not related by blood, marriage, or adoption to the owner or operator of the facility whether or not the facility is operated for profit and whether or not the facility makes a charge for services offered by it.” This definition includes, but is not limited to, day nurseries, nursery schools, childcare centers, group childcare homes, and family childcare homes. The term does not include: Educational facilities, whether private or public, which operates solely for educational purposes; 5-yr old kindergarten programs; Kindergartens or nursery schools or other daytime programs, with or without stated educational purposes, operating no more than 4 hours a day and receiving children younger than lawful school age; Summer camps for children; Bible schools conducted during vacation periods; Childcare centers and group childcare homes owned and operated by a local church congregation or an established religious denomination or a religious college or university which does not receive state -- 10 of 13 -- December 2, 2024 Page 11 of 13 or federal assistance for childcare services; and facilities that are operated for more than 4 hours a day in connection with a shopping center or service or other similar facility, where the same children are cared for less than 4 hours a day and not on a regular basis while parents or custodians of the children are occupied on the premises or are in the immediate vicinity and immediately available. These types of facilities must meet local fire and sanitation requirements and maintain documentation on these requirements on file at the facility available for public inspection. The City’s UDO defines a child daycare center is very similar to that of the state’s definition. The UDO defines “after school programs” as “any organized program which invites youth to participate outside of the traditional school day. Some programs are run by a primary or secondary school and some by externally funded non-profit or commercial organizations. Additionally, after school programs are permitted as a conditional use in most of the residential zoning districts; subject to requirements for proof of licensing or proof of exemption, limitations on hours of operation and no more than 4 consecutive hours per day, and fencing requirements for any designated play areas. After school programs are also permitted as an accessory use to all schools or religious institutions and daycare facilities in the Institutional and Professional zoning districts. The current requirements for after school programs eliminates the ability for other types of facilities, such as a part-time child-care facility located within shopping centers, to be permitted under the city’s current ordinance, even though state law exempts such facilities from licensing requirements. It also eliminates the option as far as zoning because unless the proposed facility is in the Institutional or Professional zoning districts, is an accessory use to a church or school, or is proposed to operate from a residence, the use is not allowed. Hucks said that staff wanted to bring the issue up to Council to see if there was a desire to open up the use in commercial districts in accordance with how the state permits such facilities. Even though such a facility would be considered “legally exempt,” the owner or operator of these facilities would still be required to apply for legally exempt status, meaning it would be determined by the state whether the facility is legally exempt, and this status would be required to be provided prior to the issuance of any city business license. After some discussion, Council advised staff to amend the ordinance as presented. Balloons as Signage vs. Decoration – Hucks informed Council that the city’s sign ordinance was amended a few years ago to eliminate temporary signage from the types of signs that are regulated within the city, as a result of a 2015 Supreme Court decision (Reed v. Town of Gilbert) regarding temporary signs, citing that the temporary sign regulations of the Town of Gilbert were a violation of the first amendment and the restrictions were content-based rather than content-neutral. In summary, a church installed small temporary directional signs throughout the town to inform churchgoers of where services would be held, as this particular church did not have a permanent location; however the town’s sign code contained different regulations based on the information conveyed in the signs, and the type of sign that the church had installed did not comply with the town’s sign code for that particular type of temporary directional sign. The supreme court held that a municipality cannot restrict expression because of a signs message, ideas, subject matter or content, and in most cases, content-based restrictions are considered unconstitutional unless the municipality can prove that the restrictions are narrowly tailored to serve a compelling governmental interest, such as public safety or aesthetics. In the case of the Town of Gilbert, the -- 11 of 13 -- December 2, 2024 Page 12 of 13 court found that Gilbert’s sign code was NOT narrowly tailored because it allowed an unlimited number of ideological signs but placed significant limits on directional signs. The court offered some guidance on regulations that would not be considered content-based; mainly, that the sign regulations include restrictions on time, place, and manner. This could include the size of signs, sign lighting, electronic message displays, sign placement, on-premises v. off- premises signs, number of signs, sign materials, and time restrictions. Hucks stated that the reason this was brought up to Council is because Planning has had some businesses that have displayed items that could be considered “temporary” in nature and could be considered signage. The list of prohibited signs in the city’s sign ordinance lists 21 different types of signs that would be prohibited, one of those being attention-seizing or wind activated devices, such as inflatable signs, feather flags, and balloons, among other items. The argument being made by these businesses is that there are instances where decorations have been displayed – including balloons, that were not considered “signage” and were displayed for an extended period of time. Granted, the supreme court decision dealt with non-commercial signage; however, the same content-neutral restrictions would likely still apply, and as with any regulation or law, it is always possible for such regulations to be challenged if the regulations are not narrowly tailored to achieve the city’s interest; which in the case of the list of prohibited signs, exists in the interest of public safety and aesthetics. As a sidenote, to staff’s knowledge, there are no regulations that would permit balloons or similar devices for noncommercial activities, and within the UDO, the only place where balloons or other wind-activated or attention seizing device is mentioned is under the Prohibited Signs section of the UDO. Further, the UDO defines a sign as “any device designed to attract the attention of the public for commercial or advertising purposes that is attached, painted or otherwise affixed to, or a part of a building, structure, material, surface, vehicle, or object. Signs shall include any artificial light source, time or temperature units, clocks and any device that animates or projects a visual representation that attracts the attention of the public for commercial purpose. Staff does not dispute that balloons are used to attract the public’s attention for a commercial purpose is in fact a sign, based on the city’s definition of a sign. However, staff’s concern is the issue content neutrality and whether the prohibition of balloons for commercial purposes while noncommercial balloon displays are not necessarily prohibited (although not expressly permitted) would meet the strict scrutiny test if they are prohibited for commercial purposes in order to promote the public health, safety and aesthetics of the city. Hucks again said that staff wanted to present the issue to council and see if there was any interest in allowing balloons for businesses for temporary display – which would still not be permitted by the city but may provide an avenue for businesses to have balloons for special sales, promotions or a community event. After much discussion, Council advised staff to amend the ordinance, separate out balloons prohibiting them except for special sales/events and limit the number of days. -- 12 of 13 -- -- 13 of 13 --

ISSUE: Resolution accepting dedication of roadways & drainage and the financial guarantee for the roadway warranty for the Collins Walk, Phase 1, subdivision (Blueback Herring Way, American Shad Street, Bluegill Street, and Yellow Perch Place). BACKGROUND: Diamond Shores LLC requests to dedicate the roadways and drainage system in the Collins Walk, Phase 1. The road(s) inside this development being offered for dedication are: Blueback Herring Way, American Shad Street, Bluegill Street, and Yellow Perch Place. Upon approval of this request by City Council, the City will accept the documents from Diamond Shores LLC that are required (and applicable) to finalize acceptance of the roadways and drainage system, namely: Drainage Easement, Right-of-Way Deed, Warranty Agreement, As-Built Road Plans, Certification of Non-Litigation and the Warranty Surety in the form of a financial guarantee (in this case, a cashier’s check has been provided). The roadway warranty shall be in place for a period of three (3) years. Per the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), the required roadway warranty agreement will be for three years from the date of the acceptance of the road dedication in the amount of $72,307.20, which is calculated by multiplying $33.60 per linear foot of 2 lane roadway and $5 per linear foot for each additional lane of roadway: Public Works has inspected the roadways and drainage in the Collins Walk, Phase 1 subdivision and found them acceptable to move forward with the dedication. RECOMMENDATION Adopt the resolution accepting dedication of roadways and drainage system in the Collins Walk, Phase 1 subdivision with a financial guarantee (cashier’s check provided) for a three-year warranty in the amount of $119,451.02. 3 -- 3 of 120 -- STATE OF SOUTH CAROLINA ) COUNTY OF HORRY ) RESOLUTION CITY OF CONWAY ) ACCEPTING THE ROADWAYS AND DRAINAGE SYSTEM IN THE COLLINS WALK (PHASE 1) SUBDIVISION WHEREAS, Diamond Shores, LLC has installed a roadway and drainage system within the city limits of Conway; and WHEREAS, Diamond Shores, LLC is requesting approval to dedicate street rights of way for Collins Walk, Phase 1, subdivision, Blueback Herring Way, American Shad Street, Bluegill Street, and Yellow Perch Place; and WHEREAS, Diamond Shores, LLC also requests to convey their right, title and all interest related to the drainage system together with all public easements and rights of way thereto, located within the Blueback Herring Way, American Shad Street, Bluegill Street, and Yellow Perch Place rights-of-ways; and WHEREAS, Conway City Council has determined it would be in the best interest of Conway and its citizens to accept the street and drainage system Blueback Herring Way, American Shad Street, Bluegill Street, and Yellow Perch Place, as depicted on maps created by Thomas & Hutton, prepared 04/04/2023, titled Final Plat, and recorded in the Horry County Registrar of Deeds Plat Book 322, Page 73; and NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, by the City Council of the City of Conway, South Carolina to accept road right of way and drainage on the above stated Blueback Herring Way, American Shad Street, Bluegill Street, and Yellow Perch Place from Diamon Shores, LLC as presented in the deed and easement signed by David Schwerd of Diamond Shores, LLC. 4 -- 4 of 120 -- RATIFIED BY CITY COUNCIL, duly assembled, this day of , 2024. ISSUE: Consideration of Resolution in Support of Certification of Coastal Centre as Abandoned and qualifying under the South Carolina Abandoned Buildings Revitalization Act. BACKGROUND: Coastal Centre Plaza has recently changed ownership and has the opportunity to have new life breathed into it. The new owners are applying for certification under the South Carolina Abandoned Buildings Revitalization Act and as such need a resolution of support from the City to confirm that certain buildings within the plaza have been unoccupied for a qualifying period of time. The attached Resolution will assist the new owners in the funding of the redevelopment of the site, with the hopes that high quality national retailers will be recruited to the plaza and fill a much-needed gap in the retail availability of goods for Conway residents. RECOMMENDATION Approval of the Resolution as attached. 12 -- 12 of 120 -- STATE OF SOUTH CAROLINA ) COUNTY OF HORRY ) R E S O L U T I O N CITY OF CONWAY ) A RESOLUTION CERTIFYING THE PROPERTY IDENTIFIED AS HORRY COUNTY TAX MAP NUMBERS 123-13-07-022, 123-13-07-031, 123-13-07-004, 123-13-07-026, AND 123-13-07-002, AS ABANDONED BUILDING SITES PURSUANT TO THE SOUTH CAROLINA ABANDONED BUILDINGS REVITALIZATION ACT, CODIFIED AT TITLE 12, CHAPTER 67 OF THE CODE OF LAWS OF SOUTH CAROLINA 1976, AS AMENDED; AND OTHER MATTERS RELATED THERETO. WHEREAS, the South Carolina Abandoned Buildings Revitalization Act (the “Act”), as codified at Title 12, Chapter 67 of the Code of Laws of South Carolina 1976, as amended, was enacted to create an incentive for the rehabilitation, renovation, and redevelopment of abandoned buildings located in South Carolina; and WHEREAS, the Act provides that restoration of abandoned buildings into productive assets for the communities in which they are located serves a public and corporate purpose and results in job opportunities; and WHEREAS, Section 12-67-140 of the Act provides that a taxpayer who rehabilitates an abandoned building is eligible either for a credit against certain income taxes, license fees, or premium taxes, or a credit against local real property taxes; and WHEREAS, RP Coastal Centre, LLC or an affiliate, successor, or assign thereof (the “Taxpayer”) intends to rehabilitate certain real property identified as Horry County Tax Map Numbers 123-13-07-022, 123-13-07-031, 123-13-07-004, 123-13-07- 026, and 123-13-07-002 and more fully described on Exhibit A attached hereto and made part hereof (individually, “Parcel”); and WHEREAS, each Parcel is located entirely within the City of Conway, South Carolina (the “City”); and WHEREAS, the Taxpayer has expressed a desire to claim South Carolina state income tax credits under the Act, which shall have no negative fiscal impact on the City; and WHEREAS, Section 12-67-160(A) of the Act provides that a taxpayer may apply to the City in which an abandoned building is located for a certification of the abandoned building site, and the taxpayer may conclusively rely upon that certification in determining the credits allowed; and WHEREAS, the City and the Taxpayer, after performing their diligence activities for each Parcel, have determined that each Parcel contains at least one “abandoned building” or portion of an “abandoned building” as defined in Section 12-67-120(1) of the 13 -- 13 of 120 -- Act, and the geographic area of each Parcel is consistent with the term “building site” as defined in Section 12-67-120(2) of the Act; and WHEREAS, the Taxpayer has requested that the City certify each Parcel as an abandoned building site under Section 12-67-160(1) of the Act in order to facilitate Taxpayer’s claim for income tax credits; and WHEREAS, given that the claim for income tax credits will have no negative fiscal impact on the City and that certification would enhance the likelihood of restoring non- productive property in the City to productive use, it appears that each Parcel meets the requirements of the Act for certification. NOW THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED by the City Council of the City of Conway in meeting duly assembled, as follows: Section 1. Each Parcel satisfies the criteria for an “abandoned building” as described by Section 12-67-120(1) of the Act, namely that it has been closed continuously to business or otherwise nonoperational for income producing purposes for more than five years, and the geographic area of the “building site” on each Parcel is consistent with Section 12-67-120(2) of the Act, namely that it consists of the abandoned building itself together with the parcel of land upon which it is located and other improvements located on the parcel, provided that the area of the building site is limited to the land upon which the abandoned building is located and the land immediately surrounding such building used for parking and other similar purposes directly related to the building's income producing use. Future re-platting or re-drawing of parcel lines referenced in this Resolution shall not affect the City’s findings contained herein. Section 2. The City hereby certifies that (i) the abandoned building site is an abandoned building as defined in Section 12-67-120(1) of the Act, and (ii) the geographic area of the abandoned building site is consistent with Section 12-67-120(2) of the Act. Section 3. All orders, resolutions, and parts thereof in conflict herewith are, to the extent of such conflict, hereby repealed. This resolution shall take effect and be in full force from and after its passage by the City Council. 14 -- 14 of 120 -- RATIFIED BY CITY COUNCIL, duly assembled this ___ day of _____________, 2024. ___________________________________ ____________________________________ Barbara Jo Blain, Mayor Larry A. ISSUE: Acceptance of bids for the replacement of the pool dehumidifier unit at the Conway Sports and Fitness Center, which has exceeded its expected operational life. BACKGROUND: The pool dehumidifier unit at the Conway Sports and Fitness Center was installed in 2012 and was designed to withstand the demands of a coastal environment for 5-8 years. After more than a decade in operation, the unit has surpassed its intended lifespan, increasing the risk of unexpected failures. Such failures could result in critical issues, including mold growth, corrosion, and hazardous air quality conditions. These risks pose potential health and safety concerns for facility users and could lead to costly repairs or operational interruptions. Regular maintenance and proactive replacement are crucial to prevent these risks and ensure a safe and functional environment within the pool area. BIDS: Two vendors have submitted proposals for replacing the pool dehumidifier unit, including sales tax: Vendor Bid Amount MSS Solutions $561,247.00 Daikin Applied $549,000.00 RECOMMENDATION: We recommend awarding the contract to MSS Solutions for the pool dehumidifier unit replacement. While their bid is slightly higher, MSS Solutions provided the most comprehensive and detailed proposal, which closely aligns with the specific needs of the Conway Sports and Fitness Center. Their proposal reflects a clear understanding of the facility’s requirements, ensuring that the new dehumidifier unit will effectively support the safety and operational needs of the pool area. This expenditure is included in the approved capital budget, underscoring the importance of investing in quality equipment to maintain a safe and reliable environment for all users of the Conway Sports and Fitness Center. 20 -- 20 of 120 -- 21 -- 21 of 120 -- 22 -- 22 of 120 -- 23 -- 23 of 120 -- 24 -- 24 of 120 -- November 4, 2024 Page 1 of 7 CITY OF CONWAY CITY COUNCIL MEETING CONWAY CITY HALL 229 MAIN STREET, CONWAY MONDAY, NOVEMBER 4, 2024 - 4:00 P.M. Presentation of Longevity Awards – October 2024 – 5 Years: Katie Dennis, Planning and Development (absent); 5 Years: Theodore Probst Jr., Solid Waste; 5 Years: Kenneth Hemingway, Recreation; 15 Years: Bess Harry, Construction Services – Emrick and Goldfinch presented the longevity awards. B. Presentation of a Proclamation Honoring Native American Heritage Month – Blain presented the Proclamation honoring Native American Heritage Month. C. Discussion of a request to annex approximately 0.80+/- total acres of property located at 2689, 2691, 2693, 2695, 2697 and 2699 Oak Street (PIN 325-15-01-0010), and rezone from the Horry County Neighborhood Commercial (NC) district to the City of Conway Neighborhood Commercial (NC) district. Hucks stated that the applicant applied for annexation as a requirement to connect to city utilities. There has been a restrictive covenant on file since 2009. When the property transferred to the current owner of the property, Summit Fuels, LLC in September of this year, and then application for a new utility account in the new owner’s name was made, the requirement to annex was triggered. The property contains two structures; one of which is the primary structure that includes several tenant spaces; the primary one being the gas station/convenience store. The smaller tenant spaces fronting on Oak Street include a pet grooming business, a restaurant, and the smaller structure in the rear of the property is used for storage. The property is currently zoned Horry County Neighborhood Commercial, and the City’s future land use map also identifies the property as Neighborhood Commercial. While the property is within the city’s utility service area and is identified on the future land use map, there are concerns that were noted by the city’s Technical Review Committee regarding the annexation of this property, including a high call volume for the police department, reoccurring violations related to business license and zoning – such as illegal vending, signage, and yard sales, and property maintenance violations. Hucks said that Planning Commission is scheduled to consider this request at their November 7 meeting and will hold the required public hearing. Planning Commission’s recommendation will be forwarded to council with first reading. PUBLIC HEARING AND FIRST READING: Public Hearing and First Reading of Ordinance #2024-11-18 Regarding the Proposed Riverfront and Downtown Redevelopment Plan – Rogers stated that this is the TIF District and Redevelopment Plan that has been discussed over the last few months. The TIF District requires cooperation from the county and the school district to create a special tax district that would affect them over the life of the TIF. Rogers said that both governing boards were sent notice and they 27 -- 27 of 120 -- November 4, 2024 Page 4 of 7 both voted against it in its current form and have asked to continue negotiations down the line. Gary Pope of Pope Flynn was present to introduce first reading. Blain reminded all that Council has already heard today regarding portions of what would be redeveloped and asked for any others that wanted to speak in favor of or against the redevelopment plan for downtown. David Jordan, Horry County Attorney, stated that Horry County does officially object with the intention of future discussions on the project. Motion: Goldfinch made a motion, seconded by Hardwick to close the public hearing. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. Gary Pope of Pope Flynn further explained the Tax Increment Financing District as what was included in Council’s packet. Discussions included future negotiations with the county and school district, time period, amount of acreage included, multi county business park potential, affordable housing, housing authority partnership, better living conditions for Lee Haven residents, parking needs, Ashpond amenities, funding mechanisms, grant money, and community education, among others. Motion: Blain made a motion, seconded by Hardwick to approve first reading of Ordinance #2024-11-18. Vote: Hardwick, Jordan, Goldfinch, Blain, Helms voted yes. White voted no. Motion carried with a 5-1 vote. CONSIDERATION: Consideration of a Resolution Authorizing a Deductible Adjustment for the South Carolina Municipal Insurance Recovery Fund (SCMIRF). Hendrick stated that staff has researched the SCMIRF, consulted with the Municipal Association and recommends changing the deductibles per incident to $5,000 for the property and auto physical damage deductible and the liability deductible to $25,000 per incident. These lower deductibles would give the city an annual savings of $152,534.78. Motion: White made a motion, seconded by Jordan, to approve the resolution authorizing a deductible adjustment for the SCMIRF. Vote: Unanimous. Motion carried. CITY ADMINISTRATOR’S REPORT: Emrick informed Council of the following: • Halloween is in the books and next year the city will go bigger. Staff has made notes on what worked well, what needs to change, and what need to be better. Emrick asked Council to please get similar notes to him while they are fresh. • For the month of October, the city had 235,000 visits. This is up 21% over last year and up 50.2% over the last two years. The busiest day of the month was the 19th with nearly 17,000 visitors. Emrick said what is an even better indicator of the success of Halloween, is a comparison to last year’s December. Last December was very busy. It was the city’s busiest 28 -- 28 of 120 -- November 4, 2024 Page 5 of 7 December ever. Last December the city had 175k visits, 60k less than this October. In fact, the busiest day of December 23, was the Parade Day, when Conway welcomed 13k, visitors to the city. That number would tie for the third busiest day in October. Emrick said he heard from a retail business that was up 103% over last year for the month with a week left to go. That same business found sales between 5 p.m. and closing out paced sales during normal hours several times over. One restaurant owner who owns two downtown businesses asked the city to have food trucks next year, because the restaurants could not keep up with the demand. • A final thought on Halloween, a new event was introduced this year in partnership with Coastal Carolina University, the Nightmare on Elm Street. The event had a fantastic turnout and hope that it is a harbinger of good luck for the season, which starts tonight at 7 pm! Go Chants. • This Thursday is the Coastal vs. App State Blackout game. Emrick said if any Council members would like to hand out towels to the first 10,000 people to attend, please meet Emrick at 6 pm at Gate 1. Emrick said he just got word earlier today that ESPN Sportscenter will be on campus at Coastal broadcasting live starting at 3pm prior to the game. Great chance for more exposure for our city. • The Stars and Strides 5k is this Saturday downtown. • An RFP is issued for interest in operating the Marina Store. The deadline is November 22. Staff will have proposals to Council at the first meeting in December for consideration. • While there is still another meeting of Council before the official kickoff of Christmas, Emrick wanted to make sure you have December 5th on your calendars for the Christmas Tree lighting. Thanksgiving is late this year, so our Christmas calendar is abbreviated, but our events and activities will not be. • Two weeks ago, our Planning Director, Jessica Hucks, presented on the successes of our last Master Plan Update and accepted on the City’s behalf, from the South Carolina Chapter of the American Planning Association, the 2024, Outstanding Planning Project for a Small Urban community for our Riverfront and Downtown Master Plan. Planning Efforts like our Master Plan are meant to guide the future of our city for the next 5, 10, even 20 years. Conway has been successful in implementing a large number of the projects in a very short 2-year window, which has greatly contributed to the ongoing successes of our downtown and riverfront area. • The city is closed on Monday for Veterans Day, but Solid Waste will be running routes as usual. • The Riverwalk Expansion has been delayed due to high water from the multiple hurricanes that hit over the summer. The water has returned to a lower level, so we hope to resume and finish construction soon. The former completion date was November 15th, we are likely a month or so behind that date. • There is one Department Head report tonight from Chief Le Hendrick. • There is no workshop tonight, although there are a few Executive Session items to consider. Fronting Hwy 501 is the University Commons commercial strip center, which is within the City limits and zoned Highway Commercial. CITY OF CONWAY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN: The future land use map of the Comprehensive Plan also identifies the property as Industrial; although it does not specify light v. heavy industrial. Per Section 3.2.13 – Light Industrial (LI), of the UDO, the intent of the LI district is to provide areas for light industrial uses, such as manufacturing, processing, repairing of goods, storage, packaging, distribution and retailing while ensuring adjacent and nearby properties are not adversely affected. BACKGROUND: The applicant submitted an annexation and rezoning application for the subject property on October 15. The property is located in the city’s water utility service area. It is adjacent to property that is within the city limits, also zoned Light Industrial, a building where other industrial-related uses are located. Other properties along Gardner Lacy Rd within the City limits includes a City of Conway water tower, the former MB National Golf Course entrance road, and Alpha Omega Construction Group. The applicant did not specify the reason for requesting annexation; however, upon review, staff noticed that 2 other adjacent properties have the same owner (501 Properties LLC), and per city ordinance, all properties owned by the applicant seeking to annex are also subject to annexation. Therefore, those properties have been included by staff in this request. Surrounding uses/Zoning Districts: Zoning immediately adjacent to the subject property is primarily industrial, but some surrounding properties within frontage on Hwy 501 is zoned Highway Commercial. To the rear of one of the parcels, closest to the railroad, adjacent zoning is Horry County Office, Professional, Institutional (OPI). Gardner Lacy Rd is a mixture of industrial and commercial uses. CITY OF CONWAY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN: The future land use map of the Comprehensive Plan also identifies the property as being industrial. Per Section 3.2.13 – Light Industrial (LI), the intent of the LI district is to provide areas for light industrial uses, such as manufacturing, processing, repairing of goods, wholesaling, storage, packaging, distribution and retailing while ensuring adjacent and nearby properties are not adversely impacted. PLANNING COMMISSION: Planning Commission will hold the required public hearing on the request at their December 12th meeting. ISSUE: Special Presentation of a request to rezone approximately 0.70+/- total acres of property located at 1318 and 1320 Fourth Ave (PINs 368-04-01-0021 and -0022) from the Core Commercial (CC) and Medium- Density Residential (R-2) districts to the Core Commercial (CC) district. BACKGROUND: The applicant applied to rezone the subject properties following inquiring about leasing the building(s) for a beauty salon. One of the properties had been vacant for six (6) months or longer, triggering the requirement to bring the site into compliance with the current requirements of the UDO. Upon review, staff realized that the adjacent property (1320 Fourth Ave), owned by the same property owner, along with the property seeking to be utilized, was split-zoned CC and R-2. The parking lots for both properties are located behind the buildings and zoned R-2 (medium-density residential). As such, staff recommended that both properties be rezoned to remove the R-2 zoning designation and split zoning status of the properties, bringing the zoning into compliance. Per Section 3.2.4 – Medium Density Residential (R-2), the intent of the R-2 district is to provide for areas for medium density attached, detached, semi-attached, and multifamily residential development in the City of Conway, and to prohibit uses that would substantially interfere with the development or continuation of residential structures in the District. Per Section 3.2.11 – Core Commercial (CC), the intent of the CC district is to establish a thriving commercial and mixed-use district adjacent to the Central Business District that provides form and use of development compatible to that of the CBD, but not as strict with regards to design standards. Surrounding uses/Zoning Districts: A majority of the properties surrounding the subject properties are zoned CC, with one property that fronts on Fifth Ave zoned R-2. Surrounding businesses include professional services, such as financial institutions, insurance companies, legal services, accounting services, etc. CITY OF CONWAY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN: The future land use map of the Comprehensive Plan identifies the property as being mixed-use and medium-density residential. ISSUE: First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2024-12-02 (A), to annex approximately 0.45 acres located at 2408 Cultra Rd (PIN 325-15-02-0017), and rezone from the Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF20) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district. BACKGROUND: The annexation application was submitted as a requirement for a name change in the city utility services (considered a new account). This property is within the city’s water and sewer utility service area. This property is across the road from a new development, Kingston Bay, currently being constructed. There have been a few other properties on this side of Cultra Rd over the past few years that have been required to request annexation since the Kingston Bay property was annexed. In those instances, Council chose not to annex the properties. The closest properties on this side of Cultra Rd between Oak Street and Main Street that are currently within the city limits are those within or directly adjacent to the Ivy Glen subdivision. The property contains a single-family residence. A restrictive covenant was recorded on December 2, 2003. CITY OF CONWAY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN: The Future Land Use Map of the Comprehensive Plan identifies this property as Low/Medium Density Residential (R-1). BACKGROUND: The property is requesting annexation as a requirement to connect to city service. The property was transferred in September of this year to Summit Fuel, LLC. The property has had a restrictive covenant on file since August of 2009. Currently there are two buildings and a gas canopy on the property. The building units are used for a variety of different businesses including a convenience/gas station, dog groomer, a restaurant and the rear building is used as a storage facility. Per Section 3.2.9 Neighborhood Commercial (NC)-The NC District is intended to provide small-scale retail, and service uses for nearby residential areas. Dimensional requirements and design standards of the NC district are intended to promote compatibility to surrounding residential areas and accommodate pedestrian use and access. Strip commercial development, designed primarily to accommodate vehicular access and parking, and development that is insensitive or incompatible with the scale and character of the surrounding residential areas, is discouraged in this district. Surrounding uses/Zoning Districts: The property abuts parcels zoned City of Conway Neighborhood Commercial (NC) District, Horry County Neighborhood Commercial (NC), Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF20) district, Horry County Residential, including mobile homes (MSF20) district, and Horry County Commercial Forest and Agriculture (CFA) district. Additionally, there have been instances of unauthorized vending occurring within the parking lot, including yard sales and a mobile food truck, which disrupts operations of convenience store and poses potential risks. -Business License • The property would be subject to the city property maintenance requirements. It is recommended that the landscaping be maintained, and parking lot be fixed prior to annexation.- Construction Services 103 -- 103 of 120 -- • The county has done nothing for stormwater issues at this location and staff in concerned about what issues would be inherited by the city. -Public Works CITY OF CONWAY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN: The future land use map of the Comprehensive Plan also identifies the property as Neighborhood Commercial. There was no public input. However, the city has been consistently annexing properties along Oak Street, and staff foresees other properties along Oak Street being annexed in the near future as properties change hands. As it stands, this property is a donut hole, it is within the city’s utility service area, and it’s located on the same side of Cultra Rd / Oak Street as other properties that have been annexed in recent years. ISSUE: First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2024-12-02 (C), regarding proposed amendments to Article 6 – Design Standards, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) to remove El Bethel Road from the Village Corridor Overlay (VCO). BACKGROUND: The Village Corridor Overlay (VCO), per Section 3.4.3 of the UDO, is intended to promote compact, pedestrian-scale development with residential, neighborhood commercial, professional, and office uses. The VCO zoning includes properties fronting on minor arterials and collector streets designated on the city’s zoning map. The VCO extends 250 feet from the right-of-way line for properties along these streets, and any property or building that has any portion within the 250-ft overlay boundary is subject to the regulations of the VCO. Regulations within the VCO include building massing/modulation, access management, connectivity, landscaping and buffer requirements, site design and parking, and sign limitations. Currently, the following roads are subject to the requirements of the VCO: • El Bethel Rd (+/-150’ right-of-way width) • Cultra Rd (right-of-way width varies but majority is 66’) • Mill Pond Rd (right-of-way width varies from +/-80’ to +/-125’. A small portion of Mill Pond exceeds 150’ in right-of-way width) • Sixteenth Ave, between Main Street & Church St (Hwy 501) (right-of-way width varies from +/- 60’ to +/-88’) • 16th Ave, between Church St (Hwy 501) & Hwy 378 (right-of-way width varies from +/-50’ to +/-80’) The El Bethel Rd right-of-way (150’) is wider than most of the other roadways within the VCO. Additionally, the landscape and character of El Bethel Rd has changed within the last few years, with several rezoning requests approved for institutional or medical uses. As such, there are some standards within the VCO that could be difficult for these types of uses to adhere to, with the potential for variances to be sought on signage, height limitation, connectivity requirements, landscaping/buffer requirements, etc. Horry County Schools applied for and was granted a variance on signage last year for the new Whittemore Park Middle School on El Bethel Rd. As such, staff proposes to amend Section 6.5.3 (B) – Applicability, of the VCO to exclude El Bethel Rd from the requirements of the VCO, therefore making the properties along El Bethel Rd subject to the standard requirements of the City’s Unified Development Ordinance. 115 -- 115 of 120 -- PLANNING COMMISSION Planning Commission held the required public hearing at their November 7, 2024 meeting and recommended approval to remove El Bethel Road from the Village Corridor Overlay (VCO). RECOMMENDATION Staff recommends approval of First Reading of Ordinance #ZA2024-12-02 (C), regarding revisions to remove El Bethel Road from the Village Corridor Overlay (VCO). 116 -- 116 of 120 -- ORDINANCE #ZA2024-12-02 (C) AMENDMENT TO ARTICLE 6 – DESIGN STANDARDS, OF THE CITY OF CONWAY UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE (UDO) TO REMOVE EL BETHEL ROAD FROM THE VILLAGE CORRIDOR OVERLAY (VCO). WHEREAS, Pursuant to Title 6, Chapter 29 of the Code of Laws of South Carolina 1976, as Amended known as the “South Carolina Local Government Comprehensive Planning Enabling Act of 1994” enabled the City of Conway to adopt the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) of the City of Conway, South Carolina; and WHEREAS, Article 13, Section 13.1.7 of the UDO provides that the regulations, restrictions, and boundaries set forth in said Ordinance may from time be amended, supplemented, changed, or repealed in accordance with S.C. State Code §6-29-760; and WHEREAS, the Village Corridor Overlay (VCO) is intended to promote compact, pedestrian-scale development within the City limits of Conway; and WHEREAS, El Bethel Rd has a right of way of 150-ft; wider than the other corridors that are identified as being within the VCO and the character of El Bethel Rd has changed significantly over the last several years, with more properties being rezoned for educational and medical development; and WHEREAS, El Bethel Rd is also proposed to be part of the Conway Perimeter Rd, which will become another gateway corridor into the city; and WHEREAS, following a review by Planning Commission and the required public hearing, it has been determined that the UDO should be amended relative to the removal of El Bethel Rd from the Village Corridor Overlay (VCO). Therefore, be it ORDAINED by the City Council of the City of Conway, in Council duly assembled, that the UDO be amended as attached hereto; and be it further ORDAINED, that all ordinances or parts of ordinances inconsistent with this Ordinance are hereby repealed to the extent of such inconsistency. EFFECTIVE DATE: This ordinance shall become effective upon final reading. 117 -- 117 of 120 -- Article 6. Design Standards 6.5.3 Village Corridor Overlay Zone (VCO) B. Applicability The boundaries of the VCO shall be as shown on a map titled Village Corridor Overlay Zone which is hereby adopted and made a part of the UDO, and which may be amended from time to time in accordance with the procedures established in the UDO. The VCO shall only include El Bethel Road, Cultra Road, Mill Pond Road, and Sixteenth Avenue between Main Street and Church Street (Highway 501). The VCO shall include all properties fronting on these roads designated on the overlay zone map. Properties annexed into the City of Conway shall be required to conform to the VCO regulations. Any property or building that has any portion within the 250-feet overlay boundary shall comply with these regulations. Construction or renovation of any buildings located beyond the 250-feet overlay boundary shall be required if visible from the corridor. Single-family developments (less than 5 homes) are exempt from the VCO standards. Renovated or newly constructed commercial, multi-family residential, or office developments that are located partially or completely within the boundaries indicated above shall comply with the regulations established below.
