title: APPD-BZA MINUTES 1.25.24
text: Board of Zoning Appeals 1/25/24 CITY OF CONWAY BOARD OF ZONING APPEALS MEETING THURSDAY, JANUARY 235, 2024 BUILDING & PLANNING DEPARTMENT 196 LAUREL STREET Present: Paul Lawson, Lesley Hill, Sandra James, Catherine Dingle, Jay Sellers Absent: Blake Hendrick Staff: Kym Wilkerson, Zoning Administrator, Anne Bessant, Planning Assistant; Jeff Leveille, IT Others: Megan Newbold, Terry Buchmann, Jorome Simiyon, Jon Michael Williamson, Rein Mungo, Lloyd R. Dunn, Betty Grissett, Marc Monley, Charles Rietman, Nobi Rietman, Van Davenport, Kenneth Williams I. CALL TO ORDER Chairman Lawson called the meeting to order at approximately 5:31 p.m. IL. ELECTION OF OFFICERS James made a motion to elect Lawson as the Chairman of the Board of Zoning Appeals for 2024, Dingle seconded the motion and the motion carried unanimously. James made a motion to elect Dingle as the Vice-Chairperson of the Board of Zoning Appeals for 2024. Hill seconded the motion and the motion carried unanimously. I. APPROVAL OF MINUTES Hill made a motion, seconded by Lawson to approve the December 14, 2023 minutes as written. The vote in favor was unanimous and the motion carried. Lawson swore in the applicants and staff. Iv. CRITERIA Lawson read the following four criteria required to be met in order for the Board to grant a variance: Extraordinary conditions: There are extraordinary and exceptional conditions pertaining to the particular piece of property; Other Property: The extraordinary and exceptional conditions do not generally apply to other property in the vicinity; Board of Zoning Appeals 1/25/24 Utilization: Because of the extraordinary or exceptional conditions, the application of the ordinance to a particular piece of property would effectively prohibit or unreasonably restrict the utilization of the property; Detriment: The authorization of a variance will not be of substantial detriment to the adjacent property or the public good and the character of the district will not be harmed by granting a variance. Vv. VARIANCE REQUESTS/PUBLIC INPUT A. Betty Grissett, agent for her husband, Mark Onley, property owner, request a variance from the strict application of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), Article 6-Design Standards, for the property located at 604 McCray Alley. (PIN 368-03-01-0038) Wilkerson stated that the applicant’s home, located at 604 McCray Alley, suffered fire damage. The applicant’s originally intended to renovate what is left of the structure; however, the Building Department posted the structure as “unsafe” due to damage from the fire. Per the Building Inspector, the home suffered major damage including rafters and roof damage. The house will need to be rewired and plumbed due to the fire. Additionally, the foundation needs support added in several areas and exterior wall studs/supports show evidence of termite damage. The applicants have chosen to build a new home and have building plans ready to submit for a permit; however, they were advised to apply for the variance first. The parcel is zoned R1 and is considered “/egal non-conforming” since the width of the lot at the ROW does not meet the current UDO standards of 75-ft. The lot is only 34.76-ft wide. The only dwelling type permitted in the R1 zoning district is single family detached. The setbacks in the R1 zoning district are 20- ft Front, 20-ft Rear and 10-ft Sides. The applicant is requesting a 5-ft variance on both side setback requirements from 10-ft to 5-ft in order to build a single family detached home. The applicant is seeking a variance from: e Table 6.1: Dimensional Requirements for Residential Zoning Districts The applicant requests a variance of 5-ft on the side setback allowing for a 5-ft side setback on both sides of the property Staff recommends that the BZA conduct a thorough review of the request and determine if a legal hardship exists and if the best interests of the City of Conway would be served by granting the request. The applicant was present to answer any questions. Board of Zoning Appeals 1/25/24 There was no public input. Lawson made a motion to grant the variance as requested. Hill seconded the motion and the motion carried unanimously. B. Megan Newbold, AIA, with Garvin Design Group and agent for Coastal Carolina University, property owner, request a variance from the strict application of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), Article 6-Design Standards, for the property located at Highway 544 and University Boulevard. (PIN 382-00-00- 0039) Wilkerson stated the applicant currently has plans in review for a new CCU Indoor Practice Facility. The parcel is zoned Institutional (IN) and is within the Gateway Corridor Overlay (GCO). The initial submittal made the applicant aware that the facility must meet the requirements of the Gateway Corridor Overlay (GCO). Per Section 6.3.1-Nonresidential Architectural Design Standards of the UDO: D: P, NC, HC, CC, CBD, GCO, and VCO: Properties that are located outside of the HDRDs shall be reviewed and approved by the Planning Department and shall meet the following architectural design standards: 9: “No portion of a building constructed of unadorned concrete masonry units or corrugated metal, sheet metal, exposed metal, and / or manufactured panelized metal wall systems shall be visible in any manner from adjoining developed properties, from existing public rights-of-way, or from adjoining properties which are eligible for future development.” Though staff can appreciate that the structure is atheistically appealing, our role is to enforce the UDO as written. The applicant is seeking a variance from: e Section 6.3.1-Nonresidential Architectural Design Standards The applicant requests a variance from D-9 of the above section in order to allow exposed metal as part of the facade of the new CCU Indoor Practice Facility Staff recommends that the BZA conduct a thorough review of the request and determine if a legal hardship exists and if the best interests of the City of Conway would be served by granting the request. Rein Mungo, agent for owners, was present and further explained the request. Charles Rietman spoke during public input. Board of Zoning Appeals 1/25/24 Lawson made a motion to grant the variance as requested. Sellers seconded the motion and the motion carried unanimously. C. Matthew Norris with DN Engineering and T. Van Davenport, agents for Shannon Burchett, property owner, request a variance from the strict application of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), Article 6-Design Standards, for the property located at 2206 Church Street. (PIN 338-08-04-0001) Wilkerson stated the parcel is zoned Highway Commercial (HC) and was annexed into the City of Conway as Highway Commercial in 2006. The applicant is proposing a Commercial Strip Center on this parcel. The City of Conway’s Technical Review Committee (TRC) has reviewed a one-page sketch plan which triggered a comment concerning the dumpster location. Per Section 6.6.2 —- Mechanical Equipment, Dumpster, Recycling, and Trash Handling, of the UDO: e B: Location. The location of all utilities and trash handling facilities shall be in the rear or side yards. No such facilities shall be located in any yard adjacent to a public street. The parcel is a corner lot with Highway 501 (Church Street) as the front yard and Village Street as the comer front yard. If the dumpster is placed on the parcel meeting the UDO requirements, it will be against the residential parcels that abut this parcel in the rear and on the side. Reggie Jenerette, Sanitation Director, has approved the location along Village Street for the purposes of sanitation trucks entering and exiting with the condition that the applicant follow the City of Conway’s Double Dumpster Specs. (attached) Section 6.6.2 —- Mechanical Equipment, Dumpster, Recycling, and Trash Handling, of the UDO also states: e C-2: Screening. The Appropriate screening includes: A wall OR opaque fence (excluding chain- link), a minimum of six (6) feet in height and constructed of materials approved by TRC. Shrubs, earth berm, and/or understory trees may be required in conjunction with a fence/wall to further obscure such facilities. Staff has not seen a landscaping plan yet but should the variance be granted, staff would like the board to consider adding a condition that additional landscaping be utilized in conjunction with the wall or fence to further obscure the dumpster facility. The applicant is seeking a variance from: e Section 6.6.2 — Mechanical Equipment, Dumpster, Recycling, and Trash Handling A variance to allow the dumpster facility to be located in the corner front yard along Village Street with the condition that the dumpster facility be screened by the required wall or fence as well as additional landscaping to further obscure the facility from the public right-of-way and Board of Zoning Appeals 1/25/24 adjacent properties. Van Davenport, owner was present to answer any questions. Lloyd Randall Dunn and Kenneth Williams expressed concerns during public input about the lack of an effective sound barrier between the dumpster and their residence when it is emptied early in the mornings. Lawson made a motion to grant the variance with the condition that the dumpster facility be screened by the required wall or fence, as well as additional landscaping to further obscure the facility from the public right-of-way and adjacent properties. Dingle seconded the motion and the motion carried unanimously. VI. AJOURN There being no further business to come before the Board, a motion was made and seconded to adjourn the meeting. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried and the meeting was adjourned at 6:07p.m. “7 7 Le J Approved and signed this (“C-<—dayof 7 CUM& _. 2024. \ ——— « : = —_ Phot son, Chain

According to the legend, on Sept. 22, 1989, then-South Carolina Gov. Carroll Campbell Jr. and famed evangelist Rev. Billy Graham flew in by helicopter to Garden City to survey the damage done by the hurricane. Thompson — who has been taking photos in the area since the early 1950s — met them to photograph Graham’s sermon at a local Baptist church. Campbell asked Graham “have you met my good friend, the photographer Jack Thompson?” Graham turned to the governor and replied “I was about to ask you the same thing.” Turns out, truth is far stranger than fiction. “Yeah ... that’s actually a true story,” Thomp- son said with a smile. “History is a web we weave ... a mysterious web.” Thompson — who just turned 90 last month — has been taking photographs in the Myrtle Beach area since 1953 ... chronicling the visual history of the Grand Strand for more than 75 years. “Jack is a living legend,” Myrtle Beach Mayor Mark Kruea said. “He’s a living history book ... he’s seen Myrtle Beach grow and change. “Jack probably knows more about Myrtle Beach than anyone,” Kruea said. The City of Myrtle Beach officially pro- claimed his birthday, Sept. 21, as “Jack Thomp- son Day,” although that is hardly the first honor he has received for his life’s work docu- menting a small tourist town that became one of the most visited city’s in the world. Last year, Thompson received the Order of the Palmetto, South Carolina’s highest civilian award. Thompson received the honor in the Myrtle Beach Train Depot, a building he peti- tioned to save and restore back when the city had plans to tear it down more than 20 years ago. Thompson also was awarded an honorary fine arts doctorate degree from Coastal Caroli- na University in 2006. “My dad always told me if I worked hard I’d become a doctor one day ... he was right after all,” Thompson said holding up the ring he received from the CCU. Thompson shrugs off his living legend sta- tus, but does acknowledge that he’s had an incredible journey. “A lot of people make a fuss over an old photographer like me,” Thompson said. “But I guess I’ve been everywhere and done just about everything ... it does seem kind of unbe- lievable at times.” “SOUNDED LIKE FUN” Thompson and some of his friends ran away from home and hitchhiked to Myrtle Beach in 1953 when Thompson was 13 years old. “Some of the older guys were coming back after weekends and talking about Myrtle Beach and the shagging and the girls ... It sounded like fun.” One of Thompson’s fellow runaways was Carroll Campbell Jr., the future governor of South Carolina. “Carroll was one of those guys that would always button the top button of his shirt because his mother told him it was good man- ners,” Thompson said. “I remember telling him that we were hitchhiking and we were run- aways ... just lighten up a little.” The day Thompson got to Myrtle Beach, he landed a job at a photo booth on the Pavilion ... which set him in on the course that would guide him for the next 75 years “I was lucky to find out what I wanted to do early in life,” Thompson said. Although the families of his friends came to Myrtle Beach and took them back to Green- ville, Thompson’s luck held out when his brother arrived to the Grand Strand to take him home. “My brother told me that he was taking me home and that I had done a bad thing,” he said. “But he said that he wasn’t going to take me back until the next day because he was going to go out into the beach and get a tan that day. “He came back that night with his arm around a pretty girl,” Thompson said. “Then he said those famous words to me ... ‘I’m not going home either.’” Thompson and his brother received permis- sion from their parents to stay in Myrtle Beach provided that they would remain in school and secure jobs. “I was able to get my brother a job at Skip’s Photos with me,” Thompson said. “Although most days I would work my shift and his shift while he was at the beach with Doris.” “IT WAS A WONDERFUL LIFE” Thompson continued his education, work- ing at the photo booth on weekends through the school year. However, during the summer season, Thompson discovered why he origi- nally was drawn to photography. “Oh, I would take a picture of a pretty girl in front of a crescent moon or something,” Thompson said. “I worked in a one-hour photo booth and would take them in the booth and they would watch as I would put the print in four different solutions. They were always amazed at how the image would just appear. “During the summer, I had to put a stool in the booth for girls to sit on,” he said. “I remem- ber being sad when the girls would go back home on Sunday morning ... but by Sunday evening, there was always another girl sitting on that stool.” Kruea, who has been friends with Thomp- son for decades, was not surprised. “I’ve heard Jack was a bit of a ladies man,” he said laughing. “He took full advantage of all that Myrtle Beach had to offer.” Thompson briefly considered a career change as a teenager after winning a local tal- ent show. “I would always sing to the girls when we walked on the beach,” Thompson said. “I won $500 at a talent show singing a Frankie Valli song. I thought about becoming a singer. “But back then, Myrtle Beach was about Shag dancing and beer,” he said. “There wasn’t a lot of demand for a romantic singer in those days so I stuck with photography.” “EVERYONE AND EVERYTHING” After graduating from Myrtle Beach High School, Thompson took a photographer job which allowed him to travel for several years throughout the United States. “I was photographing children for J.C. Penny, for a couple of years,” Thompson said. “I was going to do a book about it called ‘I shot a million kids’ ... but then I realized that proba- bly wasn’t the best title for a book.” After about two years, Thompson returned to the Grand Strand, where he started the work that would make him the unofficial historian of the area, eventually opening his own studio in 1967. “I came back and started shooting every- thing and everybody,” Thompson said. “My father worked in journalism and he told me to photograph everything I could because it would become part of history ... so that’s what I did.” Thompson said that even through leaner times, his commitment to capturing the histo- ry of the area remained strong. “My wife at one point wanted me to go and sell shoes for this company that existed back then,” Thompson said. “I wouldn’t give up my camera, though ... this was what I had chosen to do and I stuck with it.” Thompson said some of his most icon- ic images were taken with a Graflex Speed Graphic — a famous large-format folding press camera produced from 1912 to 1973 that became the defining tool for American photo- journalism. “I had this beautiful Speed Graphic that I shot everything with,” Thompson said. “I loved that camera and I swore that I would never stoop to using a 35 mm camera. I did eventu- ally get a Nikon and used it for a majority of my career, but I really missed my old camera. Some of my best work was shot with that.” Through the decades, Thompson’s work has visually captured the history of the area ... places are packed with businesses and houses today were captured by Thompson when they were little more than grass, trees and gravel roads. “Looking at Jack’s work is like stepping back in time,” Kruea said. “He captured Myrtle Beach for an entire generation.” Thompson not only captured the places in the Myrtle Beach area, he also captured the people that lived and visited the Grand Strand for the past 75 years, including a fair share of celebrities. “There have been so many that have come through here,” Thompson said. “Dolly Parton, Billy Graham, Slim Pickens, that fella that played Hoss on Bonanza ... and many more. “Of course, I photographed Vanna White since she was a kid,” Thompson said. “I took her school pictures when she was in the sev- enth grade and she told me to stop showing that picture to people because she thought she looked terrible.” Thompson said he captured many of his iconic images “completely in the spur of the moment.” “Most of my work wasn’t planned,” Thomp- son said. “It was more like I was guided to a spot where I could capture something that only existed for that exact moment.” APPRECIATING THE SUNSETS In 2022, Thompson had to pack up his stu- dio on 9th Avenue North after the property was sold and the owners planned on redeveloping the building. All his photographs and neg- atives currently are in four different storage buildings in the city. Thompson, who still meets customers inter- ested in his work, does his business in the lobby of the Surfside Beach Oceanfront Hotel at 15 Ocean Boulevard in Surfside Beach, which is not surprising since the entire hotel is decorated with his photos. “They let me use the lobby whenever I need to meet someone,” he said. “They’re really great about it.” Thompson said that lately he has been considering letting someone else become the caretaker of his life’s work. “I’m beginning to admire the sunset more than the sunrise,” Thompson said. “Maybe it’s time someone becomes the caretaker of the history of the Grand Strand.” Thompson said he is considering selling his archives, which is acknowledged as the defin- itive visual history of the area with more than 100,000 images. Thompson said the bidding would start at $1 million. “I guess I’ll put it out there that I’m offering my archive to the highest bidder,” he said. “I am looking for an investor that is interested in purchasing the history of the Grand Strand, especially Myrtle Beach.” Of course, any potential buyer can expect a few more images from Thompson to add to the collection. “The mayor asked me on my 90th birthday what I thought my best shot was,” Thompson said. “I’ll tell you what I told him ... I haven’t taken my best shot yet.” PO # 10139 FILE PHOTO Longtime Myrtle Beach photographer Jack Thompson. In place of a second external access point, the plan shows two (2) gates drives connecting to an unnamed County-maintained road. The applicant proposes that these drives be used for emergency access only. The unnamed road and Mill Berry Lane, which connects to it, are unpaved roads surfaced with granular millings. The staff illustration shows field measurements of approximately 12, 14, and 15 feet at locations along the access route. Staff took these measurements during a September 2026 field inspection. The subdivision plan and staff illustration are included with this report, in addition to aerial photos and photos taken by staff during a previous site visit. Note: The “measuring tool” icons shown on the staff illustration depict travel-lane widths as measured by staff during a field inspection in: Sep. 2026. Access Management Access management standards are intended to provide sufficient ingress and egress under normal traffic conditions, reduce the effect of development traffic on adjoining roadways, and provide alternative access in the event of an emergency or a roadway repair or obstruction. -- 11 of 114 -- STAFF REPORT Design Modification: Maplewood Estates Sec. 7.2.1(E)(1) of the UDO requires a minimum of 2 points of ingress and egress for single-family developments of 30 or more lots. The UDO (Sec. 2.2.1) defines “External Access” as access points along a development’s boundaries that connect to existing paved public roadways abutting the project. The proposed subdivision has one external access point from Long Ave Ext. The two proposed gated drives connect to the unnamed, unpaved County-maintained road. Because that road is not paved, the proposed drives do not appear to qualify as the second external access point under the UDO’s definition. The drives are proposed for emergency use only and do not meet the minimum fire-apparatus access standards. The City’s Fire Marshal does not support the proposed emergency-access management. He stated that the proposed route does not meet fire-apparatus access requirements, which include: • A minimum unobstructed width of 20 feet, exclusive of the shoulder; • A road designed, constructed, and maintained to support imposed loads of at least 75,000 pounds; • Asphalt, concrete, or another approved all-weather, dust-free driving surface; and • An unobstructed vertical clearance of at least 13 feet, 6 inches. Andy Markunas, Horry County’s Engineer, stated that Mill Berry Lane is in Group 3 of the RIDE 4 dirt-road list and is not expected to be paved for at least 10 to 15 years, or later. He also stated that the unnamed road currently has millings and is not included in RIDE 4. Right-of-Way The existing, unnamed road has a right-of-way width of 30 feet. The applicant proposes to provide an easement along the project frontage, rather than fee-simple right-of-way dedication, to accommodate a sidewalk and area for future road improvements by the County or City. Sec. 10.5.2(B) of the UDO states that when a development fronts an existing street segment maintained by the City, Horry County, or SCDOT that does not meet the minimum standards for its street classification, the applicant shall dedicate additional right-of-way. Sec. 10.5.2(C) requires the applicant to construct a sidewalk when one does not exist in the right-of-way. Finally, Sec. 7.1.2(D) requires a land dedication when sidewalk construction is not possible within a right-of-way, unless special circumstances apply. The County Engineer prefers fee-simple right-of-way dedication to 25 feet from the centerline of the roadway to avoid uncertainty over the right-of-way and its relationship to the future HOA. The applicant’s proposed easement would not provide the fee-simple dedication requested by the County Engineer. Requiring the additional right-of-way and applicable improvements during development would: • Allow perimeter landscape buffers to be established without later disturbance from road acquisition or construction; • Provide land for future road improvements without requiring a later acquisition process; -- 12 of 114 -- STAFF REPORT Design Modification: Maplewood Estates • Help ensure that lots and open space remain compliant with UDO dimensional standards if the road is widened; • Maintain the approved building setbacks relative to the property lines established on the final plat rather than structures becoming nonconforming in the future due to relation of property boundaries; and • Address the right-of-way and required roadway improvements as part of the subdivision approval, ensuring that infrastructure needed to serve the development is provided when the lots are created rather than deferred to a future owner or public agency. The City’s Public Works Director, Brandon Harrrelson, stated that the road may eventually be conveyed to the City. He advised that the City is not in a position to accept a gravel road and that required improvements should be completed by the developer as part of the project. He also noted that accepting the road without the required improvements could leave the City responsible for bringing it up to City standards at taxpayer expense. PLANNING COMMISSION MTG DATE: November 5, 2026 AGENDA ITEM: VI.A. ISSUE: Consideration of amendments of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), to amend Article 2 – Definitions, Article 6 – Design Standards, and Article 8 – Off-Street Parking & Loading, to define Driveway Throat Length, establish driveway throat-length requirements for development within the Gateway Corridor Overlay (GCO) district, and establish separate minimum and maximum parking requirements for Shopping Centers and Strip Commercial development. BACKGROUND (Updated): The original amendments to Article 8 proposed separate parking standards for Shopping Centers and Strip Commercial development and minimum driveway throat length requirements applicable throughout the City. Planning Commission held a public hearing on these proposed amendments at its September 3rd meeting, and recommended approval of the amendments. City Council subsequently remanded the amendment for further review after concerns were raised from developers about applying the proposed throat lengths to smaller commercial and infill properties. The parking component was not the focus of the remand and remains substantively unchanged. The driveway throat length component has been revised to apply only within the Gateway Corridor Overlay District and to authorize the TRC to modify or waive the minimum requirement when strict compliance is impracticable and a safe alternative design is provided. Parking Requirements Table 8.3 currently applies the same parking range to Shopping Centers and Strip Commercial development. The amendment would retain the Shopping Center standard and establish a separate Strip Commercial range of one space per 150 sq. ft. minimum and one space per 100 sq. ft. maximum. Parking is calculated using the building’s total gross floor area, not the number of tenants. For example, a 7,500 sq. ft. Strip Commercial building currently requires a minimum of 27 spaces. The proposed standard would require a minimum of 50 spaces, while the maximum permitted parking would increase from approx. 45 spaces to 75 spaces. The revised standard is intended to better accommodate future tenant changes and reduce parking shortages and spillover parking. Driveway Throat Length / Revisions following September 21st City Council meeting: Driveway throat length is the unobstructed distance between the adjoining street and the first onsite point of vehicular conflict. Article 2 – Definitions, of the UDO, would define the term, Article 6 – Design Standards (Sec. 6.5.2), would establish the GCO-specific standards, and Article 8 – Off-street Parking and Loading (Sec. 8.2.7), would cross-reference those standards, as well as incorporate housekeeping revisions. -- 98 of 114 -- The revised amendment makes the following changes: 1. Limits the minimum throat length requirements to development within the Gateway Corridor Overlay District, where development is generally more automobile-oriented and access is commonly provided from major roadway corridors. 2. Applies the standards to new development, redevelopment requiring site plan approval, new or relocated driveways, and changes to internal circulation that affect the available throat length. 3. Establishes ranges of 20 to 50 feet for entrances serving major residential subdivisions and multifamily development; 30 to 50 feet for small commercial sites, individual commercial outparcels, and Strip Commercial development; and 200 to 250 feet for Shopping Centers and bib- box retail establishments. 4. Authorizes TRC to determine the required distance within each range based on development intensity, anticipated traffic and queuing, access-control features, roadway classification, driveway location, internal circulation, and an approved traffic impact analysis, where applicable. 5. Authorizes TRC to modify or waive the minimum requirement when strict compliance is impracticable because of site configuration, existing development or access limitations, environmental or topographic constraints, the nature and intensity of the proposed use, or other site- specific conditions. Any modified design must provide the maximum throat length practicable and safely accommodate anticipated traffic without causing vehicles to queue, stop, or back into the adjoining street. 6. Updated related GCO provisions governing inter-parcel access, shared access points, paving, and recorded access and maintenance agreements, and revised Section 8.2.7 to clarify general driveway access standards and cross-reference the GCO requirements. STAFF ANALYSIS: Limiting the throat length standards to the GCO focuses the requirement on the City’s principal automobile- oriented corridors, where development intensity, turning movements, drive-thru uses, and shared commercial access are most likely to create queuing and circulation conflicts. It also avoids imposing the same dimensional standard on smaller commercial properties elsewhere in the City that may not generate comparable traffic or have sufficient depth to comply. TRC’s authority to select the appropriate distance within each range and to modify or waive the minimum provides additional flexibility for constrained properties in the GCO. The proposed findings require the relief to be based on site-specific conditions and continued safe operation, while allowing TRC to require a traffic analysis or other supporting documentation. -- 99 of 114 -- The parking amendment remains prospective and aligns Table 8.3 with the definitions adopted in May 2026. Establishing a separate Strip Commercial standard will better accommodate changes in tenant occupancy over the life of a development and reduce the likelihood of parking shortages and spillover parking, while leaving the existing Shopping Center standard unchanged. PLANNING COMMISSION: Staff recommends that in addition to holding the required public hearing, that Planning Commission review the proposed amendment, and make an informed recommendation to City Council. ISSUE: Consideration of amendments of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), to amend Article 2 – Definitions and Article 6 – Design Standards, to revise the definition and method of measuring building height and to clarify the applicability and exceptions to the City’s building height regulations. BACKGROUND AND ANALYSIS: The current definition of ‘building height’ establishes a measurement as the highest vertical distance from finished grade at the building line to the “average height of the roof.” However, the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) does not define “average height of roof” or provide a method for calculating it. This ambiguity may result in differing interpretations, particularly for buildings containing pitched roofs, multiple rooflines, varying ridge and eave elevations, parapets, or other architectural features. Under the current language, it is unclear whether the average roof height should be determined by measuring to the midpoint between the eave and ridge, averaging the elevations of multiple roof sections, or applying another methodology. Consequently, the existing definition may be difficult to administer consistently and may create uncertainty during building design and plan review. The proposed amendment removes the undefined reference to the “average height of the roof” and establishes the highest applicable point of one building as the controlling point for measuring building height. This provides a clear and more objective standard that can be depicted on architectural elevations and verified during plan review. The revised definition also addresses variations in finished grade. When the finished grade varies around a building, building height would be measured from the average grade elevation. This establishes a consistent point of reference for buildings located on sloping or uneven sites and avoids relying on a single isolated high or low point. Section 6.1.12 is also proposed to be amended to incorporate the revised measurement method and ensure consistency with the definition contained in Article 2. The revised section will continue to direct applicants to the applicable height limitations established in Table 6.1 for residential uses and Table 6.2 for nonresidential uses. It will also retain the existing exceptions for architectural features identified in Section 6.1.13. -- 112 of 114 -- STAFF REPORT UDO Amendment regarding Building Height Figure 6.3 (right) will illustrate the revised measurement method, providing additional guidance for applicants, design professionals, and staff. The proposed amendments are intended to: • Eliminate the undefined and potentially subjective reference to the “average height of roof”; • Establish the highest applicable point of the building as the controlling measurement; • Provide a consistent method for buildings located on sites where finished grade varies; • Ensure consistency between the Article 2 definition and the building height provisions of Sec. 6.1.12; • Preserve the existing exceptions for architectural features identified in Sec. 6.1.13; and • Improve predictability and consistency during plan review and ordinance administration. PROPOSED AMENDMENTS: Article 2 – Definition of Building Height Building Height (new definition): The measurement from the finished grade to the highest vertical distance (highest point), excepting that those architectural features identified in Sec. 6.1.13. If the finished grade varies, the measurement is determined from the average grade elevation. Art. 6, Sec. 6.1.12 – Building Height Buildings and structures are subject to the height limitations established in Table 6.1 for Residential Uses or Table 6.2 for Nonresidential Uses. Building height shall be measured from the finished grade to the highest vertical distance (highest point), excepting those architectural features identified in Sec. 6.1.13, as illustrated in Figure 6.3 (below). See Article 2 for a complete definition of Building Height. RECOMMENDED ACTION: The proposed revisions remove an undefined and potentially subjective measurement method and establish a more objective standard for determining building height. The amendments also ensure consistency between the definition contained in Article 2, the measurement provisions of Section 6.1.12, and the accompanying illustration. Request to rezone approximately 26.98+/- acres of property located at 585 and 605 Century Circle (PIN: 383-00-00-0344), from Horry County Planned Unit Development (PUD) district to the City of Conway Institutional (IN) district upon annexation. Hucks stated the rezoning request was intended to facilitate development of the property in conjunction with Coastal Carolina Athletics, including a proposed track and field complex. The Institutional district is intended to accommodate educational and higher educational facilities, and the request is consistent with the future land use map. The surrounding area includes university athletic facilities, commercial uses, industrial uses, and undeveloped property. Adjacent property within the City limits is part of the Wild Wing Planned Development. No one spoke during public input. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Ulrich. The motion carried unanimously. The applicant Ryne Hardwick was present. Anderson made a motion to approve the rezoning request, seconded by Ulrich. The motion carried unanimously. B. DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT(S) Applicant requested to defer Consideration of the applicant’s request to defer the public hearing and Planning Commission consideration of a proposed Development Agreement with the City of Conway, pursuant to the South Carolina Local Government Development Agreement Act, for approximately 67.49+/- acres of property located along on Mill Pond Rd, Hwy 501 (Church Street), Camelot Street, Carolyn Street, and Lochwood Lane, identified by PIN’s 338-00-00-0037, 338-07- 04-0015, 338-07-01-0033, 338-00-00-0015, and a portion of 338-08-03-0064. Wise made a motion to defer the rezoning request, seconded by Anderson III. The motion was carried unanimously. C. TEXT AMENDMENTS Proposed Amendment to Article 8 – Off-Street Parking & Loading, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance, regarding driveway throat length and parking requirements for Shopping Centers and Strip Commercial uses. Hucks stated the proposed amendment to Article 8 concerns two separate but related site design issues: parking requirements for strip commercial development and minimum driveway throat length. Council -- 4 of 233 -- PC 8/6/2026 3 adopted revised definitions that were part of a broader amendment for ‘shopping center’ and ‘strip commercial’, recognizing that these are different forms of development. However, the parking requirements table still combines them under one parking standard of 1 space per 275 sq. ft. That shared standard works different in practice for the two types of development. A larger shopping center generally has a substantial common parking field that is shared among many tenants. A smaller strip commercial building has fewer total spaces, often divided among several different tenant spaces. Under the current calculation, they may technically satisfy the UDO when initially developed but have too little parking to accommodate a restaurant or another high-turnover use later. The intent is not to require every strip center to provide the max number of spaces. Rather, the amendment establishes a more realistic minimum while allowing sufficient parking capacity to accommodate a broader range of tenants over the life of the development. Shopping centers would remain subject to the existing 1 space per 275 sq. ft. standard. The second part of the amendment establishes driveway throat length requirements. Driveway throat length is the unobstructed distance between the public street and the first internal location where a vehicle can turn, park, enter a drive aisle, or encounter another conflicting traffic movement. Currently, the UDO does not establish a minimum throat length. In instances when a vehicle must stop immediately after turning into the site, following vehicles may be left waiting or slowing within the public roadway. These standards are intended to improve internal circulation, reduce conflicts near site entrances, and help prevent vehicle queues from backing into public streets. The proposed amendments would align the parking table with the definitions adopted earlier this year and add a site access standard that is currently missing from the UDO. The current proposed standards would be: 20 ft for residential entrances (entrances to subdivisions), 30 to 50 ft for small commercial sites and strip commercial development; and 200 to 250 feet for shopping centers and big box retail establishments. Planning Commission may want to consider the ranges in the throat length table: ranges—30 to 50 feet and 200 to 250 feet— and determine the required distance within each range and what criteria should apply. Otherwise, an applicant may argue that only the lower number is enforceable. A simple provision could say: Where a range is provided, the required driveway throat length shall be determined by the Planning Director and City Engineer based on the size and intensity of the development, anticipated traffic volume, roadway classification, driveway location, internal circulation, and recommendations of an approved traffic impact analysis, where applicable. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Ulrich. The motion carried unanimously. Sligh made a motion to approve the rezoning request with the additional language of throat length presented by staff, seconded by Anderson III. The motion carried unanimously. V. Jessica Wise, Meeting Chair -- 6 of 233 -- STAFF REPORT Design Modification: Maplewood Estates PLANNING COMMISSION MTG DATE: Oct. 8, 2026 AGENDA ITEM: IV. A. ISSUE: The applicant is requesting a waiver from; a) the Access Management standards of the U.D.O. and b) the requirements to widen the road right-of-way for a substandard roadway. APPLICANT(S): G3Engineering and Surveying PIN(s): 294-00-00-0025 BACKGROUND: Oct. 2025 – a Master Plan for a conservation subdivision was submitted and reviewed; Sep. 2026 – the application for this Design Modification was submitted along with a rendering of the proposed layout ANALYSIS: The applicant proposes to create 69-single family lots, accessing via only one external entrance, off Long Avenue Extension and in lieu of a second entrance, provide 2 gated emergency access drives, along an un- named county-maintained road, constructed of granulate millings. This un-named road is accessed via Mill Berry Lane, also a county-maintained road of similar construction. The travel-lanes of these two roads vary; being as narrow as 12-feet (near the intersection with Long Avenue Ext) and only as wide as 15-feet (closer to the proposed emergency driveways). The “measuring tool” icons shown on the staff illustration are to depict travel-lane widths as measured by staff during a field inspection in: Sep. 2026. The photos provided are from the Horry County 2026 Aerial Photography as well as some on-site street view images taken by staff during a site visit in: Oct. 2025 Access Management Required access is; (a.) to provide sufficient ingress and egress in normal traffic patterns, while reducing the impact to traffic volumes along the adjoining roadways, from which access is provided – and – (b.) to provide adequate alternative methods of ingress and egress in the event of an emergency or during roadway repair or obstruction… Sec. 7.2.1 E (1) of the Unified Development Ordinance states that “single-family developments consisting of 30 or more lots, the City shall require a minimum of 2 points of ingress and egress” and Sec. 2.2.1 defines “External Access” as: “Access points provided along the boundaries of a development, to provide connection to the existing paved public roadways abutting the project”. The proposed 2 entrances off the un-named county road would not qualify as external access points, as the adjoining road is not paved. Nor would the drives be sufficient as emergency access, as the Fire Marshall (David Parker) noted that the proposed route “Does not meet the requirements for fire apparatus” and goes on to express that “Fire apparatus access roads shall; • have a minimum unobstructed width (exclusive of shoulder) of not less than 20 feet …. • be designed, constructed and maintained to support the imposed loads of not less than 75,000 pounds, • be constructed of asphalt, concrete or other approved all weather (dust-free) driving surface, -- 7 of 233 -- STAFF REPORT Design Modification: Maplewood Estates • have an unobstructed vertical clearance of not less than 13 feet 6 inches, etc.…” Andy Markunas (County Engineer) for: Horry County Engineering Department, stated that: “Mill Berry Lane is in group 3 of the Ride 4 dirt road list , this means that this road won’t be paved for at least 10 to 15 years (2035 to 2040 -- or later) However the “no name” road currently has millings and it’s not part of Ride 4”. Roadway Widening The applicant claims that the existing roadway (of the un-maned road) is currently only 30-feet in width and is proposing to provide a road easement (along the un-named road, abutting the project), instead of a fee-simple dedication, to encompass the new sidewalk and dedicate area for road improvements by the county or City. However, Sec. 10.5.2 B of the U.D.O. states: “Where a development fronts on any existing street segment maintained by either the City, Horry County or the South Carolina Department of Transportation and the street does not meet the minimum standards of these regulations the classification of such street, the applicant shall dedicate additional right-of-way” - Furthermore - Sec. 10.5.2 C states that: “Where a development fronts on any existing street segment maintained by either the City, Horry County or the South Carolina Department of Transportation and a sidewalk does not exist in the right-of-way, the applicant shall construct a sidewalk to meet the minimum standards for that street classification.” And Sec. 7.1.2 D dictates that: “Where the construction of the sidewalk is not possible within the right-of-way, a dedication of land from a property owner shall be required unless there are special circumstances.” The dedication of additional fee-simple right-of-way is a compulsory exaction required as a condition of development (both in the county and the city). By requiring sufficient right-of-way width during development; • perimeter landscape buffers may be situated so as not to be diminished or disturbed later, during roadway acquisitions and construction, • the additional area may be dedicated lawfully as a condition of development, without the required (taxpayer funded) compensation and legal expense that occur during a condemnation process, • adequate lot sizes may be established initially, to prevent future roadway widening from reducing lot and/or open space areas to a width, depth or square footage that will no longer conform to dimensional standards or open space requirements of the U.D.O., • to assure the building setbacks (applicable to the property lines created on the final plat), will remain affixed and not be reconfigured (with the relocation of project boundaries later-on), and thus make existing structures either non-conforming or an encroachment to new property boundaries. Brandon Harrrelson (Director) of the Conway Public Works Department stated the following concerns/recommendation: “Eventually, this road will be given to the City, at which point the City would be responsible for bringing the road up to our standards at the taxpayers’ expense. SUMMARY A traffic impact study was conducted for the proposed Mill Pond Road Commercial development in accordance with SCDOT guidelines. The proposed development is located on the north side of US 501, west of Mill Pond Road in Conway, South Carolina. The development is expected to consist of 236 multi-family housing units, 270,310 square feet of retail, 13,780 square-feet of high turnover sit-down restaurant, 13,000 square feet of fast-food restaurant, a 3,500 square-foot coffee shop and a 4,800 square foot gas station/convenience store. The development is anticipated to be constructed by the end of 2029. Direct access to the site is expected to be provided through full movement driveways to Camelot Street, full movement driveways to Lochwood Lane and full movement access to Richardson Street. A turn lane analysis was conducted at the site accesses utilizing the Build (2029) volumes. Based on the build out volumes, there are no turn lanes recommended at the site accesses. The capacity analysis indicates that the intersection of US 501 and Richardson Street is expected to see higher side street delays in both the no-build and build conditions. The intersections of US 501 and Camelot Street as well as Mill Pond Road and Camelot Street are expected to see high side street delays with the addition of the proposed development trips. As stated previously, a traffic signal is warranted at both intersections. The build improved scenario shows the intersection of US 501 and Camelot Street operating at LOS C or better and the intersection of Mill Pond Road and Camelot Street operating at LOS B or better with the addition of the traffic signals. The intersection of US 501 and Mill Pond Road is expected to see a drop in LOS from the no-build to build scenarios. It is recommended to construct a westbound right turn lane on US 501 at Mill Pond Road with an overlap in addition to a second southbound left turn lane on Mill Pond Road at US 501 to increase the capacity of the intersection. The build improved scenario demonstrates the improved delays. The intersection of Mill Pond Road and Lochwood Lane is expected to see a significant increase in delays from the no-build to build scenario. Signal Warrant Analysis A signal warrant analysis was performed for the intersection of US 501 and Camelot Street as well as Mill Pond Road and Camelot Street utilizing the Build (2029) volumes. The signal warrant utilizes the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) criteria. Thirteen-hour counts were collected for both intersections. Estimated trips from the proposed development were added to the estimated no-build volumes for the 13 hours analyzed to determine the Build scenario volumes. Hourly trip generation was generated based on hourly vehicle distributions from the 12th Edition of the ITE Trip Generation Manual. The Build (2029) volumes from the peak hour capacity analysis were used for the 7-8 AM and 5-6 PM hours, as the methodology for estimating those trips was assumed to be more precise. The intersection of US 501 and Camelot Street was analyzed under existing conditions. The intersection meets the thresholds for all three of the required warrants. Therefore, it is recommended to install a traffic signal at the intersection of US 501 and Camelot Street. The intersection of Mill Pond Road and Camelot Street was analyzed under existing conditions. The intersection meets the thresholds for all three of the required warrants. Intersection LOS Analysis Using the existing, no-build, and build traffic volumes, intersection analyses were conducted for the study intersections under Existing (2026) conditions, No-Build (2029) conditions, and Build (2029) conditions. This analysis was conducted using the Transportation Research Board’s Highway Capacity Manual (HCM 6 th Edition) methodologies of the Synchro, Version 12 software. Intersection level of service (LOS) grades range from LOS A to LOS F, which are directly related to the level of control delay at the intersection and characterize the operational conditions of the intersection traffic flow. LOS A operations typically represent ideal, free-flow conditions where vehicles experience little to no delays, and LOS F operations typically represent poor, forced-flow (bumper-to-bumper) conditions with high vehicular delays, and are generally considered undesirable. Intent These standards are intended to create a cohesive development that is harmonious among buildings of different scale and location within the development while encouraging individual expression for tenants that provides a positive visual experience and improved wayfinding for visitors and customers. These standards shall replace the requirements of Section 6.5.2(E)(F), Section 6.5.3(D), and Section 6.3.1(A)(B)(C)(D) of the UDO. B. Applicability These standards shall apply to all non-residential buildings and tenants within the Planned Development. C. Standards 1. All elevations of a structure shall be in harmony with one another in terms of scale, proportion, detail, material and color. 2. All structures within the Planned Development, including gasoline station canopies, shall be designed to create a harmonious whole. It is not to be inferred that buildings must look alike to achieve a harmony of style, and trade dress or branded colors are encouraged to be used for distinct, defining, features at entrances and articulating elements (towers, awnings, storefronts, decorative inlays, etc.). Harmony of style can be created through proper consideration of scale, proportion, detail, materials, color, site planning, and landscaping. 3. The scale of accessory structures (including canopies) shall be appropriate to the scale of the buildings in the Planned Development. Canopies designed as domineering or overpowering architectural features shall not be permitted. 4. The massing of building facades that contain a primary customer entrance, face a customer parking area, and/or are oriented to Mill Pond Road shall incorporate modulation with horizontal breaks at least once every fifty (50) feet where the building is within 250’ of the public right-of-way of Mill Pond Road. Where the building is located more than 250’ from the public right-of-way of Mill Pond Road, such horizontal breaks shall occur at least once every one hundred (100) feet. Massing and modulation changes include changes in the building height, horizontal plane, building projections/recessions, roof form, and/or other architectural elements such as (but not limited to) pilasters, columns, arcades, trellises, and entrance features. 5. The architectural design and material finish of buildings, signage, gasoline pump canopies, and other necessary structures shall be compatible with one another and other structures within the Planned Development. -- 194 of 233 -- 45 207285624.v3 6. Color combinations of paints and stains shall be complimentary. Multi-occupant buildings or single- occupant buildings immediately adjacent to each other shall utilize the same primary color palette, exclusive of trade dress and branded colors. Trade dress or branded colors should generally be limited to distinct, defining, elements at entrance features, articulating elements (towers, awnings, storefronts, decorative inlays, etc.), and trim. 7. Any building’s exterior elevation shall consist of architectural materials which are equal in quality, appearance, and detail to all other exterior elevations of the same structure. Nothing in this section shall preclude the use of different materials on different exterior elevations of the same structure so long as those materials maintain the architectural unity and integrity of the entire structure. 8. Text Amendment Article 8 of the UDO -- 31 of 213 -- STAFF REPORT Text Amendment to Article 8 – Off-Street Parking & Loading PLANNING COMMISSION MTG DATE: September 3, 2026 AGENDA ITEM: IV.C. ISSUE: Amendments Article 8 – Off-Street Parking & Loading, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding driveway throat length as well as parking requirements for Shopping Centers v. Strip Commercial. BACKGROUND: On May 4, 2026, the City Council adopted Ordinance #ZA2026-05-04(O) to update and add new definitions, including distinct definitions for “Shopping Center” and “Strip Commercial.” However, Table 8.3 (Parking Requirements) currently combines these into a single category: “Commercial Strip Center/Shopping Center,” applying a blanket minimum parking ratio of 1 space per 275 sq. ft. Maintaining this shared calculation results in severely under-parked strip centers and creates unintended zoning barriers. For example, under current minimums, a recent review for a four-unit commercial strip center required only 20 total parking spaces. This averages out to just 5 spaces per unit, including employee parking. While this allocation may suffice for low-intensity office use, it mathematically eliminates the possibility of permitting a restaurant in any of the units due to the higher parking demands of food service. Separating these two commercial uses in Table 8.3 will accommodate a wider range of tenants within strip commercial developments. By implementing the proposed ratio of 1 space per 150 sq. ft., the required parking for the previously mentioned four-unit development would increase from 20 to 38 spaces. This adjusted capacity ensures the site can support higher-turnover uses, such as restaurants, without creating local parking deficits. Also, the UDO does not address “Throat Length”. The core benefits of regulating Throat Length includes maximizing public safety and capacity. When a driveway lacks adequate throat length, entering vehicles are forced to slow down or stop immediately upon turning into a site. Keeping the public right-of-way clear minimizes the risk of speed differentials and abrupt braking on adjacent major arterials or collector streets. PLANNING COMMISSION: Staff recommends that in addition to holding the required public hearing, that Planning Commission review the proposed amendment, and make an informed recommendation to City Council. PURPOSE AND INTENT PURPOSE. The primary purpose of this PD is to establish a flexible, master-planned framework capable of accommodating the specialized operational, architectural, and site-design standards of a diverse mix of commercial and premier multifamily occupants. By utilizing a PD format rather than rigid individual districts, the development can integrate varied occupant user prototypes, specialized parking logistics, and distinct site-geometry requirements into a more functional, cohesive ecosystem that standard UDO text cannot dynamically support. Further, the PD format facilitates a more environmentally sensitive site layout by clustering development density onto less impactful upland zones. This framework ensures, to the extent feasible, the preservation of existing on-site undisturbed wetlands as high-value, integrated passive open space and spatial buffers, exceeding the environmental outcomes typical of piecemeal baseline development. INTENT. This PD is established to: 1. Encourage innovative and flexible site design that cannot be achieved through strict application of conventional zoning districts; 2. Promote integrated, unified development of a site under a single development concept; 3. Allow for limited, site-specific modifications to the standards of the UDO where such modifications result in equal or better outcomes; and 4. Ensure that development is consistent with the Comprehensive Plan and compatible with surrounding uses. South Carolina has long recognized that wetlands “are valuable habitat for wildlife and plant species and serve as hydrologic buffers, providing for absorption of storm water runoff and aquifer recharge, [therefore] commercial development is discouraged in these areas.” CMP at p. III-40. As recognized in the South Carolina Coastal Management Program Document, wetlands are valuable habitat that should not be filled indiscriminately. CZMP-62 § IX(B). The Clean Water Act contains similar language. 40 C.F.R. 230.41(b) (wetland fill may reduce “the system’s productivity” and “can degrade water quality by obstructing circulation patterns that flush large expanses of wetland systems” and may “change the wetland habitat for fish and wildlife”). Among the factors DES must both consider and address in reaching a determination about water quality impacts of this project are “(a) whether the activity is water dependent and the intended purpose of the activity; (b) whether there are feasible alternatives to the activity; (c) all potential water quality impacts of the project, both direct and indirect, over the life of the project including: (1) impact on existing and classified water uses; (2) physical, chemical, and biological impacts, including cumulative impacts; (3) the effect on circulation patterns and water movement; (4) the cumulative impacts of the proposed activity and reasonably foreseeable similar activities of the applicant and others.” S.C. Code Ann. Regs. § 61-101 F. 3. (a)-(c). DES “shall condition the certification upon compliance with all measures necessary to minimize adverse effects, including stormwater management.” S.C. Code Ann. Regs. § 61-101 F. 4. This project is not water dependent, there are likely feasible alternatives, and there will be direct and indirect water quality impacts. The construction process and presence of impervious surfaces would generate significant stormwater runoff, which will introduce pollutants and litter into nearby waterways. Studies show that impervious surfaces significantly increase stormwater runoff compared to natural areas. On average, only 15% of rainfall on pervious surfaces becomes runoff, whereas 90% of rainfall on impervious surfaces becomes runoff, carrying pollutants with it.2 The project area is located in wetlands associated with Crabtree Swamp and Crabtree Canal, which discharge into the Waccamaw River.3 Polluted runoff is a major threat to water quality for the swamp and the river, 2 See https://cms7files1.revize.com/birmingham/Document_Center/Department/Treasurers%20Office/Property%20Tax% 20Information/A1_Runoff%20Potential.pdf. 3 Attachment A, Corps Restoration Project, p. 1; Attachment B, Crabtree Plant Survival. -- 141 of 213 -- 3 contributing to declines in plant and animal diversity in affected waterbodies.4 The proposed project includes retail shops, a grocery store, restaurants, a coffee shop, a fuel station, and extensive associated parking lots. Buffers carry out the important functions of preventing erosion, reducing pollution, and protecting wildlife.5 Of particular concern is the fuel station, which is currently proposed to be located in a wetland. The fuel station will likely require underground storage tanks. The League’s water quality concerns do not only relate to runoff, but also to having USTs immediately adjected to the wetlands, and the resulting threat to groundwater. The Applicant Failed to Provide Adequate Information on the Project Purpose and Alternatives. South Carolina law requires a presentation of alternatives when making decisions about activities with water quality impacts. The state’s regulations implementing the Clean Water Act also emphasize the importance of considering alternate plans: “In assessing the water quality impacts of the project, the Department will address and consider the following factors… whether there are feasible alternatives to the activity.” S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 61-101(F)(3). “Certification will be denied if… there is a feasible alternative to the activity, which reduces adverse consequences on water quality and classified uses.” S.C. Code Ann. Regs. 61-101(F)(5) (emphasis added). The Clean Water Act itself requires a search for alternatives: “Except as provided under section 404(b)(2), no discharge of dredged or fill material shall be permitted if there is a practicable alternative to the proposed discharge which would have less adverse impact on the aquatic ecosystem.” 40 C.F.R. § 230.10(a). An alternative is considered practicable if it is “available and capable of being done after taking into consideration cost, existing technology, and logistics in light of overall project purposes.” 40 C.F.R. § 230.10(a)(2). For projects that are not water-dependent, such as this one, the CWA regulations create a presumption that practicable alternatives exist that do not involve impacts to special aquatic sites like wetlands. 40 C.F.R. § 230.10(a)(3). The Applicant has the burden of demonstrating that practicable alternatives do not exist. Despite these clear regulatory mandates, the Applicant has not provided a description of the project purpose nor satisfied its burden of clearly demonstrating that no practicable alternative exists. The public notice does not clearly articulate the project purpose, but instead, merely states that, “[t]he project purpose requires contiguous developable area and road frontage limiting the practicability of complete avoidance of all wetlands.” Without further explanation, the asserted needs for a “contiguous developable area” and “road frontage” appear to reflect the Applicant’s preferred layout rather than an actual necessity. Courts have recognized that while the Corps must consider the applicant’s project objectives, it cannot allow overly narrow purpose definitions that artificially constrain the alternatives analysis. See Sylvester v. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, 882 F.2d 407, 409 (9th Cir. 1989) (“[A]n applicant cannot define a project in order to preclude the existence of any alternative sites and thus make what is practicable appear impracticable.”). 17 See EPA https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2015-09/documents/bbfs3cost.pdf; https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2017-10/documents/lid_fs10_rainfall_epa_508.pdf; https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2018-08/documents/bbfs11space508.pdf; https://www.epa.gov/sites/production/files/2015-09/documents/bbfs4aesthetics.pdf. 18 http://www.scseagrant.org/pdf_files/Stormwater_Assessment_Report_WEB.pdf. -- 144 of 213 -- 6 The public notice lacks an alternatives analysis, particularly regarding an evaluation of offsite alternatives and onsite configurations that would further minimize or avoid wetland impacts. The public notice does not identify whether alternative project locations were considered or whether different designs within the proposed site were explored to achieve the project purpose with fewer wetland impacts. For a non-water-dependent project, the failure to adequately consider or document these alternatives raises serious concerns about compliance with the Clean Water Act guidelines. The deficiencies in the public notice, including the lack of a description of the project purpose and a clear demonstration that practicable alternatives are unavailable, prevent the public from meaningfully evaluating the project’s compliance with regulatory standards. The Applicant has failed to justify the proposed impacts. Therefore, the Corps must either deny the permit application or require the applicant to submit a revised public notice with sufficient information, followed by an extension of the public comment period. Authority and Purpose. Section 206 of the Water Resources Development Act of 1996 provides authority for the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) to carry out aquatic ecosystem restoration and protection projects if the Secretary of the Army determines that the project will improve the quality of the environment and is in the public interest while being cost-effective. This study was initiated following receipt of a December 3, 2014 letter request from Horry County seeking assistance from the USACE to develop ecological restoration along one or more waterbodies located in Horry County, South Carolina. Prior to channelization to support development, Crabtree Swamp was a bottomland hardwood wetland ecosystem. Historic channel modifications resulted in dredge material placement on the streambanks, disconnecting the floodplains and adjacent wetlands from the channel. As more intense urban land uses replaced agricultural uses, with subsequent increased stormwater runoff, reaches of Crabtree Swamp started to exhibit associated stressors such as bank failure, erosive channel velocities, incising and scouring, loss of aquatic life habitat, episodic flooding, invasive vegetation, and blockages that prevented aquatic life passage. Crabtree Swamp is now an incised, trapezoidal channel with little remaining structural diversity, and prone to bank failures. The lack of aquatic habitat and physical barriers are inhibiting aquatic life passage. The purpose of this project is to restore aquatic habitat and improve stream functions by restoring floodplain connectivity and improving bedform diversity. This will provide flood storage capacity and, when combined with the removal of invasive species and re-planting of the riparian zone with native woody tree and shrub species, will allow for a more natural riverine ecosystem. c. Crabtree swamp is located in the Kingston Lake Watershed (HUC 03040206-08-03) in northeastern SC. The swamp flows around the City of Conway and discharges into the Waccamaw River. Since the 1960's, the US Army Corps of Engineers have dredged an eight-mile canal through the swamp to prevent and control flooding. The dredge materials were piled onto the adjacent banks, creating a very steep, unstable levee system that isolated the remaining floodplain, increased water velocities, and eliminated habitat and fish spawning grounds. Horry County and the City of Conway, with assistance from federal agencies and two universities, are restoring the natural floodplain to stabilize the canal and improve water quality. In April 2009, a half-mile stretch along one streambank was restored by removing dredge materials, regrading the bank slopes and revegetating with native trees, shrubs and wetland plants. Their health status has been assessed periodically and data archived in GIS datalayers. By restoring the natural floodplain, the energy of the floodwater is dissipated, permitting deposition of sediment and improved water quality. Partners learned important lessons such as the need for 1) strong partner commitment; 2) overall coordination; 3) maintenance guidelines; 4) project assessment and sharing results; and 5) enabling natural processes. Future restoration work is needed to address continuing erosion and water quality problems in unrestored stream reaches. A second segment of the canal is being restored in 2012. INTRODUCTION The Waccamaw River is a blackwater river that flows from Lake Waccamaw, NC, and winds through Conway on its way to the mouth of Winyah Bay in Georgetown, SC. Crabtree canal, a channelized tributary, and the adjacent swamp are part of the Kingston Lake watershed that is approximately 20 sq. mi. in area and represents a major conduit for water through Conway before discharging into the Waccamaw. The canal runs approximately eight miles through Conway, in northeastern Horry County, SC (see Figure 1.) Crabtree Canal, as it is now known, was the solution to major flooding in Conway after a storm event that dropped 10.38 inches of rain in a 14 hour period on June 6th, 1964. The rising water caused major transportation corridors in Conway (U.S. highways 701, 501, and 378) to be closed or impassable. Approximately $4,000,000 in tobacco crops were destroyed by flooding, as well as small businesses and homes suffering severe damage. Farmers and residents declared Crabtree swamp was harmful to their livelihood. Farmers and land owners petitioned the state to establish the Crabtree Watershed Conservation District for the purposes of funding. Mayor Huckabee, George Jenkins Sr. and Col. S. Y. Coker of the US Army Corps of Engineers (USACOE) spearheaded the flood control project. Through this effort, the swamp was dredged and channelized, in an effort to prevent future flooding from destroying residential, commercial, and agricultural areas. In 1965-66, the USACOE excavated a 6.5-mile canal through Crabtree Swamp to improve drainage, piling the dredged materials along the bank, effectively cutting off the floodplain. Another 1.5 miles was channelized in the 1980’s. Over time, the canal banks have steepened due to the increased water flow through the canal (Figure 2a), causing bank instability and increased erosion rates. Channelization of the formerly winding swamp has significantly impacted the hydrology of the ecosystem, affecting the frequency, degree and duration of flooding. Water quality has also declined. -- 161 of 213 -- The area around Conway has experienced a change in land use over the past 50 years, shifting from an agricultural to an urban landscape. The increase in the impervious surfaces within the watershed causes the water flow in Crabtree Canal to be flashy during rain events. Currently, Crabtree Canal is listed on South Carolina’s 303(d) list of impaired waters for dissolved oxygen and fecal coliforms. The waters also experience high suspended sediment concentration after rain events. The net effect of these impairments has been to diminish the quality of aquatic habitat in the Crabtree Canal. OBJECTIVES A watershed management plan was developed for the Kingston Lake Watershed in 2010 (Libes and Fuss 2010). The restoration of Crabtree Canal was included as an action item. To implement this component of the watershed management plan, Horry County, the City of Conway, and Coastal Carolina University devised a restoration plan to improve conditions in Crabtree Canal that was based on findings from a hydrological and pollution source tracking study completed in 2008 and a floral survey of adjacent swamps performed in 2009. In May 2009, construction began at the chosen demonstration site to reconnect the floodplain along a ½- mile segment of one bank of Crabtree Canal (Figures 1 and 2b). A second ½-mile segment is undergoing restoration, 0.3 miles upstream of the first site on the opposite bank. The three main objectives of the floodplain restoration are to: 1) slow the flow of water; 2) increase water storage; and 3) reduce erosion (Fuss et al. 2010.) The restoration was designed by Coastal Carolina and Clemson Universities, in collaboration with the City of Conway and Horry County. Expert advice in selection of suitable indigenous plants was provided by Dr. Will Conner (Professor of Forestry and Natural Resources, Clemson University). Species were selected to encompass a broad range of plants indigenous to southeastern bottomland hardwood swamps. Permission to engage in this work was obtained from the property owners in the Crabtree Watershed Conservation District who signed a Memorandum of Understanding in 2008 with Horry County and the City of Conway to partner on restoration efforts (Fuss et al. 2010). The main objective was to restore a more natural bank slope and revegetate the project site with indigenous trees and shrubs. Restoring a site’s hydrology is the most important factor to consider in a bottomland hardwood restoration (Allen et al 2001; Clewell and Lee 1990).
