An additional objective of the project was to provide accessible recreation for the community, to help them reconnect with this important resource. METHODS The first phase of the restoration began in 2009, when ½-mi along one streambank was restored by removing the original dredge materials and re-grading the bank slopes. The restored floodplain was re-vegetated with indigenous trees, shrubs and wetland plants. In May 2009, 251 trees (11 species) and 297 shrubs (7 species) were planted across an 18’-wide aquatic zone and a 42’-wide upland zone. Species indigenous to local hardwood floodplain swamps were obtained from local nurseries in sizes ranging from 3 to 50 gallons. Several 100-ft long segments of pre-planted wetland carpets, with about 12 species of native emergent vegetation were installed at elevations above, at, and below the mean water line. These carpets were constructed using 5 foot wide coir mats and were made by Charleston Aquatics, Inc. The plantings had been grown out to a height of about 1 foot prior to planting. The planting plan was designed to test which species were best suited to the aquatic and upland zones. To track survival rates, the plants were tagged with a unique identification number and locations recorded with a Real Time Kinematic (RTK) GPS. Their health status has been assessed periodically and data archived in GIS datalayers. The trees have been retagged over the years as Table 1. Tree counts based on surveys conducted periodically since planting and survival rate to date. Survival rates > 75% are highlighted in red. Trees with low planting numbers are highlighted in yellow. See text for an explanation of the persimmon survival rate that exceeds 100%. -- 163 of 213 -- the original tags have weathered or gone missing. Tree and shrub conditions were classified as either: 1) Green; 2) Mixed (brown and green); 3) Brown; 4) Dead; and 5) Mixed with New Growth. “Green” surviving trees were regarded as 100% green, whereas “Dead” trees were considered 0% green. For a tree to be considered “Mixed”, at least 50% of the tree had to be brown and to be considered “Brown”, less than 20% of the tree would be green. “Mixed/ new growth” meant that there was evidence of new growth. RESULTS Since the planting of 548 trees and shrubs in May 2009, tree status has been assessed at least once a year. The results are presented in Table 1. In July 2012, the overall survival rate was found to be 66% with 361 of the planted flora being observed as either “green”, “mixed” or “mixed with new growth”. High mortality rates (<50% survival) were exhibited by seven species: Atlantic white cedar, beauty berry, black gum, swamp ti ti , eastern red cedar, southern red oak, and sugarberry. Note that three of these species had low planting numbers (Atlantic white cedar, sugarberry, and southern red oak). Six species had very high survival rates (≥75%), i.e., button bush, bald cypress, dahoon holly, river birch, persimmon and green ash. Note that the tree counts performed in May and October 2010 were likely incomplete as more of the trees tagged in 2009 were counted in May 2011. The total trees counted over time should decline as dead trees fall to the ground and are potentially washed downstream. DISCUSSION As shown in Figure 3, plant mortality was highest in areas subject to high-energy floodwater regimes, i.e. the aquatic zone. This area also had a higher percentage of plants categorized as mixed, a sign of stress. Data are available to infer flood inundation frequencies and hence how species survival relates to floodplain function. Since species were deliberately planted to test tolerance to challenging environmental conditions, individual species survival rates reflect effects of less than optimal plantings. Native plants that have volunteered at the restoration site include blue vervain (Verbena hastate) and groundsel bush (Baccharis halimifolia), both of which have colonized the section closest to the channel. Along the upper border, long leaf pine (Pinus palustris) and sweet gum (Liquidambar styraciflua) have re-populated open spaces. The original stand of persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) has multiplied, leading to a survival rate >100% as some recruits were tagged during the 2011 monitoring effort. A site maintenance plan has been implemented to manage invasive species and to guide brush trimming. Invasive species include Johnsongrass (Sorghum halepense) in the aquatic zone and Alligator weed (Alternanthera philoxeroides) in the channel. Chinese tallow (Triadica spp.), rattlebox (Crotalaria spp), and Chinese/Japanese privet (Ligustrum spp) are found in the in the upland border. A second segment of floodplain is being restored with planting scheduled for winter 2012. This site is located 0.3-mile upstream of the first segment on the opposite streambank. Based on the survival results from the first restoration, which was designed as a pilot to guide future efforts, this second segment will be planted with a lower density of trees and shrubs. A test plot will also be seeded with native grasses. It will be important to continue to monitor plant status at the site, not only to watch for early detection of invasive or nuisance species, but to monitor natural revegetation to be sure that desired species are colonizing the site. Some plant species may have limited dispersion mechanisms that won’t be mimicked in the newly restored site. Due to extensive development and channelizing of the former swamp upstream of the project site, there may Figure 3. GIS datalayer showing status of planted trees following a survey conducted in July 2012. -- 164 of 213 -- be limited opportunity for some species to recolonize the site. Natural regeneration has been found to be effective when the desired bottomland hardwood ecosystem is found in close proximity to the restoration site (Allen et al. 2001). Efforts to restore hydrologic conditions at a site in the Savannah River watershed have resulted in colonization of plants that in the future will provide a similar canopy to pre-disturbance conditions, likely due to the project site being directly adjacent to the targeted ecosystem (Nelson et al. 2000). One lesson learned is the importance of establishing a written maintenance plan that all stakeholders have agreed to. In 2009, herbicide spraying in a utility right of way killed several hundred willows that are not included in Table 1. In 2010, mowing led to the death of several trees. As a result, a maintenance plan was formulated and adopted by all the project partners. Nevertheless, in the 2012 survey, tree damage was observed that could be tied to a recent over application of herbicide intended to control invasive species in a utility right of way. SUMMARY A traffic impact study was conducted for the proposed Mill Pond Road Commercial development in accordance with SCDOT guidelines. The proposed development is located on the north side of US 501, west of Mill Pond Road in Conway, South Carolina. The development is expected to consist of 236 multi-family housing units, 270,310 square feet of retail, 13,780 square-feet of high turnover sit-down restaurant, 13,000 square feet of fast-food restaurant, a 3,500 square-foot coffee shop and a 4,800 square foot gas station/convenience store. The development is anticipated to be constructed by the end of 2029. Direct access to the site is expected to be provided through full movement driveways to Camelot Street, full movement driveways to Lochwood Lane and full movement access to Richardson Street. A turn lane analysis was conducted at the site accesses utilizing the Build (2029) volumes. Based on the build out volumes, there are no turn lanes recommended at the site accesses. The capacity analysis indicates that the intersection of US 501 and Richardson Street is expected to see higher side street delays in both the no-build and build conditions. The intersections of US 501 and Camelot Street as well as Mill Pond Road and Camelot Street are expected to see high side street delays with the addition of the proposed development trips. As stated previously, a traffic signal is warranted at both intersections. The build improved scenario shows the intersection of US 501 and Camelot Street operating at LOS C or better and the intersection of Mill Pond Road and Camelot Street operating at LOS B or better with the addition of the traffic signals. The intersection of US 501 and Mill Pond Road is expected to see a drop in LOS from the no-build to build scenarios. It is recommended to construct a westbound right turn lane on US 501 at Mill Pond Road with an overlap in addition to a second southbound left turn lane on Mill Pond Road at US 501 to increase the capacity of the intersection. The build improved scenario demonstrates the improved delays. The intersection of Mill Pond Road and Lochwood Lane is expected to see a significant increase in delays from the no-build to build scenario. Therefore, it is recommended to construct a second egress lane on Lochwood Lane. The build improved scenario shows the decreased delays with the additional egress lane. The site access capacity analysis indicates that all approaches of the site accesses are expected to operate at LOS B or better in all scenarios. Signal Warrant Analysis A signal warrant analysis was performed for the intersection of US 501 and Camelot Street as well as Mill Pond Road and Camelot Street utilizing the Build (2029) volumes. The signal warrant utilizes the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) criteria. Thirteen-hour counts were collected for both intersections. Estimated trips from the proposed development were added to the estimated no-build volumes for the 13 hours analyzed to determine the Build scenario volumes. Hourly trip generation was generated based on hourly vehicle distributions from the 12th Edition of the ITE Trip Generation Manual. The Build (2029) volumes from the peak hour capacity analysis were used for the 7-8 AM and 5-6 PM hours, as the methodology for estimating those trips was assumed to be more precise. The intersection of US 501 and Camelot Street was analyzed under existing conditions. The intersection meets the thresholds for all three of the required warrants. Therefore, it is recommended to install a traffic signal at the intersection of US 501 and Camelot Street. The intersection of Mill Pond Road and Camelot Street was analyzed under existing conditions. The intersection meets the thresholds for all three of the required warrants. Therefore, it is recommended to install a traffic signal at the intersection of Mill Pond Road and Camelot Street. Intersection LOS Analysis Using the existing, no-build, and build traffic volumes, intersection analyses were conducted for the study intersections under Existing (2026) conditions, No-Build (2029) conditions, and Build (2029) conditions. This analysis was conducted using the Transportation Research Board’s Highway Capacity Manual (HCM 6 th Edition) methodologies of the Synchro, Version 12 software. Intersection level of service (LOS) grades range from LOS A to LOS F, which are directly related to the level of control delay at the intersection and characterize the operational conditions of the intersection traffic flow. LOS A operations typically represent ideal, free-flow conditions where vehicles experience little to no delays, and LOS F operations typically represent poor, forced-flow (bumper-to-bumper) conditions with high vehicular delays, and are generally considered undesirable. text: Il. Il. Iv. PC 8/6/2026 CITY OF CONWAY PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING THURSDAY, September 3, 2026 Planning & Building Dept. Conference Room — 196 Laurel Street Present: George Ulrich, Allan Comell, Thomas J. Anderson III, Stacy Knotts, Jessica Wise, David Sligh, Greg Bryson Absent: Kendall Brown Staff: Jessica Hucks, Planning Director; Nancy Alvarez, Assistant Planner; Charlotte Peterson, Assistant Planner; Charlie Crosby, IT Others: Rebecca Harper, Geof Smith, Jeanette DeMartini, Ryne Hardwick, Laurel Schwinger, Kurt Schwinger, Mark Carlson, Monica Whaler, Deborah Goff, Kenny Pokorny, April O'Leary, Bangert Renneth, Sara Rich, Tim Stephens CALL TO ORDER Wise called the meeting to order at approximately 5:30 pm. APPROVAL OF MINUTES Ulrich made a motion, seconded by Cornell to approve the August 6, 2026, minutes as written. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. PUBLIC INPUT Wise made a motion to open public input. No one spoke during public input. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Ulrich and the motion carried unanimously. PUBLIC HEARINGS A. REZONING REQUEST(S) 1. Applicant requested to defer. Consideration of the applicant’s request to defer the public hearing and Planning Commission consideration of a request to rezone approximately 67.49+/- acres of property located on Mill Pond Rd, Hwy 501 (Church Street), Camelot Street, Carolyn Street, and Lochwood Lane (PIN’s 338-00-00-0037; 338-07-04-0015; 338-07-01-0033; 338-00- 00-0015; and a portion of 338-08-03-0064), from the Highway Commercial (HC), Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) and Conservation Preservation (CP) districts to a Planned Development (PD) district. PC 8/6/2026 Wise made a motion to defer the rezoning request, seconded by Sligh. The motion carried unanimously. 2. Request to rezone approximately 26.98+/- acres of property located at 585 and 605 Century Circle (PIN: 383-00-00-0344), from Horry County Planned Unit Development (PUD) district to the City of Conway Institutional (IN) district upon annexation. Hucks stated the rezoning request was intended to facilitate development of the property in conjunction with Coastal Carolina Athletics, including a proposed track and field complex. The Institutional district is intended to accommodate educational and higher educational facilities, and the request is consistent with the future land use map. The surrounding area includes university athletic facilities, commercial uses, industrial uses, and undeveloped property. Adjacent property within the City limits is part of the Wild Wing Planned Development. No one spoke during public input. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Ulrich. The motion carried unanimously. The applicant Ryne Hardwick was present. Anderson made a motion to approve the rezoning request, seconded by Ulrich. The motion carried unanimously. B. DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT(S) Applicant requested to defer Consideration of the applicant’s request to defer the public hearing and Planning Commission consideration of a proposed Development Agreement with the City of Conway, pursuant to the South Carolina Local Government Development Agreement Act, for approximately 67.49+/- acres of property located along on Mill Pond Rd, Hwy 501 (Church Street), Camelot Street, Carolyn Street, and Lochwood Lane, identified by PIN’s 338-00-00-0037, 338-07- 04-0015, 338-07-01-0033, 338-00-00-0015, and a portion of 338-08-03-0064. The subject properties are currently zoned Highway Commercial (HC), Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-3), and Conservation Preservation (CP), and are proposed to be rezoned to a Planned Development (PD) district for commercial and multifamily residential development. Wise made a motion to defer the rezoning request, seconded by Anderson III. The motion was carried unanimously. C. TEXT AMENDMENTS Proposed Amendment to Article 8 — Off-Street Parking & Loading, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance, regarding driveway throat length and parking requirements for Shopping Centers and Strip Commercial uses. Hucks stated the proposed amendment to Article 8 concerns two separate but related site design issues: parking requirements for strip commercial development and minimum driveway throat length. Council 2 PC 8/6/2026 adopted revised definitions that were part of a broader amendment for ‘shopping center’ and ‘strip commercial’, recognizing that these are different forms of development. However, the parking requirements table still combines them under one parking standard of 1 space per 275 sq. ft. That shared standard works different in practice for the two types of development. A larger shopping center generally has a substantial common parking field that is shared among many tenants. A smaller strip commercial building has fewer total spaces, often divided among several different tenant spaces. Under the current calculation, they may technically satisfy the UDO when initially developed but have too little parking to accommodate a restaurant or another high-turnover use later. The intent is not to require every strip center to provide the max number of spaces. Rather, the amendment establishes a more realistic minimum while allowing sufficient parking capacity to accommodate a broader range of tenants over the life of the development. Shopping centers would remain subject to the existing 1 space per 275 sq. ft. standard. The second part of the amendment establishes driveway throat length requirements. Driveway throat length is the unobstructed distance between the public street and the first internal location where a vehicle can tum, park, enter a drive aisle, or encounter another conflicting traffic movement. Currently, the UDO does not establish a minimum throat length. In instances when a vehicle must stop immediately after turning into the site, following vehicles may be left waiting or slowing within the public roadway. These standards are intended to improve internal circulation, reduce conflicts near site entrances, and help prevent vehicle queues from backing into public streets. The proposed amendments would align the parking table with the definitions adopted earlier this year and add a site access standard that is currently missing from the UDO. The current proposed standards would be: 20 ft for residential entrances (entrances to subdivisions), 30 to 50 ft for small commercial sites and strip commercial development; and 200 to 250 feet for shopping centers and big box retail establishments. Planning Commission may want to consider the ranges in the throat length table: ranges—30 to 50 feet and 200 to 250 feet— and determine the required distance within each range and what criteria should apply. Otherwise, an applicant may argue that only the lower number is enforceable. A simple provision could say: Where a range is provided, the required driveway throat length shall be determined by the Planning Director and City Engineer based on the size and intensity of the development, anticipated traffic volume, roadway classification, driveway location, internal circulation, and recommendations of an approved traffic impact analysis, where applicable. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Ulrich. The motion carried unanimously. Sligh made a motion to approve the rezoning request with the additional language of throat length presented by staff, seconded by Anderson III. The motion carried unanimously. V. DISCUSSION Mill Pond Planned Development and Development Agreement. Presentation and discussion regarding the proposed rezoning and Development Agreement for approximately 67.49+/- acres of property located on Mill Pond Rd, Hwy 501 (Church Street), Camelot Street, Carolyn Street, and Lochwood Lane (PIN’s 338-00-00-0037, 338-07-04-0015, 338-07-01-0033, 338-00-00-0015, and a portion of 338-08-03-0064). The subject properties are proposed to be rezoned to a Planned 3 PC 8/6/2026 Development (PD) district for commercial and multifamily residential development. This item is for discussion only; no formal action will be taken. VI. BOARD INPUT VIL. STAFF INPUT IX. ADJOURNMENT Wise made a motion was made to adjourn the meeting, seconded by Ulrich. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. The meeting adjourned at approximately 6:48 p.m. Approved and signed this ‘ 4 day of Nueces" , 2026. ONE Jessica Wise, Meeting Chair

Graham died unexpectedly Saturday night following a ruptured aorta related to cardio- vascular disease, according to preliminary findings from the District of Columbia medical examiner released by his office. Graham, who never married and had no children, shared a tight bond with his sister. Even before their parents died, she said, she relied on her brother. “My parents, since they had to work a lot, Lindsey was kind of the one there that took care of me. If I fell down and scraped my knee, Lindsey was the one I ran to,” she said in a 2014 campaign ad for Graham. Hours before the governor’s announcement, President Donald Trump publicly backed her as the choice, writing on social media, “This would be a fabulous tribute to Lindsey, who loved her dearly!” Lawmakers, past and present, quickly endorsed the idea, including U.S. Sen. Tim Scott, who called her a “fantastic pick. “There is no one better who understands Lindsey’s love for family, our state, and our country,” he wrote on X. McMaster indicated Trump’s post didn’t influence a decision he’d already made: She “agreed to serve through tears,” the governor said about his phone call with her early Sun- day. “I was humbled by your quickness to see the duty that you had to serve,” McMaster said at the news conference. “I called the president afterward, and he thought it was a great idea.” Graham Nordone, who was 13 when their parents died, periodically joined her brother on the campaign trail, including his short-lived bid for president in 2015, which started his relationship with Trump on rocky grounds. Graham, however, quickly became a golfing buddy, friend and confidante to the president. MOURNING On Monday, white flowers sat atop a black cloth draped over Graham’s desk on the U.S. Senate floor, and flags flew at half-staff across the country. Funeral arrangements have yet to be announced. McMaster on Sunday ordered flags above the Statehouse dome to fly at half-staff in Gra- ham’s honor until further notice. Normally, such orders last through a funeral service. On Monday, Trump ordered the same for flags on public buildings nationwide until 6 p.m. Saturday. Tributes to Graham that flooded inboxes and social media platforms came from politi- cians, as well as current and former staff. “Senator Graham never forgot who he was or where he came from. He loved Chick-fil-a so much that in the pre-smart phone era, staff provided a map of Chick-fil-A restaurants in South Carolina for his car so he could get a meal while on the road,” Scott Farmer, Gra- ham’s campaign manager of 22 years, wrote on X. “He loved SC and her people. If you needed help with Social Security benefits, the V.A., or a passport, the Senator’s constituent service team was second to none – modeled after his predecessor, Senator Strom Thurmond,” Farm- er added. “If the Port of Charleston needed to be deepened to keep our state’s economy humming, Senator Graham made sure it hap- pened. South Carolina’s congressional dele- gation hit above its weight because of Lindsey Graham and his tenacity to get things done.” College leaders offering condolences included the president and board chairman of South Carolina State University, an alma mater of Graham Nordone. She earned a master’s degree in rehabilitation counseling in 2009 from the state’s only public historically Black university. “He devoted himself to serving both our state and our nation. His commitment to national defense, the men and women of our armed forces and the security of our country defined much of his public life,” reads the joint statement from the president, retired Col. Alex- ander Conyers, and board Chairman Douglas Gantt. “His legacy of leadership, public service and dedication to South Carolina and the nation will endure,” it continued. Other women who filled vacancies Graham Nordone, who earned her bache- lor’s in sociology from the College of Charles- ton, is not the first South Carolinian to fulfill a deceased family member’s term. In the 20th century, four South Carolina women, all Democrats, were elected to finish serving their husband’s term in the U.S. House following his death. None sought election to the next full term: • Rep. Elizabeth Hawley Gasque (Sep. 13, 1938-Jan. 3, 1939) • Rep. Clara Gooding McMillan (Nov. 7, 1939-Jan. 3, 1941) • Rep. Willa Lybrand Fulmer (Nov. 7, 1944- Jan. 3, 1945); and • Rep. Corinne Boyd Riley (April 10, 1962- Jan. 3, 1963). In all, 47 women nationwide have been elected or appointed to fill congressional vacancies created by the deaths of their hus- bands: eight to the U.S. Senate and 39 to the U. S. House, according to the Center for Amer- ican Women and Politics. Four additional widows took office — three by election, one by appointment — after their husband won an election but died before his term started, according to the Office of the Historian of the U.S. House. The most recent include Rep. Julia Letlow, R-Louisiana, who won a 2021 special election after her husband, Luke Letlow, died before taking office. Rep. Doris Matsui, D-California, won a 2005 special election to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Rep. Robert Matsui. She’s since been re-elected to 10 terms. And acting Missouri Gov. Roger Wilson appointed the late Sen. Jean Carnahan to the Senate in 2001 after voters posthumously elected her husband, Gov. Mel Carnahan, who died in a plane crash three weeks before the election. POOL HALL TO CAPITOL HILL Graham’s is a story of a self-made man who went from humble beginnings in small town South Carolina to the halls of political power in Washington, D.C. Born July 9, 1955, Graham grew up in the Upstate town of Central, just 5 miles outside Clemson. His family lived in the back room of the San- itary Cafe, the restaurant and pool hall his par- ents owned. His father, Florence “Dude” James Graham, and mother, Millie, ran the pool hall six days a week. It was a textile bar during the industry’s heyday, serving up hotdogs and hamburg- ers to the local millworkers. It had a pinball machine, a jukebox and a rocking chair where his mother sat at the end of the bar, according to multiple media accounts of an e-book auto- biography Graham self-published during his 2016 presidential bid. The family cooked its meals in the bar’s kitchen and shared a bathroom with patrons. To bathe, they heated water on the stove and washed in a metal tub, Graham wrote. When some customers left to use the restroom, Graham wrote he sometimes snuck swigs of their beers or puffs of their cigarettes, earning him the nickname “Stinkball.” A “C” student in high school, Graham once told a teacher, “I want to be governor,” gar- nering snickers from his classmates, Graham wrote. After scoring an 800 on his SAT, he became the first person in his family to attend college, enrolling at the University of South Carolina. Not long after he started school, the family went to Disney World for their first vacation. But when they returned home, tragedy struck. His mother became exhausted and nau- seous. A few months later, she was diagnosed with Stage 4 Hodgkin lymphoma. The doctors gave her six months to live. The next spring, Graham’s father was diag- nosed with prostate cancer. Graham and his younger sister were in and out of the hospital with their ill parents. On June 9, 1976, Millie Graham died holding her son’s hand. Then, 15 months later, their father died of a massive heart attack. “I remember that day, Lindsey came run- ning in and just grabbed me up and hugged me and he was like, ‘I’m so sorry, but it’s going to be OK. I’m going to take care of you.’ And he did. He’s always been there for me no mat- ter what,” she said in a May campaign ad and mailer for Graham’s latest Senate bid. Graham was 22 and his sister was 13. An aunt and uncle took his sister in, but Graham still helped raise her, driving home from col- lege every chance he had. Graham graduated with his bachelor’s degree from the University of South Carolina and became a commissioned Air Force officer before starting law school. To help pay his parents’ lingering medical bills and care for his sister, he sold pots and pans door to door in Columbia and tended the family’s liquor store on weekends. After the bar exam, Graham began four years of active duty. The Air Force assigned him to the legal office at Shaw Air Force Base, where he took on cases related to the military’s flawed drug testing program. His sister was in college when Graham was assigned as one of four Air Force prosecutors in Europe at the tail end of the Cold War. He adopted her so she could receive his mil- itary benefits. In all, he served in the U.S. Air Force for 33 years, more than six of those on active duty as a lawyer. He joined the Air National Guard in 1989 and joined a small-town law practice in Walhalla. His political career began with a run for the state House, beating out the Democratic incumbent in 1992. He served just one term in the state Legisla- ture. In 1994, he won a U.S. House seat, replac- ing retiring U.S. Rep. Butler Derrick to become the first Republican from the 3rd District since Reconstruction. Around this time, Graham also joined an Air Force reserve unit, serving for a decade before retiring as a colonel. Graham spent four terms in the U.S. House, where in 1999 he gained public attention as one of the House managers during the Sen- ate’s impeachment trial of then-President Bill Clinton. After the House voted to impeach Clinton on charges of perjury and obstruction of justice over his relations with White House intern Monica Lewinsky, the Senate found him not guilty. In 2002, Graham won election to the U.S. Senate as the chosen successor to retiring Sen. Strom Thurmond, who remains the only senator in U.S. history to reach age 100 in office. Thurmond, who died within six months of retiring, ranks fourth among longest-serving senators in history at 47½ years. WHO WILL RUN? A special primary to select a new Republi- can nominee to the seat Graham held for 23½ years is scheduled for Aug. 11. Last month, Graham soundly defeated five GOP competitors to win the primary with 57% of the vote. A long list of candidates is expected to file to replace on the ballot. A runoff Aug. 25 will almost certainly be needed. In South Carolina, a runoff is neces- sary if no candidate receives more than 50% of the vote. So far, U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman has said he will run. U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace also is consid- ering it, a former campaign staffer told the S.C. Daily Gazette. Both lost their bids for gover- nor last month. Norman placed third, while Mace placed fifth in the GOP primary. On the other hand, U.S. Rep. BY TERRY WARD TERRY.WARD@MYHORRYNEWS.COM CONWAY, S.C. — Park View Road has officially reopened to traffic after a five-month clo- sure, sporting a fresh new look and some notable upgrades. Park View Road, located off Main Street at 16th Avenue, borders Collins Park — a popular park for walkers, children and pickle ballers. But the street has been closed since late February for aesthetic and functional improvements. The road reopened on Saturday, July 10 and one- way traffic is again moving through. The goal of the project was to make the street safer by incorporating traffic calming measures according to June Wood, Conway’s Public Infor- mation Officer. Wood said back in March that “the road is a cut-through for some drivers and we want to make sure the traffic coming through there is not too fast.” To help with that, the city has added some curving mechanisms to help slow down traffic. Another addition to Park View Road includes new side- walks to improve walkability for the people who use Collins Park. There is also new landscap- ing including the addition of trees that were planted, to enhance curb appeal. The parking place design was also changed. Park View Road has been converted from a parallel parking system to angled, or head-in, parking to increase the number of available spaces and make parking faster and easier. The head-in parking is also helps maintain a consistent traffic flow and make it less likely for vehicles to stick out too far into the street. Underground, the project included a complete storm- water overhaul, with waterline improvements, and drainage upgrades, Wood said. STAFF ANALYSIS: Staff has conducted a preliminary review along with a subsequent review of the applicant’s revised conceptual plan. Since the initial submittal, the applicant has made several modifications in response to staff comments, including: • Revising the parking calculations and parking ratios; • Providing a proposed parking management plan utilizing resident parking permits, designated guest parking, and customer-only commercial parking; • Continue to limit commercial uses to the ground floor of the building; • Refining the ordinance to better align permitted uses with the proposed mixed-use development concept. Staff recognizes these revisions as meaningful improvements over the original proposal. However, several planning considerations remain in Planning Commission’s evaluation. Remaining considerations: • Breadth of permitted commercial uses. The ordinance permits a range of commercial uses within the building, including retail, dining, professional services, food and convenience stores, and entertainment/venue uses. • Integration of commercial uses. The ordinance appropriately limits commercial uses to the ground floor; however, it does not establish any maximum square footage, tenant size limitations, or proportional limits relative to the residential component. • Rooftop amenity and event space. The ordinance permits rooftop uses, including pool amenities, outdoor kitchen and event space, which will require compliance with City noise and lighting regulations. -- 17 of 154 -- STAFF REPORT Hwy 544 & Buccaneers Cove (Rezoning) • Parking and Site functionality. The revised proposal provides 470 parking spaces, including 330 permit-controlled resident parking spaces, 28 designated guest spaces, and parking reserved for commercial customers. The applicant proposes to regulate parking through an onsite property management program utilizing parking permits and guest passes. While these revisions improve the overall parking framework, the proposal continues to rely on modified parking ratios that are lower than those required by the UDO. The reduced parking demand is based, in part, on anticipated residential travel behavior and property management practices, including permit controls and roommate matching. Because these operational practices are not land use regulations and may change over time, Planning Commission should consider whether the proposed parking supply will adequately accommodate long-term residential, guest, commercial, employee, and service vehicle parking demands. • Potential Offsite Parking Staff understands the applicant is exploring acquisition of an adjacent parcel or parcels on Covery Lane for additional parking. However, new conflicts over the acquisition of 906 Covery Lane may further complicate and conflict with current site plans provided. Therefore, staff’s review is based solely on the parking shown within the current PD proposal. • Open Space and Landscaping calculations. The ordinance includes both a minimum of 20% pervious area and a requirement for 25% open space based on buildable area. While both standards are defined, staff notes that the methodology for calculating these requirements differs. Clarification of how these metrics are applied may improve overall consistency and ease of administration. • Design Modifications / Exceptions. The ordinance includes a number of modifications to standard UDO requirements, including, parking modifications, reduced interior landscaping requirements, and buffer flexibility. While flexibility is a key component of a PD, staff notes that these modifications should remain proportional to the development concept and continue to provide compatibility with adjacent properties. • Transportation Improvements. During agency coordination, Horry County has indicated that improvements to Buccaneers Cove will be required to accommodate the proposed development. In addition, SCDOT has indicated that a turn lane from Hwy 544 into Buccaneers Cove will be required. Planning Commission may wish to consider how and when these improvements should be incorporated into the final development approval. -- 18 of 154 -- STAFF REPORT Hwy 544 & Buccaneers Cove (Rezoning) Since the previous Planning Commission review, the applicant has revised the proposed development by reducing the total number of dwelling units from 199 to 180, revising the parking calculations, increasing the number of guest parking spaces, and proposing an operational parking management program that includes resident parking permits, designated guest parking, and commercial customer parking. While these revisions represent an improvement over the previous submittal, the overall parking strategy continues to rely on reduced parking ratios and operational management techniques rather than an increase in the physical parking supply. The long-term effectiveness of permit parking, roommate matching, and parking management policies depends on future property management practices that are not regulated through zoning. ISSUE: Request to rezone approximately 120.71+/- acres of property located along Hwy 378, upon annexation into the City of Conway, from Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) district to the City of Conway Medium-Density Residential (R-2) and Conservation Preservation (CP) districts. APPLICANT(S): Kingston Engineering, agent PIN(s): 337-00-00-0023 CURRENT ZONING: Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) PROPOSED ZONING: Medium Density Residential (R-2) and Conservation Preservation (CP) districts BACKGROUND: City Council approved first reading of the annexation ordinance for the subject property at its May 4, 2026 meeting. Planning Commission is now being asked to hold the required public hearing and provide a recommendation to City Council regarding the appropriate zoning upon annexation. The subject property contains approx. 120.71+/- acres and is located along Hwy 378, and is currently within Horry County’s jurisdiction, where it is zoned Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA). The property is located within the City’s utility service area, and future development of the property will require connection to City water and sewer services. Concurrent with the annexation request, the applicant has submitted a Development Agreement outlining the proposed development of the property. The applicant intends to develop the site for single-family residential purposes and is requesting Medium-Density Residential (R-2) zoning for the developable portions of the property. The associated Development Agreement is being considered separately and establishes the proposed development framework, public benefits, and other obligations associated with the project. Portions of the property contain mapped flood hazard areas, wetlands, and other environmentally sensitive features. Consistent with the City’s policy of protecting floor-prone and environmentally sensitive areas that may be unsuitable for residential development, staff recommends that these areas be zoned Conservation Preservation (CP) upon annexation. DEFINITION / INTENT OF PROPOSED ZONING: Per Sec. 3.2.4 of the UDO, the Medium-Density Residential District is intended to provide areas for medium density attached, detached, semi-attached and multifamily residential development in the City of Conway, -- 103 of 154 -- STAFF REPORT Hwy 378 (Rezoning) while prohibiting uses that would substantially interfere with the development or continuation of residential structures in the district. Per Sec. 3.2.15 of the UDO, the CP district is intended to provide needed open space for general outdoor and indoor recreational uses, and to protect environmentally sensitive areas and flood-prone areas from the encroachment of any residential, commercial, industrial, or other uses capable of adversely affecting the relatively undeveloped character of the district. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: The subject property is adjacent to a mix of institutional, residential, commercial, and undeveloped land, including: • To the rear: Conway High School (Institutional – IN) and two vacant parcels zoned Conservation Preservation (CP) • Along Radio Lane: properties zoned Highway Commercial (HC) and Low/Medium-Density (R-1); and • All other adjacent properties are located in the County’s jurisdiction and zoned Highway Commercial (HC) and Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA). COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s future land use map designates the majority of the property as Medium-Density Residential, with a portion of the Highway 378 frontage identified as Highway Commercial (HC). The requested R-2 zoning is generally consistent with the Future Land Use Map for the majority of the property and reflects the applicant’s intent to develop the site for residential purposes. The proposed CP zoning for flood-prone and environmentally sensitive areas is also consistent with the City’s policy of protecting areas that may be unsuitable for residential development. Planning Commission should note that the Hwy 378 frontage is identified as HC on the Future Land Use Map. However, the applicant is not currently proposing commercial development as part of the zoning request or associated Development Agreement. Planning Commission may consider whether the proposed R-2 zoning is appropriate for the frontage based on the applicant’s stated residential development intent, surrounding conditions, and the overall zoning framework proposed upon annexation. STAFF ANALYSIS: The proposed R-2 zoning would allow a range of residential housing types and is generally consistent with the Medium-Density Residential designation shown on the Future Land Use Map for a majority of the property. The proposed CP zoning for flood-prone and environmentally-sensitive areas would provide additional protection for portions of the site that may be unsuitable for development. -- 104 of 154 -- STAFF REPORT Hwy 378 (Rezoning) Although a portion of the Hwy 378 frontage is designated Highway Commercial (HC) on the Future Land Use Map, the applicant has indicated an intent to develop the property for residential purposes. The associated Development Agreement is also being reviewed in connection with the proposed residential development of the site. Because negotiations related to the Development Agreement remain ongoing, the zoning request should be reviewed based on the appropriate zoning designations upon annexation, while recognizing that specific development obligations may continue to be refined through the Development Agreement process. Staff finds that R-2 zoning for the developable portions of the property, together with the CP zoning for flood-prone or environmentally sensitive areas, provides a reasonable zoning framework upon annexation. RECOMMENDATION: In addition to holding the required public hearing, staff recommends that Planning Commission conduct a thorough review of the request and make an informed recommendation to City Council regarding the appropriate zoning(s) upon annexation. ISSUE: Review and recommendation regarding a proposed Development Agreement for approx. 120.71+/- acres of property located along Hwy 378, in connection with annexation and rezoning of the property into the City of Conway. APPLICANT(S): Kingston Engineering, agent PIN(s): 337-00-00-0023 BACKGROUND: City Council approved first reading of the annexation ordinance for the subject property at its May 4, 2026 meeting. In conjunction with annexation and zoning of the property, the City and Developer have been discussing a proposed Development Agreement pursuant to the South Carolina Local Government Development Agreement Act. The proposed development agreement is intended to establish rights and obligations of the City and Developer related to development of the property, including vested development rights, infrastructure responsibilities, environmental protection, public improvements, and negotiated public benefits. The property is proposed to be developed primarily for residential purposes, with flood-prone and environmentally sensitive portions of the property proposed to be zoned Conservation Preservation (CP) upon annexation. Negotiations between the City and the developer remain ongoing, and several provisions of the Agreement have not been finalized. Among the outstanding issues are the scope of transportation improvements, which cannot be finalized until completion of the Traffic Impact Analysis (TIA), and the extent of the Developer’s obligations regarding the construction of the proposed Greenway trail improvements, and the extent to which the negotiated tree preservation and mitigation provisions will modify or satisfy the requirements of the Tree Preservation Ordinance. Accordingly the Agreement presented to Planning Commission should be considered a working draft that may include additions revisions prior to City’s Council’s consideration. **July 30, 2026 – DA Update – Please note the revised draft Development Agreement was submitted shortly before preparation of the packet; therefore, staff has not had adequate time to complete a full review of the proposed revisions. However, the applicant provided a brief detail below of the revisions made. The applicant submitted a revised draft Development Agreement that incorporates a commitment to construct a paved walking trail within the proposed park property. The revised agreement also clarifies the applicant's proposal that the dedication of the park property to the City, construction of the walking trail, -- 114 of 154 -- STAFF REPORT Development Agreement - Hwy 378 Property and provision of internal access connections collectively satisfy the tree mitigation requirements associated with the development. As proposed, the applicant would construct an approximately 2,600-linear-foot, 8-foot-wide paved walking trail along the eastern side of Altman Branch, extending from Highway 378 to the south side of Crabtree Canal. The proposed trail would consist of 2 inches of asphalt over 6 inches of base course and 12 inches of prepared subgrade. Under the proposed Development Agreement, the City would assume responsibility for any future improvements to the park property or extensions and improvements to the Crabtree Trail beyond the infrastructure proposed by the applicant. The applicant has indicated that additional revisions to the Development Agreement may be made following further discussions with City staff. DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT OVERVIEW: Pursuant to the SC Local Government Development Agreement Act (S.C. Code Ann. § 6-31-10 et seq.), local governments may enter into Development Agreements with property owners or developers to establish the terms and conditions under which property may be developed. Development Agreements are intended to provide certainty regarding applicable development regulations while allowing local governments to negotiate public benefits, infrastructure improvements, environmental protections, and other obligations that serve the public interest. Under the Act, the initial term of a Development Agreement depends on the size of the property. Because the subject property contains approx. 120.71 acres, the Agreement is limited to an initial term of 5 years, unless extended in accordance with the Act and the terms of the Agreement. The proposed Development Agreement is being considered concurrently with the requested annexation and zoning and is intended to establish the respective rights and obligations of the City and Developer should the property be annexed and developed. The law requires that the Planning Commission conduct a public hearing and make a recommendation to City Council prior to Council’s consideration of the proposed Agreement. City Council is the governing body authorized to approve, modify, or deny the Development Agreement following the required public hearing process. KEY PROVISIONS: The draft Development Agreement currently proposes or contemplates provisions including: • Vesting certain development rights for the property pursuant to the South Carolina Local Government Development Agreement Act; • Assigning responsibility for construction of public infrastructure serving the project; -- 115 of 154 -- STAFF REPORT Development Agreement - Hwy 378 Property • Requiring transportation improvements identified through the Traffic Impact Analysis (TIA) or otherwise required by the City or SCDOT; • Providing roadway and utility stub-outs to adjacent undeveloped properties; • Conveyance of approx. 21 acres to the City for public park and greenway (trail) purposes; • Protection of environmentally sensitive and flood-prone areas through Conservation Preservation (CP) zoning; • Annual compliance review requirements; and • Other provisions governing future development approvals, environmental protection, and implementation of the Project. Staff notes that negotiations remain ongoing regarding certain public benefits, including whether the Developer will construct the Greenway Trail improvements or convey only the land upon which the City would construct those improvements. STAFF ANALYSIS: Staff continues to work with the developer to negotiate the terms of the proposed Development Agreement. While substantial progress is being made, several material provisions remain under discussion and may change prior to City Council’s consideration. In particular: • The review of roadway and transportation improvements cannot be finalized until completion of the TIA; • The parties continue to negotiate to what extent the developer will construct the trail improvements or instead only convey the land for future construction by the City; and • The parties continue to negotiate the extent to which the developer will receive relief from the City’s Tree Preservation Ordinance and mitigation requirements in exchange for the public benefits provided under the Agreement. Planning Commission’s review should focus on the overall framework of the proposed Agreement, whether the proposed Agreement is consistent with the City’s Comprehensive Plan, and whether the public benefits being negotiated are appropriate for the vested development rights proposed to be granted. In addition to the original draft provided by the applicant, there is another draft in the packet that includes the original language of the Agreement (in black) and staff’s recommended revisions in red. Also attached is a document outlining the key provisions and a summary of revisions. RECOMMENDATION: In addition to holding the required public hearing, staff recommends that Planning Commission review the proposed Development Agreement, receive public comment, and make a recommendation to City Council -- 116 of 154 -- STAFF REPORT Development Agreement - Hwy 378 Property regarding the Agreement in concept, recognizing that negotiations between the City and the Developer remain ongoing and that revisions may occur prior to final consideration by Council. title: APPD MINUTES 8.6.26
text: PC 8/6/2026 CITY OF CONWAY PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING THURSDAY, August 6, 2026 Planning & Building Dept. Conference Room — 196 Laurel Street Present: George Ulrich, Allan Cornell, Thomas J. Anderson III, Stacy Knotts, Jessica Wise, David Sligh, Greg Bryson Absent: Kendall Brown Staff: Jessica Hucks, Planning Director; Nancy Alvarez, Assistant Planner; Charlotte Peterson, Assistant Planner; Louis Smith, IT Others: CALL TO ORDER Wise called the meeting to order at approximately 5:30 pm. Il. APPROVAL OF MINUTES Ulrich made a motion, seconded by Anderson to approve the July 9, 2026, minutes as written. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. I. PUBLIC INPUT IV. Wise made a motion to open public input. Scott Saba, Bob Moore, Margret Ramsey, and Robert Godwin spoke during public input. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Cornell and the motion carried unanimously. SUBDIVISIONS A. Brookhaven, Phase 1- The applicant is requesting approval of Phase 1 of the Brookhaven subdivision (PIN: 336-00-00-0060) Hucks stated the item is a request for preliminary plan approval for Phase 1 of the Brookhaven Planned Development. The overall Brookhaven project was annexed and zoned as a PD in 2024, in conjunction with a development agreement. The master plan was subsequently reviewed and approved by the Technical Review Committee in September 2025. Phase 1 includes 83 SF residential lots. Of those, 39 will have a min. lot width of 40-ft, and 44 will have amin. lot width of 50-ft. This phase also includes approx. 34.6 acres of open space and a 3.25-acre amenity site. The proposed lot mix, open space, and amenity area are consistent with the approved master plan. Vv. PC 8/6/2026 The developer will also provide an all-weather access road connecting this phase of the development to Juniper Bay Rd for emergency response purposes, in accordance with a previously approved design modification. The plans are still undergoing final Technical Review. If Planning Commission recommends approval, staff recommends that it be contingent upon final review and approval by the Technical Review Committee. The applicant John Richards, representing Thomas and Hutton, was present. Wise made a motion to approve the request, seconded by Anderson. The motion carried unanimously. PUBLIC HEARINGS A. REZONING REQUEST(S) 1. WITHDRAWN - Request to rezone approximately 1.54+/- acres of property located at 906 Covery Lane (PIN 382-12-04-0005), from the Horry County Neighborhood Commercial (NC) and Residential, no mobile homes allowed, (SF20) districts to the City of Conway Planned Development (PD) district upon annexation. Previously Deferred...Request to rezone approximately 5.27+/- acres of property located at the intersection of Hwy 544 and Buccaneer’s Cove (PIN 382-12-04-0006), from the Neighborhood Commercial (NC) district to the Planned Development (PD) district. Request to rezone approximately 1.17+/- acres of property located at 908 and 916 Buccaneers Cove (PIN 382-13-01-0002 and 382-13-01-0001), from Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF20) district to the City of Conway Planned Development (PD) district upon annexation. Wise made a motion to combine agenda items A.1 — A.3, seconded by Ulrich. The first three agenda items were related to a proposed mixed-use Planned Development. Staff noted that the first item had been withdrawn by the property owner, and although the owner later attempted to rescind the withdrawal, a new application would be required. The second item involved the primary development parcel, while the third added two adjacent parcels associated with the project. Staff provided an overview of the revised proposal, which includes a multi-story mixed-use building with residential units, ground-floor commercial space, rooftop amenities, and parking. Revisions since the original submission included a reduced building height, fewer residential units, and updates to the site layout. Staff also identified several outstanding comments regarding the Planned Development narrative, open space calculations, landscaping, lighting, architectural standards, and site design. Prior to the meeting, the applicant requested that the entire application be deferred to allow the withdrawn parcel to be resubmitted and to address staff comments. Staff explained that the decision to grant a deferral rests with the Planning Commission. Given the significant public interest and multiple public notices, staff recommended opening the public hearing to allow public comment before determining whether to defer the request. Wise made a motion to open public input. PC 8/6/2026 6. Annette Stephenson, Ryan Edgington, Carley Veux, Andrew Brown, Bob Moore, Scott Saba, and Ann Hawa spoke during public input. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Cornell. The motion carried unanimously. The applicant Tommy Holt was present. Ulrich made a motion to table the rezoning request until the project is complete and can be brought back to the board, seconded by Cornell. The motion carried unanimously. Request to rezone approximately 2.56+/- acres of property located on Hwy 501, across from Sioux Swamp Dr. (PIN: 326-14-04-0010), from Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) and Highway Commercial (HC) districts to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district upon annexation. Hucks stated this request is for zoning upon annexation of approximately 2.56 acres located along Hwy 501, across from Sioux Swamp Dr. The property is currently in Horry County and is zoned Commercial Forest Agriculture and Highway Commercial. Upon annexation, the applicant is requesting City of Conway Highway Commercial zoning. The annexation is being pursued primarily to facilitate the future construction of a right of way that will provide access to potential development of the adjacent properties already within the City limits. The surrounding properties are currently vacant. The City’s future land use map designates the highway frontage as Highway Commercial and the remainder as low/medium-density residential. Given the property’s frontage along Hwy 501, the surrounding City zoning pattern, and its intended use for future access, staff finds that the requested zoning is generally consistent with the area. Council approved first reading of the ordinance annexing the property at their July 20 meeting. Staff recommend that Planning Commission hold the required public hearing and forward a recommendation to City Council. Wise made a motion to open public input. No one spoke during public input. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Ulrich and the motion carried unanimously. The designated agent, Dan Stacy, was present. Ulrich made a motion to approve the request, seconded by Anderson III. The motion was carried unanimously. Request to rezone approximately 1.74+/- acres of property located on Hwy 501 and Gardner Lacy Rd, including properties at 101 and 103 Gardner Lacy Rd (PINs: 399-01-04-0001, 400-04- 03-0001, and 400-04-03-0002), from Horry County Limited Industrial (LI) district to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district upon annexation. Request to rezone approximately 9.49+/- acres of property located at 2899 E. Hwy 501 (PIN: 400-04-02-0002), from Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) district to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district upon annexation. Ulrich made a motion to combine agenda items A.5 and A.6, seconded by Wise. PC 8/6/2026 Hucks stated agenda items five and six are related and involve the same applicant and potential future development project, staff recommended hearing both items together. The request includes four properties totaling 11.23 acres along Hwy 501 and Gardner Lacy Rd being considered for annexation and rezoning to the Highway Commercial Zoning District. The first request includes approximately 1.74 acres consisting of a vacant parcel adjacent to Domino's Pizza and two commercially developed properties at 101 and 103 Gardner Lacy Road. Although the Future Land Use Map designates the properties as Industrial, the requested Highway Commercial zoning is consistent with the existing commercial development pattern in the area. The second request includes approximately 9.49 acres at 2899 E. Highway 501; a vacant property formerly used as a used-car dealership. The requested Highway Commercial zoning is consistent with the Future Land Use Map and surrounding zoning pattern. Wise made a motion to open public input. No one spoke during public input. The applicant Franklin Daniels was present. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Ulrich and the motion carried unanimously. Anderson III made a motion to approve the request, seconded by Cornell. The motion was carried unanimously. 7. Request to rezone approximately 0.13+/- acres of property located at 124 Quail Run (PIN: 383- 09-04-0058), from Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF10) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district upon annexation. Hucks stated that the property is located in the Quail Creek Subdivision, near Coastal Carolina University. Ownership of the property was transferred to the current owner in June of 2026, and restrictive covenants were recorded on that dat. The property contains a single-family residence, and the request to annex is submitted to facilitate a name change on the city utility service account. City Council approved the first reading of annexation the property at their July 20" meeting. The requested zoning upon annexation will be the Low-Medium Density Residential District. Wise made a motion to open public input. No one spoke during public input. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Anderson IIJ and the motion carried unanimously. The applicant was not present. Wise made a motion to approve the request, seconded by Ulrich. The motion was carried unanimously. 8. WITHDRAWN...Request to rezone approximately 0.34+/- acres of property located at 2857 Hwy 378 (PIN: 337-16-02-0028), from Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF40) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district upon annexation. 9. Previously Deferred...Request to rezone approximately 120.71+/- acres of property located along Hwy 378, between Mill Pond Rd and Radio Lane (PIN: 337-00-00-0023), from the Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) to the City of Conway Medium-Density Residential (R-2) and Conservation Preservation (CP) districts upon annexation. PC 8/6/2026 Hucks stated the applicant is requesting annexation and zoning of approximately 120.71 acres located along Hwy 378. The property is currently in Horry County and zoned Commercial Forest Agriculture. Upon annexation, the applicant is requesting Medium-Density Residential (R-2) for the developable portions of the property and Conservation Preservation (CP) for the flood hazard areas of the property. This request is being considered alongside a Development Agreement, which will be discussed separately. For this item, Planning Commission is only being asked to consider whether the proposed zoning upon annexation into the City is appropriate and consistent with the City’s adopted plans and policies. Issues related to engineering and construction of the property are addressed later through subdivision, permitting, and other regulatory review processes. The applicant has indicated that the property is intended to be developed for single-family residential purposes. The proposed R-2 zoning is generally consistent with the Future Land Use Map for the majority of the property. Staff is recommending that the flood hazard areas be zoned Conservation Preservation upon annexation to provide long-term protection of those areas and limit development where environmental constraints exist, and for the 21 acres proposed to be conveyed to the City to be entirely zoned Conservation Preservation as well. Staff notes that a portion of the Hwy 378 frontage is identified as Highway Commercial on the future land use map. However, the applicant is not proposing commercial development, and staff notes that much of that frontage contains environmentally sensitive areas that reduce its practical suitability for standalone commercial development. The City’s adopted Pathways and Trails Plan identifies a future greenway or trail connection through this property. As proposed, the accompanying Development Agreement contemplates conveyance of approximately 21 acres of property to the City for installation of the trail, and further negotiations to include construction of the trail by the developer prior to conveyance. These proposed public benefits are part of the Development Agreement and will be discussed under the next agenda item. From a zoning standpoint, the R-2 zoning for the developable portions of the property, together with the CP zoning for the environmentally sensitive areas, provides a reasonable rezoning framework upon annexation. The applicant is present to provide additional information as needed or answer any question you may have. This is also a public hearing item. Wise made a motion to open public input. No one spoke during public input. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Ulrich and the motion carried unanimously. The applicant Clint Richardson, representing Kingston Engineering, was present. Wise made a motion to approve the request, seconded by Anderson III. The motion was carried unanimously. PC 8/6/2026 B. DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT(S) 1. Previously Deferred...Request to enter into a Development Agreement with the City of Conway, for approximately 120+/- acres of property located along Hwy 378, between Mill Pond Rd and Radio Lane and identified by PIN 337-00-00-0023. The subject property is proposed to be developed for single-family detached residential purposes and is concurrently proposed to be annexed and rezoned to the Medium-Density Residential (R-2) district upon annexation, with portions of the property potentially designated Conservation Preservation (CP). Hucks stated that the proposed development agreement establishes the specific rights and responsibilities of the City and the developer as the property is developed. In this case, the developer would receive development rights for an initial 5-year term, and the agreement establishes obligations related to infrastructure, transportation improvements, environmental protections, public access, and other negotiable benefits. Current provisions include responsibility for public infrastructure, transportation improvements, roadway and utility connections to adjacent undeveloped properties; approx. 21 acres proposed for conveyance to the City for park and greenway purposes and annual compliance reviews. The latest draft adds construction of approximately 2,600 linear feet of an 8-foot-wide paved walking trail along Altman Branch. The applicant proposes that the park land dedication, trail construction, and internal access connections satisfy the project's tree mitigation requirements. Staff explained that the agreement remains a working draft. Review of the latest revisions is ongoing, the Traffic Impact Analysis has not yet been submitted, and several provisions, including transportation improvements, park conveyance, trail construction, and tree mitigation language, remain under development. Staff clarified that the Planning Commission's role is to conduct the required public hearing and make a recommendation on the overall framework and consistency of the agreement with the Comprehensive Plan. Final action will be taken by City Council following a second public hearing. Wise made a motion to open public input. No one spoke during public input. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Ulrich and the motion carried unanimously. The applicant, Clint Richardson from Kingston Engineering, was present. Wise made a motion to approve the request, seconded by Bryson. The motion was carried unanimously, VI. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN STEERING COMMITTEE SELECTION Peterson and Alvarez presented the list of steering committee candidates for the City of Conway Comprehensive Plan rewrite. Wise made a motion to approve the steering committee selection, seconded by Comell. The motion carried unanimously. VII. BOARD INPUT PC 8/6/2026 IX. STAFF INPUT X. ADJOURNMENT Wise made a motion was made to adjourn the meeting, seconded by Ulrich. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. The meeting adjourned at approximately 6:51pm. Approved and signed this 2——_day of ~EYRINEE RL, 2026. CNUtue. Jessica Wise, Meeting Chair

A5 www.myhorrynews.com Local author shares tale of betrayal, heartbreak and finding true love A STORY ‘ONLY GOD COULD HAVE WRITTEN’ SHANNON KEITH info@myhorrynews.com Marti Schutte said the front porch of her “little county home” in Aynor is where she feels closest to God. “That’s my peace ... I can sit there and see how his designs on my life have come true,” she said Schutte, 50, a Physical Education teacher with Horry County Schools, lives an admittedly “sim- ple” life, with and her husband, Jon, occupying about seven acres of the 50-acre farm she grew up in. However, Schutte said her 2,200 square foot home is her “fairytale” and her “happily ever after” and that the story of her life could only have been written by one author. “My story is one that only God could have writ- ten,” Schutte said. “I look back on my life and I can see his grand design so clearly. I know that God always had plans for me.” Schutte, a native of Del- aware, moved to South Carolina when she was in the fifth grade, raised on a 50-acre farm in Aynor, the same farm she came back to about a decade ago. “My life has come full circle,” Schutte said. “God’s plan took me across the country and took many years ... but he gave me the storybook ending every girl dreams of.” Last month, Schutte published ‘The Porch God Promised’ .. which chroni- cles her struggles through her first marriage, which ended in divorce but ulti- mately led her to “the man God intended for me” ... her husband, Jon. “I wrote this book because God wanted me to,”, Schutte said. “I think it can give people hope and peace.” “It was a fairytale ... If you didn’t look too close” Schutte met her first husband, who she renamed Trevor in her book, while attending col- lege in 1995. “I talk about it in my book ... It was like a fairy- tale,” she said. “It was textbook ... We both grew up in Christian homes, we shared the same values ... I thought I was living the dream.” Schutte said Trevor was a successful businessman, which allowed her to be a stay-at-home mother after the birth of their first two sons. “We had it all. On paper, our life was perfect,” Schutte said. “It was fairy- tale ... If you didn’t look too close.” Schutte said that even through the early, happy, years of their marriage, Trevor always begrudged her one thing. “Before I had my porch, I had a balcony,” Schutte said of the home she shared with her first husband. “That’s where I found peace ... where I could truly pray and hear God’s voice. Trevor never liked that I had such a place... He resented it even. It wasn’t until many years later that I learned, that people who carry secrets cannot sit quietly in the presence of peace.” While she was pregnant with her third son, Schutte said Trevor’s secrets start- ed to unveil. Eight months into her pregnancy with her third child, Schutte said “the cracks in our foundation appeared.” “I saw a message on my husband’s phone from someone he worked with and I listened to it,” she said “it was like, ‘hey handsome, you’re proba- bly working on that beau- tiful body of yours’ ... I was devastated.” Schutte said that although her husband ini- tially denied the affair, her marriage would never be the same. “That was the beginning of the end,” Schutte said. “But even then, God was telling me to move forward ... I just didn’t know where he was leading me.” “I DON’T LOVE YOU ANY- MORE” Shortly after the birth of her third son, Schutte said Trevor announced that he was taking a job in Las Vegas, Nevada, tearing her from her family and friends in South Carolina. “I was scared for myself and my family” she said. “But I still moved forward, because I believed God had a plan for me.’ Shortly before leaving for his new job, Schutte said her husband said five words to her that changed her life. “Trevor said that I prob- ably shouldn’t move to Vegas,” she said. “He told me, ‘I don’t love and you anymore’ ... that absolute- ly devastated me.” Schutte said that even though her husband recanted his statement and purchased a “mil- lion-dollar” home in Las Vegas with a balcony, the disconnect in their mar- riage continued to grow. “He had taken away my balcony ...my peace,” she said. “Still, I knew, God had moved me all the way across the country for a reason.” About two years after she moved to Las Vegas, Schutte said she met the man that would change her life. “SIMPLY ELECTRIC” Schutte said she was first introduced to Jon through mutual friends. She was 32 at the time and he was 25. Although she was married, Schutte said the “spark” upon meeting Jon was undeniable. “I can’t begin to describe it ... It was simply electric,” she said. “We both felt it, but we didn’t know where it would lead at the time.” Schutte said that after a few interactions with Jon, he admitted to having feelings for her, yet urged her to try and save her marriage. “He told me he couldn’t be friends with me because of the way he felt about me,” Schutte said. “And he told me that mar- riage was forever and that we have to honor God. “I mean, what kind of a man does that?” She asked. “They just don’t make men like Jon any- more.” Schutte said she tried to make her marriage work through the next several months, but she knew in her heart that it was over. “I tried,” she said. “I tried for my family ... I tried for my children ... I tried for God. But nothing helped in the end.’ “SHELTER IN THE STORM” About two years after moving to Las Vegas, Schutte said Trevor admit- ted to having a five-year affair and that he was leav- ing her. “I sensed it was coming,” she said. “It started out with things like him sug- gesting we have an open marriage. Later, he even offered me $200,000 to leave him. One day, he just told me he was leaving me ... and walked out casually like he was going to the gym.” Devastated, Schutte said she called on family and friends for support, then called on Jon. Their friendship eventually turned to “absolute true love.” “I don’t know what made me call him,” she said. “But somehow I knew he was the person I needed. I just knew he was my shel- ter in the storm.” Over the next few months, Schutte and Jon started dating, eventually marrying and having a daughter together. “The thing that almost broke me ended up lead- ing me to the best thing that ever happened to me,” Schutte said. “I didn’t know it at the time, but now I see God’s vision clearly. He had a plan for me all along.” “FULL CIRCLE” About two years after they were married, still liv- ing in Las Vegas, Schutte said she and Jon visited her family farm in Aynor, a visit she calls a “God wink.” “I had taken some pic- tures of the farm and posted them on Facebook, saying I missed South Car- olina and didn’t want to leave,” Schutte said. “Jon saw the post and imme- diately told me that he wanted to bring me back home to South Carolina. I knew in that moment that God had brought me full circle ... everything that happened to me was him guiding me back home.” Shortly after moving back to South Carolina, Schutte and her family took over about seven acres of her childhood farm and built their cur- rent home. And in place of the balconies of her past, Jon replaced them with a front porch .. the porch God had always promised her, Schutte said. It’s amazing to look back on it now,” she said. “I couldn’t see his vision when I was a mother of three crying on the floor because her world had shattered. But now I’m able to see God’s plan full scope.” Schutte said she hopes her readers can find peace ... and hope ... in her story. “When I first started writing my story, it was more of a steamy romance,” she said. “About a year and a half ago, I started to rewrite my story from the perspective of someone who has seen God’s plan for me come to life. “I just want people to have hope,” she said. “Hope that even in the worst moments of your life, God is preparing you for the best parts of your life.”The Porch God Prom- ised” is available through Amazon and is download- able on Amazon Kindle. In addition to being available on Amazon and at Peony & Fig, The Porch God Promised is also car- ried locally at The Ferry Market and The Aynor Family Pharmacy in Aynor. Readers can learn more about the book, upcom- ing events, and purchase at www.theporchgod- promised.com (http:// www.theporchgod- promised.com/). Schutte also started an email for readers to reach out to. The email is Martschutte0@ gmail.com. The cover of Marti Schutte’s new book. The project is approximately 6.81 acres and identified by PINs 382-12-04-0006 and 382-12-04-0005. The Planned Development envisions a mixed-use community comprised of multifamily housing and a variety of commercial uses to meet the needs of the existing and future residents of the City of Conway and the University. The development will be accessed from Buccaneer’s Cove. CURRENT CONDITIONS Currently, PIN 382-12-04-0006 is currently vacant and wooded. PIN 382-12-04-0005 contains a single- family detached structure, which is proposed to be removed. PURPOSE AND INTENT PURPOSE. The purpose of this Planned Development is to allow a vertically integrated mixed-use development consisting of commercial and residential uses designed for a student-oriented population. INTENT. The Planned Development (PD) District is established to: 1. Encourage innovative and flexible site design that cannot be achieved through strict application of conventional zoning districts; 2. Promote integrated, unified development of a site under a single development concept; 3. Allow for limited, site-specific modifications to the standards of the UDO where such modifications result in equal or better outcomes; and 4. Ensure that development is consistent with the Comprehensive Plan and compatible with surrounding uses. CONSISTENCY WITH THE COMPREHENSIVE PLAN This Planned Development is consistent with the City of Conway’s Comprehensive Plan by advancing its goals for coordinated growth, mixed-use development, and enhanced quality of life. The project introduces a thoughtfully designed mixed-use center that supports both population and economic growth associated with the University and the broader Conway community. The development integrates residential and commercial uses within a unified, multi-level building, promoting efficient land use and creating a cohesive, walkable environment. By combining these uses, the project encourages reduced vehicle trips and fosters a more connected, pedestrian-oriented community, in alignment with the City’s vision for sustainable development patterns. A variety of open space and recreational amenities are incorporated to support active lifestyles, social interaction, and accessible gathering spaces. These elements reinforce the Comprehensive Plan’s emphasis on livability, placemaking, and community engagement. -- 38 of 198 -- 2 CCU HOUSING PLANNED DEVELOPMENT DISTRICT – PIN 382-12-04-0006 & -0005 The residential component provides a housing type that responds to local demand, particularly in proximity to the University, while the commercial spaces offer services and amenities that meet the needs of nearby residents and businesses. Together, these uses create a balanced and complementary development pattern. Overall, the scale, design, and mix of uses are compatible with the surrounding area and contribute to an integrated, vibrant environment that supports the long-term planning objectives of the City of Conway.
