A3 www.myhorrynews.com SC’S VOTING LINES FROM A2 LOCAL ECONOMIC BOOST, FROM A1 what the president’s asking. Trump “has made his expectations unmistakable. There is no more time for hesitation or half measures,” she said. She seemed to blast South Carolina’s existing map as drawn on “identity politics or left-wing social engineering,” though it was drawn by the GOP-dominated Legislature. It also brought lawsuits from the NAACP, American Civil Liberties Union, and the League of Women Voters, which ultimately lost in court. “No more delays, no more excuses, no more indifference to activist courts,” Evette said. “We must finish this redistricting work now, by any means necessary.” Wilson said it’s a “cause worth taking up,” while acknowl- edging there’s a lot of frustration and anger. Just two legislative days remain in the 2026 regular session. Republicans on the House Judiciary Committee forged ahead on advancing the redistricting legislation even after acknowledging the Senate rejected the whole effort. The com- mittee voted 15-9 on party lines to send the bill to the floor to potentially take up if senators change their minds. As for what’s next, “All I can tell you is, I believe the House has done what we can do to further the process,” said Rep. Jay Jordan, R-Florence. A do-over vote in the Senate is possible. But Massey said that’s highly unlikely. If the session ends without a resolution governing the off-session, McMaster could call the Legislature back. But even then, he would have no authority to set the parameters for what legislators do. And he can’t require them to do any- thing. He has previously declined to say whether he supported the redistricting push, calling it a legislative matter. On Tuesday night, McMaster posted on social media that legislators still have two days to finish their work, to include considering “the important question of redistricting,” but stopped short of saying how they should resolve it. THE HOUSE BILL While the House proposal would delay primaries for South Carolina’s seven congressional seats, it would leave contests for U.S. Senate, state House and statewide elections on schedule for June 9, with runoffs two weeks later. Holding a second set of primaries in August could also cost taxpayers more than $3 million, when factoring in almost-certain runoffs. That does not include spending by county elections offices. It also doesn’t include the redis- tricting process itself. The House bill originally suggested an Aug. 11 primary. But a House panel voted Tuesday morning to bump that back a week to give the elections agency time to retool its databases and mail out overseas ballots the required 45 days in advance. Even so, elections Director Conway Belangia warned everything would have to go exactly right, otherwise “staff would have to work probably 24 hours a day to meet the deadlines.” Any runoffs would be Sept. 1. In South Carolina, primary runoffs are required if no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote. The vote tallies would then have to be certified by the fed- eral deadline of Sept. 19 to make the cutoffs for mailing out overseas ballots for the November general election. “All of the work that goes into election integrity would be compressed into 10 days,” Rep. Spencer Wetmore said. “We have spent years talking about election integrity, and it has been a Republican talking point that we have been rigging elections,” the Folly Beach Democrat said. “I don’t ever want to hear that again, because if this isn’t questioning election integrity and rigging maps, I don’t know what is.” played in the celebrity pro-am tournament on Wednesday. PGA stars like Brandt Snedeker (the even- tual winner) and Brooks Koepka played in the event and spoke highly of the tourna- ment. And for the greater Myrtle Beach area, the economic impact looks as though it again will be a needle-mover for the community. In 2025, Butler says that 58 percent of ticket sales came from non-locals. The boost in visitors and golf fans into the area for the event, he says, continues to be a major help and a driving force for why many are trying to keep the PGA Tour in town for years to come. “Those people are coming in and they’re staying for a few nights. They’re staying in our hotels and they’re eating in our restau- rants. Some of them are even taking time on our beaches or seeing other attractions if they aren’t staying at the golf tournament the whole time,” Butler said. “That money is going right into our econ- omy and helping keep our taxes low. It helps pay for our first responders, our roads, our teachers… that’s the direct impact.” But that’s just one side of the impact coin. Throughout the weekend, the course at the Dunes Club was praised for its ability to host golf at the sport’s highest level. The fairways and greens were in tremendous shape, and the course itself provided stunning views that made for great television. That impact, Butler said, is equally as sig- nificant. “The indirect impact is that we have this beautiful commercial running on the Golf Channel, showing this amazing golf course,” Butler said. “We see an increase in booking in our tee times during and for a few weeks after the tournament. Everyone sees it on TV and they want to come to Myrtle Beach and play golf. So, it’s a great advertisement.” Russell Long, President of the Dunes Golf and Beach Club, says the week was an over- whelming hit for members and guests alike. And the members at the Dunes Club are no longer the only ones who understand just how special the property is. Snedeker, after winning the event, called the course “phenomenal”, mentioning he wished that part of the reward for winning the tournament was the ability to become a member. That praise, Long says, will stick with those at the club for years to come. “When you hear a guy like Brandt Snedeker say that the course was so great and so spec- tacular that he wishes he could play it every day like we do, that’s the greatest compliment of all,” Long described. “This is a guy who is a golf hero… he knows golf as well as anyone in the world and he thinks that highly of our golf course, that’s incredible. It’s something to really be proud of.” Total numbers on attendance, economic impact and more are not available quite yet. But, anyone involved in the event will tell you that 2026 was a success — an that’s important given what could potentially lie ahead for Horry County’s relationship with the PGA Tour. 2027 will be the fourth and final year of the current contract for the ONEflight Myrtle Beach Classic. The hope, from the start, has been for these four years to be such a hit that the PGA Tour couldn’t turn down the possi- bility of returning to the area, potentially even making the Myrtle Beach Classic a stand- alone event. Right now, the Classic is paired with the Truist Championship at Quail Hollow Club in Charlotte, which draws the biggest names on the Tour — think the likes of Rory McIlroy and Justin Rose. But, there is real hope and belief that the event in Myrtle Beach could be such a suc- cess that the PGA Tour would explore making the Grand Strand tournament a standalone event, which would bring the very best play- ers on Tour into the area for an event starting in 2028. And while nothing has been confirmed, things are trending in the right direction. “We have one more year on the current contract… We’re already preparing for next year to be better than this year,” Butler said. “Beyond that, the PGA Tour just got a new CEO and they’re evaluating what 2028’s schedule looks like. We are certainly a part of those conversations and we hope to make some announcements in the future of some- thing positive for the Grand Strand.” Long agrees, and says that if it happens, the Dunes Club continues to be ready to host. Many believe that the tournament being in Myrtle Beach is a win-win-win for everyone involved. Between successful charitable efforts, impact on the local economy and the PGA Tour having a first-class host, many believe the ONEflight Myrtle Beach Classic has been the first step toward a very long-term partnership that could see professional golf returning to the area for many years to come. “I feel like we have been extremely suc- cessful in showing what we can do and showing we can handle it,” Long said. “We have shown that we can shine. We can attract. They know that… I think they’re going to give it every effort they have to give us an opportunity moving forward. We’re really fired up about grabbing that opportu- nity, running with it and being even better.” BY CHARLIE LENGAL | INFO@MYHORRYNEWS.COM Thousands of fans attended the 2026 ONEflight Myrtle Beach Classic at the Dunes Golf and Beach Club. Amendment(s) to Article 5 – Specific Use Regulations, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding revisions to the Non-commercial Keeping of Livestock or Fowl. The proposed amendment would establish new standards and restrictions to regulate the use of targeted grazing on city owned property in the City of Conway. Alvarez stated that many City-owned parcels that are vacant or difficult-to-maintain, require ongoing vegetation management to prevent overgrowth, improve neighborhood appearance, and reduce maintenance costs. Traditional mowing and clearing methods can be expensive, labor intensive, and in some cases limited due to access and difficult terrain. City Council has directed staff to research targeted grazing as an alternative approach used successfully in other communities to resolve these challenges. Targeted Grazing is a temporary vegetative land management practice that utilizes livestock, often goats, to clear brush, invasive species, and dense vegetation. In section 5.2.5 of the UDO the non-commercial keeping of livestock or fowl is permitted only as an accessory use under certain conditions in the Rural Residential District (RR), Residential Agricultural District (RA), and Forest Agricultural District (FA). However, some exceptions do exist. The provision is based on a definition of targeted grazing that was incorporated into Article 2- Definitions, which was adopted by City Council on May 4, 2026, as part of broader amendments to the UDO. The proposed amendment includes the following standards to properly regulate targeted grazing as a governmental service ; only occurring on property owned, leased, or otherwise controlled by the City, operating only under the authorization of the city or its designated contractor, adequately containing and supervising livestock with temporary fencing, herding practices, or other appropriate control measures, grazing to be defined as a temporary land management practice and shall not be classified as a principal, accessory, or private livestock keeping use, operations are not to be a nuisance, and all activities shall comply with applicable state and local animal welfare laws and regulations. APPLICANT(S): Marcus Thomas PIN(s): 368-01-03-0072 CURRENT ZONING: Low/Medium Density Residential (R-1) PROPOSED ZONING: Medium Density Residential (R-2) BACKGROUND: The property was transferred to the current owners in March of 2026 and is currently vacant. The applicant is requesting to rezone the property to the Medium-Density Residential (R-2) district to allow for the development of townhomes. Townhomes are not permitted within the current zoning district of R-1 and require a minimum zoning classification of R-2. Because the Future Land Use Map currently designates the property as Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1), the applicant has also submitted a concurrent request to amend the Future Land Use Map to Medium- Density Residential (R-2). DEFINITION / INTENT OF PROPOSED ZONING: Per Section 3.2.4 of the UDO, the R-2 District is intended to provide areas for medium density attached, detached, semi-attached and multifamily residential development in the City of Conway, while prohibiting uses that would substantially interfere with the development or continuation of residential structures in the District. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: The subject property is surrounded by parcels zoned Low/Medium-Density (R-1), with existing development consisting primarily of detached single-family residences. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The City’s future land use map designates the property as Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). However, the applicant has applied for a future land use map amendment for the Medium-density Residential district (Sec. 3.2.4): intended to accommodate a variety of housing types while protecting residential character from incompatible uses. -- 30 of 144 -- STAFF REPORT Sycamore St. (Rezoning) STAFF ANALYSIS: The proposed rezoning would permit a housing type that is not currently allowed on the property and would introduce Medium-Density Residential (R-2) zoning into an area that is otherwise developed and zoned predominately for detached single-family residential development. While Medium-Density Residential (R- 2) zoning exists within the general vicinity, no R-2 zoned properties are contiguous to the site. Planning Commission should consider: • Whether the proposed Future Land Use Map amendment is justified; • Whether the requested zoning is compatible with the surrounding development pattern; • Whether the site represents a logical location for attached residential development; • Whether the request advances the City’s housing goals while maintaining neighborhood compatibility; and • The precedent that approval may establish for similar requests within established R-1 neighborhoods. The request to amend the Future Land Use Map should be considered first before considering the rezoning request, as the rezoning request is largely dependent upon the Future Land Use Map amendment. Because the parcel is only 1.07 acres and is surrounded by R-1 zoning, the Commission should first determine whether Medium-Density Residential is an appropriate future land use designation for the property. If not, the rezoning request would be inconsistent with both the Comprehensive Plan and the City’s adopted rezoning criteria. RECOMMENDATION: In addition to holding the required public hearing, staff recommends that Planning Commission conduct a thorough review of the request and make an informed recommendation to City Council. Planning Commission is now being asked to hold the required public hearing and provide a recommendation to City Council regarding the appropriate zoning upon annexation. The subject property contains approx. 118.71 acres and is located along Hwy 378. The property is currently within Horry County’s jurisdiction, zoned Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA). The site is located within the City’s utility service area, and future development of the property will require connection to City utilities. The applicant has indicated an intent to develop the property for residential purposes consistent with the Medium-Density Residential (R-2) district. The R-2 district permits a mix of residential dwelling types, including single-family detached, single-family attached, and multifamily housing. A portion of the property is located within mapped flood hazard areas and wetland areas. Staff recommends that these areas be evaluated for Conservation Preservation (CP) zoning upon annexation, consistent with the City’s policy of protecting flood-prone and environmentally sensitive areas from future development impacts. DEFINITION / INTENT OF PROPOSED ZONING: Per Section 3.2.4 of the UDO, the Medium-Density Residential District is intended to provide areas for medium density attached, detached, semi-attached and multifamily residential development in the City of Conway, while prohibiting uses that would substantially interfere with the development or continuation of residential structures in the District. The requested R-2 zoning is generally consistent with the Future Land Use Map for the majority of the property. However, Planning Commission should consider whether the Hwy 378 frontage should remain consistent with the HC designation or whether the proposed residential zoning is appropriate for the frontage based on the applicants intent. STAFF ANALYSIS: The proposed R-2 zoning is generally consistent with the Future Land Use Map designation for the majority of the property and would allow for a range of residential housing types; however, a portion of the property’s frontage along Hwy 378 is designated Highway Commercial (HC). As a result, Planning Commission may wish to consider whether a single zoning classification is appropriate for the entire tract or whether multiple zoning districts should be established upon annexation to more closely align with the Future Land Use Map. Potential zoning approaches include: • Medium-Density Residential (R-2) for the developable residential portions of the property; • Conservation Preservation (CP) for flood-prone and environmentally sensitive areas; and • Highway Commercial (HC) for portions of the Hwy 378 frontage designated for commercial development on the Future Land Use Map. While the applicant has requested R-2 zoning, the Future Land Use Map contemplates a mixed land use pattern for the site, including both residential and commercial development opportunities. ISSUE: Request to rezone an approximate 10 +/- acre portion of 110 +/- acres of property located on Cultra Road and Oak Street, from the City of Conway Medium-Density Residential (R-2) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district. APPLICANT(S): Burroughs & Chapin Company, Inc. (Blake Arp) PIN(s): 325-00-00-0011 CURRENT ZONING: Medium-Density Residential (R-2) PROPOSED ZONING: Low/Medium Density Residential (R-1) BACKGROUND: The applicant is requesting to rezone approximately 10+/- acres in connection with a proposed subdivision and combination plat. If approved, the 10+/- acre portion would be conveyed to Conway Christian School and combined with the school’s existing campus property located adjacent to the subject property. The subject property is currently part of a larger tract containing split zoning of Conservation Preservation (CP) and Medium-Density Residential (R-2). The split zoning was originally established due to the presence of environmentally-sensitive areas and flood-prone land associated with portions of the tract. Under the City’s Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), split zoning of parcels is generally prohibited except in circumstances involving environmentally sensitive lands, where Conservation Preservation (CP) zoning is utilized to protect those areas. The proposed 10-acre subdivision area appears to be located outside of the environmentally sensitive portions of the parent tract and is intended to be combined with the adjacent Conway Christian School property, which is currently zoned Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). Rezoning the proposed subdivision area to R-1 would prevent the creation of a split-zoning condition on the newly combined parcel and maintain consistency with the zoning of the adjoining school campus. A large portion of the remaining tract will continue to contain flood-prone and environmentally sensitive areas currently zoned Conservation Preservation (CP). DEFINITION / INTENT OF PROPOSED ZONING: Per Section 3.2.3 of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), the intent of the R-1 district is to preserve and expand areas for low- to medium-density detached single-family residential development within the City of Conway. The district is intended to maintain a relatively spacious residential character, promote quiet and livable neighborhoods, and prohibit uses incompatible with the surrounding residential environment. -- 94 of 144 -- STAFF REPORT Cultra Rd/Oak St. (Rezoning) Educational facilities are permitted in both the R-1 and R-2 districts, subject to applicable standards in Sec. 5.1.9 of the UDO. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: The subject property is located adjacent to existing Conway Christian School campus and is surrounded by a mix of residential development, school/institutional uses, and undeveloped land. Surrounding zoning classifications include: • Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) • Medium-Density Residential (R-2) • High-Density Residential (R-3) (Midtown Village subdivision), and • Residential districts within Horry County’s jurisdiction. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The Future Land Use Map identifies the property primarily as Medium-Density Residential (R-2), with environmentally sensitive portions of the larger tract identified for Conservation Preservation (CP), and a portion along the Cultra Rd boundary identified as Neighborhood Commercial (NC). While the proposed R-1 zoning is not identical to the Medium-Density Residential designation shown on the Future Land Use Map, it represents a less intensive residential classification than currently contemplated for the property. The requested zoning would reduce, rather than increase, the development intensity of the approximately 10-acre tract. The proposed zoning is intended to facilitate the combination of the property with the adjacent Conway Christian School campus, which is currently zoned Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). As such, the request promotes zoning consistency across the combined parcel and does not create a more intensive development pattern than currently anticipated by the Comprehensive Plan. STAFF ANALYSIS: The proposed zoning request is primarily administrative in nature and is associated with a proposed subdivision and recombination of property between adjacent parcels. Because the City’s UDO generally prohibits split-zoned parcels except where necessary to preserve environmentally sensitive lands, rezoning the proposed 10-acre tract to R-1 would prevent the creation of a split-zoning condition once it is combined with the Conway Christian School property. The Conservation Preservation (CP) zoning on the environmentally sensitive portions of the remaining parent tract would remain unchanged. -- 95 of 144 -- STAFF REPORT Cultra Rd/Oak St. (Rezoning) Although the Future Land Use Map identifies the majority of the parent tract as Medium-Density Residential, the requested zoning represents a reduction in allowable residential intensity and is intended to create a consistent zoning designation across the combined school property. The request does not introduce a new land use pattern or increase allowable density. Rather, it aligns the zoning of the proposed subdivision tract with the adjacent school campus and supports a logical zoning configuration for the combined property. Staff finds the request is consistent with: • The intent of the UDO; • The surrounding zoning pattern; • The zoning of the adjacent Conway Christian School campus; and • Prior City policy regarding split-zoned parcels and environmentally sensitive lands. RECOMMENDATION: In addition to holding the required public hearing, staff recommends that Planning Commission conduct a thorough review of the request and make an informed recommendation to City Council. ISSUE: Amendments Article 5 – Supplemental and Accessory Uses, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding mobile vending requirements; specifically, to remove the fixed cap on mobile vending permits and establish administrative provisions for permit management. BACKGROUND: On July 21, 2025, the City Council adopted Ordinance #ZA2025-07-21(E), establishing a maximum of twenty (20) mobile vending permits for the 2026-27 fiscal year, with certain exemptions. On April 23, 2026, the annual cap was reached, effectively limiting the issuance of additional permits for the remainder of the current licensing cycle. Following implementation of the cap, staff identified several challenges associated with administering a fixed numerical limit: • Once the cap is reached, otherwise qualified vendors are unable to obtain permits regardless of available locations, operational capacity, or compliance history. • Modifying the permit limit requires a formal UDO text amendment, reducing the City’s ability to respond to changing circumstances and market conditions. • A fixed cap does not account for annual fluctuations in staffing resources, enforcement capacity, demand for permits, or the availability of suitable vending locations. The proposed amendment would not alter the operational standards applicable to mobile vending units, including licensing requirements, health and safety regulations, insurance requirements, waste management standards, location restrictions, or other applicable provisions of Sec. 5.1.16. Rather, the amendment is limited to revising how the annual number of permits is determined and administered. STAFF ANALYSIS: Staff believes the proposed amendment provides a more flexible and responsive framework for managing mobile vending activity while maintaining the regulatory safeguards currently contained within the UDO. The proposed framework retains City oversight of mobile vending operations while allowing the annual number of permits to be adjusted based on actual operational conditions rather than a fixed number established in the ordinance. Permit availability would be determined annually by the Planning Director, in coordination with the Zoning Administrator and Fire Marshal, utilizing objective criteria identified in the ordinance and supporting administrative policy. The number of permits available each year would be publicly established prior to the application period to ensure transparency and consistency. -- 125 of 144 -- Because all existing operational standards for mobile vending would remain in effect, staff does not anticipate that the proposed amendment would create adverse impacts on surrounding properties or alter the compatibility standards currently applicable to mobile vending operations. CITY COUNCIL: City Council has already approved First Reading of an Ordinance amending Sec. 5.1.16 of the UDO, as currently proposed, at their May 4, 2026 meeting. If Planning Commission provides a recommendation, final reading will be held at the June 15, 2026 Council meeting. PLANNING COMMISSION: Staff recommends that in addition to holding the required public hearing, that Planning review the proposed amendment, and make an informed recommendation to City Council. Each vending unit may submit multiple location sites, subject to staff approval. Commercial plan review fees will apply to each location. [ZA#2018-04-16 (B); ZA2019-03-18(B)] E. Appearance. The appearance of vending units shall be approved by the Planning Department with the following conditions: 1. The vendor shall be responsible to ensure that the vending unit is in good condition, free from evidence -- 129 of 144 -- of deterioration, weathering, discoloration, and rust. 2. Advertising consisting of the name and logo, and a listing of items available for sale may be displayed on the vending unit. No other form of advertising or signs shall be allowed. Additionally, the vendor shall follow the requirements in Sec. 11.2.2, Prohibited Signs, of the UDO. 3. If already constructed, the vendor shall submit three photographs and the dimensions of the vending unit. If not constructed, the vendor shall submit a copy of the plans and color renderings of the vending unit. 4. A vendor shall be entitled to appeal the decision of the Planning Department to revoke or deny a permit based on the appearance of the vending unit by submitting a Conway CAB (Community Appearance Board) Application. Appeals must be filed within thirty (30) days from the date the notice of revocation or denial is issued. The basis for the appeal must be included in the request for an appeal. -- 130 of 144 -- City of Conway Administrative Policy: Mobile Vending Permit Management PURPOSE The purpose of this policy is to establish a clear and consistent framework for the issuance and management of mobile vending permits within the City of Conway. The policy is intended to implement the requirements of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) by providing procedures for determining permit availability, processing applications, and managing permit allocation. By administering permit volumes through this policy, the City seeks to remain responsive to operational capacity, public safety considerations, and market conditions, while maintaining a fair, transparent, and predictable process for applicants. This policy does not create a right to a permit and shall not be interpreted as guaranteeing issuance to any applicant. ANNUAL PERMIT DETERMINATION 1. Capacity Review Prior to April 30 of each year, the Planning Director, in coordination with the Zoning Administrator and Fire Marshal, shall determine the number of mobile vending permits to be issued for the upcoming licensing cycle. 2. Evaluation Criteria This annual permit availability shall be based on the following factors: a. Availability of suitable vending locations on public and private property b. Administrative capacity for application review, inspections and enforcement c. Public health and safety considerations d. Feedback from the local business community, including organizations such as Conway Downtown Alive. 3. Public Notice The total number of permits available for the licensing cycle shall be published on the City of Conway Business License webpage prior to the opening of the application period. APPLICATION & ISSUANCE PROCEDURES 1. Submission Window Applications for permit renewals and new permits shall open 30 days prior to the expiration of the current licensing cycle. 2. Prioritization Process -- 131 of 144 -- a. Renewals Existing permit holders in good standing, with no unresolved code violations, shall be provided a defined priority period to submit renewal applications. b. New Applicants Following the renewal period, any remaining permits shall be issued to new applicants on a first-come, first-served basis, based on complete application submittals. 3. Waitlist Management If the number of complete applications exceeds the number of permits available, the City shall maintain an official waitlist. Applicants will be placed on the waitlist in the order in which complete applications are received. Permits that become available due to non-renewal, revocation, or withdrawal shall be offered to waitlisted applicants in order of placement. OPERATIONAL COMPLIANCE All mobile vending permit holders shall comply with applicable provisions of the Unified Development Ordinance and all other applicable local, state, and federal regulations, including but not limited to: 1. Maintaining a current food safety inspection report from the South Carolina Department of Agriculture (SCDA), as applicable. 2. Maintaining general liability insurance in accordance with the South Carolina Business License requirements (see SC Business License Handbook) and as specified in the UDO. 3. Proper waste management, including the removal of all trash and debris generated within a 25- foot radius of the vending unit. MID-CYCLE ADJUSTMENTS The number of permits established for a licensing cycle may be adjusted during that cycle only in response to documented: 1. Public safety concerns 2. Infrastructure or site capacity limitations 3. Significant changes in administrative or enforcement capacity. Any such adjustment(s) shall be documented in writing and made publicly available through the City’s website or other official means. POLICY ADMINISTRATION This policy shall be administered by the Planning Director or designee and shall be applied in a consistent and non-discriminatory manner. Administrative procedures established under this policy shall remain consistent with the requirements of the Unified Development Ordinance. -- 132 of 144 -- -- 133 of 144 -- 5.1.16 Mobile Vending The intent of this ordinance is to regulate how mobile food and beverage vendors sell food and / or non- alcoholic beverages to the public. A. Mobile vending shall be permitted with the following conditions. 1. The vendor shall obtain and carry at all times any SCDHEC (South Carolina Department of Health and Environmental Control) food handler and / or other applicable health safety licenses. 2. If the vendor wants to operate on public property or on private property under a special event permit, he or she shall obtain notarized written permission from the owner to conduct business. 3. The vendor shall obtain and carry at all times a valid City of Conway Business License. Vendors must obtain an annual zoning compliance. Food truck permits issued under this ordinance will be valid beginning on date of this Ordinance’s enactment until June 30 of the ensuing year. In the following year, a permit shall be from May 1 until April 30 of the ensuing year. [Amended 4-16-18 ZA# 2018-04-16 (B)] 4. The vendor can operate through an approved City of Conway Special Event Permit. Mobile vendors shall not be permitted to operate in the location of Special Event activities without the permission of the Special Event permit holder. 5. The vendor is subject to a background check by the Conway Police Department prior to issuance of a zoning permit. 6. The vendor shall provide a list of the items to be sold and shall be limited to selling food and non- alcoholic beverages. 7. All sales shall be made to pedestrians and bikers only. Vendors may not solicit or conduct business with persons in motor vehicles. 8. The vendor may use only music or bells to attract attention but shall not violate the noise ordinance regulations (City of Conway Code of Ordinances Sec. 9-1-21). 9. The vendor shall not operate in any manner that blocks, obstructs or restricts the free passage of vehicles or pedestrians in the lawful use of the sidewalks or highways or ingress or egress to the abutting property. The vendor shall maintain, at a minimum, four feet of passage for pedestrians and shall follow ADA (Americans with Disabilities Act) and ANSI (American National Standards Institute) Regulations. 10. Vending units shall be in compliance with all ANSI (American National Standards Institute) regulations. 11. The vendor shall be actively engaged in vending operations at all times while occupying any property. 12. The vendor shall pick up all refuse generated by his or her operation before the vending unit is moved. 13. All vending units must be self-contained with a waste receptacle. 14. The vendor shall not discharge items from any vending unit onto the sidewalk, gutter, storm inlets, streets, or planters. 15. The vendor shall keep the area surrounding their vending unit maintained in a safe, clean, orderly, and sanitary condition at all times. Mats shall be used in the food preparation area to keep the area clean. 16. No tables, chairs, fences, shade structures, or other site furniture shall be permitted. 17. Exterior storage or display of surplus refuse, equipment, materials, goods, wares, or merchandise associated with the vending unit shall be prohibited. 18. The vendor shall display, in plain view and at all times, current permits and licenses in or on their vending unit. 19. Any damage to landscape or vegetation caused by the mobile vending operation shall be immediately compensated by the vendor upon request of the City. 20. The vendor shall provide the location of an appropriate storage facility where the vending unit is when not in operation. -- 134 of 144 -- 21. Excluding properly licensed dining establishments located within the City limits of Conway, as well as mobile food vending units operating in conjunction with a special event permit and those which are operating under an approved franchise agreement with the City of Conway, the number of mobile food vending permits issued shall be limited to a maximum of twenty (20) each year, from May 1st – April 30th, and shall be done on a first-come, first-serve basis. a. Applications for a mobile food vending permit shall be complete at the time of submittal. Partial or incomplete applications will NOT be accepted. b. Applications for renewal of a previously issued permit does not guarantee that such permit will be approved or reserved. B. Transient Mobile Vending. In addition to the requirements in Section 5.1.16 A, transient mobile vending shall be permitted in the R, RA, RR, R-1, R-2, R-3, R-4, IN, HI, and LI Zoning Districts and legitimate construction sites only with the following conditions: 1. The vending unit shall not stop within 300 feet of any school, religious institution, or cemetery. 2. The vending unit shall only be stationary for a maximum of 30 minutes per stop and move at least one block before making another stop. 3. The hours of operation shall be anytime between sunrise and sunset. 4. The vehicle shall park legally. 5. The vending unit shall not stop in congested areas where it may impede or inconvenience the public or create a traffic hazard. 6. No door-to-door solicitation shall occur. 7. The vending unit shall incorporate flashing lights or signage indicating frequent stops of the vehicle. 8. Transient mobile vending may be permitted on City Property in the zones referenced in this section with the written approval of City Council. [ZA2018-12-17(A)] C. Franchise Mobile Vending. In addition to the requirements stated in Section 5.1.16, A, franchise mobile vending shall be permitted on Public Property in the CBD, CC, WRD, and City Parks with the following conditions: 1. Shall be granted through a franchise agreement approved by Conway City Council. 2. City Council shall determine the hours of operations. 3. City Council shall determine the approved location(s) of the vending unit. 4. Vendors shall not store, park, or leave any vending unit overnight on any public property. 5. The vendor shall complete a release and indemnification agreement, which will hold the City of Conway harmless for any loss, liability or damage, including expenses and costs, for bodily or personal injury, and for property damage sustained by a person as a result of the negligent installation, use, or maintenance of a permitted public space within the City of Conway. 6. The vendor shall submit a Certificate of Insurance verifying the following minimum coverage and specifically identifying the City of Conway as an additional insured. The mobile vendor will not be permitted to operate without a Certificate of Insurance. The City of Conway must be listed as the “Certificate Holder” on the Certificate of Insurance. Minimal acceptable coverage: a. Each Occurrence: $1,000,000 b. Personal Injury: $1,000,000 c. General Aggregate: $2,000,000 -- 135 of 144 -- D. Vending on Private Property. In addition to the requirements stated in Section 5.1.16, A, mobile vending shall be permitted on private property in the CBD, CC, WRD, P, IN, NC, HC, LI, HI, and commercial areas of PD with the following conditions: 1. A letter and/or copy of an official lease agreement from the property owner to vend on the subject parcel must be obtained. 2. No vendor shall operate within 150 feet from the principal public entrance to any food service business, unless the adjacent food service business owner provides a notarized letter agreeing to the lesser distance. If a food services business opens within the zone after the vending unit has continuously operated the business in the location for at least 6 months, the vending unit may remain in that location. 3. The vending unit shall meet a 15’ front setback from the property line, a 10’ clearance between units, 10’ from any fire hydrant, and a 10’ emergency access setback between the unit and any buildings. If adjacent to a residential area, then the vending unit must meet the side and rear property setback requirements of its underlying zoning district. 4. A list of all requested vending sites, including property owners and physical addresses, must be provided to the City. The applicant must submit a site plan, to scale, for all proposed locations of the vending operation(s) for Commercial Plan Review by the Technical Review Committee (TRC). 5. A minimum of two (2) parking spaces must be provided per vending unit and maintained in addition to the minimum parking required for the principal business (except in the CBD, CC, and WRD Zoning Districts). 6. The vending units are to be located only on parcels with no less than a paved 30 feet driveway (except in the CBD, CC, and WRD Districts). 7. The maximum number of vending units per parcel: a. For parcels up to 10,000 sq. ft., up to two vending units may be permitted at a time; b. For parcels more than 10,000 sq. ft. and less than 20,000 sq. ft., up to three vending units may be permitted at a time; c. For parcels greater than 20,000 sq. ft. in size, a maximum of 4 vending units is permitted at the same time (with the exception of city-sponsored or special events). 8. Each vending unit may submit multiple location sites, subject to staff approval. Commercial plan review fees will apply to each location. [ZA#2018-04-16 (B); ZA2019-03-18(B)] E. Appearance. The appearance of vending units shall be approved by the Planning Department with the following conditions: 1. The vendor shall be responsible to ensure that the vending unit is in good condition, free from evidence of deterioration, weathering, discoloration, and rust. 2. Advertising consisting of the name and logo, and a listing of items available for sale may be displayed on the vending unit. No other form of advertising or signs shall be allowed. Additionally, the vendor shall follow the requirements in Section 11.2.2, Prohibited Signs, of the UDO. 3. If already constructed, the vendor shall submit three photographs and the dimensions of the vending unit. If not constructed, the vendor shall submit a copy of the plans and color renderings of the vending unit. 4. A vendor shall be entitled to appeal the decision of the Planning Department to revoke or deny a permit based on the appearance of the vending unit by submitting a Conway CAB (Community Appearance Board) Application. Appeals must be filed within thirty (30) days from the date the notice of revocation or denial is issued. The basis for the appeal must be included in the request for an appeal. -- 136 of 144 -- -- 137 of 144 -- STAFF REPORT Text Amendment to Art. 5, Sec. 5.2.5 re: keeping of livestock or fowl PLANNING COMMISSION MTG DATE: June 4, 2026 AGENDA ITEM: V.C.2. ISSUE: Amendments to Article 5 – Supplemental and Accessory Uses, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to the requirements for Non-commercial Keeping of Livestock of Fowl, establishing an exception for certain residential properties twenty (20) acres or greater in size and containing a single-family dwelling. BACKGROUND: Sec. 5.2.5 of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) currently permits the non-commercial keeping of livestock or fowl as an accessory use within the Rural Residential (RR), Rural Agriculture (RA), and Forest Agriculture (FA) zoning districts, subject to specific acreage, containment, and operational standards. The ordinance also contains limited exceptions for certain properties zoned FA and educational facilities located within the Institutional (IN) zoning district. As the City continues to grow through annexation and development, portions of the City now include or may include large residential properties that exceed twenty (20) acres in size. While these properties may be located within zoning districts that permit single-family detached dwellings, the current ordinance does not provide a mechanism for property owners to keep livestock or fowl for personal enjoyment, sustenance, passive agriculture activities, or similar non-commercial purposes unless the property is located within the RR, RA, or FA zoning districts. The proposed amendment would establish an additional allowance for properties containing twenty (20) acres or more and a single-family detached dwelling as the principal use, regardless of the underlying zoning district, provided the district permits single-family detached dwellings. Livestock and fowl permitted under this provision would remain subject to all applicable requirements of Sec. 5.2.5, including standards related to acreage, animal type, containment, setbacks, nuisance prevention, and prohibitions on commercial operations. In addition to the substantive amendments, the proposed ordinance reorganizes Sec. 5.2.5 to improve readability, administration, and ease of interpretation. The current ordinance is organized primarily by animal type, which can make it difficult for property owners and staff to determine where certain permissions, restrictions, and exceptions apply. The proposed amendment restructures the section by zoning district and applicability, incorporates definitions for key terms, consolidates related standards, and clearly identifies exceptions and special circumstances. These changes are intended to make the ordinance more user-friendly while preserving the City’s existing regulations regarding nuisance prevention, animal containment, setbacks, and non-commercial use limitations. -- 138 of 144 -- STAFF REPORT Text Amendment to Art. 5, Sec. 5.2.5 re: keeping of livestock or fowl STAFF ANALYSIS: Staff finds that the proposed amendment provides a reasonable accommodation for large residential properties while maintaining the City’s existing standards intended to protect neighboring properties from potential nuisances and adverse impacts. The proposed twenty (20) acre minimum ensures that the allowance is limited to properties of sufficient size to support the keeping of livestock or fowl in a manner that remains compatible with surrounding development patterns. Staff further finds that the proposed reorganization of Sec. 5.2.5 improves the clarity and administration of the ordinance by clearly identifying where livestock and fowl are permitted, the standards that apply, and the circumstances under which exceptions may be granted. STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends that in addition to holding the required public hearing, that Planning Commission review the proposed amendments and make an informed recommendation to City Council. text: PC 6/4/2026 CITY OF CONWAY PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING THURSDAY, June 4, 2026 Planning & Building Dept. Conference Room — 196 Laurel Street Present: George Ulrich, Greg Bryson, Allan Cornell, Thomas J. Anderson II, Kendall Brown, Stacy Knotts Absent: Jessica Wise, David Sligh Staff: Jessica Hucks, Planning Director; Nancy Alvarez, Assistant Planner; Charlotte Peterson, Assistant Planner; Louis Smith, IT Others: Blake Arp, Thomas Harrison, Jackie Bromtll, Joann Waldrop, Denise Holt, Clifayetta Floyd, Il. Ii. Iv. Marcus R. Thomas, Gibbs Knotts, and others. CALL TO ORDER Ulrich called the meeting to order at approximately 5:30 pm. Anderson III made a motion to nominate Ulrich as the meeting chair, seconded by Cornell. The motion carried unanimously. APPROVAL OF MINUTES Bryson made a motion, seconded by Anderson III to approve the May 7, 2026, minutes as written. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. PUBLIC INPUT Ulrich made a motion to open public input. No one spoke during public input. Brown made a motion to close public input, seconded by Knotts to close public input and the motion carried unanimously. SUBDIVISIONS A. Hainer Place, Phase 1 - The applicant is requesting renewal of the infrastructure Letter of Credit for Phase one (1) of the Hainer Place subdivision, located on Hwy 65 and Lite Road. PC 6/4/2026 Hucks stated Phase 1 of the Hainer Place subdivision contains 53 single family lots and the current financial guarantee is set to expire June 30". The current letter of credit amount is $404,481.88, and the applicant is asking to renew the letter of credit in its current amount for an additional year. Staff recommends renewal of the letter of credit in that amount. The applicant was not present. Anderson III made a motion to approve the request, seconded by Knotts. The motion carried unanimously. PUBLIC HEARINGS A. Future Land Use Map Amendment(s) 1. Request to amend the City of Conway Future Land Use Map of the Comprehensive Plan, for approximately 1.07+/- acres of property located on Sycamore Street (PIN 382-01-03-0072), from Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) to Medium-Density Residential (R-2). Hucks stated that the applicant requested to amend the Future Land Use Map of the Comprehensive Plan and rezone the subject property from Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) to Medium-Density Residential (R- 2). A related rezoning request from Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) to Medium-Density Residential (R-2) has also been submitted and is intended to allow for the development of townhomes. The subject property is approximately 1.07 acres in size and is currently vacant. Townhomes are not permitted within the R-1 district and require a minimum zoning classification of R-2. B. 1. The applicant Marcus Thomas was present. Ulrich made a motion to open public input. Jakie Bromtll, Andrea Dennison, and Clifayetta Floyd spoke during public input. Ulrich made a motion to close public input, seconded by Bryson and the motion carried unanimously. Cornell made a motion to deny the request, seconded by Anderson. The motion was approved in a 5 to 1 vote, Brown voted against the denial. REZONING REQUEST(S) Requesting Deferral...Request to rezone approximately 1.54+/- acres of property located at 906 Covery Lane (PIN 382-12-04-0005), from the Horry County Neighborhood Commercial (NC) and Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF10) districts to the City of Conway Planned Development (PD) district upon annexation; and Request to rezone approximately 5.27+/- acres of property located at the intersection of Hwy 544 and Buccaneer’s Cove (PIN: 382-12-04-0006), from the Neighborhood Commercial (NC) district to the Planned Development (PD) district. PC 6/4/2026 Hucks stated that the applicant has requested this item be deferred until the July 9" meeting. The applicant was not present to answer questions. Anderson III made a motion to defer public input and the rezoning request until next month’s meeting, seconded by Brown. The motion carried unanimously. 2. Request to rezone approximately 1.07 +/- acres of property located on Sycamore Street (PIN: 368-01-03-0072), from the City of Conway Low/Medium Density Residential (R-1) district to the City of Conway Medium-Density Residential (R-2) district. Hucks stated that this is a rezoning request concurrent to item V.A.1. but was advertised as a public hearing separately. The property is currently vacant surrounded by single family detached homes. The rezoning request should be considered in conjunction with the future land use map amendment. Therefore, if the amendment was recommended for approval the rezoning would be consistent. If the amended was not considered for approval the rezoning would not be consistent with the comprehensive plan, nor the city’s criteria for rezoning. Ulrich made a motion to open public input. No one spoke during public input. Ulrich made a motion to close public input, seconded by Bryson to close public input and the motion carried unanimously. Ulrich made a motion to deny the request, seconded by Anderson III. The motion was carried by a vote of 5 to 1. Brown voted in opposition of the motion. 3. Request to rezone approximately 118.71 +/- acres of property located at 2080 HWY 378 (PIN: 337-00-00-0023), from the Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) district to the City of Conway Medium-Density Residential (R-2) district, or alternatively, the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) and Medium-Density Residential (R-2) districts, as may be recommended by Planning Commission. Knotts made a motion to defer the request, seconded by Anderson. The motion carried unanimously. 4. Request to rezone approximately 1.93 +/- acres of property located at 235 Singleton Ridge Road (PIN: 383-10-03-0025), from the Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) district to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district upon annexation. Peterson stated that the property located at 235 Singleton Ridge Road contains an existing urgent care and medical office facility and is located currently in Horry counties jurisdiction. Restrictive covenants were recorded in July of 1998, and annexation and rezoning are required due to a change in city utility services. 3 PC 6/4/2026 The property is currently zoned Horry County highway commercial and the requested rezonings is City of Conway highway commercial. The rezoning request is consistent with the future land use map and would fill a “donut hole” of surrounding city properties also zoned HC. The applicant was not present. Ulrich made a motion to open public input. No one spoke during public input. Ulrich made a motion to close public input, seconded by Anderson and the motion carried unanimously. Anderson made a motion to approve the request, seconded by Cornell. The motion carried unanimously. Request to rezone approximately 1.68 +/- acres of property located at 321 Rainwood Road (PIN: 324-07-03-0006), from the Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF-40) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district upon annexation. Peterson explained that the property currently contains a single-family dwelling and an accessory structure. Annexation and rezoning are required due to restrictive covenants and a change in connection to city utilities. The property is currently zoned Horry County residential SF40, no mobile homes allowed the requested rezoning is City of Conway low/medium density residential, (R-1). The request is consistent with the future land use map, and the zoning of adjacent properties. The applicant was not present. Ulrich made a motion to open public input. No one spoke during public input. Ulrich made a motion to close public input, seconded by Anderson. The motion carried unanimously. Ulrich made a motion to approve the request, seconded by Cornell. The motion carried unanimously. Request to rezone approximately 0.65 +/- acres of property located at 3154 W HWY 501 (PIN: 326-15-02-0001), from the Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) district to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district upon annexation. Hucks stated that this rezoning request was submitted as part of an annexation petition that the property owner was required to submit after the existing well system on site would not adequately serve the 4 PC 6/4/2026 property. The current zoning of the property is Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) and the proposed zoning upon annexation is City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC). The site contains an existing commercial building that has historically been occupied by a number of commercial uses, including glass companies, produce stand, medical supply companies, and most recently a mobile food vender. There have been numerous inquiries for future business have been submitted to the County; however, no final approval or inspections have been completed through the county. The property is adjacent to residentially zoned property that is within the City’s jurisdiction. Thus, any future redevelopment or site improvements would be subject to city standards upon annexation, including access, signage, landscaping, and permitting requirements. From a land use perspective, the Highway Commercial district is consistent with the City’s future land use map for this portion of the Highway 501 Corridor and is consistent with the existing commercial character of the property and the surrounding highway-oriented development pattern. The applicant was not present. Ulrich made a motion to open public input. No one spoke during public input. Ulrich made a motion to close public input, seconded by Knotts and the motion carried unanimously. Bryson made a motion to approve the request, seconded by Anderson. The motion carried unanimously. 7. Request to rezone approximately 0.96 +/- acres of property located at 3372 HWY 378 (PIN: 370- 03-02-0003), from the Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) district to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district upon annexation. Peterson stated that the subject property is located along Highway 378 near Juniper Bay Road and is currently within Horry County’s jurisdiction. The property was transferred to Sunhouse Petroleum LLC in August 2004 and contains an existing convenience store and gas station that has been in operation since the 1990s or earlier. The site currently includes two fuel canopies and one storage building. Restrictive covenants for the property have been recorded since August 2004. Annexation and assignment of City zoning are now being required in accordance with the restrictive covenants on file. The property is currently rezoned Horry County Highway Commercial, and the requested rezoning is City of Conway Highway Commercial. The applicant was not present. Ulrich made a motion to open public input. No one spoke during public input. Ulrich made a motion to close public input, seconded by Bryson, and the motion carried unanimously. 5 PC 6/4/2026 Ulrich made a motion to approve the request, seconded by Anderson. The motion carried unanimously. 8. Request to rezone an approximate 10 +/- acre portion of 110 +/- acres of property located on Cultra Rd and Oak Street and adjacent to Conway Christian School (PIN: 325-00-00-0011), from the City of Conway Medium-Density Residential (R-2) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district. Hucks stated that the applicant is proposing to subdivide a 10-acre portion of a larger tract of land located along Cultra Road, Oak Street, and Midland Parkway to convey it to Conway Christian School. The 10- acre portion is currently zoned medium density residential or R-1. In order to combine the properties into a single parcel, the applicant proposes to rezone a 10-acre portion to R-1 so that the combined property has a consistent zoning classification as split zoning of parcels is generally prohibited. The parent track was annexed last year, zoned Medium Density Residential or R-2 as well as Conservation Preservation. This split zoning was permitted due to the environmentally sensitive and flood prone condition of the property. The areas zoned Conservation Preservation remain unchanged. The rezoning would only apply to the 10-acre portion conveyed to the school. This request is primarily administrative in nature, and does not increase density, expand development rights or introduce a new land use, but rather reduces the intensity of the designation from R-2 to R-1. The applicant, Blake Arp was present. Ulrich made a motion to open public input. No one spoke during public input. Ulrich made a motion to close public input, seconded by Anderson and the motion carried unanimously. Cornell made a motion to approve the request, seconded by Anderson. The motion carried unanimously. 9. Request to rezone approximately 0.53 +/- acres of property located at 550 Dunn Shortcut Road (PIN: 337-08-02-0021), from the Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium Density Residential (R-1) district upon annexation. Alvarez stated the request to rezone is coupled with the annexation as a requirement associated with a name change to the exiting City utility services account. The parcel was transferred to the current owners in June of 2009, and restrictive covenants have been on file for this property since September of 1987. The property currently contains a single-family residence and is adjacent to the Woodcreek Subdivision which is located within City limits and zoned Low/Medium Density Residential (R-1). The request is also 6 PC 6/4/2026 consistent with the Future Land Use Map as it identifies the property to be Low/Medium Density Residential (R-1). Council approved the first reading of annexation at their May 18" meeting. Planning Commission’s recommendation of the requested zoning, if provided, will be forwarded for consideration of the first reading of the rezoning at the July 20" council meeting. The applicant Dennise Holt was present and requested annexation of her property be denied. Ulrich made a motion to open public input. No one spoke during public input. Ulrich made a motion to close public input, seconded by Cornell and the motion carried unanimously. Ulrich made a motion to approve the rezoning request and made a recommendation for City Council to thoroughly review the request and accommodate the concerns of the property owner to consider denial of the annexation. Cornell seconded the motion, the motion carried unanimously 10. Request to zone approximately 71.82+/- acres of property located behind property commonly referred to as “Lake Busbee” and adjacent to New Road (PIN 368-00-00-0019) as City of Conway Conservation Preservation (CP) district upon annexation into the City of Conway. Alvarez stated that the parcel was acquired by the City in 2025 as part of the same acquisition involving the property commonly known as Lake Busbee and the former site of the Grainger Steam Plant. During the subsequent plating activity in 2025, this portion of the overall tract was either subdivided or part of a resurvey of the existing parcels. As a result, the property does not currently appear within either the City or County zoning jurisdiction on GIS mapping, and the zoning classification of the property is therefore unknown. A significant portion of the property contains a Santee Cooper powerline right-of-way, however; staff notes that the request would not affect the powerline right-of-way. The remainder of the tract is heavily wooded and contains mapped flood hazard areas. The City is requesting annexation and zoning of the property to Conservation Preservation (CP) to maintain consistency with surrounding City-owned properties and to preserve flood-prone and environmentally sensitive land. The surrounding Lake Busbee properties and adjacent City-owned parcels are zoned either Conservation Preservation or Waccamaw Riverfront District. The Pecan Grove Subdivision, zoned Low/ Medium Density Residential (R-1) is also adjacent to the subject parcel. Ulrich made a motion to open public input. No one spoke during public input. PC 6/4/2026 VI. Ulrich made a motion to close public input, seconded by Anderson, and the motion carried unanimously. Bryson made a motion to approve the request, seconded by Brown. The motion carried unanimously. TEXT AMENDMENT(S) 1. Amendments to Article 5 — Supplemental and Accessory Uses, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to the requirements for mobile vending; specifically, to remove the cap on mobile vending permits and establish administrative provisions. Hucks stated that the proposed text amendment has been brough forth to remove the cap on mobile vending permits. In July of 2025, City Council adopted an ordinance limiting the number of mobile vending permits to 20 each year, with exceptions for vendors operating under special event permits, franchise agreements, and licensed dining establishments. The cap on permits was originally set due to concerns of oversaturation of food trucks, and a lack of staff capacity to process the volume of applications received by the city. However, planning staff has grown since the previous year and has an increased capacity to process more applications. This text amendment adds flexibility is staffs discretion to process addition permits administratively based on objective factors such as enforcement and inspection capacity, public safety considerations, availability of appropriate vending locations, and operational impacts associated with the program. The proposed amendment does not eliminate permitting requirements, inspections, location restrictions, operational requirements, and does not create an unlimited number of permits. Rather, it changes the method used to determine the number of permits available each year. Staff and the Board discussed at length. Ulrich made a motion to open public input. There was none. Ulrich made a motion to close public input, seconded by Anderson. Cornell made a motion to approve the proposed text amendment as presented, seconded by Bryson. The motion carried unanimously. 2. Amendments to Article 5-— Supplemental and Accessory Uses, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to the requirements for Non- commercial Keeping of Livestock of Fowl, establishing an exception for parcels twenty (20) acres or greater in size and containing a single-family dwelling. Hucks stated this item is another proposed amendment to the UDO regarding the noncommercial keeping of livestock or fowl. This section of the UDO was recently amended to permit targeted grazing as a 8 VI. VII. IX. PC 6/4/2026 vegetation management practice for City-owned or City-controlled properties. That amendment received final reading at the June 1" council meeting. The version that went out of the packet did not include the most recent amendments because they had not yet been adopted. Currently, the ordinance allows noncommercial keeping of livestock or fowl as an accessory use within the Rural Agriculture, Rural Residential and the Forest Agriculture districts, subject to meeting specific standards related to acreage, containment, setbacks and nuisance prevention. As the city continues to grow through annexation, we are beginning to encounter larger residential properties that are not zoned by one of the zoning districts that permit the noncommercial keeping of livestock or fowl. The proposed amendment would create a limited exception for properties containing 20 or more acres that also contain a single-family detached dwelling as its principal use. The intent is to allow property owners of these larger residential tracts to keep livestock or fowl for personal enjoyment, passive agricultural actives, or similar noncommercial proposals. The proposed amendment incorporates definitions, groups standards by zoning applicability, and clearly identifies exceptions and special circumstances. These changes are intended to make the ordinance easier for property owners, applicants, and for staff to understand and administer. Staff and the Board discussed at length. Ulrich made a motion to open public input. There was none. Ulrich made a motion to close public input, seconded by Anderson HI Anderson III made a motion to approve the proposed text amendment as presented, seconded by Bryson The motion carried unanimously. ADJOURNMENT -- 3 of 180 -- BY JOE WEDRA JOE.WEDRA@MYHORRYNEWS.COM For local students looking to get into the golf industry, Monday morning was some- what of a dream experience. Horry County Schools partnered with the ONE- flight Myrtle Beach Classic — the upcoming PGA Tour event — to host an immer- sive day at the Dunes Golf and Beach Club on Monday, April 13. Ahead of next month’s tournament, students from across the district had the golf industry’s curtain peeled back, getting a behind-the-scenes look at what it takes to pull off one of Myrtle Beach’s largest events of the calendar year. “It’s really, really beautiful out here,” said Isabella Jus- tice, a student at Socastee High. “I’ve never seen any- thing like this. It’s been fun. The tour has shown me a lot, and this is giving me an opportunity to learn about things I didn’t ever even imagine before.” Justice and several hun- dred other HCS students rotated stations on Monday morning, getting a closer look at how a PGA tourna- ment is operated. Some students spent time with the tournament mar- keting team, learning about things like placing strate- gic signage along the golf course for fans or how to properly price out hospitali- ty suite ticket packages. Others took a tour of the course itself, learning from the Dunes Club’s agronomy team on how to perfectly manicure the greens or how to get fairways ready for PGA Tour-level competitions. Notably, the ordinance: • Limits residential uses to multifamily development • Removes single-family, duplex, and townhome uses • Introduces a clear accessory use framework for amenities and recreational features • Establishes that development shall consist of a vertically integrated mixed-use building in substantial conformance with the Concept Plan • Limits nonresidential uses to the ground floor of the principal building • Includes a prohibited use section These revisions represent a significant improvement and better align the ordinance with the development concept presented. Remaining considerations (not recommendations): • Breadth of permitted commercial uses. The ordinance permits a wide range of commercial uses within the building, including retail, dining, professional services, food and convenience stores, and entertainment/venue uses. • Integration of commercial uses. The ordinance appropriately limits commercial uses to the ground floor; however, it does not establish any maximum square footage, tenant size limitations, or proportional limits relative to the residential component. • Rooftop amenity and event space. The ordinance permits rooftop uses, including pool amenities, outdoor kitchen and event space, which will require compliance with City noise and lighting regulations. • Parking and Site functionality. The proposed parking ratio (1.7 spaces per unit), along with shared parking for commercial uses, reflects an effort to balance residential and mixed-use demands. The ordinance does permit for parking within setbacks and reduced commercial parking requirements. Given the combination of residential units, commercial activity, and potential for event-related users, Planning Commission may wish to consider whether the proposed parking framework adequately addresses peak demand conditions. • Open Space and Landscaping calculations. The ordinance includes both a minimum of 20% pervious area and a requirement for 25% open space based on buildable area. While both standards are defined, staff notes that the methodology for calculating these requirements differs. Clarification of how these metrics are applied may improve overall consistency and ease of administration. • Design Modifications / Exceptions. Stormwater Stormwater runoff from this project will be collected, detained, and treated by a stormwater conveyance system on site. The system is comprised of a series of catch basins, underground reinforced concrete pipes, a proposed underground storage chamber system, and stormwater outlet control structure. The system will outfall to the wetlands located to the North of this site. Utilizing a control structure at the outfall of the underground detention system, the drainage system will control peak discharge for the post-developed area to be less than the peak discharge for the pre-developed area. The proposed stormwater system will be designed in accordance with both state and local stormwater regulations for post development discharge, conveyance, and sedimentation trapping. 12. BACKGROUND: Following multiple flood events, the City acquired numerous properties through the FEMA buyout program. These parcels, along with other vacant or difficult to maintain City-owned properties, require ongoing vegetation management to prevent overgrowth, improve neighborhood appearance, and reduce maintenance costs. Traditional mowing and clearing methods can be costly, labor intensive, and in some locations, impractical due to terrain or limited site access. An alternative approach used successfully in other communities is targeted grazing, where utilizes livestock - typically goats – to naturally manage vegetation, including brush, invasive species, and dense overgrowth. This method is environmentally friendly, reduces reliance on fuel-powered equipment and chemical herbicides, and allows for maintenance of areas that are otherwise difficult to access with conventional machinery. Targeted grazing has also demonstrated effectiveness in controlling invasive plant species and promoting long-term land health. Locally, residents may recall that Santee Cooper previously utilized goats for vegetation management along Hwy 501 in front of the Grainger plant. That effort demonstrated that managed grazing can be both practical and well received within the community. Similar programs have been implemented nationwide as a cost- effective and sustainable land management strategy. In addition to operational benefits, targeted grazing can serve as a visible example of the City’s commitment to sustainable and innovative practices. These programs often generate positive community engagement and provide educational opportunities related to environmental stewardship. From an operational standpoint, the City would lease qualifying parcels to a professional grazing service provider. The provider would be responsible for animal care, temporary fencing, transportation, and onsite supervision, while the City benefits from reduced maintenance costs and improved property conditions. The proposed amendment introduces a provision to Sec. 5.2.5 – Non-commercial Keeping of Livestock or Fowl, to allow and regulate targeted grazing strictly as a vegetation management tool on city-owned or city- controlled properties. A definition of targeted grazing was incorporated into Article 2 – Definitions, which is scheduled for final reading by City Council at their May 4th meeting. STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends, that in addition to holding the public hearing, that Planning Commission review the proposed amendments and make an informed recommendation to City Council. -- 165 of 180 -- DRAFT – Targeted Grazing ARTICLE 2 – Definitions Targeted Grazing The controlled and intentional use of livestock, including but not limited to goats, by or on behalf of the City, for the purpose of managing, reducing, or eliminating vegetation, such as grasses, brush, invasive species, and understory growth on designated properties. Targeted grazing is a form of vegetation management and shall not be considered a principal agricultural use or the keeping of livestock.
