All targeted grazing operations shall be conducted only under authorization of the City or its designated contractor. 3. Livestock shall be adequately contained and supervised through temporary fencing, herding practices, or other appropriate control measures to prevent animals from leaving the designated grazing areas. 4. Targeted grazing shall be considered a temporary land management practice and shall not be classified as: a. A principal use; b. An accessory use; or c. A form of private livestock keeping 5. Operations shall be conducted in a manner that does not create a nuisance or adversely impacts adjacent properties. 6. All activities shall comply with applicable state and local animal welfare laws and regulations. -- 168 of 180 -- STAFF REPORT Text Amendments to Art. 10 re: Open Space fee-in-lieu calculations PLANNING COMMISSION MTG DATE: May 7, 2026 AGENDA ITEM: V.B.2 ORDINANCE: NA AGENDA SECTION: Public Hearings ISSUE: Amendments to Article 10 – Park and Open Space Dedication, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), a modification to the fee-in-lieu of open space process. BACKGROUND: This text amendment was initiated in response to repeated design modification requests for major residential developments related with the fee-in-lieu of required open space dedication. Through this process, staff identified a need to standardize the method for calculating the fee in lieu in order to improve consistency, predictability, and administrative efficiency. Alternative approaches to amending Article 10 have been provided in the packet. Staff recommends Option 1, as described below. Currently, the fee-in-lieu amount is calculated based on an applicant-provided appraisal of the subject property. The applicant is required to submit a written appraisal estimating the market value of the land as if the proposed development were completed in accordance with the submitted plans. This value is then divided by the total square footage of the site to determine a per-square-foot value, which is multiplied by the amount of required open space not being provided. An additional 25% is applied to the resulting figure to establish the final fee amount. Following this calculation, the proposed fee must be presented to the Planning Commission for recommendation and subsequently approved by City Council prior to preliminary plan approval. ANALYSIS: This current fee-in-lieu process presents several challenges. First, because the calculation relies on an applicant-provided appraisal based on a hypothetical post- development condition, there is inherent variability in how market value is determined. This can result in inconsistent fee calculations across similar projects and introduce a level of subjectivity into what is intended to be a standardized requirement. Second, the current process requires multiple levels of review, including Technical Review Committee (TRC), Planning Commission, and City Council approval, prior to preliminary plan approval. This multi-step process increases review time and creates uncertainty for applicants, particularly in the early stages of development when project feasibility is being evaluated. Finally, the existing method can disproportionately impact certain types of development, including infill or smaller-scale projects, where higher appraised land values may result in significantly higher fee-in-lieu amounts relative to project scale. -- 169 of 180 -- STAFF REPORT Text Amendments to Art. 10 re: Open Space fee-in-lieu calculations OPTIONS CONSIDERED (refer to packet for details): OPTION 1: Administrative and Predictable Key elements of proposed amendments: • Planning Commission approves fee-in-lieu administratively • Only goes to Council if applicant deviates • Differentiates active v. passive open space values What it means in practice: • Faster approvals • More certainty for developers • Council only sees exceptions/negotiations Bottom line: fast, predictable, and only comes to Council when something unusual is proposed OPTION 2: Council-controlled and flexible Key elements: • Everything goes to Council • Council can: - Increase fee - Decrease fee - Consider proximity to parks, etc. • Differentiates by development type (fee simple v. in-common) What this means in practice: • Maximum policy control • Case-by-case decision making • Less predictability Bottom line: gives Council full control, but every project becomes a negotiation OPTION 3: Simple flat fee (cleanest) Key elements: • One flat fee: $10/sf regardless of anything • Council retains approval authority (like current structure of ordinance) What this means in practice: • Easiest to administer • Easiest to explain • Least nuanced Bottom line: simplest and most consistent, but least flexible. Staff recommended option: Option 1 -- 170 of 180 -- STAFF REPORT Text Amendments to Art. 10 re: Open Space fee-in-lieu calculations PROPOSED AMENDMENT: The proposed amendment replaces the existing appraisal-based methodology with a standardized, flat fee per square foot for deficiencies in required open space. Under the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), a minimum of 25% of required open space must be provided as active open space, with the remaining portion as passive open space. Active open space, such as amenity centers, pools, playgrounds, and athletic courts, typically involves significantly higher development and construction costs than passive open space areas. As such, the proposed amendment establishes a differentiated fee structure. Based on research of estimated costs associated with the development of both active and passive open space amenities (see supporting materials in the packet), staff recommends the following rates: • Active Open Space: $12.00 per square foot for any deficiency in required active open space • Passive Open Space: $8.00 per square foot for any deficiency in required passive open space In addition to revising the fee calculation methodology, the amendment modifies the review process for fee- in-lieu requests. Under the proposed structure: • The Planning Commission may approve fee-in-lieu requests administratively when the applicant utilizes the prescribed fee structure established in the Ordinance; and • If the applicant proposes an alternative compliance method – such as a modified fee amount, conservation easement, land donation, or offsite improvement, PC shall forward a recommendation to City Council, which will retain final decision-making authority. This approach streamlines the review process for standard applications while preserving City Council oversight for requests involving discretion or deviation from the established procedures. Real World Scenarios, using recommended option: Ex: Multifamily project, in-common. 24 units  24,000 sq. ft. of open space required (1,000 sq. ft. per unit). Developer would be required to either pay the total fee in lieu, or provide at least one acre of open space, meeting the requirements for features and suitability, in Sec. 10.3.9(C). Scenario 1: No Open Space provided (full fee-in-lieu) Type Required Provided Deficiency Rate Fee Active 9,600 sf 0 9,600 sf $12/sf $115,200 Passive 14,400 sf 0 14,400 sf $8/sf $115,200 Total fee: $230,400  Planning Commission approves administratively  No City Council action required -- 171 of 180 -- STAFF REPORT Text Amendments to Art. 10 re: Open Space fee-in-lieu calculations Scenario 2: Only PASSIVE open space provided (common issue) Type Required Provided Deficiency Rate Fee Active 9,600 sf 0 9,600 sf $12/sf $115,200 Passive 14,400 sf 14,400 sf 0 --- $0 Total fee: $115,200 ! Scenario 3: Partial Compliance (more realistic) Type Required Provided Deficiency Rate Fee Active 9,600 sf 6,000 sf 3,600 sf $12/sf $43,200 Passive 14,400 sf 10,000 sf 4,400 sf $8/sf $35,200 Total fee: $78,400  Reduced fee based on open space provided  Approved administratively Scenario 4: Developer proposes alternative (triggers requirement for Council review) Developer proposes the following alternatives: • Reduced fee • Land donation • Offsite improvements (e.g. greenway, park expansion) Review Process • Planning Commission  Recommendation • City Council  Final decision SUMMARY: The proposed amendment to Sec. 10.3.9(D) is intended to: • Establish a consistent and predictable fee calculation method • Reduce subjectivity associated with appraisal-based valuations • Improve administrative efficiency by streamlining the review process • Provide greater cost certainty for applicants early on in the development process • Maintain flexibility for alternative compliance methods through City Council review STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends, that in addition to holding the public hearing, that Planning Commission review the proposed amendments and make an informed recommendation to City Council. -- 172 of 180 -- DRAFT (includes all options) 10.3.9 Park and Open Space Dedication A. General Requirements for Parks and Open Space Dedication for Major Residential Developments 1. B. Minimum Open Space Required 1. Major residential developments shall provide a minimum of 1,000 square feet of suitable open space area per lot and/or unit . 2. A minimum of twenty-five percent (25%) of the required open space shall be suitable for active areas and/or features as defined in Section 10.3.9, C. The remainder of the required open space shall be suitable passive areas as defined in Section 10.3.9, C. 3. Park and Open Space Features and Suitability. Open Space areas shall be comprised of three (3) main elements: Passive, Active, and Ancillary Areas. 1. Passive Open Space Areas. Passive areas within open space are characterized as un- encumbered upland areas, dedicated to preserve the existing natural environment for the enjoyment of the residents of the community. Passive areas have no designated sports fields. Criteria for suitable passive areas are defined below: a. Unity: passive areas are to be provided within a parcel of a minimum one acre in size and designed to minimize the number of open space lots being split. b. Location: passive areas may be centrally located or utilized to enlarge or provide special buffering along the perimeter of the project. c. Conformity: Passive areas should preserve existing on-site woodlands (interior to or along the perimeter of the project), safeguard protected and landmark trees in their natural state and create a spatial buffer around wetlands, ponds and floodways that may still be enjoyed by the residents of the community. 2. Active Open Space Areas and Features a. Active Open Space Areas. Active areas within open space are characterized as amenity sites and/or features to provide members of the community with opportunities for recreational activity as well as social interaction. Unity: active areas are to be provided within a parcel a minimum of one acre in size and designed to minimize the number of open space lots being split. ii. Active features are to be within upland area(s) only, free of obstructions and topographical constraints that would impede pedestrian access. v. Connectivity: Amenity Sites areas shall have both pedestrian and vehicular access and shall not be isolated by topographical constraints. Active features shall provide adequate pedestrian access internal to the project. vi. Conformity: Amenity Sites shall be incorporated into the Stormwater Management and Sediment Control plans to be elevated to at least two (2) feet above the one hundred (100) year flood elevation and provide positive drainage away from the building site. b. Active Open Space Features. Active Features within Open Space are characterized as tangible facilities designed to facilitate community and recreational activities. Suitable active features may include, but not be limited to items listed below: i. amenity centers / clubhouses / gymnasium and/or fitness centers, ii. community pools & pool houses, iii. playgrounds / tot lots, iv. athletic courts and/or designated sport fields, -- 174 of 180 -- DRAFT (includes all options) v. community gardens, vi. walking trails / bike paths / boardwalks, vii. elevated wetland trails / pedestrian and/or bike water body crossings, viii. existing homes, barns or buildings of historic value, and/or ix. any additional features as deemed acceptable by Planning Commission. c. text: Il. Til. IV. PC 5/7/2026 Present: Absent: Staff: Others: CALL CITY OF CONWAY PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING THURSDAY, MAY 7, 2026 Planning & Building Dept. Conference Room — 196 Laurel Street Jessica Wise, George Ulrich, Greg Bryson, Allan Cornell, Thomas J. Anderson III, David Sligh, Kendall Brown, Stacy Knotts Jessica Hucks, Planning Director; Katie Dennis, Planner; Nancy Alvarez, Assistant Planner; Charlotte Peterson, Assistant Planner; Marcus Cohen, IT Margaret Ramsey, Carlee N. Vieux, Diane Moore, Monica Wey, Kaitlyn Weimer, George Stephenson, Jamie McLain, Theresa Coffin, Bob Moore, John Creul, Dery] Bruotom, Jennifer Bruotom, Amy Richardson, Brad Richardson, Chris Esposito, Tommy Holt, Anne Kawa, Bradley Lloyd, Chance Gilmore, Willis Mitchell, and others. TO ORDER Chairperson Wise called the meeting to order at approximately 5:30 pm. APPROVAL OF MINUTES Ulrich made a motion, seconded by Bryson to approve the April 2, 2026, minutes as written. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. PUBLIC INPUT Wise made a motion to open public input. No one spoke during public input. Sligh made a motion to close public input, seconded by Ulrich to close public input and the motion carried unanimously. SUBDIVISIONS A. Design Modifications 1. Previously Deferred... Snowhill Estates - the applicant, Diamond Shores, LLC, is requesting a design modification regarding the requirements for lots and building sites; specifically, the requirement that lots are to be accessed via internal roads only (Sec. 10.3.8, D), for a proposed major subdivision on East Country Club Dr. and Hwy 905 (PIN 339-00-00-0023). The applicant was not present and requested the item be withdrawn from the agenda. 1 PC 5/7/2026 B. Letters of Credit 2. Kingston Bay, Phase 2 — The applicant, Dimond Shores, LLC, is requesting renewal of the infrastructure Letter of Credit for Phase 2 of the Kingston Bay subdivision, located between Cultura Rd and Oak Street. The applicant was not present. Hucks explained that the applicant was seeking an extension to the infrastructure letter of credit for the Kingston Bay subdivision. The letter of credit insures completion of infrastructure installation in phase two of the subdivision. The current letter of credit, in the amount of $473,260.60, is set to expire May 14, 2026, the extension would be for one year. Staff recommended approval based on TRC review. Wise made a motion to approve the request, seconded by Ulrich. The motion carried unanimously. Vv. PUBLIC HEARINGS A. REZONING REQUEST(S) 1. Previously Deferred...Request to rezone approximately 5.28+/- acres of property located at 2578 HWY 378 (PIN 337-10-03-0010), from the Highway Commercial (HC) district to the Heavy Industrial (HD) district. The applicant, Brad Richardson, was present. Dennis explained the request followed a business license request to sell heavy equipment. This use is not consistent with the current highway commercial zoning classification. The applicant has requested to rezone the property to the heavy or light industrial district. Surrounding uses of the property include a mix of uses including some of industrial nature, such as the adjacent recycling center. The property has historically operated as an industrial use. A light industrial rezoning would be appropriate for this property, as it would allow for less intense use of the site for production, storage, and distribution activities. Wise made a motion to open public input. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Ulrich. The motion carried unanimously. Sligh made a motion to rezoning the subject property from the highway commercial district to the light industrial district, seconded by Cornell. The motion carried unanimously. 2. Request to rezone approximately 0.59 +/- acres of property located at 5003 Converse Drive (PIN: 383-08-02-0061), from the Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF 10) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R1) district upon annexation. Hucks stated this property was requesting annexation due to restrictive convenience that has been on file 2 PC 5/7/2026 since 2014 and for connection to city utilities. The property is within the College Park Subdivision where several lots have been annexed over recent years. The current zoning is Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF10) which requires a lot size no less than 10,000 square feet. The proposed zoning is Low/medium Density Residential (R-1). PC 5/7/2026 TEXT AMENDMENT(S) A. Amendment(s) to Article 5 — Specific Use Regulations, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding revisions to the Non-commercial Keeping of Livestock or Fowl. The proposed amendment would establish new standards and restrictions to regulate the use of targeted grazing on city owned property in the City of Conway. Alvarez stated that many City-owned parcels that are vacant or difficult-to-maintain, require ongoing vegetation management to prevent overgrowth, improve neighborhood appearance, and reduce maintenance costs. Traditional mowing and clearing methods can be expensive, labor intensive, and in some cases limited due to access and difficult terrain. City Council has directed staff to research targeted grazing as an alternative approach used successfully in other communities to resolve these challenges. Targeted Grazing is a temporary vegetative land management practice that utilizes livestock, often goats, to clear brush, invasive species, and dense vegetation. In section 5.2.5 of the UDO the non-commercial keeping of livestock or fowl is permitted only as an accessory use under certain conditions in the Rural Residential District (RR), Residential Agricultural District (RA), and Forest Agricultural District (FA). However, some exceptions do exist. The provision is based on a definition of targeted grazing that was incorporated into Article 2- Definitions, which was adopted by City Council on May 4, 2026, as part of broader amendments to the UDO. The proposed amendment includes the following standards to properly regulate targeted grazing as a governmental service ; only occurring on property owned, leased, or otherwise controlled by the City, operating only under the authorization of the city or its designated contractor, adequately containing and supervising livestock with temporary fencing, herding practices, or other appropriate control measures, grazing to be defined as a temporary land management practice and shall not be classified as a principal, accessory, or private livestock keeping use, operations are not to be a nuisance, and all activities shall comply with applicable state and local animal welfare laws and regulations. Staff and the Board discussed at length. VII. VIII. IX. PC $/7/2026 Peterson explained the amendment establishes a flat fee to be paid in lieu of providing on site open space in major residential developments. Currently Article 10’s calculation for the fee-in-lieu process is complicated and includes subjectivity in the determination of a projects post construction market value in which the fee-in-lieu of open space is calculated by. The proposed amendment suggests a flat fee of $12 per square foot of deficient active open space, and $10 per square foot of deficient passive open space. Changes to the ordinance would also permit Planning Commission to approve fee-in-lieu payments from a development administratively if the developer abides by the flat fee established in this ordinance. In the case of a variance request from the specified fee-in-lieu, planning commission would provide a recommendation to city council and city council will continue to have final decision-making powers to accept or deny the variance request. ADJOURNMENT -- 3 of 393 -- BY MIKE DUPREZ MIKE.DUPREZ@MYHORRYNEWS.COM Pat Mallett picked up a shoebox and held it up to her audience, asking if they remembered why it had once been an essential companion on any train journey. The older attendees in the classroom at the Horry County Library in Conway remembered. Mallett, an Atlantic Beach historian, related how blacks had to pack their lunch in a shoe- box since segregation in the Jim Crow era there weren’t any restaurants available along the route for blacks. “It was against the law to stop,” Mallett said. In a humorous aside, Mallett opened the shoebox and took out the contents. There was an apple, banana and peanut butter sandwich, not props. She passed them out as the audience chuckled. Mallet’s session was part of Gullah Geechee Community Day on Saturday, Feb. 21, when several events were held in locations in down- town Conway. Participants were able to look back at Atlantic Beach history and learn of plans for the future. Atlantic Beach was founded in 1934 when George W. Tyson, a Wilmington, N.C. native, bought 29th Ave. and 30th Ave. from R.W. Ward for $2,000. The purchase covered 47 acres. In 1941, Tyson bought 31st Ave. and 32nd Ave. from Viola Bell for $600 and took on her mortgage. The purchase was for 49 acres. The town has remained in those boundaries ever since. Atlantic Beach chose to remain a separate municipality when Cherry Grove, Crescent Beach, Ocean Drive and Windy Hill all combined to form North Myrtle Beach in 1966. It did so to maintain its identity as a historic black town. Due to segregation, Atlantic Beach, known as the Black Pearl, became a Mecca for black busi- nesses and tourists. Among other things, there was an amuse- ment park that contained a merry-go-round, bumper cars, swings and carousels. The dance and music scene was vibrant. “I thought it was the greatest thing since sliced bread,” said Ralph Gore, 83, a native of Little River. “...Atlantic Beach was a great place. It was only four blocks.” Times were difficult, too, because of segre- gation. The beach was roped off and fenced on both sides and blacks were not allowed on the Crescent Beach and Windy Hill. The fence even extended into the water. “We didn’t think much about it because you were programmed to have that mindset,” Gore said. “These people are better than you.” But the shag has a lot of its roots in black music and there was some quiet crossover. Stories have been told — and confirmed by some — that male shaggers would sneak over to Atlantic Beach, watch the black guys dance and copy their moves. “They wanted to come to our beach,” Gore said. “But they couldn’t because it was against the law. The law said you could not socialize. ... They would ride over in their cars on Sunday afternoon and look at all of us on the patio dancing and having fun.” Gore spoke of people “tripping” the juke box so it would play 10-15 records for free. The town also benefited in terms of its music scene from famous black musicians like Bo Diddley staying in Atlantic Beach. “They had to stay here because there was nowhere else they could stay,” Mallett said. Visitors came from all over and they arrived in all forms of transportation — horse and buggy, school buses, church buses and cars. Some even hitchhiked. Ironically, the argument could be made that integration hurt Atlantic Beach. “At the end of segregation the black dollars left because they had all of these options,” said Atlantic Beach realtor Jaye Divine, who led another presentation at the Horry County Museum. “So people no longer came here and it fell into decline. ... By the time we came down here 20 years ago, it was still in that state.” Divine heads up an organization known as Supporters of the Tyson Ancestral Restrictions on the Deed (STARD). During her slide presentation, Divine showed STARD’s mission statement. “Atlantic Beach aspires to preserve its historic small-town charm and cultural identity while promoting inclusive community life, respon- sible growth, environmental stewardship, and a resilient local economy, using transparent governance and enhanced appeal to strengthen its public image and ensure a high quality of life for all.” Divine showed a video she recently shot from the beach. A3 www.myhorrynews.com North Myrtle Beach announces retirement of fire chiefBY MIKE DUPREZ MIKE.DUPREZ@MYHORRYNEWS.COM North Myrtle Beach Fire Chief Billy Floyd will retire effective May 16, 2026, the city announced Wednesday morning. Floyd has been fire chief nearly three years and has been with the department just over 16 years. “It has been an absolute honor and privilege to serve the City of North Myrtle Beach and this Fire Department through vari- ous roles throughout my tenure here, especially these last three years as Fire Chief,” Floyd said in a statement. “This department and city hold a special place in my heart, and I am thankful as well as grateful for the opportunities they have provided me during my time here.” Those feelings were mutual. “On behalf of the City Council and our entire community, I want to thank Chief Floyd for his years of dedicated service and steady leadership,” said North Myrtle Beach J. Baldwin in a statement. “He has served this City with professionalism, integrity, and a true passion for public safety. His contributions will have a lasting impact on North Myrtle Beach.” Floyd has also served as the city’s emergency preparedness director, which involved coordination with department heads for the city’s response to large scale incidents and events, especially weather-re- lated events. “Chief Floyd’s leadership has made a meaningful and lasting impact on our Fire Department and our organization as a whole,” said North Myrtle Beach City Manager Ryan Fabbri in a statement. “His dedication to preparedness, training and service has helped ensure the safety of our residents, visitors and employees. We are deeply appreciative of his commitment to the City of North Myrtle Beach and wish him the very best in his retirement.” Floyd got his start as a volunteer firefighter in his native Nich- ols in 1996 and then spent five years with the fire department in Mullins before coming to North Myrtle Beach. Floyd joined the North Myrtle Beach Fire Department in May 2005 as a firefighter/public safety officer. He worked his way up to the rank of Training Captain before leaving the city to work for Horry County Fire Rescue in November 2008. After just over four years, Floyd returned to the North Myrtle Beach Fire Department in January 2013 as Division Chief of Fire Training. He was promoted to Deputy Fire Chief in May 2021. Floyd became the city’s seventh fire chief in April 2023. There are 91 uniformed personnel in the department. “I cannot say enough about the employees throughout this city who are making a difference each day,” Floyd said. “I am excited to watch this department continue to progress for- ward, thanks in part to the outstanding men and women who make up the fire department, and with the full support of city Administration, as well as our mayor and city ouncil behind them.” Deputy Fire Chief John Galganski will serve as interim chief upon Floyd’s retirement while the city evaluates its next steps in naming a permanent replacement, according to the news release. BY JOE WEDRA JOE.WEDRA@MYHORRYNEWS.COM Meredith Kennedy, chair of the Myrtle Beach Middle School Improvement Council, has announced she will be running for the Republican nomination for the Horry County Board of Education District 2 seat. The District 2 seat is being vacated by board member Debbie Edmonds, who confirmed with MyHorryNews on Monday, March 2 that she will not be running for reelection. Kennedy previously worked 18 years with for-profit technical colleges and is now a licensed Realtor in South Carolina. “I’m here and I’m ready to work,” Kennedy said. “I’ll treat this like a job. I am really pas- sionate about investing in the schools that our students and our communities deserve. I will invest in preparing academically-strong, fiscally-responsible students and preparing them for their futures. “I want every child in the district to have an opportunity to thrive, no matter what corner of the district they live in or what socioeco- nomic background they come from. They all should have the opportunity to thrive.” Kennedy says she first became involved in an increased level with Horry County Schools after a February 2024 incident at Myrtle Beach Middle School, when a student brought a gun to the school. She and her husband, J.B., have a 14-year- old son who attends Myrtle Beach Middle. “I jumpstarted off of that conversation and started talking to other parents about what they knew about how secure their school was,” Kennedy said. She describes that from there, her involve- ment and conversations “snowballed” as she became more active at Myrtle Beach Middle and involved in overall Horry County Schools activities. One of her primary campaign goals is to help support “future-ready students”. “Whether that is college, post-secondary four-year education and beyond, whether it’s community college education, or just some type of formal training for a trade, the mili- tary… The options kids have are a lot,” Kenne- dy said. “I want to get them to graduation and make sure there is a plan for every child.” Kennedy praised the board’s decision to hire new Superintendent Clifford Jones, who she says she would be excit- ed about working with if she was elected to the board. Jones, she feels, has similar goals of sup- porting students’ future preparations. “Future-ready stu- dents, that includes supporting our new leadership in the district. The Board made a really great decision in hiring new leadership. I think they made a really smart decision with the current superintendent,” she said. “He is community-driven, because he realizes the school can’t do it on its own. And, he is leading the biggest employer in Horry County right now. I thought it was really critical. And, I voiced my opinion on how I thought they needed to search externally and hire an actual search firm. And, they did that. It was great. I was very impressed with the Board for doing that and going and looking at other options outside of Horry County.” Kennedy says her two other priorities are fiscal responsibility and improving the way that the district works with special needs stu- dents. Her son, Gabe, has autism. She says that some “revamping” is needed in some areas surrounding special needs across the district. “[Gabe] has had a phenomenal run, mainly because he has had really talented teachers along the way,” Kennedy said. “But the way we approach special needs is not the most progressive way we could be doing it. We want those kids to be future-ready as well, and for them to be productive members of society.” Horry County Board of Education elections are partisan elections. Dawson seeks reelection to Horry County Board of Education District 6 Pam Dawson Landfill expansion debate reaches Loris City Council BY TERRY WARD TERRY.WARD@MYHORRYNEWS.COM Horry County’s landfill needs to expand, according to Edwin Marr, assistant executive director of the Horry County Solid Waste Authority. He delivered that message Mon- day night, March 2, in front of Loris City Council. The three-phase expansion that is being proposed would extend its capacity that would allow for 23.4 million tons of waste and provide capacity until the year 2068. Why is there a need to expand the land fill? The latest projections show the Horry County landfill, on S.C. Highway 90 — just over six miles from Conway — reaching capacity for construction and demolition (C and D) debris by 2029. C and D debris is non-haz- ardous solid waste generated during the con- struction, remodeling, repair, or demolition of homes, buildings, roads, and bridges. C&D debris includes objects like: doors, hardwood flooring, furniture, asphalt, drywall and more. The Horry County Solid Waste Authority manages both the landfill and the county’s recycling centers. The Waste Authority start- ed the arduous process of requesting permits from the Army Corps of Engineers last year. The permits are required to increase the area of the landfill. Marr said the Environmen- tal Protection Agency, and state agencies, would also have to approve the expansion. If approved, it would take four to five years before phase one of the expanded landfill area would be ready for use. Marr said the first cell is expected to add capacity for about 17 years of waste and would collect C and D debris. APPLICANT(S): Diamond Shores Surveying LLC PIN(s): 339-00-00-0023 BACKGROUND: March 2026 – the application for this design modification, along with the Sketch Plan (displayed on the monitors) was submitted to the Planning Dept. for a proposed major subdivision with lots fronting E. Country Club Dr. and Hwy 905, containing 43 single-family lots. ANALYSIS: The applicant is proposing to provide direct access to 35- lots via 19- individual residential driveways along E. Country Club Drive and located across the street from the 95-lot phase 1 of “Homestead” subdivision (a 127-lot conservation subdivision developed from the same parent tract). See image “A” below …. as well as Four (4) individual residential driveways, providing direct access to eight (8) SF lots, along the portion of Hwy 905 located between the traffic light (at E. Country Club & Hwy 905) and the intersection of Inlet Lane. See image “B” below. Per Section 10.3.8 (D): “Lots within major residential developments are to access via internal streets only”… in order to maintain traffic-flow and minimize the frequency of vehicular collisions, between residents entering/exiting individual driveways and motorists traveling along higher-order roadways, the -- 19 of 393 -- STAFF REPORT Snowhill Estates – Design Mod. city requires that residential lots within a major development, utilize lower-order streets that were designed for such movements. Roadway intersections are designed with wide travel surfaces and larger pavement radiuses, so vehicular motion may be more fluid and require less deceleration in turns, whereas Residential driveways are narrow with little to no radius, requiring motor vehicles to slow dramatically or even stop to maneuver into. Also typically, residential driveways provide very little throat length to facilitate vehicular deceleration on-site and often no maneuvering room to turn around, so that vehicles exiting the lot may do so in a forward motion. For these reasons, residential roadways are designed to be lower-order streets with posted speed limits of 15 MPH. • East Country Club Drive is a Collector roadway with a posted speed limit of 45 MPH and an average daily trip count of: 6,000 in 2025 (data by GSATS). • Hwy 905 is a Major Arterial roadway with a posted speed limit of 45 MPH and an average daily trip count of: 10,800 in 2024 (data by SCDOT)…. Also, this section of the parent tract is zoned: WRD, which does not permit single-family dwellings. Comments from TRC David Parker (Conway Fire Dept): “The proposed houses with several driveways would be located on E. Country Club which is a main road with several curves that moves heavy traffic through the region and is not well lit up at night. Possible increased risks for motor vehicle crashes with all the driveways instead of an internal street with two access points. 905 area is proposing four properties and they may present some of the same challenges.” Brandon Harrelson (Conway Public Works): “E. Country Club has a high volume of traffic as is. Adding 19 driveway cuts will further increase the risk of accidents. Due to the lack of lighting at night and the amount of traffic, Public Works is opposed to the design mod.” Construction Services Dept.: “High traffic area to have so many driveways and no turn lanes, especially with the new subdivision already approved on E. Country Club (Homestead). Lots of flooding in this area.” Planning Director (J. Hucks): Single-family residential is not a permitted use in the Waccamaw Riverfront District (WRD). The lots that are proposed along Hwy 905 are located on a portion of the overall tract zoned WRD, not R-1. ISSUE: Request to rezone approximately 5.28 +/- acres of property located at 2578 Hwy 378, from the Highway Commercial (HC) district to the Heavy Industrial (HI) district. APPLICANT(S): Brad Richardson, Richardson Family Holdings, LLC PIN(s): 337-10-03-0010 CURRENT ZONING: Highway Commercial (HC) PROPOSED ZONING: Heavy Industrial (HI) BACKGROUND: The subject property was annexed into the City in 2001 [#ZA2001-06-11(C)] and has been zoned Highway Commercial (HC) since annexation. The applicant applied for a business license to sell and display heavy equipment. While “heavy equipment sales and repair” is not (currently) expressly listed as a use in Article 4 – Use Tables, of the UDO, the operational characteristics of the proposed activity are most consistent with industrial uses involving outdoor storage, equipment staging, and heavy vehicle display. The UDO provides that: • Storage/Shed sales and similar outdoor display uses are permitted only in Light Industrial (LI) and Heavy Industrial (HI) districts; • Manufactured and modular home sales are permitted only in industrial districts; • Wholesaling, Storing and Distributing (heavy) is permitted exclusively in the Heavy Industrial (HI) district. Heavy equipment sales typically involve large machinery, outdoor display areas, equipment loading/unloading, and service or repair activities. These characteristics align more closely with industrial districts than with the intent of the Highway Commercial (HC) district. Section 3.2.14 of the UDO establishes the Heavy Industrial (HI) district as intended to accommodate heavy manufacturing, distribution, and processing activities, including uses with outdoor storage and operational characteristics not suitable for commercial corridors. The City’s UDO is “permissive” in nature. Uses are allowed only where they are expressly listed. If the use is not listed, it must be evaluated for similarity to existing categories. Heavy equipment sales share operational characteristics with industrial uses that are permitted only in industrial districts. Therefore, it is not an appropriate use in the Highway Commercial district simply because it is not specifically named. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: Adjacent properties are zoning Highway Commercial (HC), including: -- 38 of 393 -- STAFF REPORT 2578 Hwy 378 (rezoning) • Waste Management (sanitation service company) • Property owned by the applicant While zoned HC, the operational characteristics of some of the surrounding uses are more industrial in nature. Additionally, properties located across Hwy 378 are zoned industrial. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The Future Land Use Map identifies the property as Highway Commercial. Per Section 3.2.10 of the UDO, HC district is intended to: • Serve automobile-oriented commercial activities • Provide corridor compatibility • Reduce traffic congestion • Enhance the aesthetic atmosphere of the City The Highway Commercial (HC) district is not intended to accommodate heavy equipment sales, outdoor industrial storage, or repair operations involving large machinery. Rezoning the property to Heavy Industrial (HI) would: • Introduce an industrial zoning designation into an area identified as HC on the Future Land Use Map; • Potentially expand industrial zoning along the Hwy 378 corridor; • Establish precedent for similar requests along other commercial corridors. STAFF ANALYSIS: Staff has consistently maintained that heavy equipment sales and repair constitute an industrial use based on scale, operational characteristics, and impact profile. Allowing such a use within the Highway Commercial (HC) district undermines the intent of the HC district and creates interpretive ambiguity in the UDO. However, rezoning this property to Heavy Industrial (HI) presents a policy question for Planning Commission and City Council: • Whether the corridor segment is transitioning toward industrial character; or • Whether maintaining Highway Commercial zoning along Hwy 378 remains the City’s long-term policy objective. The request represents a departure from the Future Land Use Map designation and the established intent of the Highway Commercial district. Because the request is inconsistent with the Future Land Use Map and represents a policy shift along the Hwy 378 corridor, staff recommends that Planning Commission carefully evaluate: • Long-term corridor planning objectives; -- 39 of 393 -- STAFF REPORT 2578 Hwy 378 (rezoning) • Potential precedent impacts; • Compatibility with surrounding HC-zoned properties; and • Whether Light Industrial (LI) may be a more appropriate transitional district than Heavy Industrial (HI), if industrial zoning is deemed appropriate. STAFF RECOMMENDATION (and public hearing): In addition to holding the required public hearing, staff recommends that Planning Commission conduct a thorough review of the request and make an informed recommendation to City Council. The proposed amendments revise the classification and regulation of certain commercial uses across multiple zoning districts. The amendments establish updated and new definitions, clarify use classifications, and implement additional use-specific standards and location-based restrictions for certain higher-impact uses, including, but not limited to: tobacco/vape/smoke shop establishments, alternative financial services (e.g., payday loan/title loan/cash advance/check-cashing services), gas/service stations (with or without convenience stores), outdoor event facilities/spaces, and similar uses. BACKGROUND: Over the past several months, staff has evaluated regulatory approaches to address land use compatibility concerns with certain commercial uses, particularly within the Highway Commercial (HC) district and along key corridors. This effort was initiated following a rezoning request involving property zoned HC and located adjacent to an established single-family residential neighborhood. While the rezoning request was ultimately denied, it highlighted broader concerns that the HC district and other zoning districts currently permits a range of higher-intensity commercial uses without sufficient locational standards or mitigation measures when located in proximity to residential areas. In response, staff conducted a comprehensive review of the Use Tables in Article 4 as well as Article 5 of the UDO to identify uses that: • Are currently permitted by right without additional standards; and • May generate operational or site impacts incompatible with nearby residential uses, including traffic, noise, lighting, hours of operation, and other intensity-related factors. Staff also reviewed regulatory approaches utilized by comparable municipalities in South Carolina and other jurisdictions, including the use of separation requirements, conditional or special exception approval processes, and district-based regulations, to identify tools appropriate for implementation in Conway. Proposed Amendments: The proposed amendments establish a comprehensive and coordinated regulatory framework for certain commercial uses that may have greater potential for land use impacts. Key components of the amendments include: -- 127 of 393 -- • Revisions to Article 2 (Definitions): Updated and newly established definitions to clarify use classifications and eliminate ambiguity, including distinctions for similar or overlapping uses. • Revisions to Article 4 (Use Tables): o Clarification that only uses expressly listed in the Use Table are permitted. o Reclassification of certain uses from “Permitted” to “Supplemental” or “Accessory” where appropriate. o Establishment of a formal process for classification of similar or unlisted uses based on primary business activity. • Revisions to Article 5 (Supplemental and Accessory Uses): o Renaming and restructuring of the Article to reflect its function as a set of objective, use-specific standards. o Implementation of location-based criteria, including separation requirements and proximity triggers. o Establishment of Special Exception review in limited circumstances where site- specific impacts warrant additional evaluation. o Adoption of clear, measurable standards addressing operational and site design considerations. • Nonconformities: Existing lawful uses established prior to the adoption of these amendments will be considered legal nonconforming uses and may continue in accordance with Art. 12 – Nonconformities. However, re-establishment of certain uses subject to separation or special exception requirements will be required to comply with current standards. • Housekeeping amendments: Additional revisions are included to improve clarity, consistency, and internal alignment across multiple Articles of the UDO. Regulatory Approach: The proposed amendments represent a multi-layer regulatory approach intended to balance economic development opportunities with neighborhood compatibility. Rather than eliminating uses entirely, the amendments: • Establish objective standards to mitigate potential impacts; • Apply separation requirements where appropriate to prevent overconcentration of certain uses; • Utilize Special Exception review as a targeted tool to address site-specific conditions; and • Align use classifications with actual operational characteristics through updated definitions and administrative interpretation authority. -- 128 of 393 -- This approach ensures that similarly situated uses are regulated consistently while providing flexibility to address unique site conditions. Consistency with Comprehensive Plan: The proposed amendments are consistent with the goals and policies of the City’s Comprehensive Plan, including: • Protection of established residential neighborhoods; • Promotion of compatible land use patterns; • Improved design and redevelopment of commercial corridors; and • Support for balanced and sustainable growth. Additional Information: These amendments will ensure that uses with similar impacts are regulated consistently and that staff has tools to address location-specific issues, rather than treating every site the same regardless of context. The complete text of the proposed amendments (with amendments and as amended) are provided for review. STAFF RECOMMENDATION: In addition to holding the required public hearing, staff recommends that Planning Commission review the proposed amendments and make an informed recommendation to City Council. If a recommendation is provided, these amendments will be considered for first reading at the April 20th Council meeting. -- 129 of 393 -- Key revisions since last review: 1. [Ord. #ZA2013-08-05(A)] 2.2.2 Sign-related Definitions *Refer to Article 11 for Signage Regulations. Animation The movement, or the optical illusion of movement of any part of the sign structure, design or pictorial including the movement of any illumination or the flashing, scintillating or varying of light intensity. The automatic changing of all or any part of the facing of a sign or any part of a sign shall be considered to be animation. Also, included in this definition are signs having “chasing action” which is the action of a row of lights commonly used to create the appearance of motion. Time and temperature units and electronic message centers are not included in this definition. Foot Candle A unit of illumination equal to that given by a source of one (1) candela at a distance of one foot (equivalent to one (1) lumen per square foot or 10.764 lux). Illumination Lighting; the act / condition of being illuminated (Merriam Webster definition). Lumen A unit for measuring the amount of light something produces (Cambridge dictionary definition). Lux A unit of illumination equal to the direct illumination on a surface that is everywhere one meter from a uniform point source of one candle intensity or equal to one lumen per square meter (Merriam Webster definition). Sign Any device designed to attract the attention of the public for commercial or advertising purposes that is attached, painted or otherwise affixed to, or a part of a building, structure, material, surface, vehicle, or object. Integral decorative or architectural features of buildings except letters or trademarks, fences, walls and works of art, which -- 157 of 393 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 2 – Definitions 2-26 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended November 3, 2025 are noncommercial in nature, are not to be construed as being a sign. Sign shall include any artificial light source, time or temperature units, clocks and any device that animates or projects a visual representation that attracts the attention of the public for commercial purpose. Sign Area (also referred to as the gross surface area) The square foot area individual symbols, letters, figures, illustrations, messages, forms, or panels, sign area shall be considered to include all lettering, wording, and accompanying designs and symbols, together with the background on which they are displayed, any frame around the sign and any “cutouts” or extensions but shall not include any supporting structure or bracing. The aggregate sign area is the summation of the area of all sign faces combined. Sign Copy The portion of a sign which contains the name, logo, advertising message, or business identification and consists of all such symbols, letters, figures, insignia, illustrations, messages or forms. Sign copy does not include the border, molding or decorative framing. Sign Face The part of the sign that is or can be used to identify, advertise, communicate information or for visual representation which attracts the attention of the public for any purpose. Sign face includes any background material, panel, trim, color, and direct or self-illumination used that differentiates that sign from the building, structure, backdrop surface or object upon which or against which it is placed. The sign structure shall not be included as a portion of the sign face provided that no identifying/advertising message, symbol or any of the aforementioned sign face criteria are displayed on or designed as part of the sign structure, whether structurally necessary or not. In the case of signs designed with integral sign face and sign structure, the blank (support) area equivalent to a maximum of 50% of the allowable sign area shall be exempt from computations of sign area. Sign Height The vertical distance measured from the average lowest adjacent street crown finished grade at the base of the sign to the highest point top of the sign face or supporting sign structure, whichever is greater. Where a sign is located on a berm or artificial raised grade, height shall be measured from the average surrounding natural grade. Sign Panel The primary surface of a sign that carries the identifying/advertising message. Sign Structure A supporting structure erected or intended for the purpose of identification or advertising with or without a sign thereon, situated upon or attached to the premises upon which any sign may be fastened, affixed, displayed or applied, provided however, said definition shall not include a building or fence. If the total width of the sign structure exceeds fifty (50) percent of the total width of the sign face, the sign structure area shall be included as part of the sign area. Arm Post Sign A sign supported by a structure on one post not exceeding 8 feet in height, that is placed in the ground, and which is wholly independent of any building, fence, vehicle or object other than the off centered structure for support. Animation The movement, or the optical illusion of movement of any part of the sign structure, design or pictorial including the movement of any illumination or the flashing, scintillating or varying of light intensity. The automatic changing of all or any part of the facing of a sign or any part of a sign shall be considered to be animation. Also, included in this definition are signs having “chasing action” which is the action of a row of lights commonly used to create the appearance of motion. Time and temperature units and electronic message centers are not included in this definition. Foot Candle A unit of illumination equal to that given by a source of one (1) candela at a distance of one foot (equivalent to one (1) lumen per square foot or 10.764 lux). Illumination Lighting; the act / condition of being illuminated. Lumen A unit for measuring the amount of light something produces. Lux A unit of illumination equal to the direct illumination on a surface that is everywhere one meter from a uniform point source of one candle intensity or equal to one lumen per square meter. Sign Any device designed to attract the attention of the public for commercial or advertising purposes that is attached, painted or otherwise affixed to, or a part of a building, structure, material, surface, vehicle, or object. Integral decorative or architectural features of buildings except letters or trademarks, fences, walls and works of art, which are noncommercial in nature, are not to be construed as being a sign. Sign shall include any artificial light source, time or temperature units, clocks and any device that animates or projects a visual representation that attracts the attention of the public for commercial purpose. Sign Area (also referred to as the gross surface area) The square foot area individual symbols, letters, figures, illustrations, messages, forms, or panels, sign area shall be considered to include all lettering, wording, and accompanying designs and symbols, together with the background on which they are displayed, any frame around the sign and any “cutouts” or extensions but shall not include any supporting structure or bracing. The aggregate sign area is the summation of the area of all sign faces combined. Sign Copy The portion of a sign which contains the name, logo, advertising message, or business identification and consists of all such symbols, letters, figures, insignia, illustrations, messages or forms. Sign copy does not include the border, molding or decorative framing. Sign Face The part of the sign that is or can be used to identify, advertise, communicate information or for visual representation which attracts the attention of the public for any purpose. Sign face includes any background material, panel, trim, color, and direct or self-illumination used that differentiates that sign from the building, structure, backdrop surface or object upon which or against which it is placed. Sign Height The vertical distance measured from the average finished grade at the base of the sign to the highest point of the sign or supporting structure. Custom Manufacturing Custom manufacturing refers to the on-site production of goods by hand manufacturing or artistic endeavor, which involves only the use of hand tools, individually powered tools or domestic mechanical equipment and the incidental sale of these goods directly to consumers. High Technology (Hi-Tech) Industry Research, development and controlled production of high-technology electronic, industrial or scientific products. Typical uses include biotechnology firms and computer component manufacturers. Light Industrial Production processes which use already manufactured components to assemble, print or package a product such as cloth, paper, plastic, leather, wood, glass or stones, but not including such operations as paper, saw or mills, steel, iron or other metalwork’s, rolling mills, or any manufacturing uses involving primary production of commodities from raw materials. By the nature of the activity performed and/or the scale of the operation, these uses can be located near residential or commercial uses with minimal impact to adjacent uses. Typical uses include apparel manufacturing, paper products finishing, furniture production and production of fabricated metal products. Where a proposed use is not specifically listed, the Zoning Administrator, or their designee, may determine that the use is substantially similar in character, intensity, and impact to a listed use. The classification of a use shall be based on the primary or principal business activity conducted on the premises, considering operational characteristics, services provided, or goods offered for sale, regardless of the name of the business, signage, business registration, or marketing description used by the operator. The Zoning Administrator’s determination shall be given substantial weight and shall not be overturned unless clearly erroneous based on the evidence presented. 2. Basis for Determination. Such determination shall be based on objective consideration of operational characteristics, traffic generation, hours of operation, and other relevant land use impacts. The use shall then be regulated in the same manner as the most similar use. 3. Unclassified Uses. If the proposed use cannot be reasonably classified as substantially similar to a listed use, it shall be deemed prohibited unless and until the Use Table is amended by City Council. The Planning Director or their designee has the authority to consider and treat a proposed use that is similar to a specific use in Article 4. 4. Record of Determination. Determinations made under this subsection shall be documented by the Zoning Administrator and maintained as part of the official zoning records of the City. Such determinations may be relied upon in the interpretation and administration of this Ordinance. Table Organization a. Use Categories Column. The first column identifies general use groupings (e.g. ‘Residential Uses, Commercial Uses, Industrial Uses). b. Specific Use Column. The second column lists specific uses within each use category. c. Zoning District Columns. The middle columns correspond to each zoning district within the City of Conway. Each cell contains a letter classification code indicating whether the use is permitted within that district. 2. Use Classification Codes. The letter codes used in the Use Table have the following meanings: P Use is permitted in the zoning district S Use is permitted subject to compliance with applicable Supplemental Use Standards listed in the Applicable Standards column A Use is permitted as an accessory use that is incidental or subordinate to the principal use. Applicable supplemental standards may apply P1/S1/A1 Indicates a footnote with additional information (see Sec. 4.3) SE Use is permitted only through Special Exception approval by the Board of Zoning Appeals and may be subject to additional conditions Blank Use is not permitted in the zoning district 3. Applicable Standards Column. The Applicable Standards column identifies ordinance sections containing supplemental standards applicable to the specific use. 4. Permitted Uses. The uses listed in the Use Table of this Article are the only uses permitted within each zoning district, subject to the standards of this Ordinance. A use that is not specifically listed as Permitted (P), permitted subject to Supplemental Use Standards (S), Permitted as an Accessory Use (A), or permitted as a Special Exception (SE), shall be deemed prohibited. The absence of a use from the Use Table shall not be interpreted as permission to establish such use. B. Determination of Similar or Unlisted Uses 1. Authority. Where a proposed use is not specifically listed, the Zoning Administrator, or their designee, may determine that the use is substantially similar in character, intensity, and impact to a listed use. The classification of a use shall be based on the primary or principal business activity conducted on the premises, considering operational characteristics, services provided, or goods offered for sale, regardless of the name of the business, signage, business registration, or marketing description used by the operator. -- 210 of 393 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 4 – Use Tables AS PROPOSED TO BE AMENDED 4-2 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended November 3, 2025 The Zoning Administrator’s determination shall be given substantial weight and shall not be overturned unless clearly erroneous based on the evidence presented. 2. Basis for Determination. Such determination shall be based on objective consideration of operational characteristics, traffic generation, hours of operation, and other relevant land use impacts. The use shall then be regulated in the same manner as the most similar use. 3. Unclassified Uses. If the proposed use cannot be reasonably classified as substantially similar to a listed use, it shall be deemed prohibited unless and until the Use Table is amended by City Council. 4. Record of Determination. Determinations made under this subsection shall be documented by the Zoning Administrator and maintained as part of the official zoning records of the City. Such determinations may be relied upon in the interpretation and administration of this Ordinance. Applicability The provisions of this Article establish supplemental use and development standards applicable to certain uses permitted within the zoning districts of the City. These standards address use-specific characteristics and potential site impacts that are not fully addressed by base district regulations. Uses subject to Supplemental Use Standards, as identified in Article 4 – Use Tables, shall comply with the provisions of this Article in addition to all other applicable requirements of the zoning district in which the use is proposed. Uses lawfully established prior to the adoption of these standards that do not conform to the requirements of this Article shall be considered legal nonconforming and shall be subject to the provisions of Article 12 – Nonconformities, including the limitations on re-establishment of discontinued nonconforming uses. Where this Article references zoning districts by name or by use category (e.g., residential zoning districts), such references shall be interpreted in accordance with Article 4 – Use Tables. Uses described as permitted in districts where a principal residential use is allowed shall include all zoning districts in which such residential use is permitted. Nothing in this Article shall be construed to authorize the re-establishment of a use that has lost its legal nonconforming status, except in accordance with Article 12. B. Relationship to Zoning District Regulations. The supplemental use standards in this Article apply in addition to the regulations of the district in which the use is located. Compliance with these standards shall not exempt a use from meeting all other applicable requirements of this Ordinance. C. Administrative Review and Special Exception Approval. Where expressly provided in this Article and/or identified in Article 4 – Use Tables, certain uses or site conditions may require administrative review or special exception approval by the Board of Zoning Appeals in order to evaluate and mitigate site-specific impacts. Such review shall be conducted in accordance with Article 14 – Boards and Procedures. Special exception approval shall be based on the applicable criteria set forth in Article 14, in addition to any applicable use- specific standards identified in this Article. 5.1.1 Adult Entertainment Establishments Adult entertainment establishments include, but are not limited to: cabarets, bookstores, drive-in theaters, theaters, peep shows, adult model studios, sexual encounter centers, escort services and motels, as defined herein, and any other establishment which contains activities characterized by the performance, depiction or description of “specified sexual activities”, or “specified anatomical areas”. Adult entertainment establishments shall be permitted in the Light Industrial (LI) and Heavy Industrial (HI) districts provided the following standards are met: A. Number No more than one (1) adult use as classified above shall be located on any lot. B. Location Adult entertainment establishments shall not be located closer than: 1. 1,000 feet from residential zoning districts or residential use in the City of Conway (R, RA, RR, R-1, R-2, R- 3, R-4, or residential within a MU or PD Zoning District) or equivalent residential zoning districts or use in Horry County. -- 225 of 393 -- Article 5 – Supplemental and Accessory Uses 5-4 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended XX City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance [ZA2018-12-17(A)] 2. 1,000 feet from any religious institution, day care facilities, public or private education facility, Community Support Services / Facility, Outpatient Treatment Facility, public park, public library, cemetery, or any motion picture establishment which shows G or PG rated movies to the general public on a regular basis. [ZA2019-04-01(D)] 3. 2,000 feet from any other adult use, provided that this shall not apply to any establishment or cabaret that does not provide adult entertainment more than twelve (12 times per calendar year). 4. Basis of Measurement. Distances shall be measured in a straight line from the closest property line of the parcel in which the proposed use is located to the closest property line of the parcel containing the protected use or zoning district, without regard to intervening structures, rights-of-way, or property ownership. C. Ownership Disclosure If a person who applies to operate an adult entertainment business is an individual, he must sign the application for a permit as applicant. If a person who applies to operate an adult entertainment business is other than an individual, each individual who has a ten (10%) percent or greater interest in the business must sign the application for a permit and/or license as applicant. If a corporation is listed as owner of an adult business, or as entity which wishes to operate such business, each individual having a ten (10%) percent or greater interest in the corporation must sign the application for a permit and/or license as applicant. All corporate officers shall also sign the application. The fact that a person possesses other types of state or county permits and/or licenses does not exempt him from the requirements of obtaining a sexually oriented business permit and/or license. D. Sale and/or Consumption of Alcohol Prohibited The sale and/or consumption of alcoholic beverages in conjunction with any adult entertainment establishment shall be prohibited. E. An adult entertainment establishment shall neither employ nor permit the admittance / patronage of any person who is under 18 years of age. F. Inspections The management of any adult entertainment establishment shall permit representatives of the Police, Fire, Construction Services, Planning/Development Department or other City or State Agencies to inspect the premises at any time it is open for business. G. Revocation of Zoning Compliance The Planning Director shall revoke a Certificate of Zoning Compliance, thereby suspending the operation of any adult entertainment establishment, for any of the following: 1. The giving of false or misleading information by the applicant at any time in the application process; 2. For the illegal sale of any controlled substance on the premises; 3. For the arrest and conviction of any owner or employee (unless said employee is discharged immediately) for any violation of Title 44 of the Code of Laws of South Carolina, 1976 as amended, relating to controlled substances; and/or violation of any State or Federal crime involving moral turpitude and/or violation of Title XVI, Chapters 3, 15, 23, and 25 of the Code of Laws of South Carolina, 1976, as amended; and/or for the arrest and conviction of any owner or employee for any violation of Title 16 of the Code of Laws of South Carolina, 1976, as amended; 4. Failure to permit inspections by authorized City and State agencies or personnel; 5. Violation of the age restrictions as set forth herein. H. Exterior Portions of Regulated Establishments 1. BACKGROUND (updated): This amendment is a companion to a related set of amendments addressing use classifications and supplemental standards within Articles 2, 4 and 5 of the UDO. As part of that broader effort, staff evaluated the need for a formal Special Exception process to address certain uses that, while appropriate within a zoning district, may have the potential to create site-specific impacts depending on location and operational characteristics. A Special Exception is a permitted use within a zoning district that requires case-by-case review to evaluate potential impacts, such as traffic generation, operational intensity, noise, lighting, and compatibility with surrounding properties. The purpose of the special exception process is to provide a structured and consistent mechanism for evaluating these impacts in accordance with established ordinance criteria. A special exception: • Is a permitted use within an applicable zoning district; • Is not a variance from dimensional or development standards; • Does not authorize a use that is otherwise prohibited; • Requires a finding that the proposed use complies with applicable ordinance standards and will not result in demonstrable adverse impacts; and • May be approved with reasonable conditions directly related to identified impacts and necessary to ensure compliance with the UDO. If adopted, the special exception process would require an applicant, where specified in the Use Table or in Article 5, to obtain approval from the Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA) following a duly noticed public hearing conducted in accordance with Article 14. Evaluation of Uses: As part of this process, staff evaluated a range of uses to determine whether Special Exception review was appropriate, including bed and breakfast establishments, outpatient treatment facilities, alternative financial services, adult entertainment establishments, body piercing and tattoo establishments, tobacco/vape/smoke shops, taverns/bars/nightclubs, and gas/service stations. The evaluation focused on whether existing ordinance standards – such as separation requirements, -- 332 of 393 -- STAFF REPORT Amendment(s) to Articles 2 – Definitions, 4 – Use Tables, & 14 – Boards & Procedures operational limitations, and location-based criteria – were sufficient to address potential impacts, or whether additional discretionary review would provide a meaningful benefit. Based on this analysis, staff determined that certain uses are already adequately regulated through objective standards and do not warrant additional special exception review. These include adult entertainment establishments, taverns/bars/nightclubs, tattoo and body piercing establishments, bed and breakfast establishments, and outpatient treatment facilities, all of which are subject to existing locational, operational, and/or separation requirements within the UDO. Conversely, for selected uses, the special exception process provides an additional layer of review to address site-specific conditions that cannot be fully anticipated through objective standards alone. Proposed amendments: The proposed amendments to Articles 2, 4 and 14: • Establish a formal Special Exception process within the UDO; • Define the scope and criteria for Special Exception review; • Identify specific uses and circumstances under which special exception approval is required; and • Clarify the role of the Board of Zoning Appeals in evaluating such requests based on established criteria. These amendments are intended to work in coordination with the updated Use Table (Art. 4) and Supplemental and Accessory Use standards (Art. 5), creating a consistent framework in which: • Uses are clearly classified; • Objective standards are applied where appropriate; and • Discretionary review is used selectively to address site-specific impacts. Consistency with the Comprehensive Plan: The proposed amendments are consistent with the goals and policies of the City’s Comprehensive Plan, including: • Protection of established residential neighborhoods; • Promotion of compatible land use patterns; and • Implementation of regulatory tools that support balanced and context-sensitive development. Extraordinary conditions: There are extraordinary and exceptional conditions pertaining to the particular piece of property. 2. Other Property: The extraordinary and exceptional conditions do not generally apply to other property in the vicinity. 3. Utilization: Because of the extraordinary or exceptional conditions, the application of the ordinance to a particular piece of property would effectively prohibit or unreasonably restrict the utilization of the property. 4. Special exceptions are permitted uses that are permitted within a zoning district upon approval by the Board of Zoning Appeals, subject to compliance with specific standards. These uses, due to their size, location, design, or potential impacts, require additional review to ensure compatibility with surrounding uses. Copies of all notices, correspondence, documentary evidence, orders and forms shall be maintained as public records. -- 351 of 393 -- STAFF REPORT Amendments to Article 12 - Nonconformities PLANNING COMMISSION MTG DATE: April 2, 2026 AGENDA ITEM: V.B.3 ISSUE: Amendments to Article 12 – Nonconformities, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding the re-established of certain uses that require special exception approval under the UDO. This amendment will clarify revisions related to the discontinuance and re-establishment of nonconforming uses, establish consistent standards for nonconforming lots, structures, sites, signs, and ensure alignment with recently proposed amendments to Articles 2, 4, 5, and 14. BACKGROUND: Article 12 of the UDO establishes the framework for regulating nonconforming lots, structures, and uses. Nonconformities typically arise when properties or uses were lawfully established prior to the adoption or amendment of zoning regulations but no longer comply with current standards. As part of the City’s broader effort to modernize and clarify the UDO, staff has undertaken a comprehensive review of Article 12 to address inconsistencies, improve clarity, and ensure that the provisions function cohesively with other sections of the Ordinance—particularly those governing supplemental use standards (Article 5) and Board of Zoning Appeals procedures (Article 14). These amendments are a companion to related updates establishing a formal Special Exception process and refining use-specific standards for certain uses that may have greater potential impacts on surrounding properties. Summary of Proposed Amendments: The proposed amendments to Article 12 include the following key updates: 1. Discontinuance and Re-establishment of Nonconforming Uses • Clarifies that a nonconforming use is considered discontinued after 180 days of inactivity. • Establishes a clear process for re-establishment of nonconforming uses, subject to review and approval by the Board of Zoning Appeals. • Introduces objective criteria for re-establishment, including: o Lawful prior establishment of the use o No increase in intensity or impact o Demonstration that discontinuance was due to circumstances beyond the property owner’s control • Limits the scope of re-established uses to their prior conditions. -- 352 of 393 -- STAFF REPORT Amendments to Article 12 - Nonconformities 2. Separation-Based and Location-Restricted Uses • Establishes that uses rendered nonconforming due to separation requirements, location restrictions, or special exception standards may continue as legal nonconforming uses. • Clarifies that once such uses are discontinued, they may not be re-established unless they comply with current ordinance requirements. This provision ensures consistency with recently proposed standards for uses such as tobacco/vape establishments and alternative financial services. 3. Change in Ownership • Clarifies that a legal nonconforming use may continue despite a change in ownership, tenancy, or business name, provided the use has not been discontinued. 4. Nonconforming Lots of Record • Establishes that lawfully created lots that do not meet current dimensional standards may still be used for permitted purposes. • Requires combination of commonly owned adjacent lots where necessary to meet minimum standards. 5. Nonconforming Structures and Sites • Clarifies provisions for expansion, reconstruction, and modification of nonconforming structures. • Establishes consistent standards for site elements such as parking, access, landscaping, and buffering. • Ensures that improvements do not increase the degree of nonconformity. 6. Damage and Reconstruction Standards • Establishes a consistent threshold for reconstruction: o Structures damaged 50% or less may be rebuilt to prior nonconforming conditions. o Structures damaged greater than 50% must be brought into full compliance. 7. Nonconforming Signs • Modernizes provisions to remove outdated material-specific standards. • Clarifies maintenance, repair, and replacement allowances. • Establishes clear limitations on reconstruction and expansion of nonconforming signage. 8. General Clarifications and Housekeeping • Improves organization, terminology, and cross-references throughout Article 12. -- 353 of 393 -- STAFF REPORT Amendments to Article 12 - Nonconformities • Aligns provisions with Article 5 (Supplemental Use Standards) and Article 14 (Boards & Procedures). • Eliminates redundant or conflicting language. ANALYSIS The proposed amendments improve the overall clarity and functionality of Article 12 by: • Providing a clear and consistent framework for determining when nonconforming uses may continue, be discontinued, or be re-established; • Aligning nonconforming use provisions with recently updated standards for uses subject to separation requirements or special exception review; • Eliminating ambiguity regarding the role of the Board of Zoning Appeals in reviewing re- establishment requests; • Ensuring that nonconforming uses are not expanded or intensified over time, while still allowing reasonable relief in limited circumstances. These updates also reinforce the City’s ability to manage uses with greater potential impacts while maintaining fairness for property owners with legally established uses. STAFF RECOMMENDATION: In addition to holding the required public hearing, staff recommends that Planning Commission review the proposed amendments and make an informed recommendation to City Council.
