[ZA2012-09-04 (A)] -- 376 of 393 -- STAFF REPORT Amendments to UDO (ART.’s 2, 6, 7, 10, and 12) regarding private roads and access to substandard streets PLANNING COMMISSION MTG DATE: April 2, 2026 AGENDA ITEM: V.B.4 ISSUE: Amendments to Article 2 – Definitions, Article 6 – Design Standards, Article 7 – Street Design and Circulation, Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development, and Article 12 – Nonconformities, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), to establish standards for private roads in the City of Conway. This amendment in intended to address existing lots of record that lack adequate frontage on a public street accepted for maintenance by the City, County, or State, and to establish regulations for development proposed on roads not constructed to City standards. BACKGROUND: The City’s current UDO requires all lots to front on a public street constructed to City standards and accepted for maintenance by the City. While this requirement is appropriate for new subdivisions, it has created challenges in situations involving: • Lots of record created prior to adoption of the UDO; • Properties annexed into the City that are served by private or substandard roads; • Existing roads that were assumed to be public but were never formally dedicated; • Roads under the jurisdiction of other entities that do not meet City standards; and • Parcels lacking adequate frontage due to historic platting patterns. Under the current ordinance, these properties may be unable to obtain building permits or certificates of occupancy unless a public street is constructed to full City standards. In many cases, this requirement is impractical due to cost, ownership constraints, or existing development patterns. ANALYSIS The proposed amendment establishes a coordinated framework across multiple sections of the UDO to address these conditions while maintaining the City’s standards for new development. Key Components of the Amendment 1. Definition of Private Road (Article 2) Adds a definition clarifying that private roads are not publicly maintained and are not part of the City street system unless constructed to City standards and formally accepted. 2. Frontage Requirement Modification (Article 6) Revises the requirement that all lots must front on a public street to allow access via private roads or access easements in limited circumstances, as governed by Article 10. -- 377 of 393 -- STAFF REPORT Amendments to UDO (ART.’s 2, 6, 7, 10, and 12) regarding private roads and access to substandard streets 3. Street Design Consistency (Article 7) Updates existing provisions to remove the blanket prohibition on private roads and instead allow them only where specifically permitted by Article 10. Private roads remain prohibited for major subdivisions. 4. Subdivision Regulations (Article 10) Creates a new Section 10.10 – Private Roads and Access to Substandard Streets, which: • Allows private roads only in limited circumstances, such as lots of record and annexed properties; • Establishes minimum design and safety standards, including fire access requirements; • Requires recorded maintenance agreements and clarifies that the City has no maintenance responsibility; • Prohibits the use of private roads for major subdivisions; • Provides administrative approval authority for individual lots of record; and • Establishes standards for development accessing substandard roads, including the ability to require improvements or deny development where adequate access cannot be provided. 5. Nonconforming Lots (Article 12) Clarifies that legally created nonconforming lots of record may be developed, including those lacking frontage, provided access is established in accordance with Section 10.10. PURPOSE AND INTENT The proposed amendment is intended to: • Address longstanding issues related to access for legally created lots of record; • Provide a clear and consistent framework for evaluating development on private or substandard roads; • Maintain public safety through minimum access and fire standards; • Protect the City from long-term maintenance obligations associated with private roads; and • Preserve existing requirements for public streets in new and major subdivisions. This amendment does not reduce development standards for new subdivisions and does not permit private roads as an alternative to required public infrastructure for large-scale development. IMPACTS Positive Impacts • Provides a practical solution for development of existing lots lacking public frontage; • Reduces the need for case-by-case exceptions or informal interpretations; -- 378 of 393 -- STAFF REPORT Amendments to UDO (ART.’s 2, 6, 7, 10, and 12) regarding private roads and access to substandard streets • Improves clarity and consistency in the UDO; • Enhances public safety by establishing minimum access standards; • Protects the City from assuming maintenance of substandard or private roads. Potential Concerns • Perception that private roads are being broadly permitted (mitigated by limitations within the ordinance); • Need for careful administrative review to ensure compliance with safety standards. STAFF RECOMMENDATION: In addition to holding the required public hearing, staff recommends that Planning Commission review the proposed amendments and make an informed recommendation to City Council. If a recommendation is provided, the proposed amendments will be forwarded for consideration of first reading at the April 20, 2026 City Council meeting. -- 379 of 393 -- PREVIOUS STAFF REPORT OUTLINING ROAD ISSUES ISSUE: Discussion of existing issues regarding roadway standards, including: development of lots fronting private or substandard roadways, external access points for major developments onto substandard roadways, and roadway warranty timeframes in relation to the completed installation of the road. BACKGROUND: Prior to the 1975 Home Rule Act, which, among other things, authorized the adoption of subdivision regulations by local governments, the subdivision of properties had no regulatory oversight. Severing of parcels occurred through legal descriptions provided in title deeds, some such descriptions referenced recorded & un-recorded survey maps, while other properties were split by description alone. To facilitate access, many such properties were created with private roadways or easements, and without the governance of such actions, no road design standards were codified or improvements to said roadways required as a condition of severance. Road Issue 1: Development of lots fronting private or substandard roadways The City’s UDO requires all proposed lots to front a public street built to City standards and formally dedicated to the City; however, there are several pre-existing lots of record that do not front public roads or public right of ways where the road was never installed. As annexation expands outward and development pressure increases, we are encountering a growing number of legacy properties (i.e. pre- existing, legal nonconforming lots of record) that do not meet or cannot meet these requirements. These situations include: • Lots of record created decades ago without public frontage • “Paper streets” that were platted but never constructed • Roads historically assumed to be public but never formally dedicated • Former state-maintained roads where maintenance ceased but right-of-way remains • Landlocked parcels where homes once existing but cannot now be rebuilt Policy Questions: 1. Continue strict enforcement requiring full public street construction and dedication in all cases? OR 2. Establish narrowly tailored provisions to address legacy lots and minor situations while maintaining standards for new subdivisions? Possible amendments could include below options: • Legacy lot relief: allow development of pre-existing lots without public frontage if minimum access and safety standards are met and no further subdivision occurs. • Minor subdivision private access standards: permit limited private access easements for small- scale divisions (i.e. 3 or less) with fire approval and recorded maintenance agreements. • Private street clarification: allow private streets under defined standards without obligating City maintenance unless built to full public specifications. Providing policy clarity will: ➢ Reduce litigation exposure and associated costs -- 380 of 393 -- PREVIOUS STAFF REPORT OUTLINING ROAD ISSUES ➢ Protect long-term infrastructure integrity ➢ Provide predictable standards for staff and property owners ➢ Avoid future unfunded infrastructure liabilities Examples Examples of where these issues exist are attached. Example 3 of the attachment shows a current, ongoing legal situation that is yet to be resolved. The home is currently under construction and is expected to seek a Certificate of Occupancy (C.O.) in late April / early May. At the time the property was annexed (2023), City records showed the road as “public.” However, the road was never conveyed to anyone, private or public, at the time adjacent properties were conveyed to new owners going back to the 1950’s. The property owner will not be able to receive a C.O. until the road is constructed, in accordance with the UDO, and an approved design modification granted by Planning Commission. The City has retained legal representation to pursue all legal avenues available in which the road could be dedicated to the City for perpetual maintenance, once the road has been improved. To date, the issue has not been resolved. As such, staff is pursuing alternatives in the interim, such as: • Accepting a financial guarantee in lieu of the improvements being completed until the issue can be resolved and the property owner installs the road improvements and dedicates it to the City. • Allowing a C.O. to be issued upon inspection and approval from the Fire Dept. • Recording a no-maintenance acknowledgement Road issue 2: External access points for major subdivisions onto substandard roadways As previously stated, the UDO requires that any street / road that will serve as frontage for one or more lots shall be improved and dedicated to the City, OR already be a public road maintained by SCDOT or Horry County. It does not, however, address a criteria for existing roads that will be utilized for external access to new developments. Since many roadways in the county are privately maintained or publicly maintained yet unpaved, it would be advantageous for the City to require that all external access point to major residential developments originate from a paved, publicly maintained roadway. Example: The City is currently reviewing a development located off of Long Ave, which is proposed to be developed as a conservation subdivision. One of the entrance points to the development is off of a 12 foot wide dirt road, proposed to be used to satisfy the minimum ingress/egress requirements for the proposed number of lots. This issue will become more and more prevalent as the City’s footprint continues to expand into the unincorporated areas, where substandard roads are more common. Key Principle for the UDO: • “No subdivision shall be approved unless safe and adequate access is provided to a public street built to standards sufficient to accommodate the proposed development.” Currently, the UDO does not specifically address access via another jurisdiction’s substandard facility. Possible additions to the UDO to address the issue of adequate access: -- 381 of 393 -- PREVIOUS STAFF REPORT OUTLINING ROAD ISSUES • Add an “adequate access” standard, stating “where a subdivision proposes access from a street not owned or maintained by the City, the applicant shall demonstrate that such street meets minimum width, paving, drainage, and fire access standards sufficient to serve the proposed development. • Also consider adding: “if the existing street does not meet such standards, the applicant shall be responsible for improvements necessary to provide safe and adequate access prior to final plat approval.” • Amendments could also be tied to fire code standards, to include: - A minimum unobstructed width for the roadway - An all-weather / dust free surface - Appropriate turnarounds • Amendment could include a “capacity & functional classification” clause, such as “the City may require offsite roadway improvements where an existing access street lacks the capacity or structural integrity to accommodate projected traffic volumes generated by the development.” Road Issue 3: Roadway warranty timeframes in relation to the completion of the roadway in which the warranty covers The City requires a roadway warranty for all roads dedicated to the City with major residential subdivisions. The UDO requires this after the final plat is recorded, but BEFORE any Certificate of Occupancies can be issued for new homes in the development in which the street dedicated serves as the required frontage. This warranty covers the roadway, curb/gutter, sidewalks, and stormwater/drainage within the rights-of-way being dedicated. The warranty is for a three-year period. The issue is not the warranty itself, which includes a financial guarantee to cover the cost of repairs that could be necessary within the 3-year period, but the trigger point in which the warranty starts. The basic steps are outlined below: 1. Roads must be built 2. Roads must be dedicated before first C.O. issued 3. Warranty runs for 3 years from “completion” 4. Final asphalt layer often installed much later 5. Heavy construction traffic occurs after dedication 6. Warranty expires before the road truly stabilizes. This creates a mismatch between legal acceptance and functional completion. The City requires new subdivision roads to be public because the City maintains them forever. To protect taxpayers, a 3-year warranty is required when dedicated and accepted. In practice, the clock starts running before the road is truly finished and before it has experienced normal residential use conditions. Developers typically only install base surface asphalt layers and intermediate layers, then they dedicate roads so that the homes being built can be issued C.O.’s. They will subsequently build out the entire phase of the subdivision, which could include 50-100 homes, with heavy trucks using the roads during this time, and the final surface layer is not installed until near the end. By this time, the warranty period -- 382 of 393 -- PREVIOUS STAFF REPORT OUTLINING ROAD ISSUES may be close to expiration, and the City is close to assuming full, long-term maintenance responsibility; essentially inheriting early deterioration risk. Left unaddressed, this could result in premature resurfacing costs, a maintenance burden on Public Works, reduced pavement life cycles, and capital improvement impacts. Current Ordinance Dedication → Acceptance → Warranty Start Instead of: Final pavement completion → Warranty Start Practical solutions: • Start warranty at final surface installation and amend the UDO to state, “the roadway warranty period shall commence upon installation and City acceptance of the final surface layer.” - Add a clause stating that roads could be dedicated sooner but the warranty period resets or begins upon final satisfactory inspection of the completed roads. • Two stage acceptance. Create: - Conditional acceptance. Allows or C.O.’s to be issued so that roads are public for access, and warranty clock does not start. - Final acceptance. Occurs after final surface layer installed and final inspection, then warranty begins. • Extend warranty to a five-year period (less ideal). This would address timing but it wouldn’t fix the clock-start issue. As previously stated, with the continued growth of the area, subdivision road inventory will increase rapidly, and if warranty timing remains misaligned, the City absorbs hidden long-term costs, and pavement management becomes unreliable. -- 383 of 393 -- 12 3 Example 1: Access Easement– platted in accordance with county requirements City does not allow lots to be accessed via an easement. All lots must front a public street. The lots depicted here are essentially “landlocked.” If annexed, a permit could not be issued under current requirements. -- 384 of 393 -- Example 2: City right of way but road is not installed Carpet Alley is classified as a City road. The road goes from Ninth Ave to Racepath Ave. However, the right-of- way is cut off so there is no outlet from Carpet Alley other than Ninth Ave. The subject parcels would be required to install the roadway to the city’s minimum road design standards. A cul- de-sac may be required for emergency vehicle turnaround. -- 385 of 393 -- Grainger Circle Eagle Street 20+ lots with no access meeting City Standards -- 386 of 393 -- Example 3: Private Road leading to property being developed (not within a major subdivision) Ownership of underlying property is not surrounding property owners. Previous plats identified the road as public, including City GIS, which identified road as a county road. County GIS identified road as a city road. Roadway to be installed to match conditions of the connecting city road. Must be complete prior to CO being issued. -- 387 of 393 -- Example 4: Parcel in city limits. Sixth Ave is a state right-of-way. However, state maintenance ends before the paved right-of-way reaches this lot. -- 388 of 393 -- Roadway Amendments to UDO Proposed Article 2 – Definitions: Section 2.2 – Definitions 2.2.1 General Definitions Private Road / Private Street: A privately owned vehicular accessway that is not dedicated to or accepted for maintenance by the City that provides access to one or more lots. Private roads may be located within a recorded easement or private tract and shall be constructed and maintained by the property owner(s), homeowner’s association, or other responsible entity. Private roads are not part of the City street system and the City shall have no obligation for their maintenance, repair, or reconstructed unless and until accepted by the City. Private roads shall not be eligible for acceptance into the City street system unless constructed or improved to meet all applicable City standards in effect at the time of dedication. Substandard Road: A road that does not meet the City’s minimum design or construction standards for public streets, including but not limited to, paving, drainage, or structural capacity. ARTICLE 6 – Design Standards Section 6.2 – Residential Design Standards 6.2.1, Dimensional Requirements Current language: Except as specified for each dwelling type (below), the following dimensional requirements shall apply: A. Minimum Lot Size. The minimum lot sizes for each zoning district and/or dwelling type can be found in Table 6.1: Dimensional Requirements for Residential Zoning Districts. B. Setbacks: the front, side, corner front, and rear yard setbacks shall adhere to the requirements set forth in Table 6.1. C. Each lot shall front on a public street. Proposed language: Except as specified for each dwelling type (below), the following dimensional requirements shall apply: A. Minimum Lot Size. The minimum lot sizes for each zoning district and/or dwelling type can be found in Table 6.1: Dimensional Requirements for Residential Zoning Districts. B. Setbacks: the front, side, corner front, and rear yard setbacks shall adhere to the requirements set forth in Table 6.1. C. Frontage. Each lot shall front on a public street; however, lots may obtain access from an approved private road or access easement where permitted in accordance with Article 10 (Subdivision and Land Development) of this Ordinance. -- 389 of 393 -- Roadway Amendments to UDO Proposed ARTICLE 7 – Streets and Circulation Section 7.1 – Street Design 7.1.12, Reserve Strips, Half Streets and Private Streets Current language: Reserve strips and non-access easements adjoining street rights-of-way for the purpose of preventing access to or from adjacent property, (except those required by the Technical Review Committee to prevent access to thoroughfares), private streets and half-streets shall not be permitted under any condition. Proposed language: 7.1.2 Reserve Strips, Half Streets, and Private Roads A. Reserve Strips and Non-Access Easements Reserve Strips and non-access easements adjoining street rights-of-way for the purpose of preventing access to or from adjacent property shall not be permitted, except where required by the Technical Review Committee to restrict access to thoroughfares. B. Half-Streets Half-streets shall not be permitted under any condition. C. Private Roads 1. Private roads shall not be permitted except in accordance with the provisions of Article 10 (Subdivision and Land Development) of this Ordinance. Private roads shall not be considered part of the City street system and shall not be maintained by the City unless and until constructed to City standards and formally accepted. 2. Design and construction requirements for private roads shall be as established in this Ordinance and subject to review and approval by the City. 3. Private roads shall not be permitted for major subdivisions. ARTICLE 10 – Subdivision and Land Development Section 10.3 Subdivision Design Standards 10.3.5 Reserve Strips, Half Streets, and Private Streets Current language: Reserve strips and non-access easements adjoining street rights-of-way for the purpose of preventing access to or from adjacent property, private streets, and half-streets shall not be permitted under any condition (except as required to restrict access to existing or proposed arterial streets, collector streets, or thoroughfares). Proposed language: 10.3.5 Reserve Strips, Half Streets, and Private Roads A. Reserve Strips and Non-Access Easements Reserve strips and non-access easements adjoining street rights-of-way for the purpose of preventing access to or from property shall not be permitted, except where required by the Technical Review Committee to restrict access to thoroughfares. B. Half-Streets Half-streets shall not be permitted under any condition. -- 390 of 393 -- Roadway Amendments to UDO Proposed C. Private Roads 1. Private roads or streets shall not be permitted except in accordance with Section 10.10 of this Ordinance. Private roads or streets shall not be considered part of the City street system and shall not be maintained by the City unless and until constructed to City standards and formally accepted. 2. Design and construction requirements for private roads shall be as established in this Ordinance and subject to review and approval by the City. 3. Private roads shall not be permitted for major subdivisions. NEW SECTION: Section 10.10 Private Roads and Access to Substandard Streets 10.10.1 Private Roads A. Purpose The purpose of this Section is to provide limited flexibility for development in situations where access to a public street does not exist or cannot reasonably be constructed, including lots of record that were legally created prior to adoption of this Ordinance or prior to annexation, and annexed properties, while ensuring safe access and protecting the City from maintenance obligations. B. General Standard Public streets shall remain the required standard for subdivisions. Private roads shall be permitted only in limited circumstances as provided in this section. C. When Permitted Private roads may be approved in the following circumstances: 1. Lots of record created prior to adoption of this Ordinance or prior to annexation; 2. Annexed properties lacking frontage on a public street; 3. Minor subdivisions consisting of _____ lots or fewer; (I recommend 3 or less) 4. Where strict application of public street requirements is determined by the City to be impractical due to existing conditions. D. Limitations Private roads shall be subject to the following limitations: 1. Private roads shall not be permitted for major subdivisions 2. Private roads shall not be approved where extension of a public street is reasonably feasible 3. No further subdivision of lots served by a private road shall be permitted unless the road is upgraded to City standards. 4. Private roads shall not be used to avoid the construction of public streets where such streets are otherwise required. E. Minimum Standards Private roads shall meet the following minimum requirements, unless otherwise approved by the City: 1. Minimum travel surface width: twenty (20) feet; (Fire said 20’ is the minimum) 2. All-weather driving surface capable of supporting emergency apparatus vehicles; 3. Adequate drainage shall be provided; 4. Turnaround facilities where required; 5. Compliance with applicable fire access requirements. F. Maintenance 1. Private roads shall be maintained by the property owner(s), homeowners’ association, or other responsible entity. -- 391 of 393 -- Roadway Amendments to UDO Proposed 2. A recorded maintenance agreement shall be required prior to final plat approval or issuance of building permits, as applicable. 3. The City shall have no responsibility for maintenance, repair, or reconstruction of private roads. G. Plat Requirements All private roads shall be clearly identified on plats with the following note: “Private road – not maintained by the City of Conway.” H. Administrative Approval The Planning Director, or their designee, may approve private road access for individual lots of record or minor subdivisions where compliance with public street requirements would create an undue hardship due to existing conditions. I. Acceptance as Public Streets Private roads shall not be accepted into the City street system unless constructed or improved to meet all applicable City standards in effect at the time of dedication. 10.10.2 Access to Substandard Streets A. Applicability This section shall apply to development proposed to be accessed by a road that: 1. Is not constructed to City standards; 2. Is not publicly maintained; 3. Has unknown or unclear ownership; or 4. Is otherwise determined by the City to be substandard. B. General Requirement 1. Development shall not be approved unless safe and adequate access is provided. Access via a substandard road may be permitted only when the City determines that such access is sufficient to serve the proposed development or can be improved to meet minimum standards acceptable by the City. 2. Approval of access to a substandard road shall not be construed as acceptance of such road for public maintenance. C. Required Improvements The City may require improvements to a substandard road as a condition of development approval, including but not limited to: 1. Widening of the travel surface; 2. Installation of an all-weather surface; 3. Drainage improvements; 4. Turnaround facilities; 5. Intersection improvements; 6. Additional access points where necessary for public safety. D. Fire Access All development served by a substandard road shall comply with applicable fire access requirements. Approval from the Fire Department may be required prior to issuance of permits. E. Limitations 1. The City may limit the number of lots or intensity of development served by a substandard road. 2. The City may deny development where adequate access cannot be provided. 3. Major Subdivisions and Substandard Roads -- 392 of 393 -- Roadway Amendments to UDO Proposed a. Major subdivisions shall not be approved where primary access is proposed via a substandard road, including roads maintained by another governmental entity, unless such road is improved to meet minimum City standards for access and public safety prior to or concurrent with development. b. Where such access is proposed, the applicant shall be responsible for securing all necessary approvals from the applicable jurisdictions and completing required improvements as a condition of development approval. F. Coordination with Other Jurisdictions Where access is provided via a road under the jurisdiction of another governmental entity, the applicant may be required to obtain approval from that entity for any necessary improvements. -- 393 of 393 --

title: APPD MINUTES 4.2.26
text: I. Il. IV. PC 3/5/2026 CITY OF CONWAY PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING THURSDAY, April 2, 2026 Planning & Building Dept. Conference Room — 196 Laurel Street Present: Jessica Wise, George Ulrich, Greg Bryson, Allan Cornell, Thomas J. Anderson III, David Sligh Absent: Kendall Brown Staff: Jessica Hucks, Planning Director; Katie Dennis, Planner; Nancy Alvarez, Assistant Planner; Charlotte Peterson, Assistant Planner; Marcus Cohen, IT Others: David Shwerd, Holly Wilczewski, Jack Wilczewski, Rob Shelton, Cam Armstrong, Marshal McMillan, Nathan Pound, Jerry Stalvy, George Debush CALL TO ORDER Chairperson Wise called the meeting to order at approximately 5:30 pm. APPROVAL OF MINUTES Ulrich made a motion, seconded by Bryson to approve the March 5, 2026 minutes as written. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. Ulrich made a motion to combine the public hearing and zoning request for item request 4 through 10 due to their common ownership and identical rezoning request. The motion was seconded by Bryson and carried unanimously. PUBLIC INPUT Wise made a motion to open public input. Holly Wilczewski spoke during public input. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Ulrich to close public input and the motion carried unanimously. SUBDIVISIONS A. Design Modifications 1. Clearbrook - the applicant, Thomas & Hutton, is requesting design modifications regarding access management requirements and roadway design criteria for the Clearbrook subdivision, located on Hwy 905 and John Doctor Rd (PIN 339-00-00-0013). Dennis stated that the project had previously come before the board, including approval of two design modifications in December 2024. The current plan proposed 200 lots. The applicant requested three design modifications related to access management requirements and one related to roadway design criteria in the UDO for the Clearbrook subdivision located on HWY 905 and John Doctor Road. 1 PC 3/5/2026 2. The applicant first requested that Phase 1, with 31 lots, be served by a single entrance from John Doctor Road. Second, they are requested that Phase 2, with an additional 66 lots, also use that same entrance resulting in 97 lots served by a single point of access. Third, the applicant requested that 48 proposed lots in Phase 3 be accessed by a single entrance from Padgett Lane. Dennis stated in section 7.1.2 of the UDO requires developments with 30 or more lots to have at least points of ingress and egress. That standard is intended to ensure safe access, reduce congestion, and provide reliable emergency access. The fourth request is to allow a block length of approximately 2,525 feet, where the UDO limits block length to 1,200 feet to promote connectivity and emergency access. Staff also noted safety and traffic concerns from the Technical Review Committee including Fire Department and the Police Department. Dennis clarififed that Planning Commission does have the authority to grant design modifications; however, Fire Code requirements would still apply. The applicant Nathan Pound was present. The board discussed at length. Bryson made a motion to approve, install a complete all weather surface road during Phase 1 from John Doctor Rd to Padgett Lane through Phase 1 to Phase 4, contingent to fire code, and an approval for the block length request, Anderson seconded the motion. The motion carried unanimously. Snowhill Estates - the applicant, Diamond Shores, LLC, is requesting a design modification regarding the requirements for lots and building sites; specifically, the requirement that lots are to be accessed via internal roads only (Sec. 10.3.8, D), for a proposed major subdivision on East Country Club Dr. and Hwy 905 (PIN 339-00-00-0023). The applicant David Schwerd and Rob Shelton were present. Dennis stated that the applicant was requesting a design modification for a 43-lot subdivision on East Country Club Dr. The plan proposed 19 individual driveway connections to serve 35 lots on E Country Club Dr, and four additional driveways to serve 8 lots along HWY 905. Dennis further explained Section 10.3.8(D) of the UDO requires that lots within major residential developments access via internal streets. This standard is intended to maintain traffic flow and reduce conflicts between residential driveways and higher-speed roadways. In this case, East Country Club Drive is a collector road with a posted speed of 45 miles per hour and approximately 6,000 daily trips, and Highway 905 is a major arterial with similar speeds and over 10,000 daily trips. These roadway types are not designed for frequent driveway access. Staff also noted concerns from the Technical Review Committee. Fire, Public Works, and Construction Services have all expressed safety concerns related to the number of driveway cuts, traffic speeds, limited lighting, and overall crash risk. 2 PC 3/5/2026 The board discussed at length. Cornell made a motion to defer this item to allow the applicant to modify the proposed design to better meet TRC safety recommendations, Bryson seconded the motion. The motion carried unanimously. B. Letters of Credit 1. Collins Walk — the applicants, Thomas & Hutton and Diamond Shores, LLC, are requesting approval of an extension and reduction of the infrastructure letter of credit (LOC) for the Collins Walk subdivision, located off Hwy 501/Church St., near the intersection of Hwy 501/Church St. and Cultra Rd. The applicant, David Schwerd was present. Dennis explained the applicant was seeking an extension to and a reduction of the infrastructure letter of credit for the Colins Walk subdivision. The letter of credit insures completion of infrastructure installation in phase one of the subdivision. The current letter of credit is set to expire April 9, 2026, the extension would be for one year and a reduction of $462,799.06 to a $239,456.25. Staff recommended approval based on TRC review. Ulrich made a motion to approve the request, seconded by Cornell. The motion carried unanimously. Vv. PUBLIC HEARINGS A. REZONING REQUEST(S) 1. Previously Deferred...Request to rezone approximately 5.28+/- acres of property located at 2578 HWY 378 (PIN 337-10-03-0010), from the Highway Commercial (HC) district to the Heavy Industrial (HI) district. The applicant was not present. Dennis stated the applicant requested this item be further deferred. Wise made a motion to defer until the applicant can be present, seconded by Ulrich. The motion carried unanimously. 2. Request to rezone an approximately 0.73+/- acres of property located at 424 Maplewood Circle from the Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed, (SF40) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district (PIN 324-06-01-0002). Dennis stated this rezoning request is a result of a requirement to request annexation upon connecting to city utility services. The subject parcel is located in the Maplewood subdivision near Long Avenue Extension, with restrictive covenants in place since May of 1988. The property is contingent to City limits, with two adjacent parcels having been annexed in 2020 and 2024. The request is consistent with the Future Land Use Map and surrounding uses, which reflect the use of 3 PC 3/5/2026 the subject property being a single-family residence with a detached garage. City Council did approve the annexation at the March 16" meeting. Staff will forward Planning Commission’s recommendation to Council at the April 20th meeting. The applicant was not present. There was no public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Ulrich to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. Wise made a motion to approve the rezoning request from Horry County Residential; no mobile homes allowed (SF 40) to City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). Anderson seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. 3. Request to rezone approximately 3.92+/- (total) acres of property located at 1121, 1125, and 1135 HWY 501 E. from the Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) district to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district (PINs: 367-14-03-0011 and -0008). David Sligh recused himself. Dennis stated that these properties are currently being considered for annexation due to a new water connection request from the mobile home located on the property. The parcels are currently zoned Horry County Highway Commercial, and the proposed zoning is City of Conway Highway Commercial. The proposed rezoning is consistent with the future land use map. The properties are located along the Highway 501 corridor and are developed with existing commercial uses, including an older commercial building used as a tire center and another parcel containing Skyline Signs. One of the parcels also contains a manufactured home that is currently vacant. Dennis noted that the applicant has expressed his desire to not be annexed and requested a dollar amount of what annexation would cost annual; specifically pertaining to property taxes and business licensing fees. Staff and the board discussed at length. The applicant was not present. There was no public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Ulrich to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. Wise made a motion to approve the recommendation for rezoning, Ulrich seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. City of Conway Properties 4. Request to rezone approximately 0.42+/- acres of property located at 103 Azalea Dr. from the Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district to the Conservation Preservation (CP) district (PIN 339-01-02-0005). 5. Request to rezone approximately 0.38+/- acres of property located at 1508 Little St. from 4 PC 3/5/2026 the Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district to the Conservation Preservation (CP) district (PIN 339-08-01-0007). 6. Request to rezone approximately 8.15+/- (total) acres of property located on Hawthorne Dr. from the Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district to the Conservation Preservation (CP) district (PINs 339-01-02-0004, 0001, -0002, and -0008). 7. Request to rezone approximately 8.0+/- (total) acres of property located on Freeman Dr. and Godfrey Ave from the Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district to the Conservation Preservation District (CP) (PINs 338-04-03-0001, -0002, -0004; 338-05-02- 0017, -0018, -0019, -0021, -0022, -0023, -0024, -0025; 339-01-04-0001, -0002, -0003, -0004; 339-08-01-0001, and -0002). 8. Request to rezone approximately 3.29+/- acres of property located on Long Ave (181, 205, 207, 210, 212, 213, 214, 216, 217 and 218 Long Ave) from the Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district to the Conservation Preservation (CP) district (PINs 339-01-04- 0016; 339-08-01-0009, -0010; 338-05-02-0016, -0015, -0014, -0013, -0012, -0006, and -0004). 9. Request to rezone approximately 83.5+/- (total) acres of property located on/adjacent to Long Ave and Sherwood Dr. from the Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district to the Conservation Preservation (CP) district (PINs: 338-04-03-0003, 338-00-00-0027, -0028, 339-08-01-0006, -0043, -0001, -0002, 339-01-04-0005, -0007, -0008, -0009, -0010, -0011, and -0012). 10. Request to rezone approximately 61.2+/- acres of property located on or adjacent to Sherwood Dr. from the Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district to the Conservation Preservation (CP) district (PINs 338-00-00-0024, -0025; 338-05-02-0010; - 0026, -0027, -0028, -0030, -0033; and 338-05-03-0053). Dennis stated items 5.4.4 through 5.A.10 include approximately 57 parcels that have been purchased by the city following repetitive flooding with the intent to return as much as possible back to the flood plain and its natural state within reason. In accordance with those efforts, the requested zoning to Conservation Preservation will act as an added layer of protection for surrounding community members. The Conservation Preservation District promotes outdoor and indoor recreational uses and is commonly used to protect environmentally sensitive areas as well as flood prone areas from the encroachment of commercial, industrial, or any other uses that could adversely impact the relatively undeveloped nature of the properties. Hucks, then stated, that all of the subject properties are shown on the Future Land Use Map as Conservation Preservation. While many of the subject parcels were already owned by the city, a majority were FEMA buyout lots, meaning the city purchased the lots after Hurricane Florence to prevent them from being developed again. There are two proposed stormwater projects on some of the parcels including the Chestnut Bay Project and the McKeithen Watershed Project for the purpose of storing stormwater, mitigating flooding, and providing a recreational aspect for the community. Staff and the board discussed at length. PC 3/5/2026 Holly Wilczewski and George Debush spoke during public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Ulrich to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. Wise made a motion to approve the rezoning request of items 5.4.4 through 5.A.10 from Low/Density Residential (R-1) to Conservation Preservation (CP). Anderson seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. Ulrich dismissed himself and was not present for the remainder of the meeting. TEXT AMENDMENT(S) 1. Previously Deferred...Amendment(s) to Article 2 ~ Definitions, Article 4 — Use Tables and Article 5 — Specific Use Regulations, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding revisions to Permitted and Conditional uses in various zoning districts. The proposed amendment(s) would establish new or additional standards and restrictions for new and/or existing regulated commercial uses, including, but not limited to, vape/smoke/tobacco shops, alternative financial services (i.e. payday loan/title loan/cash advance services), gas/service stations (with or without a convenience store), outdoor event facilities/spaces, and other high impact uses in the City of Conway. Dennis stated that At a high level, the amendments do three things: e First, update definitions in Article 2 to better reflect how uses actually function and to eliminate ambiguity in classification. e Second, clarify the Use Tables in Article 4, including establishing that only listed uses are permitted and providing a consistent process for classifying similar or unlisted uses. e Third, restructure Article 5 to focus on objective, use-specific standards—such as separation requirements, location-based criteria, and operational limitations—to better address potential impacts, particularly near residential areas. Since the last Planning Commission meeting, staff has made several refinements based on Commission feedback, including: e Standardizing how distance and separation requirements are measured across all applicable uses; e Clarifying that rights-of-way do not negate required separation distances; e Refining definitions to better distinguish between similar use types; e Reorganizing Article 4 for improved clarity and usability; and e Ensuring alignment between Articles 2, 4, and 5, as well as the other Articles proposed to be amended, so that use classifications and standards function consistently. e Ensured that distances are from a residential zoning district OR use, so zoning districts, such as a PD, or a commercial district that contains a residential use is also afforded the same separation requirements from the restricted uses. Existing lawful uses will be considered legal nonconforming and may continue in accordance with Article 12. Overall, these amendments are intended to create a more consistent, predictable, and balanced regulatory framework, one that allows for appropriate commercial development while better protecting adjacent residential areas. PC 3/5/2026 Wise made a motion to open public input. There was none. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Sligh. Sligh made a motion to approve the proposed text amendments, seconded by Wise. The motion carried unanimously. 2. Previously Deferred...Amendment(s) to Article 2 — Definitions, Article 4 — Use Tables, and Article 14 — Boards and Procedures, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding the adoption of a special exception process and uses in which a special exception will be required. Dennis explained the amendment establishes a special exception process. This amendment would provide a new definition of a “Special Exception” in Article 2 of the UDO. Amendments to Article 4 identify which zones require a special exception under specific uses, and in Article 14, amendments establish the review criteria for the Zoning Board of Appeals. Wise made a motion to open public input. There was none. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Bryson. The motion carried unanimously. Wise made a motion to approve the amendments with the inclusion of Sligh’s comments, seconded by Cornell. The motion carried unanimously. 3. Amendment(s) to Article 12 — Nonconformities, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding the re-establishment of certain uses that require special exception approval under the UDO. Dennis explained the amendments to Article 12 focus on claying when a non-conforming use is considered discontinued and under what limited circumstances it may be re-established. It maintains the 180-day discontinuance standard but clarifies that vacancy or lack of activity, rather than simply maintaining a business license, to determine whether a use is still active. The amendment also eliminates use variance-type interpretations by establishing that nonconforming uses cannot be re-established except in very limited hardship situations, and only if strict criteria are met. Finally, it creates a stricter standard for uses subject to separation or location requirements, requiring continuous operation and prohibiting re-establishment once those uses cease. The proposed language will prohibit the restricted uses from re-establishing once the nonconforming use ceases for any period of time, and should the use seek to re-establish, it will only be permitted to do so in compliance with the UDO. Overall, Article 12 has been updated to not only address specific policy concerns, but also to improve clarity, consistency, and usability across the entire section as well as close known loopholes and provide a more consistent and defensible framework. Staff and the Board discussed at length. Wise made a motion to open public input. There was none. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Cornell. VIL. VIII. PC 3/5/2026 Sligh made a motion to recommend the changes in option 4 of the proposed text amendments to items 5.B.3, seconded by Wise. The motion carried unanimously. 4. Amendment(s) to Article 2 — Definitions, Article 6 — Design Standards, Article 7 — Street Design & Circulation, Article 10 — Subdivision and Land Development, and Article 12 —- Nonconformities, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), to establish standards for private roadways in the City limits. The proposed amendment is intended to address existing lots of record that lack adequate frontage on a public street accepted for maintenance by the City, County, or State, and to establish regulations for development proposed on roads not constructed to City standards. Dennis stated the proposed amendments for Articles 2, 6, 7, 10 and 12 of the UDO seeks to establish standards for private roads in the City limits in limited circumstances. The intent is to address a growing issue that staff is seeing as the City continues to annex property and deal with older development patterns. This amendment creates a limited framework to allow access to those lots through private roads or existing substandard roads, while still maintaining safety and infrastructure standards. The key points of the proposed amendments are: e Private roads are only allowed in limited situations, such as lots of record and annexed properties; e They are not permitted for major subdivisions; e The city will not maintain private roads; and e All access must meet minimum safety and fire requirements, and the city can require improvements or deny development if access is inadequate. Dennis noted that the proposed text amendments are not about lowering standards for new development but rather about addressing existing conditions in a safe and practical way. The packet and the PowerPoint include some examples of what staff has been encountering and while the proposed amendments will not address every scenario, it may address situations like in examples 3 and 4; provided all other standards can be met. The amendments provide staff with a structured way to handle situations we’re already seeing, instead of dealing with them on a case-by-case basis. Staff and the Board discussed at length. Wise made a motion to open public input. There was none. Wise made a motion to close public input, seconded by Cornell. Wise made a motion to approve the proposed text amendments to items 5.B.4 as presented, seconded by Sligh. The motion carried unanimously. DISCUSSTION ITEMS A. ADJOURNMENT -- 2 of 162 -- BY SAZIE EAGAN SAZIE.EAGAN@MYHORRYNEWS.COM Grand Strand Health hosted a groundbreak- ing ceremony for a $220 million in-patient hospital located in the southend of Myrtle Beach on Monday, Feb. 9. CEO of Grand Strand Health Mark Sims said the groundbreaking represents the healthcare organization’s commitment to improving access to care in the fast-growing population of the Grand Strand. “By building South Strand Hospital, we’re increasing access to inpatient, surgical and diagnostic services right where growth is hap- pening. This investment means shorter travel times, more timely care, and better access for our community when it matters most,” Sims said in a statement. The South Strand Hospital will be a two-sto- ry facility constructed adjacent to the South Strand Medical Center that is currently oper- ating at the intersection of U.S. 17 Bypass and Sheffield Parkway. The new healthcare facility will be equipped with 59 beds, four operating rooms and full imaging and surgical capabilities, according to the press release. The construction of South Strand Hospital is part of Grand Strand Health’s $350 million multi-year investment into regional expan- sion. In 2025, the healthcare organization broke ground on three freestanding emergen- cy rooms in Murrells Inlet, Conway and Little River, citing fast-growth concentrated in those areas’ residential populations. Improvements to Grand Strand Health’s main campus are also included in the expan- sion plan. Grand Strand Medical Center, locat- ed at 805 82nd Parkway, is getting upgrades to its emergency department, laboratory services and operating room. BY TERRY WARD TERRY.WARD@MYHORRYNEWS.COM If the walls could talk... The former Waccamaw Elementary School on Highway 90 at East Cox Ferry Road, is get- ting a facelift. The 1950s-era school has sat empty for decades, in rural peace and in disre- pair. But volunteers are breathing life back into the stately old brick building. “Windows were broken out, there were holes in the walls and the hardwood floors were covered with adhesive,” said Andrew McDonald. He’s the president of The Center, a faith- based, nonprofit that was established to help those struggling with addiction. To fulfill its role, The Center has the unique zoning classification as a school, church and hospital facility, in recognition of the edu- cation, spiritual, and restorative healing The Center provides. So far the windows have been replaced, the floors are being reclaimed and the walls have been repaired and painted. Skutchi Designs donated $40,000 in furniture for The Center’s classrooms that once housed grammar school students. “We’ve replaced 180 window panes,” said Lisa Hastings, The Center’s operations man- ager. “We’ve sanded decades of wear from the floors, revealing the beauty that had been hid- den for years.” And not only is the building being reclaimed, so are lives. The Center offers a variety of programs, cur- rently in the soft-opening stage. Some of those programs include: crisis intervention; 12-step recovery; GED-training; vocational education; trauma counseling; and Bible study. Many help sessions now are held in The Center’s Rock Bottom Chapel, adjacent to the main school building. When the renovations are fin- ished at the school, programs will move to the classrooms in a “School for Hope.” McDonald said he doesn’t deserve credit for The Center, instead he is working on the plan that God wants him to follow. “We’re here to help broken people and we’ll meet you right where you are. We want you to understand that you are loved and you have a purpose. It’s a healing place for the whole family.” The Center is not a stand-alone project. It is a coordinated network that connects with other resources across Horry County and South Carolina. But the first step to get it off the ground required some fortuitous funding. Melissa Miller is the treasurer for The Center. Her husband, Steven, is now five years sober after battling a nearly 20-year drug addiction. He serves as the nonprofit’s CEO. Melissa explained how the seed money for the project came about. “My husband, Steven, is an over-the-road truck driver,” Miller said. “He bought a tick- et out on the road, waited a couple of days, scratched it off, and it was actually a winner.” Melissa and Steven donated a part of the lottery winnings to help refurbish the old school. Steven said he can’t wait to help those find their way to the experience he has had. “I always tell people the gift of desperation is the greatest blessing I’ve ever received,” Steven said. “Inside of these doors, people will find hope, help, and someone to just put their hand on their shoulder to listen to peo- ple in their darkest times and help them find a way out.” Go to The Center’s website to find out more, or to donate. Your mobile home also qualifies. If you meet the require- ments to qualify your property as a legal residence, you can reduce your tax bill significantly. South Carolina law sets the assessment ratio for real property at 6% of market value. To receive the 4% assessment ratio as a legal residence, you may apply online at https://www.horrycountysc.gov/tax-payer-services/ or to the Assessor’s Office between January 1, 2026 and January 15, 2027. If you have applied in a prior year and received 4% assessment ratio, you do not need to reapply if your legal residence is still the same and there have been no changes in ownership. Any time your legal residence changes or a change is made in ownership an application must be filed with the Assessor to receive the 4% assessment ratio. TO QUALIFY FOR LEGAL RESIDENCE If you are a resident, you must have owned and lived in your home, as your primary residence, prior to application and apply to the Horry County Assessor’s Office on or before January 15, 2027. Only one residence qualifies for the 4% ratio. A mem- ber of the household may not hold the 4% ratio on any other property. A member of the household includes the spouse and dependent children of the owner. The burden of proof for eligibility of the 4% ratio lies with the owner. To prove residency the Assessor may require a copy of the owner’s South Carolina individual income tax return, copies of South Carolina motor vehicle registrations for all motor vehicles owned by the owner or any proof required by the Assessor. AGRICULTURE USE If you owned a tract of real property in Horry County between January 1, 2026 and December 31, 2026 and it is used for Bona Fide Agricultural use “to raise, harvest, or store crops, feed, breed or manage livestock, or to produce plants, trees, fowl, or animals useful to man ...” you may qualify for a “special assessment” that will reduce your taxes. PHOTO PROVIDED Grand Strand Health leaders broke ground on a $220 million healthcare facility, South Strand Hospital, located at 5100 Highway 17 Bypass. -- 3 of 162 -- ISSUE: Workshop discussion regarding the full rewrite of the City’s Comprehensive Plan, including project scope, timeline, growth management framework, and public engagement strategy to guide long-term land use and infrastructure policy. BACKGROUND: Pursuant to SC Code §6-29-510 (E), the Comprehensive Plan must be reviewed at least every five (5) years and fully updated every 10 years. While Conway has updated individual elements of the current 2035 Comprehensive Plan between 2017 and 2023, those updates occurred incrementally and reflect varying data sets, assumption, and planning priorities. The City is now entering the required 10-year update period and must adopt a new Comprehensive Plan by 2029. Given the pace of growth and changing development patterns, staff recommends a coordinated, full rewrite to ensure internal consistency across all elements, updated data integration, and alignment across land use, infrastructure, resiliency, housing, and economic development strategies. Why a full rewrite vs. amendments? Because prior updates were completed at different times using different base data, inconsistencies now exist among population projections, land use assumptions, infrastructure planning, and resiliency strategies. A comprehensive rewrite will: • Establish consistent population and growth projections across all elements • Align land use policies with infrastructure capacity and capital planning • Integrate resiliency, mobility, and housing strategies • Provide updated goals and implementation actions • Ensure compliance with state law requirements Project Organization The Planning Department has two new staff members who will be dedicated to the Comprehensive Plan rewrite. The Transportation Element is proposed to be prepared by a third-party consultant due to its technical complexity. Consultant selection will occur during the early project phase. Planning Commission will appoint a Steering Committee consisting of approximately 12-15 community members representing diverse stakeholder interests (e.g. business owners, residents, board members, institutional representatives). The Steering Committee will serve in an advisory capacity throughout the project, assisting in the development of goals, strategies, and draft materials. Planning Commission will serve as the primary policy review body throughout the rewrite process and will ultimately recommend adoption of the updated Plan to City Council. -- 4 of 162 -- Growth Management Framework Conway has experienced significant population growth since 2000, increasing by approximately 150 percent, with more than 30,000 residents in 2026. This sustained growth underscores the need for a coordinated growth management strategy that balances development demand with infrastructure capacity, fiscal sustainability, and preservation of community character. The updated Comprehensive Plan will evaluate strategies to: • Promote infill and redevelopment within existing service areas • Preserve established residential neighborhoods • Support workforce housing opportunities across income levels • Align new development with infrastructure capacity • Identify priority capital investment areas • Encourage connectivity, walkability, and context-sensitive design The Plan will also assess targeted reinvestment within the Core Commercial (CC), Central Business District (CBD), and Gateway Corridors to reinforce established activity centers and maximize infrastructure investments. Policies may address transition strategies to protect residential neighborhoods while allowing appropriate, compatible redevelopment. The growth management framework will emphasize data-driven analysis to ensure that land use policy decisions are fiscally responsible and infrastructure-supported. Technology and Community Engagement The Comprehensive Plan rewrite will utilize enhanced digital engagement tools to broaden community participation and improve transparency. An interactive ArcGIS StoryMap platform is being developed to: • Provide access to project updates • Share data and mapping tools • Present draft materials • Offer interactive survey opportunities Social media platforms and digital outreach will supplement traditional public meetings, workshops, and stakeholder sessions to expand participation and ensure representation across demographics and geographic areas. -- 5 of 162 -- Anticipated Timeline (preliminary): 2026 – Data Collection and community engagement 2027 – Drafting of core elements and Steering Committee review 2028 – Public review and revisions 2029 – Formal adoption Conclusion The Comprehensive Plan rewrite represents a significant multi-year initiative to establish a coordinated, forward-looking framework for Conway’s continued growth and development. By integrating updated data, consistent policy direction, and broad community engagement, the new Plan will provide clear guidance for future land use decisions, infrastructure investments, and development regulations. Request to rezone approximately 0.43+/- acres of property located at 1322 and 1324 Cottage Lane (PINs 338-10-02-0005 and -0006) upon annexation, from the Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district, or alternatively, the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district. Hucks stated that these properties are located on Cottage Lane and both are currently zoned Horry County Highway Commercial. Hucks explained that this amendment has been discussed at previous Planning Commission meetings, and it has grown since staff began drafting the amendment. Whereas previously, it only included certain uses that warranted additional regulation, the amendment was advertised this time to include other items, such as “Outdoor Event Facilities / Spaces”, which was previously its own amendment. There have also been issues that have arose over the last couple of months that staff felt needed to be addressed in this amendment. The intent of this amendment, which will include Article 2, 4, 5 and 14 of the UDO is to restrict certain uses that have had secondary negative impacts to surrounding properties, or that there may be a proliferation of in certain areas; particularly when these uses are in close proximity to residential uses. Whereas previously, the amendment focused on uses in Highway Commercial and the Industrial districts, the amendment has evolved into a focus on uses, and all the districts in which the use is currently permitted, and where the use is permitted, but with additional standards. Some of these uses will also require special exception approval from the Board of Zoning appeals under certain circumstances. This amendment also provided staff the ability to correct administrative errors, make housekeeping revisions, define terms that are already used throughout the UDO, or that would be necessary as part of the other amendments being proposed. One of the biggest changes proposed is to the Use Tables, which will have different codes than currently. Whereas, conditional uses were identified with a “C”, they will now be uses in which supplemental standards will apply and will be coded with an “S”. Accessory uses will be identified with an “A” rather than Pa. Special Exceptions, where required, will be identified with an SE in the table. Article 5 will be renamed to Supplemental Use and Development Standards, to be in line with the intent of Article 5 and the Use Tables of Article 4. The biggest issue with the “conditional use” language is that it implies that a conditional use permit is given for certain uses, which is not the case. The proposed amended title of Article 5 better reflects what the Article actually does: it establishes additional, site-specific standards that apply to certain uses beyond those of the base zoning district, clarifies what uses can be approved administratively, without additional review, or those that are subject to needing a special exception when additional review is needed. Because there will be uses that will require special exception approval under certain situations, using the term “conditional use” could blur standards and expose decisions to being challenged. Additionally, these changes align with modern UDO best practices that have moved away from the term “conditional use” and in favor of supplemental standards, use-specific criteria, and clearly defined review triggers. So, the biggest changes to Article 5 include the addition of restricting certain uses by adopting supplemental use standards for those uses, which include the requirement for them to receive special exception approval based on proximity to residential uses or residential zoning districts. ISSUE: Request to rezone approximately 5.28 +/- acres of property located at 2578 Hwy 378, from the Highway Commercial (HC) district to the Heavy Industrial (HI) district. APPLICANT(S): Brad Richardson, Richardson Family Holdings, LLC PIN(s): 337-10-03-0010 CURRENT ZONING: Highway Commercial (HC) PROPOSED ZONING: Heavy Industrial (HI) BACKGROUND: The subject property was annexed into the City in 2001 [#ZA2001-06-11(C)] and has been zoned Highway Commercial (HC) since annexation. The applicant applied for a business license to sell and display heavy equipment. While “heavy equipment sales and repair” is not (currently) expressly listed as a use in Article 4 – Use Tables, of the UDO, the operational characteristics of the proposed activity are most consistent with industrial uses involving outdoor storage, equipment staging, and heavy vehicle display. The UDO provides that: • Storage/Shed sales and similar outdoor display uses are permitted only in Light Industrial (LI) and Heavy Industrial (HI) districts; • Manufactured and modular home sales are permitted only in industrial districts; • Wholesaling, Storing and Distributing (heavy) is permitted exclusively in the Heavy Industrial (HI) district. Heavy equipment sales typically involve large machinery, outdoor display areas, equipment loading/unloading, and service or repair activities. These characteristics align more closely with industrial districts than with the intent of the Highway Commercial (HC) district. Section 3.2.14 of the UDO establishes the Heavy Industrial (HI) district as intended to accommodate heavy manufacturing, distribution, and processing activities, including uses with outdoor storage and operational characteristics not suitable for commercial corridors. The City’s UDO is “permissive” in nature. Uses are allowed only where they are expressly listed. If the use is not listed, it must be evaluated for similarity to existing categories. Heavy equipment sales share operational characteristics with industrial uses that are permitted only in industrial districts. Therefore, it is not an appropriate use in the Highway Commercial district simply because it is not specifically named. SURROUNDING USES/ZONING: Adjacent properties are zoning Highway Commercial (HC), including: -- 17 of 162 -- STAFF REPORT 2578 Hwy 378 (rezoning) • Waste Management (sanitation service company) • Property owned by the applicant While zoned HC, the operational characteristics of some of the surrounding uses are more industrial in nature. Additionally, properties located across Hwy 378 are zoned industrial. COMPREHENSIVE PLAN / FUTURE LAND USE MAP: The Future Land Use Map identifies the property as Highway Commercial. Per Section 3.2.10 of the UDO, HC district is intended to: • Serve automobile-oriented commercial activities • Provide corridor compatibility • Reduce traffic congestion • Enhance the aesthetic atmosphere of the City The Highway Commercial (HC) district is not intended to accommodate heavy equipment sales, outdoor industrial storage, or repair operations involving large machinery. Rezoning the property to Heavy Industrial (HI) would: • Introduce an industrial zoning designation into an area identified as HC on the Future Land Use Map; • Potentially expand industrial zoning along the Hwy 378 corridor; • Establish precedent for similar requests along other commercial corridors. STAFF ANALYSIS: Staff has consistently maintained that heavy equipment sales and repair constitute an industrial use based on scale, operational characteristics, and impact profile. Allowing such a use within the Highway Commercial (HC) district undermines the intent of the HC district and creates interpretive ambiguity in the UDO. However, rezoning this property to Heavy Industrial (HI) presents a policy question for Planning Commission and City Council: • Whether the corridor segment is transitioning toward industrial character; or • Whether maintaining Highway Commercial zoning along Hwy 378 remains the City’s long-term policy objective. The request represents a departure from the Future Land Use Map designation and the established intent of the Highway Commercial district. Because the request is inconsistent with the Future Land Use Map and represents a policy shift along the Hwy 378 corridor, staff recommends that Planning Commission carefully evaluate: • Long-term corridor planning objectives; -- 18 of 162 -- STAFF REPORT 2578 Hwy 378 (rezoning) • Potential precedent impacts; • Compatibility with surrounding HC-zoned properties; and • Whether Light Industrial (LI) may be a more appropriate transitional district than Heavy Industrial (HI), if industrial zoning is deemed appropriate. STAFF RECOMMENDATION (and public hearing): In addition to holding the required public hearing, staff recommends that Planning Commission conduct a thorough review of the request and make an informed recommendation to City Council. (843) 488 -9888 ph (84 3) 4 88-98 90 fax 2940 JERRY BARNHILL BLVD - CONWAY, SC 2 9527 PIN #: 383-14-02-0001 REVISED 2019 FLOOD ZONES 0.2 PCT ANNUAL CHANCE FLOOD HAZARD A AE VE PARCELS -- 36 of 162 -- STAFF REPORT Amendments to Articles 2 – Definitions, 4 – Use Tables, & 5 – Specific Use Regulations, of the UDO PLANNING COMMISSION MTG DATE: March 5, 2026 AGENDA ITEM: VIII.B.1 ISSUE: (previously deferred) Amendments to Article 2 – Definitions, Article 4 – Use Tables, and Article 5 – Specific Use Regulations, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to Permitted and Conditional Uses in various zoning districts. The proposed amendments would establish new or additional standards and restrictions for new and/or existing regulated commercial uses, including, but not limited to, vape/smoke/tobacco shops, alternative financial services (payday loan/title loan/cash advance services), gas/service stations (with or without a convenience store), outdoor event facilities/spaces, and other high impact uses in the City of Conway. BACKGROUND: Over the past several months, staff has been researching various options for limiting or restricting certain uses in some of the City’s commercial zoning districts; particularly in the Highway Commercial district. This came as a result of a request to rezone a property, already zoned HC, which sought to rezone to a district that allowed multifamily development and was ultimately denied; however, the concern that the existing Highway Commercial (HC) zoning designation, where located directly adjacent to established single-family residential neighborhoods, permits a range of higher- intensity commercial uses without additional buffering or locational limitations. Staff began looking at the Use Table in Article 4 of the UDO to determine which uses did not currently have specific conditions associated with the use, including those that there have been a proliferation of over the past several years, which may generate land use impacts that are incompatible with adjacent residential neighborhoods, including increased traffic activity, extended hours of operation, lighting, noise, and other operational characteristics. Staff reviewed regulatory approaches utilized by comparable municipalities in South Carolina and other jurisdictions, including separation requirements, conditional use approvals, amortization provisions, and district limitations, to evaluate potential regulatory tools appropriate for Conway. Options discussed with Planning Commission the past couple of months included separation requirements, sunset clause/amortization, adoption of a special exception process, and removing certain uses from the HC district entirely and limiting these uses to the LI and HI districts only, or a combination of the aforementioned options. The proposed amendments represent a multiprong approach intended to balance economic opportunity with neighborhood compatibility. The amendments include separation requirements in certain circumstances, additional use-specific standards, and in some cases, the requirement for -- 37 of 162 -- Special Exception approval when located near residential districts. Existing lawful uses established prior to adoption of these amendments will be considered legal nonconforming uses and may continue subject to the provisions of Article 12 – Nonconformities. Other changes include reclassifying uses that were “Permitted” uses to “Supplemental” uses, or to “Accessory” uses, or removal of certain uses in certain zoning districts entirely. Several housekeeping changes are included in the proposed amendments as well. The proposed amendments are consistent with the Comprehensive Plan’s goals related to neighborhood protection, compatible land use patterns, and corridor redevelopment. The complete proposed amendments are included for your review. NOTE: areas highlighted in gray in Article 5 are revisions from the last draft that was reviewed.
