Definitions Section 2.1 – Interpretation of Certain Words and Phrases 2.1.1 Interpretation • Words used in the present tense include the future tense. • Words or phrases not specifically defined herein shall have their customary meanings as defined in a standard dictionary. • Words used in the singular number include the plural, and words used in the plural include the singular. • The word LOT shall include the words TRACT, PLOT, PARCEL and PROPERTY. • The word SHALL is always mandatory, and the words MAY and SHOULD are permissive. • The words SHOULD and MAY always indicate OPTIONAL. • The words USED or OCCUPIED as applied to any land or building shall be construed to include the words INTENDED, ARRANGED or DESIGNED TO BE USED OR OCCUPIED. • The word BUILDING includes the word STRUCTURE. • The word PERSON includes a FIRM, ASSOCIATION, PARTNERSHIP, TRUST, COMPANY, CORPORATION or any other entity usually defined in legal usage as a person. • The words HE or HIS shall mean the words SHE or HERS. • The word STRUCTURE includes the word BUILDING. • The phrase SET FORTH HEREIN refers to all Articles of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance. • The phrase HISTORIC DESIGN REVIEW DISTRICT(s) shall also be identified as HDRD(s). • The phrase ON PREMISES (or onsite) shall be interpreted to mean ON THE SAME LOT. • The term CITY OF CONWAY UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE shall also be identified as the UDO. • The term PLANNING DIRECTOR shall mean the Planning & Development Director for the City of Conway, South Carolina. • The term COUNCIL or CITY COUNCIL shall mean the Conway City Council. • The term PLANNING COMMISSION or PC shall mean the City of Conway Planning Commission. • The term COMMUNITY APPEARANCE BOARD or CAB shall mean the City of Conway Community Appearance Board. • The term BOARD OF ZONING APPEALS or BZA shall mean the City of Conway Board of Zoning Appeals. • The term TECHNICAL REVIEW COMMITTEE shall also be identified as the TRC. • The word USE includes the terms ARRANGED, DESIGNED and/or INTENDED for use, activity and/or purpose. [Ord. #ZA2025-01-2I] -- 53 of 162 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 2 – Definitions 2-2 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended November 3, 2025 Section 2.2 – Definitions 2.2.1 General Definitions Access Management: The process of providing and managing access to land development while preserving the regional flow of traffic in terms of safety, capacity, and speed. [Ord. #ZA2020-09-02(A)] • External Access - access points provided along the boundaries of a development, to provide connection to the existing paved public roadways abutting the project. • Internal Access - access points provided to paved public roadways within a project. Accessory Dwelling Unit (ADU): A housing unit not exceeding one thousand (1,000) square feet, with cooking facilities, sanitary facilities, and an independent means of access, either attached to a single-family detached dwelling or located on the same lot as a single-family detached dwelling. Accessory Structure: A subordinate structure, the use of which is incidental to and customary in connection with the principal structure or use, and which is located on the same lot with such principal structure or use. Accessory Use: A subordinate use which is incidental to and customary in connection with the principal structure or use and which is located on the same lot with such principal structure or use. Active Open Space: see Section 10.3.9 A.D.T. (Average Daily Trip): The average number of vehicles per day that pass over a given point. Alternative Financial Service: An establishment whose primary business is the provision of short-term, high-cost consumer financial products or services, including but not limited to payday loans, title loans, check-cashing services, installment lending, deferred-presentment transactions, or similar consumer credit products. For purposes of this definition, an establishment shall be considered an Alternative Financial Service establishment when more than fifty (50%) of its gross revenue or business activity is derived from such products or services. The sale of ancillary financial products, such as money orders, prepaid cards, or wire transfers shall not, by itself, exempt an establishment from this definition where consumer lending is the primary activity. This term shall not include state or federally chartered banks, savings institutions, or credit unions. Amenity Center: A clubhouse or similar structure owned by a homeowners’ association, property owner’s association or development/property management company for use by residents of a specific apartment, condominium, or townhome complex or a specific subdivision including recreational facilities, social rooms and other non-commercial activities. The structure shall fit with the residential character of the surrounding development. Amplified Sound: Any sound that is increased in volume or power by electrical, electronic, or mechanical means, including but not limited to loudspeakers, public address systems, amplifiers, musical instrument amplifiers, sound systems, or similar devices, and which shall comply with all applicable provisions of the City’s Noise Ordinance. Amplified sound does not include low-volume background music played entirely indoors and not intended to be audible beyond the premises. Armory: A building/structure where firearms and ammunition are stored, maintained and/or repaired by and for the express use of law enforcement and/or the US Armed Forces. [Ord. #ZA2023-07-17(B)] Artisan: A person skilled in an applied art or artistic discipline (also known as Artist, Craftsman). Artists’ Studio & Gallery: An establishment for the preparation, display, and/or sale of individually crafted artwork, jewelry, furniture, sculpture, pottery, leathercraft, hand-woven articles, watercraft, baked or prepared food and -- 54 of 162 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 2 – Definitions 2-3 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended November 3, 2025 drink, and similar items by one or more artisans (also known as Artisan Workshop) Assembly: The use of a building or structure, or a portion thereof, for the gathering of persons for purposes such as civic, social, or religious functions. Bail Bond Establishment: A building in which a “Professional Bondsman” (any person who is approved and licensed under the provisions of the South Carolina Code of Laws; Statute 38-53-10) makes a business of furnishing bail in criminal cases or who furnishes bail in five or more criminal cases in any one year, whether for compensation or otherwise. Banquet Hall: An establishment used regularly for serving food and beverages to groups that, before the day of the event, have reserved the facility. Food shall be brought in from off-site. Live entertainment may be featured as accessory to the meeting or banquet. See also “Indoor Event Facility”. Bars & Taverns: Bars and taverns are defined as an establishment primarily engaged in the sales and service of alcoholic beverages for on-premises consumption. The incidental sale or provision of food on the premises does not entitle the establishment to be considered a restaurant under the provisions of this code, unless 60% or greater of total revenue is generated from the sale of food. Synonymous with bars and taverns are other establishments, such as pubs, saloons, barrooms, tap rooms, and watering holes – all of which shall be considered a bar or tavern for the purposes of this code of ordinances. This does not include nightclubs or adult entertainment establishments, which are elsewhere defined herein. Beauty Salon / Barber Shop: an establishment that provides cosmetic treatments for people (haircuts / treatments / styling, manicures, pedicures, waxing, etc.) Bed and Breakfast Home: A private residence which provides lodging and meals for guests, in which the host or hostess resides at the same time and which, while it may advertise and accept reservations, does not hold itself out to the public to be a restaurant, hotel, or motel, and serves food only to overnight guests. Berm: A mound of soil, either natural or man-made, intended to buffer land uses or limit access (Section 9.3.1). Big Box Retail Establishment: a single-tenant retail establishment occupying a freestanding building with a gross floor area of 50,000 square feet or greater, measured in accordance with the definition of “Gross Floor Area” in this ordinance, and primarily engaged in the sale of merchandise directly to the general public. For the purposes of this definition, a freestanding building is a principal structure not physically integrated into a multi-tenant shopping center development through shared walls or unified site design approved as a shopping center under this Ordinance. This term shall not include retail establishments located within or developed as part of an approved Shopping Center, as defined in this ordinance. Body Piercing: The creation of an opening in the body of a human being so as to create a permanent hole for the purpose of inserting jewelry or other decoration. This includes, but is not limited to, piercing of an ear, lip, tongue, nose, or eyebrow, but does not include piercing an ear lobe with a disposable, single-use stud or solid needle that is applied using a mechanical device to force the needle or stud through the ear lobe. Book Exchange Box: An outdoor accessory structure maintained by a property owner on private property where books and recorded performing arts and media are kept for public and/or exchanges with no fees or sales and are publicly accessible. Boxes are limited to a maximum height of 6.5 feet of the highest vertical distance measured from the finished grade at ground level to the highest point on the structure, and a maximum width and depth of three feet. [Ord. #ZA2018-01-02(C)] -- 55 of 162 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 2 – Definitions 2-4 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended November 3, 2025 Borrow Pit: A pit in close proximity to and worked solely in conjunction with a large-scale construction project. The working provides the development with bulk filling minerals and is restored with any surplus soils that may arise. Buffer: Open spaces, landscape areas, fences, walls, berms, or any combination thereof used to physically separate or screen one use or property from another so as to visually shield or block noise, lights, or other nuisances. Buildable Area: The area of a lot remaining after the minimum yard and open space requirements of the UDO have been met. Building: Any structure having a roof supported by columns or walls and intended for the shelter, housing, or enclosure of any individual, animal, process, equipment, goods, or materials or any kind. Building Height: The highest vertical distance measured from the finished grade at ground level at the building line to the average height of the roof. Building, Principal: The building in which the main or principal use of the lot on which said building is located is conducted. Building Frontage: The linear length of a building facing the street right-of-way. Build-to line: An alignment that dictates the front yard setback from a street or public right-of-way, to be followed by buildings fronting thereon. The build-to line does not apply to building projections or recesses. Build-to Zone: The Build-to Zone includes the area of a front yard from the Build-to Line to any allowed variance from that line indicated in the applicable code sections. Café, Coffee Shop: A small establishment in which beverages, light meals, and snacks are served. If the building where this establishment is located is greater than one thousand (1,000) square feet, it shall be considered a restaurant. Caliper: The measurement of the size in inches of a tree’s trunk diameter at one (1) foot above the ground elevation six (6) inches above the soil line, or across the stump, in the event the tree has been severed at less than 12 inches above the soil line. Centralized Mail Delivery Systems: • Cluster Mail Box Unit (aka Cluster Box Unit (CBU)): A centralized form of mail delivery containing between 8 and 16 individually locked mailboxes and parcel compartments intended to serve residential dwellings within a development for the purpose of mail delivery by the United States Postal Service (USPS). • Centralized Mail Delivery Kiosks: A group of cluster mailbox units serving more than 16 residential dwellings from one central location within a development. Centralized mail delivery kiosks may contain multiple cluster- type mailbox units (Cluster Box Unit (CBU); freestanding or pedestal mounted, or other clustered mailbox units mounted on a wall or shelter, approved by the USPS. [Ord. #ZA2020-09-02 (B)] Commercial Short-Term Rental (CSTR): A conditional use whereby a structure is converted and/or created into a fully functioning, private accommodations use, which may include cooking, living, sanitary and sleeping facility within one dwelling unit, to be rented to one (1) family for a period of not more than ninety (90) consecutive days. -- 56 of 162 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 2 – Definitions 2-5 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended November 3, 2025 Hotels, motels, Inns, bed and breakfast establishments, and other land uses explicitly defined and regulated in the UDO separately from Commercial Short-Term Rentals (CSTR’s) are not considered Commercial Short-Term Rentals. [Ord. #ZA2021-06-21(B)] Community Residential Care Facility (CRCF): A facility which offers room and board and which, unlike a boarding house, provides/coordinates a degree of personal care for a period of time in excess of twenty-four (24) consecutive hours for two (2) or more persons, eighteen (18) years old or older, not related to the licensee within the third degree of consanguinity. It is designed to accommodate residents' changing needs and preferences, maximize residents' dignity, autonomy, privacy, independence, and safety, and encourage family and community involvement. Included in this definition is any facility (other than a hospital), which offers or represents to the public that it offers a beneficial or protected environment specifically for individuals who have mental illness or disabilities. These facilities may be referred to as "assisted living" provided they meet the above definition of community residential care facility. • Assisted Living Facility: Residences for the frail and elderly that provide rooms, meals, personal care, and supervision of self-administered medication. Such facilities may also provide other services, such as recreational activities, financial services, and transportation. • Congregate Housing: A multi-unit rental housing complex with self-contained apartments designed to provide a supportive environment for the elderly and accommodate a relatively independent lifestyle. Such facilities generally provide support services, such as meals, laundry, housekeeping, transportation, and social and recreational activities. • Continuing Care Retirement Community: A community in which there is furnished, pursuant to a continuing care contract, to two (2) or more persons not related to the administrator or owner of the facility within the third degree of consanguinity, board or lodging together with nursing, medical, or other health-related services, regardless of whether the services or lodging are provided at the same location or not. It does not include an institution operating solely as a nursing home or community residential care facility licensed by the Department. • Group Home: A licensed facility offering room and board, and which, unlike a boarding house, provides / coordinates a degree of personal care for a period of time in excess of twenty-four (24) consecutive hours for two (2) or more persons, eighteen (18) years old or older, not related to the licensee within three degrees of relation. Included in this definition is any facility (other than a hospital) which offers or represents to the public that if offers a beneficial or protected environment specifically for individuals who have mental illness or disabilities. • Nursing Home: A facility with an organized nursing staff to maintain and operate organized facilities and services to accommodate two (2) or more unrelated persons over a period exceeding twenty-four (24) hours, which is operated either in connection with a hospital or as a freestanding facility for the express or implied purpose of providing intermediate or skilled nursing care for persons who are not in need of hospital care. Community Support Services • Community Support Facilities: An agency which provides a variety of support services to adult individuals, including those with disabilities, whose primary goal is to help individuals increase or maintain their independence and quality of life through interaction and participation in the community, as well as teaching concepts such as self-determination, self-advocacy and socialization and training to enhance skills they already possess or want to learn. Other services may include providing assistance with linking to or accessing community resources. Such services do not include day care facilities. • Outpatient Treatment Facilities: A facility licensed through the South Carolina Department of Health and Environmental Control (SCDHEC) that provides outpatient treatment for alcoholism and drug addiction, with licensed medical staff to provide diagnosis and treatment on an outpatient basis only. Such facilities may -- 57 of 162 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 2 – Definitions 2-6 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended November 3, 2025 participate in a Narcotic Treatment Program (NTP), which uses methadone or other narcotic treatment medications, as defined by SCHEC, on an outpatient basis. [Ord. #ZA2013-08-05(A)] -- 71 of 162 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 2 – Definitions 2-20 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended November 3, 2025 2.2.2 Sign-related Definitions *Refer to Article 11 for Signage Regulations. Animation: The movement, or the optical illusion of movement of any part of the sign structure, design or pictorial including the movement of any illumination or the flashing, scintillating or varying of light intensity. The automatic changing of all or any part of the facing of a sign or any part of a sign shall be considered to be animation. Also, included in this definition are signs having “chasing action” which is the action of a row of lights commonly used to create the appearance of motion. Time and temperature units and electronic message centers are not included in this definition. Foot Candle: a unit of illumination equal to that given by a source of one (1) candela at a distance of one foot (equivalent to one (1) lumen per square foot or 10.764 lux). Illumination: lighting; the act / condition of being illuminated (Merriam Webster definition). Lumen: A unit for measuring the amount of light something produces (Cambridge dictionary definition). Lux: A unit of illumination equal to the direct illumination on a surface that is everywhere one meter from a uniform point source of one candle intensity or equal to one lumen per square meter (Merriam Webster definition). Sign: Any device designed to attract the attention of the public for commercial or advertising purposes that is attached, painted or otherwise affixed to, or a part of a building, structure, material, surface, vehicle, or object. Integral decorative or architectural features of buildings except letters or trademarks, fences, walls and works of art, which are noncommercial in nature, are not to be construed as being a sign. Sign shall include any artificial light source, time or temperature units, clocks and any device that animates or projects a visual representation that attracts the attention of the public for commercial purpose. Sign Area (also referred to as the gross surface area): The square foot area individual symbols, letters, figures, illustrations, messages, forms, or panels, sign area shall be considered to include all lettering, wording, and accompanying designs and symbols, together with the background on which they are displayed, any frame around the sign and any “cutouts” or extensions but shall not include any supporting structure or bracing. The aggregate sign area is the summation of the area of all sign faces combined. Sign Copy: The portion of a sign which contains the name, logo, advertising message, or business identification and consists of all such symbols, letters, figures, insignia, illustrations, messages or forms. Sign copy does not include the border, molding or decorative framing. Sign Face: The part of the sign that is or can be used to identify, advertise, communicate information or for visual representation which attracts the attention of the public for any purpose. Sign face includes any background material, panel, trim, color, and direct or self-illumination used that differentiates that sign from the building, structure, backdrop surface or object upon which or against which it is placed. The sign structure shall not be included as a portion of the sign face provided that no identifying/advertising message, symbol or any of the aforementioned sign face criteria are displayed on or designed as part of the sign structure, whether structurally necessary or not. In the case of signs designed with integral sign face and sign structure, the blank (support) area equivalent to a maximum of 50% of the allowable sign area shall be exempt from computations of sign area. Sign Height: The vertical distance measured from the average lowest adjacent street crown finished grade at the base of the sign to the highest point top of the sign face or supporting sign structure, whichever is greater. Where a sign is located on a berm or artificial raised grade, height shall be measured from the average surrounding natural grade. Sign Panel: The primary surface of a sign that carries the identifying/advertising message. -- 72 of 162 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 2 – Definitions 2-21 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended November 3, 2025 Sign Structure: A supporting structure erected or intended for the purpose of identification or advertising with or without a sign thereon, situated upon or attached to the premises upon which any sign may be fastened, affixed, displayed or applied, provided however, said definition shall not include a building or fence. If the total width of the sign structure exceeds fifty (50) percent of the total width of the sign face, the sign structure area shall be included as part of the sign area. (Section 11.4.8) Awning Sign: Signage or text located on the front face of an awning projection. Billboard (Traditional): A traditional sign identifying/advertising and/or directing the public to a business or merchandise or service or institution or residential area or entertainment which is located, sold, rented, leased, produced, manufactured and/or furnished at a place other than the real property on which said sign is located. Traditional Billboards do not display messages by electronic means but instead utilizes materials such as paint, vinyl and/or paper substrates. The advertisement does not rotate but is stationary. Canopy (sign): Any sign that is a part of or attached to a canopy. Changeable Copy: An element of a sign in which a message is changed manually in the field, through the utilization of attachable letters, numbers, symbols, and other similar characters of changeable pictorial panels. Directional Sign: A sign permanently erected or permitted in the public right-of-way or private property by the state of South Carolina, or other governmental agency to denote the name of any thoroughfare, the route to any city, town, village, educational institution, public building, historic place, shrine, or hospital, to direct and regulate traffic, to denote any railroad crossing, bridge, or other transportation or transmission company for the direction or safety of the public. Typical uses include canning of fruits and vegetables, processing of dairy products, and the production of prepared meats (from purchased, previously slaughtered animals). Agricultural Research: Agricultural research use type refers to establishments for experimental greenhouse and field growing of agricultural commodities, landscaping and seeds, including experimental use of herbicides, pesticides and other agricultural practices. High Technology (Hi-Tech) Industry: Research, development and controlled production of high-technology electronic, industrial or scientific products. Light Industrial: Production processes which use already manufactured components to assemble, print or package a product such as cloth, paper, plastic, leather, wood, glass or stones, but not including such operations as paper, saw or mills, steel, iron or other metalwork’s, rolling mills, or any manufacturing uses involving primary production of commodities from raw materials. These standards are intended to address subject use-specific characteristics and a determination by the Planning Director that such use(s) conform(s) to all potential site impacts that are not full addressed by base district regulations. Uses subject to this Article shall comply with all applicable regulations standards set forth herein in addition to the regulations of for that specific use and the zoning district in which such the use is proposed to be located. Applications to construct or alter conditional uses shall be processed in accordance with the standards set forth herein for permitted uses. Uses subject to Supplemental Use Standards are identified Applicable conditional uses shall be shown in Article 4, Use Tables. Where expressly stated, certain uses or site In addition to the conditions may require administrative review or special exception approval by the Board of Zoning Appeals in order to evaluate and mitigate site-specific impacts set forth in this Article, the Planning Director and/or the Technical Review Committee (TRC) may require additional provisions reasonable as deemed necessary to protect the health, safety, and welfare of the general public. Such review shall be limited to the criteria identified in the applicable section(s) of this Article. 5.1.1 Adult Entertainment Establishments Adult entertainment establishments include, but are not limited to: cabarets, bookstores, drive-in theaters, theaters, peep shows, adult model studios, sexual encounter centers, escort services and motels, as defined herein, and any other establishment which contains activities characterized by the performance, depiction or description of “specified sexual activities”, or “specified anatomical areas”. Adult entertainment establishments shall be permitted as conditional uses in the Light Industrial (LI) and Heavy Industrial (HI) districts provided the following requirements standards are met: A. Number. No more than one (1) adult use as classified above shall be located on any lot. B. Location. Adult entertainment establishments shall not be located closer than: 1. 1,000 feet from residential zoning districts or residential use in the City of Conway (R, RA, RR, R-1, R-2, R- 3, R-4, or residential within a MU or PD Zoning District) or equivalent residential zoning districts or use in Horry County. [ZA2018-12-17(A)] 2. 1,000 feet from any religious institution, day care facilities, public or private education facility, Community Support Services / Facility, Outpatient Treatment Facility, public park, public library, cemetery, or any motion picture establishment which shows G or PG rated movies to the general public on a regular basis. [ZA2019-04-01(D)] 3. 2,000 feet from any other adult use, provided that this shall not apply to any establishment or cabaret that does not provide adult entertainment more than twelve (12 times per calendar year). 4. Measurements of distance separation shall be in a straight line from the closest points of the buildings in which the adult uses are located. C. Ownership Disclosure. If a person who applies to operate an adult entertainment business is an individual, he must sign the application for a permit as applicant. If a person who applies to operate an adult entertainment business is other than an individual, each individual who has a ten (10%) percent or greater interest in the business must sign the application for a permit and/or license as applicant. If a corporation is listed as owner of an adult business, or as entity which wishes to operate such business, each individual having a ten (10%) percent or greater interest in the corporation must sign the application for a permit and/or license as applicant. All corporate officers shall also sign the application. The fact that a person possesses other types of state or county permits and/or licenses does not exempt him from the requirements of obtaining a sexually oriented business permit and/or license. D. Sale and/or Consumption of Alcohol Prohibited. The sale and/or consumption of alcoholic beverages in -- 90 of 162 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 5 –Specific Supplemental and Accessory Use Regulations Standards 5-4 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended XX conjunction with any adult entertainment establishment shall be prohibited. E. An adult entertainment establishment shall neither employ nor permit the admittance / patronage of any person who is under 18 years of age. F. Inspections. The management of any adult entertainment establishment shall permit representatives of the Police, Fire, Construction Services, Planning/Development Department or other City or State Agencies to inspect the premises at any time it is open for business. G. Revocation of Zoning Compliance. The Planning Director shall revoke a Certificate of Zoning Compliance, thereby suspending the operation of any adult entertainment establishment, for any of the following: 1. The giving of false or misleading information by the applicant at any time in the application process; 2. For the illegal sale of any controlled substance on the premises; 3. For the arrest and conviction of any owner or employee (unless said employee is discharged immediately) for any violation of Title 44 of the Code of Laws of South Carolina, 1976 as amended, relating to controlled substances; and/or violation of any State or Federal crime involving moral turpitude and/or violation of Title XVI, Chapters 3, 15, 23, and 25 of the Code of Laws of South Carolina, 1976, as amended; and/or for the arrest and conviction of any owner or employee for any violation of Title 16 of the Code of Laws of South Carolina, 1976, as amended; 4. Failure to permit inspections by authorized City and State agencies or personnel; 5. Violation of the age restrictions as set forth herein. H. Exterior Portions of Regulated Establishments. 1. BACKGROUND (updated): This amendment is a companion amendment to a related amendment under consideration addressing specific uses within certain zoning districts (Articles 2, 4 and 5). As part of that discussion, the adoption of a Special Exception process for selected uses was evaluated. A Special Exception is a permitted use within a zoning district that requires case-by-case review due to the potential for site-specific impacts, such as traffic generation, operational intensity, noise, or other compatibility considerations. The purpose of the special exception process is to evaluate such impacts in accordance with established ordinance standards and ensure compatibility with surrounding properties. A special exception: • Is a permitted use within the zoning district; • Is not a variance from dimensional or development standards; • Does not authorize a prohibited use; • Requires a finding that the proposed use complies with applicable ordinance standards and will not create demonstrable adverse impacts; and • May be approved with reasonable conditions directly related to identified impacts and necessary to ensure compliance with the UDO. If adopted, the special exception process would require an applicant, where specified in the Use Table, to obtain approval from the Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA) following a duly noticed public hearing conducted in accordance with Article 14. During evaluation of potential uses, the following were considered bed & breakfast establishments, outpatient treatment facilities, payday/title loan establishments, adult entertainment establishments, body piercing/tattoo parlors, vape/smoke/tobacco shops, taverns/bars/nightclubs, and gas/service stations. After review, certain uses – including adult entertainment establishments, taverns/bars/nightclubs, tattoo and body piercing establishments, bed & breakfast establishments, and outpatient treatment facilities – were not identified as requiring special exception approval. These uses are currently subject to established locational criteria, operational standards, and/or separation requirements -- 155 of 162 -- STAFF REPORT Amendment(s) to Articles 2 – Definitions, 4 – Use Tables, & 14 – Boards & Procedures within the UDO. Add “or special exception” to sentence -- 156 of 162 -- Section 14.2 – Board of Zoning Appeals 14.2.1 Duties and Powers Duties and powers of the Board of Zoning Appeals are derived from Section 6-29-800 of the South Carolina Code of Laws. A. To hear and decide appeals where it is alleged the City Zoning Administrator or their designee, erred in an order, requirement, decision, or determination. In such cases, the Board may reverse or affirm, wholly or in part, the City Zoning Administrator or their designee’s action. The Board shall have all the powers of the City Zoning Administrator or their designee in such cases and may direct the issuance of a permit. B. To hear and decide appeals for variances in specific cases when a strict application of the zoning ordinance would cause an unnecessary hardship, and approval of such variance would not be contrary to public interest or undermine the spirit of the zoning ordinance. The fact that property may be used more profitably if a variance is granted is not grounds for a variance. The Board may attach conditions to a variance that address location, character, or other features of a proposed building, structure, or use, in order to protect the established property values in the surrounding area or to promote the public health, safety, or general welfare of the community. The Board may grant a variance for an unnecessary hardship if it makes and explains in writing all of the following findings. 1. Extraordinary conditions: There are extraordinary and exceptional conditions pertaining to the particular piece of property. 2. Other Property: The extraordinary and exceptional conditions do not generally apply to other property in the vicinity. 3. Utilization: Because of the extraordinary or exceptional conditions, the application of the ordinance to a particular piece of property would effectively prohibit or unreasonably restrict the utilization of the property. 4. Detriment: The authorization of a variance will not be of substantial detriment to adjacent property or the public good, and the character of the district will not be harmed by granting a variance. C. An affirmative vote of two-thirds (2/3) of the Board members present and voting shall be required before a variance may be granted for a use of land, a building or a structure that is prohibited in a given district, provided however that City Council may overrule the decision of the Board within thirty (30) days following the decision of the Board. In order to grant a use variance, the following finding must be determined and made part of the record: the use requested can be documented to have been a past use of the property; however, historic use alone may not be sufficient to grant a use variance. The fact that property may be utilized more profitably, should a variance be granted, may not be considered grounds for any variance. D. Special Exceptions 1. Authority and Purpose The Board of Zoning Appeals shall hear and decide Special Exception requests only where such approval is expressly required by this UDO. Special exceptions are permitted uses that, due to their size, location, design, or potential impacts, require additional review to ensure compliance with applicable standards and compatibility with surrounding uses. In evaluating a request for a special exception, the Board shall consider the following criteria: a. The special exception complies with all applicable standards in Article 5 of this ordinance. b. The proposed use is compatible with surrounding land uses and consistent with the intent of the zoning district. c. Adequate provision is made for setbacks, buffering, screening, and similar design elements as required by this UDO. -- 157 of 162 -- d. The proposed use will not create demonstrable adverse impacts, including excessive noise, odor, dust, vibration, glare, overcrowding, or traffic, beyond those normally associated with permitted uses in the zoning district. e. The use will not hinder or endanger vehicular or pedestrian movements on adjacent streets. 2. Conditions of Approval In granting a special exception, the Board may impose reasonable conditions of approval directly related to identified impacts and necessary to ensure compliance with this UDO. 3. Time Limits The Board may include, as a condition of approval, a time limit within which the action for which the special exception approval is required shall begin or be completed, or both. Failure to comply with the time limit imposed shall void the special exception approval. The Board’s review shall be limited to the criteria set forth herein and any additional use-specific factors identified in Article 5. 14.2.2 Procedure for Appeals, and Variances and Special Exceptions A. Application: Any person aggrieved by an administrative action or decision or seeking relief from a requirement in the Zoning Ordinance, shall make a formal request on an application supplied by the City Zoning Administrator or their designee. Such application shall be completed in full and returned to the office of the City Planning & Development Department or emailed to Planning@ConwaySC.gov. B. Stay of proceedings: An appeal shall stay all legal proceedings in furtherance of the action appealed from, unless the officer from whom the appeal is taken certifies to the Board, after the notice of appeal is filed that by reason of facts stated in the certificate, a stay would, in the opinion of the officer, cause imminent peril to life or property. In that case, proceedings shall not be stayed except by a restraining order which may be granted by the Board of Zoning Appeals or by a court of record on application, on notice to the officer from whom the appeal is taken and on due cause shown. C. Notice of hearing: Notice of regularly scheduled meetings of the Board of Zoning Appeals shall be published in a general circulation newspaper fifteen (15) days prior to the date of the meeting. D. Posting of lot: In cases involving variance requests, a notice of a variance request, special exception request or appeal shall be posted on or adjacent to the affected property in a conspicuous place fifteen (15) days prior to the date of the scheduled meeting. One such notice shall be visible from each public right-of-way that abuts the property. E. Decisions of the Board: All final decisions and orders of the Board of Zoning Appeals shall be in writing and be permanently filed in the office of the Board as a public record. All findings of fact and conclusions of law must be separately stated in final decisions or orders of the Board of Zoning Appeals, which must be addressed to parties or interest by certified mail. 14.2.3 Appeal of Board of Zoning Appeals Decision to Court Appeal of the Board of Zoning Appeals is derived from Section 6-29-820 of the South Carolina Code of Laws. A. Any person or persons jointly or severally aggrieved by a final decision of the Board of Zoning Appeals may present to a court of record a petition duly verified setting forth that the decision of the Board of Zoning Appeals is illegal, in whole or in part, specifying the grounds of the illegality. Such petition shall be presented to the court within thirty (30) days after the filing of such decision of the Board. -- 158 of 162 -- B. Upon the filing of the appeal, the clerk of court shall give immediate notice of such appeal to the City Zoning Administrator, and within thirty (30) days from the time of the notice, the City Zoning Administrator shall file with the clerk a certified copy of the proceedings held before the Board of Zoning Appeals, including transcript of the evidence heard before it, if any, and the decision to the Board including its findings of fact and conclusions. C. The filing of an appeal from a decision of the Board of Zoning Appeals shall not ipso facto act as a supersedes, but the judge of the court may, in his at their discretion, grant a supersedes upon such terms and conditions as may seem reasonable and proper. 14.2.4 Organization The rules of procedure are adopted pursuant to S.C. Code § 6-29-790 for the City of Conway Board of Zoning Appeals which consists of members appointed by the City Council. A. Officers. The officers of the Board shall be a chairman and vice-chairman elected for one (1) year terms at the first meeting of the Board in each calendar year. Such officers shall be eligible to succeed themselves. Vacancies in office shall be filled immediately for unexpired terms by regular election procedures. The Board shall appoint a member of the staff of the City of Conway as secretary of the Board B. Chairman. 1. The chairman shall be a voting member of the Board and shall: 2. Call meetings of the Board; 3. Preside at meetings and hearings; and swear in witnesses; 4. Act as spokesperson for the Board; 5. Sign documents for the Board; 6. Have orders of the Board served on parties; and 7. Perform other duties approved by the Board. C. Vice-Chairman. The vice-chairman shall exercise the duties of the chairman in the absence, disability, or disqualification of the chairman. In the absence of the chairman and vice-chairman, an acting chairman shall be elected by the members present. D. Planning Staff. The secretary shall: 1. Provide and publish notice of appeals and meetings; 2. Prepare the meeting agenda; 3. Assist the chairman in preparation of agenda’ 4. See that property involved in appeals for variances is properly posted; 5. Keep recordings and minutes of meetings and hearings; 6. Maintain Board records as public records; 7. Serve Board decisions on parties; 8. Attend to Board correspondence; and 9. Perform other duties as needed. 14.2.5 Meetings A. Time and Place. An annual schedule of regular meetings shall be adopted, published and posted in the City of Conway Planning & Development Department in December of each year. Special meetings may be called by the -- 159 of 162 -- chairman upon 24 hours’ notice, posted and delivered to all members and local news media. Meetings shall be held at the place stated in the notices and shall be open to the public. B. Agenda. A written agenda shall be furnished by City Staff to each member of the Board and the news media and shall be posted at least five (5) days prior to each regular meeting, and at least twenty-four (24) hours prior to a special meeting. Items may be removed from the agenda or postponed at a meeting by a majority vote. C. Quorum. A majority of the members of the Board shall constitute a quorum. A quorum shall be present before any business is conducted other than rescheduling the meeting. A recusal by a member does not affect the quorum, which is determined by the membership present. D. Rule of Order. Robert’s Rules of Order, Revised, shall govern the conduct of meetings except as otherwise provided by these Rules of Procedure. 14.2.6 Appeals Procedure A. Form of Appeal. Appeals from administrative decisions and applications for variances or special exceptions shall be filed on forms approved by the Board and provided to applicants by City Staff. B. Time for Appeal. An appeal from an administrative decision must be filed within fifteen (15) days after actual notice of the decision by delivery of the approved appeal form to the Planning & Development Staff of the Board who shall notify the official appealed from. C. Calendar. Appeals and applications shall be marked with the date of receipt and placed on the hearing calendar in the order in which received. Appeals shall be heard in the order on the calendar unless otherwise set by the Board for good cause shown. D. Withdrawal of Appeal. Any appeal or application may be withdrawn by written notice delivered to the Zoning Administrator or their designee prior to action by the Board. An appeal from an administrative decision which is withdrawn may not be re-filed after the fifteen (15) day time for appeal has expired. Withdrawn applications for variances may be refilled after six (6) months and shall be placed on the calendar according to the date re-filed. E. Continuances. The hearing of an appeal or application may be continued one time by the Board for good cause shown. F. Notice. Public notice of hearing of the Board shall be published in a local newspaper and posted on or adjacent to the property affected at least fifteen (15) days prior to the hearing. The notice shall contain a description of each matter to be heard and identify the applicant and property affected. -- 160 of 162 -- 14.2.7 Hearing Procedure A. Appearances. The applicant or any party in interest may appear in person or by agent or attorney. The Board may postpone or proceed to dispose of a matter on the records before it in the absence of an appearance on behalf of an applicant. B. Witnesses. Parties in interest may present testimony under oath. Witnesses may be compelled to attend by subpoena requested at least ten (10) days prior to a hearing and signed by the chairman. The Board may call its own witness when deemed appropriate. C. Cross Examination. No party shall have the right to cross-examine witnesses; however, the opportunity to examine opposing witnesses may be freely extended when conducted in an orderly manner. Intimidation of witnesses will not be allowed. D. Evidence. Relevant documents, photographs, maps, plans, and drawings will be received in the record without authentication in the form of legible copies. Relevant testimony which is not cumulative, or hearsay will be received. The chairman will rule on all evidentiary matters. Evidence may be placed in the record with or without an objection noted. 14.2.8 Conduct of Hearing A. Conduct of Hearing. The normal order of hearing, subject to modification by the chairman, shall be: 1. Statement of matter to be heard (chairman or secretary); 2. Presentation by the City Zoning Administrator; 3. Presentation by applicant; 4. Presentation by official appealed; or 5. Presentation by opponents; 6. Rebuttal by applicant; 7. Unsworn public comment when appropriate; 8. The Board may question participants at any point during the hearing; 9. Matter in which additional time is granted may be moved to the end of the agenda. B. Disposition. The Board may deliberate and make a final disposition of a matter by a majority vote of the members present at the hearing and qualified to vote; provided that not less than a quorum is qualified to vote. The vote may be taken at the same or a subsequent meeting. A member may not vote on a matter which the member has not heard. Deliberations and voting shall be conducted in public. C. Form of Order. An order shall be issued disposing of a matter by granting or denying relief with such conditions may be deemed necessary; or affirming, modifying, or reversing an administrative decision. A matter may be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction or prosecution. Findings of fact and conclusions of law shall be separately stated in an order. D. Service of Order. City Staff shall deliver a copy of an order to each party in interest by certified mail immediately upon execution of the order by the chairman. -- 161 of 162 -- E. Rehearing. The Board may grant a rehearing of an application which has been dismissed or denied upon written request filed with the Zoning Administrator or their designee within fifteen (15) days after delivery of the order accompanied by new evidence which could not reasonably have been presented at the hearing, or evidence of a clerical error or mutual mistake of fact affecting the outcome. 14.2.9 Records A. Minutes. The City Staff shall record all meetings and hearings of the Board which shall be preserved until final action is taken on all matters presented. The City Staff shall prepare minutes of each meeting for approval by the Board at the next regular meeting. Minutes shall be maintained as public records. B. Orders and Documents. The City Staff shall assist in the preparation and service of all orders of the Board in appropriate form. Copies of all notices, correspondence, documentary evidence, orders and forms shall be maintained as public records. -- 162 of 162 --

ADJOURNMENT -- 2 of 137 -- BY TERRY WARD TERRY.WARD@MYHORRYNEWS.COM The Myrtle Beach Regional Economic Development Cor- poration’s Annual meeting played to a packed house of business, industry and agency leaders, Jan. 8, at the Barefoot Resort Conference Center in North Myrtle Beach. A crowd of approximately 350 people came out to get an economic development review of Horry County from local business leaders and elected officials, a significant increase from 87 people showing up to its first annual meeting. KEYNOTE SPEAKER Chuck Sexton, founder and CEO of Strategic Location Advisors, was the keynote speaker and addressed the importance of economic development in the county. Sexton started his pre- sentation with a slide of a single-wide mobile home in rural Kentucky. It was where he and his family lived when he was a child. “Why does economic development matter?” Sexton asked the packed crowd. He said his father struggled to find a steady job until a company came to his home- town because of the effort of an economic development team. “My father got a job and we were able to get a house. Economic development is important to who I am,” Sex- ton said. Sexton has a 25-year track record in economic develop- ment, site selection, industrial supply chain and strategic planning. His work, according to his bio, has resulted in the creation of more than 8,000 jobs and more than $3 billion in capital investment. He advised local economic developers to respond fast if they get a site visit from a potential business or indus- try. Sexton, who developed the City of Conway’s strategic plan in 2025, also presented a list of county-related data points. The data showed in the last 10 years, there has been an increase in Horry County in: wages; per capita income; household income; and population, while labor force participation has declined by almost 3%. The top five income pro- ducing occupational areas in Horry County are: financial and insurance services; infor- mation technology; profes- sional services; healthcare; and wholesale trade, accord- ing to Sexton. Sexton showed another graphic indicating that South Carolina is gaining jobs and that decreases the chance for recession. He also praised Horry County for being a receptive host to economic develop- ment inquiries and he ended with some advice. “Make sure people feel like they are at home when they come to Horry County.” OTHER SPEAKERS MBREDC President and CEO Sandy Davis and the organization’s Board Chair- man Gregg Smith, talked about the “wins” Horry Coun- ty experienced in 2025 and the growth MBREDC has seen since 2014. Davis spoke to: - the $10 million Galivants Ferry Sawmill that is billed as a boon to the timber indus- try, adding 18 jobs, with the potential for expansion. - the Ocean Craft Marine selection of Bucksport for its $10.8 million boat manufac- turing facility was another big development, Davis said. She said MBREDC staff had to respond on short notice to accommodate the team that was searching for a site for the industry. Ocean Craft Marine will provide 93 jobs when in operation. - and the Coastal Ready Mix Concrete was another com- pany opening a site in Horry County in 2025, accounting for 19 new jobs. A LOOK BACK AT 2025 Last year, the MBREDC hosted 193 existing industry visits and helped attract $225 million in new capital invest- ment, accounting for the cre- ation of 130 new jobs. Smith referred to MBREDC as the “architects of Horry County’s future,” who will refuse “to let our region stand still.” He said the small team at the MBREDC is a “dedicat- ed advocate” for growth. Horry County Council Chairman Johnny Gardner told the crowd that the entire county is in the “hospitality business.” He also said getting a fifth precinct (for the Carolina Forest area) was a signifi- cant accomplishment for the county in 2025. Gardner said that gaining the fifth percinct will allow for faster response times for fire and law enforcement personnel in the Carolina Forest area. He also touted the passage of the Ride 4 referendum for roads improvement and bridge replacements in the county. The MBREDC has helped account for $241.381 million in capital investment since 2020, and 639 jobs, according to the corporation’s annual report. OCEAN BLVD. An item Kruea said he brought forward on behalf of the down- town business community is to stop blocking off Ocean Boule- vard for the Summer Emergency Vehicle Access Plan (SEVAP) traffic pattern. During the summer months, the Myrtle Beach Police Department closes several blocks of Ocean Boulevard’s northbound lane beginning at 4 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays. On the block between 8th and 9th Avenue North, traffic is closed entirely. “It needs to be lively, it needs to be family-friendly. We want people to have a good time and just shutting the street off because you can’t adequately provide a police presence isn’t the answer,” he said. Kruea said businesses reported to him a 40% difference in sales for the summer of 2025 and largely attributed the decrease in sales to the MBPD’s traffic plan. “Ocean Boulevard is our living room,” he said. “And when you’ve blocked off traffic to Ocean Boulevard, as a driver or as a pedestrian — you wonder what’s going on down there. Is there something bad going on down there? So, just visually it sends the wrong message.” He said positioning three or four officers on foot or bicycles per block would be more effective even if this strategy puts an emphasis on hiring more police officers. A business owner from the Ocean Boulevard community said officers on foot would be a better representation of police pres- ence. “Police officers need to be visible, but on the street. Not so much sitting in cars with tinted windows,” Kruea said. “Just clos- ing off traffic automatically at 4 o’clock on Friday and Saturday because it’s easier for the police to do that is not the answer.” Eliminating the traffic pattern received some pushback from Simons and he said it is worthwhile to keep the SEVAP traffic plan in the public safety tool kit for high volume visitor times including North Carolina spring break. The council seemed in agreement that keeping the plan as an option is different from automatically utilizing the SEVAP traffic plan each summer weekend at 4 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays. The council approved the motion unanimously. PLANNING AND ZONING DEPARTMENT Another initiative brought from conversations along the campaign trail is to separate the city’s Planning and Zoning Department into two separate commissions. “Daily I hear how difficult it is to deal with the city of Myr- tle Beach,” he said. “Apparently there’s a restaurant in the north end that’s been trying to get an awning permit for eight months. It shouldn’t take eight months to get an awning per- mit.” He said the Myrtle Beach Planning & Zoning Department is currently serving two functions; the department creates rules, establishes zones and also enforces those rules and zones. Council approved a motion for the city manager to evaluate separating the department as part of the upcoming budget. “At the end of the day people who write the rules should not be the people who enforce the rules and vice versa,” he said. Simons said the challenge of this separation will involve sep- arating financial accounts and that process can and will take place during upcoming budget discussions. The Zoning Code is currently undergoing a rewrite and another motion was approved by council to include the Plan- ning Commission to contribute to the rewrite with a policy consultant. CITY CONSULTANTS AND STATE REPRESENTATION An agenda item not brought by Kruea, but with his support was to direct Simons to create a list of consultants hired by council during the calendar year 2025. “We thought it was a good idea,” Kruea said. “As part of the conversion during the election season we talked about consul- tants and whether they are contributors or not. It’s one of those fuzzy areas that you just don’t see the hard numbers on and this is a chance to see the hard numbers.” The list included a deadline of March 1, 2026. In addition to examining the city’s previous consultants, Kruea would like to re-evaluate the city’s current representa- tion in Columbia and potentially Washington D.C. Council approved a motion to provide a 60-day notice of cancellation to the current Columbia lobbying firm and look at other options for representation in the General Assembly. “It’s time for a change, it’s time to look at that differently,” Kruea said. The current representing firm is Denny’s Public Affairs. “I’ve met with plenty of the legislative delegation already to let them know that when we do come, it will be as a unified voice that the city and the chamber and the business commu- nity will be on the same page,” he said. BUDGET RETREAT The city council will no longer conduct their budget retreat in Pinopolis, South Carolina at Santee Cooper’s Wampee Confer- ence Center. The council approved a motion to have a budget workshop in the city of Myrtle Beach on Feb. 3. OTHER COMMENTS FROM KRUEA Since launching his campaign in March, Kruea has said that the Myrtle Beach Area Chamber of Commerce’s cut of the Tourism Development Fee would need to be revisited. The TDF is a 1% sales tax on items purchased in city limits. Eighty per- cent is allocated to the MBACC, to invest in tourism and adver- tisements, and the remaining 20% the city uses as a property tax credit to full-time residents, required by the state. The Myrtle Beach residents are increasing at a rate greater than the city’s cut of funds from the TDF and Kruea said the percentage of the distribution of funds needs to change. With new leadership at the MBACC, including the CEO Matt Pivar- nik hired within the last year, he is inclined to say it will be a collaborative change. “I’ve met briefly with the chamber board. I’ve met several times with Matt [Pivarnik]. He’s aware that the TDF needs to be revisited so that it serves the community as a whole,” he said “How that looks yet, we haven’t figured out.” The MBACC currently receives about $35 million for adver- tising. The business community would point out the tourism numbers are flat or down a little bit, so it is important they get the bang for their buck, Kruea added. “We’ve not had a next-big-thing since before COVID. The city, in this year’s budget, used all of its 20% of the property tax credit and had to add an extra $1.2 million to make up the property tax credit. That’s not responsible financial spending, to use somebody else’s money to pay somebody else’s property tax credit,” Kruea said. CITY MANAGER AND CITY ATTORNEY SALARIES Simons’ 5% cost-of-living adjustment went into effect on January 1, 2026 along with the city council’s attorney salary increase. The previous council approved a 5% COLA to be added to the city manager’s $278,262 annual salary and the city attorney’s $203,320 annual salary at their final Dec. 9 meeting. The increase in salary was applied only for the second half of FY 2025-2026, according to the city. Kruea said the salary adjustment was a decision he felt should have been left to the newly-elected council. “Percentages are a weird thing. Five percent of $300,000 is a lot more than five percent of $40,000 and the public is smart enough to understand that,” Kruea said. “And if you look behind the curtain there, the council just let their contract roll over last year. They did not do an annual review. “It probably shouldn’t have been termed that because when you’re making $278,000, you can afford the cost of living. It should have been a performance or a merit increase – not a cost of living adjustment. And yet there was no measurement of performance or merit that I could see.” JANUARY 15, 2026 | LOCAL | THE HORRY INDEPENDENT | CONWAY, S.C. CALL TO ORDER Chairperson Wise called the meeting to order at approximately 5:30 pm. II. ELECTION OF OFFICERS Bryson made a motion to nominate Wise as Chairperson, seconded by Ulrich. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. Ulrich made a motion to nominate Sligh to serve as Vice Chairman, seconded by Anderson. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. III. APPROVAL OF MINUTES Ulrich made a motion, seconded by Cornell to approve the December 11, 2025, minutes as written. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. IV. PUBLIC INPUT There was no public input. V. SUBDIVISIONS A. University Suites – The applicant(s) is requesting approval of: University Suites Expansion, a multi-family project and is requesting a waiver from the post-development appraisal requirement for the project (PIN 383-10-03-0020). Hucks gave an overview of the request and a background summary, noting the following: Under the current requirements of the UDO, any development in which less than one acre of open space would be required, the applicant is required to pay a fee in lieu of providing the open space onsite, unless the open space to be provided onsite complies with the suitability standards, including that it is a minimum of one acre in size. Based on the current requirements for open space, 1,000 sq. ft. of open space is required for each unit proposed, which would be 24,000 sq. ft. in this case. -- 4 of 137 -- PC 1/8/2026 2 The applicant is proposing to pay the fee in lieu of providing open space; however, the applicant is asking for a modification from the way in which the fee in lieu amount is determined. The applicant has provided a contracted amount of $569,000 in lieu of the written appraisal, and using that dollar amount, the fee in lieu would amount to $179,142 (or $7.46/sq. ft.) and when you include the recent amendment to the open space ordinance which requires the fee in lieu amount to be 125% of the determined amount, the required fee in lieu amount for the 24-unit project would be $224,000. The applicant contends that while they are providing the fee in lieu, the project will still provide some open space, although it does not meet the suitability standards of the UDO. Items regarding University Suites 1 – a request to approve a design modification from the requirement for a written appraisal in determining what the open space fee in lieu amount would be and to instead, accept the applicant’s amount of $569,000 as being a satisfactory amount to be used in determining that fee, and 2 – preliminary plan approval. Staff recommend that, should the Planning Commission choose to recommend approval of the applicant’s requests, such recommendation be made contingent upon final review and approval by the Technical Review Committee (TRC). The applicant, Schwerd, was present and further explained the request. The board and staff discussed the request at length. Cornell made a motion to approve the overall layout of the University Suites Expansion and the waiver from the post-development appraisal requirement. Anderson seconded the motion; Wise opposed, and the motion carried. B. University Suites – The applicant is requesting a reduction on the required fee-in-lieu amount (PIN 383-10-03-0020). Hucks gave an overview of the request and a background summary, noting the following: As part of the open space fee in lieu request, if the design modification is granted, the applicant would like to get credit for the open space being provided onsite and have it deducted from the overall required square footage. Per their application, using the per square footage rate of $7.46 per square foot, and the open space deficit of 6,991 sq. ft., the fee in lieu amount would be $52,152.86. Granted, this amount does not take into account the 25% additional fee that the ordinance requires. Should their dollar amount be accepted, the fee in lieu amount will also need to be approved by City Council. If approved by City Council, the fee must be satisfied prior to preliminary plan approval by the Technical Review Committee. Staff recommend that, should the Planning Commission choose to recommend approval of the applicant’s requests, such recommendations be made contingent upon final review and approval by the Technical Review Committee (TRC). The applicant, David Schwerd, was present and further explained the request. -- 5 of 137 -- PC 1/8/2026 3 The board and staff discussed the request at length. Wise made a motion to deny a reduction from the required fee-in-lieu amount. Seconded by Bryson and supported by Cornell, Sligh, Anderson, and Ulrich opposed the motion. The vote tied 3-3, and the motion failed. The proposed amendments would establish new or additional standards and restrictions for new and/or existing regulated commercial uses, including, but not limited to, vape/smoke/tobacco shops, alternative financial services (payday loan/title loan/cash advance services), gas/service stations (with or without a convenience store), outdoor event facilities/spaces, and other high impact uses in the City of Conway. BACKGROUND: Over the past several months, staff has been researching various options for limiting or restricting certain uses in some of the City’s commercial zoning districts; particularly in the Highway Commercial district. This came as a result of a request to rezone a property, already zoned HC, which sought to rezone to a district that allowed multifamily development and was ultimately denied; however, the concern of the existing zoning of HC directly adjacent to an established single-family residential neighborhood and the potential uses that could be established remained. Therefore, staff was asked to look at the uses and ways to limit them when adjacent to residential areas. Staff began looking at the Use Table in Article 4 of the UDO to determine which uses did not currently have specific conditions associated with the use, including those that there have been a proliferation of over the past several years, and which often have secondary negative impacts on surrounding properties. Staff researched how other cities and towns regulated these uses, if at all, and explored options for additional regulation in the City of Conway of certain uses; particularly, vape shops/smoke shops/tobacco shops and payday/title loan establishments, known as “alternative financial services.” Other uses considered were gas stations/convenience stores and the proximity to residential areas where the use is directly abutting a residentially zoned property or use. Options discussed with Planning Commission the past couple of months included separation requirements, sunset clause/amortization, adoption of a special exception process, and removing certain uses from the HC district entirely and limiting these uses to the LI and HI districts only, or a combination of the aforementioned options. The proposed amendments that have been included are a multiprong solution, with some uses becoming more limited or restricted, such as establishing separation requirements, as well as the requirement of some uses to obtain a special exception in certain instances. Animation: The movement, or the optical illusion of movement of any part of the sign structure, design or pictorial including the movement of any illumination or the flashing, scintillating or varying of light intensity. The automatic changing of all or any part of the facing of a sign or any part of a sign shall be considered to be animation. Also, included in this definition are signs having “chasing action” which is the action of a row of lights commonly used to create the appearance of motion. Time and temperature units and electronic message centers are not included in this definition. Foot Candle: a unit of illumination equal to that given by a source of one (1) candela at a distance of one foot (equivalent to one (1) lumen per square foot or 10.764 lux). Illumination: lighting; the act / condition of being illuminated (Merriam Webster definition). Lumen: A unit for measuring the amount of light something produces (Cambridge dictionary definition). Lux: A unit of illumination equal to the direct illumination on a surface that is everywhere one meter from a uniform point source of one candle intensity or equal to one lumen per square meter (Merriam Webster definition). Sign: Any device designed to attract the attention of the public for commercial or advertising purposes that is attached, painted or otherwise affixed to, or a part of a building, structure, material, surface, vehicle, or object. Integral decorative or architectural features of buildings except letters or trademarks, fences, walls and works of art, which are noncommercial in nature, are not to be construed as being a sign. Sign shall include any artificial light source, time or temperature units, clocks and any device that animates or projects a visual representation that attracts the attention of the public for commercial purpose. Sign Area (also referred to as the gross surface area): The square foot area individual symbols, letters, figures, illustrations, messages, forms, or panels, sign area shall be considered to include all lettering, wording, and accompanying designs and symbols, together with the background on which they are displayed, any frame around the sign and any “cutouts” or extensions but shall not include any supporting structure or bracing. The aggregate sign area is the summation of the area of all sign faces combined. Sign Copy: The portion of a sign which contains the name, logo, advertising message, or business identification and consists of all such symbols, letters, figures, insignia, illustrations, messages or forms. The sign structure shall not be included as a portion of the sign face provided that no identifying/advertising message, symbol or any of the aforementioned sign face criteria are displayed on or designed as part of the sign structure, whether structurally necessary or not. In the case of signs designed with integral sign face and sign structure, the blank (support) area equivalent to a maximum of 50% of the allowable sign area shall be exempt from computations of sign area. Sign Height: The vertical distance measured from the lowest adjacent street crown ground at the natural grade at the natural grade at which the sign occurs, adjacent to the sign, to the top of the sign face or sign structure, whichever is greater. Sign Panel: The primary surface of a sign that carries the identifying/advertising message. Sign Structure: A supporting structure erected or intended for the purpose of identification or advertising with or without a sign thereon, situated upon or attached to the premises upon which any sign may be fastened, affixed, displayed or applied, provided however, said definition shall not include a building or fence. If the total width of the sign structure exceeds fifty (50) percent of the total width of the sign face, the sign structure area shall be included as part of the sign area. Typical uses include canning of fruits and vegetables, processing of dairy products, and the production of prepared meats (from purchased, previously slaughtered animals). Agricultural Research: Agricultural research use type refers to establishments for experimental greenhouse and field growing of agricultural commodities, landscaping and seeds, including experimental use of herbicides, pesticides and other agricultural practices. Alternative Energy Production: Energy production sites dedicated to the commercial production of electricity by means of wind, solar, or other non-petroleum energy sources. Custom Manufacturing: Custom manufacturing refers to the on-site production of goods by hand manufacturing or artistic endeavor, which involves only the use of hand tools, individually powered tools or domestic mechanical equipment and the incidental sale of these goods directly to consumers. Typical uses include ceramic studios, custom cabinet making, crafts making, candle making, custom jewelry manufacturers, woodworkers, custom furniture craftsmen, metal craftsmen, blacksmiths, and glass blowers. High Technology (Hi-Tech) Industry: Research, development and controlled production of high-technology electronic, industrial or scientific products. Typical uses include biotechnology firms and computer component manufacturers. Light Industrial: Production processes which use already manufactured components to assemble, print or package a product such as cloth, paper, plastic, leather, wood, glass or stones, but not including such operations as paper, saw or mills, steel, iron or other metalwork’s, rolling mills, or any manufacturing uses involving primary production of commodities from raw materials. Typical uses include apparel manufacturing, paper products finishing, furniture production and production of fabricated metal products. Heavy Industrial: Heavy industry refers to production processes, which should not be located near residential or commercial uses due to the insensitive nature of the industrial activity and/or the scale of the operation. These uses may be located near other manufacturing uses exhibiting similar characteristics although special control measures may be required for some extremely intensive operations to ensure compatibility with similar industrial uses.
