Conference Room – 196 Laurel Street Present: Jessica Wise, George Ulrich, Thomas J. Anderson III, Greg Bryson, Ellen Watkins Absent: Allan Cornell, David Sligh, Kendall Brown Staff: Jessica Hucks, Planning Director; Katie Dennis, Planner; Marsha Ponder, Planning & Development Assistant; Brent Gerald, Planner; Charlie Crosby, IT Others: Ballery Skipper, David Schwerd, Keith Skinner and Casey Jones I. CALL TO ORDER Chairperson Wise called the meeting to order at approximately 5:30 pm. II. APPROVAL OF MINUTES Ulrich made a motion, seconded by Watkins to approve the September 4, 2025, minutes as written. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. III. PUBLIC INPUT No public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Ulrich to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. IV. SUBDIVISIONS A. The Reserve at Millpond. The applicant(s) is requesting approval of: The Reserve at Millpond, an in- common townhome development and the associated street names for the project (PIN 3385-00-00-0018). Hucks provided a brief overview. Stating that in September of 2024 – a Sketch Plan was submitted and reviewed. March thru August of 2025 – initial submittal and 2 revised Preliminary Plan sets were submitted and reviewed. The development site is located on a 41.28-acre tract, behind the Turtle Creek subdivision and proposes: 45 buildings, containing a total of: 234 in common townhome units. Access to the project is to be provided by extending the two existing stub-outs, provided within Turtle Creek development (Tortoise Drive & Turtle Creek Drive), as well as the construction of a new stub-out within the development site connecting to the future phase of Elmhurst (currently in review). A total of: 5.37-acres of Open Space is required on-site. The project design proposes to provide a total of: 8.60-acres of Open Space, with 1.66- acres being active Open Space and containing such active features as; a 6-ft wide elevated boardwalk, a 6-ft wide walking trail (constructed of aggregate base materials), a 10-ft X 20-ft stationary dock as well as a future Amenity Site. The applicant is also requesting approval of the following street names. Horry County has reserved these names for this development: • Soul • King Solomon -- 3 of 29 -- PC 10/2/2025 2 • King David Staff recommended that if Planning Commission approved of the applicant’s request, that such approval be contingent upon final review and approval by the Technical Review Committee (TRC). The applicant, David Schwerd, was present to discuss the request and answer questions from the Board. The board, staff and applicant discussed the request at length. Wise made a motion to approve the development and the associated street names contingent on TRC approval and ask that TRC consider a pervious paving detail or edging, to help stabilize the walking paths. Ulrich seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. V. PUBLIC HEARINGS A. REZONING REQUEST(S) 1. WITHDRAWN…Request to rezone approx. 10.97+/- acres of property located at 1808 Rhue Street (PIN 368-00-00-0002) from the Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district to the Institutional (IN) district. 2. Request to rezone approximately 2.15+/- acres of property located at 1001 Creel Street (PIN 368-08-01-0103) from the Horry County General Residential (GR) district to the City of Conway Professional (P) district upon annexation into the City of Conway. Hucks stated that the applicant is seeking to zone the subject property as Professional (P) upon annexation into the City. of the subject property, and upon annexation, zone the property to the Professional (P) district. is seeking annexation into the City as the property is within the city’s utility service area, and multiple neighboring properties are also owned by the same property owner. The property contains a single-family residence which would be allowed to remain upon rezoning as residential is an allowable use in the Professional (P) zoning district. The City’s future land use map identifies the property as Low Density Residential. Per Section 3.2.3 of the UDO, the R-1 district is to provide for the preservation and expansion of areas for low to medium density, detached single-family residential development in the City of Conway. The district shall present a relatively spacious character, promote quiet, livable neighborhoods, and prohibit uses that are incompatible with the residential nature of the surrounding area. Council approved 1st reading of the annexation request at their September 15th meeting and staff will forward Planning Commission’s recommendation to Council for consideration at their October 20th meeting. The applicant was present to answer questions. There was no public input and Wise made a motion, seconded by Ulrich to close public input. The motion carried unanimously. The board, staff, and applicant discussed the request at length. Anderson made a motion to approve the rezoning request as presented. Bryson seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. -- 4 of 29 -- PC 10/2/2025 3 B. TEXT AMENDMENT(S) 1. Previously Deferred… Amendments to Article 2 – Definitions, Article 4 – Use Tables, & Article 6 – Design Standards, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding the requirements and subdistricts of the Waccamaw Riverfront District (WRD). Hucks stated that the Waccamaw Riverfront District is currently split between 2 subdistricts: WRD-1 and WRD- 2. However, the only mention of the subdistricts is within Section 6.4.1 (A) of the UDO. There is nothing that “defines” the difference in the 2 subdistricts. Section 6.4.1 (D) provides requirements for the WRD-1 subdistrict to be mixed-use. This is in order to promote pedestrian related activity and public access to the riverfront. It requires that all ground level floors of any building in the WRD-1 subdistrict be devoted to permitted uses as outlined in the Use Tables of Article 4, aside from residential (multifamily) uses. Recently, the property containing the old Santee Cooper smoke stacks and ash ponds that is now owned by the City was annexed (portions of) and rezoned to WRD-2, as that was the zoning district directly adjacent to the subject property which also has direct access to the river. Some portions of the property are across Hwy 501, on New Rd, which was zoned WRD-2 as well due to it being a portion of the parcels adjacent to the river and not split out from the parcels. These two separate parcels total approx. 224 acres. Currently, the Use Tables (Art. 4), footnote #5 for the WRD (WRD5), states, “Permitted uses and conditional uses listed under the WRD column shall meet the mixed use requirements in Section 6.4.1 if located in the WRD-1 subdistrict.” However, several of the parcels that would be considered as WRD-1 do not have direct access to the riverfront, and the intent of the district is to “provide for the physical, social, and economic development of the City’s riverfront area.” Additionally, there may be future plans for the 224+/- acres now owned by the City where the mixed-use requirement for portions of the property should be adhered to, in accordance with the intent of the district; specifically, where there is riverfront and/or riverwalk access. The proposed amendment(s) would eliminate the subdistricts for WRD. Instead, the mixed-use requirement would be applicable to properties that adjoin the riverwalk, with multifamily uses prohibited on ground-level floors. Other amendments proposed include minor changes to the wording of certain sections of the WRD ordinance, identifying which areas are subject to review by the Community Appearance Board (CAB) (not currently in the UDO) and revise the locations of the WRD. These amendments are attached for your review. There was no public input and Ulrich made a motion, seconded by Wise to close public input. The motion carried unanimously. The board and staff discussed the request at length. Wise made a motion to approve the amendments to Article 2, Article 4, and Article 6 regarding requirements and subdistricts of the WRD district. Anderson seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. 2. Amendments to Article 2 – Definitions and Article 13 – Administrative Agencies and Functions, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), to establish provisions for requiring a Development Agreement for developments that involve a zoning map amendment and/or annexation into the City of Conway. -- 5 of 29 -- PC 10/2/2025 4 Hucks stated that over the past several years; in particular, the last 2-3 years, there has been an increase in the number of properties in the county’s jurisdiction that have sought annexation into the City, either due to the requirement to annex for city services, or by contiguity at the choice of the property owner. One of the most notable annexations occurred in 2024 – The Warden Station PD. Due to the size and nature of some of these requests, the developer entered into a Development Agreement (DA) with the City for development of the properties, which included provisions that would help ensure quality and sound development and that the growth that would result from the development would pay for itself. Since the annexation of Warden Station and other large properties, Council asked staff to prepare options for requiring a development agreement for certain types of developments, which was discussed during Council’s budget retreat earlier this year. Staff recommended that should such a requirement be established, that it be limited to property seeking annexation into the City for residential development OR property in the City seeking a zoning map amendment to a district that would permit residential development, and that a particular threshold be established, such as a certain number of lots/units and minimum acreage. In South Carolina, the requirement for developments to enter into a Development Agreement (DA) is not uniformly mandated across the state. State law does determine a municipality’s ability to use development agreements, through the South Carolina Local Government Development Agreement Act, which authorizes local governments to establish procedures and requirements to consider and enter into such agreements with developers. DAs are typically utilized for substantial developments that involve large tracts of land, as the minimum acreage for a DA is 25 acres of highland. However, developers cannot be “required” to enter into such an agreement; they must be voluntary, and both parties must agree to the terms of the agreement. Local governments can make zoning approvals, plan approvals, or annexations contingent on entering into a development agreement. The proposed amendment(s) provides a definition of “Development Agreement” for inclusion in Article 2 of the UDO as well as a Section within Article 13, outlining the Purpose, Applicability, Procedure, and Relationship to Zoning Decisions for Development Agreements in the City of Conway. Any residential development seeking annexation and/or a zoning map amendment to a district that permits residential uses and proposing 150 or more lots and/or units OR involving 25 acres or more of uplands will be subject to the requirement for a development agreement. Minor subdivisions/developments would be exempt from the requirement for a development agreement. In addition to the proposed amendments, a table which outlines the state’s requirements for a development agreement are attached for your review. There was no public input and Wise made a motion, seconded by Anderson to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. The board and staff discussed the request at length. Anderson made a motion to approve the text amendments for Article 2 – Definitions and Article 13 – Administrative Agencies and Functions of the city of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), incorporating the recommended revisions for properties containing 25 acres or more of uplands, a development agreement shall be required, with 50 or more lots/units proposed. Bryson seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. -- 6 of 29 -- PC 10/2/2025 5 3. Deferred… Amendments to Article 2 – Definitions, Article 4 – Use Tables, Article 5 – Specific Use Regulations, and Article 6 – Design Standards of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding uses in the Highway Commercial (HC) and Light Industrial (LI) zoning districts. C. AMENDMENT(S) TO THE CITY OF CONWAY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN 1. Amendment to the City of Conway Comprehensive Plan, to adopt, by reference, the 2025 Conway Parks and Recreation Master Plan. Jessica Wise recused herself from this agenda item. Bryson made a motion to appoint George Ulrich as Vice Chair to preside in place of Chairperson Wise during her recusal. Watkins seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. Hucks stated that in April 2024, the City of Conway advertised publicly to select a firm to provide professional design services for a City of Conway Parks Master Plan, and the team of Greenberg Farrow + Brandstetter Carroll Inc was chosen. A portion of this Master plan is funded by a grant awarded from the SC Department of Parks, Recreation & Tourism Park and Recreation Development Fund (PARD). Over the past year, City staff has been working with the design team, including: • Needs assessment and inventory of all existing facilities • Defining the mission, vision, values, goals and objectives for Parks, Recreation facilities, and their usage • Providing short, intermediate, and long-range management and development plans for recreation, park and facility planning • Establishing priorities and recommendations for existing and future park and facility development, including types of parks, size of parks, timing of development, and developer-led allocation of park lands • Developing a systematic plan that maximizes the park, recreation, and natural open space opportunities for Conway residents • Identify appropriate staffing needs to support park maintenance operations and recreation operations • Future trends recommendations • Providing recommendations for physical improvements to existing and future recreation and park facilities to create a uniform and cohesive look and feel that is distinctly Conway, including branding and signage. A draft of the 2025 Parks & Recreation Master Plan was attached for the boards review. Council approved 1st reading of the amendment(s) at their August 18th meeting and final reading is scheduled to occur at the October 6th meeting, pending Planning Commission’s review & recommendation. There was no public input and Ulrich made a motion, seconded by Watkins to close public input. The motion carried unanimously. The board and staff discussed the request at length. -- 7 of 29 -- PC 10/2/2025 6 Bryson made a motion to approve the amendment as presented. Anderson seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. Ulrich signed the Resolution, formalizing the adoption of the Master Plan. VI. BOARD INPUT Bryson inquired about the future plans for Lake Busby. VII. STAFF INPUT Hucks addressed the board to explain the deferral of Text Amendment Number 3 on the agenda. She provided context regarding the need for additional review. VIII. ADJOURNMENT A motion was made to adjourn the meeting. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. A5 www.myhorrynews.com ‘IS THIS NOW THE NORM’ Horry County Board of Education talks school choice, student withdrawals BY JOE WEDRA JOE.WEDRA@MYHORRYNEWS.COM Horry County Schools Superintendent Clifford Jones listened to a lengthy conver- sation regarding school choice, the mar- keting efforts of the district and more at a board work session on Monday, Sept. 8. Among the topics discussed by the HCS Board of Education was withdrawal infor- mation since the start of the 2025-26 school year. Velna Allen, HCS’ chief officer of student services, reported to the board that 2,475 students have withdrawn from HCS since the first day of school. The data, which was up to date as of late last week, include stu- dents who were enrolling in new programs for the current school year, were being homeschooled, and more. Of those 2,475, 1,100 students were remaining in Horry County and attending charter, private, virtual school or home- school options. Of that total, 1,069 moved out of the county, while 306 were listed as “other.” “This creates a disruption in our bud- geting process,” Jones said. “This creates a disruption in our building programs. This creates a disruption in anything related to future-casting. Because the question is — is this now the norm? That’s the question.” Allen reported to the board that 320 stu- dents -- 256 elementary, 64 middle -- were attending the new Discovery School at Myr- tle Beach, a charter school in Conway on Highway 90. Atlantic Collegiate Academy, a charter school in Conway off of Bear Bluff Road, had 188 former HCS students enroll this year, while Coastal High School, a char- ter high school in Myrtle Beach on Palmetto Pointe Boulevard, enrolled 93 former HCS students. As a whole, current enrollment in Horry County Schools (47,253) is 1,038 students less than what the district had projected this year (48,291). Neil James, who represents Carolina For- est, Conway, Green Sea Floyds and Loris areas in District 10, initiated the discussion on school choice and related topics. “If you look at these other schools, char- ter schools, they are offering choice. We may need to take a look at some ways to improve or increase our choices for parents and their students,” James said. Pam Dawson, who represents Carolina Forest, St. James and Socastee in District 6, called the current situation a “competitive market environment.” “I am sure the superintendent and staff are very aware of this competitive market environment that we are now in,” Dawson said, continuing to say that “customer ser- vice” could play a big role for the district over time. “When school choice first became a topic of conversation in South Carolina, my first reaction was ‘we are currently in a compet- itive market environment,’” Dawson said. “Many of the things I know Superintendent Jones is focusing on will help us in that regard. That has to do with responsiveness to parents. If you translate customer service as applied to the education environment, I believe our teachers and administrators do yeoman’s work and do the best they can do. “But, parents are sensitive to things like that. How quickly their emails are respond- ed to; do they get a full and complete answer when we reply to them? Things like that are going to make the difference over the long haul. Because, as we say, they have a choice.” Debbie Edmonds, who represents the Carolina Forest and Myrtle Beach areas in District 2, also highlighted the “mar- ketplace” trend that rippled through the night’s conversation. Edmonds agreed with Dawson’s and James’ comments, expanding to say that the district could look at things like smaller class sizes as a solution to competing with alternative academic options that exist. “It’s a marketplace,” Edmonds said. “So, if it’s an open marketplace, I’m a business- woman. How can I compete? What can I do? “Even a smaller class size, that’s a great advantage to children who are struggling with learning. If I have 28 in one class and then this other class has 16, my kid is going to get more attention in a class size of 16 than the one with 28, or whatever the max is. I just want to say I’m glad we’re having these conversations, and I hope we will continue to look at ourselves in a compet- itive nature because I don’t think this is going to change any time soon. I think it’s going to continue down this path.” Howard Barnard, who represents Surf- side Beach and the St. James service area in District 5, asked Allen, the student services officer, if there was any indication of “feder- al government intervention” in schools as a part of discussion on potential deportation of students. Said Allen: “Not to my knowledge. Not that I’m aware of. We will continue to mon- itor that, though. But, the data did not indi- cate that. Again, some people may be afraid to share that. But at this point, I am not led to believe that.” Other members, including Wendy Hodges, who represents the Myrtle Beach, Socastee and St. James area in District 4, indicated it was too early to make changes, noting a belief that many students could return back to Horry County Schools. Jones, after listening to the conversa- tion, told the board that the conversation is something they would “monitor” and would revisit at a conversation topic on a quarterly basis. The superintendent also sent a message to parents who might have been listening to the meeting take place and had their stu- dents at another academic option. “My hope is, if you’re listening today, my hope is that you come back,” Jones said. The intent of the FA district is to establish and preserve areas for agricultural or passive recreation. Most agricultural uses require structure(s) for farming equipment or stables for animals. However, the current language of the UDO would not permit such structures without there being a principal use and structure (i.e. in conjunction with a single-family dwelling). The proposed amendment carves out an exception for the FA district only for the ability to have accessory structures relating to farming; particularly, the keeping of livestock / fowl, without the requirement to have a principal structure, but with conditions, including that it would be applicable to parcels zoned FA that are a minimum of 5 acres in size. This amendment also includes other revisions relating to the noncommercial keeping of livestock / fowl and adds the Rural Residential (RR) district as one of the districts in which the use is permitted as a conditional use. The amendments are included on the following pages. Note that the amendments are applicable to “noncommercial” activities, not commercial activities. Commercial agriculture uses in FA already require a minimum lot size of 10 acres. Additional information can be found in the packet for the September 4, 2025 PC mtg. There was no public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Anderson to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. The board and staff briefly discussed the request. Bryson made a motion to approve the amendment as presented. Cornell seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. V. BOARD INPUT None VI. STAFF INPUT Hucks shared details regarding the upcoming text amendments scheduled for presentation. VII. ADJOURNMENT A motion was made to adjourn the meeting. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. The meeting adjourned at approximately 6:57 pm. Approved and signed this ___________ day of ______________, 2025. ISSUE: Amendments to Article 4 – Use Tables and Article 6 – Design Standards, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding the requirements and subdistricts of the Waccamaw Riverfront District (WRD). BACKGROUND: Currently, the Waccamaw Riverfront District is split between 2 subdistricts: WRD-1 and WRD-2. However, the only mention of the subdistricts is within Section 6.4.1 (A) of the UDO. There is nothing that “defines” the difference in the 2 subdistricts. Section 6.4.1 (D) provides requirements for the WRD- 1 subdistrict to be mixed-use. This is in order to promote pedestrian related activity and public access to the riverfront. It requires that all ground level floors of any building in the WRD-1 subdistrict be devoted to permitted uses as outlined in the Use Tables of Article 4, aside from residential (multifamily) uses. Recently, the property containing the old Santee Cooper smoke stacks and ash ponds that is now owned by the City was annexed (portions of) and rezoned to WRD-2, as that was the zoning district directly adjacent to the subject property which also has direct access to the river. Some portions of the property are across Hwy 501, on New Rd, which was zoned WRD-2 as well due to it being a portion of the parcels adjacent to the river and not split out from the parcels. These two separate parcels total approx. 224 acres. Currently, the Use Tables (Art. 4), footnote #5 for the WRD (WRD5), states, “Permitted uses and conditional uses listed under the WRD column shall meet the mixed use requirements in Section 6.4.1 if located in the WRD-1 subdistrict.” However, several of the parcels that would be considered as WRD- 1 do not have direct access to the riverfront, and the intent of the district is to “provide for the physical, social, and economic development of the City’s riverfront area.” Additionally, there may be future plans for the 224+/- acres now owned by the City where the mixed-use requirement for portions of the property should be adhered to, in accordance with the intent of the district; specifically, where there is riverfront and/or riverwalk access. The proposed amendment(s) would eliminate the subdistricts for WRD. Instead, the mixed-use requirement would be applicable to properties that adjoin the riverwalk, with multifamily uses prohibited on ground-level floors. Other amendments proposed include minor changes to the wording of certain sections of the WRD ordinance, identifying which areas are subject to review by the Community Appearance Board (CAB) (not currently in the UDO) and revise the locations of the WRD. These amendments are attached for your review. Amendments to the WRD district 6.4.1 Waccamaw Riverfront District (WRD) The Waccamaw Riverfront District defines the area south of Second Avenue and east of Beaty Street, Marina Drive, and portions on either side of New Road (refer to the City’s zoning map for more specific locations). Historically a manufacturing and rail transportation corridor, it is important to honor the area’s past while continuing to support new quality development. The purpose of this district is to help increase the economic vitality of the downtown, enhance the riverfront approach, provide opportunity for new mixed-use development, provide for the public’s use and enjoyment, and to provide for the protection of the riverbank. New buildings and uses that locate in the Waccamaw Riverfront District should be of pedestrian scale and orientation; ensure the public’s visual access and enjoyment of the river; evoke a feeling of the industrial and transportation history of the area; include design orientation both to the river and to the public way; and integrate public outdoor activity. The area’s configuration is linear and narrow and provides limited potential for on-site vehicular circulation or storage. It’s an area primarily served and occupied by people, not vehicles, although some provision has been made for public and private parking. Uses in the Waccamaw Riverfront District are not to be automobile-oriented or dependent. [Amended ZA2019-02-18(C) ZA2023-10-02(E)] A. ISSUE: Amendments to Article 2 – Definitions and Article 13 – Administrative Agencies and Functions, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), to establish provisions for requiring a Development Agreement for developments involving a zoning map amendment and/or annexation into the City of Conway. BACKGROUND: Over the past several years; in particular, the last 2-3 years, there has been an increase in the number of properties in the county’s jurisdiction that have sought annexation into the City, either due to the requirement to annex for city services, or by contiguity at the choice of the property owner. One of the most notable annexations occurred in 2024 – The Warden Station PD. Due to the size and nature of some of these requests, the developer entered into a Development Agreement (DA) with the City for development of the properties, which included provisions that would help ensure quality and sound development and that the growth that would result from the development would pay for itself. Since the annexation of Warden Station and other large properties, Council asked staff to prepare options for requiring a development agreement for certain types of developments, which was discussed during Council’s budget retreat earlier this year. Staff recommended that should such a requirement be established, that it be limited to property seeking annexation into the City for residential development OR property in the City seeking a zoning map amendment to a district that would permit residential development, and that a particular threshold be established, such as a certain number of lots/units and minimum acreage. In South Carolina, the requirement for developments to enter into a Development Agreement (DA) is not uniformly mandated across the state. State law does determine a municipality’s ability to use development agreements, through the South Carolina Local Government Development Agreement Act, which authorizes local governments to establish procedures and requirements to consider and enter into such agreements with developers. DAs are typically utilized for substantial developments that involve large tracts of land, as the minimum acreage for a DA is 25 acres of highland. However, developers cannot be “required” to enter into such an agreement; they must be voluntary, and both parties must agree to the terms of the agreement. Local governments can make zoning approvals, plan approvals, or annexations contingent on entering into a development agreement. The proposed amendment(s) provides a definition of “Development Agreement” for inclusion in Article 2 of the UDO as well as a Section within Article 13, outlining the Purpose, Applicability, Procedure, and Relationship to Zoning Decisions for Development Agreements in the City of Conway. Any residential -- 38 of 408 -- STAFF REPORT Amendment(s) to UDO establishing provisions for requiring a Development Agreement for developments involving a zoning map amendment and/or annexation into the City of Conway development seeking annexation and/or a zoning map amendment to a district that permits residential uses and proposing 150 or more lots and/or units OR involving 25 acres or more of uplands will be subject to the requirement for a development agreement. Minor subdivisions/developments would be exempt from the requirement for a development agreement. In addition to the proposed amendments, a table which outlines the state’s requirements for a development agreement are attached for your review. D-9 DRAFT -- 51 of 408 -- Plan Envision Engage Evaluate EXECUTIVE SUMMARY EXECUTIVE SUMMARY vii The Need for a P laN Conway is a small city located adjacent to Myrtle Beach in Horry County, South Carolina. Conway experienced rapid growth over the past 25 years and that trend is expected to continue for at least the next 10 years. Conway’s population is also aging with an increased percentage of residents 65 and over and a decreased percentage of residents under 18. The population is also slightly less diverse in 2022 compared to 2010 with white residents making up a larger percentage of the population. Overall, approximately 12% of Conway residents live within a 10-minute walk to a neighborhood or community park. Many residents live beyond a 5-minute drive to a neighborhood or community park and several areas of the city are more than a 10-minute drive to a neighborhood or community park. These areas could be served with strategically targeted park development and by requiring new subdivision developments to provide parks and open space available to all Conway residents. These investments are highlighted in Chapters 5 and 6. Meant to instill focus, establish priorities, and inspire action, the plan was produced with guidance from an active steering committee appointed by and including some city officials. The plan is supported by robust data collection, including hours of in-person engagement, and provides a foundation for continuous improvement of Conway’s parks and recreation offerings. The P rocess – why are These acTioNs Needed Existing Conditions of Parks and Recreation A park system should be evaluated as a composite of recreation areas with each meeting a particular public need. The system should provide a combination of smaller neighborhood parks, larger community parks, special use parks, and indoor recreation facilities. For all residents, whatever their background, parks and recreation facilities help provide a variety of passive and active recreational opportunities. Proximity to these valuable resources invariably improves community health and wellness while creating more adaptable, robust local economies.1 Demographic and Benchmarking Analysis Conway experienced significant population growth in the recent past that is expected to continue. The city is becoming older and slightly less diverse. As these trends continue, they may create new demands for recreation programs and facilities. 1 https://www.fastcompany.com/90624316/great-parks-dont-just-haverec-space-they-create-jobs?mc_cid=105f89bd93&mc_eid=6c9b6b28d4 Conway falls below the benchmark departments for the overall number of parks and a few key park features, including playgrounds, splash pads, and multipurpose rectangular fields. The Parks and Recreation Department employs more staff than the benchmark departments, largely due to Conway managing a large indoor recreation center with an indoor swimming pool. Service Area Analysis Maps of service areas for various parks and facilities were used to identify service gaps or underserved areas within Conway based on walking and driving times. Conway’s overall level of service for recreation facilities is relatively low, with most parks and facilities concentrated in two areas: Downtown and the neighborhoods near Collins Park and the Billy Gardner Recreation Complex. The analysis indicated that only 12% of Conway residents live within a 10-minute walk to a neighborhood or community park. A composite service areas map shows the overall level of service for parks and facilities, ranked from high to low, in turn revealing areas of need and opportunity. Shades of green indicate high service levels, while red areas show those with the lowest level of service to parks and recreation facilities. Approximately 14% of Conway residents live in areas with high or medium-high levels of service. whaT coNway resideNTs said Understanding the needs and wants of Conway residents was essential to developing the Master Plan. A recent report, The Power of Parks to Promote Health,2 breaks down the new data to show communities how to make parks a more formal part of their health programs, helping to ensure more are able to experience the physical and mental health benefits of public parks and green spaces. TPL found that “people are on average 9% less likely to suffer from poor mental health and 21% less likely to be physically inactive” in the top 25 ranking cities, compared to the lower-ranked cities, even after controlling for race/ethnicity, income, age, and population density. The City of Conway currently offers four neighborhood parks. Collins Park Collins Park is located in the north-central area of the city. The park includes an arched entry, paved parking, a restroom building, paved sidewalks, fountain, sculpture area, mature landscape, a playground, basketball court, four tennis courts, five pickleball courts, a community building (Mary Thompson Center), seating, and two picnic shelters. Collins Park is well-maintained and in good general condition. There is easy pedestrian and vehicular access to the park and concrete sidewalks throughout. The playground area and sports courts are in need of minor maintenance due to use. The existing restroom building is in good condition; however, the community building is in need of renovation. At the time of this plan, the city was in the process of upgrading the shelters and adding a new one between the pickleball and basketball courts. Riverfront Park Riverfront Park is located on the Waccamaw River in the downtown area of the city. The park includes an arched entry, paved parking, a restrooms building, wide paved sidewalks, a playground, one picnic shelter, a pavilion, fountain, seating, an amphitheater, mature landscape, boardwalk, and paved trail connecting to the Riverwalk. There is easy pedestrian and vehicular access to the park and either a wide concrete sidewalk or wooden boardwalk throughout. Riverfront Park is well-maintained and in good general condition, although it is sometimes subject to flooding. The city has invested in several projects to make the park more resilient, including planting Cypress trees to stabilize the bank, replacing rip rap, flood proofing several structures and the playground. The mature plant material provides a good amount of shade. The playground area is in need of minor maintenance due to use. The amphitheater is in need of minor maintenance due to weathering. The existing restroom building, picnic shelter, and pavilion are in good condition. This growth is an encouraging reflection of the community’s engagement and Conway’s success in promoting its offerings. However, continued efforts will be needed to maintain this trajectory, especially given the increasing competition and shifting interests. Significant Growth in Older Adult Programs Older Adult Programs experienced remarkable growth, with participation more than doubling between 2022 and 2024. This is consistent with national trends that show increasing demand for wellness, fitness, and social opportunities among older demographics. This group often values programs that foster both physical health and social connections, making it essential to enhance offerings such as low-impact exercise classes, recreational sports, and community-building events. Additionally, happy participants tend to encourage their friends to join, creating a powerful word-of-mouth marketing cycle. Stability in Youth Sports & Athletics Participation in Youth Sports & Athletics remained stable, fluctuating only slightly from 3,339 in 2022 to 3,446 in 2024. However, this stability may indicate that current offerings are reaching capacity due to limited field availability, natural grass field challenges, and weather constraints. To address this, the development of synthetic turf fields could allow for increased participation and decreased weather cancellations. Declines in Key Program Categories Health, Fitness, and Wellness programs remain the most popular category. However, participation declined from 9,693 in 2022 to 8,451 in 2024. This may reflect shifting fitness trends, growing competition from private fitness centers, and a natural leveling off after the pandemic-related boom in participation. Adapting programs to incorporate current fitness trends and ensuring they remain innovative and competitive will be crucial. Active Adult programs saw a sharp decline, falling from 539 in 2022 to just 210 in 2024, suggesting a potential misalignment with the target audience’s interests or a need for refreshed programming. Partnerships with local organizations and the introduction of more dynamic or collaborative activities could help revive interest. Aquatics programs saw steady declines (from 477 in 2022 to 260 in 2024), which indicate challenges in attracting participants. There may also be an issue with incomplete data capture for swim lessons and pool activities. A review of data systems and program evaluation is recommended to ensure a clearer understanding of trends. Drop-in participants to both aquatics centers should be measured. According to department records, youth program participation (not including sports leagues) has grown since 2021 with a large spike in 2022. For continued growth, Parks and Recreation should continuously evaluate factors such as changing interests among youth, program variety, and scheduling conflicts. Engaging with families and youth through surveys or focus groups could also reveal valuable insights. Community & Special Events This category showed some volatility, declining in 2023 but rebounding in 2024. Fluctuations may be influenced by factors such as inclement weather, competing local events, or varying levels of interest in specific types of events. Tracking attendance trends, gathering participant feedback, and conducting detailed evaluations can help improve future event planning. Essentially, the following descriptions help to indicate which portions of the city are most likely to benefit from community services. 2�10�1 Methodology Designed to identify communities most likely to need support before, during, or after a hazardous event, the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) uses 16 social factors to calculate a score (between 0 and 1) that compares all census tracts in the USA to each other – a score of 0 being the least vulnerable and 1 being the most. The 16 factors make up four categories as seen in Figure 2.12. Each factor is scored individually, and they are combined to create the category scores. The category scores are combined to determine the overall SVI score.4 Figure 2�18: Social Vulnerability Factors 4 Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, “CDC/ATSDR Social Vulnerability Index,” https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/place-health/php/svi/index.html This information provides a valuable data source because vulnerable populations are most likely to need other types of assistance as well, lacking the resources needed to respond to all types of threats. Accordingly, vulnerable populations are most likely to need community services overall, including parks and recreation. The demographic data used for the 2022 SVI (the most recent available) comes from the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates from (2018-2022). 2�10�2 Results Once the SVI was collected for each census tract that includes part of Conway, the results were divided into five categories which can be seen in Figure 2.19. Conway should consider adding bike trails and features in the future at Waccamaw River Park and other future suitable land. 2�12�11 Creative Placemaking The Trust for Public Land – a nonprofit organization with a mission to bring high-quality parks within a 10-minute walk of every person in the U.S. – is a leading champion of creative placemaking as a strategy for affecting change. Creative placemaking is a collaborative, community-based process that captures the power of art, vibrancy of local heritage, and potential of place to build memorable spaces rooted in culture and local identity. Parks and recreation agencies around the nation offer community connection in physical and social forms; creative-placemaking is just another tool for ensuring successful parks that equitably reflect the people who use them.18 Creative-placemaking can take countless forms. It may look like an outdoor sculpture walk featuring local artists’ work at the center of the neighborhood park. It might be an annual arts performance downtown that showcases immigrant and refugee cultures in the community. It can also be as low- profile as a pollinator garden, including interpretive signage about the plants chosen and why. Whatever it may look like, it is essential that the community be inclusively integrated into every phase: ideation, selection (of artist(s), piece(s), feature(s), etc.), installation, activation, and long-term care. When parks and recreation agencies prioritize local traditions, cultural identities, and native resources, making sure these are reflected in program and facility offerings, users will be more likely to participate and do their part to sustain the system� A reciprocal relationship forms, where the community engages with parks and recreation to provide place-based resources. Creative placemaking would provide opportunities to make every park unique and to build and connect community around these parks. Setting acreage targets – aiming for a certain number of parkland acres overall – is one way of achieving a desired level of open space. Target acreage can be a useful way for evaluating the progress of open space acquisition, but effective conservation also requires more intentional acquisitions based on a specific resource and where it is found. In other words, looking at open space acquisitions through a conservation lens, the amount of land preserved depends on aspects of that resource not just on the number of acres. Land preservation in general has many benefits, such as increased quality of life for residents and elevated property values. In order for these benefits to be shared equitably – benefits typically are higher the closer the proximity – open space should be looked at from a holistic perspective taking into additional consideration natural resources and distribution. For this analysis, travel times (walking or driving) based on the street network were used to determine service areas for parks by park type and for specific facilities within parks. The size of service areas varies depending on the amenity in question. This analysis used ArcGIS Online and ArcGIS Pro by ESRI for the development of both the spatial data and the maps used in the report. The process to develop the service area consisted of six steps for each service area distance. 1. Create shapefile with park entrances in ArcGIS Pro 2. Upload shapefile with park entrance points to ArcGIS online 3. Select “Perform Analysis” → “Use Proximity” → “Create Drive-Time Areas” 4. Select Walking Time or Driving Time (depending on measurement)  Toward facility at 12pm on Saturday 5. Select “Run Analysis” 6. “Export to Shapefile” and download This process was repeated to generate service areas representing the following travel times:  10-minute walk  5-minute drive  10-minute drive The shapefile for park entrances was created using the “PARK_PARCELS” shapefile provided by the City of Conway, combined with aerial imagery. Once the service areas were generated, the results were reduced to a single polygon for each site using the “Dissolve” function in ArcGIS Pro. The service area shapefiles were then linked to the inventory table presented in Chapter 2 (Table 2.5) to allow for the selection of the service area of each site by facilities/features offered. The next step in the process was to assign service areas to parks by park type and various recreational facilities. The travel times associated with each park or facility are based on common travel time measurements. For example, a 10-minute walk is a commonly used measurement for the distance a person will travel for a frequently used service. The travel times assigned are based on the use level of the amenity, which corresponds with the length of time a user is likely to spend at the destination. For example, users are likely willing to travel a greater distance to use a large community park than a small neighborhood park, because the larger park will likely keep visitors and their families occupied for longer. The travel time shapefiles from the previous step were used to create a series of service area maps. For each map, the locations of each amenity in question were selected using “Definition Query” from the travel time layers. For example, the neighborhood park service areas map (Figure 2.10) show a 10-minute walk to any park (green for Conway and orange for parks by others). In contrast, 5- and 10-minute drive measurements were used for community park service areas (Figure 2.11). All three measurements were used for specific park amenities (dark green for 10-minute walk, light green for 5-minute drive, and yellow for 10-minute drive) in Figures 2.12 to 2.16. These areas were turned-on (or the other areas were turned-off) in the corresponding travel time layers within ArcGIS Pro (using “Definition Query”) because they contained the specific park feature represented in the map. The composite service areas map (Figure 2.17) consists of a weighted overlay of each of the park and facility service areas. A single shapefile was created for each of the 21 facilities and three park classifications listed in Table B.1 below with the levels of service (travel times) indicated in the table. Scores were assigned to the travel time from each facility as indicated with a higher score for a shorter travel time. The “Union” function in ArcGIS Pro was used to combine these 24 layers into one composite layer. Once the scoring for all layers was combined into a single layer, a Field was added to the Attribute Table to indicate the composite score. The scores for the 21 facilities and park classifications were totaled to represent this composite score for all areas in Conway. Each of the five ranges represents approximately 8 points since the highest scoring location scored a 70.5 (out of 83 possible points). Therefore, each category represents the score of the area as a percentage of the points between the lowest (0) and highest score (70.5). These areas were then presented in the composite service areas map. The five areas were then exported to a new shapefile and uploaded to ESRI Business Analyst to estimate the population and demographics for those living within each level of service. Major residential developments must allocate a minimum of 1,000 square feet of suitable open space per lot and/or unit. Additionally, a minimum of 25% of the dedicated open space must be suitable for active areas. The ordinance provides specific requirements for the design of both active and passive areas. Additionally, the ordinance offers developers the option to offer off-site land or amenities to the City or make a fee- in-lieu payment to the City in instances where open space is unavailable or the community would be better served with the provision/expansion of a public park and/or trail. Steering Committee Member • Robbie Watkins - Steering Committee Member • Beth Helms - Steering Committee Member • Don Rockey - Steering Committee Member Notes: • Approx 1,400-1,500 residents have been added to the City in recent years (Horry County fastest growing area in SC). • The median resident age has been increasing yearly (Horry County popular for retirement- age residents). • Based on current demographics, there is a need for affordable programs. • City should consider development of parks and recreational parks/programs for the demographics it wants to attract. • There are a lot of programs currently advertised. Understanding times offered, attendance numbers and demographics, cost to host/maintain, etc could be key to understanding needs. • It was noted that dog parks attract young people and foster community, especially when located within walking distance of housing. • Steering committee • A challenge was presented to staff to monitor program users (ie: City vs County residents, Youth vs Adult participants, etc). City could provide benchmarking locations during events, breakdown membership home addresses, etc. DRAFT -- 233 of 408 -- E-18 2025 CONWAY PARKS AND RECREATION MASTER PLAN • Policy decisions (ie: limiting County memberships / program users, additional fees to cover costs, whether the City’s goal is to cover programs or make a profit, etc) should be considered and applied across all programs. • Overall national parks and rec cost recovery is 10%. • Standardizing services with prototypical buildings could make maintenance / replacement / upgrades easier. • Powerful stance on parks and rec programs (offered by City staff) – Opportunities for individual improvements and empowerment vs subsidizing for community benefit. • City should seek partnerships and require developers to contribute parks and rec spaces, especially if annexed into the City. o Donate properties for parks and “quality of life” (ie: wetlands). o Pay impact fees. o Develop public amenity areas. title: APPD_10.2.25 PC MINUTES
text: PC 10/2/2025 CITY OF CONWAY PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING THURSDAY, October 2, 2025 Planning & Building Dept. Conference Room — 196 Laurel Street Present: Jessica Wise, George Ulrich, Thomas J. Anderson III, Greg Bryson, Ellen Watkins Absent: Allan Cornell, David Sligh, Kendall Brown Staff: Jessica Hucks, Planning Director; Katie Dennis, Planner, Marsha Ponder, Planning & Development Assistant; Brent Gerald, Planner; Charlie Crosby, IT Others: Ballery Skipper, David Schwerd, Keith Skinner and Casey Jones CALL TO ORDER Chairperson Wise called the meeting to order at approximately 5:30 pm. Il. APPROVAL OF MINUTES Ulrich made a motion, seconded by Watkins to approve the September 4, 2025, minutes as written. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. I. PUBLIC INPUT No public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Ulrich to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. IV. SUBDIVISIONS A. The Reserve at Millpond. The applicant(s) is requesting approval of: The Reserve at Millpond, an in- common townhome development and the associated street names for the project (PIN 3385-00-00-0018). Hucks provided a brief overview. Stating that in September of 2024 —a Sketch Plan was submitted and reviewed. March thru August of 2025 — initial submittal and 2 revised Preliminary Plan sets were submitted and reviewed. The development site is located on a 41.28-acre tract, behind the Turtle Creek subdivision and proposes: 45 buildings, containing a total of: 234 in common townhome units. Access to the project is to be provided by extending the two existing stub-outs, provided within Turtle Creek development (Tortoise Drive & Turtle Creek Drive), as well as the construction of a new stub-out within the development site connecting to the future phase of Elmhurst (currently in review). A total of: 5.37-acres of Open Space is required on-site. The project design proposes to provide a total of: 8.60-acres of Open Space, with 1.66- acres being active Open Space and containing such active features as; a 6-ft wide elevated boardwalk, a 6-ft wide walking trail (constructed of aggregate base materials), a 10-ft X 20-ft stationary dock as well as a future Amenity Site. The applicant is also requesting approval of the following street names. Horry County has reserved these names for this development: e Soul e King Solomon PC 10/2/2025 e King David Staff recommended that if Planning Commission approved of the applicant’s request, that such approval be contingent upon final review and approval by the Technical Review Committee (TRC). The applicant, David Schwerd, was present to discuss the request and answer questions from the Board. The board, staff and applicant discussed the request at length. Wise made a motion to approve the development and the associated street names contingent on TRC approval and ask that TRC consider a pervious paving detail or edging, to help stabilize the walking paths. Ulrich seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. PUBLIC HEARINGS A. REZONING REQUEST(S) 1. WITHDRAWN...Request to rezone approx. 10.97+/- acres of property located at 1808 Rhue Street (PIN 368-00-00-0002) from the Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district to the Institutional (IN) district. 2. Request to rezone approximately 2.15+/- acres of property located at 1001 Creel Street (PIN 368-08-01-0103) from the Horry County General Residential (GR) district to the City of Conway Professional (P) district upon annexation into the City of Conway. Hucks stated that the applicant is seeking to zone the subject property as Professional (P) upon annexation into the City. of the subject property, and upon annexation, zone the property to the Professional (P) district. is seeking annexation into the City as the property is within the city’s utility service area, and multiple neighboring properties are also owned by the same property owner. The property contains a single-family residence which would be allowed to remain upon rezoning as residential is an allowable use in the Professional (P) zoning district. The City’s future land use map identifies the property as Low Density Residential. Per Section 3.2.3 of the UDO, the R-1 district is to provide for the preservation and expansion of areas for low to medium density, detached single-family residential development in the City of Conway. The district shall present a relatively spacious character, promote quiet, livable neighborhoods, and prohibit uses that are incompatible with the residential nature of the surrounding area. Council approved 1* reading of the annexation request at their September 15" meeting and staff will forward Planning Commission’s recommendation to Council for consideration at their October 20th meeting. The applicant was present to answer questions. There was no public input and Wise made a motion, seconded by Ulrich to close public input. The motion carried unanimously. The board, staff, and applicant discussed the request at length. Anderson made a motion to approve the rezoning request as presented. Bryson seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. PC 10/2/2025 B. TEXT AMENDMENT(S) 1. Previously Deferred... Amendments to Article 2 — Definitions, Article 4 — Use Tables, & Article 6 — Design Standards, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding the requirements and subdistricts of the Waccamaw Riverfront District (WRD). Hucks stated that the Waccamaw Riverfront District is currently split between 2 subdistricts: WRD-1 and WRD- 2. However, the only mention of the subdistricts is within Section 6.4.1 (A) of the UDO. There is nothing that “defines” the difference in the 2 subdistricts. Section 6.4.1 (D) provides requirements for the WRD-1 subdistrict to be mixed-use. This is in order to promote pedestrian related activity and public access to the riverfront. It requires that all ground level floors of any building in the WRD-1 subdistrict be devoted to permitted uses as outlined in the Use Tables of Article 4, aside from residential (multifamily) uses. Recently, the property containing the old Santee Cooper smoke stacks and ash ponds that is now owned by the City was annexed (portions of) and rezoned to WRD-2, as that was the zoning district directly adjacent to the subject property which also has direct access to the river. Some portions of the property are across Hwy 501, on New Rd, which was zoned WRD-2 as well due to it being a portion of the parcels adjacent to the river and not split out from the parcels. These two separate parcels total approx. 224 acres. Currently, the Use Tables (Art. 4), footnote #5 for the WRD (WRDs), states, “Permitted uses and conditional uses listed under the WRD column shall meet the mixed use requirements in Section 6.4.1 if located in the WRD-1 subdistrict.” However, several of the parcels that would be considered as WRD-1 do not have direct access to the riverfront, and the intent of the district is to “provide for the physical, social, and economic development of the City’s riverfront area.” Additionally, there may be future plans for the 224+/- acres now owned by the City where the mixed-use requirement for portions of the property should be adhered to, in accordance with the intent of the district; specifically, where there is riverfront and/or riverwalk access. The proposed amendment(s) would eliminate the subdistricts for WRD. Instead, the mixed-use requirement would be applicable to properties that adjoin the riverwalk, with multifamily uses prohibited on ground-level floors. Other amendments proposed include minor changes to the wording of certain sections of the WRD ordinance, identifying which areas are subject to review by the Community Appearance Board (CAB) (not currently in the UDO) and revise the locations of the WRD. These amendments are attached for your review. There was no public input and Ulrich made a motion, seconded by Wise to close public input. The motion carried unanimously. The board and staff discussed the request at length. Wise made a motion to approve the amendments to Article 2, Article 4, and Article 6 regarding requirements and subdistricts of the WRD district. Anderson seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. 2. Amendments to Article 2 — Definitions and Article 13 — Administrative Agencies and Functions, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), to establish provisions for requiring a Development Agreement for developments that involve a zoning map amendment and/or annexation into the City of Conway. PC 10/2/2025 Hucks stated that over the past several years; in particular, the last 2-3 years, there has been an increase in the number of properties in the county’s jurisdiction that have sought annexation into the City, either due to the requirement to annex for city services, or by contiguity at the choice of the property owner. One of the most notable annexations occurred in 2024 — The Warden Station PD. Due to the size and nature of some of these requests, the developer entered into a Development Agreement (DA) with the City for development of the properties, which included provisions that would help ensure quality and sound development and that the growth that would result from the development would pay for itself. Since the annexation of Warden Station and other large properties, Council asked staff to prepare options for requiring a development agreement for certain types of developments, which was discussed during Council’s budget retreat earlier this year. Staff recommended that should such a requirement be established, that it be limited to property seeking annexation into the City for residential development OR property in the City seeking a zoning map amendment to a district that would permit residential development, and that a particular threshold be established, such as a certain number of lots/units and minimum acreage. In South Carolina, the requirement for developments to enter into a Development Agreement (DA) is not uniformly mandated across the state. State law does determine a municipality’s ability to use development agreements, through the South Carolina Local Government Development Agreement Act, which authorizes local governments to establish procedures and requirements to consider and enter into such agreements with developers. DAs are typically utilized for substantial developments that involve large tracts of land, as the minimum acreage for a DA is 25 acres of highland. However, developers cannot be “required” to enter into such an agreement; they must be voluntary, and both parties must agree to the terms of the agreement. Local governments can make zoning approvals, plan approvals, or annexations contingent on entering into a development agreement. The proposed amendment(s) provides a definition of “Development Agreement” for inclusion in Article 2 of the UDO as well as a Section within Article 13, outlining the Purpose, Applicability, Procedure, and Relationship to Zoning Decisions for Development Agreements in the City of Conway. Any residential development seeking annexation and/or a zoning map amendment to a district that permits residential uses and proposing 150 or more lots and/or units OR involving 25 acres or more of uplands will be subject to the requirement for a development agreement. Minor subdivisions/developments would be exempt from the requirement for a development agreement. In addition to the proposed amendments, a table which outlines the state’s requirements for a development agreement are attached for your review. There was no public input and Wise made a motion, seconded by Anderson to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. The board and staff discussed the request at length. Anderson made a motion to approve the text amendments for Article 2 — Definitions and Article 13 — Administrative Agencies and Functions of the city of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), incorporating the recommended revisions for properties containing 25 acres or more of uplands, a development agreement shall be required, with 50 or more lots/units proposed. Bryson seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. PC 10/2/2025 3. Deferred... Amendments to Article 2 — Definitions, Article 4 —- Use Tables, Article 5 — Specific Use Regulations, and Article 6 — Design Standards of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding uses in the Highway Commercial (HC) and Light Industrial (LI) zoning districts. C. AMENDMENT(S) TO THE CITY OF CONWAY COMPREHENSIVE PLAN 1. Amendment to the City of Conway Comprehensive Plan, to adopt, by reference, the 2025 Conway Parks and Recreation Master Plan. Jessica Wise recused herself from this agenda item. Bryson made a motion to appoint George Ulrich as Vice Chair to preside in place of Chairperson Wise during her recusal. Watkins seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. Hucks stated that in April 2024, the City of Conway advertised publicly to select a firm to provide professional design services fora City of Conway Parks Master Plan, and the team of Greenberg Farrow + Brandstetter Carroll Inc was chosen. A portion of this Master plan is funded by a grant awarded from the SC Department of Parks, Recreation & Tourism Park and Recreation Development Fund (PARD). Over the past year, City staff has been working with the design team, including: e Needs assessment and inventory of all existing facilities e Defining the mission, vision, values, goals and objectives for Parks, Recreation facilities, and their usage e Providing short, intermediate, and long-range management and development plans for recreation, park and facility planning e Establishing priorities and recommendations for existing and future park and facility development, including types of parks, size of parks, timing of development, and developer-led allocation of park lands e Developing a systematic plan that maximizes the park, recreation, and natural open space opportunities for Conway residents e Identify appropriate staffing needs to support park maintenance operations and recreation operations e Future trends recommendations e Providing recommendations for physical improvements to existing and future recreation and park facilities to create a uniform and cohesive look and feel that is distinctly Conway, including branding and signage. A draft of the 2025 Parks & Recreation Master Plan was attached for the boards review. Council approved 1* reading of the amendment(s) at their August 18" meeting and final reading is scheduled to occur at the October 6" meeting, pending Planning Commission’s review & recommendation. There was no public input and Ulrich made a motion, seconded by Watkins to close public input. The motion carried unanimously. The board and staff discussed the request at length. PC 10/2/2025 Bryson made a motion to approve the amendment as presented. Anderson seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. Ulrich signed the Resolution, formalizing the adoption of the Master Plan. VI. BOARD INPUT Bryson inquired about the future plans for Lake Busby. VII. STAFF INPUT Hucks addressed the board to explain the deferral of Text Amendment Number 3 on the agenda. She provided context regarding the need for additional review. Vill. ADJOURNMENT A motion was made to adjourn the meeting. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. The meeting adjourned at approximately 7:00 pm. Approved and signed this Uy day of WIRUACE , 2025. Qqyins el . : Jessica Wise, Chairperson

A5 www.myhorrynews.com REBRANDING, FROM A3 edith Denari said in addition to the logo, the rebranding package will also include an official font, color palette, brand guidelines, and brand and implementation strategy. Denari said these materials will eventually be reflected on the city’s website, official city documents, marketing, stationary, future art and more. “It’s a business investment,” Denari said. “This is not just a logo design; this was a branding project. There are many layers to it – a government, a city, a municipal agency. This is a big government project. This is a big government bid. These agencies specialize in this caliber of a project.” The project was advertised on the city’s bids and purchases page in October 2024 for branding agencies to submit proposals for “a comprehensive branding initiative aimed at enhancing the city’s identity, promoting tourism, supporting economic development and fostering civic pride.” The city announced the Florida-based Zimmerman Agency was awarded the project in February of 2025. The city faced criticism from local artists and advertising agencies for hiring an out-of- state agency rather than searching for local talent. Altman is not confident a Myrtle Beach business or artist would have qualified for the project, explaining his perspective comes from his own work in advertising and editorial pho- tography on a national level. “Where I think that people missed the mark is locally, somebody comes to a designer and says, ‘I need a logo’ and a designer designs a logo,” Altman said. “What they don’t do is they don’t look up market research behind that brand to see what their competitors are doing. They don’t build a strategy behind the brand and they don’t build an identity behind the brand. They just make a logo. So, people aren’t seeing that aspect.” The image circling around social media was not the final product and its debut from the city would have accompanied a survey for the public to give feedback prior to an official roll- out. The presentation at the Aug. 5 city council workshop was the third update Denari gave to council, but the first time the logo made its way around social media. The presentation at the workshop said the city seal was created in 1976 and will contin- ue to function as the official legal emblem of the municipality. Denari said the city seal is traditional, historical and not meant to be changed. The city was motivated to invest in branding with a logo because the individual departments seek an identity in tandem with the expanding economy of Myrtle Beach. “Like our parks and rec department, they have a ton of swag. They work with kids all the time. The city seal doesn’t resonate with the hundreds or thousands of children that partic- ipate in our recreation programs. They wanted something more fun and reflective for parks and recreation,” Denari said. The parks and recreation department cre- ated their own logo and merchandise and Denari said there are about a dozen logos that exist within the municipality and this brand- ing project will also create consistency. Altman said the logo will help Myrtle Beach’s reputation of being outdated. “I think that revamping a logo that was designed in the ‘70s is a really good idea to start uplifting the image of the area and draw a potentially different type of consumer base here from the tourism perspective,” Altman said. Denari said since the project was for brand- ing rather than a simple logo design, the cho- sen bid had to meet certain qualifications of a firm. “The city, per law, per city ordinance, we have a whole procurement purchasing divi- sion page on our website. There’s links for local vendors to sign up to be part of our regis- try. So, when projects like this that are up their alley, so to speak, come up they get an auto- matic notice sent to them so they know that it is out and they can bid it,” Denari said. Altman said this procurement process is standard in the industry. “In the grand scheme of things, I think that if local designers want to do this, they can go get that work. All it takes is a little under- standing and know-how. And that know-how can be found online. It’s not a secret; it’s not something that’s hidden. There are plenty of websites devoted to creatives and the selling process, and how to pitch to larger agencies and other creatives,” he said. Nancy Mace on Monday, Aug. 4 offi- cially announced her campaign for governor of South Carolina, saying the state is at a piv- otal point and can’t afford to have “another empty suit” in the governor’s office. “South Carolina is tired of politicians who smile for the cameras, lie to your face and then vanish when it’s time to lead,” Mace said during her campaign announcement in Charleston. “I’m not one of them.” Mace is the latest to join a growing field of Republicans running for governor which include Attorney General Alan Wilson, Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette Congressman Ralph Norman and state Sen. Josh Kimbrell. After jumping into the race, Rep. Nancy Mace’s team announced the ‘Mother of all Town Halls Tour,’ a statewide series where she will travel across the state and meet voters face to face, share her message, and take questions directly from South Carolinians. And the first stop in her campaign came at the Veterans Cafe and Grille in Myrtle Beach. Almost two months since Lt. Gov. Pamela Evette — who is also seeking the Republican nomination for governor — held a town hall of her own at the same location. While it was her first stop in the county, Mace made it clear it wouldn’t be her last. Whenever any provision of this Ordinance refers to or cites a section of the South Carolina Code of Laws and that section is later amended, this Ordinance shall be deemed amended to refer to the amended section. 1.1.3 Jurisdiction This Ordinance shall apply to all property (land, buildings, structures, and uses) located within the corporate limits of the City of Conway, South Carolina, as permitted by law, and as may be expanded, contracted, or modified from time to time. 1.1.4 Applicability A. All development and use of land within the City of Conway shall conform to the requirements of this Ordinance. B. The provisions of this Ordinance shall apply to all zoning, land subdivision, site development, signage, landscaping, and related land use activities occurring after its effective date, unless specifically exempted. C. Applicability to Governmental Facilities. To the extent allowed by law, the provisions of this ordinance shall apply to development by the County, State, or federal government or its agencies, departments, or corporate services, or on land owned or otherwise controlled by the County, State, or federal government. 1.1.5 Relationship to Other Laws A. Where this Ordinance imposes a greater restriction than imposed by other local ordinances, regulations, private covenants, or agreements, the provisions of this Ordinance shall control. B. Compliance with this Ordinance does not relieve any person from complying with other applicable local, state or federal laws or regulations. C. Private Restrictions / Covenants 1. In accordance with SC Code of Laws § 6-29-1145, as amended, local planning agencies are required to inquire in application for a permit if the parcel of land is restricted by a recorded covenant that prohibits the proposed activity. Nothing within this Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) shall be construed to authorize the use of any land or structure in a manner that violates private deed restrictions, covenants, or other private agreements governing the use of land. The City of Conway does not enforce private deed restrictions or covenants and assumes no responsibility for interpreting or enforcing such agreements. -- 49 of 144 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 1 – General Provisions 3-3 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended xx, xx xxxx 1.1.6 Severability If any section or provision of this Ordinance (UDO) is declared invalid or unconstitutional by a court of competent jurisdiction, such declaration shall not affect the validity of this Ordinance (UDO) as a whole or any part thereof which is not specifically declared to be invalid or unconstitutional and shall continue in full force and effect. 1.1.7 Effective Date This Ordinance (UDO) shall take effect and be enforced from and after the date of its adoption by the City Council for the City of Conway, and supersedes and repeals any previous zoning, subdivision, or development regulations by the City of Conway to the extent of any conflict. 1.1.8 Preamble (Informational Reference) The City’s policy goals and planning philosophy underlying this ordinance are described in the Preamble, which is the original Ordinance adopting the Unified Development Ordinance, Ordinance 2011-12-12 (A), and is attached as Appendix A – Preamble, to this Article. The UDO is enacted and designed to exercise the full range of authority available to the City in accordance with State law to: A. Provide for adequate light, air, and open space; B. Prevent the overcrowding of land; C. Avoid undue concentration of population; D. Lessen congestion in the streets; E. Facilitate the creation of a convenient, attractive and harmonious community; F. Protect and preserve scenic, historic, or ecologically sensitive areas; G. Regulate the density and distribution of populations and the uses of buildings, structures, and land; H. Facilitate the adequate provision and availability of public facilities or services; I. Secure safety from fire, flood, and other dangers; and J.
