Single lots are two (2) acres or larger. 3.2.2 Rural Residential (RR) The intent of the RR District is to provide for the preservation and expansion of areas for very low density, detached single-family residential development in the City of Conway. The district shall present a rural character, promote quiet, livable neighborhoods, and prohibit uses that are incompatible with the residential nature of the surrounding area. 3.2.3 Low/Medium Density Residential (R-1) The intent of the R-1 District is to provide for the preservation and expansion of areas for low to medium density, detached single-family residential development in the City of Conway. The district shall present a relatively spacious character, promote quiet, livable neighborhoods, and prohibit uses that are incompatible with the residential nature of the surrounding area. [Amended 12/17/18 #ZA2018-12-17(A)] 3.2.4 Medium Density Residential (R-2) The intent of the R-2 District is to provide areas for medium density attached, detached, semi-attached and multi- family residential development in the City of Conway, and to prohibit uses that would substantially interfere with the development or continuation of residential structures in the District. 3.2.5 High Density Residential (R-3) The intent of the R-3 District is to provide areas for high-density attached, detached, semi-detached, and multifamily residential development in the City of Conway and to prohibit uses that would substantially interfere with the development or continuation of residential structures in the District. 3.2.6 Traditional Residential (R-4) The intent of the R-4 District is to allow undeveloped parcels of land to be subdivided and developed in a manner that utilizes traditional residential neighborhood principles that were common in the early part of the 20th Century. More specifically, the district is intended to provide for the configuration of blocks, lots, streets, open spaces, and other amenities that lend to creating a sense of community and social interaction. The characteristics of such developments generally include rectangular block configurations where streets run parallel and perpendicular to one another, intersect at or near 90-degree angles, and form blocks of similar size and shape. Centrally located open space for community recreation and leisure is required in order to compensate for the uniquely smaller lots of such developments. Service alleys providing access to the rear of lots are necessary in order to accommodate vehicular storage and public utility services. The design aspect of the individual homes is as critical to the creation of the sense of community as the design standards of the platted subdivision. Typically, homes should be built closer to streets and on raised foundations. Front porches, which create an ‘outside room’ combined with the close proximity of the homes to the sidewalks, promote social interaction which lends to creating a sense of community. -- 57 of 144 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 3 – Zoning Districts 3-4 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended July 21, 2025 3.2.7 Professional (P) The intent of the P District is to accommodate office, institutional, and residential uses in areas whose character is neither exclusively business nor residential in nature. ZA2018-12-17(A)] -- 59 of 144 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 3 – Zoning Districts 3-6 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended July 21, 2025 Section 3.3 – Special Use Districts 3.3.1 Waccamaw Riverfront District (WRD) The intent of the WRD District is to provide for the proper physical, social, and economic development of the City’s riverfront area in order to protect, promote and improve the public health, safety, morals, convenience, order, appearance, prosperity, and general welfare, including but not limited to: safeguarding the cultural, scenic, economic, environmental, and social heritage of the Waccamaw Riverfront on behalf of the City, Horry County and South Carolina; providing for adequate light, air, and public open space; encouraging efficient and economic practices in the process of development and redevelopment; making adequate provision for pedestrian and vehicular traffic; supporting the wise and efficient expenditures of public funds promoting safe and proper drainage; protecting lives and properties from the hazards of flooding; safeguarding water quality; promoting attractive and economically beneficial community and architectural appearance; protecting valuable wetlands trees, and other vegetation; encouraging natural and environmentally sound shoreline stabilization, promoting economic prosperity for the district and the City, and providing for adequate public access to the river and its shores. 3.3.2 Planned Development District (PD) The intent of the PD District is to provide for large-scale, quality development projects (three acres or larger) with mixed land uses which create a superior environment through unified development and provide for the application of design ingenuity while protecting surrounding developments. More specifically, the intent of the PD District is to permit: A. Flexibility in design to take the greatest advantage of natural land, trees, historical and other features; B. Accumulation of large areas of usable open space for recreation, preservation of natural amenities, and provision of community facilities; C. Creation of a variety of residential and compatible neighborhood arrangements that give the home occupant greater choice in selecting types of environments and living units; D. Clustering of one residential type for better use of land and open space; E. Allowance of sufficient freedom for the developer to take a creative approach to the use of land and related physical development, as well as utilizing innovative techniques to enhance the visual character of the city; F. Efficient use of land which may result in reduction in development and maintenances cost of street and utility systems; G. Simplification of the procedure for obtaining approval of proposed developments through simultaneous review by the city of proposed land use, site consideration, lot and setback consideration, public needs and requirements, and health and safety factors. -- 60 of 144 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 3 – Zoning Districts 3-7 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended July 21, 2025 3.3.3 Mixed Use Flexible Zone (MU) The intent of the Mixed-Use Flexible Zone is to encourage a mix of residential, professional and limited commercial development throughout the City of Conway that does not create excessive demands for vehicular parking. The requirements of the district are designed to promote mixed uses and provide a transition between residential and commercial properties and minimizing adverse effects to adjoining properties. The Mixed-Use District is a ‘floating zone’ which is defined as a zone that is described in the text of a zoning ordinance, but is unmapped (S.C. Code of Laws, Title 6, Chapter 29). Once a property is designated Mixed Use, it will then be mapped by amending the Official Zoning Map of the City of Conway. The floating zone may be applied to properties throughout the city through a rezoning application process – this applies only to properties that are identified as Mixed Use on the City of Conway’s official Future Land Use Map in the City of Conway Comprehensive Plan. 3.3.4 Mineral Mining Zone (MM) The Mineral Mining District (MM) is a flexible zoning district established for the purpose of providing for the development of needed mineral resources in areas where such resources exist subject to adequate safeguard for the conservation of the environment. Mineral mining, as used herein, applies to the extraction and processing of crushed stone, building stone, sand, clay, limestone, gravel deposits, and other minerals mined in a quarry type operation. The standards set forth in this section do not regulate or permit the extraction of metallic minerals, fossil fuels or other minerals not specifically enumerated above. 3.3.5 Institutional Campus District (IC) The intent of the IC, Institutional Campus district is to accommodate universities, colleges, or other large institutional schools in campus-like settings. The IC district is intended to promote and enhance the development and expansion of institutional campuses while minimizing the adverse impacts that can result when such uses are located near residential neighborhoods, and to ensure development that is coordinated with the provision of local infrastructure and public service capacities. Intent. Residential design standards are not an attempt to stifle design but are meant to inspire good architectural design while protecting and enhancing the aesthetic and visual character of residential developments within the City of Conway. More specifically, to: 1. avoid monotony in design; 2. protect and preserve the character of residential areas within the city and permit continued development of a compatible nature on vacant properties that are or will be proposed for residential development within the city limits; 3. enhance the character and function of city streets; 4. promote original and high-quality design, and reduce tract or production-style homes; 5. maintain and enhance property values through appropriate aesthetic and functional design considerations; 6. deemphasize garages as major visual elements along local residential streets; 7. encourage design details, which add visual interest and encourage outdoor living spaces; and 8. implement the city’s goals and objectives within the city’s comprehensive plan related to providing a mix of housing types and promoting quality site development and design that enhances Conway’s sense of place within neighborhoods. Applicability The IC District provides flexibility for large institutional uses, including college campuses, universities, medical facility complexes and similar campus-oriented institutions, to develop and function as independent campus areas with unique needs and characteristics. The district provides flexibility beyond the IN District by allowing the applicant to create their own master plan for future development, rather than submitting individual developments for review under the IN District. The master plan allows flexibility and provides uniformity and arrangement of buildings and spaces that is not possible when development occurs on a lot-by-lot basis. Development within the IC District that complies with an approved, valid and unexpired master plan shall be exempt from individual zoning review. B. Permitted Uses The principal use within the IC District shall include colleges, universities, technical schools, or hospitals, as well as uses supporting and ancillary to those institutions, including but not limited to: campus housing, bookstores, food services, recreational and athletic fields and facilities, auditoriums, parking lots and structures, clinics, research facilities, and utility facilities. C. Minimum General Requirements Flexibility from the dimensional and design requirement of the IC District shall be provided by allowing a unique Institutional Master Plan. However, the following minimum requirements shall be adhered to throughout the IC District: 1. Open Space Requirement. A minimum of 25% of net developable land within the IC District shall be provided as public open space, including parks, plazas, trails, greenways, water features, or natural open space. 2. General Requirements. All other standards under the GCO and VCO shall apply. D. Boards and Procedures Section 14.2 – Board of Zoning Appeals 14.2.1 Duties and Powers Duties and powers of the Board of Zoning Appeals are derived from Section 6-29-800 of the South Carolina Code of Laws. A. To hear and decide appeals where it is alleged the City Planner Zoning Administrator or their designee, erred in an order, requirement, decision, or determination. In such cases, the Board may reverse or affirm, wholly or in part, the City Planner’s Zoning Administrator or their designee’s action. The Board shall have all the powers of the City Planner Zoning Administrator or their designee in such cases and may direct the issuance of a permit. B. To hear and decide appeals for variances in specific cases when a strict application of the zoning ordinance would cause an unnecessary hardship, and approval of such variance would not be contrary to public interest or undermine the spirit of the zoning ordinance. The fact that property may be used more profitably if a variance is granted is not grounds for a variance. The Board may attach conditions to a variance that address location, character, or other features of a proposed building, structure, or use, in order to protect the established property values in the surrounding area or to promote the public health, safety, or general welfare of the community. The Board may grant a variance for an unnecessary hardship if it makes and explains in writing all of the following findings. 1. Extraordinary conditions: There are extraordinary and exceptional conditions pertaining to the particular piece of property. 2. Other Property: The extraordinary and exceptional conditions do not generally apply to other property in the vicinity. 3. Utilization: Because of the extraordinary or exceptional conditions, the application of the ordinance to a particular piece of property would effectively prohibit or unreasonably restrict the utilization of the property. 4. Detriment: The authorization of a variance will not be of substantial detriment to adjacent property or the public good, and the character of the district will not be harmed by granting a variance. C. An affirmative vote of two-thirds (2/3) of the Board members present and voting shall be required before a variance may be granted for a use of land, a building or a structure that is prohibited in a given district, provided however that City Council may overrule the decision of the Board within thirty (30) days following the decision of the Board. In order to grant a use variance, the following finding must be determined and made part of the record: the use requested can be documented to have been a past use of the property; however, historic use alone may not be sufficient to grant a use variance. The fact that property may be utilized more profitably, should a variance be granted, may not be considered grounds for any variance. 14.2.2 Procedure for Appeals and Variances A. The property shall be a minimum of one (1) acre in size for every The keeping of fowl is limited to five (5) birds or other domesticated types of fowl per acre. C. Setbacks & Fencing: All domestic livestock or fowl must be kept at least 25 feet from all property lines with fencing adequate to retain any livestock within the required setbacks. For properties abutting a residential district (R, R-1 through R-4), the minimum setbacks shall be increased to 50 feet from all property lines adjacent to the residential district. [Amended 12/17/18 #ZA2018-12-17(A)] C. Accessory Requirement. Livestock and/or fowl, as well as any structures related to the keeping of such animals, shall be located upon the same property as the residential use, except as provided below: 1. Exemption for properties zoned FA and five (5) acres or more in area. Structures associated with the non-commercial keeping of livestock / fowl may be permitted as a standalone use in the FA district, under the following provisions: a. Such structure(s) shall comply with the setbacks for the zoning district in which it is located, and not less than twenty-five (25) feet from all property boundaries; whichever is greater. b. Such structure(s) shall comply with all requirements for accessory structures in Section 5.2.1 in the event a residential dwelling or other permitted principal use is constructed. 1. Non-Commercial: The keeping, breeding, or training of any animals for monetary gain or profit shall be deemed a commercial business and is prohibited in all residential districts. D. Properties zoned IN. In addition to the above, The non-commercial keeping of chickens or other domesticated fowl is permitted as a conditional use in the IN zoning district under the following -- 143 of 144 -- provisions under the following conditions: 1. Roosters are prohibited. 2. The breeding of chickens or any other type of fowl is prohibited. 3. Non-domesticated or exotic species, including but not limited to peacocks, ostriches, emus, raptors, etc., are prohibited. 4. Fowl shall be adequately contained within the property and shall not be permitted to run at large. A chicken coop with a fenced in area adequate for the chickens/fowl health and to safely and healthy move about is required. Said coop shall be considered an accessory structure and subject to the conditions in Article 5.2.1. Chickens shall be penned at all times. 5. It shall be unlawful for any person to permit or allow any chickens to run at large. 6. No person shall keep chickens within the city limits in such a manner that a nuisance is created. 7. The keeping of fowl chickens must be for educational purposes only. [Ord. ZA2017-10-16 (C)] E. Use Not to be a Nuisance. No person shall keep livestock or fowl within the city limits in such a manner that a nuisance is created. F. Non-Commercial Use Only. The keeping of livestock and fowl, as provided herein, is for non- commercial purposes only. The keeping, breeding, or training of such animals for monetary gain or profit shall be deemed a commercial business and shall be prohibited. -- 144 of 144 --

title: APPD_9.4.25 PC MINUTES
text: PC 9/4/2025 CITY OF CONWAY PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING THURSDAY, September 4, 2025 Planning & Building Dept. Conference Room — 196 Laurel Street Present: Jessica Wise, George Ulrich, Allan Cornell, Thomas J. Anderson III, David Sligh, Greg Bryson, Ellen Watkins, Kendall Brown Absent: Staff: Jessica Hucks, Planning Director; Katie Dennis, Planner; Marsha Ponder, Planning & Development Assistant; Brent Gerald, Planner; Louis Smith, IT Others: Vicki Smink, John Powell, Ellen Powell, Sue Taylor, Orion Loftis, Frank Derosa, James Baldwin, Michael McCarty, Brenda McCarty, Susan Carr, Maureen Strittmatter, Edward Poole, James Riley Best, Susan Daniels, Roger Daniels, Lew Daniels, Joe Ruggio, Mary Ruggio, AnneMarie Olinger, Casey Jones, Anthony Motola, Haylee Clark, Alex Bates, Louis Malfara, Debra Malfara and Others. I. CALL TO ORDER II. Il. IV. Chairperson Wise called the meeting to order at approximately 5:30 pm. APPROVAL OF MINUTES Ulrich made a motion, seconded by Cornell to approve the August 7, 2025, minutes as written. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. PUBLIC INPUT AnneMarie Olinger, Joe Ruggio, Joseph Palmier, and Edward Poole spoke during public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Sligh to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. PUBLIC HEARINGS A. REZONING REQUEST(S) 1. Previously Deferred...Request to rezone approximately 109.13 +/- acres of property located at or near the corner of Cultra Rd. and Oak Street (PIN 325-00-00-0011) from the Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) district to the City of Conway Medium-Density Residential (R-2) and Conservation Preservation (CP) districts upon annexation into the City of Conway. Board member Anderson submitted a Recusal Statement form and abstained from voting on this item due to a declared conflict of interest. Anderson did not participate in the discussion or decision-making process. Hucks stated the subject property is proposed to be annexed into the City for residential development. The property is within the city’s utility service area, thus requiring annexation to be requested. Surrounding developments — Rivertown Row North, Kingston Bay and Elmhurst, are also zoned Medium-Density Residential (R-2). Midtown Village, which directly abuts this property, is zoned High-Density Residential (R-3). A large portion of the subject property is located within the AE flood zone, which runs through the middle of the parcel (see attached maps). While development is permitted within flood zones, provided the affected property meets the required elevation, staff does not support rezoning portion(s) of property within a flood zone to a district 1 PC 9/4/2025 that would permit residential development. In 2023, Council adopted an ordinance that permits parcels containing environmentally sensitive areas to be split-zoned, which is otherwise prohibited, with such areas being zoned Conservation Preservation (CP) upon annexation of property or when property is proposed to be rezoned. Given that there is a small portion of the property within the floodway, in which no development can occur, and that the general area has been prone to flooding, should annexation proceed, this would be an opportunity to discuss the possibility of zoning the portions within a flood zone / floodway to CP with the applicant. In this instance, the applicant would need to submit a survey showing the areas within the flood zone / floodway so that they could be mapped accordingly should the split zoning be preferred. Surrounding in-City zoning includes Neighborhood Commercial (NC), High-Density Residential (R-3), Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1), and Medium-Density Residential (R-2). The area is primarily single- family residential, with limited established commercial uses. There is a gas station/convenience store (Sun House) with a few tenant spaces containing limited commercial uses, including a dog grooming business, immediately adjacent to the subject property. Surrounding County zoning includes mostly residential, including Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF20) on 20,000 sq. ft. min. lot sizes, and Residential, including mobile homes (MSF20), also on 20,000 sq. ft. min. lot sizes. Abutting property is also zoned Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA). The John T. Henry Auction location is near the subject property, which is also zoned CFA. Horry Electric is also nearby, on the opposite side of Cultra Rd, which is zoned Office/Professional/Institutional (OPI). The City’s future land use map provides three (3) future land use designations for the subject property. For the portion with frontage along Cultra Rd, the future land use is shown as Neighborhood Commercial (NC). A larger portion of the property is shown as Conservation Preservation (CP) on the city’s future land use map. The portion abutting Midtown Village and Conway Christian School is shown as High-Density Residential on the future land use map. Additional information can be found in the packet for the September 4, 2025 PC mtg. Staff recommends, in addition to holding the required public hearing, that Planning Commission conduct a thorough review of the request and make an informed recommendation to City Council. The applicant was present to answer questions. Michael McCarty, Louis Malfara, Ellen Powell, Brenda McCarty, AnneMarie Olinger and others spoke during public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Sligh to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. The board, staff and applicant discussed the request at length. Wise made a motion to approve the rezoning request as presented. Ulrich seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. 2. Request to rezone approximately 0.39 +/- acres of property located at 5206 Columbia Street (PIN 383-08-03-0002) from the Horry County Single Family Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF10) district to the City of Conway Low- Medium Density Residential (R-1) district upon annexation. Hucks stated that the property was transferred to the current owners on August 4, 2025. The property is lot 4 in block 3 of the College Park subdivision. Restrictive Covenants were recorded on August 6, 2025. The property contains a single-family dwelling. Property abutting the subject parcel was annexed in May of 2024 and property directly across the subject parcel was annexed in August of 2024. Annexation is being requested due to the requirements for connection to city utilities. PC 9/4/2025 The property abuts the Oakbrook development (city limits, zoned R-2). County zoning, including CFA and MSF20 (Residential, including mobile homes, on min. lot sizes of 20,000 sq. ft.), containing residential dwellings or vacant property, is also adjacent to the subject property. The City’s future land use map identifies the property as Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). Additional information can be found in the packet for the September 4, 2025 PC mtg. Staff recommends, in addition to holding the required public hearing, that Planning Commission conduct a thorough review of the request and make an informed recommendation to City Council for appropriate zoning. The applicant was not present. No public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Ulrich to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. The board and staff discussed the request at length. Wise made a motion to approve the rezoning request as presented. Anderson seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. 3. Request to rezone approximately 10.68 +/- acres of property located at the intersection of Hwy 501 and Hwy 548 (PINs 326-00-00-0026 & 326-09-03-0006), from the Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) district to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district upon annexation. Hucks stated that the applicants are seeking to annex the subject parcels into the City for commercial development. The proposed type of commercial establishments are not known at this time; however, the requested zoning upon annexation is Highway Commercial (HC), which is also consistent with the future land use map designation. The property abuts Pinnacle Storage (PS Southeast), which is zoned Light Industrial (City limits); Tractor Supply, zoned Highway Commercial (HC) (City limits), and is directly across the Parker’s Kitchen development, which is currently under construction in the city limits, zoned HC. The City’s future land use map also identifies the property as Highway Commercial (HC). Additional information can be found in the packet for the September 4, 2025 PC mtg. Staff recommends, in addition to holding the required public hearing, that Planning Commission conduct a thorough review of the request and make an informed recommendation to City Council for appropriate zoning. The board and staff discussed the request at length. No public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Ulrich to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. The applicant was present to answer questions. Sligh made a motion to approve the rezoning request as presented. Anderson seconded the motion, and the motion carried. B. TEXT AMENDMENT(S) 1. Requesting Deferral...Amendments to Article 2 — Definitions, Article 4 — Use Tables, Article 5 — Specific Use Regulations, and Article 6 - Design Standards of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding uses in the Highway Commercial (HC) and Light Industrial (LI) zoning districts. PC 9/4/2025 Ulrich made a motion to defer the amendments to Article 2 — Definitions, Article 4 — Use Tables, Article 5 — Special Use Regulations, and Article 6, to the October 2” meeting. Sligh seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. 2. Requesting Deferral...Amendments to Article 2 — Definitions, Article 4 — Use Tables, and Article 6 - Design Standards, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding the requirements and subdistricts of the Waccamaw Riverfront District (WRD). Ulrich made a motion to defer the amendments to article 2 — Definitions, Article 4 — Use Tables, Article 5 — Special Use Regulations, and Article 6, to the October 2"4 meeting. Sligh seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. 3. Previously Deferred...Amendments to Article 1 — Preamble, Article 2 — Definitions, Article 3 — Zoning Districts, Article 6 — Design Standards, Article 13 — Administrative Agencies and Functions, and Article 14— Boards and Procedures, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding requirements for annexation and amendments to the city’s official zoning map, amendments relating to City Boards and procedures, adoption of a special exception process for specific uses, and revisions to language in these Articles of the UDO for clarity and consistency. Hucks provided an overview of the request, the proposed amendments are part of a larger effort to clean up several parts of the UDO, which has been in process since early 2024. In addition to this cleanup effort, some of the proposed amendments will address recent guidance provided by the Municipal Association with respect to the process for annexation and zoning of property. Going forward, annexation and zoning map amendments will be separate ordinances considered by Council. These changes are outlined in Article 13. Several of these amendments are simply relocated from Article 6. Other amendments include, but are not limited to, the following: e Article 1 has been amended to include several provisions, such as an intent and purpose, applicability of the UDO, transition rules/vested rights, limitation of liability, among other legal provisions. The “preamble” of the UDO will be moved to an appendix in Article 1. e Article 3: moved the CCU Neighborhood Overlay ordinance to Article 6, to be in the overlay section of the UDO, similar to the GCO, VCO, and MSO are located. e Article 6: removed language to add to Article 13 instead. e Article 14: Minor revisions to the language regarding the BZA and TRC. Additional information can be found in the packet for the September 4, 2025 PC mtg. Staff recommends, that in addition to holding the public hearing, that Planning Commission review the proposed amendments and make an informed recommendation to City Council. There was no public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Anderson to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. The board and staff briefly discussed the request. Wise made a motion to approve the amendments as presented. Ulrich seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. PC 9/4/2025 4. Amendments to Article 4-— Use Tables and Article 5 — Specific Use Regulations, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) regarding requirements for noncommercial keeping of livestock or fowl and related accessory uses and/or structures in the Forest Agriculture (FA) zoning district. Hucks provided an overview of the request, the city’s footprint is extending to more rural areas of the county, and several large tracts are shown as being Forest Agriculture (FA) on the future land use map; many of them exceeding 100 acres in size. The intent of the FA district is to establish and preserve areas for agricultural or passive recreation. Most agricultural uses require structure(s) for farming equipment or stables for animals. However, the current language of the UDO would not permit such structures without there being a principal use and structure (i.e. in conjunction with a single-family dwelling). The proposed amendment carves out an exception for the FA district only for the ability to have accessory structures relating to farming; particularly, the keeping of livestock / fowl, without the requirement to have a principal structure, but with conditions, including that it would be applicable to parcels zoned FA that are a minimum of 5 acres in size. This amendment also includes other revisions relating to the noncommercial keeping of livestock / fowl and adds the Rural Residential (RR) district as one of the districts in which the use is permitted as a conditional use. The amendments are included on the following pages. Note that the amendments are applicable to “noncommercial” activities, not commercial activities. Commercial agriculture uses in FA already require a minimum lot size of 10 acres. Additional information can be found in the packet for the September 4, 2025 PC mtg. There was no public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Anderson to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. The board and staff briefly discussed the request. Bryson made a motion to approve the amendment as presented. Cornell seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. V. BOARD INPUT None VI. STAFF INPUT Hucks shared details regarding the upcoming text amendments scheduled for presentation. VI. ADJOURNMENT A motion was made to adjourn the meeting. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. The meeting adjourned at approximately 6:57 pm. Approved and signed this z day of OUBEC , 2025. . a : Jessica Wise, Chairperson

Conference Room – 196 Laurel Street Present: Jessica Wise, George Ulrich, Allan Cornell, Ellen Watkins, Thomas J. Anderson III, David Sligh Absent: Greg Bryson, Kendall Brown Staff: Katie Dennis, Planner; Marsha Ponder, Planning & Development Assistant; Brent Gerald, Planner, Kym Wilkerson, Zoning Administrator; Charlie Crosby, IT; Sydney Livingston, Summer Intern Others: Fred Archer, Beverly Marlowe, Ann Hutson, Mack Hutson, Andreas Hoppe, Cecil Brown, Monica Brown, Ruth Cronin, Charles Pency I. CALL TO ORDER Chairperson Wise called the meeting to order at approximately 5:30 pm. II. APPROVAL OF MINUTES Ulrich made a motion, seconded by Cornell to approve the June 5, 2025, minutes as written. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. III. PUBLIC INPUT There was no public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Cornell to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. IV. PUBLIC HEARINGS A. ANNEXATION/REZONING(S) 1. Previously Tabled … Request to annex approximately 1.43+/- acres of property located at 104 Gardner Lacy Rd (PIN 399-01-04-0006), and request to rezone from the Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) district to the City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) district. Dennis stated on August 27th of 2024, the applicant went to the City’s Water Dept. to apply for water services on the subject property. The applicant was informed at that time that because the property is contiguous to property in the City limits, they would have to request annexation. Upon review of the property, staff noticed that per County land records, there were permits pending for the subject property. The only thing holding up permit issuance at that point was the requirement for the applicant to provide proof that City utilities would be connected. The permit was applied for at Horry County on February 27, 2024. The use specified on the permit was for a new auto shop. At the time the permit was applied for at the county, the subject property was NOT contiguous. However, the adjacent parcel, the Founders -- 3 of 98 -- PC 7/10/2025 2 National Golf property, was currently going through the annexation process and had received First Reading on February 19 th . Final Reading occurred on March 18 th , subsequently making this parcel contiguous to City limits. As such, staff informed the County at the time that no permits could be issued for the property due to the requirement to annex before permitting, which would then need to occur once the property is annexed and would be issued by the City. Surrounding uses/Zoning Districts: The property abuts parcels zoned City of Conway City of Conway Highway Commercial (HC) and Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) and Horry County Limited Industrial (LI). Adjacent uses include the property containing the former entrance road for the MB National Golf Course, a gas station (fronting Hwy 501), Southern Sun Awnings, and Domino’s Pizza is located across Gardner Lacy Rd. The zoning designation applied for on the annexation and rezoning paperwork is the Highway Commercial (HC) district. Per Section 3.2.10 of the UDO, the intent of the Highway Commercial (HC) district is to provide compatible locations to serve the automobile-oriented commercial activities in harmony with major highway developments, reduce traffic congestions and to enhance the aesthetic atmosphere of the City. City Council approved first reading of the annexation and rezoning at their September 3 rd meeting. However, during a workshop at their September 16, 2024 meeting, staff made council aware that the applicant has received his stormwater approval, DHEC approval and SCDOT encroachment permits, and the civil plans had already been approved through the County. If the applicant were forced to start this process over in the City’s jurisdiction, it would create an unnecessary financial hardship that may be impossible for the property owner and business owner to overcome. For this reason, staff preferred tabling final reading at the time until the county issued Certificate of Occupancies for the property. Update – July 2025: The structure is still in the process of being constructed. Council still has the ability to defer or table final reading of the annexation, should they choose to do so. Regardless, the request is required to receive a recommendation from Planning Commission with regard to the proposed zoning upon annexation. Additionally, property directly across from this property was annexed into the city limits in January 2025 (former Wolverine Brass properties) as Light Industrial (LI). Additional information can be found in the packet for the July 10, 2025 PC mtg. Staff recommends, in addition to holding the required public hearing, that Planning Commission conduct a thorough review of the request and make an informed recommendation to City Council. The applicant, Fred Archer, was present to answer any questions. No public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Sligh to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. -- 4 of 98 -- PC 7/10/2025 3 The board and staff discussed the request at length. Wise made a motion to approve the annexation and rezoning request to city of Conway Highway commercial district. Cornell seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. 2. Request to annex approximately 0.79+/- acres of property located at 150 Amber Lane (PIN 367-14-04-0004), and rezone from the Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) district to the City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1) district. Dennis stated the annexation application was submitted by the property owners, as a requirement for connection to city services. According to Horry County Land Records, the property was transferred into the owner’s names on July 24, 2024. The property contains an existing brick single-family home as well as a mobile home. A restrictive covenant was recorded on April 17, 2025. As part of the required review by the Technical Review Committee (TRC), all were asked to comment on the request for annexation. Below are their comments: Building: recommends disapproval – This is not an area we normally patrol with property maintenance and the building inspectors are too busy as it is. Flood: Approved Fire: Approved GIS: NA Police: recommends disapproval – We currently have few properties nearby and creates a reverse donut hole where we generally do not patrol the area. It also brings us closer to another school, and we are at capacity for our SRO program. If all contiguous properties associated with this owner come in, we will have Hwy 501 corner and frontage access, which takes us away from the school and into a more commercial area. Public Utilities: Approved Public Works: Approved Sanitation: Approved The Future Land Use Map of the Comprehensive Plan identifies this property as Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1). While development is permitted within flood zones, provided the affected property meets the required elevation, staff does not support rezoning portion(s) of property within a flood zone to a district that would permit residential development. In 2023, Council adopted an ordinance that permits parcels containing environmentally sensitive areas to be split- zoned, which is otherwise prohibited, with such areas being zoned Conservation Preservation (CP) upon annexation of property or when property is proposed to be rezoned. Given that there is a small portion of the property within the floodway, in which no development can occur, and that the general area has been prone to flooding, should annexation proceed, this would be an opportunity to discuss the possibility of zoning the portions within a flood zone / floodway to CP with the applicant. In this instance, the applicant would need to submit a survey showing the areas within the flood zone / floodway so that they could be mapped accordingly should the split zoning be preferred. Dear Planning Director, I am writing to formally express my objection to the proposed annexation and rezoning of approximately 107.75 acres located on Cultra Road and Oak Street from Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA) to City of Conway Medium-Density Residential (R-2). Trees play a vital role in stormwater absorption, and their removal could exacerbate flooding during hurricanes and severe storms, which are common in our area. 2. ORDINANCE: NA AGENDA SECTION: Public Hearings ISSUE: Previously Tabled – Amendments to Article 2 – Definitions, Article 4 – Use Tables, and Article 5 – Specific Use Regulations, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding requirements for Day Care Facilities. BACKGROUND: This issue was initially discussed at the February 2025 Planning Commission meeting. The issue arose out of an inquiry from a prospective childcare provider, looking to open a part- time child-care facility in a strip mall setting. Currently, the City’s ordinance does not address part- time child care, or any other type of child care which the state deems to be “legally exempt”, meaning the child care center / program is open less than four (4) hours per day, no more than two (2) days per week, and on an irregular schedule, such as on school holidays. Upon closer review, staff looked at ways to include more options for child care within the UDO, compliant with state law, without compromising the safety and security of children. There were several factors considered when drafting the proposed amendments: • According to a 2024 article from the Children’s Trust of South Carolina, one of the most significant reasons for the lack of workforce participation is the shortage of childcare. Childcare challenges center around three primary factors: access, affordability, and quality. - Access: 42% of South Carolinians live in a childcare “desert”, meaning there are 3 young children for every licensed “spot.” - Affordability: the low supply of available slots drive up costs. The average cost for center- based childcare for an infant (in 2024) is approximately $9,000 per year. - Quality: finding high-quality childcare can be a challenge due to the high (employee) turnover rates and poor employee compensation. • Disparities relating to childcare (cost; access) disproportionately affect low-income and minority families because they limit workforce participation, and exacerbate inequalities in education, health and economic opportunities. Even middle-income families struggle to afford high-quality childcare, and subsidy programs often have long waiting lists or strict eligibility requirements. • Many localities include childcare regulations in their ordinances that create a barrier to home- based providers, such as requirements for home modifications, and zoning codes – including Conway’s, have not been updated to accommodate home-based care. These requirements also disproportionately affect minority or low-income women, who are most likely to seek licensing for an in-home childcare program. -- 79 of 98 -- STAFF REPORT Amendment to UDO regarding requirements for Day Care Facilities - Lack of centralized coordination between the multiple agencies who provide oversight of childcare (i.e. DSS, First Steps, DHEC) contribute to the gaps in service, inefficiencies, and frustration of families and providers trying to navigate the complex systems in place. What changes are advocated by the American Planning Association? • Reviewing current regulations regarding childcare facilities and amend, as needed, to remove barriers to parents entering or re-entering the workforce. • Support legislation (i.e. zoning amendments) which provide for childcare in locations convenient to neighborhoods and in public facilities such as schools, recreation centers and social service centers. Procedures should not be overly burdensome and should be related to size and land use impacts associated with the proposed facility. • Remove obstacles to group and family childcare in all zoning districts, in safe and appropriate locations for children. • Support legislation (local or state) which provides for small childcare homes as permitted land uses in all zoning districts without standard home occupation restrictions. • Support federal, state and local legislation providing for childcare needs assessments and for planning to be performed at the state and local level. Where the proposed amendments included in the proposed ordinance could make a real impact: • Permits family and group child care homes in residential areas as conditional uses, removing a major zoning barrier; • Provides economic opportunities for individuals looking to become a family or group child care home provider; • Aligns local definitions and use standards with DSS categories, helping to prevent conflicts; • Helps small providers navigate compliance without confusion; • Helps reduce regulatory burdens for home-based providers. Please review the attached amendments to Section 5.1.7 of the UDO and the Table (attached) breaking down the proposed amendments. While the proposed amendments are a first step in addressing child care disparities at a local regulatory level, there are still opportunities to strengthen equity impacts for low-income families, minority entrepreneurs, and working parents with nontraditional schedules.
