Purpose. Through the use of Best Management Practices (BMP’s) to protect onsite and offsite water resources, a variety of BMP’s can preserve site hydrology and maintain or reduce pre-development run-off volumes and rates. New development shall minimize off-site stormwater runoff, promote on-site filtration, and minimize the discharge of pollutants to ground and surface water. Every development over three acres shall at all times have in place a plan approved by the City of Conway that articulates sustainable stormwater management initiatives. In addition to other requirements set by the City of Conway, the Storm Water Management Plan shall include storm water management performance standards. Post development peak discharge rates should not exceed pre- development peak rates. B. Storm Water Management Performance Standards 1. Provisions for Stormwater Management. a. Rate Control. Storm water drainage systems shall manage the peak rate of discharge from the Development, incorporating the maximum permissible release rate allowed by the City of Conway. Untreated, direct stormwater discharges to wetlands or surface waters are not allowed. b. Volume Control. Storm water drainage systems shall reduce the volume of runoff from a development by one of the following measures: 1) Capture first one-half inch of runoff from all impervious surfaces in accordance with volume control BMP’s; or 2) achieve a fifteen (15) percent reduction in impervious surfaces from existing conditions. 2. Provisions for Sediment and Erosion Control. Erosion and sediment controls must be implemented to remove 80% of the average annual load of total suspended solids. C. Stormwater Management Design Techniques. Multiple Storm Water Management Techniques (Best Management Practices or BMPs) shall be applied to a development parcel in order to accomplish the above stated rate and volume controls. BMPs shall include the following methods of infiltration. 1. Bioswale. Bio-swales are open, linear channels that filter stormwater as the water flows through vegetation to the discharge point. Although their width and length vary as needed to achieve function, at a minimum they are two feet wide at the bottom and have a maximum slope of 2.5:1. Rain will not stand for more than four (4) hours in a bioswale before infiltrating. A bioswale often includes a perforated pipe for emergency overflow situations. 2. Filter Strips. A landscape strip usually underlain by open graded aggregate with no fines. 3. Permeable Pavers. A paving system that allows water to move through the driving surface into the stone base below. Permeable pavers are individual clay or concrete pavers that provide a solid ground surface and strong enough to take heavy loads, like large vehicles, while at the same time allowing water to filter through the surface and reach the underlying soils. Permeable pavers shall be utilized in commercial and residential paved areas such as parking lots, sidewalks, storage yards, building entryways, plazas and patios. Design requirements include the following: a. Use surface material that allows infiltration. b. A minimum 6-inch depth of aggregate base/storage bed shall be used below the permeable pavement surface. c. Provide positive drainage from the permeable surface (slope surface at 1% to 2%). -- 115 of 128 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 9 – Landscaping, and Buffering and Tree Preservation Standards 9-26 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended d. Provide surface conveyance system as if material was impervious. Drain stormwater to a designed discharge point. e. Perforated overflow pipe design shall be designed and evaluated by project engineer or geotechnical engineer. 4. Vegetated Roof. A vegetated roof system designed to detain rain water on the building’s roof. In general, the vegetated roof is planted with species adaptable to drought conditions. 5. Cistern. A closed system that re-uses rain water for various landscape uses and/or internal building recycling. 6. Rain Garden. A vegetated garden space that filters rain water. Rain gardens are shallow depressions in the landscape and are designed to hold and filters runoff. They are amended with bioengineered soil and vegetated with plants that are adapted to both wet and dry conditions. 7. Native Vegetation. See Section 9.5.3 for approved plants and trees for bio retention areas. 8. Perforated Pipe. The use of permeable pipe embedded in open-graded aggregate, in lieu of concrete pipe, shall be the preferred method for stormwater conveyance. D. Few communities can actually boast that they build streets around trees as Conway does. Few communities attach names and historical significance to particular trees as Conway does. The live oak trees, which line many streets within the city, are probably the city's most prized and most protected natural resource. Local legend has it that when the large oaks along Main Street were threatened by the construction of the railroad in 1887, Mrs. Mary Beaty, who lived near the Wade Hampton Oak, appeared with a loaded shotgun and demanded that the construction workers "touch not a single bough." The actions of Mary Beaty have inspired the citizens of Conway to actively protect the live oak trees as well as certain other native tree species. It is felt that Mrs. Beaty's actions that day were the genesis of tree protection, not only in Conway, but in the State of South Carolina. 9.8.2 Intent A. The intent of the City of Conway tree protection ordinance is to accomplish the following: 1. To provide for the protection, preservation, proper maintenance, and use of trees and woodlands; 2. To minimize disturbance and prevent damage from erosion and destruction of the natural habitat without denying the reasonable use and enjoyment of the property within the city; 3. To protect trees and woodlands (including other forms of vegetation) for their economic support of local property values and for their natural beauty, wilderness character, or geological, ecological or historical significance; 4. To address the public concern for these valued natural resources in the interest of health, safety, and general welfare of the residents of the City of Conway; 5. To encourage the beautification, air-cooling and purification, noise abatement, property value enhancement and the other attributes of trees within a city; 6. To naturally control flooding and erosion, moderate noise pollution, dust, and other airborne pollutants, moderate the city climate and shelter and feed wildlife; 7. To enable citizens to prevent and control the spread of diseases, to preserve trees in the path of development, and to avoid the unnecessary cost associated with sewer clogging, sidewalk replacement and tree-related accidents. 9.8.3 Applicability This chapter shall apply to all trees of any type protected or landmark trees located on public or private property inside the city limits of the City of Conway, South Carolina. Please refer to Section 9.8.10, Tree permits required, for the applicability of each type of permit. 9.8.4 Jurisdiction The city arborist, or their designee shall be responsible for the administration of all provisions of this chapter and for public tree management. Best Management Practices: Forest management practices developed pursuant to federal water quality legislation, to minimize or prevent non-point source water pollutions established by the SC Forestry Commission. -- 118 of 128 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 9 – Landscaping, and Buffering and Tree Preservation Standards 9-29 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended D. Caliper: A caliper measurement shall be measured six (6) inches above the soil line, or across the stump, in the event the tree has been severed at less than 12 inches above the soil line. E. Critical root zone: That area of tree roots under the canopy measured to be no less than one and one- half (1 ½) feet in radius for every inch of trunk diameter measured four and one-half (4 ½) feet above the ground. F. Diameter at breast height (d.b.h.): The diameter measurement of a tree is measured at four and one- half (4 ½) feet above ground level, commonly referred to as d.b.h. 1. Forks located less than one (1) foot from the ground are to be treated as separate trees and measured at standard DBH. The square root of each DBH (sum of the square of each) is used to derive total DBH. a. Total DBH= where: b. "a" and "b" are the DBH of split trunks. 2. Forks located between one (1) foot and four and a half (4.5) feet from the ground are to be treated as separate trees and calculated with the formula above but measured from three and a half (3.5) feet from the pitch, or at the start of the fork. 3. Forks located at or greater than four and a half (4.5) feet from the ground are measured just below the fork beneath the swelling. See Figure 7 (below): Figure 7: DBH for Forks located at or above 4.5 feet F. Drip line: An imaginary vertical line extending downward from the outermost tips of the tree branches to ground level. G. Grading: the process of leveling / releveling the ground to a specific elevation or slope to create a more suitable topography for development of a site, to ensure proper stormwater drainage, and control soil erosion and sedimentation during and after construction. “Mass” grading typically involves the clearing of trees and other vegetation. H. Grubbing: The removal of understory vegetation, stumps, roots and other debris which does not remove any trees with a d.b.h. of four (4) inches or greater. I. Hazard tree: A tree, or tree part that may be dangerous and is likely to fail and cause damage or injury, and the likelihood of failure exceeds an acceptable level of risk. The city arborist shall make such determination. -- 119 of 128 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 9 – Landscaping, and Buffering and Tree Preservation Standards 9-30 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended J. Pruning: The cutting or removing of any part of the branching structure of a tree in the crown, trunk or root areas. K. Public nuisance trees (trees that have become): Any tree with an untreatable disease or insect pest problem; dead trees or trees in irreversible decline; a tree or limb(s) that obstruct streetlights, traffic signs, the free passage of pedestrians or vehicles; a tree that poses a threat to public safety or property. L. Silviculture: The art and science of controlling the establishment, growth, competition, health, and quality of forests and woodlands to meet the diverse needs and values of landowners and society on a sustainable basis. M. Tree: Any self-supporting woody plant growing upon the earth that provides single or multiple trunks with potential d.b.h. of two (2) inches and grows to an overall height of 15 feet or more. N. Tree Protection Plan: a plan identifying the location, species and size (d.b.h.) of existing trees as well as trees that are proposed to be removed, including the tree protection areas and the means of protection. The Tree Protection Plan shall also include the location, species and size of all trees proposed to be replanted on the site as mitigation. O. Tree removal: The cutting or removal of 50 percent or more of the crown, trunk, or root system of a tree, or causing the death of a tree through damaging, poisoning, or other direct or indirect action. P. Tree survey: A survey plan prepared by a South Carolina Licensed Surveyor, registered forester or ISA certified arborist indicating an accurate location, size, and species, and/or other desired measurements or information on protected or landmark trees present on a property or given location. 9.8.8 Licensing It shall be unlawful for any person who is being paid a fee for the business of planting, cutting, trimming, pruning, removing, or otherwise modifying trees within the city limits of Conway to conduct such business without first signing an affidavit stating that he or she has received and read the City of Conway Tree protection Preservation Ordinance and 2001 ANSI A300 Standards (current edition), or any current revision of these documents. Such affidavit shall be completed and submitted when making an application for, or renewing, a City of Conway business license. 9.8.9 Tree Preservation and Protection The removal or destruction of any protected or landmark tree as referenced below within the city limits of Conway without the necessary tree removal permit shall be prohibited. No person shall intentionally damage, cut, carve, transplant, or remove any tree, attach any signs with rope, wire, nails, or other contrivance to any tree, allow any substance which is harmful to such trees to come in contact with them or be placed within their dripline over pervious areas; or intentionally set fire or permit any fire to burn when such fire or the heat thereof will injure any portion of any tree listed below. Any such actions shall be subject to the penalties established in Section 3-4-14 9.8.15. All trees required for preservation mitigation shall be in addition to any landscaping required by the this Conway zoning ordinance as part of the overall development of the site. A. Protected trees: The following trees shall be considered protected trees and shall not be removed from any lot in the city limits of Conway without a protected tree removal permit (Table 9.1): Table 9.1: City of Conway Protected trees Common Tree Name Scientific Name Protected Size 1 Flowering Dogwood Cornus florida 4″ d.b.h. or greater Crape Myrtle Lagerstroemia Indica 4” d.b.h. or greater -- 120 of 128 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 9 – Landscaping, and Buffering and Tree Preservation Standards 9-31 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended 2 Redbud Cercis Canadensis 4″ d.b.h. or greater 3 American Holly Ilex opaca 8″ d.b.h. or greater 4 Live Oak Quercus virginiana 8″ d.b.h. or greater 5 Southern Magnolia Magnolia grandiflora 8″ d.b.h. or greater 6 Red maple Acer rubrum 8″ d.b.h. or greater 7 Bald cypress Taxodium distichum 8″ d.b.h. or greater 8 River Birch Betula nigra 8″ d.b.h. or greater 9 Sycamore Plantanus occidentalis 8″ d.b.h. or greater 10 Cottonwood Populus deltoides 8” d.b.h or greater 11 Dawn Redwood Metasequoia glyptostroboides 8” d.b.h or greater 12 Tulip Liriodendron tulipifera 8” d.b.h or greater 13 Red Cedar Juniperus virginiana 8” d.b.h or greater 14 Tupelo Nyssa sylvatica 8” d.b.h or greater 15 Iron Wood Carpinus caroliniana 8” d.b.h or greater 16 All other Oak Species Quercus 14″ d.b.h. or greater The proposed removal of any tree listed above may be subject to mitigation of trees approved for removal, Section 3-4-10 9.8.11. B. Landmark trees. The following trees shall be considered landmark trees and shall not be removed from any lot in the city limits of Conway without a landmark tree removal permit: 1. All live oak trees designated on the map entitled "The Oaks of Conway, South Carolina," researched and prepared by Evelyn Snider, Joseph N. Pinson, Jr., and Eugene Holbert; 2. Any live oak tree equal to or in excess of 30 24 inches d.b.h.; 3. Any tree that city council designates as a landmark tree; The proposed removal of any tree listed above shall be subject to mitigation of trees approved for removal, per Section 3-4-10 9.8.11. C. Required landscaping. Any tree planted to meet the City of Conway landscape landscaping regulations requirements of the this Unified Development ordinance, including street trees (per Section 9.3.6), may not be removed without a tree removal permit. The proposed removal of any tree listed above shall be subject to mitigation of trees approved for removal in accordance with, Section 3-4-10 9.8.11. D. Mitigation Plantings. Any tree planted to meet mitigation requirements as described in this Section may not be removed without tree board approval and shall be subject to the required mitigation as described in Section 9.8.11. Any mitigation tree removed without approval shall be subject to penalties, as described in Section 9.8.16. E. Setback and Buffer Area(s). For all non-residentially zoned lots, and all proposed or approved major residential development sites as defined in this UDO, all protected and landmark trees equal to or greater than eight (8) inches d.b.h. may not be removed from the exterior setback and/or required buffer area without a tree cutting removal permit. Exceptions shall may be made for ingress/egress to the parcel. 9.8.10 Tree Permits Required A. Protected tree removal permit: This permit is necessary to remove any protected tree on any lot within the City of Conway. Requests to remove protected trees shall be reviewed on a case-by-case basis by the city arborist or their designee. -- 121 of 128 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 9 – Landscaping, and Buffering and Tree Preservation Standards 9-32 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended 1. Prior to the issuance of a tree removal permit for a protected tree, the city arborist or their designee shall determine that one (1) or more of the following conditions exist: a. The tree is considered hazardous per the definition in Section 9.8.7; b. The tree is dead or in irreversible decline as determined by the city arborist or their designee; c. The tree has an untreatable disease or insect pest problem as certified by a registered forester or a certified arborist or by the city arborist; d. The tree or its root system is causing visible damage to structures, and/or areas used for pedestrian and vehicular traffic; e. The tree or its root system is causing damage to structures or underground utilities, as certified by a structural engineer; f. Trees within power line easements that cannot be properly pruned by the local utility company; g. Trees, which after proper pruning, which remain classed classified as hazard trees; h. The tree is located in the footprint of a proposed building, addition or expansion, and there are no practical alternative locations on the lot for the addition or expansion or practical means to build around the tree. 2. Protected trees may only be removed with the written approval of the city arborist, or their designee. a. All protected tree removal permits are valid for six (6) months from the date of issue. b. A condition of the protected tree removal permit shall be mitigation, as defined provided for in Section 9.8.11. B. Tree Removal Permits Required for Non-residential developments and major subdivisions: 1. All developments shall strive to minimize the removal of existing trees. 2. The following items shall be submitted in conjunction with an application to remove protected trees: a. Site / construction plans; b. A tree survey depicting all protected and landmark trees, all waterways, wetlands, buffers, and setback areas, where applicable; c. A tree preservation plan, prepared in accordance with Section 9.8.9. The plan shall indicate the location, size, (DBH), and species of all trees proposed for protection; d. A tree protection plan, in accordance with Section 9.8.12; e. A tree mitigation plan, prepared in accordance with Section 9.8.9. The plan shall indicate the location, size (DBH), and species of all trees proposed for mitigation planting. 3. All trees proposed for protection or preservation shall be clearly identified in the field (i.e. clearly marked) prior to the issuance of any tree removal permits. 4. All tree removal permits that are issued for non-residential developments and major subdivisions shall be valid for two (2) years from the date of issuance. C. Landmark tree removal permit: This permit is necessary to remove any landmark tree on any lot within the City of Conway. Requests to remove landmark trees shall be reviewed on a case-by-case basis by the city arborist, then by the Conway tree board. 1. The tree board may authorize the city arborist to issue issuance of a landmark tree removal permit for the removal of a landmark tree provided the board determines one (1) or more of the following: a. The tree is classed as classified a hazard tree, is in irreversible decline, and cannot be properly pruned to alleviate such condition; -- 122 of 128 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 9 – Landscaping, and Buffering and Tree Preservation Standards 9-33 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended b. The tree is diseased or infectious as certified by a registered forester or certified arborist or the city arborist and cannot be properly treated or pruned to alleviate such condition; c. The tree is located on an undeveloped lot in such a position that the lot cannot be developed in a reasonable and prudent manner. In this instance, the Conway tree board staff shall consider a require the applicant to request for a variance from a particular zoning requirement if it would alleviate the need to remove such landmark tree; and if so determined, initiate such request with the Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA). i. In this instance, if no alternative to the removal of the landmark tree can be obtained through the BZA, the Tree Board may attach any conditions to the permit the tree board deems deemed necessary to ensure compliance with the intent of this section chapter if the tree board grants removal of the landmark tree is granted by the board. d. The tree is causing visible structural damage to a building and no feasible alternative other than removal of such tree exists, as certified by a structural engineer. 2. All landmark tree removal permits are valid for six (6) months from the date of issue. 3. A condition of the landmark tree removal permit shall be mitigation, as defined provided for in Section 3-4-10 9.8.11. (c) Tree cutting permit . This permit is necessary to remove any tree from any nonresidentially zoned lot in the city limits of Conway, any proposed or approved major residential development sites (more than five (5) lots or units or the creation of a new street proposed for dedication) or any residentially zoned lot two (2) acres or greater. All developments should strive to minimize the removal of existing trees. The following items shall be submitted to the city arborist when requesting a tree cutting permit and may be submitted on the same map: (1) A tree survey depicting all protected and landmark trees, all waterways, wetlands and setback areas. (2) A tree preservation plan prepared in accordance with section 3-4-8. This plan shall show the location, size and species of all trees proposed for protection. (3) A tree mitigation plan prepared in accordance with section 3-4-10. This plan shall show the location, size and species of all trees proposed for planting. All trees proposed for protection or preservation must be clearly identified in the field prior to the issuance of a tree cutting permit by the city. All tree cutting permits are valid for two (2) years from the date of issue. 9.8.11 Mitigation of Trees Approved for Removal A. In cases where any type of tree removal permit is issued, Mitigation planting(s) may shall be required to compensate for the loss of any removed tree(s).The species of replacement trees shall be selected from one (a) of the following sources: in cases where a tree removal permit has been issued, unless otherwise determined by the city arborist or their designee. 1. The species of replacement trees shall be selected from one (1) of the following sources: a. Shade Canopy trees or ornamental trees listed in the recommended plant list of the Conway zoning ordinance (section 11.1115); in Section 9.5.1; unless located within a bioretention area; then see Section 9.5.3. b. Trees listed as protected trees in Section 3-4-8 (a) 9.8.9, A. of this chapter; c. Other trees as approved by the city arborist or their designee. 2. All mitigation tree selections shall be reviewed and approved by the city arborist, their designee, or the Conway tree board. An effort should be made to include a diversity of species when planting mitigation trees. -- 123 of 128 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 9 – Landscaping, and Buffering and Tree Preservation Standards 9-34 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended 3. Where the city arborist or their designee determines that a site cannot sustainably support the required replacement, due to the size and shape and/or structures and/or viable site constraints, a fee based on the current nursery market value plus installation costs shall be paid to the City of Conway Tree City USA mitigation account. 4. All trees planted to satisfy the mitigation requirements shall be healthy living trees. The owner, occupant, tenant, or agent shall be jointly and severally responsible for the maintenance of all trees. Any dead or damaged tree shall be promptly replaced with a tree of a similar size and type. Mitigated trees shall be maintained in perpetuity. 5. All trees required for mitigation shall be in addition to any landscaping required by the City of Conway zoning ordinance UDO as part of the overall development of the site. B. Mitigation for trees removed with any approved protected or landmark tree removal permit. The following table (Table 9.2) shall be used to calculate mitigation tree requirements for protected and landmark trees removed with a permit. Table 9.2: Mitigation Requirements for trees removed with a tree removal permit Type of Tree to be removed Number of Replacement Minimum Caliper of Replacement Alternate Fee Protected Trees; Any tree other than Landmark Trees Equal to number of d.b.h. inches removed 4″ *Current nursery market value for required replacement plus associated installation costs Landmark Trees Two times the number of d.b.h. inches removed 4” *Two times the current nursery market value for required replacement plus associated installation costs *To be used in the event mitigation trees cannot be replanted on the site in question. 1. All required mitigation trees must be planted within 12 months of the issuance of the removal permit. 2. All violations of the required tree planting shall be subject to the penalties outlined in Section 9.8.15, Table 9.3. C. Mitigation for property unable to retain replant the required number of trees with any approved tree cutting removal permit. 1. If a property owner obtains a tree removal permit for any tree planted or retained to meet the City of Conway’s landscape landscaping and buffer requirements from the zoning ordinance, they shall be required to replant the minimum landscape requirements for the use as stated provided for in the Conway zoning ordinance Section 9.2. 2. If a property owner/applicant cannot preserve or if there is less than a minimum of 10 trees (minimum six (6) inch d.b.h.) or 60 inches of d.b.h. per actual acre, the property owner/applicant shall re-establish the number of three (3) inch d.b.h. replacement trees necessary to meet the 60 d.b.h. per acre requirement. If the site is less than an acre in size, the fractional requirement (rounded up to the nearest whole number) shall prevail. 3. A property owner/applicant may apply to the Tree Board for relief from the tree mitigation requirements. The tree board may waive the tree mitigation requirements if the applicant illustrates that there are unique topographic conditions that prevent the planting of the replacement trees. In this case, the tree board may require that payment in the amount equal to the current nursery market value for the required replacement trees plus associated costs of -- 124 of 128 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 9 – Landscaping, and Buffering and Tree Preservation Standards 9-35 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended installation for as many three (3) four (4) inch d.b.h. caliper trees necessary to meet the total required d.b.h. inches of removed from the site. 4. All mitigation trees required as a condition of a tree removal permit must be installed prior to the issuance of a certificate of occupancy, of any commercial building or residential home or the recording of a final plat on for any proposed major development. The property owner or developer may post a financial guarantee for mitigation trees in accordance to with the standards of Section 11.1105 9.4.7. of the landscape requirements of the Conway zoning ordinance. 9.8.12 Tree Protection During Clearing, Grubbing, Grading and Construction A. During any type of clearing, grubbing, grading, development or construction, the following measures shall be utilized to protect any on- site tree that is not designated for removal: 1. It shall be the responsibility of the person in charge of the erection, repair, alteration or removal of any building or structure to place a guard or protector around any tree or shrub on subject lot or in the public rights-of-way so as to prevent injury to such tree or shrub arising out of such erection, repair, alteration or removal. 2. Protective barriers, such as silt fences, bollards, roping or other such devices as approved by the city arborist, or their designee, shall be placed by the person requesting construction permits around each tree at the drip line of the canopy of each tree to prevent any type of encroachment under the drip line, or six (6) times the diameter at breast height (d.b.h.) whichever is greater. 3. Trenching shall be no closer than six (6) times the diameter at breast height to the affected tree, nor disrupt more than 30 percent of the drip line root area. 4. No other types of disturbance, equipment or material storage, or construction shall be allowed under the drip line of any tree without prior approval of the city arborist. 5. The city arborist, or their designee, may make an on-site inspection at any time in order to verify compliance with the above and may place a stop work order on the work site for infractions or violations of this section or this chapter. 6. It shall be unlawful for any person to willfully fell, remove, prune, undermine, burn or otherwise damage or destroy any tree or shrub in or upon any public area or right-of-way. 7. No soil disturbance, trenching, grading, paving or storage of equipment/materials shall take place within the critical root zone of any protected or landmark tree. 8. When retained trees are damaged or the critical root zone is disturbed, the property owner shall be subject to the requirements in Section 9.8.15. 9. Unnecessary cutting, breaking or skinning of roots, skinning and bruising of bark, smothering trees by stockpiling construction or excavation materials within the drip line is prohibited. Also prohibited is excessive foot or vehicular traffic and parking of vehicles within the pervious area within the drip line. 10. Tree Protection Plan. A tree protection plan shall include the following: a. Designation of tree protection zones identifying the trees to be protected (location, species, size – d.b.h.); b. Limits of clearing and land disturbance (i.e. grading, clearing, grubbing, etc.); grading plan; c. Details for protecting / avoiding tree roots in trenching plans for underground construction, such as utility placements; d. Details for barricades or fencing for tree protection zones. Such protection (barricades, -- 125 of 128 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 9 – Landscaping, and Buffering and Tree Preservation Standards 9-36 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended fencing, silt fencing, etc.) is required to be installed prior to commencement of land disturbance. e. Tree mitigation table illustrating compliance with this article; f. Stormwater ponds, swales, easements, drains, etc. g. Trees within protection zones shall be protected from sediment erosions material; h. Prior to land disturbance, suitable protective barriers shall be erected and maintained around all protected and landmark trees to be retained during development of the site, so as to prevent damage. 9.8.13 Tree pruning A. Tree pruning shall be accomplished in accordance with the procedures set forth in the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) A300 Tree Care Operations standards, or its revision / replacement in effect at the time of application or at the time of pruning. B. The use of unnatural pruning techniques shall be considered an unauthorized removal of a tree unless the tree is designated on an approved landscape plan to be shaped or formed in an unnatural pattern or to be maintained at a certain height. Examples of unnatural pruning are topping, stubbing, dehorning, lion- tailing, or lopping. These practices are detrimental to tree health and are specifically prohibited. C. Any tree on any public street, highway right-of-way, easement, owned or maintained by the City of Conway, or any tree on private property defined as a hazard tree or public nuisance tree in Section 9.8.6 may be pruned based upon the recommendation of the city arborist, or their designee. D. The city arborist or their designee may have hazard trees or public nuisance trees on public or private property pruned in the interest of public safety. A proper form of written notification will be used to alert the owners that crews will be in the area within a three (3) day period. Contact information will be provided for the City of Conway. E. Any property owner requesting the pruning of a landmark tree shall obtain a tree pruning permit. Property owners shall apply directly to the city arborist City of Conway Planning & Development Department for this permit. 9.8.14 Exemptions from this chapter A. If any tree is determined by the city arborist to be diseased, injured or located in a manner that endangers the public health, safety or welfare of city residents, the city arborist or their designee may authorize its immediate removal. B. In case of emergencies such as windstorms, ice storms, hurricanes, tornadoes, drought or other disasters, the city arborist or their designee may waive the requirements of this chapter during the emergency period so that the requirements of this chapter would in no way hamper private or public work to restore order to the City of Conway. C. The removal of live trees in conjunction with tree farms, agricultural practices, or commercial nurseries. D. Silviculture so long as the following conditions are met: -- 126 of 128 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 9 – Landscaping, and Buffering and Tree Preservation Standards 9-37 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended 1. Property must contain at least five (5) acres. 2. Activities occurring on the tract must be devoted of the production of marketable forest products. 3. No trees may be removed within 50 feet of the entire perimeter of the lot. 4. No protected or landmark trees may be removed. 5. The silviculture activity shall be in compliance with the latest South Carolina Best Management Practices Manual for Forestry. 6. A silviculture permit is obtained from the city arborist, or their designee. The application for such permits must include a boundary survey of the area to be harvested, depiction of the buffer area, location, size and species of any protected or landmark tree on the site and tree protection and silt fencing devices for preservation of trees in the buffer area, protected trees and landmark trees. Also, the permit application must include a narrative detailing proposed reforestation method. 7. No development may take place on a parcel that has been issued a silviculture permit within three (3) years of the cutting unless the property owner meets the replacement standards detailed in Section 3-4-14 9.8.16, Violations and enforcement. 8. All silviculture permits are valid for two (2) years from the date of issue. 9.8.15 Violations and Enforcement A. The city arborist, or their designee, shall have the authority to inspect property for compliance with this chapter and issue stop work orders on any actions found in violation of this section. 1. The city arborist, or their designee, has the right to use aerial photography/ video, site inspections, existing stump measurements, previous plan submittals, or any other appropriate method to aid in determining the total d.b.h of the tree(s) removed. B. Protected and landmark tree violations: Protected and landmark trees cut, removed, or pruned in violation of this chapter are subject to the following penalties: 1. Plant replacement trees on site; and/or; 2. Pay a fine mitigation fees to the City of Conway Tree City mitigation account, as prescribed by the Tree Board. The Tree Board shall make the final determination of any penalty for the removal of a protected or landmark tree without a permit. Any fees collected as a result of the enforcement of this ordinance shall be placed in the City of Conway Tree City USA mitigation account. The following table (Table 9.3) may be used by the tree board as a guide for penalties of violations. Table 9.3. Penalties—Removal of Protected or Landmark Trees Without a Permit. Diameter of Tree Removed (d.b.h.) Rounded Up Number of Replacement Minimum Caliper of Replacement Alternate Fee 4″ through 12″ Double the total d.b.h. of the removed tree 4” Current nursery market value for required replacement plus associated costs of installation 13″ or greater Triple the total d.b.h. of the removed tree 4″ Same as above 3. All other violations. Trees removed from any non-residentially zoned lots, proposed, or approved major residential developments found to be in violation of this section, are subject to the penalties listed in Table 9.3. -- 127 of 128 -- City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance Article 9 – Landscaping, and Buffering and Tree Preservation Standards 9-38 Adopted December 12, 2011 Last Amended 4. The tree board shall make the final determination of Any penalty assessed for violation of this Section shall be determined by the Tree Board. trees removed without a permit in violation of this Section. 9.8.16 Appeals A. Denial of protected tree removal permit, tree cutting permit, silviculture permit or landmark tree pruning permit: Any person denied a tree removal permit, silviculture permit, or landmark tree pruning permit by the city arborist may appeal to the Tree Board. An appeal must be filed in writing within 10 working days of the denial of the permit to the city arborist Planning & Development Department. B. Denial of landmark tree removal permit: Any person denied a landmark tree removal permit by the Conway tree board may appeal to the Conway City Council Board of Zoning Appeals. An appeal must be filed in writing within 10 working days of the denial of the permit to the city arborist Zoning Administrator. C. Appeal of violation penalty: Any person assessed a penalty for the violation of this chapter by the Conway tree board may appeal to the Conway City Council Board of Zoning Appeals. An appeal must be filed in writing within 10 working days of the denial of the permit to the Zoning Administrator. D. Appeal of mitigation amounts requirements: Any person (property owner, applicant, etc.) seeking relief from the mitigation requirements, including the fee-in-lieu of onsite mitigation, that has have been assessed determined by the city arborist, or their designee, may appeal the mitigation amount(s) to the Tree Board. E. Decisions of the Conway Tree Board may be appealed to Circuit Court, in accordance with Section 14.1.15; except as provided for herein. 9.8.17 Damage to trees on public property No person shall damage, destroy, remove, or otherwise harm a tree located on public property or within the right- of-way without a tree removal permit or the written consent of the Tree Board or an authorized city official. The City of Conway shall require compensation for the damage or destruction of a public tree equal to the appraised value of such tree prior to the damage or cost of repair to the tree as determined by a certified arborist. -- 128 of 128 --

title: APPD_1.9.25 PC MINUTES
text: PC 1/9/2025 II. Til. CITY OF CONWAY PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING THURSDAY, January 9, 2025 Planning & Building Dept. Conference Room — 196 Laurel Street Present: Jessica Wise, Kendall Brown, David Sligh, Greg Bryson, Ellen Watkins, Danny Hardee, Thomas J. Anderson III, George Ulrich Absent: None Staff: Jessica Hucks, Planning Director; Brent Gerald, Planner; Marcus Cohen, IT; Katie Dennis, Planner; Marsha Ponder, Planning & Development Assistant Others: Kelvin Causey, Kelvin Chadwick, Jay Sellers, O’Brian Martin, Daniel Asmonga CALL TO ORDER Chairperson Wise called the meeting to order at approximately 5:30 pm. ELECTION OF OFFICERS Ulrich made a motion to nominate Sligh to serve as Vice Chairman, seconded by Anderson. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. Ulrich made a motion to nominate Wise as Chairperson, seconded by Watkins. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. APPROVAL OF MINUTES Sligh made a motion, seconded by Ulrich to approve the December 12, 2024, minutes as written. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. PUBLIC INPUT There was no public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Sligh, to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. DESIGN MODIFICATIONS A. Previously Tables... Buchanan Lane — The applicant, Sellers Construction, is requesting a design modification from the required street improvements and roadway design standards for future development of property located on an existing private roadway — Buchanan Lane (PIN 324-16-01- 0005), including the requirement for the property to have frontage onto a publicly maintained street. Wise stated that this request had been previously tabled and entertained a motion to untable. Ulrich made a motion, seconded by Watkins, and the motion carried unanimously. Hucks stated the 4.04-acre tract was annexed into the city limits in 2023 as Low-Density Residential (R). The property owner proposes to develop a single-family dwelling on the property at some point in the near future; however, no permits for the structure have been applied for at this time. Buchanan Lane is a 50’ unimproved right-of-way. PC 1/9/2025 Per Section 10.5.2 — Street Improvements, of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), “all proposed streets shall be graded to the full width of the right-of-way and improved with a pavement width and standard curb and gutter and storm drainage section as required for the particular classification of street. All grading, pavement and curb and gutter shall be designed and installed in accordance with City of Conway standards and the approved construction plan”. Section 10.9.3 — Basic Design Requirements, provides several standards for construction of streets to be dedicated to the City upon completion, including right of way standards, drainage system/stormwater requirements, sub-grade/surface material requirements, underdrain requirements, standards for shoulders/ditches, etc. The applicant is seeking a design modification to allow Buchanan Lane to be improved to the same standards as Graham Rd; provided that the 24’ pavement width requirement is still met. Granting the modification would exempt the applicant from the requirement to install curb/gutter, sidewalks, and street trees along either side of Buchanan Lane. The design modification, if granted, will not exempt the applicant from having to comply with other construction standards, including base/binder course/subgrade requirements, surface course requirements, minimum paving tolerances, installation of street signage (if applicable), applicable drainage/stormwater improvements, etc. Public Works may also require that a geotechnical report and pavement design be provided if the native soil’s conditions are considered unsatisfactory or of questionable suitability. Additionally, Buchanan Lane will be required to be dedicated to the City for perpetual maintenance once the improvements have been completed AND before any permits for any construction on the property can be issued. The requirements of Section 10.5.2 (A) — Street Improvements, regarding the requirement for all lots to be directly connected to the public street system and not an “island”, are and wiil continue to be applicable to this property. Staff Recommendation, before this request was tabled at the July 2024, PC meeting, it was the understanding of staff that the applicant intended to dedicate the road to the city, once improvements were installed. However, the underlying owners of Buchanan Lane do not wish to dedicate the improvements to the City although they have no issue with the applicant installing the road improvements. The issue of the lot — already created and not fronting a public street — is an issue that has come up more frequently the past few years. Bill Mack Blvd, on the other side of Graham Rd, has several lots that do not access a public street and some of which rely on city services. Bill Mack is not paved, and residents are required to bring their roll carts to Graham Rd in order for sanitation trucks to empty. Other properties throughout the city either front unimproved rights of way that ARE owned by the city, county, or state — but not maintained, or the right-of- way doesn’t exist at all. Many of these properties are heirs’ property and even if the heir was willing to improve the right-of-way, they would likely not have the right to do so unless the underlying property owners were still alive and knew who they were. Planning Commission may be most familiar with property on Sixth Ave that was considered last year for similar reasons as Buchanan Lane. However, unlike Sixth Ave, in the case of Buchanan Lane, not knowing the ownership of the underlying property is not an issue. The underlying ownership is identified, and the owner also gets their access from Buchanan Lane. They too would benefit from the improvements proposed by the applicant. However, they do not wish to deed the portion of the road being improved to the City for perpetual maintenance. This does pose an issue with perpetual maintenance of Buchanan Lane. Ultimately, if 2 VI. PC 1/9/2025 Planning Commission wishes to grant the design modification, the underlying owner will continue to own the private roadway, and maintenance of the road will be a civil issue. A possible solution may be to require a maintenance agreement to be recorded showing the roadway (as well as any realignments of the easement) that details the maintenance responsibilities of all tenants of Buchanan Lane. The applicant, Jay Sellers, Sellers General Construction, LLC was present to answer any questions. The board and staff discussed the request at length. Sligh made a motion to approve the design modification, allowing the road width, curb, and gutter requirements to be substantially similar to Graham Road, as opposed to the full requirements under the UDO. Anderson seconded the motion, and the motion carried with Wise and Hardee voting no. PUBLIC HEARINGS A, ANNEXATION/REZONING REQUEST(S) 1. Request to annex approximately 7.62+/- (total) acres of property located at 1705 Hwy 501 and on E. Cox Ferry Rd (PINs 383-01-02-0030 & 383-01-03-0002), and rezone from the Horry County Highway Commercial (HC) and High Bulk Retail (RE4) districts to the City of Conway Light Industrial (LI and Highway Commercial (HC) districts. Hucks gave the board an overview of the request, stating that the applicant submitted an annexation and rezoning application for the subject properties November 2024. The property is located in the city’s water utility service area and is contiguous to property in the city limits. This annexation is part of a broader enforcement issue related to the subject property that has been ongoing for a few years now. The applicant relocated his business, H&H Builders, from another property on Hwy 501 (in county’s jurisdiction) to this location, which has been owned by the applicant for some time. Both properties are still in the county’s jurisdiction; however, there were and continue to be issues related to business licensing, unpermitted structures, and uses on the subject properties, in that the county’s zoning compliance approval for the sales office is solely for a sales office only and not for any outdoor display, and a large metal building (more than 3,000 sq. ft.) in size, was erected on one of the parcels without a building permit (aerial photograph from April 2024 included in packet). Complicating matters, the properties were one parcel before being split in 2007 (plat book 221, pg. 175). The railroad right-of-way separates the two parcels. Now that they are separated, they cannot be recombined, due to the right-of-way that exists. However, both parcels include the use of manufactured homes sales, and in order for the manufactured home sales business to be compliant, the sales office, parking, etc., must be located on the same property as the display models are located; otherwise, the use is considered outdoor storage, which is prohibited except in conjunction with a permitted use. The applicant was attempting to become compliant with Horry County’s requirements; however, in order for them to do so, they would need to provide water to the unpermitted metal building on the same parcel as the displays (manufactured home units) are located on. Being that it would be an extension of (water) service, or a new service if none currently exists, the requirement to annex becomes applicable. The issue for staff is that if the property is annexed under the current condition, then the city is inheriting a use on a property that was never legally permitted on the property as well as structures that were never issued PC 1/9/2025 a building permit. Yet, the only way for the property to comply would include the requirement for city water to be extended to the property, which requires the applicant to request annexation. Staff has been working with the applicant’s attorney on the issues and has agreed that if Council chose to annex the properties, that they would be given the opportunity to request variances for some of the outstanding issues without the threat of further enforcement, pending the outcome of the variance requests, as they cannot request any variances (from the City’s requirements) until and unless the property has been annexed. If Council chooses not to annex, the applicant would need to comply with the requirements for the county. While manufactured home sales is the current use of one of the properties, the applicant has stated that they would be phasing that use out in the near future and would pursue approval to develop mini-storage and/or other commercial / industrial uses. The requested zoning upon annexation is Highway Commercial (HC) (0.47-acre parcel with frontage on Hwy 501) and Light Industrial (LI) (7.15-acre tract with frontage on E, Cox Ferry Rd). The future land use map of the Comprehensive Plan also identifies the larger tract fronting E. Cox Ferry Rd as being Industrial, and the smaller parcel with frontage on Hwy 501 as Highway Commercial (HC). The future land use map does not distinguish between light and heavy industrial, only “industrial”, but because Light Industrial (LI) is the requested zone for the larger parcel upon annexation, that district is defined below: Staff recommends, in addition to holding the required public hearing, that Planning Commission conduct a thorough review of the request and make an informed recommendation to City Council. There was no public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Anderson, to close public input. Motion carried unanimously, O’ Brian Martin, agent for applicant, was present to answer any questions. The request was discussed at length. Bryson made a motion to recommend approval of the request to City Council, as presented. Sligh seconded the motion, and the motion carried with Hardee voting no. B. REZONING REQUEST(S) 1. Request to rezone approximately 5.63+/- acres of property located on Shoffner Road (PIN 325-13-02-0002) from the Light Industrial (LI) district to the Heavy Industrial (HD) district. Hucks provided the board with an overview of the request, stating that the applicant submitted a rezoning application for the subject property in December 2024. The property is already in the city limits, zoned Light Industrial (LI). The property is currently owned by UFP Real Estate, LLC. The current use / business on the subject property is UFP Mid-Atlantic, LLC, a building materials supplier (i.e. roof trusses, etc.). The use of the property is split onto 2 separate properties, which are zoned differently. The larger property that contains the main building (not part of the request) is zoned Heavy Industrial (HI). The other property, which is proposed to be rezoned, is currently zoned Light Industrial (LI), The applicant wishes to combine 4 PC 1/9/2025 the properties but because they are zoned differently, one of the properties must be rezoned to have the same zoning as the other property it’s proposed to be combined with. Staff recommends, in addition to holding the required public hearing, that Planning Commission conduct a thorough review of the request and make an informed recommendation to City Council. There was no public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Anderson to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. The applicant, Kelvin Causey was present to answer any questions. The board and staff discussed the request at length. Ulrich made a motion to defer the request. Anderson seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. C. TEXT AMENDMENT(S) 1. To be DEFFERED...Amendments to Article 2 — Definitions and Article 5 — Specific Use Regulations, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding requirements for Day Care Facilities. The above item was deferred. 2. Previously Deferred... Amendment(s) to Article 11 — Signage, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding general provisions, exempt and prohibited signs, sign standards by zoning district and sign type, and applications and permits for signs. Hucks stated that since early 2023, city staff has been going through the UDO to identify inconsistencies, typos, and other items that may be lacking within each Article of the UDO. The sign ordinance, although amended a few times through the years, has not had a comprehensive review of all sign requirements, and as part of the city’s UDO cleanup effort, staff is seeking to amend Article 11 to address several issues that have been identified through the years and/or that have caused confusion amongst staff and the sign community, as well as different interpretations. Some of the amendments include, but are not limited to: Revisions to requirements for signage in residential zoning districts; Addition of murals to signage that is considered to be exempt from permitting procedures, provided that it does not contain text or images that identify the business or business product(s) Clarification of number of wall signs permitted on corner buildings or lots; Removal of balloons as being ‘prohibited’ signage; Revisions to requirements for EMC/LED signs — regarding distance to residential structures or properties; Minor revisions to design requirements for monument signs (deletion of repetitive language); Revisions to requirements for drive-thru signs (i.e. menu panel options); and Housekeeping revisions to sign permit requirements PC 1/9/2025 Staff recommends that Planning Commission conduct a thorough review of the proposed amendments to Article 11 and make an informed recommendation to City Council. There was no public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Ulrich, to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. The board and staff discussed the request at length. Wise made a motion to recommend approval of the requested amendment to City Council as presented. Sligh seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. 3. Amendment(s) to Article 9— Landscaping and Buffer Requirements, the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding Landscaping, Buffer, and Tree Preservation requirements. Hucks stated that staff is proposing an amendment to Article 9 that would allow for a more clarification on commonly misinterpreted aspects of the Tree Preservation Ordinance, penalties for violations of the ordinance, as well as a more appropriate course of action for Tree Board appeals, as well as other minor amendments to the landscaping requirements; part of the ongoing effort to cleanup articles of the UDO. Amendments include (but are not limited to) the following: 1. Codify the Tree Preservation Ordinance into the UDO. Then the Tree Ordinance falls under the purview of the Planning & Development Dept. 2. Designate that the Community Appearance Board (CAB) will continue to act as the Tree Board; however, appeals of the decisions of the Tree Board would instead be directed to the Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA). 3. Amend the Tree Preservation Ordinance, including the Appeals Section (Sec. 3-4-15 — Appeals, that directs appeals of the Tree Board to Conway City Council, to direct appeals of the Tree Board decision to Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA) instead of City Council. Decisions of BZA would be appealable to circuit court. 4, Adopt an application fee ($250) for Tree Board Appeals. Staff proposes to begin charging $250 for Tree Appeal applications. Should applicants seek to appeal the decision of the Tree Board, and these requests go to BZA, the property will need to be posted, the appeal would need to be advertised, letters would need to be sent to adjacent property owners, and decisions from the BZA would need to be mailed certified to interested parties. 5. Upon the request of tree board, staff has made some housekeeping changes throughout the ordinance to ensure a more uniform and concise understanding of the processes and terminology used throughout the ordinance. These items include clarity of the process of tree mitigation, implementation of higher penalties for improper removal of protected or landmark trees, and clarification on definitions that were commonly misinterpreted. 6. Addition and deletion, upon the request of the tree board, of trees from the protected tree list. The tree board asked to remove non-native trees, Crepe Myrtle and Dawn Redwoods, from the protected list but to rather include native trees, such as a Tulip tree, Red Cedar, and a Tupelo tree. 6 PC 1/9/2025 VIL. VIIl. Staff recommends, in addition to holding the required public hearing, that Planning Commission conduct a thorough review of the proposed amendments and make an informed recommendation to City Council. There was no public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Ulrich, to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. The board and staff discussed the request at length. Wise made a motion to recommend approval of the requested amendment to City Council as presented. Sligh seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. BOARD INPUT None. STAFF INPUT None. ADJOURNMENT A motion was made to adjourn the meeting. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. The meeting adjourned at approximately 6:54 pm. Approved and signed this &Y day of EBRUREY, , 2025. S H] , CYMSAUDUNE, \ Jessica Wise, Chairperson

Conference Room – 196 Laurel Street Present: Jessica Wise, Kendall Brown, George Ulrich, Thomas J. Anderson III, David Sligh, Greg Bryson Absent: Danny Hardee, Ellen Watkins Staff: Jessica Hucks, Planning Director; Brent Gerald, Planner; Marcus Cohen, IT; Anne Bessant, Planning & Development Coordinator; Marsha Ponder, Planning & Development Assistant Others: John Richards I. CALL TO ORDER Chairperson Wise called the meeting to order at approximately 5:30 pm. II. APPROVAL OF MINUTES Ulrich made a motion, seconded by Anderson to approve the October 3, 2024 minutes as written. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. III. PUBLIC INPUT There was no public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Ulrich, to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. IV. SUBDIVISIONS A. Maple Grove Subdivision, Phase 1, 2 &3 – The applicant is requesting preliminary plan approval for Phases 1, 2 & 3 of the Maple Grove subdivision, located on Collins Jollie Rd (PIN 295-00-00- 0037). Hucks stated that Maple Grove is one of the developments within the Collins Jollie Conservation Subdivision, located on Collins Jollie Rd. There are a total of 10 phases within the development, and the applicant is requesting preliminary plan approval for the first 3 phases, which contains a total of 176 lots – 53 in phase 1, 60 in phase 2 and 63 in phase 3. The master plan, street names and design modifications were approved by Planning Commission in March of this year. If approved, staff recommends that it be contingent upon final review and approval of the Technical Review Committee. John Richards, Thomas & Hutton, was present to answer any questions. The board, applicant, and staff discussed the request at length. Wise made a motion to approve the request as presented pending any further TRC review comments. Sligh seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. -- 3 of 139 -- PC 11/7/2024 2 B. Rivertown Row North, Phase 1 – Letter of Credit extension / renewal. Hucks stated that Phase 1 of Rivertown Row North contains 108 lots. The original letter of credit was approved in November 2022 for $1,249,500. The ordinance allows staff to renew and if necessary, reduce the original letter of credit amount the first time it is set to mature, which was done in 2023 for an additional year and reduced to $636 thousand. If the letter of credit is to be extended for an additional year, Planning Commission must approve the extension along with the amount. 71 lots within Phase 1 are either vacant or currently under construction. Remaining work and infrastructure include sidewalks and street trees for the remaining lots, as well as landscaping, fencing, the surface layer of asphalt for the roads in Phase 1 and a percentage of the amenity center. The applicant is seeking to reduce the letter of credit to $430,999. Staff has performed a site visit and TRC has approved the proposed reduction. The applicant was not present. Sligh made a motion to approve the request as presented. Ulrich seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. V. PUBLIC HEARINGS A. ANNEXATION/REZONING REQUEST(S) 1. Request to annex approximately 0.80+/- total acres of property located at 2689, 2691, 2693, 2695, 2697 and 2699 Oak Street (PIN 325-15-01-0010), and rezone from the Horry County Neighborhood Commercial (NC) district to the City of Conway Neighborhood Commercial (NC) district. Hucks gave the board an overview of the request, stating that the applicant has applied for annexation of the subject property as a requirement to connect to city utilities. There has been a restrictive covenant on file since 2009. When the property transferred to the current owner of the property, Summit Fuels, LLC in September of this year, and then application for a new utility account in the new owner’s name was made, the requirement to annex was triggered. The property contains two structures; one of which is the primary structure that includes several tenant spaces; the primary one being the gas station/convenience store. The smaller tenant spaces fronting on Oak Street include a pet grooming business, a restaurant, and the smaller structure in the rear of the property is used for storage. The property is currently zoned Horry County Neighborhood Commercial, and the City’s future land use map also identifies the property as neighborhood commercial. While the property is within the city’s utility service area and is identified on the future land use map, there are concerns that were noted by the city’s technical review committee regarding the annexation of this property, including a high call volume for the police dept., reoccurring violations related to business license and zoning – such as illegal vending, signage, and yard sales, and property maintenance violations. Staff recommends that Planning Commission provide a thorough review of the request and make an informed recommendation to City Council. -- 4 of 139 -- PC 11/7/2024 3 The applicant was not present. There was no public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Anderson, to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. After much discussion, Bryson made a motion to recommend approval of the request to City Council, as presented. Anderson seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. B. TEXT AMENDMENT(S) 1. DEFFERED…Amendment(s) to Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to the requirements for Conservation Subdivisions. 2. DEFERRED…Amendment(s) to Article 2 – Definitions, Article 3 – Zoning Districts, and Article 4 – Use Tables, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding revisions to various items within the Articles of the UDO. The above items were deferred. 3. Amendment(s) to Article 6 – Design Standards, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), to remove El Bethel Road from the Village Corridor Overlay (VCO). Hucks stated the Village Corridor Overlay is intended to promote compact, pedestrian scale development with residential, neighborhood commercial, and professional uses. The current overlay includes properties with frontage along minor arterials and collector streets per the city’s zoning map. This includes 16th Ave, between Church St & Main St, Mill Pond Rd, Cultra Rd, and El Bethel Rd. In addition to the typical zoning requirements, overlays add an additional layer of requirements for properties that are located within them. The Village Corridor Overlay include requirements for access management, connectivity, landscaping & buffer standards that could be in addition to standard landscaping requirements, and sign limitations. The character of El Bethel Road has changed over the last several years, with the rezoning of several properties to Institutional to allow for educational or medical facilities. Some of the overlay’s standards may create hardships for some of the properties yet to be developed, particularly with regard to height limitation and signage. Regardless of the zoning district, the maximum height for properties in the VCO is 40’, while the institutional zoning district allows a maximum height of 80’. Signs are limited to a size of 24 sq. ft. for a single tenant and 40 sq. ft. for a multi-tenant building. More recently, the new middle school requested and received a variance for the sign they have installed as it exceeded the square footage that was permitted – not in the zoning district or the type of sign, but due to the property being within the overlay. El Bethel Rd also has a wider right-of-way than other streets that are within the Village Corridor Overlay, with a right-of-way width of 150-ft. With the addition of the perimeter road, once completed, it will be a heavier traveled road for vehicles and tractor trailers to get from 701 north or west of Conway to 701 South and Hwy 501 bypass. At that point, it could be considered more of a gateway corridor. -- 5 of 139 -- PC 11/7/2024 4 Staff recommends that Planning Commission provide a thorough review of the request and make an informed recommendation to City Council. There was no public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Ulrich, to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. Wise made a motion to recommend approval of the request to City Council, as presented. Sligh seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. 4. Amendments to Article 11 – Signage, of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), regarding general provisions, exempt and prohibited signs, sign standards by zoning district and sign type, and applications and permits for signs. Hucks stated that the sign ordinance has been amended a few times over the years, and more recently, amendments to the EMC / LED section of the ordinance. However, Article 11 has not had a comprehensive review like other Articles of the UDO, and it remains to be one of the most misinterpreted ordinances, or that has different interpretations for the same requirements. Most of the variance requests that staff receives is for setback requirements and signage, and sign standards tend to be the most violated of all zoning requirements. Some of the items that are proposed to be amended include adding language to clarify standards for signs in disrepair, unsafe, obsolete and abandoned signs, making it clear that any sign deemed to be obsolete or abandoned cannot be re-established or reused and must be removed from the property in its entirety, adding murals to the list of signs that are exempt from permitting procedures, clarifying requirements for signs in residential zoning districts, standards for wall signs – particularly with regard to where a second wall sign is permitted if the property or building is located on a corner lot, as well as adding a minimum separation for EMC/LED signs from residentially zoned properties and/or structures, and several other housekeeping items. Staff recommends that Planning Commission provide a thorough review of the request and make an informed recommendation to City Council. There was no public input. Wise made a motion, seconded by Anderson, to close public input. Motion carried unanimously. Wise made a motion to defer the request until the next meeting to give staff time to revise the amendment relating to distances from EMC signs to residential properties/structures. Sligh seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. VI. DISCUSSION ITEMS None. VII. BOARD INPUT Wise thanked everyone. -- 6 of 139 -- PC 11/7/2024 5 VIII. BACKGROUND: August 2024 The project development tract was annexed into the city and zoned: R (low- density residential) September 2024 The initial master plan and yield plan were submitted and reviewed November 2024 An application for this proposed design modification was submitted as well as the first revised master plan and yield plan, depicting the project layout as shown on the attached illustrations. ANALYSIS: (A.) Block Length: “Blocks shall not be…more than twelve hundred feet in length, except as the Planning Commission considers necessary to secure efficient use of land or desired features of street pattern.” Sec. 7.1.10…. The distance between the Padgett Lane entrance to the intersection, providing inner-connectivity, is approximately: 3,800-linear feet. The maximum design length for blocks are to provide suitable alternative routes throughout a community, both for daily travel as well as emergency access. However, as development expands into the more rural areas, topographic constraints will steer design away from the traditional grid pattern street systems found in many urban developments. Both the configuration of the project boundaries, along with the existing wetlands located on-site, do appear to impede the developer’s ability to connect certain internal roadway intersections and provide multi-block segments within the project. Furthermore, the spine road being proposed will create the only connection between John Doctor Road and Padgett Lane: • John Doctor Road is an approximately: 0.97-mile dead-end public street used as access by approximately 50-individual properties with an additional 32-lots to be created with phase 2 of Rivers Edge Village – and - • Padgett Lane is an approximately: 0.95-mile dead-end road used as access by approximately 30- individual properties, sole access to Padgett Lane Subdivision (containing 36-lots) and as -- 9 of 139 -- secondary access to Lockhaven (a 362-lot residential subdivision). The connection between John Doctor Road and Padgett Lane will provide an alternative means of ingress and egress for both emergency vehicles and daily travelers. (B.) Cul-de-sac Length: “The maximum length of a cul-de-sac shall be 800 feet, unless necessitated by topography or property accessibility and approved by the Planning Commission” Sec. 7.1.11 A (1.)…. The distance between the proposed street intersection and the circular cul-de-sac, where such street terminates , is: 1,040- linear feet The maximum length for a dead-end cul-de-sac is to limit the distance and number of lots that are served through the used of a singular route, without an alternative means of ingress and egress. However, existing wetlands do constrain accessibility to the upland area, at the north-east corner of the development. BACKGROUND: Earlier this year, Council approved a text amendment to Article 10 – Subdivision and Land Development, of the UDO to correct several issues that are inconsistent or outdated, or that were inconsistent with current policy; however, two sections within Article 10 were left out of the update – Open Space Requirements and requirements for Conservation Subdivisions, due to the comprehensive nature of the amendments. Open Space amendments were recently adopted. The amendments proposed to the Conservation Subdivision ordinance are intended to correct several flaws and inconsistencies that staff has found over the years; particularly when the Collins Jollie Conservation Subdivision was being reviewed. The main issue is the current requirement for conservation subdivisions, even when there are multiple neighborhoods owned by separate developers, to plat all of the open space and conservation areas up front and at the same time, regardless of the status of project. For this reason, Collins Jollie has a development agreement that allows these areas to be platted with each project/tract within the entire conservation subdivision; however, these areas must be shown on the approved Master Plan. Other changes include a reorganization of the entire ordinance, to group like requirements together, such as open space requirements, permitted uses, general requirements, and the requirements for permanent protection of open space and conservation areas. Included is Section 10.4 of the UDO containing the requirements for Conservation Subdivisions and the proposed amendments.
