title: APPD-12.20.23 PC WORKSHOP MINUTES
text: PC 12/20/2023 CITY OF CONWAY PLANNING COMMISSION WORKSHOP WEDNESDAY, DECEMBER 20, 2023 Planning & Building Dept. Conference Room — 196 Laurel Street Present: Brian O’Neil, Jessica Wise, Danny Hardee, Julie Hardwick, Kendall Brown, David Sligh, George Ulrich Absent: Samantha Miller, Ellen Watkins Staff: Jessica Hucks, Planning Director; Brent Gerald, Planner; Katie Dennis, Planning Concierge; Brandon Harrelson, Public Works Director; Le Hendrick, Fire Chief; David Parker, Fire Marshall; James Friday, Public Utilities Director; Johnny Lewis, Public Utilities; Charlie Crosby, IT; Anne Bessant, Planning Assistant Others: Walter Warren, Scott Withington, Charles Jordan, Jamie Steele, McKenzie Jordan, Charlie Jordan, & others I. CALL TO ORDER Chairman O’Neil called to order at 3:00 p.m. Il. DESIGN MODIFICATION A. Previously Deferred ...2208 Sixth Ave — requesting a design modification to allow a structure to be constructed on an existing lot of record that lacks the required frontage onto a publicly maintained (and improved) street. Hucks stated that in November of 1941 lot 90 was created via a subdivision map recorded at Horry County Clerk of Court in plat book 2 page 118. A paved street was constructed within the adjacent 40-ft wide right-of-way; such street extended from Pittman Street, yet terminating before reaching the subject property. Maintenance of the street is South Carolina Department of Transportation (SCDOT). In July of 2023 a permit application was submitted to construct a single-family residence on the subject lot. The prospect of a residents being constructed along an un-improved section of roadway raises two primary concerns: (a.) Will the physical condition of the land, by which the lot is accessed, delay or even prevent emergency apparatus and/or city service vehicles from performing their duties? (b.) If improved to any lesser standard, then that of a public street, who will assume responsibility for the perpetual maintenance of the drive? The creation of this lot pre-dates municipal design standards, such as: lot dimensions, access managements standards or subdivision regulations, thus as it sits, is a legal non-conforming lot. However the proposed PC 12/20/2023 development on this site does trigger roadway improvements as stated in both: Section 10.5.2, A: “Any existing street segment that has not been accepted for maintenance by either the City of Conway, Horry County or the South Carolina Department of Transportation, and that is to serve as the required frontage for one or more lots created pursuant to these regulations, shall be improved and dedicated to the public, as provided for above, in such a way that the street segment meets the standards of these regulations for the particular classification of street, including right-of-way width. Such street segment shall be directly connected to the existing public street system by way of at least one public street accepted for maintenance by either the City of Conway, Horry County or the South Carolina Department of Transportation. No development shall be permitted on any street that is an “island” not connected directly to the public street system”. Section 12.4.1, D of the UDO states: “Where an existing nonconforming structure or site is nonconforming in regard to street access, the site shall be brought into conformity with the provisions of this UDO for street access or shall be brought as close to conformity as the physical circumstances made possibly allow”. Beyond the paved section of 6th Ave, the remainder of the roadway appears to be untreated soil... Uncompacted soil, when dry, may support the weight of an average passenger vehicle; such as; ¢ acompact car (average weight of 2,500-Ibs), e amid-sized vehicle (average weight of 3,000-Ibs), e an SUV or pick-up truck (average weight of 4,000-Ibs) or e a full-size truck (which can weigh anywhere between 4,000 to 5,700-Ibs). However uncompacted soil will not support the weight of emergency apparatus or city service vehicles such as; e Fire Engines (equipped with gear to put the fire out, including water tanks, pumps, and hoses), which typically weigh between: 35,000 to 40,000-Ibs, e Fire Trucks (fuli of rescue and ventilation equipment to safely and efficiently rescue victims), which typically weigh between: 36,000 to 60,000-Ibs, - or - non-emergency city service vehicles such as e Sanitation trucks which can weigh between: 20,000 to 30,000-Ibs. As a comparison: suitable sub-grade materials (select soil base materials to be laid beneath any all-weather surface material) is required to be compacted to 95% modified proctor to sufficiently support a 40,000-Ibs loaded tandem axle dump truck temporarily (as exposure to inclement weather will rapidly deteriorate the base road materials), and another 8 to 11-inches of all-whether surface material (such as coquina or GABC), compacted to 100% modified proctor, would need to be laid atop the sub-grade to support such weight long-term. Sufficient drainage facilities and a minimum 2-inches of “Type 1” asphalt would be required to meet the standards of a “Local Access Street”. Maintenance: staff also has concerns regarding, who will be take on responsibility to perpetually maintain the drive/access? as the state likely will not construct nor may not extend their maintenance system to cover PC 12/20/2023 this section of roadway, even if such roadway is constructed, and, the owner of the subject lot does not appear to own the underlying property to which the road right-of-way was dedicated. Staff recommends a thorough review of the applicant’s request. Jamie Steele, Diamond Shores, agent for owner was present to answer any questions. After much discussion, O’Neil made a motion to deny the design modification based on staff's concerns outlined in their report; however, after discussion, he withdrew his motion, as the motion made was too broad and the board suggested that the PC’s authority, specific to the request, should be more narrow than broad. Sligh made a motion to deny the design modification request as presented. Wise seconded the motion and the motion carried unanimously. I. DISCUSSION A. Request to annex and/or rezone approximately 486 +/- acres of property, located at or near the corner of HWY 378 & Juniper Bay Rd, HWY 378 & Airport Rd, Dayton Drive, and on Dunn Shortcut Rd (PIN’s 336-00-00-0043, -0044, -0045, 336-13-04-0006, 336-14-04-0011, 336-15- 03-0003, 337-00-00-0009, -0011, -0012, 337-08-01-0004, 370-00-00-0011, and 370-04-01- 0004), and rezone from the Horry County Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA), Horry County Highway Commercial (HC), Horry County Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF40), the City of Conway Heavy Industrial (HI), City of Conway Low/Medium-Density Residential (R-1), and City of Conway High-Density Residential (R-3) districts to the City of Conway Planned Development (PD) district. Hucks stated that the applicants are seeking to annex and/or rezone the aforementioned properties for the purposes of developing as a Planned Development (PD). Also proposed is a Development Agreement for the subject property. Per the applicant’s submittal, the planned development envisions a mixed-use community consisting of differing types and styles of single-family homes and a variety of commercial uses to meet the needs of the existing and future residents of Conway. The development will be accessed from Hwy 378, Juniper Bay Rd, Dunn Shortcut Rd, Airport Rd (commercial tract) and Dayton Dr. The proposed PD will also be bound by a Development Agreement; the details of which are included in this packet (draft document), and is on this agenda for consideration. Per the most recent master plan submitted, the proposed density was 1,459 units. However, there are a couple of tracts within the master plan that are “flex tracts”, which could contain multifamily uses instead of commercial, bringing the maximum density to 1,767 units. Refer to the table provided in the narrative for density proposed for each tract within the PD. With the exception of these flex tracts, the residential will consist of single-family detached, single-family semi-attached, and townhouses. There are no flood zones within the project area. There are approximately 59 acres of wetlands identified on the Open Space Master Plan. PC 12/20/2023 Current Zoning of properties currently in the county’s jurisdiction include: Commercial Forest Agriculture (CFA), Highway Commercial (HC), and Residential, no mobile homes allowed (SF40). This project is within the City’s utility service area. The City’s Future Land Use Map identifies these properties as the following: PIN’s 336-00-00-0043, -0044, -0045, and 370-00-00-0011: identified as Industrial on the future land use map. The future land use map does not distinguish between Light and Heavy Industrial. PIN’s 336-13-04-0006, 336-15-03-0003, 336-14-04-0011, and 370-04-01-0004: identified as Highway Commercial (HOC) on the future land use map. PIN’s 337-00-00-0009, -0012, and 337-08-01-0004: identified as Low-Density Residential on the future land use map. PIN 337-00-00-0011 is identified as High-Density Residential on the future land use map. Proposed Modifications from Design Standards (Section 5 of PD Narrative): 1. Landscape buffers to not be required between commercial uses. 2. Where multipurpose trails are proposed in landscape buffers, buffer widths to be reduced to a Type A (5° width) buffer. 3. Minimum block lengths to be 270’ (v. the standard of 400’) 4. Landscape buffers on the F-2 tract to meet the Type A (5’) buffer requirements on side and rear property lines. 5. To exempt sidewalk and pathway requirements on the perimeter of the PD (i.e. portions of tracts that abut Hwy 378, Juniper Bay Rd, Dunn Shortcut Rd, Airport Rd, and Dayton Dr.). 6. Streets to be designed and constructed per the Street Cross Section exhibits provided in the narrative (attached). 7. Up to 50% of garages facing the street on single-family detached and duplex semi-attached units shall be eligible to protrude more than 10’ past the front fagade. In such instances, garage faces shall have decorative design treatments to minimize their appearance. One deviation that was not mentioned above is the interconnectivity requirements between developments. Tract R-4 abuts the existing Macala Acres subdivision. The UDO would typically require that a stub-out be provided to connect to future development. In this case, when Macala Acres was platted, there was property platted as future access on the Final Plat for Phase 3 of Macala Acres. This can be found between lots 87 and 88 on the plat, recorded in Plat Book 222 at Page 187 (copy of plat attached). The applicant has shown a stub out to be provided on Tract R-4. This does not achieve the required connection, and the residents of Macala Acres do not wish to have the connection made. At the time of the plat approval for this phase of Macala Acres, it is unclear whether the requirement to install the stub-out would have been required, or reserving access only. The current requirements dictate that a stub-out be provided for future connection, or that the connection be made if a stub-out on the adjoining property or access has been set aside, if recommended by the Technical Review Committee. PC 12/20/2023 Planning Commission will need to decide if the connection should be installed, on both sides (R-4 tract and Macala Acres access), whether the stub-out should be provided only on the R-4 tract, or whether the connection can be omitted entirely. Walter Warren, Scott Withington, Charles Jordan, Charlie Jordan, and McKenzie Jordan, applicants were present and further explained the request. The commissioners, applicants and staff discussed the request in length. The following items were discussed during the meeting: Flex districts Stormwater concerns. (The need a detailed stormwater management plan) Infrastructure concerns for the area (traffic improvements needed) Connection to Macala Acres (staff supports the connection) Street width within the development (pavement width should be a min of 24’) Residential design standards (snout houses) (PC would prefer all lots to meet the design standards, but a reduction in the percentage of lots that would be considered a snout house would have to be reduced) Development agreement (Development agreement enhancement fees, potential land swaps, city park acreage, canal trail, etc.) Lot size requirements for the single-family portion of the development (PC seems to support a min. of 50’) Landscape buffer & trail (applicant seeking a reduction in buffer to a Type A buffer along the canal trail) Connectivity of the R-5 tract to the rest of the development (possible connection to be made in the form of a pathway / open space connection. Some members of PC would prefer that interconnectivity be provided via a road system, or to remove the R-5 tract from the PD) Proposed roadway connection on City property (applicant states they do have another option if necessary and are looking to do a land swap (potentially) with the city). Possible future strains of city utility services for the develop. The need for a new water tower with the addition of the project. Distance from closest fire station. Le Hendrick stated that the 5-mile radius to maintain the city current ISO rating would be maintained (addition of county fire station on el bethel rd.) Fire training facility located on the stormwater pond side of the proposed roadway going through city shops — training facility is brand new and there are no other locations for the facility to be located at this time. PC requested a schematic of a block in the development to see what a typical street would look like with the requested lot widths and the style of homes proposed. Revise a portion of the Flex district tract(s) to a Commercial only tract (portion fronting on Hwy 378). PC 12/20/2023 IV. ADJOURMENT A motion was made to adjourn the meeting. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. The meeting adjourned at approximately 5:09 pm. Approved and signed this “ TA day ot KA cf 2024. LEE GALE ELE Brian O’Neil, Chairman

Previously Tabled…1501 Ninth Ave: The applicant, Dr. Daniel Falk, is appealing staff’s decision to deny a tree removal request for the property, located at 1501 Ninth Ave. (PIN 338-14–03-0031). Dennis gave an overview that on June 9th staff received a request to remove a tree from the property located at 1501 Ninth Ave. Upon inspection staff determined the tree is a 29” Magnolia tree, which is a protected tree, in good health and did not appear to show any signs of decline. Staff did observe some damage to the nearby gutter system, but did not see any structural damage directly caused by the tree in question. There was also no apparent damage outside of age to the deck directly below the tree canopy. In accordance with Section 9.8.10 (A) (1) of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) staff’s determination was to deny the removal of the tree. Staff informed the applicant of the decision and ultimately the applicant decided to appeal staff’s decision. On June 13, 2025, an application to appeal was submitted. Staff spoke with the owner and informed the owner of the criteria staff must use to allow for the removal of a protected tree as well as that the plan to develop the site in the future is not a sufficient reason to grant removal of the tree at this time. If the board chooses to grant the removal of the 29” Magnolia tree, mitigation would still be a requirement. Mitigation is based on the number of inches being removed, 29 (x), divided by the minimum number of inches required for each replacement tree, 4 (y), to equal the number of trees to be replaced, 8 (z). X / Y = Z 29 / 4 = 7.25 (8) Tree City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance:  Section 9.8.7: Definitions -- 2 of 16 -- CAB 8/13/2025 2  Section 9.8.10 (A): Protected Tree Removal Permit  Section 9.8.11: Mitigation of Trees Approved for Removal  Section 9.8.16: Appeals Staff recommends the board discuss the appeal of the mitigation requirements and instruct staff and the applicant on how to proceed. The applicant, Linda Koretic, was present. Staff, board and the applicant discussed at length. Kurlowski made a motion to approve the removal of the Magnolia Tree given the arborist reports. Roehm seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. Kurlowski made a motion to waive any mitigation requirements related to the removal of the Magnolia tree. McLain seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. B. Previously Tabled…1501 Ninth Ave: Determination of penalties assessed due to failure to mitigate an approved Landmark Tree removal, located at 1501 Ninth Ave. (PIN 338-14-03-0031). Dennis gave an overview that in July of 2024 the owner received approval to remove a 36” Live Oak tree closer to the commercial structure on the property. That tree did show signs of decline due to plumbing upgrades done to the commercial building. Ultimately the board approved the removal of the tree but did require mitigation of 9 (nine) 4” (four-inch) caliper canopy trees to be planted on site. That permit has since expired, and the mitigation plantings have not been completed. This does place the property owner in violation of the ordinance and is subject to the penalties listed in Table 9.3 of the UDO. Mitigation penalties are based on the number of inches being removed, 36 (v), multiplied by the applicable number found in Table 9.3 of the UDO 3 (w), then divided by the minimum number of inches required for each replacement tree, 4 (y), to equal the number of trees to be replaced, 27 (z). Millpond Townhomes (PIN 338-00-00-0018): The applicant, David Schwerd, is requesting a reduction of mitigation requirements for the project located at PIN 338-00-00-0018. Dennis gave an overview that the applicant, David Schwerd, is requesting a reduction of mitigation requirements for the project located at Pin 338-00-00-0018. The applicant is requesting the board grant approval to use the retention of trees on an upland area of the parcel as credit towards their mitigation requirements as well as a reduction in the caliper requirement of the mitigation trees from 4” caliper to 2.5” caliper. Mitigation is based on the number of inches being removed, 2264 (x), divided by the minimum number of inches required for each replacement tree, 4 (y), to equal the number of trees to be replaced, 566 (z). X / Y = Z 2264 / 4 = 566 Trees However, the applicant is requesting first that the caliper size of the mitigation trees be reduced to 2.5” caliper meaning, 2264 (x), divided by 2.5(y), to equal the number of trees to be replaced, 906 (z). X / Y = Z 2264 / 2.5 = 905.6 (906) Trees Staff is amenable to the reduction in the caliper size of the trees as our concern is the number of inches being replaced. Secondly, the applicant would like to receive credit for existing trees located on a portion of the property that is not being developed. Staff would like to point out that this area is not being developed because of the choice to save trees but rather due to the need for this area to count towards their open space requirements for the project as well as the highly improbable ability to adequately develop the area. The uplands the trees are proposed to be retained on are almost surrounded by flood zones, or wetlands and have a floodway as a barrier between the main portion of the development and the upland area of trees being discussed. This presents the issue of development, such as crossing the wetlands and a floodway with a road constructed to city standards, although not impossible, would be extremely expensive as well as restrictive and based on approvals from the Army Corps of Engineers as well as FEMA. This area also creates an issue for development due to its size and the shaping of the floodzones around the area. In recent years City Council has made it abundantly clear that they do not support development within floodzones, which could be an added challenge to development in this area. The applicant has requested that 2,200 trees within this area be used as credit towards mitigation requirements. -- 4 of 16 -- CAB 6/25/2025 4 The Tree Preservation ordinance does not allow for retention to count as mitigation but does give the board the ability to assess mitigation how they see fit. However, staff would not support the ability of 254 trees of Protected size or species to count towards mitigation as these trees, if removed, would trigger their own mitigation requirements. The remaining 1966 trees are of protected species, as stated by the applicant, but not illustrated or specified on the plan, would be what staff would be open to the board’s decision on. Staff is hesitant to support any ability to allow retention as mitigation, but the board does have the ability to consider the request, with the exception of the 254 protected or landmark trees identified within the area. If the board chooses to grant approval to allow the 1966 existing trees totaling 10,077” in d.b.h., then mitigation plantings would not be required. However, the applicant is offering to plant 252 additional trees on the site at a 2.5” minimum caliper assuming the board chooses to grant the reduction in caliper size. If the board chooses to grant a credit of any kind for retention of trees staff would recommend it be capped at the remaining d.b.h needed to meet mitigation requirements for this project. Or consider a reduction in d.b.h. with additional plantings rather than granting retention as mitigation opportunities that staff is also worried could become a request for many future development sites. Only the trees that are outside the protected or landmark size for a species will count. All these combined are to provide the remaining 1,634-inches needed for mitigation, but no additional inches shall be credited for the project. ISSUE: Appeal of staff’s decision to deny a tree removal request, 1501 Ninth Ave APPLICANT(S): Dr. Daniel Falk PIN(s): 338-14-03-0031 CURRENT ZONING: City of Conway Professional (P) PREVIOUS MEETING(S): June 25, 2025 BACKGROUND: On June 25th the board tabled this item and requested that the owner proceed with the PiCUS Sonic Tomography Testing recommended by the arborist for the 29” Magnolia tree in question. After the test the results show a large hollow hole internal to the tree. The results are as follows. “The PiCUS Sonic Tomography machine detected a large hollow cavity. The software depicted the hollow cavity with the color blue. The cavity is likely formed due to a fungal plant pathogen. Unfortunately, a full and green tree canopy is not an indication of a stable tree.” The arborist recommends the following. “Because at this stage in the tree’s life corrective pruning of the codominant stems in not recommended, and the hollow cavity detected is not likely to improve with antifungal supplementation, and finally because the clinic as well as a neighboring home is within the trees drop zone, I recommend removal of the tree in question.” Following the results of the PiCUS Sonic Tomography Test staff does agree that the removal of this tree would be best. We also appreciate the applicant’s cooperation and willingness to obtain further testing during this process. If the board chooses to apply the mitigation requirements for this tree the applicant would be responsible for the mitigation of 7 trees in the form of plantings or a fee-in-lieu if the board so chooses. Staff would like to point out that this area is not being developed because of the choice to save trees but rather due to the need for this area to count towards their open space requirements for the project as well as the highly improbable ability to adequately develop the area. The uplands the trees are proposed to be retained on are almost surrounded by flood zones, or wetlands and have a floodway as a barrier between the main portion of the development and the upland area of trees being discussed. This presents the issue of development, such as crossing the wetlands and a floodway with a road constructed to city standards, although not impossible, would be extremely expensive as well as restrictive and based on approvals from the Army Corps of Engineers as well as FEMA. This area also creates an issue for development due to its size and the shaping of the floodzones around the area. In recent years City Council has made it abundantly clear that they do not support development within floodzones, which could be an added challenge to -- 19 of 24 -- development in this area. The applicant has requested that 2,200 trees within this area be used as credit towards mitigation requirements. The Tree Preservation ordinance does not allow for retention to count as mitigation but does give the board the ability to assess mitigation how they see fit. However, staff would not support the ability of 254 trees of Protected size or species to count towards mitigation as these trees, if removed, would trigger their own mitigation requirements. The remaining 1966 trees are of protected species, as stated by the applicant, but not illustrated or specified on the plan, would be what staff would be open to the board’s decision on. Staff is hesitant to support any ability to allow retention as mitigation, but the board does have the ability to consider the request, with the exception of the 254 protected or landmark trees identified within the area. If the board chooses to grant approval to allow the 1966 existing trees totaling 10,077” in d.b.h., then mitigation plantings would not be required. However, the applicant is offering to plant 252 additional trees on the site at a 2.5” minimum caliper assuming the board chooses to grant the reduction in caliper size. If the board chooses to grant a credit of any kind for retention of trees staff would recommend it be capped at the remaining d.b.h needed to meet mitigation requirements for this project. Ultimately the board approved the removal of the tree but did require mitigation of 9 (nine) 4” (four-inch) caliper canopy trees to be planted on site. That permit has since expired, and the mitigation plantings have not been completed. This does place the property owner in violation of the ordinance and is subject to the penalties listed in Table 9.3 of the UDO. Mitigation penalties are based on the number of inches being removed, 36 (v), multiplied by the applicable number found in Table 9.3 of the UDO 3 (w), then divided by the minimum number of inches required for each replacement tree, 4 (y), to equal the number of trees to be replaced, 27 (z). Plus, the originally required mitigation amount of 9 trees, for a grand total of 36 mitigation trees. V*W=X X/Y=Z 36*3= 108, 108 / 4 = 27 Trees 27+9 (original mitigation) = 36 Trees total CAB 6/25/2025 Staff is open to working with the applicant however the board sees fit. City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance: Section 9.8.7: Definitions Section 9.8.10 (C): Landmark Tree Removal Permit Section 9.8.11: Mitigation of Trees Approved for Removal Section 9.8.15: Violations and Enforcement Section 9.8.16: Appeals VV VV WV Staff recommends the board discuss the appeal and reduction of the mitigation requirements and instruct staff and the applicant on how to proceed. The applicant was present. Staff, board and the applicant discussed at length. Jordan made a motion to amend item B, deferring it until after the July 9th meeting to allow time for the originally anticipated tree mitigation efforts to proceed. Hall seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. C. Millpond Townhomes (PIN 338-00-00-0018): The applicant, David Schwerd, is requesting a reduction of mitigation requirements for the project located at PIN 338-00-00-0018. Dennis gave an overview that the applicant, David Schwerd, is requesting a reduction of mitigation requirements for the project located at Pin 338-00-00-0018. The applicant is requesting the board grant approval to use the retention of trees on an upland area of the parcel as credit towards their mitigation requirements as well as a reduction in the caliper requirement of the mitigation trees from 4” caliper to 2.5” caliper. Mitigation is based on the number of inches being removed, 2264 (x), divided by the minimum number of inches required for each replacement tree, 4 (y), to equal the number of trees to be replaced, 566 (z). X/Y=Z 2264 / 4 = 566 Trees However, the applicant is requesting first that the caliper size of the mitigation trees be reduced to 2.5” caliper meaning, 2264 (x), divided by 2.5(y), to equal the number of trees to be replaced, 906 (z). X/Y=Z 2264 / 2.5 = 905.6 (906) Trees Staff is amenable to the reduction in the caliper size of the trees as our concern is the number of inches being replaced. Secondly, the applicant would like to receive credit for existing trees located on a portion of the property 3 CAB 6/25/2025 that is not being developed. Staff would like to point out that this area is not being developed because of the choice to save trees but rather due to the need for this area to count towards their open space requirements for the project as well as the highly improbable ability to adequately develop the area. The uplands the trees are proposed to be retained on are almost surrounded by flood zones, or wetlands and have a floodway as a barrier between the main portion of the development and the upland area of trees being discussed. This presents the issue of development, such as crossing the wetlands and a floodway with a road constructed to city standards, although not impossible, would be extremely expensive as well as restrictive and based on approvals from the Army Corps of Engineers as well as FEMA. This area also creates an issue for development due to its size and the shaping of the floodzones around the area. In recent years City Council has made it abundantly clear that they do not support development within floodzones, which could be an added challenge to development in this area. The applicant has requested that 2,200 trees within this area be used as credit towards mitigation requirements. The Tree Preservation ordinance does not allow for retention to count as mitigation but does give the board the ability to assess mitigation how they see fit. However, staff would not support the ability of 254 trees of Protected size or species to count towards mitigation as these trees, if removed, would trigger their own mitigation requirements. The remaining 1966 trees are of protected species, as stated by the applicant, but not illustrated or specified on the plan, would be what staff would be open to the board’s decision on. Staff is hesitant to support any ability to allow retention as mitigation, but the board does have the ability to consider the request, with the exception of the 254 protected or landmark trees identified within the area. If the board chooses to grant approval to allow the 1966 existing trees totaling 10,077” in d.b.h., then mitigation plantings would not be required. However, the applicant is offering to plant 252 additional trees on the site at a 2.5” minimum caliper assuming the board chooses to grant the reduction in caliper size. City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance: > Section 9.8.7: Definitions > Section 9.8.11: Mitigation of Trees Approved for Removal >» Section 9.8.16: Appeals Staff does not recommend granting a 10,077” d.b.h. credit as staff is concerned with the desire to apply that credit to other projects. If the board chooses to grant a credit of any kind for retention of trees staff would recommend it be capped at the remaining d.b.h needed to meet mitigation requirements for this project. Or consider a reduction in d.b.h. with additional plantings rather than granting retention as mitigation opportunities that staff is also worried could become a request for many future development sites. CAB 6/25/2025 The applicant was present. Staff, board and the applicant discussed at length. Jordan made a motion to approve the planting of 252 trees at 2.5-inch caliper minimum, these trees are to count towards the mitigation requirements assessed for the project. The remaining 1,634-inches of required mitigation is to come from the cumulative number of DBH for the exiting trees within the upland area of the project site. Only the trees that are outside the protected or landmark size for a species will count. All these combined are to provide the remaining 1,634-inches needed for mitigation, but no additional inches shall be credited for the project. Watts seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. Iv. PUBLIC INPUT None. v. BOARD INPUT None VI. STAFF INPUT Dennis provided a reminder about a proposed joint workshop with the Board, involving both the CAB and Tree Board, which may be scheduled at a later date. vol. ADJOURN There being no further business to come before the board, a motion was made and seconded to adjourn the meeting at 4:55 pm. The vote in favor was unanimous and the motion carried. 7H / me Approved and signed this 8 day of A UGY. 57 , 2025. Gerald Wallace III, Chairperson

The tree is already dangerously leaning towards homes and will impact home if weather is severe. When the underground storm drainage was being installed all the dirt was removed on that side of the tree base of the root ball system and a cement tile was installed in its place. My next-door neighbor has already has a much larger (oak) tree within 20 feet of this one that was on my property to fall on his property and destroyed the roof and two rooms on his home.” Staff spoke with the owner on site and on the phone and was informed by the owner that the sewer lines were observed via camera by a city employee during the construction along the roadway, but it is staff’s understanding that a plumber had not identified any issues with the underground piping. Although, there does appear to be some cosmetic damage to the owner’s sidewalk and a column along their fence line staff could not grant the removal as the damage is not structural, nor does it cause immediate harm to pedestrians or vehicular traffic. The board is now tasked with determining if staff ruled in error and if the removal of the tree should be granted. If the board chooses to grant the removal of the tree, mitigation would still be a requirement. Mitigation is based on the number of inches being removed, 25 (x), divided by the minimum number of inches required for each replacement tree, 4 (y), to equal the number of trees to be replaced, 7(z). -- 2 of 47 -- CAB 4/23/2025 2 X / Y = Z 25 / 4 = 6.25 (7) Trees The homeowner would also like to request a reduction in mitigation, and they are open to planting on site but are concerned with the number of plantings and the size of the property with available planting space. Staff does support the UDO which allows the Tree Board the ability to waive or reduce mitigation requirements, however they see fit. Staff recommends the board discuss the appeal and reduction of the mitigation requirements and instruct staff and the applicant on how to proceed. The applicant was present. Staff and the board discussed at length. Jordan made a motion to table the request to allow public works to look at it and let the homeowner get a letter from the plumber that shows that the tree is messing the sewer line up. Watts seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. B. 1129 Glossy Ibis Dr.: The applicant, Cynthia Gorlaski, is appealing staff’s decision to deny a tree removal request for the property, located at 1129 Glossy Ibis Dr. (PIN 383-05-03-0018). Dennis gave an overview that on March 18th staff received a request to remove a tree from the property located at 1129 Glossy Ibis Dr. The owner provided a letter from a certified arborist identifying the tree as an 87” Water Oak in good health, qualifying this tree as a protected tree. Staff’s inspection revealed that the tree is in a rear corner of the property and the root system appears to extend under a newly poured concrete pad but did not observe any structural damage to the home itself at the time of inspection. In accordance with Section 9.8.10 (A) (1) of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) staff’s determination was to deny the removal of the tree. Staff informed the applicant of the decision and ultimately the applicant decided to appeal staff’s decision. On March 31, 2025, an application to appeal was submitted referring to the arborist letter that reads as follows. “One Water Oak tree at left rear corner, approximately 30 feet tall and 87 inches in diameter, is a well- established tree in good health, but it poses a problem to the homeowners. The root system is under the new concrete pad and growing towards the foundation of the house. This could cause structural damage to the house. I recommend the removal of the tree before the damage occurs.” The board is now tasked with determining if staff ruled in error and if the removal of the tree should be granted. If the board chooses to grant the removal of the tree, mitigation would still be a requirement. Mitigation is based on the number of inches being removed, 87 (x), divided by the minimum number of inches required for each replacement tree, 4 (y), to equal the number of trees to be replaced, 22(z). X / Y = Z 87 / 4 = 21.75 (22) Trees The homeowner would also like to request a reduction in mitigation, and they are open to planting on site but are concerned with the number of plantings and the size of the property with available planting space. Staff can only support the UDO which states protected trees cannot be removed without meeting one or more of the criteria listed in Section 9.8.10 (A)(1) of the UDO, which is what the decision to deny was based upon. -- 3 of 47 -- CAB 4/23/2025 3 However, the board does have the ability to grant approval to remove the tree if they feel staff ruled in error as well as the ability to waive or reduce mitigation requirements, however they see fit. Staff recommends the board discuss the appeal and reduction of the mitigation requirements and instruct staff and the applicant on how to proceed. The applicant was present. Staff and the board discussed at length. Jordan made a motion that staff was correct in denying the removal of the tree. However, since the tree is a protected Water Oak and due to the species type, the board does have the ability to allow the removal at the owner’s request, but the owner needs to mitigate per the ordinance without any reduction. Mitigation will be based upon staff’s determination of the true DBH of the tree before mitigation calculations are solidified. Kurlowski seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. Jordan amended his motion to include mitigation to be carried out through a fee in lieu of or planting trees of approved sizes or any combination of the two on the owner's property, as outlined in the ordinance, based on the owner’s preference. Wallace seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. C. 1201 3rd Ave.: The applicant, Brady Norris, with the Horry County Maintenance Department, is requesting approval for the removal of a Landmark Live Oak tree, located at 1201 3 rd Ave. (PIN 368-04- 02-0043). Dennis gave an overview that on April 8th staff received a request to remove a tree from the property located at 1201 3 rd Ave. The applicant stated the tree was in a state of decline. Upon inspection staff found the tree is a 24” Live Oak tree that does appear to be in a state of severe decline. In accordance with Section 9.8.10 (C) of the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) staff could not grant approval to remove the tree and informed the applicant that the request would be deferred to the Tree Board. This tree is also a part of the Patriot Tree Project that was implemented to honor Civil War Veterans from Horry County by dedicating Live Oak Trees or planting Live Oak Trees in their honor. This tree was dedicated on September 12, 2014, in Honor of Robert T. Anderson. The board must determine if the tree meets the criteria described in Section 9.8.10 (C) (1) to grant the approval of removal. Those requirements are as follows. Landmark tree removal permit: This permit is necessary to remove any landmark tree on any lot within the City of Conway. Requests to remove landmark trees shall be reviewed on a case-by-case basis by the city arborist, then by the Conway tree board. 1.The tree board may authorize the issuance of a landmark tree removal permit for the removal of a landmark tree, provided the board determines one (1) or more of the following: a. The tree is classified a hazard tree, is in irreversible decline, and cannot be properly pruned to alleviate such condition; b. The tree is diseased or infectious as certified by a registered forester or a certified arborist and cannot be properly treated or pruned to alleviate such condition; c. The tree is located on an undeveloped lot in such a position that the lot cannot be developed in a reasonable and prudent manner. In this instance, the applicant shall be required to request a variance from a particular zoning requirement if it would alleviate the need to remove such landmark tree; and if so determined, initiate such request with the Board of Zoning Appeals (BZA). -- 4 of 47 -- CAB 4/23/2025 4 i. In this instance, if no alternative to the removal of the landmark tree can be obtained through the BZA, the Tree Board may attach any conditions to the permit deemed necessary to ensure compliance with the intent of this section if removal of the landmark tree is granted by the board. d. The tree is causing visible structural damage to a building and no feasible alternative other than removal of such tree exists, as certified by a structural engineer. If the board chooses to grant the removal of the tree, mitigation would still be a requirement. Mitigation is based on the number of inches being removed, 24 (x), divided by the minimum number of inches required for each replacement tree, 4 (y), to equal the number of trees to be replaced, 6(z). X / Y = Z 87 / 4 = 6 Trees The applicant is also asking the board to waive the mitigation requirements. Staff can only support the UDO which states Landmark trees cannot be removed without the approval of the Tree Board. However, the board does have the ability to grant approval to remove the tree if the tree meets one or more of the criteria listed in Section 9.8.10 (C) (1) of the UDO as well as the ability to waive or reduce mitigation requirements, however they see fit. Staff recommends the board discuss the request and reduction of the mitigation requirements and instruct staff and the applicant on how to proceed. The applicant was present. Staff and the board discussed at length. Jordan made a motion to approve the tree's removal and to address mitigation separately after the motion's approval. However, he withdrew his motion to allow the board to combine the removal and mitigation into a single motion. Jordan then made a motion to approve the removal of the tree, citing confirmation from a forestry expert that the tree is dead, and that mitigation would be set at half the requirement stipulated by the ordinance involving the planting of three 4-inch DBH trees on county property within the city. Watts seconded the motion, and the motion carried with a 3 to 2 vote, with Kurlowski and Roehm voting no. IV. PUBLIC INPUT None. V. Staff can only support the UDO which states protected trees cannot be removed without meeting one or more of the criteria listed in Section 9.8.10 (A)(1) of the UDO, which is what the decision to deny was based upon. 2 CAB 4/23/2025 However, the board does have the ability to grant approval to remove the tree if they feel staff ruled in error as well as the ability to waive or reduce mitigation requirements, however they see fit. Staff recommends the board discuss the appeal and reduction of the mitigation requirements and instruct staff and the applicant on how to proceed. The applicant was present. However, since the tree is a protected Water Oak and due to the species type, the board does have the ability to allow the removal at the owner’s request, but the owner needs to mitigate per the ordinance without any reduction. Mitigation will be based upon staff's determination of the true DBH of the tree before mitigation calculations are solidified. Kurlowski seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. Jordan amended his motion to include mitigation to be carried out through a fee in lieu of or planting trees of approved sizes or any combination of the two on the owner's property, as outlined in the ordinance, based on the owner’s preference. Wallace seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. In this instance, if no alternative to the removal of the landmark tree can be obtained through the BZA, the Tree Board may attach any conditions to the permit deemed necessary to ensure compliance with the intent of this section if removal of the landmark tree is granted by the board. d. The tree is causing visible structural damage to a building and no feasible alternative other than removal of such tree exists, as certified by a structural engineer. Mitigation is based on the number of inches being removed, 24 (x), divided by the minimum number of inches required for each replacement tree, 4 (y), to equal the number of trees to be replaced, 6(z). X/Y=Z 87/4 =6 Trees The applicant is also asking the board to waive the mitigation requirements. Staff can only support the UDO which states Landmark trees cannot be removed without the approval of the Tree Board. However, the board does have the ability to grant approval to remove the tree if the tree meets one or more of the criteria listed in Section 9.8.10 (C) (1) of the UDO as well as the ability to waive or reduce mitigation requirements, however they see fit. Staff recommends the board discuss the request and reduction of the mitigation requirements and instruct staff and the applicant on how to proceed. The applicant was present. Staff and the board discussed at length. Jordan made a motion to approve the tree's removal and to address mitigation separately after the motion's approval. However, he withdrew his motion to allow the board to combine the removal and mitigation into a single motion. Jordan then made a motion to approve the removal of the tree, citing confirmation from a forestry expert that the tree is dead, and that mitigation would be set at half the requirement stipulated by the ordinance involving the planting of three 4-inch DBH trees on county property within the city. Staff performed an extensive review and determined that due to the amount of pruning being requested the tree would be at a tremendous risk of decline if this amount of pruning took place. This determination lead to the denial of the application to prune the Landmark Live Oak Tree. The reasoning for the pruning request does play a role in staff’s determination as we try to understand and work with applicants in situations that are difficult. The applicant informed staff that the reason for the pruning was due to overhead powerlines. However, staff reviewed all the approved plans along with the tree survey in great detail and found more questions than answers with the location of the tree in comparison to the powerlines. The plans show that the tree is well within their silt fence line and the powerlines are on the opposite side of that same silt fence line. Furthermore, -- 2 of 11 -- CAB 1/8/2025 2 staff was unable to find where the tree would interfere with the powerlines as depicted on the approved plans page C9.0 and per Section 6.5.2 (I), Utilities, of the Gateway Corridor Overlay, new utility lines, including electric, telephone, etc. are required to be underground. The tree is also located within the 15’ landscape setback area and a portion of the 30’ building setback area as shown on page C4.0. Once the applicant’s application was denied staff explained the next steps available to the applicant. Which involved appealing staff’s decision to the Tree Board. The applicant ultimately decided to appeal staff’s decision to deny the pruning of a 36” Live Oak Tree. Staff, agent and the board discussed at length. A mitigation penalty will be imposed if the pruning is not conducted according to the approved plan. Hall seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. ISSUE: 1302 10th Ave: The applicant, Robert Ahlborn, with Better Tree Service, is requesting approval to remove a Landmark Live Oak tree from the property, located at 1302 10th Ave (PIN 338-14-02-0043). ZONING DISTRICT: Low Density Residential (R-1) SCOPE OF WORK: In February the applicant applied to remove a tree that is located at 1302 10th Ave. Upon, inspection staff determined the tree was a Live Oak with a DBH of 32”. Staff notified the applicant the tree permit was being referred to the tree board. The tree in question does present signs of decline with a large portion of the center of the tree being hollow and beginning to break open. The tree board must determine if one or more of the following conditions are met before granting approval to remove the tree. • The tree is classed as a hazard tree, is in irreversible decline, and cannot be properly pruned to alleviate such condition; • The tree is diseased or infectious as certified by a registered forester or certified arborist or the city arborist and cannot be properly treated or pruned to alleviate such condition; • The tree is located on an undeveloped lot in such position that the lot cannot be developed in a reasonable and prudent manner. In this instance, the Conway tree board shall consider a request for a variance from a particular zoning requirement if it would alleviate the need to remove such landmark tree; and if so determined, initiate such request with the board of zoning appeals. In this instance, if no alternative to the removal of the landmark tree can be obtained, the Conway tree board may attach any conditions to the permit the tree board deems necessary to ensure compliance with the intent of this chapter; • The tree is causing visible structural damage to a building and no feasible alternative other than removal of such tree exists, as certified by a structural engineer. If the board chooses to grant removal the board must also determine mitigation in accordance with Section 3-4- 10. The mitigation requirement is the number of inches removed, 32 (x), divided by the minimum number of inches for each replacement tree, 4 (y), to equal the number of trees to be replaced, 8 (z). X / Y = Z 32 / 4 = 8 Trees The board does have the ability to waive all mitigation requirements or reduce mitigation however they see fit. -- 8 of 11 -- Applicable Standards City of Conway Tree Board Ordinance:  Section 3.4.6: Definitions  Section 3.4.9 (b): Landmark Tree Removal Permit  Section 3.4.10: Mitigation of trees approved for removal  3.4.15: Appeals STAFF RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends the board discuss the removal of the tree and mitigation requirements and instruct staff and the applicant on how to proceed. -- 9 of 11 -- -- 10 of 11 -- -- 11 of 11 --

TREE PROTECTION NOTES 1. ALL TREES SHOWN ON THIS PLAN TO BE RETAINED SHALL BE PROTECTED DURING ALL PHASES OF DEMOLITION/CONSTRUCTION WITH TEMPORARY FENCING. IT SHALL BE THE GENERAL CONTRACTORS RESPONSIBILITY TO COORDINATE WITH LANDSCAPE CONTRACTOR. 2. TREE PROTECTION FENCES SHALL BE INSTALLED PRIOR TO THE COMMENCEMENT OF ANY SITE PREPARATION WORK (CLEARING, GRUBBING OR GRADING). CLEARING SHALL BE DONE BY HAND. 3. FENCES SHALL COMPLETELY SURROUND TREE OR CLUSTERS OF TREES; SHALL BE LOCATED 5' FROM THE OUTERMOST LIMITS OF THE TREE BRANCHES (DRIP LINE); AND SHALL BE MAINTAINED THROUGHOUT THE CONSTRUCTION BY CONTRACTOR. PROJECT IN ORDER TO PREVENT THE FOLLOWING: A. SOIL COMPACTION IN THE ROOT ZONE AREA RESULTING FROM VEHICULAR TRAFFIC OR STORAGE OF EQUIPMENT OR MATERIALS. B. ROOT ZONE DISTURBANCES DUE TO GRADE CHANGES (GREATER THAN 6 INCHES CUT OR FILL) OR TRENCHING. C. WOUNDS TO EXPOSED ROOTS, TRUNK OR LIMBS BY MECHANICAL EQUIPMENT. D. OTHER ACTIVITIES DETRIMENTAL TO TREES SUCH AS CHEMICAL STORAGE, CEMENT TRUCK CLEANING, AND FIRES. 4. EXCEPTIONS TO INSTALLING FENCES 5' FROM TREE DRIP LINES MAY BE PERMITTED IN THE FOLLOWING CASES: A. WHERE PERMEABLE PAVING IS TO BE INSTALLED: ERECT THE FENCE AT THE OUTER LIMITS OF THE PERMEABLE PAVING AREA. B. WHERE TREES ARE CLOSE TO THE PROPOSED BUILDING: ERECT THE FENCE NO CLOSER THAN 6 FEET TO THE BUILDING. 5. WHERE ANY OF THE ABOVE EXCEPTIONS RESULT IN A FENCE BEING CLOSER THAN 4 FEET TO A TREE TRUNK, PROTECT THE TRUNK WITH STRAPPED-ON PLANKING TO A HEIGHT OF 8 FEET (OR TO THE LIMITS OF LOWER BRANCHES) IN ADDITION TO THE REDUCED FENCING PROVIDED. 6. PRIOR TO EXCAVATION OR GRADE CUTTING WITHIN TREE DRIP TO EVAPORATION. LINES, MAKE A CLEAN CUT BETWEEN THE DISTURBED AND UNDISTURBED ROOT ZONES WITH A ROCK SAW OR SIMILAR EQUIPMENT TO MINIMIZE DAMAGE TO REMAINING ROOTS. 10. ZONING DISTRICT: Highway Commercial (HC); Gateway Corridor Overlay (GCO) SCOPE OF WORK: The applicant is appealing staff’s decision to deny the removal of 6 protected trees. 3-19-2024: Staff approved the removal of 6 protected trees with the condition that mitigation plantings be installed. 7-31-2024: Applicant requested a reduction in mitigation plantings. 8-28-2024: Tree Board deferred the applicates request of tree mitigation reduction due to the applicant not being present for the meeting as well as more information from the applicant being needed for staff to calculate mitigation amounts. 9-24-2024: the applicant’s Engineer provided a new tree survey showing 4 additional trees for removal. 9-26-2024: the applicant requested a variance from the GCO Front Buffer requirements and Article 9 Landscaping and Buffer Requirements within the UDO. The applicant requested the decision be deferred to the October 24th meeting. 10-15-2021: The applicant’s engineer provided an updated tree survey showing another 4 additional trees for removal. 10-22-24: Staff responded to the applicant’s engineer outlining that the original 6 trees that were previously approved on 3-19-2024 for removal and one additional 18” Willow Oak were approved for -- 53 of 75 -- removal and required mitigation plantings. The remaining 7 trees were denied removal. The applicant was informed that they could appeal this decision to the Tree Board within 10 days of the decision. 10-24-2024: The Board of Zoning appeals denied the applicants variance request for landscaping reductions. 10-28-2024: The applicant provided a fourth tree survey now highlighting two trees that are “dead”, one of which was denied removal and the other was never proposed for removal in any previous submittals. The applicant also identified one previously approved for removal tree that would remain. Staff’s determination to deny the removal of the remaining 7 trees, which this appeal is based on, was prior to being made aware of potentially dead and or diseased trees. Staff denied removal of those trees because, in the staff’s opinion, the applicant does have adequate space and could design around or incorporate the protected trees into the overall design. Since this determination the applicant has stated there are two potentially dead trees. Staff would be willing to accommodate the removal and mitigation of those two trees provided an arborist determination is supplied stating the condition of the trees. The applicant previously requested a reduction in mitigation based on the original approval of 6 trees, but that determination can not be made until the appeal is first determined. Once the board rules on this appeal the applicant will then be required to provide mitigation plantings for any trees removed. The applicant must make all attempts to include the mitigation plantings in addition to the required landscaping and buffering. A landscaping plan identifying the required landscaping or buffering as well as the mitigation plantings must be provided to staff prior to consideration of a reduction by the tree board. (PIN’s 326-00-00-0025, 326-09-01- 0002, & 326-09-01-0001) BACKGROUND: The applicant currently has commercial plans in review for a new car dealership at the above location. The parcels are zoned Highway Commercial (HC) and fall within the Gateway Corridor Overlay (GCO). The three (3) parcels are to be combined via a platting action to create one parcel. Per Section 6.5.2-Gateway Corridor Overlay - Parking Lots over 30,000 square feet: The front buffer for non- residential establishments shall be 15-ft along corridor rights-of-way. This buffer is intended for aesthetics, rather than screening purposes. The buffer shall contain the following minimum ornamental plantings per 100-linear feet of frontage: 3-canopy trees, 3-understory trees & 20-shrubs Per Section 9.3.4-Landscape Requirements for the Interior of Parking Areas - Each landscape island or peninsula shall contain a minimum of 1-canopy tree & 5-shrubs. The applicant is concerned about the visibility as well as increased maintenance of the future dealership’s automobile displays based on the UDO’s landscape requirements. The applicant is requesting a reduction in the GCO front landscape buffer requirements as far as Canopy and Understory Trees are concerned. The applicant would also like to use Understory Trees in lieu of Canopy Trees in nine (9) of the parking islands at the front and to the south side of the project. (see Variance Request Plan attached) This project is also on the agenda for the Tree Board on Wednesday, October 23 for a request to mitigate additional protected trees beyond what the City Arborist has previously approved. The proposed trees in blue on the attached Variance Request Plan may be trees that are used to meet the Mitigation Requirements. Per the Variance Request Plan, the applicant is also proposing a Commercial Center on the remainder of the combined parcels. The Highway 501 frontage for the Commercial Center, based on the Variance Request Plan, will meet the GCO front landscape buffer requirements. This project will be completed in two (2) phases. -- 72 of 75 -- Variance: 3525 W Highway 501 Variances requested: Section 6.5.2 – Gateway Corridor Overlay (GCO): • A variance to reduce the number of Canopy Trees from eight (8) to two (2) and reduce the number of Understory Trees from eight (8) to four (4) in the front GCO landscape buffer on the dealership side of the property only. Section 9.3.4 – Landscape Requirements for the Interior of Parking Areas: • A variance to replace Canopy Trees with Understory Trees in nine (9) of the landscape islands on the dealership side of the property only. The applicant cites the following reasons for which a variance should be granted: **See attached application. CITY OF CONWAY UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE (UDO) & ANALYSIS In Section 14.2.1 of the UDO, the duties and powers of the Board of Zoning Appeals reflect Section 6-29-800 of the South Carolina Code of Laws. According to Section 14.1035, the Board of Zoning Appeals duties are “to hear and decide appeals for variances in specific cases when a strict application of the zoning ordinance would cause an unnecessary hardship, and approval of such variance would not be contrary to public interest or undermine the spirit of the zoning ordinance. The fact that property may be used more profitably if a variance is granted is not grounds for a variance. The Board may attach conditions to a variance that address location, character, or other features of a proposed building, structure, or use, in order to protect the established property values in the surrounding area or to promote the public health, safety, or general welfare of the community. The Board may grant a variance for an unnecessary hardship if it makes and explains in writing all of the following findings. 1. Extraordinary Conditions: There are extraordinary and exceptional conditions pertaining to the particular piece of property. 2. Other Property: The extraordinary and exceptional conditions do not generally apply to other property in the vicinity. 3. Utilization: Because of the extraordinary or exceptional conditions, the application of the ordinance to a particular piece of property would effectively prohibit or unreasonably restrict the utilization of the property. 4. Detriment: The authorization of a variance will not be of substantial detriment to adjacent property or the public good, and the character of the district will not be harmed by granting a variance. RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends that the BZA conduct a thorough review of the request and determine if a legal hardship exists and if the best interests of the City of Conway would be served by granting the request. -- 73 of 75 -- PLANNING & DEVELOPMENT 196 Laurel Street  Post Office Box 1075 Conway, South Carolina 29528-1075 Telephone (843) 488-9888 www.ConwaySC.gov MAYOR Barbara Jo Blain MAYOR PRO TEM Larry A. (PIN’s 326-00-00- 0025, 326-09-01-0002, & 326-09-01-0001) Dear Applicant(s): After consideration of the evidence and arguments presented at the October 24, 2024 meeting, the Board made the following findings of fact and conclusions: 1. Extraordinary conditions: There are extraordinary and exceptional conditions pertaining to the particular piece of property. “All properties in the Gateway Corridor Overlay are required the front landscape buffer.” 2. Other Property: The extraordinary and exceptional conditions do not generally apply to other property in the vicinity. “The applicant answered No on the application.” 3. Utilization: Because of the extraordinary or exceptional conditions, the application of the ordinance to a particular piece of property would effectively prohibit or unreasonably restrict the utilization of the property. “The applicant answered Not Applicable on the application.” 4. Detriment: The authorization of a variance will not be of substantial detriment to adjacent property or the public good, and the character of the district will not be harmed by granting a variance. “There does not appear to be a hardship with this requirement of the UDO.” -- 74 of 75 -- 196 Laurel Street  Post Office Box 1075 Conway, South Carolina 29528-1075 Telephone (843) 488-9888 www.ConwaySC.gov THE BOARD, THEREFORE, ORDERED the requests for the variances from the strict application of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), Section 6.5.2-Gateway Corridor Overlay (GCO) and Article 9-Landscaping & Buffering, for the property located at 3525 W Highway 501 were Denied. title: APPD_1.8.25 TREE BOARD MINUTES
text: CAB 1/8/2025 CITY OF CONWAY TREE BOARD MEETING WEDNESDAY, January 8, 2025 Planning & Building Dept. Conference Room — 196 Laurel Street Present: Jacqueline Kurlowski, Duc Watts, Gerry Wallace, Coker Hall Absent: Troy Roehm, Jamie McLain, McKenzie Jordan Staff: Katie Dennis, Planner; Marcus Cohen, IT; Louis Smith, IT; Marsha Ponder, Planning Assistant; Jessica Hucks, Planning Director Other: Franklin Williams, Trent Hardee, Daniel Ben-Yisrael, Kathy Ropp I. CALL TO ORDER Chairperson Wallace called the meeting to order at approximately 4:09 p.m. I. APPROVAL OF MINUTES Kurlowski made a motion to accept the minutes as written. It was seconded by Hall to approve the November 13, 2024, minutes. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. II. ELECTION OF OFFICERS Kurlowski made a motion to nominate Jordan to serve as Vice Chairman, seconded by Watts. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. Watts made a motion to nominate Wallace as Chairman, seconded by Kurlowski. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. IV. TREE APPEALS A. 3500 W Hwy 501 (Parker’s Kitchen): The applicant, Parker’s Kitchen, is appealing the decision of staff to deny the pruning of a Landmark Live Oak tree for the property, located at 3500 W Hwy 501 (PIN 326- 09-03-0008). Dennis gave an overview that in December of 2024 the applicant submitted an application request to prune a 36” Landmark Live Oak Tree that is located at 3500 W Hwy 501. Staff performed an extensive review and determined that due to the amount of pruning being requested the tree would be at a tremendous risk of decline if this amount of pruning took place. This determination lead to the denial of the application to prune the Landmark Live Oak Tree. The reasoning for the pruning request does play a role in staff's determination as we try to understand and work with applicants in situations that are difficult. The applicant informed staff that the reason for the pruning was due to overhead powerlines. However, staff reviewed all the approved plans along with the tree survey in great detail and found more questions than answers with the location of the tree in comparison to the powerlines. The plans show that the tree is well within their silt fence line and the powerlines are on the opposite side of that same silt fence line. Furthermore, 1 CAB 1/8/2025 staff was unable to find where the tree would interfere with the powerlines as depicted on the approved plans page C9.0 and per Section 6.5.2 (I), Utilities, of the Gateway Corridor Overlay, new utility lines, including electric, telephone, etc. are required to be underground. The tree is also located within the 15? landscape setback area and a portion of the 30’ building setback area as shown on page C4.0. These reasons alone were not the greatest factor in staffs reasoning or decision for denial but did prove difficult for staff to understand the reasoning for such a large amount of pruning to be requested. Once the applicant’s application was denied staff explained the next steps available to the applicant. Which involved appealing staffs decision to the Tree Board. The applicant ultimately decided to appeal staff's decision to deny the pruning of a 36” Live Oak Tree. The Tree Board is now responsible for determining if staff ruled in error and if the tree should be allowed to be pruned as described by the applicant. Should the board choose to grant the applicants appeal, staff recommends the following: e A certified arborist must submit a pruning plan to staff prior to the pruning permit being issued and the pruning taking place explaining the process being used and ensuring the pruning practices being used are in accordance with ANSI A300 standards and will not be a detriment to the tree. Renderings were included in the packet. Daniel Ben-Yisrael, Real estate Development Manager and Frank Williams, Horry Electric further explained the request and discussed with the board at length. Staff, agent and the board discussed at length. Kurlowski made a motion to approve the requirement that a certified arborist must submit a pruning plan to staff prior to the issuance of the pruning permit and the commencement of pruning activities. The plan should explain the process being used, ensure that the pruning practices adhere to ANSI A300 standards, and confirm that the practices will not be detrimental to the tree. A mitigation penalty will be imposed if the pruning is not conducted according to the approved plan. Hall seconded the motion, and the motion carried unanimously. B. 3525 Hwy 501 (Hardee Auto Sales): The applicant, Trent Hardee, is appealing the decision of staff to deny the removal of Protected trees for the property, located at 3525 Hwy 501 (PIN 326-00-00-0025). Dennis provided an overview, noting that the applicant is appealing staff's decision to deny the removal of six protected trees. Staff approved the removal of six protected trees on March 19, 2024, with the condition that mitigation plantings be installed. On July 31, 2024, the applicant requested a reduction in mitigation plantings. The Tree Board deferred the applicant's request for a reduction in tree mitigation on August 28, 2028, due to the applicant's absence from the meeting and the need for additional information from the applicant for staff to calculate the mitigation amounts.9-24-2024: the applicant’s Engineer provided a new tree survey showing 4 additional trees for removal. CAB 1/8/2025 On September 26, 2024, the applicant requested a variance from the GCO Front Buffer requirements and Article 9 Landscaping and Buffer Requirements within the UDO. The applicant requested that the decision be deferred to the October 24th meeting. On October 15, 2021, the applicant’s engineer provided an updated tree survey that showed an additional four trees marked for removal. On October 22, 2024, staff responded to the applicant's engineer, outlining that the original six trees that were previously approved on March 19, 2024, for removal, and one additional 18” Willow Oak, were approved for removal with required mitigation plantings. The remaining seven trees were denied removal. The applicant was informed that they could appeal this decision to the Tree Board within 10 days of the decision. The Board of Zoning appeals denied the applicants variance request on October 24, 2024, for landscaping reductions. The applicant provided a fourth tree survey on October 28, 2024, now highlighting two trees that are “dead”, one of which was denied removal and the other was never proposed for removal in any previous submittals. The applicant also identified one previously approved for removal tree that would remain. Staff's determination to deny the removal of the remaining 7 trees, which this appeal is based on, was prior to being made aware of potentially dead and or diseased trees. Staff denied removal of those trees because, in the staff's opinion, the applicant does have adequate space and could design around or incorporate the protected trees into the overall design. Since this determination the applicant has stated there are two potentially dead trees. Staff would be willing to accommodate the removal and mitigation of those two trees provided an arborist determination is supplied stating the condition of the trees. The applicant previously requested a reduction in mitigation based on the original approval of 6 trees, but that determination can not be made until the appeal is first determined. Once the board rules on this appeal the applicant will then be required to provide mitigation plantings for any trees removed. The applicant must make all attempts to include the mitigation plantings in addition to the required landscaping and buffering. A landscaping plan identifying the required landscaping or buffering as well as the mitigation plantings must be provided to staff prior to consideration of a reduction by the tree board. Renderings were included in the packet. Staff Recommend(s) Approval to remove 5 of the originally approved trees, one 18” Willow Oak within the proposed roadway, the two newly stated dead trees with the condition that the applicant provides an arborist determination that they are dead and or dying, preserve the 20” Willow Oak by moving the storm drainage system as stated by the applicant as well as the remaining 6 trees by incorporating them into the design of the property. The applicant, Trent Hardee further explained the request and discussed with the board at length. Staff, applicant and the board discussed at length. Kurlowski made a motion to defer the item until the applicant can provide a detailed landscape plan showing mitigation plantings in the event the appeal is granted, to provide clarification to staff and the board. Watts seconded the motion. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. CAB 1/8/2025 Vv. PUBLIC INPUT None. VI. BOARD INPUT None. VI. STAFF INPUT Dennis mentioned that the tree preservation ordinance will be on the Planning Commission agenda tomorrow, January 9th. If the board members are interested, they can tune in or be in attendance. Additionally, the finalized presentation will be available online in the Planning Commission’s packet. VI. ADJOURN There being no further business to come before the board, a motion was made and seconded to adjourn the meeting at 4:48 pm. The vote in favor was unanimous and the motion carried. TREE PRESERVATION ORDINANCE AMENDMENT(S) Dennis stated staff presented the board’s recommendation of amendments to the Tree Preservation Ordinance to City Council at their October 21st meeting. Council asked for clarification on the removal of Crepe Myrtle trees as well as the higher penalties that are being assessed. Staff informed the board about the penalty allowability and that they are, in staffs’ opinion, within the legal confounds for the City to enforce. Jordan provided detail on the request to remove Crepe Myrtle trees from the protected trees list. These reasons include the fact that they are not native trees, they are rapidly growing and would be protected rather quickly, as well as the extreme measures required for pruning techniques on these specific types of trees to provide the best- looking tree. These pruning techniques could very rapidly be restricted by the Preservation Ordinance requirements of pruning protected trees. Staff and the board discussed at length. McLain made a motion to approve the amendments to the Tree Preservation Ordinance. Rohem seconded the motion. The vote in favor was unanimous. The motion carried. IV. BOARD INPUT None V. (PIN’s 326-00-00-0025, 326-09-01- 0002, & 326-09-01-0001) BACKGROUND: The applicant currently has commercial plans in review for a new car dealership at the above location. The parcels are zoned Highway Commercial (HC) and fall within the Gateway Corridor Overlay (GCO). The three (3) parcels are to be combined via a platting action to create one parcel. Per Section 6.5.2-Gateway Corridor Overlay - Parking Lots over 30,000 square feet: The front buffer for non- residential establishments shall be 15-ft along corridor rights-of-way. This buffer is intended for aesthetics, rather than screening purposes. The buffer shall contain the following minimum ornamental plantings per 100-linear feet of frontage: 3-canopy trees, 3-understory trees & 20-shrubs Per Section 9.3.4-Landscape Requirements for the Interior of Parking Areas - Each landscape island or peninsula shall contain a minimum of 1-canopy tree & 5-shrubs. The applicant is concerned about the visibility as well as increased maintenance of the future dealership’s automobile displays based on the UDO’s landscape requirements. The applicant is requesting a reduction in the GCO front landscape buffer requirements as far as Canopy and Understory Trees are concerned. The applicant would also like to use Understory Trees in lieu of Canopy Trees in nine (9) of the parking islands at the front and to the south side of the project. (see Variance Request Plan attached) This project is also on the agenda for the Tree Board on Wednesday, October 23 for a request to mitigate additional protected trees beyond what the City Arborist has previously approved. The proposed trees in blue on the attached Variance Request Plan may be trees that are used to meet the Mitigation Requirements. Per the Variance Request Plan, the applicant is also proposing a Commercial Center on the remainder of the combined parcels. The Highway 501 frontage for the Commercial Center, based on the Variance Request Plan, will meet the GCO front landscape buffer requirements. This project will be completed in two (2) phases. -- 23 of 26 -- Variance: 3525 W Highway 501 Variances requested: Section 6.5.2 – Gateway Corridor Overlay (GCO): • A variance to reduce the number of Canopy Trees from eight (8) to two (2) and reduce the number of Understory Trees from eight (8) to four (4) in the front GCO landscape buffer on the dealership side of the property only. Section 9.3.4 – Landscape Requirements for the Interior of Parking Areas: • A variance to replace Canopy Trees with Understory Trees in nine (9) of the landscape islands on the dealership side of the property only. The applicant cites the following reasons for which a variance should be granted: **See attached application. CITY OF CONWAY UNIFIED DEVELOPMENT ORDINANCE (UDO) & ANALYSIS In Section 14.2.1 of the UDO, the duties and powers of the Board of Zoning Appeals reflect Section 6-29-800 of the South Carolina Code of Laws. According to Section 14.1035, the Board of Zoning Appeals duties are “to hear and decide appeals for variances in specific cases when a strict application of the zoning ordinance would cause an unnecessary hardship, and approval of such variance would not be contrary to public interest or undermine the spirit of the zoning ordinance. The fact that property may be used more profitably if a variance is granted is not grounds for a variance. The Board may attach conditions to a variance that address location, character, or other features of a proposed building, structure, or use, in order to protect the established property values in the surrounding area or to promote the public health, safety, or general welfare of the community. The Board may grant a variance for an unnecessary hardship if it makes and explains in writing all of the following findings. 1. Extraordinary Conditions: There are extraordinary and exceptional conditions pertaining to the particular piece of property. 2. Other Property: The extraordinary and exceptional conditions do not generally apply to other property in the vicinity. 3. Utilization: Because of the extraordinary or exceptional conditions, the application of the ordinance to a particular piece of property would effectively prohibit or unreasonably restrict the utilization of the property. 4. Detriment: The authorization of a variance will not be of substantial detriment to adjacent property or the public good, and the character of the district will not be harmed by granting a variance. RECOMMENDATION: Staff recommends that the BZA conduct a thorough review of the request and determine if a legal hardship exists and if the best interests of the City of Conway would be served by granting the request. -- 24 of 26 -- PLANNING & DEVELOPMENT 196 Laurel Street  Post Office Box 1075 Conway, South Carolina 29528-1075 Telephone (843) 488-9888 www.ConwaySC.gov MAYOR Barbara Jo Blain MAYOR PRO TEM Larry A. (PIN’s 326-00-00- 0025, 326-09-01-0002, & 326-09-01-0001) Dear Applicant(s): After consideration of the evidence and arguments presented at the October 24, 2024 meeting, the Board made the following findings of fact and conclusions: 1. Extraordinary conditions: There are extraordinary and exceptional conditions pertaining to the particular piece of property. “All properties in the Gateway Corridor Overlay are required the front landscape buffer.” 2. Other Property: The extraordinary and exceptional conditions do not generally apply to other property in the vicinity. “The applicant answered No on the application.” 3. Utilization: Because of the extraordinary or exceptional conditions, the application of the ordinance to a particular piece of property would effectively prohibit or unreasonably restrict the utilization of the property. “The applicant answered Not Applicable on the application.” 4. Detriment: The authorization of a variance will not be of substantial detriment to adjacent property or the public good, and the character of the district will not be harmed by granting a variance. “There does not appear to be a hardship with this requirement of the UDO.” -- 25 of 26 -- 196 Laurel Street  Post Office Box 1075 Conway, South Carolina 29528-1075 Telephone (843) 488-9888 www.ConwaySC.gov THE BOARD, THEREFORE, ORDERED the requests for the variances from the strict application of the City of Conway Unified Development Ordinance (UDO), Section 6.5.2-Gateway Corridor Overlay (GCO) and Article 9-Landscaping & Buffering, for the property located at 3525 W Highway 501 were Denied.
